Russian Su-35 fighter jets collide over Kursk, killing pilot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:51:08 UTC
01:51:08 KST

- Russian military channel Fighterbomber reported that two Su-35S fighter jets collided in Russia's Kursk region, killing one pilot and seriously injuring another.
- The report claims 10 confirmed Su-35S losses since Russia's invasion began, attributed to Ukrainian air defenses, strike drones, and aviation incidents, a figure that could not be independently verified.
Two Russian Su-35S fighter jets collided in Russia’s Kursk region, according to Fighterbomber, a Telegram channel with reported ties to the Russian Aerospace Forces. Follow-up reports indicate one pilot was killed in the collision and another was seriously injured, though the full circumstances of the incident are still being determined.
Neither Russia’s Defense Ministry nor Ukrainian officials had confirmed these details independently at the time of this report. Kursk region, which borders Ukraine, has been the site of repeated Russian aircraft losses since Ukrainian forces launched a cross-border incursion there in August 2024, and it remains an active zone for Russian aviation operations.
The Su-35S is a twin-engine, highly maneuverable fourth-generation-plus fighter that Russia has used extensively during its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, both for air superiority missions and to escort strike aircraft.
The total number of confirmed Su-35S losses since the war began is 10 aircraft, attributing the losses to a mix of Ukrainian air defense systems, strike drones, and various aviation incidents.
Russian military channels and independent Russian outlets have documented several Su-35S losses over the course of the war that were not caused by Ukrainian action at all. Independent Russian investigative outlet The Insider has reported at least two cases in which Russia’s own air defense systems shot down Su-35S jets by mistake, once near Mariupol and separately near Tokmak in the Zaporizhzhia region, incidents Fighterbomber itself has publicly acknowledged and, in one case, used to warn Russian pilots that their own air defenses posed a greater danger than Ukraine’s. Ukraine’s air force has also claimed several confirmed shootdowns of Su-35S aircraft through more conventional means, including one in Kherson region in May 2023 and another along the Kursk front in June 2025.
That June 2025 engagement, first reported by German outlet Bild, involved a Ukrainian-operated F-16 that shot down a Su-35 near the town of Korenevo in Kursk Oblast, marking the first known aerial kill by an F-16 under Ukrainian command. According to Bild’s reporting, Ukraine’s air force used a Swedish ASC 890 airborne early warning aircraft to detect the Russian jet at a range of 200 to 300 kilometers and relay its position to the F-16 pilot in real time, who then fired an AIM-120 missile that forced the Su-35 pilot to eject.
The Su-35S has drawn scrutiny throughout the war both for its combat losses and for a series of incidents unrelated to enemy fire, including at least one crash attributed to engine failure. Russia has continued flying the aircraft on the front lines despite the losses, reflecting its role as one of the Russian air force’s primary fighters alongside the older Su-30SM and the Su-57 stealth fighter.
The condition of the injured pilot and further details on the collision, including whether either aircraft was destroyed on impact or during an attempted landing, have not been independently confirmed.

Israel mulls entry of Syrian Druze workers amid labour shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:45:46 UTC

Breadcrumb
Israel mulls letting in Syrian Druze workers amid labour shortages
Israeli authorities are considering a proposal that would allow members of Syria’s Druze minority to enter the country to work amid ongoing labour shortages, particularly in the agricultural sector, the Israeli news website Ynet has reported.
The proposal would allow Syrian Druze to work on farms but would also give them vocational training in a number of fields, such as agriculture, medicine, and other professions.
Since deadly sectarian violence broke out in Syria’s Druze-majority Suweida province in July 2025, most of the province has been under the control of separatist militias opposed to the Syrian government and sympathetic to Israel.
Israel has tried to position itself as a “protector” of the Syrian Druze community while Druze spiritual leader Hikmat al-Hijri recently said that Suweida province is an “integral part of Israel”.
Ynet reported that the much higher wages in Israel would provide an incentive to Syrian Druze wishing to work in Israel, pointing out that one day’s wages would be equivalent to roughly three months of wages in Syria.
The Israeli outlet also said that the country's military was planning to allow meetings between Druze in Syria and their relatives in Israel, at designated locations near the border on the Syrian side.
After the Assad regime fell in December 2024, Israel seized land in Syria beyond the Golan Heights and has frequently launched attacks and incursions in Syria.
Israel first mooted the idea of bringing in Syrian Druze workers in April 2025, amid shortages of foreign labour caused by the Gaza War.
However the Israeli government reportedly cancelled the plan at the last minute.
The plan intended to establish a “bridge” between Israel and residents of Syrian towns between 5 and 10 kilometres from the Israeli border.
However Israeli security agencies reportedly vetoed it.

Tokyo demands removal of Khabarovsk monument showing Soviet soldier smashing Japan’s chrysanthemum emblem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:42:27 UTC
01:42:27 KST

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has demanded the removal of a monument to the “victory over militarist Japan” that was unveiled in Khabarovsk on Sept. 4. The bronze sculpture depicts a Soviet soldier using the butt of his rifle to smash a stone border marker bearing a chrysanthemum, the symbol of Japan’s Imperial House.
Takaichi called said Tokyo had raised objections with the Russian side before the statue was unveiled. Her statement was published in both Japanese and Russian.
“The chrysanthemum emblem is widely recognized as a symbol of Japan, and the erection of a monument depicting its destruction is completely unacceptable,” she said.
Takaichi said her government would continue pressing for the removal of the monument. Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said separately on Sept. 5 that demands to stop the installation and dismantle the monument had been conveyed through diplomatic channels. He said the Russian side had not complied.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova responded to Takaichi’s comments, telling Russian state-controlled news agency RIA Novosti: “All that remains is to demand that the wind stop blowing and the sun stop shining.” She described Russian history as “based on facts” and said its memory had been “enshrined in a monument.”
The monument was installed on the Amur River embankment in the far-eastern city of Khabarovsk. According to a statement by the regional government, it was created on instructions from Vladimir Putin with the participation of the Russian Military Historical Society. The project was designed by sculptor Denis Stritovich, architect Vadim Frolov, and artist Ilya Khrabry.
The main figure is 15 meters (49 feet) tall, while the monument’s pylons bear the names of the Soviet Far Eastern and Transbaikal fronts, the Pacific Fleet, and the Amur Flotilla. The unveiling was attended by Khabarovsk regional governor Dmitry Demeshin, representatives of the Russian Military Historical Society, military personnel, and delegations from the Chinese and North Korean diplomatic missions.
Stritovich told the newspaper Vzglyad that the border post depicted as being smashed by a Red Army soldier was modeled on Japanese boundary markers used on Sakhalin after the island was divided following the Russo-Japanese War. The soldier is holding a Mosin rifle, and the sculptor said the specific weapon was chosen to emphasize the connection between Russia’s defeat in the 1904-1905 Russo-Japanese War and the Soviet Union’s victory in 1945.
Vzglyad reported that the first stage of another memorial was unveiled at the same time on Slavy (lit. “Glory”) Square in Khabarovsk, dedicated to Russian troops killed in the Kremlin’s ongoing war against Ukraine. A new semicircular section was added to the existing memorial to those killed in the Great Patriotic War (the Soviet term for the 1941-45 war against Nazi Germany).
According to Tatyana Fonova, secretary of the regional working group on commemorating the fallen, the names have not yet been inscribed on the new monument. The local government plans to add them following what it describes as “victory” in the current war.
The episode marks the second public protest by Takaichi in recent weeks over Russia’s actions in the Far East. In August, the Japanese prime minister called Putin’s first visit to the disputed islands “absolutely unacceptable,” and Japan’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador.
Japan claims Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai islets, which came under Soviet control at the end of World War II. The territorial dispute remains the main obstacle to a formal peace treaty between Moscow and Tokyo.

‘Slumping’ S Korean corals worry divers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:41:05 UTC
01:41:05 KST

Ko Myeong-hyo loved the vibrant color and thriving life of South Korea’s soft corals when she first began diving off the coast of Jeju island six years ago, looking to harvest seafood for sale.
“Watching the coral garden collapse and turn white, it was so disorienting,” Ko said after two years of rising temperatures and harsher weather brought by climate change have led to many corals slumping over and dying.
“I was afraid the whole sea might be collapsing,” she said.
Photo: Reuters
The “slumping” phenomenon is showing up again this year, said the Paran Ocean Citizen Science Center, a group of divers who monitor the island’s UNESCO-listed soft corals, mostly around uninhabited islets south of Jeju.
Roughly half of one cluster off the islet of Beomseom has been struggling in past months, the group said.
Unlike hard corals supported by rigid calcium carbonate skeletons, soft corals rely on internal fluid pressure to keep upright. Environmental changes can disrupt that pressure, leading them to sag or collapse.
“If another large-scale ‘slumping’ happens, corals partially recover and then a lot break off and deteriorate again, and that keeps repeating, their capacity to recover just keeps declining,” researcher Kim Taihun said.
Kim and Anna Beate Jost, a colleague at the Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology (KIOST), documented Jeju’s 2024 soft coral slumping event for the first time in a May article in the journal Scientific Reports.
In an e-mail, Korea Heritage Service, which manages the soft coral colonies designated a national monument, said it has monitored the situation this year and would keep up long-term research to identify the reasons for the changes.
The South Korean Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, which oversees marine protected species and areas such as soft corals, added that it plans detailed investigation to gauge the scale of damage.
Kim said this year’s event looked similar to that of 2024, but could worsen should high water temperatures persist through this month, and the El Nino weather phenomenon might trigger typhoons and heavy rains.
However, he called for consistent and quantitative monitoring of the loss of soft corals through slumping, citing a lack of research support.
Climate change has hit corals globally, with perhaps the world’s most famous colonies on Australia’s Great Barrier Reef getting the most attention.
A record heat wave has parched the Korean Peninsula this year while heavy rains have pelted the south.
Coral researchers say such weather conditions, as well as water flowing down from China’s Yangtze River to affect the area’s salinity, are potential triggers for “slumping.”
Jeju’s waters have given safe harbor to soft coral communities, sensitive to environmental conditions and living on the edge of tolerable conditions in the northernmost limit of coral distribution in the East China Sea.
Soft coral functions as the nursery underpinning Jeju’s marine ecosystem, and soft coral communities reside in the UNESCO-listed Jeju Island Biosphere Reserve.
“The seaweed sea, the coral sea, is the foundational ecosystem underlying Jeju’s marine ecology,” said Yoon Sanghoon, an environmental expert at Paran.
“So if this base ecosystem collapses, there’s a real possibility the entire marine ecosystem could collapse.”
Over the past decade, marine heat waves around South Korea have extended almost four times longer, at 83.3 days, weather authorities said.
Paran, formed in 2023 by Jeju residents concerned by marine changes, brings together office workers, traditional divers and documentary filmmakers who flock there for monthly dives.
They plunge to the coral bed to take photograph and document changes they provide to scientists.
While Ko, a third-generation Jeju haenyeo or “sea woman”, can dive to a depth of as much as 8m relying on her own breath, she carries an oxygen tank on coral dives to greater depths.
The warming waters have affected the seabed in other ways, said her mother, 70-year-old Son Choon-sook, who began diving 45 years ago, when species such as turban shells, abalone and sea cucumber were abundant and thick seaweed festooned the rocks.
“I’ve worked at the sea for about 45 years, earned money, and sent my children to school on it,” she said. “Now the catch has run dry, and it makes me very sad.”
The thinning catch of the past few years follows summers that make the water too hot for species to spawn, she added, and her workday has shrunk to three hours from five formerly, as there is less to gather, but partly also for reasons of health.
Ko said her most recent dives in the summer have worried her again.
“Rather than the beautiful coral shapes, I feel like I’m seeing more sick coral now,” she added.

Banning kids from social media is only half a solution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:41:01 UTC
01:41:01 KST

Australia’s pathfinding efforts to keep children off social media are a closely watched experiment that more than two dozen countries are trying to imitate. The early data suggest it is not going very well.
More than 81 percent of under-16s still used at least one restricted platform after the ban took effect last December. Usage of TikTok among children aged 10 to 12 was higher than before, one parental-control company found, and roughly unchanged for teens aged 13 to 15. Qustodio, the firm behind the data, acknowledged the figures only encompass families already using its software to restrict apps, meaning the broader picture could be worse.
It is far too early to declare the policy a failure. Judging its effectiveness could take years. Other fast followers, including Malaysia and Indonesia, are finding that children can get around restrictions (as many suspected they would). One reason age bans are struggling is that prohibition addresses only half the problem. If policymakers want children off social media, they need to give them somewhere else to go.
Illustration: Yusha
When Prime Minister Anthony Albanese first campaigned on barring youth from social media, he declared the goal was to get children “off their devices and onto the footy field.” It was a wildly popular rallying cry for parents who feel powerless against addictive algorithms. Yet data shared by Australia’s eSafety Commissioner suggest that has not happened either; there was little to no change in participation in offline activities such as sports since the policy was introduced.
Cost helps explain why. Youth sports are increasingly a privilege for the rich. An Australian survey published in August found expense was a limiting factor in the ability to participate in community-level sports for 78 percent of children. Many jurisdictions offer subsidies of up to A$200 (US$143) a year per child. The average annual cost to participate in sports was A$4,567. Commanding children to get off their phones is the easy part, actually getting them on the sports field (or in a community theater, after-school arts club or even just a safe place to play outside with peers) takes harder policy work.
Yet research has repeatedly found that increased time spent in extracurriculars is linked to less screen use. In China, where school can be highly competitive from a young age, researchers were trying to see if giving elementary children two hours of extracurricular outdoor physical activity after school would impact their test scores. They ended up finding it did not hurt academic performance, and that it had the benefit of reducing screen time relative to the control group. A separate study in Canada of almost 29,000 seventh-graders found that those who engaged in sports, arts and community programs reported significantly less recreational screen time; and students with extracurricular activities and shorter screen times had the best mental health outcomes.
Many continue to equate the global regulatory pressure on social media firms to a Big Tobacco moment. Iceland offers another policy lesson. The nation treated adolescent cigarette and alcohol use as a social infrastructure problem, dramatically increased funding for subsidized sports, extracurricular activities and youth centers. In other words, policymakers did not rely on restrictions alone, they made other ways of socializing much easier to access. This involved parents, caregivers and a whole-of-community approach. The results were dramatic: The share of 10th graders who said they had been drunk at least once in the past 30 days fell from a peak of 42 percent in 1998 to about 6 percent in 2024. Daily cigarette smokers plunged from 23 percent to less than 1 percent.
Where should this money come from? Perhaps from Big Tech itself. In the US, Meta Platforms Inc last week agreed to a settlement of up to US$18 billion to resolve a litany of lawsuits. Court documents specify that the payments to settling states can be used, among other things, for after-school or summer programs including sports, literacy and other activities. Australia could eventually collect penalties from social media companies that fail to keep children off their platforms. Lawmakers would be wise to put those funds into expanding access to offline spaces.
Ultimately, it would still be hard for these clubs to compete with the lure of the algorithm. The US settlement would force Meta to change how it operates young users’ Facebook and Instagram accounts. These updates would only apply to the jurisdictions covered by the multistate agreement. Regulators elsewhere should press for the same protections to be rolled out globally. Changing the design of these platforms would be critical to keeping young people off them. Parents, not to mention developing minds, often feel they have little agency when up against behemoth recommendation systems engineered for maximum engagement. If teens are still finding ways on, as they would likely continue to do, regulators must tackle access and the algorithms.
One of the big criticisms from the UN children’s agency and a growing chorus of academics is that booting kids off social media would sever community lifelines. It is a legitimate concern as much of teenage (and adult) social life has migrated online. That only strengthens the case for rebuilding those communities offline.
Structural problems require more than cosmetic solutions. Policymakers must confront what makes online life, even illicitly, more attractive to young people than the real world.
Catherine Thorbecke is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asia tech. Previously she was a tech reporter at CNN and ABC News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Fossil link for sea turtles found off coast of Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:41:01 UTC
01:41:01 KST

The world’s first confirmed fossil of a modern leatherback sea turtle has been discovered off Taiwan, providing new clues about the species’ evolution.
A leatherback sea turtle, which can easily grow to more than 2m long, is the largest sea turtle species alive today. However, because they have a relatively soft shell, their fossils do not generally form well, limiting scientists’ understanding of the evolutionary history of modern leatherbacks.
That might have changed with the analysis of a fossilized humerus found on the seabed between Taiwan and the Penghu Islands. National Taiwan University Department of Life Science and Institute of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology associate professor Tsai Cheng-hsiu (蔡政修) and doctoral candidate Liao Yi-ju (廖翊如) confirmed the bone belonged to a leatherback.
Photo: Screen grab from National Taiwan University’s Web site
The discovery is the first confirmed fossil of a modern leatherback found anywhere in the world and provides important clues about the species’ origins and evolution.
Leatherbacks differ markedly from other living sea turtles. Tsai said all other living sea turtles belong to the family Cheloniidae, while leatherbacks belong to the family Dermochelyidae, which now contains only one living species: the leatherback.
Unlike other sea turtles, leatherbacks do not have a hard shell. Instead, their outer covering has a leathery texture, giving rise to their English name, “leatherback sea turtle.”
The fossilized humerus studied by Tsai and Liao was donated by Hou Li-jen (侯立仁), a retired professor from Tainan. It was discovered on the seabed in the same region where fossils of ancient pre-humans were found.
After detailed comparisons and morphological analysis of the humerus, the researchers confirmed that it belonged to a leatherback.
Their findings were published in June in the international journal Acta Palaeontologica Polonica.
The fossil found off Taiwan provides clues about the evolution of leatherbacks. They have the broadest distribution of any living sea turtle, ranging from cold polar waters to the tropics. However, their nesting and feeding grounds are relatively limited.
The waters around Taiwan do not host a major nesting or feeding area for leatherbacks. Important nearby nesting grounds include Indonesia, New Guinea and the Solomon Islands.
Tsai said molecular data from modern leatherbacks suggest that the species might have originated in the Indo-Pacific, including waters around Taiwan. The discovery of the world’s first confirmed fossil of a modern leatherback in Taiwan supports this hypothesis about the species’ origins and evolution.
The research team said fossil discoveries in Taiwan have demonstrated the importance and research value of the island’s paleontological record in understanding the origins and evolution of biodiversity.

Google Taiwan is reducing its workforce as the company continues to adjust operations to improve efficiency and focus resources on core goals, the Chinese-language Liberty Times (sister paper of the Taipei Times) reported yesterday.
The Alphabet Inc unit said the organizational adjustments have begun and would continue, even though it did not put a figure on the number of potential job cuts or specify the affected departments in its Taiwan operations.
The company’s response came after rumors circulated on social media about major job cuts at Google Taiwan.
Photo: CNA
Some posts said the downsizing would target the company’s consumer electronics-related departments and high-level roles, and some even speculated a cut of 30 percent to 50 percent of staff, the Liberty Times reported.
There were also posts pointing to Google’s hardware research and development (R&D) office at the Taipei Far Eastern Telecom Park in New Taipei City’s Banciao District (板橋) as likely to be hardest hit, the report said.
The Banciao R&D center is Google’s largest hardware engineering hub outside the US.
Despite the rumors, a senior Google official said last week that the company plans to expand its artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure R&D center in Taipei’s Shilin District (士林) and increase its office space by 60 percent.
The company would increase its investment in Taiwan as local partners take on a growing role in developing its AI infrastructure, Google senior vice president and chief technologist for AI and infrastructure Amin Vahdat said on Wednesday last week at a media session after delivering a speech at the Semicon Taiwan trade show in Taipei.

Are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:48 UTC
01:40:48 KST

Picture humanity in a boat being swept down a raging river, praying there is no Niagara Falls ahead. Or imagine standing with the pioneering physicists in 1942 before they triggered the first self-sustaining nuclear fission chain reaction beneath a Chicago stadium.
These were two of the analogies used this week by Robert Trager, an expert in the nascent field of AI governance, to describe the perilous but potential-filled moment the world stands at with accelerating artificial intelligence.
Trager, the director of the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, was speaking in the week OpenAI claimed the technology had crossed the threshold known as AGI — artificial general intelligence — with its newest model, GPT-6 Astra.
Photo: EPA
That claim came as the company prepared for a potential US$850 billion stock flotation, so included a dose of marketing spin, but if true it may be significant. The San Francisco company defines AGI as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.
The tasks it claims Astra can automate include designing circuit boards, filling out tax returns, building video games, financial modeling, engineering design and helping assemble legal documents. The threat to some white-collar jobs is implicit.
AI RISKS
Yet, the AGI claim coincides with rising fears about AI risks among safety experts and political leaders, whose nerves have been jangled by the increasing power and impenetrability of AI models this summer and a spate of serious safety accidents viewed by some as possible final warning shots.
“We’re heading through the rapids and we’re really hoping there isn’t some kind of drop in front of us and we don’t really know,” Trager said. “We’re plausibly close to crossing the line to what’s called recursive self-improvement, where [AI] systems improve themselves. That kind of recursivity is actually the definition of an explosion.”
The latest worry came on Friday, just hours after Astra’s launch, with reports that a swarm of AI agents had repurposed a German Web site as a message board to share tactics to cheat on tasks, according to Reuters. OpenAI said it was reviewing the matter but would not characterize it as a hack.
There is a sense of an awakening among politicians. On Thursday, US senator Bernie Sanders cited this summer’s alarming breakout of a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents which hacked into Hugging Face, a third-party software store, when he called for “an immediate pause on advanced AI development, and a permanent ban on superintelligence.”
He said countries around the world must “work together to prevent this nightmare scenario”, which he defined as “an artificial mind smarter than any human, capable of operating independently beyond our control.”
Concerns currently focus on AIs mounting cyber-attacks that could cripple real-world social and economic infrastructure, but future concerns include their ability to create biohazards and control military hardware.
Across the Atlantic, a cross-party group of UK parliamentarians has called for AI “kill switches” to be required by law to prevent disastrous loss of control, citing “a recent spree of rogue AI incidents”.
Darren Jones, an MP and former chief secretary to Keir Starmer, is also urgently attempting to set up a body to help legislators grapple with the technology.
“AI is developing at such a pace that neither government nor parliament can keep up,” he warned.
And next week a bill will be proposed by the Labor MP Alex Sobel to prohibit superintelligent AI development in the UK.
NEW MODELS
The increasing anxiety comes amid a torrent of new AI models. Already this year, 67 have been released by the leading US companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, and their Chinese rivals Moonshot, Z.ai and Qwen, according to one count.
With every increase in power, there is a potential increase in risk. OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, which is targeting a US$2 trillion stock exchange listing, this week admitted its own AIs were “not perfectly aligned” with human values and said there had been a “failure of operational security” in July hacks by its own model, Claude. It said the incidents had “stressed that the urgency of improving our cybersecurity defenses is even higher than we previously believed.”
AI’s double edge — opportunity and risk — was on show when OpenAI launched Astra on Thursday. Its marketing video focused not on the risks but on the breezy convenience that AI could offer to a certain kind of customer. It showed an upmarket San Francisco woman simultaneously booking a tennis court and designing a presentation for her high-end rainwear collection; a thirtysomething man being helped to build his dream space invaders game and order a takeaway; a law firm executive being helped to draft some contracts.
Yet only weeks ago, this was a model whose training had to be partly paused because of safety concerns after the Hugging Face incident. An independent safety researcher drafted in to investigate, Ajeya Cotra, said it was “more than 50 percent of the way to full-blown AI takeover.”
Astra also has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability — the first time it has given a model such a label. It means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure.”
The company’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, insisted the model was properly aligned not to do that, but added that “as these models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder.”
The ability to monitor what AI models are “thinking” as they advance is another growing source of safety fears. This week it was reported that OpenAI had been training Astra to reason not only in natural language, but in a more opaque manner that is faster and more efficient — and can make models’ chains of reasoning harder to follow. It means a model’s internal calculations may not always be written out as directly readable words — as if it was thinking in its head, rather than showing its working. Some experts fear this could help AIs covertly conspire against their human overseers.
OpenAI confirmed Astra “shows a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared to previous models” and Pachocki said “as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging.”
The company played down the development, but the increase in opaque reasoning sparked concern from AI safety researchers. Ryan Greenblatt, the chief scientist at Redwood Research, a nonprofit examining AI safety and security, called it “extremely concerning.” Gary Marcus, an influential AI sceptic, compared it to kicking away an already “rickety scaffolding before we have something better.”
CONFLICTED TECHNOLOGISTS?
OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, said this week he felt conflicted about the advances of AI models. He admitted OpenAI’s security had “failed” in the Hugging Face incident and called it “a legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure.”
“We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time, and it is still discordant for us,” he said in a tweet. “We know it is much more discordant for other people.”
His rationale for releasing OpenAI’s most powerful model so soon after a safety crisis appears to be that the world needs to see how AIs perform in the real world to understand where AI is heading. He said: “An iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.”
And yet he can see the risks. On Tuesday he addressed the G20 ministerial summit in North Carolina in the US and told politicians that “some things are going to go very wrong with cybersecurity unless people act quite urgently”.
He added: “There will be other challenges in the next five years. People talk about biosecurity and the things we are going to face there. There will be bigger ones yet to come.”

On Sunday, Teng pitched a total of 0.1 innings, in which he struck out one batter but gave up two walks and allowed a run.
Photo: Erik Williams-Imagn Images
The Sunday result saw Teng allow six runs in his last three games with the team in the majors, prompting the Astros to announce that the Taiwanese pitcher will be optioned back to the Astros’ Triple-A affiliate, the Sugar Land Space Cowboys.

At the top of the first, Lee drew a walk to first base before hits from subsequent teammates allowed him to score his only run of the game.
Lee was then struck out in the top of the third and fifth innings before hitting a foul pop-up in the top of the eighth.
The eyes of Taiwanese baseball fans were on Lee in July as he went on a 12-game hitting streak, which ended at the end of the month.

Court upholds and finalizes sentences in influence junket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:48 UTC
01:40:48 KST

The Supreme Court has upheld the convictions and prison sentences of a New Taipei City borough warden and an association chairman for election offenses involving a China-funded trip intended to influence Taiwanese voters.
The court rejected appeals by Yao Wei-hua (姚韋華), warden of Cingshan Borough (青山) in Tucheng District (土城), and Chinese Youth Cultural and Educational Art Exchange Association chairman Chien An-shih (簡安仕), confirming the High Court’s guilty verdicts.
In February, the High Court overturned a lower court’s acquittal, finding Yao and Chien guilty of contravening the Public Officials Election and Recall Act (公職人員選舉罷免法) and the Presidential and Vice Presidential Election and Recall Act (總統副總統選舉罷免法). It increased their sentences pursuant to Article 7 of the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法).
Photo: CNA
Yao was sentenced to two years and six months in prison and Chien was sentenced to four years and eight months in prison, with both deprived of their civil rights.
Prosecutors said that Chien, acting under the instruction and financial backing of China’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) in Nanjing, commissioned Yao in September 2023 to invite borough wardens and residents on a trip to China.
The participants paid NT$16,500 each for airfare, while meals and lodgings were provided for free, prosecutors said.
Yao on Nov. 5, 2023, took five borough wardens and nine relatives and friends to China, where they were hosted by the Nanjing TAO, they said.
During a banquet, a red banner with the slogan “One close family on both sides of the Taiwan Strait” was displayed, while TAO officials promoted cooperation between the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party, support for New Taipei City Mayor Hou You-yi (侯友宜), who was then running as the KMT candidate for president, and opposition to the “separatist” Democratic Progressive Party in an attempt to sway elections, prosecutors said.
In 2024, the New Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office indicted Yao and Chien on suspicion of contravening the Anti-Infiltration Act, the Public Officials Election and Recall Act, and the Presidential and Vice Presidential Election and Recall Act.
The New Taipei District Court acquitted them in the first trial, citing insufficient evidence to prove that the free lodging and meals were intended as bribes or to influence the participants voting behavior.
During the High Court appeal, Chien denied seeing the red banner and said that members of a Taiwanese business association were also present at the banquet.
Chien added that he hated politics, had never voted in a presidential election and could not possibly influence others’ voting behavior.
Yao also denied the allegations, saying that he “just wanted to go have fun” and had no knowledge of which Chinese officials were attending.
However, prosecutors presented evidence showing the pair had dined with TAO officials two months prior to the elections, adding that Yao and Chien had previously admitted to discussing the itinerary with TAO personnel, who accompanied the group throughout the trip.
The seating arrangement at the banquet interspersed Taiwanese attendees with Chinese officials, demonstrating a clear quid pro quo, prosecutors said.
The Supreme Court ruling was final.
Additional reporting by CNA and Yang Hsin-hui

Movie industry backsliding on gender: director
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:46 UTC
01:40:46 KST

When Danish director May el-Toukhy was selected for the top competition at the Venice Film Festival in July, she was the only female filmmaker in a 20-strong field — with a movie “about the invisibility of women.”
She joked about the irony at a press conference on Sunday, while pointing out that progress on gender bias made in the wake of the 2017 #MeToo movement appeared to be reversing.
“After #MeToo, I think all of us were really aware of this gender imbalance,” she told reporters.
Photo: Reuters
“And something has happened over the course of the last couple of years where we’re kind of returning to, you know, what it used to be — and so we have to be better,” she added.
The protagonist of Woman Unknown is a bride-to-be struggling to hide her wartime secret — a relationship with a Nazi during the German occupation of Denmark during World War II.
Women accused of having consorted with the enemy are seen in the film violently stripped, their heads shaved and red swastikas painted on their bare flesh.
The powerful film, which drew enthusiastic applause after a press screening on Sunday, is “about being objectified on one hand and on the other hand being unseen and voiceless,” el-Toukhy said.
The dearth of females in the top Venice competition has sparked nagging questions about the selection process and female representation.
Festival artistic director Alberto Barbera angered many observers in July when he said the initial 20-1 male domination of the top competition was because the submissions from women “were not enough to put them into the competition.”
Since then, the festival has added another film co-directed by a woman, the documentary NAZA about the Israeli killing of civilians in Gaza, which is to premiere on Thursday.
El-Toukhy, a Danish-Egyptian director who has worked on Netflix’s The Queen, said she had encountered gender bias throughout her career and even with her latest film.
“When I pitched the film to people, I could see that they were glazing over because they were, like, ‘Oh, another Second World War film,’ which I feel is unfair because we’ve told so many stories about the male experience during war or post-war, and we haven’t really explored what it meant to be a woman during that time as much,” she said.
After film school, she said she struggled to find financing for her first film.
“I think it took me six or seven years, whereas my male peers, they were much faster than me,” she said.
“My second film was really hard to get done as well,” she added.
She sees the underrepresentation of women at the top of the industry as a “structural problem” — echoing a similar point made by American star Maggie Gyllenhaalm, who is head of the competition jury in Venice this year.
“I do think it’s much harder for women to get their films financed,” Gyllenhaal said in the first week of the festival.
“Also, could it be possible that the things that women, having had a different experience of being alive in the world, want to make movies about are not always deemed high art?” she added.
Award-winning Italian actress Jasmine Trinca told reporters on Sunday: “When I see that there is only one woman in competition, I’m alarmed, I’m angry.”
“I think it’s a question we really need to ask ourselves and confront,” Trinca said.
A study from the USC Annenberg Inclusion Initiative described last year as a “Great Recession” for women directors in the US: Just nine women were attached to the 100 top-grossing films at the box office.
Only three women have won an Oscar for Best Director: Kathryn Bigelow, Chloe Zhao (趙婷) and Jane Campion.

The Taipei District Court has issued an arrest warrant for an aide of independent Legislator May Chin (高金素梅) after he jumped bail on Sunday.
Judicial police had responded late on Sunday after an electronic wrist monitor belonging to Chang Chun-chieh (張俊傑), Chin’s former legislative office director, issued a low-battery alert, the court said in a statement yesterday.
Police responding to the alert were unable to locate Chang, but recovered his wrist monitor, which had been “broken and thrown away,” the court said.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
After notifying immigration authorities, the court issued an arrest warrant for Chang.
Chin, Chang and 22 others were indicted on June 8 on corruption and fraud-related charges related to the embezzlement of public funds and the importation of unapproved COVID-19 test kits from China.
Chin, who has denied wrongdoing, was accused of obtaining more than NT$7.87 million (US$249,430) in public funds through fraudulent claims for legislative assistants’ salaries, bonuses, overtime pay and childcare subsidies. This included registering several people, including Chin’s siblings, as legislative assistants, but they did not perform any duties, prosecutors alleged.
Chang was accused of conspiring with Chin to fraudulently obtain funds earmarked for assistants’ salaries, as well as using an indigenous cultural association to fraudulently obtain more than NT$9.33 million from government agencies and state-owned enterprises.
Prosecutors said that during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2022, Chin also authorized Chang to enlist others to illegally import 74,400 unapproved rapid test kits from China, circumventing medical device regulations.
Chin said the rapid test kits were intended to help indigenous communities amid a shortage of the devices in Taiwan.
In the indictment, prosecutors recommended a sentence of at least 16 years for Chang and 12-and-a-half years for Chin.
Chang, who had been detained and held incommunicado for nearly four months before his indictment, was released on NT$10 million bail in June.
At the time, Chang’s lawyers sought his release on health grounds, saying he was more than 70 years old and battling lung cancer.
During the first day of his trial on Tuesday last week, Chang denied the corruption charges, but admitted to other offenses, such as document forgery. He said that he was not just a legislative aide in name, but had performed his duties and had no criminal intent.

Admiring Cabinet’s budgetary acrobatics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:45 UTC
01:40:45 KST

Over the past few days, opposition lawmakers have harshly criticized the Cabinet for “showing contempt for the legislature” by spending all NT$500 million (US$15.85 million) of the Executive Yuan’s budget that had previously been frozen by lawmakers for the 2025 fiscal year.
The story began in December 2024, when the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) were reviewing the central government’s budget. Angered by then-Cabinet secretary-general Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) leaving that legislative committee meeting without authorization, the lawmakers in January last year responded by voting to freeze NT$500 million in Executive Yuan funding.
However, after combing through the government’s final accounts for last year submitted at the end of last month, the opposition lawmakers were nearly apoplectic. Not only had the NT$500 million not remained under lock and key, but it had been completely spent.
For those familiar with government accounting, the controversy — which opposition lawmakers have denounced as bypassing legislative oversight — is a case of a rather entertaining bureaucratic sleight of hand.
Opposition lawmakers, in their eagerness to flex their authority, had overlooked an important detail. In their proposal, the KMT and TPP’s resolution simply stated that NT$500 million of Executive Yuan funding was to be frozen, but neglected to specify any particular budget item or program.
As the legislature had not specified which funds were off-limits, the Cabinet assigned the frozen NT$500 million to personnel expenses, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said. Civil servants’ salaries, pensions and related remuneration have strong statutory and constitutional protections. The Cabinet said that it was legally obligated to make those payments.
The Executive Yuan played its apparent submission as an offensive move, finding a legal pathway for it to spend the money. In the end, the Cabinet effectively put the entire NT$500 million to use, a maneuver that spared operating expenses and construction and procurement spending from bearing the full weight of the freeze.
While KMT and TPP lawmakers have been protesting angrily, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) offered only a brief response to media questions on Friday, saying that the DGBAS had already explained the matter in accordance with the law.
With little legal recourse, it seemed that all opposition lawmakers could do is vent to the media that, in the words of KMT Culture and Communications Committee Director Charles Chen (陳以信), the Legislative Yuan “might as well close its doors” in light of the Cabinet’s workaround.
The act of budgetary subterfuge is another demonstration that, even under the political constraints of a minority government, the administration does not necessarily have to sit helplessly. When faced with politically motivated, borderline frenzied budget cuts and freezes; government officials can still respond with technical expertise and legal arguments.
This battle over government accounting not only demonstrates the political resilience of a minority government, but also shows that if legislative oversight is reduced to political score-settling without technical rigor, lawmakers might ultimately find themselves struck by their own boomerang. It has been a battle of political and bureaucratic wits, and is certainly a worthy piece of gossip.
Richard Wu is a trade promotion organization retiree.

Driver thanks ‘superhero’ rival as race safety fails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

A British racing driver thanked a “superhero” rival for pulling him from the flaming wreckage of his car after a horror crash in Shanghai, saying the quick response saved his life.
Loek Hartog on Saturday stopped and leapt out of his own car to rush to the aid of Ollie Millroy during the China GT Championship race at the Shanghai International Circuit, home of the Chinese Formula One Grand Prix. The Dutchman used a fire extinguisher on Millroy’s Ferrari as a blaze raged before yanking open the driver’s door and dragging him to safety.
“I am still alive tonight entirely thanks to one man,” Millroy posted on social media.
“Loek Hartog stopped instantly with no flag marshals or fire crews in sight and risked his own life to get me out of the car,” he added.
The 36-year-old Millroy suffered a huge impact in the multi-car crash during the race, which resulted in his car erupting instantly in flames.
“I don’t remember anything ... but I will remember his incredible act of bravery for the rest of my life,” Millroy wrote. “One day I will tell our three kids this story and Loek will be the biggest superhero in history in their eyes too.”
“I’m lying here tonight with five broken ribs, broken collar bone, broken hand and finger and a bruised lung, but it could have been much worse,” he wrote. “Thank you Loek. I owe you my life for your selfless act today.”
Hartog, 23, played down his heroics in a social media note posted after visiting Millroy in hospital.
“It was terrifying, and there were moments when I didn’t know if I’d ever manage to get Ollie out,” he said. “But it’s not about what I did. I’m sure many people in my position would have reacted exactly the same way.”
“The most important thing is that Ollie is okay. Things could have turned out very differently today, and I’m truly grateful that they didn’t,” he said.
Millroy’s team, AAI Motorsport, said they would “no longer participate in any races organised by China GT” in a statement that criticized safety standards at the circuit.
The team said Millroy’s car “continued to burn for more than a minute” after the crash, and that “no timely and effective firefighting and rescue operations were seen.”
The China GT Championship organizing committee said in a statement on Chinese social media: “We sincerely apologize for this accident and for the subsequent shock and distress it has caused.”
“We will conduct a thorough review and investigation into this accident, and draw up more comprehensive plans to address any shortcomings,” it said.
“The championship organizing committee extends its sympathies to Oliver Millroy, driver of car number 91, and the other drivers involved in the accident, and sincerely hopes for their speedy recovery,” it said. “The committee also expresses its deep gratitude and respect to Loek Hartog, who was the first driver to arrive at the scene of the accident and provide assistance.”

Germany’s far-right AfD triumphs, aims fire at chancellor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservatives yesterday licked their wounds after a crushing state election defeat in the ex-communist east, as the triumphant far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) launched a withering attack against him.
AfD national coleader Alice Weidel — basking in the almost 44 percent landslide in Saxony-Anhalt — charged that “no chancellor before has been as unpopular as Friedrich Merz, who has become a major burden on Germany’s prosperous development.”
Merz was huddling with his Christian Democrats (CDU), including defeated state premier Sven Schulze, whose party scored 17 percent, an outcome widely blamed on voter anger against the ruling coalition at a time of economic stagnation.
Photo: Bloomberg
The AfD’s lead candidate in the state, 35-year-old Ulrich Siegmund, said that voters had sent “a signal to Berlin” and took pleasure in mocking 70-year-old Merz, calling him “a very good campaigner” for the AfD.
He said that although his party had narrowly missed out on an absolute majority, it was now reaching out to other parties and individual lawmakers in an effort to build a stable ruling coalition.
“It is a very clear government mandate,” Siegmund said.
While the result sparked jubilation among the AfD’s followers, the prospect of the first far-right government taking charge of a German state since World War II has deeply unsettled other parties, migrants and minority groups.
The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt is labeled a “right-wing extremist” group by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, and some of Siegmund’s staff are former members of a since-banned neo-Nazi organization.
“I’m scared,” said a 28-year-old man who came from Afghanistan in 2015 and who asked not to be named.
“I have two children here,” he said in Magdeburg, Saxony-Anhalt. “What will happen if I have to leave?”
AfD national coleader Tino Chrupalla sought to dispel such fears, saying that “no one needs to be afraid of us.”
He told Deutschlandfunk radio that his party is not against people with a migrant background, “provided they are integrated, speak German ... and contribute to the economy here.”
Weidel struck a more combative tone, attacking the Merz government and predicting that her party would take power in 2029 national elections.
“The people in this country do not want things to continue as they are,” she said, demanding an end to “illegal migration, open borders, skyrocketing rates of crime committed by foreign nationals, and a refusal to carry out deportations.”
Weidel also slammed Germany’s “disastrous energy policy” and “rampant deindustrialization that is breaking Germany’s backbone.”
Pressure has grown on Merz not just from the far-right, but also from within his coalition, which has struggled to reboot a stagnant economy and has argued over social policy, especially pensions.
The visibly dejected CDU state Premier Schulze on Sunday said that his campaign was not always helped by national government policies, saying that “we often faced headwinds, and that wasn’t always easy.”
Daniel Guenther, the CDU premier of Schleswig-Holstein state, labeled the AfD win “a shocking moment for our country.”
“For the first time since the end of World War II, the AfD — a party whose state branch is classified as right-wing extremist — is close to securing an absolute majority,” he said.
The AfD, founded in 2013 as a euroskeptic protest party, soon transformed into an Islamophobic and anti-immigration party, railing against the open-door policy of former CDU chancellor Angela Merkel.
Merz has vowed to return the CDU to its conservative roots and launched a crackdown on irregular immigration while trying to turn the economy around.
Political scientist Oliver Lembcke of Ruhr University Bochum said: “We are witnessing a tectonic shift in the party system.”
Merz took office with the promise of pushing back the AfD, yet the party has grown stronger, despite the CDU’s shift to a more conservative course.
“This confronts Merz with a question of renewed urgency: What strategy can the CDU use to reverse this trend?” Lembcke said.

Renters should be careful of ‘walkthrough’ scams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

People looking for apartments should always view the property in person and sign a lease before making any payments, the Criminal Investigation Bureau (CIB) said, following reports of scammers posting fake rentals.
Demand for rental housing rises as a new academic year starts each year in September, prompting scammers to target inexperienced renters such as students with fake listings on online rental groups, the bureau said.
The listings often advertise rentals below market rates with attractive interiors; scammers claim they are out of town and offer to mail keys through a convenience store delivery service for self-guided viewings, it said.
Photo: CNA
They send fake convenience store delivery links to steal personal information and trick victims into making bank transfers, it added.
One person came across a rental listing on social media for a studio in Taipei’s Daan District (大安), advertised as newly renovated for NT$10,000 a month including a parking space and eligible for a rent subsidy.
She contacted the “landlord” via Line, who said they were out of town but offered to mail the keys through convenience store delivery for a walkthrough.
The scammer sent a fake delivery Web site where the victim entered her delivery information, after which the site said she had “not completed real-name verification” and instructed her to contact online customer service to verify her bank account.
Misled by the fake customer service, the victim transferred NT$30,000 and bought NT$25,000 worth of game credits at a convenience store, sending the redemption codes to the scammers.
She lost NT$55,000 and realized she had been scammed after contacting police to verify the transaction.
Past rental scams often asked prospective tenants to pay a deposit before viewing the property and then cut off contact after receiving the money, the CIB said.
Scammers have added fake delivery Web sites impersonating convenience store services, using the delivery of keys for self-guided walkthroughs to make the transaction appear legitimate, it said.
People should view the property in person, verify the landlord’s identity and only pay after signing a lease, the bureau said.
Convenience store delivery services should never ask people to transfer money or use online banking for real-name verification, it said.
Anyone who encounters such requests should stop immediately and call the 165 anti-fraud hotline or 110 to report the situation, it added.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:41 UTC
01:40:41 KST

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un put his second naval destroyer into service and called for building a more reliable nuclear deterrent, state media reported yesterday, as the US, South Korea and Japan began a trilateral military exercise he views as a security threat.
The ship’s commissioning comes as North Korea is dialing up pressure on Washington after rebuffing US President Donald Trump’s decision to scale back a major military drill with South Korea in a conciliatory step toward Kim. Observers say North Korea wants to wrest bigger US concessions.
The destroyer Kang Kon was commissioned into North Korea’s navy in the eastern port city of Wonsan on Sunday at a ceremony attended by Kim and his teenage daughter, whom South Korea’s spy service calls his likely heir. North Korean state media photos showed the girl in a white dress and blazer walking alongside her father on a red carpet, touring the warship and posing with sailors.
Photo: KCNA / KCNA VIA KNS / AFP
The ship and the Choe Hyon, which was put into service in June, are both 5,000-tonne destroyers that state media said can carry various conventional and nuclear weapons. Considered North Korea’s biggest and most advanced warships, the two destroyers were likely built with Russian assistance, experts say.
In July, North Korea said it test-fired nuclear-capable cruise missiles from the Kang Kon.
In a speech at the ceremony, Kim said the back-to-back warship additions instilled fear in the enemies as the nuclear armament of North Korea’s navy made it possible to exercise its nuclear deterrent in a more diversified, practical manner.
Photo: Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP
“The enemies’ concerns will surely be deepened,” Kim said. “We must establish more clearly a powerful and reliable nuclear war deterrent, to put into practice the diverse and effective operation of our nuclear combat systems and further strengthen our military activities for maritime defense and war deterrence.”
Meanwhile, the US, South Korea and Japan yesterday began their five-day Freedom Edge exercise near the Korean Peninsula.
South Korea’s military said the exercise is defensive in nature and meant to enhance a joint response capability against North Korean nuclear threats, and that it involves key maritime and aerial military assets from the three countries.
At the exercise’s opening ceremony at Yokota Air Base in western Tokyo, the US Pacific Command quoted Lieutenant General Stephen Jost, commander of the US forces in Japan, as saying that Washington, Tokyo and Seoul “stand together on common interests, ready to preserve the peace and security we have built and defended for more than eight decades.”

India’s resilience depends on diversified trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:40 UTC
01:40:40 KST

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s participation in the Shanghai Cooperation Council meeting in Kyrgyzstan was about more than regional security; he used the forum to push for deeper trade links between member states. This is only the latest example of India’s proactive pursuit of trade diplomacy. Last year’s free trade agreement with the UK was followed this January by the “mother of all deals,” a wide-ranging agreement with the EU. And high-level trade talks continue with the US, building on a joint statement of intent issued in February.
The backdrop to this big push is fraught. US President Donald Trump’s sweeping and erratic tariffs are only the latest body blow to the international trading system. The WTO’s Appellate Body, which adjudicates trade disputes between member states, has been decapitated since 2019. Countries are increasingly viewing trade and investment through a national security lens. The rules-based multilateral trade order that the Asian Tigers and China relied on to pursue export-led development has effectively collapsed, with no evident successor in sight. As Antonio Gramsci put it at another moment of profound global upheaval, this is “the time of monsters.”
How might a middle power such as India anchor its trade strategy in such a tumultuous period? The nascent field of geoeconomics offers useful guidance.
Consider the concept of “geopolitical distance.” Political scientists at Georgetown University have built a database measuring the gap between countries at any given point in time, based on voting patterns at the UN General Assembly. Research has shown that geopolitical distance is becoming increasingly important in determining patterns of international economic engagement. Bilateral trade, foreign direct investment and cross-border financial claims fall sharply with geopolitical distance.
This trend raises the prospect of a segmented world economy, with export markets shrinking for most countries. While such “geoeconomic fragmentation” is still limited compared to, say, the Cold War era, the trajectory is worrying. A review of several papers suggests that a full decoupling of the global economy into rival blocs could reduce global GDP by up to 7 percent in the long term. The burden would fall disproportionately on emerging and developing economies, which stand to benefit the most from external market access, unrestricted foreign direct investment and technology transfers.
In this landscape, the best strategy for a middle power is likely to be diversification: building a network of trade relationships sufficiently dispersed so that no single bilateral rupture could cause catastrophic harm. The obvious analogy is to modern portfolio theory: a well-diversified investor is not betting on any particular asset but rather seeking insulation against the failure of a subset of assets. The measure is the standard deviation of a country’s trade-weighted geopolitical distance from all trade partners.
By this metric, India is well placed. It ranks among the top quartile of countries for export diversification across the geopolitical spectrum, and near the median for import diversification. Its trade relationships range from the US and Europe to Russia and the Gulf, with many Asian and African economies in between. It has conspicuously refused to be corralled into a single bloc: abstaining from Ukraine-related votes at the UN and deepening the Quad partnership, while playing a foundational role in the BRICS group and negotiating deals with the US and the EU. Such strategic diversification is enormously valuable in a fragmenting world.
Indian policymakers should draw several lessons from these findings. First, to leverage its enviable spread of partners, India must trade much more than it does today. While the country’s trade-to-GDP ratio of about 45 percent is considerable progress from the near-autarky of the pre-liberalization era, it remains well below the levels achieved by successful East and Southeast Asian economies.
The string of free trade agreements is an excellent start, but more could be done to develop regional trade by joining major agreements such as the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership. Closer to home, trade links among the economies of South Asia remain much weaker than those among comparable groups such as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. To use one example, they could be strengthened by expanding cross-border energy markets: abundant hydropower from neighbors such as Nepal and Bhutan could reduce India’s dependence on fossil-fuel imports.
Next, India should participate in plurilateral deals struck among various subsets of WTO members seeking to deepen trade in a specific area. The economist Jagdish Bhagwati argued that plurilateral agreements impede first-best multilateral progress, but that argument is irrelevant when the WTO has not made any multilateral progress on lowering trade barriers since the Doha Development Round commenced in 2001. Consider the plurilateral agreement on e-commerce being implemented by 66 members, covering 70 percent of global trade. As a large net-exporter of digital services, India should not only sign on, but seek a leading role in the coalition.
Finally, India should zealously safeguard the diversification it has already achieved, which in turn makes it an attractive partner for countries forging a “China Plus One” strategy or, increasingly, seeking to reduce trade dependence on the US. That means being wary about any bilateral agreement that curtails its freedom of action vis-a-vis third countries. Canada has set an example by walking away from trade negotiations with the Trump administration in part because the US sought veto power over its engagement with other countries.
Of course, Canada is overwhelmingly dependent on the US as an export market, so it is unclear whether its principled stand can succeed. For India, well-diversified to begin with, the case is more clear-cut. A country that has spent decades cultivating strategic autonomy should think long and hard before trading it away for preferential market access, however attractive the terms. India must lean into its position as one of the few countries to combine economic scale, democratic legitimacy and geopolitical breadth to boost trade and remain open to all comers.
Shekhar Aiyar is director and chief executive of the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations.

Passengers are charged a booking service fee for the use of the global distribution system, which provides reservation services for airlines. The fee is based on a user-pays principle and applies regardless of whether passengers purchase tickets through an airline’s official Web site, a travel agency or other sales channels.
All four airlines collect the booking service fee as part of the ticket price and any changes to the fee do not require prior approval or reporting to the Civil Aeronautics Administration (CAA).

11 killed in avalanche
At least 11 people were killed and six injured after an avalanche struck a group of climbers in the Kabardino-Balkaria region in the North Caucasus, local emergency services said. The avalanche swept down Mount Mizhirgi, one of the highest peaks in the North Caucasus, at about 5pm on Sunday, hitting a group of 33 climbers. As of 9am yesterday, 10 climbers had made their own way down the mountain, while the fate of six others remained unknown, emergency services said. More than 50 emergency workers were involved in the search-and-rescue operation, but efforts were being hampered by difficult terrain and a high risk of further avalanches, they said.

Some ‘good deals’ can be fraudulent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:35 UTC
01:40:35 KST

The Administration for Digital Industries yesterday cautioned the public to verify online advertisements with commercial brands’ official Web site to avoid fraudulent mooncake sales ahead of the Mid-Autumn Festival.
Some people made online purchases based on a seasonal gift box ad on social media, it said. The ad claimed it was a limited-edition gift box that contained artisanal holiday treats, with refrigerated home delivery and an early-bird discount offered to attract consumers, it said.
The Web site showed product photos, gift box contents, prices, delivery options and an order form after clicking the purchase link to enter its Web site, which looked similar to that of legitimate vendors, it said.
Photo: Taipei Times
People who placed an order did not verify the offer with the brand’s official Web site or social media accounts, nor did they make sure the purchase link and the seller’s information was legitimate while entering their information and paying, it said.
They did not receive any shipment notification, and several days later, the ad Web site stopped working, it said.
No customer service or store information was ever found, the administration said, adding the complainants finally checked the brand’s official Web site and realized there was no promotion.
The ad was set up by scammers mimicking the legitimate brand, it said.
The administration reminded people to remember four anti-fraud tips while shopping online.
First, do not assume it is an official campaign just because an attractive online ad uses fine product photos or well-known brand names, it said.
Consumers should first check a brand’s official Web site or social media accounts and enter its shopping Web site via officially approved sales channels, the administration said, cautioning against clicking on links for unknown sources.
Second, people entering a shopping Web site should verify the link with the brand’s official Web site and make sure it provides comprehensive information on company name, contact information, address, returns and exchanges, and after-sales services, it said.
Third, do not trust products that come with unusually low prices or discounts before checking with the official Website, it said.
Fourth, do not follow instructions on unknown Web sites to transfer money, enter credit card numbers, or share any personal information, it said.
That can prevent data breaches, unauthorized credit card charges or getting scammed, the administration said.

No shortcut to excellence in chips: TSMC executive
Unknown

There are “no shortcuts” to excellence in chipmaking, said Y.P. Chyn (秦永沛), a top executive at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電), as he received one of Taiwan’s most prestigious industrial technology honors yesterday.
Chyn, TSMC’s executive vice president and co-chief operating officer, made the remarks during a ceremony in Hsinchu County’s Jhudong Township (竹東) at which he was inducted as an Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI, 工業技術研究院) laureate.
“For nearly 40 years, I have always believed there are no shortcuts to excellence in semiconductor manufacturing, and technology research and development,” Chyn said.
Photo: Lin Yi-ju, Taipei Times
He said he had worked with TSMC’s operations teams to overcome “countless technical bottlenecks” and turn advanced manufacturing technologies into mass-production capabilities that helped drive global technological innovation.
Chyn recounted his journey, saying that he joined the ITRI’s Electronics Research and Service Organization after graduating from National Cheng Kung University in 1982, and that the four-and-a-half years he spent there “laid the foundation for my semiconductor career.”
He later joined the newly established TSMC in 1987 as one of its early employees.
Looking back on the development of Taiwan’s semiconductor industry, Chyn called it a “Taiwan miracle” and said the government-backed ITRI had played a critical role at a pivotal time.
He said the ITRI’s efforts to cultivate talent and transfer personnel “laid the talent foundation” for TSMC when the chipmaker was established, helping pave the way for the company’s success and Taiwan’s rise as a global semiconductor powerhouse.
Chyn also thanked TSMC founder Morris Chang (張忠謀) for creating the foundry business model, which he described as “a business model that changed the world.”
He also thanked TSMC chairman and CEO C.C. Wei (魏哲家), former chairman Mark Liu (劉德音), his colleagues and his family.
President William Lai (賴清德), who presented Chyn with his laureate certificate, said Chyn had led teams in achieving yield breakthroughs in processes ranging from 28 nanometers to 2 nanometers, helping cement TSMC’s leadership in advanced manufacturing.
Chyn’s contributions have also helped Taiwan “remain at the core of the global supply chain in the era of AI and high-performance computing,” Lai added.

PRC could exploit defense gaps: Manila
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:40:31 UTC
01:40:31 KST

China could see recent cuts to US-South Korean military exercises as an opportunity to reassert itself in the Indo-Pacific region, Philippine Secretary of Defense Gilberto Teodoro said yesterday, though he said Washington had assured Manila that its commitments to the Philippines remained unchanged.
Speaking to Reuters on the sidelines of the Seoul Defense Dialogue, Teodoro said there had been no reduction in US-Philippine military activities, and that bilateral and multilateral cooperation involving Manila continued to expand.
US President Donald Trump’s decision last month to scale back military exercises with South Korea has prompted debate among security analysts over the credibility of US deterrence in Asia and whether rivals such as China could perceive a weakening of US resolve.
Photo: Reuters
“It is a possibility, of course. China is very quick to exploit gaps,” Teodoro said when asked whether Beijing could seize on the move.
“If we’re talking about the Indo-Pacific as a whole, then it may signal some opportunity for China to reassert itself,” he said.
However, Manila had received “definite assurances” from Washington and that there was “no indication” that the changes in South Korea would affect commitments under the US-Philippines Mutual Defense Treaty, he said.
Manila has deepened defense cooperation with the US under Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, including expanded joint exercises and greater access for US forces to Philippine military facilities, as tensions with China have intensified in the South China Sea.
Teodoro said Manila was also broadening security ties with other partners. The Philippines recently concluded agreements with Canada and New Zealand, signed a visiting forces agreement with France, and was negotiating a similar pact with Britain, he said.
The defense chief also accused China of relying increasingly on influence operations alongside military and maritime pressure.
“Definitely it takes advantage of democratic space to co-opt people and to use a free media to expand its distortive narratives,” he said.
The Philippines is pursuing stronger espionage and foreign influence legislation to counter such activities, he said.
Asked about Marcos’ recent remarks that progress was being made toward possible joint oil and gas exploration talks with China, Teodoro struck a cautious note, saying it would be “doubtful” that any economic cooperation could be insulated from longstanding sovereignty disputes in the South China Sea.
Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Mao Ning (毛寧) yesterday said that China “has always been committed to maintaining peace and stability in the Asia-Pacific region, refraining from great-power confrontation, and hopes that relevant countries can also play a positive role in regional peace and stability.”
Teodoro was in Seoul for talks aimed at expanding defense cooperation with South Korea, one of Manila’s largest arms suppliers.
South Korea has supplied the Philippines with FA-50 light combat aircraft, frigates and other military equipment as Manila modernizes its armed forces.
He said the Philippines was interested in deeper industrial cooperation and emerging defense technologies from South Korea, but indicated that a long-discussed submarine acquisition program remained some way off.
“The submarine program is still under review,” he said, citing questions over mission requirements and the substantial infrastructure needed to support such a capability. “I would say it will be still a way off.”
Teodoro said concerns about China’s actions were encouraging closer security cooperation among countries across the region and could ultimately lead to a more interconnected Indo-Pacific security network.
“I believe so because the motivating factor there is China,” he said.

The air force plans to build 26 more hardened aircraft shelters as the number of F-16Vs stationed along Taiwan’s east coast is expected to reach 120 when the final shipment of 66 jets procured from the US arrives.
The incoming jets would be stationed at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung County, augmenting the F-16V Block 20s operated by the 5th Tactical Fighter Wing in Hualien County, officials said yesterday.
The air force plans to allocate more than NT$6.88 billion (US$218.1 million) from next year to 2031 to build the shelters in Hualien and Taitung as part of the implementation of a “one aircraft, one shelter” policy.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
Based on the Ministry of National Defense’s budget proposal for next year, 22 of the shelters would be built in Hualien and four in Taitung. The air force plans to build five general aircraft hangars and related facilities at the Hualien base to house transport aircraft.
The air force’s budget plan calls for NT$65.53 million to be allocated next year for project management, surveying, drilling and preliminary design.
Detailed design, tendering and contract awards are scheduled for 2028 and 2029, with construction beginning in 2030, and construction, inspection and project closeout to be completed in 2031.
The air force said in its budget proposal that during defensive operations, frontline fighter aircraft would be dispersed to the Jiashan and Shihzishan facilities in Hualien and Taitung respectively to preserve combat capabilities.
It needed to reassess the number of aircraft as well as the protective capacity and requirements of existing shelters.
The new shelters would be designed to withstand high levels of explosive force, ensuring that sufficient numbers of fighter jets could be preserved to continue carrying out joint suppression, interception and homeland defense missions in the event of a sudden enemy attack or during a contingency, the air force said.
Once the 7th Tactical Fighter Wing in Taitung has received all 66 F-16V Block 70s, eastern Taiwan would have about 110 to 120 F-16Vs, based on public releases, making the region one of the most important concentrations of Taiwan’s fighter aircraft.
