Masked U.K. anti-migrant protesters condemned for "thuggish and intimidating" behavior
London — Hundreds of masked anti-migrant protesters brought traffic around one of the world's busiest maritime passenger ports, the Port of Dover in England, to a standstill over the weekend.
In the latest in a series of increasingly confrontational demonstrations across Britain, demonstrators, many wearing balaclavas, dressed in all black and carrying English and British flags, blocked roads on Saturday leading to the Dover ferry port, chanting "stop the boats" and "Christ is king."
Traffic was halted, causing a highway backup that stretched 4 miles and disrupting ferry passengers and freight.
The Kent Police force described the gathering as a "spontaneous protest" and made no arrests. But local Labour Party lawmaker Mike Tapp challenged that characterization, arguing the action appeared to have been clearly coordinated.
"Policing depends on preparation. This was clearly organized, yet Kent Police appear to have had little advance warning," Tapp wrote in The Mirror newspaper. "I will be asking why, whether intelligence was missed, and whether additional officers - including mutual aid from forces such as the Met [London Metropolitan Police] - can be mobilized quickly enough when Dover is targeted again."
Patriot Platform, a recently formed far-right network and protest group, claimed responsibility for the protest. It's led by Daniel Thomas, better known online as Danny Tommo, an anti-immigrant social media influencer and close associate of Britain's Elon Musk-endorsed, far-right activist Tommy Robinson.
Thomas took to X to celebrate Saturday's action in Dover: "You stuck to the plan and maintained complete discipline," he said, adding: "A message was sent! Now imagine how powerful the next message will be."
Thomas, who was previously jailed for involvement in an attempted kidnapping, also claimed lawyers had been available by phone to speak with senior police officers during the demonstration, and that activists were supplied with legal documentation of their rights. Kent Police has not commented on Thomas' claim.
Dover has long been at the center of Britain's debate over the "small boats." Nearly 200,000 migrants have crossed the English Channel from France since 2021, and while the number of crossings is down significantly this year, it continues to be a hot topic in British politics.
The U.K. government, led by the center-left Labour Party, condemned the Saturday demonstration, saying in a statement that while "the right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy … we condemn the behavior in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused."
Nigel Farage, leader of the right-wing populist Reform UK party and a one-time ally of President Trump, also condemned the protests, calling them "disgusting" on the GB News network.
"Nobody in any political protest, on the left or right, should appear in balaclavas," he said.
A second confrontation within 24 hours
Sunday brought a second anti-migrant confrontation, as hundreds of protesters descended on Portsmouth, a city that's home to a major naval base on England's south coast, after a boat carrying around 140 migrants was intercepted off Britain's shore.
U.K. Coastguard aircraft, a helicopter and lifeboats were involved in the operation to bring the people from the inflatable "mega-dinghy" to shore in Portsmouth.
Thomas livestreamed from the city, urging supporters to travel to Portsmouth. Videos posted online show protesters confronting police as authorities attempted to bring the migrants onto land and then transport them by bus to an initial processing facility.
Some protesters attempted to obstruct the buses, while police officers formed lines to keep them away from the arrivals.
Emma Reynolds, a lawmaker and current member of the cabinet, condemned the protests as "thuggish and intimidating behavior" in an interview with CBS News' partner network BBC News.
Migration as a political flashpoint
Anti-migrant demonstrations have become increasingly common across Britain over the last two years.
Hotels accommodating asylum seekers became regular protest sites last year, while disorder and violence linked to anti-migrant demonstrations has erupted in several cities, including Glasgow in Scotland and Belfast in Northern Ireland.
Tommy Robinson has drawn large crowds to demonstrations in central London. At one 2025 rally, Elon Musk addressed Robinson's supporters remotely, telling them: "Whether you choose violence or not, violence is coming to you, you either fight back or you die."
Robinson has continued staging demonstrations in 2026, although some have drawn smaller crowds.
During 14 previous years of Conservative Party rule, and since the Labour Party came back to power two years ago, successive British governments had pledged and largely failed to stem the flow of undocumented migrants arriving by small boats from France.
More than 40,000 people made the journey in 2025, according to government data. Around 17,000 migrants had crossed between Jan. 1 and Sept. 1 of this year, which the government likes to note is approximately 43% fewer than during the same period last year.
The events in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend appear to show that falling arrival numbers alone won't shield the government from anger over migration, especially as it is encouraged by high-profile activists determined to keep the topic front and center.

from refuge to prototype: why cabins keep redefining how we live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:38:45 UTC
01:38:45 KST

The cabin has always promised something larger than its diminutive footprint. Reduced to shelter, enclosure and a relationship with its surroundings, it seems to return architecture to its most elementary question: what do we actually need in order to inhabit a place? Yet its contemporary appeal extends well beyond construction. At a moment defined by permanent connectivity, speed and availability, the image of a small structure removed from the city has become a shorthand for another rhythm of life — quieter, slower and apparently more autonomous. The cabin is therefore both an architectural experiment and a cultural fantasy: a place onto which we project everything we feel ordinary life no longer gives us.
Spanish journalist and curator Eva Morell explores precisely this tension in ‘Refugio, una historia de cabañas’, published by Debate in 2025. Moving from prehistoric shelters to Thoreau’s Walden, Le Corbusier’s Cabanon and cabins embedded in popular culture, the book examines shelter as both physical structure and recurring human desire. ‘For me, a cabin is an ideal, a philosophy, almost a religion: a space where you feel comfortable, calm and safe,’Morell explains. ‘The cabin is more a feeling than an architecture, because it goes beyond architecture itself.’
That desire has acquired a peculiar form in the digital age. Cabins circulate endlessly through Instagram feeds, Pinterest boards and travel accounts: isolated timber structures glowing against forests, lakes or snow-covered landscapes. They offer visual access to a world imagined as the opposite of the one through which we encounter them. Morell’s own fascination developed through Tumblr and early social media before eventually becoming El Club de la cabaña, the newsletter she launched in 2021. The contradiction is central to her reading of the phenomenon. ‘We are using the internet, which is exactly what we want to escape from, as the tool to search for the offline,’she says.‘Looking at cabins on a screen is a way of disconnecting without leaving the sofa.’
For Morell, this digital obsession is less a contradiction to resolve than a symptom to examine. The imaginary cabin offers withdrawal even when no physical journey takes place. Scrolling past these images becomes a small act of projection: picturing another house also means picturing another routine, another relationship with work, technology, possessions or time. ‘It seems to me the most honest symptom of how tired we are in this hyper-technological and productivity-driven era,’she observes. The cabin’s contemporary relevance, then, may lie precisely in this distance between image and reality. We do not necessarily want the building itself; we want the conditions of life that we believe it contains.
Architecture nevertheless remains fundamental to that promise. By reducing the domestic environment to a constrained footprint, the cabin forces decisions that larger houses can postpone or conceal. What deserves space? Which elements are indispensable? How much comfort is enough? How should a dwelling meet the landscape rather than merely occupy it? From primitive shelters to modernist experiments, the cabin has repeatedly allowed architects to rehearse ideas at a scale where every material, opening and function becomes consequential. Morell’s history places Le Corbusier’s famously compact Cabanon alongside much older and more vernacular forms of refuge, suggesting that the impulse to reduce habitation is neither new nor attached to a single architectural language.
This is also where the cabin begins to look less nostalgic than experimental. Its limitations can become useful constraints for testing self-sufficiency, material economy and a more immediate relationship between building and environment. The apparent regression toward something primitive can therefore point forward. Morell describes the first refuges as the beginnings of collective human life and argues that our relationship with them has never disappeared: ‘Before we are born we already inhabit one, our mother’s body, and after coming into life we spend the rest of our time searching for places that give us that embrace again.’ For her, ‘Refugio’ is consequently not a book ‘about little wooden houses,’ but about the much older impulse to construct spaces of protection and belonging.
Yet the cabin’s promise of simplicity becomes more complicated once it enters the contemporary market. Since the pandemic, nature tourism and remote accommodation have expanded dramatically, turning isolation, silence and disconnection into desirable — and often expensive — commodities. Morell calls this process ‘cabañificación’, comparing it to the transformation of historic neighborhoods and traditional markets through gentrification. ‘Modern world has achieved something astonishing: taking the most basic things that exist — going into the countryside, being quiet, breathing — and turning them into an elite activity you have to pay for,’she says.‘We are paying for something that should be free: not being available.’
The cabin therefore occupies an uncomfortable position between resistance and consumption. It can test how little architecture we need while simultaneously becoming a highly designed symbol of privilege; it can promise proximity to nature while helping transform that landscape into a tourism product. Morell asks the question directly: ‘When we go to a cabin, are we really looking to disconnect, or are we simply replacing urban overload with a decorated version of the rural?’ Perhaps this contradiction is exactly what makes the cabin useful to contemporary architecture. Rather than proposing that everyone retreat into the woods, its renewed popularity exposes what many people increasingly miss in ordinary habitation: silence, autonomy, reduced consumption, contact with nature and the possibility of being temporarily unavailable. The real experiment may therefore not be how to build more cabins, but how to bring some of what they promise back into everyday life.
This article is part of designboom’s MODES OF HABITATION chapter, exploring how the spaces we inhabit can reshape the ways we live together. Discover more stories rethinking domesticity, shared living, and the many forms a home can take here.

‘Rhetoric differs’: How the UK’s relationship with Israel took a downturn

‘Rhetoric differs’: How the UK’s relationship with Israel took a downturn
The UK is planning to take new steps against illegal Israeli settlements as Palestinians suffer more violence.
The United Kingdom is expected to announce trade restrictions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, the latest sign, some analysts say, that UK-Israeli relations have taken another downturn.
Britain is one of Israel’s strongest allies in the West, but since the Labour Party came back to power after more than a decade in opposition, some of the government’s policies and rhetoric have shifted.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Burnham’s expected UK ban on Israeli settlement goods draws broad support
- list 2 of 4PA activists face ‘terror’ charges over Trump golf resort protest: Report
- list 3 of 4UK has billions in contracts with firms tied to illegal Israeli settlements
- list 4 of 4Yair Netanyahu, Israeli PM’s son, angers UK right over Falklands
On the one hand, the UK still maintains diplomatic ties and supplies F-35 parts through the global pool programme that Israel can access. On the other, it has suspended some arms-export licences and more regularly condemns the conduct of the Israeli military and settlers.
While campaigning ahead of the 2024 general election, then-Labour leader Keir Starmer said Israel “has the right” to withhold power and water from Gaza, during an interview with the UK’s LBC radio station. His comment upset many and he later backtracked, saying he believed Israel had a right to “self-defence”.
In May 2025, he wrote that he “strongly” opposed the “expansion of Israel’s military operations in Gaza”, in a joint letter with French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian premier Mark Carney.
Last week, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, appointed under new premier Andy Burnham, told the House of Commons that he would set out measures to prevent the UK’s involvement in projects such as the E1 settlement in the occupied Palestinian territory. It comes at a time of increasing violence towards Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
“Obviously, the rhetoric differs between them [UK prime ministers], but materially, the Israeli regime operates just as it did, irrespective of whether Andy Burnham or [former Conservative Prime Minister] Rishi Sunak was at the helm,” Zena Agha, a policy analyst with the British Palestinian Committee, told Al Jazeera.
“We’re seeing more of a continuation versus a rupture.”
In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other senior figures often mock Britain, where public opinion is increasingly turning against Israel’s oppression of Palestinians.
Last month, Netanyahu called the UK the “Islamic Republic of Britain”, according to translated comments published by Israeli media, as he criticised UK media coverage of Israel.
‘We will act’: Labour promises response to illegal settlements
While settlements and outposts are illegal under international law, the E1 project would create a continuous settlement corridor from the large settlement in Ma’ale Adumim and other illegal Israeli settlements to occupied East Jerusalem – effectively cutting the West Bank in half.
Condemning the settlement expansion project, Miliband said: “This government will not acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution.
“We will act, and I will set out a comprehensive set of measures in the coming weeks.”
Asked if he would ban trading goods and investment in both directions immediately, the foreign secretary said “a comprehensive reset of our approach on these issues” was needed because it is “high time”.
Agha said that while the move to place trade restrictions on settlements was in the right direction, it was the “bare minimum”, especially in the context of the Gaza genocide.
“These are measures we would expect any government to take in accordance with the international legal framework to which it subscribes. So it shouldn’t be celebrated in that regard. Nevertheless, it is something which the previous administration didn’t do, and so it should be welcomed,” Agha told Al Jazeera.
She explained that the main issue is how these sanctions would work in reality, or if they would end up as “lip service and rhetoric of condemnation as opposed to an actual meaningful impact on the way that the Israeli military occupation operates and profits off colonisation of Palestinian land and labour.”
So far, there are few details on how the government will impose these trade restrictions and on which goods more specifically.
But Burnham’s administration, since coming to power in July, is viewed as taking bolder steps on Israel.
Last month, the UK joined 21 countries and the European Commission in condemning the E1 project, calling on Israel to “retract these plans immediately and end its expansion of settlements in the West Bank.”
“Not only will they take us further from peace, but they further undermine Israel’s international standing,” the statement read.
Under Starmer, former Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper announced the UK, France and Canada imposed sanctions on six entities and one individual in June “involved in financing, enabling and carrying out settler violence in the occupied West Bank”, according to a government statement. Australia and New Zealand also imposed coordinated sanctions shortly before the UK announcement.
But those who sympathise with Palestinians believe Starmer did not go far enough.
“It’s clear that Palestine is a decisive issue for the British electorate,” said Agha. “I think Andy Burnham is perceptive to the shifts on the ground and how the British public feel.”
Shamiul Joarder of Friends of Al-Aqsa, a pro-Palestine group in Britain, called for a full trade ban with Israel.
“(Britain) needs to pull the mechanisms, pull the levers where they need to, in order to ensure that we are abiding by international law, that we are indeed standing up for the rights of the Palestinian people, and we’re speaking against oppression and apartheid.
“What comes from that is almost secondary. We need to do what is legally, ethically, and morally correct,” he said.
Israeli officials have condemned the sanctions plan, deepening a diplomatic dispute.
Israel Foreign Minister Gideon Saar warned last week that Israel would “act against Britain” if sanctions went ahead.
“If they act, I think they will be making a big mistake,” Saar told the Israeli news outlet Ynet.
Agha said the decision to impose sanctions on goods from illegal settlements is more of a diplomatic dispute than an economic issue.
While it is too early to know how Israel will react, she would not be surprised if Israel “bats this away” once it’s announced.
“I think if the UK or the EU had wanted to do this economically, they could have done it 50 years ago. Israel is not the only state which violates international law, and the international community has figured out how to sanction those states pretty effectively,” she said.
“So the question is not do they have the mechanism to do it, and can they figure out how to do it effectively?
“The question actually is: Do they have the diplomatic belief or ideological conviction in order to do it?”

Germany’s democracy rests on one party’s choice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:35:29 UTC
01:35:29 KST

Germany’s democracy rests on one party’s choice
The Ukraine conflict has exposed a German establishment more willing to defend its commitments to Kiev than to consider their cost to Germany. Saxony-Anhalt has delivered its verdict: an overwhelming win for the AfD (Alternative for Germany).
Now the parties it defeated may try to preserve their power through the establishment’s political firewall, while the BSW (Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance) must decide whether it will help restore political independence and relations with Russia or become the anti-Russian establishment’s last line of defense.
The war in Ukraine has posed a very basic question: whose interests should the German government serve? Kiev has its objectives. Germany has its own responsibilities, resources, and limits. The two cannot simply be declared identical. The AfD deserves credit for challenging this confusion. It has insisted that German interests are paramount and that Russia cannot be treated as a permanent enemy without serious costs to Europe. Its proposals include reducing financial and military assistance to pressure Kiev into peace negotiations, offering partial sanctions relief to encourage talks, and lifting sanctions fully once a peace agreement is reached. These are subjects for practical diplomacy. They recognize that Russia will remain a major European power whatever German ministers say about it, and that a durable settlement must be negotiated with Moscow. The AfD’s parliamentary proposal gives negotiations and the restoration of relations a place in policy that endless establishment declarations of “resolve” cannot supply.
The BSW’s opposition to arms deliveries to Ukraine and its demand for diplomacy give it substantial common ground with the AfD. This is one reason to welcome its presence in parliament. Thus, in Saxony-Anhalt, the immediate opportunity belongs to the AfD and BSW: together, they could turn their rejection of the present course into a governing coalition.
Supporters of military assistance argue that weapons strengthen Ukraine’s negotiating position. In reality, it merely prolongs the fighting and delays the inevitable defeat of Ukraine. Kiev cannot reasonably expect foreign taxpayers to shoulder indefinite financial burdens while facing economic hardship at home, especially without clear limits or a realistic plan for peace. Germany should also take Russia’s stated security concerns seriously enough to examine them in negotiations. Taking those concerns into account does not oblige Berlin to accept every Russian demand. It means recognizing that a settlement requires terms the parties will observe, rather than a declaration written for the satisfaction of only one side.
Saxony-Anhalt has now given that challenge political weight. The AfD won 43.8% and 39 seats. The CDU (Christian Democratic Union, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s party) received 17.2% and 15 seats. The BSW entered parliament with 5.3% and five seats. Together, the AfD and BSW would hold 44 of the 83 seats, exceeding the 42 needed for a majority. The CDU, SPD (Social Democratic Party), Greens, and Left have only 39 between them. An alternative majority excluding the AfD would therefore require the BSW. The reported seat allocation presents the BSW with a clear choice: negotiate a change of government with the election winner or help its opponents keep it out.
The AfD fell short of an absolute majority, but has still earned the strongest political claim to lead coalition negotiations, even though it has no automatic right to govern. The establishment’s firewall exists to prevent that claim from being tested through ordinary bargaining. Before demands are presented, before compromises are considered, before a common program is examined, the answer is already supposed to be no. The establishment then describes this refusal as a “defense of democracy.” It might more honestly describe it as a defense of its own exclusive right to supply the government.
No party is legally obliged to cooperate with the AfD. Equally, no party is entitled to escape criticism for refusing. The defenders of the firewall like to recite the first point as though it settles the second. It does not. Parties make choices, and voters are entitled to judge them. If the CDU can contemplate arrangements involving the Greens and the Left (both radical, socially destructive, and truly extremist), it must explain why differences in those directions can be managed while differences with the AfD prohibit even a discussion. Saying “we will not cooperate with the AfD because of the firewall” does not explain why cooperation would be wrong.
The CDU’s position is especially contemptuous of the conservative voters whose support it continues to solicit. During the campaign, their concerns are important. After the campaign, those concerns must wait while the party protects the firewall. What is such a party conserving? Increasingly, the answer appears to be its own place in government. Its failure to mount a serious challenge to the woke cultural agenda prevalent across German institutions makes it, in practice, a party of the left wearing a conservative label. Its clearest commitment is to keep the AfD out of power, even when that means preserving the policies its own voters want changed.
This is the practical meaning of the uniparty. The Greens and the Left openly advance the left-liberal agenda, the SPD supports it, and the CDU helps preserve it while calling itself conservative. Their campaign quarrels offer voters the illusion of choice without a real change of direction. When the AfD threatens to overturn that agenda, they unite to keep it out of government and call their cooperation “democratic responsibility.” Ministers can be replaced and coalition partners reshuffled, but the same political course survives. The firewall protects the established parties from the consequence elections should make possible: losing power to an opposition that intends to govern differently.
The firewall lets the established parties lose voters without losing power. Instead of defeating the AfD through better government and stronger arguments, they can gather enough coalition partners to keep it out. Parties rejected at the ballot box then present their survival in office as a “victory for democracy.” This gives force to the AfD’s accusation that opposition is welcome only while it cannot govern. Every additional party recruited to keep the AfD out makes the arrangement harder to disguise: the established parties are protecting their own hold on power.
The BSW should understand this danger better than most. It was founded to challenge policies that the established parties treated as beyond debate. It deserves sympathy for reopening arguments about war, economic interests, and the costs imposed on ordinary people. Its call for normal relations with Russia offers a necessary alternative to permanent confrontation, and its willingness to defend that position under political pressure deserves credit. However, if the BSW refuses to enter into a coalition with the AfD, it accepts an establishment veto over its own political freedom. It may still speak against the system, but the established parties will have allowed the BSW to criticize their policies while preventing it from forming a government that could change them.
The BSW’s refusal even to consider a coalition with the AfD amounts to surrender before negotiations begin. It gives up a possible majority without discovering which of its demands the AfD would accept. The BSW should put its policies on the table and negotiate hard. If agreement proves impossible, it can explain what prevented it. But refusing talks in advance means obeying the establishment’s command that the AfD must never govern. A party elected to oppose the old parties would then be helping keep them in office. Its voters would have supplied the seats; the establishment would collect the benefit.
Supporting individual AfD proposals is better than rejecting them on principle, but it can become an excuse for avoiding the real contest over power. The BSW could claim influence through occasional votes while leaving the government and its priorities in other hands. A government in Saxony-Anhalt cannot stop Germany’s weapons deliveries to Ukraine or negotiate peace with Russia; those decisions belong to the federal government. An AfD-BSW coalition would need an agreement on matters it could directly influence, such as schools, policing, and state spending. If it governed well, it would give voters concrete evidence that cooperation between the two parties can work. That would weaken the argument for keeping the AfD out of office. The established parties would then have to defend their record against an actual AfD-led government. The firewall spares them that comparison.

Interpol cancels Assad-era alert on 24,511 Syrian passports
Interpol has cancelled an Assad-era international alert that listed more than 24,500 Syrian passports as stolen, after Syrian authorities said the documents had in fact been legally issued to their owners.
Syria's interior ministry said the International Criminal Police Organisation had withdrawn the 2024 alert covering 24,511 passports following coordination between Interpol and its Damascus branch.
Colonel Abdul Rahim Jabara, director of international cooperation at the ministry, said the former regime of Bashar al-Assad had asked for the passports to be listed as stolen in November 2024, after opposition forces seized Aleppo.
According to Jabara, the Assad government claimed the passports had been stolen from an immigration and passports centre in the northern city.
The documents had instead been issued through official procedures and handed to their legitimate holders, he said.
The alert subsequently resulted in some Syrians being detained abroad and having their passports confiscated, disrupting their ability to travel.
The ministry did not specify how many passport holders had been affected, which countries had detained them, or whether all confiscated documents have since been returned.
It said the alert was cancelled after communication with Interpol established that it had been based on inaccurate information.
The Syrian government has not said why the Assad regime reported the passports as stolen despite their having allegedly already been issued, though it is widely believed to have been a means to punish Syrians living in opposition areas.
The request came during the dramatic collapse of Assad's control over northern Syria.
Opposition forces led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham launched a surprise offensive in late November 2024 and entered Aleppo on 29 November, forcing pro-regime forces from the city shortly afterwards.
The offensive rapidly spread south, culminating in the capture of Damascus and Assad's flight from Syria on 8 December.
Interpol maintains a global database containing information on travel and identity documents reported by member states as stolen, lost, revoked or invalid.
Police and border authorities around the world can check passports against the database at airports and border crossings, meaning a passport recorded as stolen can trigger its seizure and prevent its holder from travelling.
Only the country that issued a travel document can submit it to Interpol's stolen and lost travel documents database through its national authorities.
Interpol says the system contains around 138 million records and was searched billions of times by law enforcement agencies worldwide in 2023.
The cancellation therefore removes an international flag that Syrian authorities say had wrongly affected thousands of otherwise legitimate documents.
The episode also highlights the continuing administrative consequences of decisions taken during the final weeks of Assad's rule, almost two years after his government was overthrown.
Syria's new authorities have been working to restore the country's relations with international institutions and reassess administrative and security measures inherited from the former government.
Jabara said the cancellation followed sustained work by Syria's international cooperation department and Interpol office in Damascus.
The interior ministry said the process ultimately established that the original report concerning the passports was incorrect and based on inaccurate information.

BELGRADE — Serbia’s hopes of joining the EU were further threatened Monday by the funeral of a notorious army commander convicted of war crimes and the Srebrenica genocide.
Ratko Mladić’s send-off — attended by thousands of people in Belgrade on a balmy September afternoon — drew condemnation from Brussels, which is already at odds with Serbia over its democratic decline, its crackdown on press and judicial freedoms and failure to sanction Russia for the war against Ukraine.
“Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries,” Christian Wigand, a spokesperson for the European External Action Service, said in a statement Monday, while European Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a planned visit to Belgrade this week over what she called the “glorification” of Mladić.
Advertisement
The Serbian government officially said that it had no hand in organizing the funeral, yet Mladić’s body was flown on a government plane and members of the Serbian Armed Forces escorted the coffin to its final resting place while the military band played a funeral march. The patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Porfirije — a close ally of Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić — led the funeral mass, where Mladić’s coffin was draped in the Serbian flag.
Mladić, a general who spearheaded military campaigns across Bosnia and Croatia and was convicted of genocide for the killing of more than 8,000 people in early July 1995 in the eastern Bosnian town of Srebrenica, died in late August aged 84 while serving a life sentence at Scheveningen prison in the Netherlands.
Senior Serbian officials turned out for the service at the Church of Saint Luke on Monday, including Defense Minister Bratislav Gašić and Justice Minister Nenad Vujić. Danilo Vučić, the president’s son, was also in attendance, as was Russian Ambassador Aleksandr Botsan-Kharchenko.
Vučić, a populist nationalist who has been president of Serbia since 2017, himself skipped the funeral to meet with Shavkat Mirziyoyev, president of Uzbekistan, and made no reference to Mladić or the funeral in his public statements.
The president has often positioned himself as a pragmatic technocrat in Brussels, while Serbia continues an EU accession bid that started in 2014. But critics and human rights organizations have accused him of allowing — sometimes encouraging — nationalism to foment domestically.
Vujić, the justice minister, defended the right of Serbian citizens to pay their respects to Mladić on Friday, stressing that “the punishment ends with death.”
Advertisement
Mladić holds a particular cachet among nationalists who believe Serbs are entitled to more land and power in the Balkans, and not only those aligned with the ruling party. The young men in the funeral procession wore black T-shirts with Mladić’s face across the front, or flags printed with his smiling portrait tied around their shoulders. Others held signs reading “You did not die, General, you live in our hearts.”
Miloš Jovanović, leader of the New Democratic Party of Serbia, an opposition figure who often attacks Vučić from the right, also attended the funeral mass and said that Serbian citizens regard Mladić as “a symbol of freedom [for] Serb people.”
Since Mladić’s death, murals dedicated to him have appeared across Belgrade, while a public wake was organized on Saturday. The football clash Sunday between Serbia’s two largest clubs, Partizan and Crvena Zvezda, opened with a banner bearing his face and the message “Direction Potočari!” — a grim nod to Mladić’s seizure of the eastern Bosnian village where thousands of Bosniaks were summarily executed.
People gather for Mladić’s funeral procession in Belgrade on Sept. 7, 2026. | Oliver Bunic/AFP via Getty Images
Neighboring Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Kosovo have condemned the events. Bosnia — the country most affected by his ethnic cleansing campaigns — filed criminal complaints against figures who have promoted Mladić’s image since his death, an act punishable by law in the country.
For Serbians who have spent years watching Mladić rehabilitated by successive governments into a defender of the Serb people — his crimes watered down or denied in official retellings — the outrage from the EU has arrived far too late.
“It is rather irritating to read statements from foreign actors professing shock that an authoritarian, nationalist regime would instrumentalize the funeral of a convicted war criminal,” said Srdjan Majstorović, chairman of the board of the European Policy Center in Belgrade.

“All of this happened on their watch, so there is no room for surprise,” he continued, highlighting that Brussels has presented Vučić as “essential to the country’s progress.”
Days before the funeral, 29 EU lawmakers from five political groups penned a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and to Kos demanding that Brussels freeze all pre-accession payments to Serbia, citing reports that the country had deployed spyware against student leaders, activists and opposition politicians.
The spyware allegations land after nearly two years of student-led protests against Vučić’s government, which began after the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad in November 2024 killed 16 people and became the largest sustained challenge to his rule.
Serbia has not opened a new negotiating chapter with the EU since December 2021, blocked by eight member countries over its rule-of-law record and its refusal to sanction Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Despite launching their bids much later, Ukraine and Moldova rank ahead of Serbia in their progress, and neighboring Montenegro is widely deemed a front-runner to join the bloc.

The drone war is becoming a race to adapt, rather than perfect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:31:13 UTC
01:31:13 KST

The drone war is becoming a race to adapt, rather than perfect
A soldier launches an RQ-35 Heidrun drone used for reconnaissance and artillery fire correction in the Zaporizhzhia direction in Ukraine, on Feb. 22, 2026. (Dmytro Smolienko / Ukrinform / NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Robert Brull
CEO of FibreCoat
You don't need to have followed the Ukraine war closely to recognize the central role that drones have played in the conflict.
As I write, the Russian e-commerce giant Ozon is reeling following a third day of long-range drone strikes— an indication not only of the significance of drones, but also of how the drone war has evolved.
At the start of the war, such an attack was impossible; now, as of summer 2026, drones shape almost every act as part of wider systems. But readers of this publication will know that.
What relatively few onlookers outside of Ukraine recognize is the way in which every drone innovation on one side of the conflict has prompted innovation on the other. Ukrainian recon drones led Russia to pursue jamming and short-range air defense innovation; Russian improvements in electronic warfare and air cover led to the use of expendable quadcopters by Ukraine.
On and on in this vein the war has proceeded, all the way to where we are now, where drones are mass-produced, often by 3D printers for expediency, and long-range drones are routinely flying deep into enemy territory to target oil refineries, logistics hubs, and ostensibly civilian businesses seen to be supporting the Russian war effort.
Now Russia is responding with increasingly advanced air defense systems and spoofing technology. And that has brought into focus new and increasingly sophisticated forms of technology that can protect enough long-range drones (protecting all of them is next to impossible) that some are able to penetrate those Russian defenses and carry out their missions.
Chief among these, perhaps, is chaff, a relatively old technology that has recently been brought into the 21st century.
Used on military aircraft and warships since World War II, chaff is in effect a radar countermeasure typically made of tiny aluminum-coated glass fibers.
When dispensed, it forms a large, reflective cloud or fog in which each individual glass fiber reflects a radio frequency.
These resonate, confusing enemy radar, blinding ground systems, spamming false signals, and tricking radar-guided missiles into going for the wrong target. They can create massive uncertainty across even sophisticated radar systems and make decision-making difficult. They also impose a financial cost: enemies waste ammunition aiming at the wrong target.
But technology itself is not the most important thing. Innovation, at least by itself, is not the most important thing, either. The decisive factor in Ukraine, and it will be the decisive factor in all modern conflicts, is the ability to innovate at speed.
Warfare has become a competition to learn and apply what you learn fastest. Ukraine builds a new drone; Russia replies with drone countermeasures; Ukraine tweaks the drone to overcome those countermeasures; Russia tweaks its counter-countermeasures. A system that takes ten years to develop risks becoming useless before it's even out in the field.
Why does this matter? Because wider Europe is rearming. And there's an important lesson here. The present and the future of war are being decided not by the large, established contractors who produce a small number of highly expensive platforms able to last decades, but by smaller, more adaptable, fast-moving companies.
Indeed, the use of 3D printers in Ukraine points very clearly to what matters: pragmatism, flexibility, mobility, modularity, cost-efficiency, and, of course, efficacy.
In Ukraine, technology is designed, built, sent into the field, and used; and operators on the front line then feed back to the manufacturers, who redesign the technology, rebuild it, and send it into the field to be used.
It's a virtuous, if lethal, cycle of innovation, one in which iteration is continuous and "good enough for now" is the aim of the game. You could say that this is the ultimate free market of ideas, where the most useful solutions are adopted, and those that don't are not. The Ukrainians are picking and choosing the best products for their goals in a constantly evolving marketplace.
My view is that Europe has an opportunity to support its friends in Ukraine while testing out new technologies.
It could replicate the Ukrainian model of innovation, bolster Ukraine's armed forces, and use its battlefield as a live innovation engine: testing its systems, allowing them to break, then improving them at speed.
Indeed, assuming there was Ukrainian approval, Europe should consider allocating a portion of its budget towards battlefield testing.
At the very least, we should be more humble in how we think about modern warfare and seek to learn the many lessons that have been learned so painfully by Ukraine in its attempt to hold off their Russian aggressors.
First among these is that the aim of the game is to adapt, not perfect: to iterate quickly rather than build complex systems slowly. New chaff innovations may be the latest chapter in this technological contest. But it won't certainly be the last.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

Satellite images show Russian Ka-52 and Mi-28 helicopters destroyed in Sochi drone attack

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:30:05 UTC
01:30:05 KST

Satellite images published Sept. 6 indicate that a Ukrainian attack on Sochi and the nearby federal territory of Sirius that occurred overnight on Sept. 4 destroyed two Russian military helicopters — a Ka-52 and a Mi-28 — at a parking area at Sochi airport, while one Mi-8 was damaged.
The assessment was reported by the Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) channels Absoliutno Nadiine Dzherelo (lit. “Absolutely Reliable Source”) and Dnipro OSINT ⟨ Harbuz ⟩, which published the satellite imagery. The Russian pro-war Telegram channel Voenny Osvedomitel (lit. “Military Informant”) also agreed with the assessment that two helicopters had been lost.
According to the same OSINT sources, the damage from the raid extended beyond the helicopters. Absoliutno Nadiine Dzherelo reported that two RVS-2000 storage tanks were destroyed at an oil depot near Sochi airport, while four RVS-1000 tanks were damaged (the RVS designations refer to standard Russian vertical steel storage tanks, with the number indicating their approximate capacity in cubic meters).
The channel also published an image of a Russian radar post in the city of Adler and said there had been at least two hits on the radome — the protective radio-transparent dome covering the station.
Another satellite image published by the same channel showed an air defense position in Sirius. The analysts said two launchers and a Pantsir surface-to-air missile and gun system of an unidentified variant had been destroyed there.
The Insider had previously detected a thermal anomaly in the same area — near the Psou River — and reported that an air defense position was located there.
On the night of the attack, Ukrainian drone and missile manufacturer Fire Point said its FP-1 drones had struck several targets in Sochi, including a Lukoil oil depot, fuel infrastructure near Adler airport, and a position belonging to an S-400 air defense system.
Some of the consequences of the raid were already confirmed on Sept. 4. That day, the Krasnodar Region’s operational headquarters said a fire had broken out after drone attacks on Sochi and Sirius. Officials reported no casualties, though windows were shattered in several homes and other buildings.
The Insider then analyzed data from NASA FIRMS and found heat signatures near the airport’s fuel complex and near the aforementioned air defense position by the Psou River in Sirius. Thermal anomalies can indicate fires, explosions, or other intense heat sources, but do not by themselves establish the cause of the heat signature.
Sochi Mayor Andrei Proshunin later warned residents that publishing photographs or video showing the aftermath of the attack was prohibited.
Russia’s Defense Ministry, meanwhile, said 490 Ukrainian drones had been shot down over several Russian regions beginning on the evening of Sept. 3, including over the Krasnodar Region. The ministry did not say how many drones had attacked the Sochi and Sirius area.
Russian authorities did not report any losses of military equipment or damage to the radar post, nor to the airport oil depot or the air defense position.

Syria detains three generals amid campaign against Assad-era figures
Syrian security forces are continuing a campaign of arrests against people accused of committing crimes during the rule of the former Assad regime, detaining at least three Assad-era generals.
Syrian authorities on Monday said they had arrested a former general accused of involvement in the bloody repression of protests in 2011 that sparked the country's civil war.
In a statement, security forces said they "arrested former Major General Mohammed Ali Durgham, a prominent officer in the military establishment during the era of the former regime" of Bashar al-Assad, who was ousted in 2024.
They accused him of "issuing direct orders to his units to fire on unarmed demonstrators in the Damascus countryside" after anti-Assad protests had erupted in 2011.
Durgham was a field commander in the army's feared Fourth Division, commanded by Assad's brother Maher al-Assad, between 2009 and 2013.
Human Rights Watch in 2011 quoted a Syrian army defector who said that Durgham was one of the generals who "ordered the troops to shoot at protesters when his unit was deployed to areas in and just outside of Damascus".
He has been under European Union sanctions since 2012.
In Aleppo province, the Internal Security Forces announced the arrest of former Air Force Brigadier General Hamada Ali Murad.
The security authorities said Murad was still being interrogated, with the aim of determining the nature of his activities in previous years.
According to information circulating about his career, Murad is originally from the town of Nubl – a stronghold of the former regime - in northern Aleppo province. 
He graduated from the Air Force Academy, specialising as a helicopter pilot. He previously served with the 63rd Helicopter Air Brigade at Taftanaz Air Base in Idlib province before transferring to the Air Force Academy as an instructor and later to the Air Institute.
Following the Syrian uprising in 2011, he is believed to have been assigned to the notorious Air Force Intelligence branch in Aleppo as a liaison officer. There, he is accused of coordinating air operations and helping to identify areas for targeting.
The Assad regime notoriously used indiscriminate barrel bombs to attack opposition-held towns and cities, killing tens of thousands of civilians. He later headed the Air Training Institute in Aleppo. 
Murad’s arrest comes as part of a broader security campaign in Aleppo province.
In Latakia province, the Internal Security Forces announced on Saturday the arrest of Major General Jalal Kamel Saqr, who previously served as commander of the 18th Infantry Brigade in the former regime’s forces. 
The authorities said preliminary investigations indicated that he was involved in war crimes and arbitrary detention of civilians during the years of the Syrian uprising.
They also said he participated in military operations targeting areas in Damascus and Eastern Ghouta, as well as overseeing detention campaigns in Daraa province in the south of the country.
Over 500,000 people were killed in the Syrian conflict, which began after the Assad regime’s brutal suppression of anti-government protests in 2011 and is generally considered to have ended with the overthrow of the Assad regime in December 2024.
Most of the casualties were as a result of the regime's bombardment of civilian areas.

Nicaragua challenges German arms exports to Israel at ICJ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:26:00 UTC
01:26:00 KST

Nicaragua challenges German arms exports to Israel at ICJ
September 7, 2026
Germany on Monday asked the International Court of Justice (ICJ) to dismiss a case brought by Nicaragua, accusing Berlin of violating the 1948 Genocide Convention by supplying arms to Israel amid its war with Hamas in Gaza.
If the ICJ, otherwise known as the World Court, decided to hear the case, the process would likely take years and be contingent on the findings from separate Gaza-related cases in The Hague.
But Germany is arguing it shouldn't even go that far, saying that Nicaragua did not follow proper processes and that the dispute does not fall in the international court's jurisdiction.
Nicaragua, on the other hand, argues that the case should be heard because it and Germany are both signatories to the Genocide Convention — despite neither side being directly involved in Israel and Hamas' war in Gaza and although the ICJ hearing on whether Israel committed genocidal acts in Gaza could take years.
What is the case about?
Nicaragua accuses Germany of aiding and abetting genocide in Gaza by selling weapons to Israel, some of which it says have been used in Gaza.
An initial bid for an emergency injunction ordering a halt to exports failed in 2024 at the height of the war in Gaza, but Germany also failed in its bid to have the case summarily and permanently dismissed at the earliest opportunity.
The German government suspended weapons exports to Israel for around three months in 2025 as the conflict continued and casualty figures rose. But it has since restarted them amid the truce struck late last year that largely stopped the fighting, without ending Israeli strikes entirely.
Germany walks a fine historical and political line in the case.
On the one hand, the 1948 Genocide Convention was born in very large part from the lessons of the Holocaust and the spirit of "never again" after World War II. But to the same token, Germany has always sought to maintain close and cooperative ties with Israel, a state formed in very large part as a consequence of its mass extermination of Jews in Europe. It considers Israeli security part of its own raison d'etre as a modern democratic state.
Israel's war in Gaza was launched against Hamas after Hamas carried out the October 7, 2023 terror attacks on Israel. October 7 was the single deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. Hamas is a Palestinian Islamist group based in the Gaza Strip.
What is Germany arguing?
Germany is arguing both that the case should be dismissed on procedural grounds, and that Nicaragua's allegation of aiding and abetting genocide is unsubstantiated.
Although Germany, Nicaragua and Israel are all signatories to the Genocide Convention, a case like this where neither side is a direct party to a conflict is unusual. Its represenatives told the court that Nicaragua had not taken the proper steps before filing the legal challenge and arguing much of the case falls out of the ICJ's jurisdiction.
"Germany respectfully requests the court to reject Nicaragua's claims," Julia Monar, legal adviser to the German Foreign Ministry, told the judges.
"All German weapons exports to Israel and other countries are subject to strict review procedures that are more stringent than international regulations," Monar also told the court, a reference to Germany's intentionally restrictive weapons export policies adopted after World War II.
In mid-May this year, Germany's Bundestag parliament published information saying that between November 2025 — shortly after the truce was brokered — and March this year, exports worth around €167 million (roughly $194 million) were approved.
What's likely to happen next?
Nicaragua's case is based on the South African lawsuit at the ICJ accusing Israel of genocidal acts in Gaza.
In a preliminary hearing — the findings of which Israel rejected — the court found it plausible that Israel could have committed genocidal acts in Gaza and called for a full hearing. That process will take years, with court sessions not expected until 2029.
A full hearing in Nicaragua's case against Germany, should the ICJ choose to pursue one, could well rely on a resolution in the broader genocide allegations against Israel.
More immediately, Nicaragua is expected to lay out its arguments in The Hague on Tuesday.
A decision on Germany's bid to shelve the case entirely is tentatively expected some time this year.
The ICJ is the top UN court dealing with disputes between states and alleged violations of various international treaties. Its rulings are final and cannot be appealed.

Russia and North Korea deepen relations with symbolic road bridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:22:08 UTC
01:22:08 KST

Russia and North Korea deepen relations with symbolic road bridge
Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have grown extensively amid Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
The first road bridge connecting Russia and North Korea has been opened, forging a symbolic link between the pair.
The first flag-adorned trucks made their way across the one-kilometre (0.6-mile) two-lane bridge spanning the Tumen River on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Why is Chinese President Xi Jinping visiting North Korea now?
- list 2 of 4‘Sealed in blood’: Where does the China-North Korea alliance stand today?
- list 3 of 4Western allies warn North Korean IT workers funding nuclear arsenal
- list 4 of 4‘Tit for tat’: Why is Trump cosying up to North Korea’s Kim Jong Un again?
The two countries, which previously were only connected by air and rail routes, announced that the link marks an important milestone in their relations, which have grown considerably stronger since Russia launched its war on Ukraine.
Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korea’s Premier Pak Thae-song tuned in by video link to address workers and government officials from both countries.
The Russian official said that up to 300 vehicles would be able to cross every day and that the bridge would be linked to Russia’s federal road network.
“I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” said Mishustin.
Trucks would begin to use the bridge immediately to transport cargo, the Russian government said. At the end of this year, the bridge would be fully operational and could be used for passenger traffic, too.
Construction of the new bridge, which had been under discussion for years, began in April last year after being agreed during a visit by Russia’s President Vladimir Putin to North Korea in 2024.
There are already direct air and rail links between Moscow and Pyongyang, but until Monday there had not been a proper road link.
The project sits close to the “Friendship Bridge” – a rail link that was commissioned in 1959 after the Korean War and for decades was the sole border crossing point.
Symbolically, the new bridge is named after Yakov Novichenko, a Red Army soldier who Pyongyang credits with protecting the life of North Korea’s first leader Kim Il Sung in 1946 by intercepting a grenade thrown at him.
The opening of the link marks the deepening of relations between Moscow and Pyongyang, with cooperation having accelerated since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
That conflict has alienated Moscow from much of the Western world, a diplomatic status that North Korea has endured for years.
Pyongyang sent thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help repel a 2024 Ukrainian incursion there.
Mishustin alluded to that in his speech on Monday, referring to “the Korean heroes who, only recently, fought shoulder to shoulder with our soldiers and defended Russian soil”.
The bridge is not merely an engineering project, but “a new symbol of friendship”, the Russian prime minister added, calling the opening of the link “a genuinely historic event”.
Pak Thae-song said that the bridge will further cement the two countries’ cooperation “which fulfils the hopes and aspirations of the peoples of both countries as they seek shared development and prosperity”, according to Russia’s TASS news agency.

China Focus: Chinese Arctic expedition finds anti-freeze fish beneath high-latitude ice
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
00:17:45 CST
01:17:45 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Chinese researchers have captured five juvenile polar cod in a densely ice-covered area in the high Arctic, a discovery that may deepen scientists' understanding of the species and its habitat's ecosystem.
The young fish, aged one to two years, were caught in the northern Canada Basin above 86 degrees north latitude during a long-term ice station survey by members of China's 16th Arctic Ocean expedition aboard the icebreaker Xuelong 2.
An unmanned ecological observation system deployed at the same station captured video footage of such fish moving beneath the ice.
The species is built for life under the ice, where water temperatures can fall to minus 2 degrees Celsius.
Special antifreeze proteins keep the fish's body from freezing, allowing them to live beneath the ice and feed on zooplankton, or tiny animals, there, said Kim Vane, an onboard fish biologist from the Alfred Wegener Institute in Germany.
"An unexpected harvest," said Zhang Jichang, an expedition member from the Yellow Sea Fisheries Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Fishery Sciences, who has taken part in multiple Arctic expeditions.
During China's 13th Arctic Ocean expedition in 2023, researchers caught a single juvenile polar cod in an ice hole and treated it as a chance occurrence. "The concentrated discovery this time shows that a certain number of juvenile polar cod live beneath the ice in these high-latitude waters," Zhang said.
Chinese scientists had previously known the species inhabited the icy surface waters of the Arctic Ocean mainly through published literature, he said, and physical specimens had been hard to obtain.
Results from China's successive Arctic surveys indicate that juvenile polar cod live mainly beneath the sea ice of the central Arctic Ocean, while adults stay near the seabed over the continental shelf and slope.
The Canada Basin has long been considered mostly "barren," with low productivity, and repeated trawl surveys in its central and southern waters on this voyage failed to catch any fish at all.
Finding so many juvenile polar cod at a single ice station in the basin's far north was surprising, said Lan Musheng, assistant to the expedition's chief scientist, adding that the northern high-latitude ice zone could become an important area sustaining the development of polar cod populations.
"These polar cod are the native fish of the central Arctic Ocean, they belong here," said Vane.
A study recently published by Vane and her colleagues showed that, on the basis of fish ear stones, or otoliths, collected from the sea floor of the Lomonosov Ridge not far from where the expedition caught these fish, that polar cod have been present in the central Arctic Ocean for at least 48,000 years.
The new observations also help explain why the fish are present in the area. On the day of the catch, Zhang and Vane dissected one specimen on site and found its stomach strikingly full. A vertical plankton tow at the same station brought up dense swarms of zooplankton and abundant phytoplankton, or small algae.
"We can preliminarily conclude that some high-latitude waters hold enough prey organisms for juvenile polar cod to feed on," said Wang Honggen, an expedition member from the Institute of Oceanology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
The discovery is the latest marker of China's advancing Arctic research, which began with the icebreaker Xuelong's first Arctic expedition in 1999 and the opening of Yellow River Station in Norway's Ny-Alesund in 2004. In 2019, Xuelong 2 -- China's first domestically built polar research icebreaker -- entered service. Four years later, it carried researchers on China's 13th Arctic Ocean expedition to the vicinity of the North Pole, the first comprehensive survey there by a Chinese research vessel.
The current expedition left port in early July and has since carried out comprehensive surveys in the central Arctic Ocean, monitoring the atmosphere, the melting ice and the ecosystem beneath it.
The stakes reach beyond one species. Polar cod are considered a keystone of the ice-associated Arctic marine food web -- one of the few fish linking zooplankton to other fish, seabirds and marine mammals.
The discovery also feeds into Arctic governance. China is one of the 10 parties to the Agreement to Prevent Unregulated High Seas Fisheries in the Central Arctic Ocean, which was signed in 2018 and imposes an initial 16-year ban on commercial fishing in the area while the parties carry out a joint program of scientific research and monitoring.
Yang Lei, deputy leader of the expedition, said the discovery will provide a scientific basis for China's continued participation in the joint research and monitoring program under the agreement, helping expand and deepen international understanding of Arctic Ocean fish stocks and improve Arctic Ocean governance.
"Where do the juvenile fish come from? How do they connect with the adult populations? And what are their migration routes?" Zhang said, "If we can clarify these questions, it will be of great scientific significance for understanding the life history and population status of polar cod in the future." ■

BERLIN, September 7. /TASS/. Tino Chrupalla, co-chairman of the Alternative for Germany (AfD), has said that voter fatigue with Germany’s continued support for Ukraine was among the factors behind his party’s landslide victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliamentary elections.
"Federal policy issues significantly influenced the outcome. This was evident from the issues that proved decisive for voters, including internal security, as well as war and peace – and this is also an important message," Chrupalla told a news conference in Berlin.
"People are simply tired of this. They see how billions in tax revenues are transferred to Ukraine every day, effectively sending money abroad instead of spending it on our own people," he emphasized.
According to the AfD leader, this policy has contributed to "the current economic situation in the country."
State parliamentary elections were held in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. According to preliminary official results, the AfD won a landslide victory with 43.8% of the vote - its strongest result in any German region since the party’s founding and nearly twice its showing in the previous state election five years ago.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) finished second, receiving 17.2% of the vote - less than half of its 2021 result and its worst-ever performance in Saxony-Anhalt. The Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD) came third with 9.3%, followed by the Greens with 8.9% and the Left Party with 8.6%. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), formerly known as the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance for Reason and Justice, also cleared the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament, winning 5.3%.
Experts have described the CDU’s poor showing as a personal setback for Merz and a sign of voter dissatisfaction with his government’s policies, including its approach to Russia.

====================================================================================================

How the far-right AfD is causing a German political earthquake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
16:13:57 UTC
01:13:57 KST

Germany's AfD won a state election in a landslide, sounding an alarm for centrist politics
Berlin — Sunday's election results did not give Germany's controversial AfD party automatic control of the state of Saxony-Anhalt, but what the far-right party achieved wasn't just an election victory. It was a political landslide.
Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% of the vote in the legislative election, and while that may not be enough to form the next state government, it was the best result the party has achieved in any contest in its 13-year history.
Compared to the last state election in 2021, it more than doubled its share of the votes.
The result was even more dramatic for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union. The CDU garnered only 17.2% of the votes in Saxony-Anhalt — plummeting from the 37.1% achieved in the last state election. The CDU, which has led every Saxony-Anhalt state government since 2002, now trails the AfD by more than 26 percentage points.
The results of the election show how fundamentally Germany's political system is changing. The AfD is no longer a fringe, anti-European Union protest party.
Does the AfD still have a path to power in Saxony-Anhalt?
In Germany, winning an election does not automatically mean a party gets to run the government — whether it's a state or the nation.
If the AfD had won just another percentage point or two of the vote on Sunday, it may well have garnered the absolute majority required in the state legislature to name the state's next leader and administration.
Having not met that threshold, AfD Saxony-Anhalt still faces significant hurdles to become the state's governing party — but it isn't out of contention yet.
Following the election, the AfD will hold 39 of the 83 seats in the new state parliament. So, the AfD's leading candidate in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, is three seats short of the 42-seat absolute majority needed to form a new, all-AfD administration.
And that's where complicated German coalition arithmetic comes into play. The other parties that won a decent share of the votes on Sunday, including the CDU, have all flatly rejected joining a coalition government with the AfD.
That collective refusal — a political line of demarcation backed by virtually all parties explicitly to keep a party seen as extremist out of power — is known in Germany as a "firewall."
The firewall has held for decades, but now a left-wing populist party could be poised to poke a hole in it in Saxony-Anhalt.
The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) received 5.3% of the vote on Sunday, giving it five seats in the state legislature. It has also ruled out joining a formal coalition with the AfD. One of its two lead candidates said Monday, however, that the BSW could abstain in a possible third round of voting to elect the state's minister-president, roughly equivalent to a U.S. governor.
In that round, only a simple majority of votes is required to elect the individual to the post, and abstentions are not counted. A BSW abstention alone would not automatically put the AfD's Siegmund into the top job. While the AfD holds 39 seats, the other four parties that took a significant share of the votes, the CDU, SPD, Greens and Left, together also hold 39.
If all four of those parties remain united to maintain the firewall against the AfD, and all five BSW lawmakers abstain from the vote, the result would be a tie, and the AfD would still not be able to form a government.
But a single party defection or other deviation could be decisive, and the AfD's Siegmund has said he'll speak with other parliamentary groups and individual lawmakers, likely hoping to convince just one member to defect from their own party's position behind the firewall.
This is where the AfD's new power lies: Even if it does not form a government, its election result is already forcing other parties to at least consider political arrangements that have long been unimaginable in Germany.
The collapse of Germany's centrist power base
In the 2025 federal election, the AfD won more than 20% of the vote.
This weekend in Saxony-Anhalt, it achieved its best result in a state election with almost 44%, and that came two years after it also finished first in neighboring Thuringia state's legislative election, taking 32.8% of the vote.
That clear trajectory, for the CDU, is a snowballing political crisis.
The Christian Democrats have ruled out cooperation with the AfD for years. However, following the debacle in Saxony-Anhalt, pressure to show some flexibility in that strategy is mounting.
Before the election, Sepp Müller, deputy chairman of the CDU's parliamentary group, had argued that in the event of a clear AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt, the party should be given a mandate to form a government. Other Union politicians, however, have warned against abandoning the firewall, even a little bit.
Union parliamentary group leader Thorsten Frei said unequivocally on election night: "We do not talk to right-wing extremists."
So the CDU, which has led Germany's national government for 52 of its 77 post-World War II years, is in a dilemma. To keep the AfD out of power, it may need to partner with smaller parties far to the left, including the Left Party, with which the CDU has also ruled out a formal coalition. If, on the other hand, it opens itself up to working with the AfD, it would tear down one of the most important political boundaries in Germany.
And the CDU's crisis has now reached Berlin.
Chancellor Merz had promised to push back against the AfD politically. The party achieving its best result ever on Sunday, while Merz's own CDU sinks to its lowest representation ever in Saxony-Anhalt, has brought a lot of pressure on the national leader.
The first internal call for Merz's resignation came from Tim Brand, a board member of the CDU's youth organization in the state of Brandenburg, who called on him to step down both as chancellor and CDU chairman. The CDU youth union in Saxony-Anhalt has separately demanded the resignation of the party's state leadership.
AfD's unlikely leader sets sights on next federal election
One of the people who stands to benefit most from the AfD's gaining momentum after the Saxony-Anhalt election is Alice Weidel, co-chair of the AfD and the party's candidate to stand as Germany's next chancellor in the 2029 federal election.
Weidel doesn't fit what many may think of as the traditional image of her party. She holds a Ph.D. in economics and worked for Goldman Sachs. She is a lesbian who lives openly with her Swiss partner, a woman of Sri Lankan descent, and their two sons.
While she spends part of her time in Einsiedeln, Switzerland, Weidel says she's a registered resident in Germany and pays her taxes in the country.
All of those factors appear to contrast with elements of her party's platform: The AfD promotes a traditional view of the family, opposes some policies aimed at ensuring equal treatment of LGBTQ people, and has made drastic limits on immigration a key policy point.
The focus on immigration, in a country where the centrist government's decision to welcome hundreds of thousands of Syrian refugees a decade ago has fueled ongoing anger among many voters, has been a cornerstone of the AfD's success.
In Saxony-Anhalt, among other things, the party is calling for a "deportation and remigration campaign" and restrictions on the display of LGBTQ symbols in schools.
But Weidel seems to have made the contradictions between her personal life and her party's platform a political advantage rather than an obstacle, at least so far.
On Monday, she hailed the vote in Saxony-Anhalt as a "dream result" and made it clear her sights are now set on Berlin. In the next federal election, she aims to bring the AfD's share of the national vote to at least 40%, which would force Germany to grapple with a question that has long seemed theoretical: What happens if the firewall holds, but the party behind it keeps growing stronger?
At what point, in other words, might constitutionally legal political jockeying become fundamentally undemocratic?
