Latvian businesses to strengthen cooperation with german technology and industry leaders in Berlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:05:03 UTC
00:05:03 KST

From 14 to 17 September, a delegation of Latvian businesses will visit Berlin on a trade mission organised by the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), where they will meet German companies, investors, innovation centres and research organisations. Minister of Economics Viktors Valainis will join the business delegation’s programme on 16 and 17 September. The visit will focus on information and communication technologies, financial technologies, life sciences, as well as defence and dual-use technologies. The aim of the visit is to strengthen economic cooperation between Latvia and Germany, foster new business contacts and expand opportunities for Latvian companies in the German market.
Germany is Latvia’s second-largest foreign trade partner. Latvia’s trade in goods and services with Germany reached €5.5 billion in 2025, while Latvian exports amounted to €2.09 billion, increasing by 7% year-on-year. The positive trend has continued this year. In the first half of 2026, Latvian goods exports to Germany increased by 10% to €709.6 million. Germany is also Latvia’s largest market for services exports: in 2025, services exports reached €779 million, while in the first quarter of 2026 they increased by a further 23%.
“Over the past few years, we have worked purposefully to open up broader opportunities for Latvian companies in the German market, and this work is already delivering concrete results. Latvian companies are increasingly strengthening their presence in Germany — Olpha and several other Latvian companies have established subsidiaries in Germany, while the German market accounts for approximately 30% of demand for Latvian investment platforms. At the same time, German company SCHWENK is planning an investment project worth more than €500 million in Latvia to develop climate-neutral cement production in Brocēni. Our ambition must now be even greater — to integrate Latvian companies into European industrial supply chains, develop joint products and technologies, and attract new investment. There is a strong foundation for this: in the first half of 2026, Latvian goods exports to Germany increased by 10%, while services exports grew by 23% in the first quarter. We must use this growth to strengthen the position of Latvian companies in high value-added industries,” said Minister of Economics Viktors Valainis.
Programme Tailored to the Development Goals of Latvian Companies
Separate programmes have been developed for companies operating in information technology, defence and dual-use technologies, financial technology and life sciences. These will include meetings with potential clients, cooperation partners and investors. The visit will also feature visits to German companies, innovation centres and research institutions.
Information technology companies will participate in the Big Bang AI Festival and the sixth German-Baltic Digital Summit, as well as visit technology companies, including the Tesla factory in Berlin-Brandenburg and technology company HEIDELBERG. Defence and dual-use technology companies will discuss cooperation opportunities in unmanned and counter-drone technologies, robotics and defence supply chains. They will also visit the Marienpark Berlin resilience technology centre and German defence technology company Andres Industries AG.
Representatives of the financial technology sector will meet members of Berlin’s local FinTech ecosystem to discuss European Union rules for crypto-asset service providers under MiCA, access to the German market and investment opportunities. Berlin is one of Europe’s leading FinTech hubs, offering Latvian companies opportunities to establish new contacts with investors, banks and technology partners.
Life sciences representatives will have the opportunity to visit Campus Berlin-Buch, a major life sciences hub in Berlin, and BIOTRONIK SE & Co. KG, one of the leading medical technology companies.
German businesses will also have an opportunity to learn about the opportunities offered by Latvian companies, with particular attention paid to the development of data centres in Latvia — an area with significant growth and investment potential.
As part of the visit, a memorandum of understanding is planned to be signed between LIAA, the German-Baltic Chamber of Commerce in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania (AHK Baltikum), and the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DIHK). The agreement will enable Latvian businesses to obtain information about market opportunities in third countries where LIAA does not have representative offices under conditions equivalent to those available to German companies.
“The German market is large, technologically advanced and supported by an extensive international business network. It is therefore important for Latvian companies not only to find partners in Germany, but also to use the opportunities offered by this network in other markets. The planned trilateral memorandum of understanding between LIAA, the German-Baltic Chamber of Commerce and the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry will give Latvian companies access to information and contacts regarding business opportunities in third countries where Latvia does not have its own representation. This will broaden the export opportunities of Latvian companies and expand their network of international partners,” said LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere.

War criminal Mladic buried with military honors in Belgrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:03:00 UTC
00:03:00 KST

War criminal Mladic buried with military honors in Belgrade
September 7, 2026
Several thousand people lined the streets of Belgrade on Monday to follow the funeral service and burial of former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic.
Earlier in the day, Serbian Patriarch Porfirije personally officiated at the funeral service for the former general, who died while serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide in Srebrenica and other war crimes committed during the violent breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.
In accordance with his wishes, Mladic was laid to rest at Topcider Cemetery beside his daughter, who died by suicide in 1994.
Informer TV, a staunchly pro-government broadcaster, carried live coverage of what it described as a "magnificent farewell," without mentioning the roughly 8,000 Bosniak civilians and prisoners massacred by Mladic's Bosnian Serb forces in Srebrenica in July 1995.
President Vucic not in attendance
President Aleksandar Vucic did not attend the funeral, citing a previously scheduled visit by his counterpart from Uzbekistan.
Observers say that the president has tried to chart a middle course on the issue of Mladic's funeral.
Mladic was not buried with state honors, but with military honors, with Vucic insisting that the state was merely respecting the wishes of the family and ensuring a dignified burial.
"Were we supposed to forbid people from attending, forbid the funeral itself and create dog cemeteries?" he said in response to criticism from the EU.
The phrase "dog cemeteries" refers in Serbia to the unmarked graves of so-called "enemies of the people" who were executed by Yugoslav partisans during and immediately after World War II.
Vucic was equally dismissive of the decision by EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos to cancel a planned visit to Belgrade, calling her reaction "stupid." He has brushed aside other criticism of the public glorification of Mladic in much the same way.
An EU spokesman said in a statement that "Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries."
Politically tricky time for Vucic
For Vucic, who has long sought to balance Serbia between the European Union and Russia, the situation is politically delicate.
He is expected to call a snap parliamentary election as early as this week. The poll is likely to take place on October 25.
For the first time in years, there is a credible possibility that his ruling bloc could be defeated by the student movement, which has led anti-government protests in Serbia for nearly two years now.
Vucic is expected to head the list of his Serbian Progressive Party as its candidate for prime minister.
Elections also in Bosnia and Hercegovina
According to Dejan Bursac, a political scientist at the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory in Belgrade, all signs point to a president increasingly anxious about the upcoming vote.
"Vucic is grasping at every available lifeline," Bursac told DW. "One of those lifelines is Mladic's funeral and the nationalism it can help generate, allowing Vucic to present himself as a patriot while portraying his political opponents as traitors."
Many Serbs, Bursac said, still feel deep resentment over the outcome of the Yugoslav wars and claim that crimes committed against Serbs during these wars largely went unpunished. "That sentiment is now being deliberately inflamed and politically exploited," said Bursac.
Tanja Topic, a political analyst from Banja Luka in the predominantly Serb entity of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where Srebrenica is located, sees a similar dynamic.
"Politics here rests heavily on emotion," she told DW. "This is an issue around which citizens are mobilized. They forget how difficult their lives are because patriotic fervor takes over."
Bosnia and Herzegovina will go to the polls before Serbia, with elections there scheduled for October 4.
Students have a different focus
In Serbia, the student movement — a coalition of faculty assemblies and protest groups operating without formal leaders or public representatives — has largely avoided commenting on Mladic, the funeral or wartime crimes on its social media channels.
Analysts note that both Vucic's party and the student-backed electoral list, which is expected to include respected professors, activists and other public figures, are attempting to function as broad "catch-all" political platforms.
In Serbia, that means neither side can afford to alienate nationalistically minded voters. "Especially because the election will most likely be decided by a very narrow margin," said Dejan Bursac.
The students, he argued, have recognized that for many citizens, it is enough to campaign for the rule of law, democracy and against systemic corruption.
The protest movement began with university blockades after the collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city, in November 2024. Sixteen people were killed.
Although prosecutors have opened several investigations, including into possible corruption linked to construction contracts, no trial has yet begun.
The power of media control
Few people in Serbia place much faith in opinion polls. Nevertheless, it is widely assumed that both the ruling party and the student movement command roughly 40% support each.
The government directly or indirectly controls most television stations and major news outlets, many of which frequently publish identical content.
In recent days, pro-Vucic tabloid Informer has targeted anyone who describes Mladic as a war criminal, branding such critics as "professional haters of Serbs" and "traitors."
Yet political narratives in Serbia shift quickly. Vucic alone appeared on television roughly 400 times last year. By the time voters head to the polls in late October, he will almost certainly need a new issue to rally supporters around.
Mladic's funeral is unlikely to carry him all the way to election day.

Swiss Post plans 110 redundancies
Swiss Post has announced plans to cut costs by the end of 2027, which could result in up to 110 redundancies.
The post office justifies says the cost-cutting measures are necessary to ensure its long-term financial independence.
Swiss Post attributes these measures to the fall in the volume of letters and over-the-counter transactions. Growth in new business sectors and pricing measures have not yet managed to offset the decline in revenue.

Chancellor Merz says AfD result 'changes all of Germany'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:01:00 UTC
00:01:00 KST

Chancellor Merz says AfD result 'changes all of Germany'
September 7, 2026
There are situations in which politicians who have little left to say to each other still appear together before the press. This was certainly the case when Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) and his party colleague, Sven Schulze, the state premier of Saxony-Anhalt, discussed the results of Sunday's state election. They described the results as a catastrophe for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) — an earthquake, a disaster. Merz appeared shaken and devastated, to put it mildly.
He thanked Schulze for his work during the campaign. Then Merz added: "Not only did something change in Saxony-Anhalt yesterday but throughout all of Germany. It will have repercussions, including on the international stage."
This is because the victors in the state election, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), oppose supporting Ukraine in the face of Russia's war of aggression, and many AfD politicians maintain close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin's government, Merz explained.
No regard for the rule of law?
Speaking about the AfD, Merz adopted an almost confrontational tone. Majorities can change, he said, and democrats must always be aware of that and accept it.
But, Merz said, it is shocking that 60% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt chose parties that disregard the rule of law in Germany. Merz was talking about not only the AfD but also the socialist Left Party and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which split off from the Left Party over issues that align the BSW with the AfD.
In contrast, the chancellor said his government will always defend the values of the German constitution: "In our country, these values are not up for debate. Power is granted, not seized. And the minority is not the enemy of the majority."
Historians have long described the Nazis' rise to power in the German Reich as a "seizure of power," which is why Merz's statement is sure to be the subject of much discussion.
Seeking to reassure Germany's international partners in the EU and NATO, he said, "We know that Germany bears a special responsibility because of its history. We will always defend our political order and our firm anchoring in Europe."
Could CDU politicians in Saxony-Anhalt help the AfD come to power?
Standing next to him, Schulze remained silent. On election night the previous evening, long after his defeat had become clear, Schulze repeatedly emphasized in numerous statements that the public's widespread dissatisfaction with the Merz government in Berlin had dealt him a massive blow.
As for now, the worst-case scenario has narrowly been averted: the AfD does not have an absolute majority in the Magdeburg state parliament — but only by the narrowest of margins.
And this is a problem for Friedrich Merz: Dissatisfaction is growing, even within his own ranks. Can he prevent individual CDU lawmakers in Saxony-Anhalt from voting — against the official party line — to elect Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD election winner, as head of government?
If not, then both of Merz's seats of power would be in serious jeopardy: his position as chairman of the party and his seat in the Chancellery.
Merz defends his controversial reforms
However, as of today, Merz is still defending the difficult reforms his government has undertaken. One such reform is the overhaul of the chronically deficit-ridden pension system, which will bring great hardship to many people in Germany and faced fierce opposition during the election campaign.
On election night, Vice Chancellor and center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) leader Lars Klingbeil suggested reassessing the reforms following the defeat of the coalition government in Berlin. However, Merz has not mentioned such a change in course.
AfD displays confidence
Hours before the chancellor's appearance at the CDU headquarters, the AfD took to the stage at the Federal Press Conference. The top candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, sarcastically thanked the media, which had largely portrayed him during the campaign as a threat to democracy and the rule of law.
"It was also thanks to you that we made it," Siegmund said, adding, "Thank you very much for the great coverage during this election campaign."
For example, the influential news magazine Der Spiegel had recently labeled the AfD politician "Germany's most dangerous man" in a widely circulated cover story.
Siegmund then looked out triumphantly at the packed hall and declared, "Never before has there been such a wide gap between those members of the media who seek to dictate to us here in Saxony-Anhalt how we should live and the reality of life for the people in this state."
But Siegmund avoided the question about whether the election result is a clear mandate for his party to form a government — even one without a majority of its own, if necessary, or possibly with the tacit support of the economically left, populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).
Siegmund, however, has said he does not want to be a partner in a coalition — he wants absolute power, and he doesn't have it. The situation in Saxony-Anhalt will surely be the subject of much discussion for many days, perhaps even weeks, to come.

====================================================================================================

Dover and Portsmouth showed us a new kind of far right – and the authorities were caught out | Joe Mulhall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:00:23 UTC
00:00:23 KST

Sadly, we’ve become used to far-right protests in recent years. Whether it’s the vast demonstrations led by Stephen Yaxley-Lennon (AKA Tommy Robinson) in central London, or the hundreds of local protests outside hotels and HMOs housing asylum seekers, the sight of far-right activists chanting anti-migrant slogans has become all too common.
What we saw in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend feels different. At roughly 7am on Saturday morning, hundreds of balaclava-clad men, dressed all in black, began piling out of the backs of vans and blocked roads around Dover port. Shockingly, the police appear to have known nothing about it in advance.
Then, on Sunday evening, a group of men gathered near a Portsmouth beach to “block” the arrival of asylum seekers on a boat. The group had been monitoring maritime apps and tracking the progress of boats towards Britain. They put out a call for people to join them and dozens answered, including well-known activists from the neo-Nazi movement.
What we have seen over the past three days marks a dangerous new development in the far right. While previous protests – many of which descended into ugly racist violence – have been worrying enough, we are now faced with a new, more clandestine and confrontational threat.
Hope Not Hate was the first to identify that the Dover disturbance was organised by a far-right group called Patriot Platform. The balaclava-clad men blocking roads were part of a new network founded by Tommy Robinson’s right-hand man Daniel Thomas (AKA Danny Tommo).
Launched in June, the group unites a web of smaller localised anti-migrant groups into a single body. Current members hail from the Kent Patriots, Watford Patriots, South London Patriots, South-East Patriots, North-West Patriots, Surrey Patriots and Chertsey Patriots, to name just a few.
Patriot Platform is a self-professed Christian “army of patriots” formed to, in Thomas’s words, “reclaim our borders, restore order and send a clear message: Britain belongs to the British people”. The group functions as a vigilante unit to combat immigration and revive what it says are Christian values, ready to spring into action across the country at Thomas’s word.
Worryingly, there is an unusual degree of discipline to Patriot Platform’s organising. Rather than being a single entity, it operates as a network for the local groups. These groups utilise various social media platforms, most commonly Instagram, X, Facebook and TikTok, for their promotional output.
However, unlike organisers of previous public anti-migrant protests, Patriot Platform operates clandestinely, with event planning happening via closed groups and direct personal communication. Its means of operation have more in common with football hooligan gangs than with traditional anti-migrant protest groups. This is how its supporters managed to arrive in their hundreds in Dover unnoticed.
Rather than being met with the usual mealy-mouthed condemnations and talk of “legitimate concerns”, these “protests” need to be called what they are: far-right vigilantism. These aren’t fearful locals, they are organised far-right activists led by Thomas, a man who pleaded guilty to attempted kidnapping and was sentenced to two years in prison after taking part in an armed attempt to abduct a man during a drugs-related dispute.
Since the riots of 2024, Thomas has repeatedly spoken about the need to take to the streets and take direct action. He has been upfront about his intention to create a “patriotic army that is able to take control of the United Kingdom”.
Despite warnings from Hope Not Hate, the authorities have failed to act. They have allowed Thomas to agitate, organise and mobilise large groups around the country. Last weekend was the consequence of police inaction, and I fear that without decisive action things will only get worse.
Clearly, the government needs to be far more robust in dealing with far-right vigilantism. The Home Office is so preoccupied with being seen to be tough on immigration that it has neglected the safety of the very migrants and asylum seekers being targeted.
And the police response exposes serious failings in the authorities’ approach to far-right anti-immigrant violence more broadly. Time and again, they appear unaware of the strength of protests and unprepared for the violence that sometimes results.
The events in Dover and Portsmouth should be a wake-up call for anyone who believes that far-right extremism can be managed through inaction. This is no longer simply about angry protests or offensive rhetoric. We are seeing organised groups willing to mobilise quickly, operate covertly and confront those they see as enemies. The longer authorities fail to recognise the seriousness of this threat, the bolder these groups will become.
The government must act now, before vigilantism becomes normalised and far-right activists feel they can operate with impunity on Britain’s streets.
- 
  Joe Mulhall is director of research at the anti-fascism organisation Hope not Hate

====================================================================================================

Cravings ‘like heroin withdrawal’: what happens when weight-loss drugs don’t work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:00:21 UTC
00:00:21 KST

When Mercedes was told by her doctor that she could be prescribed GLP-1 weight loss jabs in 2024, she broke down. “[When] she said yes, I cried in her office. And I didn’t really stop crying for a week,” she said.
“Finally, after being overweight my entire life, this was going to save me. My struggle, my burden, my shame was finally going to come to an end.”
But as time went on it was hope, not weight, that fell away.
“I was on [Ozempic] for nine months. And then I went on Wegovy for four months, then Contrave [an oral, non-GLP-1 medication], and then Mounjaro, and that was for a few months, and then nine months ago I started on Zepbound,” said Mercedes. “Nothing has worked.”
A recently retired teacher in her 50s, Mercedes is among a small proportion of people for whom the powerful new weight-loss drugs, championed by celebrities for their transformative effects, do not work.
Ozempic, a type 2 diabetes medication, and Wegovy, which is licensed for weight loss, both contain a drug called semaglutide that mimics a hormone that occurs naturally in our bodies: GLP-1. These medications reduce the rate at which food is emptied from the stomach, suppresses appetite and increase the production of insulin – meaning many people lose weight.
Mounjaro and Zepbound, also now household names, have an even greater weight-loss effect. They both contain the drug tirzepatide which mimics both GLP-1 and another hormone.
The excitement around such “GLP-1s” has been hard to miss: the medications have grabbed headlines, with clinical trials suggesting they can help participants lose an average of 15% to 20% of their body weight. Studies suggest they could help with conditions ranging from heart problems and addictions to fatty liver disease. In some cases experts say the effects may not be entirely related to weight loss.
But not everyone experiences the benefits. Between 9% and a third of participants in clinical trials lose less than 5% of their body weight – depending on the type of drug and dose used.
Now researchers are trying to work out why – something they say could help doctors tailor the use of the drugs, maximise cost-effectiveness and reduce side-effects.
For Mercedes, the impact of non-response has been profound.
“Aside from the fact that it’s not working and that it’s so expensive, to say it’s hard on the self-esteem is a humongous understatement,” said Mercedes, who lives in Canada. “It’s been a real struggle, with shame and regret and big bills and disappointment that my own body is not working the way it should.”
Prof Alexander Miras, an obesity expert at Ulster University, said the efficacy of the drugs could not be blamed on patients. “If the drug does not reduce hunger and food intake for someone, it is just not going to work,” he said.
Mercedes said she has tried hard to stick to lifestyle changes alongside the medications but, for her, the jabs did not suppress constant, intrusive thoughts about food.
“I just thought: ‘No, I’ve got to get somewhere … I’m going to die of obesity’,” she said. “I was really strict with myself for a month – but the cravings, which I can only call like heroin withdrawal … it’s just overwhelming. And the food talk never ended.”
The extreme effort paid off, to an extent. “I can honestly say I lost 20 pounds in that month, but not because of the medication,” she said.
Mercedes is certainly not alone: the Guardian has heard from dozens of people for whom GLP-1 medications have had little effect.
Yury K, 57, also from Canada, said he tried a number of weight loss programmes before starting Wegovy for obesity. He exercises about five days a week, mainly with kettlebells, and does not eat junk food or fast food.
While Yury said he saw some improvements in his blood sugar levels and cholesterol while using the medication, as well as a reduction in food noise and appetite, he found his weight barely changed.
“I started Wegovy at about 242lb and, after six months, I was still about 242lb. My weight can fluctuate a little because of water, but essentially there was no meaningful weight loss,” he said. He also experienced unpleasant side effects, including constipation and sensitive skin.
“There is so much discussion about GLP-1 medications as if they work for everyone, and that was not my experience. When you put in the effort with diet and exercise, take the medication exactly as prescribed, and still see little benefit, it is difficult not to feel disappointed,” he said.
Lucille*, 53, who is based in Luxembourg, told the Guardian she has been taking GLP-1 medications for four years – initially to help with insulin resistance – starting on a daily injection of a GLP-1 medication called Saxenda, before switching to Ozempic.
Yet despite being effective at first, Lucille says the medications no longer help her lose weight – even after switching to Mounjaro and taking the highest dose. “It’s as if nothing is having an effect any more,” she says. “The Mounjaro 5mg [dose] is outrageously expensive and so far none of these medications have been approved by my health insurance,” she adds.
At present, the reason for such variations in response remains unclear. “The short answer to why some people don’t respond is we don’t really know,” said Miras.
He said research had suggested factors such as motivation, intelligence, education and socioeconomics did not predict how patients would respond to GLP-1 medications.
But other characteristics might do. “We know, for example, that age plays a role – so older people lose less weight. Sex plays a role – men lose less than women,” said Miras. “[And] people with type 2 diabetes lose less weight compared to people without.”
Studies have also suggested ancestry might have an impact, with the medications most effective in people of European ancestry, and least effective in people of African American ancestry.
Dr Mahesh Umapathysivam, an endocrinologist and clinical researcher at Adelaide University in Australia, said it was plausible that hormones could have an effect too.
“There is growing evidence that oestrogen alters GLP-1 response. We see that with the difference between male response and female response. Also, we know from some of the physiological studies that time of menstrual cycle also alters GLP-1 response,” he said.
“Finally, the use of menopausal hormone replacement therapy – which contains oestrogen – is associated with greater weight loss in semaglutide users.”
Then there is the matter of genetics. A recent study highlighted the potential role of a genetic variant that affects receptors in the brain upon which the drugs work.
“People carrying the genetic variant, we found lose about an extra 0.76kg (1.6 lbs) on average, and people who carry two copies of the variant double that,” said Adam Auton, vice-president of human genetics at the 23andMe Research Institute, and the senior author of the study.
“For people with two copies, this accounts for about 10% of the weight people might expect to lose on these medications.”
Umapathysivam and colleagues have recently published a study into two genetic variants that affect the production of an enzyme, known as PAM, that modifies many hormones including GLP-1. The team found people with such variants appear to show resistance to GLP-1.
“GLP-1 resistance simply means a given amount of GLP-1 has less effect on the body,” Umapathysivam said. “The implication for treatment is that a certain dose of GLP-1 in someone with resistance might mean less weight loss, less glucose lowering, less insulin secretion or less slowing to the gastric emptying.”
Despite emerging research, it is not yet possible to accurately predict who will respond to weight loss jabs and who won’t.
But there are reasons for people like Mercedes to be hopeful. A series of promising new drugs are in development. “Another option is to change patients to a non-GLP-1 based drug called Mysimba [the UK brand name for Contrave]. It works in the same parts of the brain, but just slightly differently and therefore may be worth trying,” said Miras. “It is not available in the NHS, just privately.”
For some who struggle to lose weight with GLP-1 medications, weight-loss surgery may be the only option left. And, Miras says, “[A] lack of response to GLP-1 based drugs does not predict lack of response to [bariatric] surgery.”
And for those who lose little to no weight on GLP-1 medications, the message is clear. “It’s not your fault and it’s not the drug’s fault either, this is purely luck,” said Miras. “I’ve seen it before, it’s not very common, but it does happen.”
Mercedes began GLP-1 medications with huge amounts of hope and expectation. “There was just so much publicity around it. So many people [using the drugs said]: ‘Oh, I forgot to eat lunch,’ that I suppose subconsciously I just sort of ignored the prospect that … the drugs didn’t work,” she said.
“I wish I knew if there were other people out there, like me, for whom [GLP-1s] are just not effective at all.”
*Some names have been changed

North Korea, Russia open first road bridge in ‘new symbol of friendship’
Unknown

North Korea, Russia open first road bridge in ‘new symbol of friendship’
The bridge can allow up to 300 vehicles to cross every day and will be linked to Russia’s federal road network, says PM Mikhail Mishustin
North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge on Monday in a carefully choreographed display of friendship, a structure which spans the Tumen river and which both sides cast as an important milestone in their deepening strategic partnership.
The first flag-adorned trucks trundled across the 1 km (0.6-mile) long two-lane bridge as Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korea’s Premier Pak Thae Song tuned in by video link to address workers and government officials from both countries.
Construction of the new bridge, which had been under discussion for years, began in April last year after the project was agreed during a visit by President Vladimir Putin to North Korea in 2024.
There are already direct air and rail links between Moscow and Pyongyang, but until Monday there had not been a proper road link. Instead, since 1959 and by special arrangement, planks had been placed on the nearby rail bridge – for decades the sole border crossing point – in order to move vehicles across the border between the two countries.
“I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” said Mishustin, who said ties between Moscow and Pyongyang were “at an unprecedented high level” and called the opening of the bridge “a genuinely historic event”.
The construction of the bridge was not merely an engineering project, he said, but “a new symbol of friendship”.
Mishustin said up to 300 vehicles would be able to cross every day and that the bridge would be linked to Russia’s federal road network and have easy access to the transport corridor which runs from the far eastern city of Vladivostok to St Petersburg. Trucks would begin to use the bridge immediately to transport cargo, the Russian government said. At the end of this year, the bridge would be fully operational and could be used for passenger traffic too.

Nearly 80% of residential buildings in Ukraine ready for heating season
The Ministry for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport announced this in a Telegram post, according to Ukrinform.
"Ukraine continues preparing its housing and utilities infrastructure and social sector for winter. Despite the risks posed by the war, work is underway in all regions. As of early September, more than 114,000 residential buildings had been prepared for the heating season, accounting for 79.2% of the planned total," the ministry said.
In addition, 14,194 boiler houses and more than 13,300 km of heating networks have been prepared, along with 2,900 water-supply pumping stations and more than 8,300 wells.
Some 20,600 social infrastructure facilities, including schools, kindergartens and healthcare institutions, are also ready.
Road services have prepared 4,124 pieces of specialized equipment, repaired 8.6 million square meters of roads, and stockpiled more than 1.3 million tonnes of road-gritting materials and reagents.
Particular attention is being paid to frontline regions, where critical infrastructure operates under the constant threat of attacks. There, it is important not only to complete repairs but also to ensure adequate reserves and readiness to promptly restore services in the event of damage.
President Volodymyr Zelensky earlier enacted a decision of the National Security and Defense Council concerning the implementation of comprehensive resilience plans for individual regions and preparations for the 2026/2027 heating season in Kyiv.

Investigation into tortured journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna wins Online Journalism Award

Investigation into tortured journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna wins Online Journalism Award
The Viktoriia Project investigation into journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna, who died in Russian captivity, has won the Excellence in Collaboration and Partnerships category at the international Online Journalism Awards.
Source: Online Journalism Awards
Details: Its competitors were Jailed and Pregnant (NBC News Digital), about pregnant women in US prisons, and The Poisonous Lead Trade (The Examination, Premium Times, The New York Times, Truth Reporting Post), about the poisonous lead trade in Nigeria.
The Viktoriia Project was initiated by the Paris-based newsroom of Forbidden Stories, with 13 media outlets, including Ukrainska Pravda, contributing to its creation.
The journalists reconstructed the route Viktoriia took through Russian prisons, uncovered details of the torture she endured in captivity, and investigated how Russian authorities delayed the return of the journalist's body.
The project also tells the stories of other civilian prisoners whom the Russians are holding in temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine and in Russia. Viktoriia had been reporting on their stories before her death.
Background:
- In March 2022, Viktoriia Roshchyna was captured by Russian forces and held for 10 days in the temporarily occupied city of Berdiansk.
- In 2022, Roshchyna wrote a series of articles for Ukrainska Pravda from the temporarily occupied territories. Her work included stories about life in occupied Crimea during the war, the sham referendum in occupied Donetsk Oblast, and a photo report from the devastated city of Mariupol.
- On 25 July 2023, Roshchyna left Ukraine for Poland, planning to make the three-day journey via Russia to the occupied part of Ukraine's east.
- On 3 August 2023, Roshchyna went missing in Russian-occupied territory.
- It was not until May 2024 that Russia admitted to having detained Roshchyna. The Russian Ministry of Defence sent a letter confirming this to her father, Volodymyr Roshchyn.
- Russia delayed the repatriation of Roshchyna's body, which was only returned in February 2025.
- The Office of the Prosecutor General reported that Roshchyna's body bore multiple signs of torture and ill-treatment: abrasions, bruises, a broken rib and evidence of electrocution.
- The investigative team conducting the inquiry confirmed that the body was brought back to Ukraine after an autopsy conducted in Russia. Journalists learned from law enforcement sources that the body was missing several internal organs – the brain, the eyeballs and part of the trachea. An international forensic pathologist believes this may have been an attempt to conceal the true cause of death, including possible suffocation.
- Viktoria's funeral was held in Kyiv on 8 August.

President Donald Trump appeared to float the idea of renaming New Mexico as “New America,” sharing several maps of the state that listed the new moniker. The images posted Monday, without context or comment, came a day after Trump uploaded an initial "New America" map via social media—an item that was later reshared by the official White House account.
Trump also posted an AI-generated video of himself slapping “America” over a road sign that had previously read “Welcome to New Mexico” and claimed that “many people” had suggested the name change. The White House has not announced any effort to rename New Mexico. TIME has reached out for comment.
The rhetoric has prompted backlash from Democratic lawmakers representing the state. “New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate—it’s been ours since before the United States existed,” said the state’s Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham. “While the White House wastes time coloring on maps, Nuevo México is busy doing the work.”

Elsewhere, some Trump allies came out in support of the floated name change. “New America? Kind of catchy,” argued Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah.
Trump's habit of renaming things—often after America or himself
The President’s social media rhetoric regarding New Mexico comes days after he floated renaming the vital trade passage the Strait of Hormuz as “Trump Strait.”
It also follows Trump signing an Executive Order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” on Aug. 27, amid a widening trade war with Canada. The change was met with widespread disapproval from both U.S. lawmakers and Canadian politicians, who vowed Lake Ontario will continue to be called by that name.
The order applies to U.S. federal references of the lake and does not determine how Canada—or others—refer to the body of water. U.S. users of Google Maps and Apple Maps, however, will notice the change reflected.
Trump has often turned to name changes as a show of power and a way to undermine his perceived adversaries.
The President has also put his stamp on Washington, D.C., renaming the Kennedy Center by adding his own surname to the title. After much back-and-forth and legal complications, the Center’s board voted in August to reinstate Trump’s name on the building’s facade, testing a judge’s order from May that mandated its removal.
Trump added his name to the U.S. Institute of Peace late last year, pointing towards his claim of ending a number of global conflicts since his return to the White House.
Outside of renaming landmarks and buildings after himself, Trump has also faced backlash over a string of what Democratic lawmakers have referred to as “vanity projects” across D.C.

Germany’s AfD wins in key state: Is far-right on cusp of national rule?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:59:32 UTC
23:59:32 KST

Germany’s AfD wins in key state: Is far-right on cusp of national rule?
The AfD, which is classified as ‘far-right extremist’ by Germany’s intelligence agency is projected to come first in the 2029 national election.
For the first time since World War II, a far-right party is within reach of power at state level in Germany, after coming first in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 44 percent of the vote, stopping short of an overall majority but making clear its wide political significance.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US envoys hold ‘substantive’ talks with Zelenskyy in first visit to Kyiv
- list 2 of 3German far-right AfD wins Saxony-Anhalt election, falls short of majority
- list 3 of 3Can AfD form Germany’s first far-right state government since World War II?
On election night, AfD’s leader in the state called on other political groups to cooperate. “As a democrat, I will reach out to all those who wish to work with us to bring about a fundamental political turnaround,” Ulrich Siegmund said.
Yet, forming a government will prove difficult. The AfD has been classified as “far-right extremist” by the domestic intelligence agency and other political groups remain wary of striking an alliance.
The AfD has dismissed accusations of extremism and mainstream parties have been unable to halt its surge in the polls over recent months. Latest polling indicates the party, which stands for strong restrictions on immigration, restoring ties with Russia, cutting support to Ukraine and quitting the euro, is Germany’s most popular at national level.
The Saxony-Anhalt election could be a harbinger of a historic return of the far-right in the 2029 national election, when forecasts say the AfD stands a realistic chance of finishing first.
What happened in Saxony-Anhalt?
Siegmund, the charismatic 35-year-old who attracted thousands to his campaign rallies, said AfD “made history”.
“The people have made it absolutely clear that they finally want political change and, above all, they have shown that they want it with us,” he told supporters.
The AfD achieved its best-ever election result in Saxony-Anhalt with 44 percent of the vote, leaving all other parties far behind. The incumbent centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU), led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, scored less than half of that share with 17 percent.
The AfD is projected to gain 39 of the 83 seats in the state parliament in Magdeburg, leaving it three short of the 42 needed for an absolute majority.
That means the party must find allies, but all other mainstream parties refuse to work with the far-right, a strategy of non-cooperation known as the “firewall”. The AfD has so far never participated in a governing coalition in Germany’s 16 states nor in its federal government.
While he now appears willing to strike deals with other parties to come to power, previously Siegmund signalled unwillingness to find middle ground with other political groups. Leading up to the vote, he stated that he was only interested in governing alone to bring about fundamental political change in Germany.
How did AfD fare in recent elections?
The election takes the AfD one step closer to advancing its agenda, while also reflecting the growing unpopularity of Germany’s ruling coalition.
In Saxony-Anhalt, the party more than doubled its vote share — from 21 percent in the last election. By contrast, the CDU’s vote halved from 37 percent to 17 percent, its worst result ever in the east-central German state.
Federal elections last year similarly resulted in a landmark performance by the AfD, which emerged as the largest opposition faction in the Bundestag, the German federal parliament in Berlin. The party came second with 21 percent of the vote, securing its highest-ever showing.
In state elections in Baden-Wurttemberg and Rhineland-Palatinate earlier this year too, the AfD more than doubled its seats — though it still finished third. In 2024, the AfD emerged victorious in the Thuringia state election and second in the Brandenburg state election — both were firsts for the party.
The AfD’s electoral gains in Saxony-Anhalt mirror growing dissatisfaction among voters — especially in the former East Germany — about the stagnant economy, high unemployment and domestic security, which the party largely pins on immigration.
What challenges lie ahead for AfD?
Since its formation in 2013, the AfD has been embroiled in various scandals and has faced major controversies, including alleged foreign espionage links, secret deportation plans and internal nepotism.
The party went from a fringe Eurosceptic group to the country’s most powerful opposition force in little more than a decade, becoming too extreme even for the European Parliament’s far-right Identity & Democracy group. It kicked the party out in May 2024 after lead AfD candidate Maximilian Krah stated that not everyone in the SS – Adolf Hitler’s infamous Nazi paramilitary organisation – was a criminal.
Krah has also been under investigation by German prosecutors for alleged illegal payments, bribery and money laundering linked to China and Russia. The German parliament last year decided to lift the far-right legislator’s immunity to help investigators.
AfD politicians have also come under fire for employing family members, including in Saxony-Anhalt, where several parliamentarians are reported to have employed relatives.
Bundestag President, Julia Klockner, banned seven AfD employees from entering the German parliament over security concerns, after they failed internal background reliability checks due to their ties to right-wing extremist networks and past criminal convictions.
Senior AfD figures also faced a backlash for attending a secretive meeting to discuss mass deportation plans for people with a migration background.
What are the AfD’s prospects for the national election in 2029?
Pollsters are unanimous in forecasting the AfD as the largest party in Germany in the next national election in 2029, with around 28 percent of the vote.
That would mark a major transformation in the German political landscape from 2025, when the CDU and its ally the Christian Social Union together won 28.5 percent of the vote.
Yet even that outcome would not necessarily give AfD the ability to govern. If other parties maintain a “firewall” policy, that could prevent the far-right party from forming a coalition government.
Still, the Saxony-Anhalt election has been received by some politicians as a call for change. “Politics begins with considering reality,” Cem Ozdemir, head of government in the southwestern state of Baden-Wurttemberg and a member of the Green Party, wrote on X.
“That means the AfD is the election winner in Saxony-Anhalt. And that must mean for all democratic forces that nothing can remain as it is, and we must fundamentally reconsider our politics and our political style.”

Why do the Falkland Islands matter to the UK and Argentina so much?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:58:56 UTC
23:58:56 KST

Why do the Falkland Islands matter to the UK and Argentina so much?
Argentina’s sovereignty claim is enshrined in its constitution, but oil production raises the economic stakes.
A dispute between Argentina and Britain over control of the Falkland Islands has flared up again, after Argentinian President Javier Milei said the “winds of change” favour his country’s claim to the self-governing overseas United Kingdom territory.
Argentina’s presidency said in a statement on Friday that it had ordered the opening of proceedings to “investigate and penalise” 45 entities “linked to the exploration and exploitation of hydrocarbons” around the Falklands, which Argentines call Las Malvinas.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Yair Netanyahu, Israeli PM’s son, angers UK right over Falklands
- list 2 of 3Argentina’s Milei threatens sanctions over Falklands oil drilling
- list 3 of 3Argentina’s Milei threatens sanctions as he refocuses on Falklands
The remarks followed comments from US President Donald Trump that the United States was reviewing its position on the Falkland Islands. Washington has threatened to oppose Britain’s sovereignty over the South Atlantic archipelago if it does not increase its NATO defence spending.
British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting responded by asserting Britain’s “unshakeable” commitment to the Falklands. “The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British,” he said in a social media post.
Residents of the Falkland Islands have indicated they prefer to remain a part of the UK, and British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the country would “resolutely uphold” their right to self-determination.
Why do the Falkland Islands matter to the UK and Argentina?
Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war in 1982 over the South Atlantic islands, located about 600km (375 miles) east of Argentina’s southernmost tip.
It ended with the surrender of Argentine troops after 74 days of fighting that killed 649 Argentines and 255 British troops.
Argentina’s sovereignty claim is enshrined in its constitution and is frequently invoked as an expression of national identity. Milei said the islands are “our future” and that Argentina needs to “recover” them as a matter of national importance.
The right-wing libertarian is preparing to seek re-election in October 2027 as his approval ratings plummet. Polls show only around 34 percent of Argentines support his drastic belt-tightening and deregulation policies.
Plans for large-scale oil production around the islands raise the economic stakes of the dispute. Milei declared that the Sea Lion deep-sea oil project, a joint UK-Israel operation, was a “clear and present danger” to the country’s claims.
Production at the field about 220km (140 miles) north of the islands is expected to begin in 2028. Argentina considers the project an illegal exploitation of resources in waters it claims as its own. “Any further advance on the Malvinas Islands will be considered a violation of our national security,” Milei said.
Rockhopper Exploration and Navitas Petroleum brushed off Milei’s threats in a joint statement on Friday, saying they would press ahead with the Sea Lion plan under licences granted by the Falkland Islands government and backed by Britain.
How is the US playing into the dispute?
The United States has signalled it may change its long-held position on the future of the Falklands. For decades, successive US administrations have remained neutral on the competing claims while recognising Britain’s de facto administration of the islands.
A departure from that position risks inflaming already high transatlantic tensions between Washington and its NATO allies.
Milei said the US was considering a change in position because it sees Argentina as a “reliable partner, aligned with Western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come”.
The Argentinian leader is a regular feature at conservative pro-Trump political gatherings in the US, and Trump has previously described the far-right populist leader as his “favourite president”.
Trump has repeatedly criticised Britain over its stance on the US-Israel war on Iran, accusing it of not assisting Washington in the fight against Tehran and of failing to help the US reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Benjamin Gedan, director of the Latin America programme at the Stimson Center in Washington, DC, said hints of a change to US neutrality in the dispute over the Falklands were clearly designed to needle British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Despite the good relationship between Trump and Milei, any resolution of the Falklands dispute still depends on persuading the UK. “Any settlement of this long-standing dispute will surely involve negotiations,” Gedan said. “And that means persuading the British, not the Americans.”

ICE crackdown laid bare at Venice festival documentary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:57:22 UTC
23:57:22 KST

ICE crackdown laid bare at Venice festival documentary
VENICE, Sept 7 - Oscar-winning filmmaker Laura Poitras said on Monday she hopes a new documentary about U.S. immigration raids will help "denormalise" violence under President Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign.
Premiering at the Venice Film Festival, the 25-minute documentary "They're Here", co-directed by Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller, follows volunteers in Minneapolis as they track the movements of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents conducting deportation operations earlier this year.
"The reality is a nightmare. The entire country is under attack and immigrants are living in fear throughout the United States right now," Poitras said ahead of the screening.
CONFRONTING PROTESTERS IN THE SNOW
Trump launched his deportation drive immediately after taking office in January 2025. He has defended ICE's tactics and argued that people who entered the U.S. illegally must be sent home.
The Minneapolis sweep drew weeks of demonstrations and confrontations between protesters and ICE agents in which immigration officers shot dead two U.S. citizens.
"In the mainstream media, this kind of violence is being normalised. We believe very strongly in the power of cinema to denormalise this violence and to show what's happening," Poitras told a news conference.
Poitras, whose full-length documentary "All the Beauty and the Bloodshed" won Venice's top Golden Lion prize in 2022, said she and Mueller decided to make a much shorter film because they felt it was urgent to show immediately what was happening.
Shot largely from the perspective of local residents tracking the movements of ICE teams, "They're Here" cuts between volunteer dispatch networks and the story of a Mexican man hiding from immigration authorities with the help of his son.
The documentary shows locals plotting the routes of unmarked ICE cars, masked agents confronting protesters on snow-covered streets and handcuffed detainees boarding deportation flights.
COMMUNITY RESPONSE
The Minneapolis crackdown became one of the flashpoints in the broader deportation campaign and the U.S. administration eventually scaled back the operation after months of unrest.
Mueller said the filmmakers wanted to document both the scope of the anti-migrant sweep and the community response it provoked across the city.
"The resistance remained one of documentation more than anything else, precisely because it was about keeping people safe rather than fighting ICE," she said. "These are our neighbours, and we don't want them stolen from us."
She said the eventual drawdown on ICE operatives showed that the community action had worked.
"ICE removed 80% of its agents. So there was a real response to this kind of resistance, which I think we can all take hope from," she said. REUTERS

Russia Burns Through $29 Million Every Hour to Fund Its War Against Ukraine

2026-09-07

Russian federal budget spending linked to the war against Ukraine reached a record 10.687 trillion rubles ($123.4 billion) in the first half of 2026.
According to an analysis of finance ministry data by Janis Kluge, a researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, the figure represents a 30% increase, or 2.46 trillion rubles ($28.4 billion), compared with the same period in 2025.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the Moscow times, military spending was 65% higher than in the first six months of 2024 and 145% above the level recorded during the same period in 2023.
Compared with the first year of Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, spending increased by 285%, while expenditures were more than five times higher than in the prewar year of 2021.
On average, Russia spent about 1.78 trillion rubles ($20.6 billion) a month on its military and weapons production during the first half of this year. That amounted to roughly 59 billion rubles ($681.4 million) per day, or 2.5 billion rubles ($28.9 million) per hour.
Military-related expenditures accounted for 43.8% of all federal budget spending during the six-month period, which Kluge described as a new record.
Measured against government revenue, the share was even higher. Russia spent the equivalent of 57.3% of all federal budget income on the military and defense industry.
A year earlier, military spending accounted for 39.2% of federal expenditures and 46.8% of revenue. Before the full-scale invasion, those figures stood at 20% and 19.8%, respectively, according to Kluge’s calculations.
Ukraine Unlocks €418M in EU Aid in August, But Billions Remain at Risk
About two-thirds of Russia’s military spending was classified, Kluge said.
During the first six months of 2026, the Kremlin spent 3.546 trillion rubles ($40.9 billion) through publicly disclosed defense budget lines and 7.141 trillion rubles ($82.4 billion) through classified expenditures.
The classified portion increased by 42% compared with the previous year and was more than seven times higher than before the war.
Since the beginning of 2022, Russia has spent a total of 57.144 trillion rubles ($660 billion) on its military and weapons procurement.
That amount is comparable to the Russian Central Bank’s entire gold and foreign currency reserves, valued at $720.3 billion as of Aug. 1. It is also about 2.2 times the estimated $292.8 billion value of Russia’s gold holdings.
The Russian government initially planned defense spending equivalent to 6.7% of gross domestic product in its 2026 budget. Actual spending was about 1.5 times higher than planned and reached an estimated 10.5% of GDP for the first half of the year, Kluge calculated.
Russia’s growing military expenditures have contributed to a widening federal budget deficit.
The deficit reached about 6.45 trillion rubles ($74.5 billion) in the first seven months of 2026, equivalent to 2.8% of GDP and roughly twice the original target for the entire year.

Moscow orders German consulate to shut in tit-for-tat move

Moscow orders German consulate to shut in tit-for-tat move
Russia has ordered the German consulate in St. Petersburg to close in a widening diplomatic dispute with Berlin. The mission must cease operations by September 18, the Foreign Ministry in Moscow said on Monday.
“Russia is withdrawing its consent for the German Consulate General in St. Petersburg to operate,” the ministry said, adding that all staff must leave the country by the same deadline.
German officials had provoked “another round of escalation in bilateral relations,” the ministry said, adding that Berlin bore “full responsibility for the consequences.”
The measures follow German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul’s September 1 announcement that Berlin would close Russia’s consulate in Bonn on September 18 and terminate an agreement governing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said it had handed Germany’s head of mission in Moscow a formal notice on the closure of the St. Petersburg consulate.
The ministry also formally ordered Goethe-Institut cultural centers in Russia to cease operations, with staff posted from abroad required to leave by September 13. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov had earlier said the centers would close in response to Berlin’s measures.
Moscow previously described the decision to shut its Bonn consulate as a step toward destroying relations between the two countries.
The dispute follows a controversial drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport, where an explosives-laden UAV was found between Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes on August 4. The German government said earlier it had grounds to believe Moscow was responsible.
Berlin subsequently announced the closures in Bonn and Berlin, along with tighter border controls for Russian citizens.
Moscow has denied involvement. President Vladimir Putin suggested the allegations were intended to distract Germans from domestic economic problems.
The latest Russian measures come as the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) won the regional election in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, finishing well ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU.
The AfD’s lead candidate in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, has criticized Berlin’s approach to Russia, arguing that arms deliveries to Ukraine and sanctions have done little to resolve the conflict. He has called for serious diplomatic engagement with Moscow.

'Findings' Exhibition to Open at the Draugu House Gallery  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:54:32 UTC
23:54:32 KST

A new permanent archaeological exhibition, “Findings” ("Atradumi"), will open at 5 p.m. on Friday, 11 September, at the Draugu House Gallery in Konrāds Quarter, Cēsis. The exhibition brings centuries-old objects together with items that were lost or discarded only recently. The exhibits have been selected by well-known public figures, while children offer their interpretations of how unique antiquities may once have been used.
The exhibition is based on archaeological finds uncovered during the restoration of Konrāds Quarter. Archaeological investigations in the area between Cēsis Medieval Castle and St John’s Church began in the spring of 2024 and continued until last autumn.
Archaeologists discovered the remains of medieval timber buildings, the castle’s defensive wall, burials and numerous objects associated with the everyday lives and crafts of the town’s inhabitants. The finds include a 13th-century casting mould, medieval writing styli, amber rosary beads, fragments of wooden vessels, footwear and other leather goods.
However, the researchers preserved more than just ancient and rare objects during the excavations. In their view, even very recent finds bear witness to their time and can tell us how a place was used, how people lived and what habits they had. This idea has become one of the central themes of “Findings”. What determines whether we regard an object as valuable historical evidence or merely as an ordinary everyday item? And do archaeologists and people with no professional connection to archaeology notice the same things?
To explore these questions from a different perspective, people whose professional work is unrelated to archaeology were invited to help select the exhibits. The contents of the exhibition’s first display cases were chosen by technology entrepreneur Anna Andersone, actor and entrepreneur Juris Žagars, journalist Inga Spriņģe, poet Jānis Rokpelnis and digital marketing specialist Artūrs Mednis.
Each participant selected objects that surprised or intrigued them or made them reflect from centuries-old antiquities to very recent and seemingly insignificant items. In conversations with archaeologist Laura Lēģere, they learned what researchers had already discovered about their chosen objects and which questions remained unanswered. The conversations were filmed, and the recordings have become part of the exhibition.
Another section of “Findings” focuses on several remarkable antiquities, but this time it is the children who offer the explanations. In front of the camera, they try to work out how the objects discovered by archaeologists may once have been used and how they were made. Their guesses and conclusions provide a captivating and touching insight into how a centuries-old past is interpreted through the experiences and imagination of a child today.
“When creating history exhibitions, I have always tried to find unconventional ways of making the distant past understandable and engaging for contemporary audiences. This time, the circumstances offered an especially good opportunity to experiment with an unusual format to let people from entirely different fields select the finds and to entrust the interpretation of some antiquities to children. It was a wonderful experience. I am particularly delighted that we were able to involve so many different people in creating the exhibition from Cēsis and Riga, seasoned professionals and children with their own perspectives and ideas. To me, this meeting of different viewpoints is the very essence of ‘Findings’,” says Gundars Kalniņš, the exhibition’s curator and the author of its concept.
Although “Findings” has been created as a permanent exhibition, its contents will evolve over time. From time to time, some of the display cases will be completely renewed to feature finds selected by other well-known public figures. The exhibition’s next transformation will reveal which objects from the rich collection of archaeological finds uncovered in the courtyard of Konrāds Quarter have been chosen by educator Edgars Plētiens, editor Nellija Ločmele, event host Valdis Melderis, entrepreneur Egija Gailuma and artist Kristians Brekte.
“Findings” will therefore have no single definitive version. As the display cases and the people whose choices they present change, the story told by the exhibition will change as well giving visitors a reason to return again and again.

Port of Klaipėda develops green methanol bunkering vessel concept  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:54:27 UTC
23:54:27 KST

As the shipping industry moves towards cleaner solutions, the Port of Klaipėda is preparing for changing market needs. Stricter environmental requirements and the growing market for alternative fuels mean that ports need to start planning now for the infrastructure and services that will be needed in the future. Together with its partners, the Klaipėda Port Authority has assessed the potential for green methanol bunkering and developed a concept for a vessel that could provide this service.
“The energy transition is changing the maritime sector and creating demand for cleaner solutions. As the alternative fuels market develops, ports will also need to adapt their infrastructure and services. We are preparing now so that, as green shipping corridors develop across the Baltic Sea, the Port of Klaipėda will be ready to meet market needs and remain competitive. Green methanol bunkering has real potential both in Klaipėda and across the Baltic Sea region,” says Algis Latakas, CEO of the Klaipėda Port Authority.
The Port Authority explored new solutions for cleaner shipping together with 14 partners from different countries through the H2Deri@BSP project. The project aims to accelerate the use of hydrogen-based fuels and support the transition towards zero-emission shipping.
As part of the project, the Klaipėda Port Authority assessed the Port’s potential to offer green methanol bunkering services in the future. The study looked at expected demand for green methanol, regulations supporting the use of alternative fuels, potential customers and fuel supply chains, as well as the environmental benefits of green methanol.
An analysis by Moffatt & Nichol Baltics found that although the green methanol market in the Baltic region is still at an early stage, ports that can offer alternative fuel bunkering are likely to become increasingly attractive to shipping lines. For Klaipėda, green methanol bunkering could also become a new business area, bringing additional revenue and expanding the range of services available at the Port.
The study also identified potential for green methanol to be produced from green hydrogen in the future. The Port of Klaipėda already has a green hydrogen production facility in operation. As the shipping industry works towards its decarbonisation goals, green methanol could see particularly strong demand from regional vessels, passenger ships and ferries, as well as vessels serving offshore wind farms.
The Port of Klaipėda continues to strengthen its role as an energy port. Since 2024, the green methanol-powered container ship Eco Umande, operated by Singapore’s X-Press Feeders, has been calling at the Port of Klaipėda. The Port has also signed a cooperation agreement with several other ports to support the development of green methanol infrastructure. Offering green methanol bunkering services could therefore further strengthen Klaipėda’s competitiveness and create new opportunities for the Port.
The project has already moved beyond analysis to a practical solution. The project developed a technical specification and concept design for a green methanol bunkering vessel for the Port of Klaipėda.The concept was developed by Western Baltic Engineering, part of the Western Shipyard Group (VLG) operating at the Port of Klaipėda.
Designed for flexible operations in shallow waters and on local bunkering routes, the vessel would have a green methanol capacity of 800 metric tonnes. It could supply up to 250,000 metric tonnes of green methanol per year.

The lunchbox came from Wa Jer Restaurant, located in the Wah Sing Industrial Building on Wah Sing Street.
A customer reportedly bought a HK$44 (US$5.60) set meal that included satay beef rice noodles, a ham omelette and a drink.
When opening the takeaway box, she discovered a live baby rat covered in satay sauce and moving among the noodles.
The customer uploaded the footage to a social media platform, where it quickly went viral and sparked heated online debate over the source of the creature.
The diner preserved the meal box intact and immediately filed a complaint with the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department.
A department spokesman said it received the complaint on Monday, seized the food for testing and found hygiene conditions in parts of the premises to be unsatisfactory.

Emor: Brand preferences vary considerably across the Baltic states, but one favourite unites them all  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:54:22 UTC
23:54:22 KST

According to Emor’s survey, brand preferences among residents of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania differ in several respects, but YouTube was rated as the most likeable brand by residents of all three Baltic states.
The survey ranked the most likeable brands among consumers. “Although the top-ranked brand is the same in all three Baltic states, the rankings quite clearly reflect the distinctive character of each market,” said Emor’s research expert Katrin Männaste. The top three brands differ considerably between the countries: in Estonia, YouTube is followed by Swedbank and Kalev; in Latvia, by WhatsApp and Apple; and in Lithuania, by Lidl and Google.
“Estonia stands out for having more brands with local roots and brands developed for the local market at the top of the ranking – in addition to Kalev, A. Le Coq, Coop, Selver and Smart-ID are also among the ten most likeable brands,” noted Katrin Männaste. In Latvia, two local food brands ranked highly: meat brand Forevers and Kārums, best known as a curd snack brand and currently in the process of being acquired by an Estonian company. The locally founded DIY and home improvement retail chain DEPO is also among Latvian residents’ favourite brands. Of the three Baltic states, Lithuania has the most international brands at the top of its ranking: among local players, retail chain Maxima and Lithuanian National Radio and Television (LRT) are represented in the top ten.
“Brand preferences across the Baltic states are united primarily by international brands and the strengthening position of digital brands – behind the leader YouTube, brands such as Apple, Google and Samsung are also among the 25 most likeable brands in all three Baltic states,” Männaste commented. Compared with the previous survey conducted across the Baltic states (2021), ChatGPT, Smart-ID and Waze have now also entered the top 25. There is, however, common ground in other sectors as well: Swedbank and the retail chains Lidl and Maxima are among the top 25 in all three countries. “The extent of change varies between countries: compared with 2021, the composition of Lithuania’s top ten has remained relatively unchanged, while the top of the Latvian ranking has changed more noticeably over the past five years,” the research expert added.
To identify the most appealing brands, Emor conducted an online survey in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in May 2026, in which respondents were asked to select up to five brands they found most appealing from a predefined list. The selection included more than 190 brand names and logos in Latvia and Lithuania and more than 160 in Estonia. The list is based on the experience gained by Emor and its Latvian and Lithuanian partners from various brand studies. The survey included 1,236 residents of Estonia, 1,609 residents of Latvia and 1,548 residents of Lithuania aged 16–74. The survey is representative of the population in this age group.

Nurkulov arrived in Lithuania shortly before his temporary residence permit was due to expire. The defendant claims he was unaware that the Al Qassem Brigades, the organisation to which he transferred money, is designated as a terrorist organisation by the European Union.
Nurkulov is accused of providing direct material support to the Al Qassem Brigades, the military wing of the Palestinian Islamist organisation Hamas, while holding a Lithuanian residence permit, with the intention that the funds be used to support terrorist activities.
The defendant maintains he did not know the Al Qassem Brigades were listed as a terrorist group in the European Union and believed the money would be used for food and other humanitarian aid. He previously told the court he deeply regretted his actions and asked for leniency. However, the prosecutor noted that during the pre-trial investigation, Nurkulov had stated he was aware of the organisation's terrorist status.
Under Lithuanian law, such an offence is punishable by three to 10 years in prison.
According to case files, officials also found posts on his accounts calling for Muslims to join a holy war against non-believers and Israel, alongside photos of masked armed individuals.
Nurkulov was detained at the airport after flying to Lithuania from Istanbul. The pre-trial investigation was conducted by the Financial Crime Investigation Service in cooperation with the State Security Department and was led by a prosecutor from the Prosecutor General's Office.
