Vilnius, Riga, Tallinn by Train: A 7-Day Baltic Route  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:43 UTC
23:53:43 KST

For most of the past two decades, travelling overland between the three Baltic capitals meant one thing: a long-distance coach. The rail network inherited from the Soviet era ran east to west rather than north to south, and the direct Vilnius-Riga passenger service disappeared in 2004. Anyone wanting to see all three capitals in a single trip either booked a bus, hired a car, or flew, which on routes of a few hundred kilometres made little sense for either cost or carbon. The accommodation side was just as fragmented: three cities, three national markets, and no single place to compare them. That gap is narrowing, and platforms such as trip1 now list hotels across all three countries under one roof, which for a trip of this shape matters more than it might sound.
The transport picture has changed too. Since December 2023, Lithuanian operator LTG Link has run a daily direct train between Vilnius and Riga, restoring a link dormant for nearly twenty years. In January 2025, the Lithuanian, Latvian and Estonian railways coordinated their timetables to create a through Vilnius-Riga-Tallinn service with a single cross-platform change at Valga on the Estonian-Latvian border, sold under one ticket. Demand has run ahead of forecasts, and from January 2026 an additional daily Riga-Tallinn service was added.
What follows is a route, and rather more detail than usual on where to sleep at each end of it, because on a three-country itinerary the hotels are the part most people get wrong.
Why seven days, and how the three hotel markets differ
Three capitals in seven days sounds ambitious but is comfortable in practice. Vilnius to Riga is 348 kilometres, Riga to Tallinn 441, and the full Vilnius-Tallinn run 789. That is less than the length of Great Britain.
Two nights in each city, with the seventh day absorbed by travel or a stopover, is the sensible allocation. Travel south to north: Tallinn has the best onward connections, with ferries to Helsinki and Stockholm and a busy airport, which makes it the natural place to finish.
The three accommodation markets behave quite differently, and knowing how before you book saves money and walking.
Vilnius is the cheapest of the three and has an unusually deep boutique segment for a city of half a million, largely because the old town is full of restored palaces and merchant houses that convert well. Five-star rates here undercut four-star rates in Tallinn.
Riga has the widest range and the sharpest price gradient. Old town rates drop noticeably once you cross into the Quiet Centre, a ten-minute walk that also puts you closer to the Art Nouveau district.
Tallinn is the most expensive, has the smallest luxury segment, and sells out earliest. The medieval core is compact, genuinely worth staying inside, and priced accordingly. Book this one first.
Vilnius: two nights
Vilnius makes the strongest case for being the first stop, partly because it is the least familiar to most visitors and partly because it holds the largest baroque old town in Northern Europe, a UNESCO World Heritage site that is still a working residential district rather than a preserved museum quarter.
Two days covers the old town, the Gediminas Tower viewpoint, Užupis across the river, and the National Museum. The contemporary city deserves an afternoon too: Vilnius has become a serious European fintech hub, and the effect on the restaurant and café scene in Naujamiestis is visible.
Where to stay in Vilnius
The old town is the obvious base, and the top end punches well above the city's size.
Hotel Pacai on Didžioji street is the standout. It occupies a baroque palace built in 1677 for the Pac family, once the grandest private residence in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and reopened in 2018 after a restoration by local architects as a 104-room Design Hotels property with a spa, restaurant and bar. The historic shell has been kept and the interiors are deliberately contemporary.
Relais & Châteaux Stikliai, on Stiklių street among the galleries and artisan workshops, is the older kind of luxury. Its restaurant has been the benchmark for fine dining in Vilnius for more than thirty years, served under a glass-roofed atrium, and the wellness area includes a pool and Roman-style baths.
Narutis, a Small Luxury Hotels of the World member on Pilies street, sits in a building first documented in 1581, which makes it one of the oldest hotel buildings in the city. It is directly on the old town's main artery, with a quiet inner courtyard and its own spa.
Radisson Collection Astorija occupies a classical 1901 building roughly thirteen minutes' walk from the railway station and includes an indoor pool. It is the reliable full-service choice, and the closest thing Vilnius has to a grand hotel in the traditional sense. Grand Hotel Vilnius, Curio Collection by Hilton covers similar ground.
In the mid-range, the Shakespeare Boutique Hotel sits in a renovated 17th-century palace fifty metres from Cathedral Square, and the Grotthuss Boutique Hotel occupies a historic building on a medieval street about eleven minutes from the station, with a small wine bar off reception. Artagonist Art Hotel, Imperial Hotel & Restaurant and Mabre Residence are all inside the old town and consistently well reviewed. For predictable business-standard rooms, Hilton Garden Inn Vilnius City Centre, AC Hotel Vilnius and Novotel Vilnius Centre are all central.
Vilnius railway station is around fifteen minutes on foot from the southern edge of the old town, so anywhere inside the walls keeps the onward journey simple. The Lithuania travel guides on trip1 break the city down by district if you are weighing the old town against Užupis or Naujamiestis.
Vilnius to Riga
The train leaves Vilnius in the morning and reaches Riga Central Station in just over four hours, comparable to driving and considerably more pleasant. Second-class fares vary between roughly 10 and 24 euros; first class is fixed at around 34 euros and includes an assigned seat and complimentary refreshments. The rolling stock is a modern Pesa diesel unit with air conditioning, Wi-Fi, power sockets and at-seat catering.
Booking opens up to sixty days ahead on this sector, and the advice is consistent: book early. The service runs full and sells out days or weeks in advance. Interrail and Eurail holders need a seat reservation.
The coach alternative is perfectly good. Lux Express and Ecolines run frequent services, journey times are broadly similar and fares often lower. The difference is comfort and the ability to move around, which on a four-hour leg matters more than it sounds.
Riga: two nights
Riga is the largest of the three cities and has the widest spread of things to see: the old town, the Art Nouveau quarter on Alberta iela with the densest concentration of Jugendstil architecture anywhere in Europe, and the Central Market housed in former Zeppelin hangars. Two nights is a minimum rather than a comfortable allocation.
Where to stay in Riga
Riga Central Station is a seven-minute walk from the edge of the old town, which makes arrival easy regardless of where you have booked.
Neiburgs is probably the definitive Riga boutique stay. It occupies a carefully restored 1903 Art Nouveau building on Jauniela, directly beside Riga Cathedral on Dome Square, and its rooms are effectively apartments, with kitchenettes, high ceilings and original plasterwork. Each room has a different footprint because the heritage building dictated it. The hotel restaurant has held a Michelin Guide listing three years running and cooks seasonal Latvian produce sourced from the Central Market.
Grand Hotel Kempinski Riga, on Aspazijas bulvāris opposite the canal gardens, is the city's flagship five-star: 141 rooms, three bars, a spa widely rated among the best in the Baltics, and a rooftop restaurant looking across the old town spires. It is about 350 metres from Town Hall Square.
Pullman Riga Old Town on Jēkaba street, renovated in 2025, is the contemporary alternative, with a spa, indoor pool, rooftop bar and large, light rooms just inside the old city gates. Grand Palace Hotel on Pils iela, a Small Luxury Hotels member five minutes from Riga Cathedral, is the more traditional five-star.
At the value end, the Eurostars Metropole on Aspazijas is Riga's oldest continuously operating hotel, open since 1871 and a seven-minute walk from the station, and remains remarkably inexpensive for the space and location. Rixwell Old Riga Palace, Hotel Gutenbergs, Konventa Sēta and Hotel Monte Kristo are all solid old town options at moderate rates.
If you would rather be near the Art Nouveau district than the medieval core, Hotel Bergs sits inside the Bergs Bazaar, an elegant 19th-century courtyard complex in the Quiet Centre, and deals almost entirely in suites. Grand Poet by Semarah and Radisson Blu Latvija are nearby and cheaper. Art Hotel Roma, in a converted early 20th-century building near the National Opera, is the most characterful mid-range choice in the centre.
The Latvia travel guides on trip1 are useful for settling the old town versus Quiet Centre question before you commit, since the two produce quite different trips.
Riga to Tallinn, via Valga and Tartu
This is the leg where train and bus genuinely diverge. The coach is faster, around four and a half hours on a good run. The train takes longer, requires a change at Valga, and costs about 30.50 euros in second class.
It is still worth taking. The route runs through the Latvian countryside and southern Estonia rather than along a motorway. And there is Valga.
Valga in Estonia and Valka in Latvia were a single town until the border was drawn in 1920. They now function as twin municipalities inside the Schengen area, with no border controls and a pedestrian bridge over which, in one of the more charming pieces of municipal design in Europe, an international swing has been installed, letting you swing between two countries. The station has free luggage lockers requiring only a small coin deposit, so a few hours here is easily arranged.
The stronger case for breaking the journey, though, is Tartu. Estonia's second city and home to its oldest university, it has a compact old town, a river, an unusually beautiful wooden railway station and an atmosphere owing more to Scandinavia than to the Baltic coast. It was a European Capital of Culture in 2024 and the investment shows.
If you stay, Antonius Boutique Hotel is the pick, a small luxury property directly opposite the main university building and about 170 metres from the Town Hall. Lydia Hotel, a contemporary building set within the historic old town, has a spa lounge with several saunas and a pool. Dorpat Hotel is the large, good-value option, 197 rooms on the Emajõgi riverfront with its own Herb Spa, near the AHHAA science centre. V Spa & Conference Hotel is the wellness-led choice, and Hotel Soho sits beside Town Hall Square.
Tallinn: two nights
Tallinn Balti Jaam is roughly eight minutes on foot from Town Hall Square, a considerably better arrival than the bus station, which needs a tram ride into the centre. On a rail itinerary this is worth factoring into where you book.
Where to stay in Tallinn
Stay inside the medieval walls. The old town is small, the alternative districts are not appreciably cheaper, and the walls are the reason you came.
Schlössle Hotel is the heritage benchmark: a restored 13th-century merchant's house in a quiet corner of the old town with just 23 rooms, a member of Small Luxury Hotels of the World, a sauna and spa, and a basement cigar lounge built around an open hearth. Queen Elizabeth II stayed here in 2006.
Hotel Telegraaf, Autograph Collection is the most complete full-service option, occupying a converted 19th-century telegraph building with a courtyard, the substantial Telegraaf Spa, and the Michelin-listed Tchaikovsky restaurant on site. If you want a polished city stay rather than a historic curiosity, this is it.
The Three Sisters spreads 23 rooms across three connected medieval merchant houses and is the design-forward choice. Hotel St. Petersbourg is the heritage option at a lower rate.
Nunne Boutique Hotel deserves particular mention on a rail trip: 74 rooms built into the city walls, about five minutes from Balti Jaam and four from Town Hall Square, with a restaurant and spa. It is hard to beat for a short stay with luggage. Go Hotel Shnelli sits directly beside the station and is the budget version of the same logic.
For views over cobbles, Swissôtel Tallinn occupies the tallest building in the city. At the value end inside or beside the old town, Meriton Old Town Garden, Merchants House Hotel, My City Hotel and Bern Boutique Hotel all review well. Kalev Spa & Waterpark is the family choice.
Tallinn sells out earliest of the three capitals, particularly across summer and the December market period. The Estonia travel guides on trip1 cover Tartu alongside Tallinn, which helps if you are still deciding whether to build in the stopover.
Booking and paying: hotels with crypto
One development worth flagging, particularly for a regional audience.
Both Lithuania and Estonia have positioned themselves as regulated hubs for digital assets under the EU's MiCA framework, and travel has been among the earlier consumer categories to reflect that. trip1 now lets travellers book hotels with crypto, paying for a room in Bitcoin, USDT or other major assets while the property is settled in euros and never has to handle digital currency at all. From the hotel's side nothing changes. From the traveller's side, it removes the conversion step.
On a single-city trip that is a marginal convenience. On a three-country itinerary it is more useful than it first appears. You are making three bookings across three markets, and a payment method that works identically for all of them, without card foreign-transaction fees and without moving funds into a bank account first, takes one variable out of the planning. For visitors arriving from outside the euro area, or for anyone holding crypto who would rather spend it than convert it, the ability to pay in trip1 for hotels with crypto is a practical advantage rather than a novelty.
It also fits the region. The Baltic states have spent a decade building a reputation for digital-first public and financial infrastructure, from e-Residency in Estonia to a dense fintech licensing environment in Lithuania. A traveller booking a Riga hotel in crypto from a Vilnius café is, in a modest way, an expression of that.
What comes next
The current rail service is a stopgap in the best sense. Rail Baltica, the 900-kilometre standard-gauge line that will eventually connect Tallinn to the Polish border via Riga and Kaunas, passed the point of no return some time ago. As of mid-2026, 267 kilometres of main line are construction-ready, around 43 percent of the first phase, with track laying underway in Lithuania and terminal works advancing at Riga Central Station and Tallinn's Ülemiste. The first phase targets 2030.
When it opens, journey times between the capitals will roughly halve and the trip described here will compress into something closer to a long weekend. Until then, the slower version has its own argument. Eleven hours from Vilnius to Tallinn, with a change at a border town where you can swing between two countries, is not the fastest way to see the Baltics. It may well be the best one.

Latvian and international defence industry to gather in Rēzekne this week  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:42 UTC
23:53:42 KST

On 6 and 7 September, the Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum will take place in Rēzekne, bringing together more than 180 participants from Latvia and abroad. The two-day programme will begin with the National Armed Forces Industry Day, featuring demonstrations of defence and dual-use technologies on land, water and in the air, as well as company visits. On 7 September, the GORS Concert Hall will host discussions with international experts, technology presentations, an EXPO and one-to-one business meetings. At the heart of the Forum is a practical question: how can Latvian companies use their technologies and manufacturing capabilities to become part of international defence industry supply chains?
Representatives from more than 15 countries are expected to attend the Forum, including more than 45 international companies and up to 120 Latvian companies. International participants include TensorOne, AJB Subsea, HISDESAT, NEST AI, Fischer Panda and Sine Engineering, while representatives of BAE Systems, Dedrone by Axon, Wolfram Europe, SAF Tehnika, Silmor, Pērkons Energy, Redwire, RAW and Origin Robotics will also take part in the programme.
More than 150 pre-arranged business meetings are planned during the Forum, giving Latvian companies an opportunity to meet potential customers, cooperation partners, investors, suppliers and representatives of the international defence industry.
“Latvian companies have technologies and manufacturing capabilities that enable them to compete internationally. The key challenge now is to turn this potential into concrete cooperation opportunities and export deals. This is why the Forum places a strong emphasis on practical cooperation, creating direct connections between Latvian companies, international industry representatives, potential customers and partners,” says Līva Stūrmane, Chair of the Board of the Latvian Exporters Association “The Red Jackets”.
6 September: technologies in action on land, water and in the air
The Forum will begin on Sunday, 6 September, with the Industry Day “Technologies in Action”. From 10:00 to 15:00, demonstrations organised by the Ministry of Defence will showcase defence and dual-use technologies operating on land, water and in the air. The programme will also include a tactical briefing and industry presentations.
The demonstrations will take place at the former Rēzekne I railway station site and in the area near Lake Kovšu, offering participants an opportunity to experience the capabilities and innovation potential of Latvia’s defence industry in practice and to establish contacts with representatives of the industry and the military. Following the demonstrations, from 15:00 to 17:30, the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) will organise visits to LEAX Rēzekne, Bee Tactics and VEREMS, where international participants will have an opportunity to learn more about the companies’ operations, manufacturing capabilities and solutions.
From 17:30, participant registration and the official opening will continue at the Latgale Embassy GORS.
“Strengthening Latvia’s defence capabilities and developing the domestic defence industry are closely interconnected. Every company capable of developing technologies, systems or components for defence needs strengthens both national security and its own export potential. It is equally important to provide the industry with opportunities to demonstrate its solutions in real-life environments while receiving direct feedback from soldiers and international partners,” emphasises Raivis Melnis, Minister of Defence of the Republic of Latvia.
7 September: from technology to international markets
On Monday, 7 September, at the GORS Concert Hall, the Forum will continue with the programme “From Technology to International Markets”, focusing on the growth of Latvia’s defence industry and opportunities to integrate into international supply chains.
The day will begin with Uģis Norītis, representing the Ministry of Defence, who will present on the development of a globally competitive Latvian defence industry. Laura Štrovalde, Diāna Baranova, Magnus-Valdemar Saar, Head of Wolfram Europa, and Mārtiņš Tiknuss, Head of Gateway&Partners, will discuss the development of the Baltic defence industry and regional cooperation.
International defence strategy consultant Thibault Normand will address opportunities for Latvian companies to enter international defence supply chains, while representatives of Silmor, Pērkons Energy, Redwire and UniLAB Defence will discuss financing, scaling up production and entering export markets.
Later in the programme, Normunds Bergs, CEO of SAF Tehnika, will speak about critical communications, spectrum analysers and electronic warfare.
Niklas Edelsvärd, Sales Director at BAE Systems Land Systems, Edgars Šadris, Deputy State Secretary at the Ministry of Economics, Reinis Purvēns, Head of RAW, and Christian Emaus, Regional Director for the Nordics, Baltics and NATO at Dedrone by Axon, will discuss the journey of dual-use technologies from development to integration into international value chains and cooperation with major system integrators.
Māris Ķuda, Head of Government Relations at Origin Robotics, will address the role of precision technologies on the modern battlefield.
The Forum will conclude with Christian Emaus, Regional Director for the Nordics, Baltics and NATO at Dedrone by Axon, sharing how interconnected data, a common operational picture and rapid decision-making can help regain control of the airspace. Following the conference programme, the EXPO and business meetings will continue until 15:00.
Growth of the defence industry creates new export opportunities
As European countries increase defence investment and strengthen supply chains, new opportunities are emerging not only for defence industry companies but also for civilian manufacturers and technology companies.
The Forum’s priority sectors include artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and ICT, drones and unmanned systems, smart energy and advanced materials, electronics and engineering, as well as the chemical and metalworking industries. The Forum programme will continue on 8 September in Riga with company visits, giving international participants an opportunity to learn more about companies’ technologies and manufacturing capabilities and to continue the discussions initiated in Rēzekne.
The Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum is organised by the Latvian Exporters Association “The Red Jackets” in cooperation with the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), the Ministry of Economics and the Ministry of Defence. Further information about the Forum, its programme and participants is available on the Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum website.

Finland's Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN, Heli Lehto, made a statement on behalf of eight countries at a UN General Assembly session addressing the situation in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
"We, the Nordic and Baltic countries, call on Russia to immediately and fully fulfill its obligations under international law. We demand the immediate, complete, and unconditional withdrawal of all Russian forces from the territory of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders," the diplomat said.

She pointed to the sharp increase in Russian attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure in 2026. "UN independent investigators continue to report mass arbitrary detentions and the widespread use of torture against civilians, detainees, and prisoners of war," she said.

"Human rights organizations have documented the large-scale forced displacement and illegal deportation of Ukrainian children. Ukrainian authorities report deliberate efforts to destroy Ukrainian national identity in the occupied areas, including through militarization, indoctrination, and the illegal adoption of children," the Finnish representative said.

"We remain firmly committed to the creation of a special tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine and continue to steadfastly support the work of the International Criminal Court," Lehto concluded.
The diplomat presented the joint statement on behalf of Denmark, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Sweden, and Finland.

Lithuania’s Luna Robotics puts 24/7 drone vision at heart of Baltic security  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:33 UTC
23:53:33 KST

Lithuanian defence technology company Luna Robotics is turning battlefield lessons from Ukraine into scalable technologies for unmanned systems, developing China-free imaging solutions that allow drones to operate around the clock. CEO Elvinas Kukys believes Lithuania can become a major European defence-tech hub if it succeeds in scaling production, investment and international market access.
“Luna Robotics was created to solve an operational gap: unmanned systems lose effectiveness in darkness and poor visibility,” Kukys emphasised to The Baltic Times.
Drawing on military experience and direct contact with Ukrainian users, the company builds compact, low-latency imaging systems for FPV drones, interceptor drones and other unmanned platforms.
The war in Ukraine has fundamentally changed the pace at which defence technology is developed and deployed.
“Ukraine has shown that defence innovation is now measured in weeks, not years. Technology must be affordable, scalable and continuously improved through operator feedback,” Kukys said.
Battlefield success, he argues, increasingly depends not on creating a theoretically perfect product but on rapid integration, dependable supplies and the ability to update software as tactics and threats evolve.
Maintaining drone capabilities after dark is one of Luna Robotics' principal areas of focus.
“Night vision is essential because modern operations do not pause after sunset,” Kukys said.
Effective low-light imaging allows operators to maintain reconnaissance, navigation, target identification and interception capabilities when conventional cameras become ineffective.
“It is becoming a baseline requirement, not a premium feature,” the CEO said.
The company's LunaCam provides low-latency, 24/7 imaging in a lightweight format, with colour and monochrome configurations and optional infrared illumination. Its onboard processing can support software including object recognition and last-mile targeting, while radar-data integration can guide operators towards aerial targets.
Luna Robotics develops and manufactures its technology in Lithuania, which Kukys sees as an important contribution to Baltic security and resilience.
“We develop and manufacture our technology in Lithuania, creating local engineering know-how, production capacity and a resilient allied supply base,” he said.
Its technology can be integrated into FPV drones, interceptors, unmanned ground vehicles, or UGVs, and other platforms. Local capabilities can help Baltic defence partners deploy systems faster while reducing dependence on geopolitically risky suppliers.
“In defence, supply chains are a security issue, not merely a purchasing decision,” Kukys said.
Luna Robotics says its hardware and software are China-free. Kukys points to availability, export restrictions, cybersecurity, traceability and long-term maintenance among the potential risks associated with reliance on Chinese components.
Kukys believes Lithuania possesses many of the ingredients needed to become a significant European defence technology hub, including engineering talent, military understanding, rapid decision-making and direct access to lessons from Ukraine.
“Its small size can be an advantage: developers, users and institutions can work closely and iterate quickly,” he said.
However, Lithuania, he says, now needs to scale procurement and manufacturing capacity, develop specialist talent, attract patient capital and improve international market access.
Luna Robotics has similarly ambitious plans for its own expansion.
“In five years, I see Luna Robotics as a leading European provider of vision and autonomy technology for unmanned systems,” Kukys said.
The company aims to serve FPV and interceptor drones, UGVs and potentially unmanned surface vehicles, or USVs, while expanding manufacturing and R&D in Lithuania and deepening partnerships with European and US manufacturers.

Archaeology sheds new light on Suleyman the Magnificent’s final campaign in Hungary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:52:14 UTC
23:52:14 KST

- Archaeologists identify remains of mosque, dervish lodge, guesthouse, guard barracks, wooden palisade and civilian buildings
 
Archaeological research near Szigetvar Castle in Hungary, where Ottoman Sultan Suleyman the Magnificent led his final military campaign, has revealed that the settlement established around his presumed place of death was considerably larger than previously thought.
The findings have provided new insights into the size, structure and daily life of the Ottoman settlement known as Turbek, which developed around a tomb built in Suleyman’s honor.
Research conducted by Hungary’s University of Pecs in 2024 and 2025 found Ottoman-era artifacts scattered across an area of approximately 80 hectares, with their concentration varying across different parts of the site.
The evidence indicates that the settlement was not only more extensive than earlier estimates suggested but also relatively prosperous.
The findings have drawn renewed attention to Suleyman’s last campaign and the Ottoman remains near Szigetvar on the 460th anniversary of his death during the siege of the castle on the night of Sept. 6-7, 1566.
 
Suleyman’s final campaign and death
Suleyman, the longest-reigning sultan in Ottoman history, who ruled for nearly 46 years, left Istanbul on May 1, 1566, to lead his 13th and final military campaign.
Despite his advanced age and declining health, he traveled at the head of the army. His imperial tent was erected on a hill overlooking Szigetvar Castle, at what is now believed to be the site of the tomb complex.
Suleyman died in his tent during the night of Sept. 6-7. The fortress fell to Ottoman forces shortly afterward.
Historical sources say the sultan’s death was concealed from the army to prevent a breakdown in morale and discipline and to ensure the peaceful accession of his son, Selim II.
According to historical accounts, Suleyman’s internal organs were removed to preserve his body, which was treated with amber and musk before being temporarily buried beneath the throne inside his tent.
Some historical sources and widely accepted accounts maintain that his internal organs were buried at the encampment.
His body was reportedly exhumed about 42 days later and placed in a carriage for the return journey, during which officials continued to act as if the sultan were alive. His death was formally announced after Selim II arrived in Belgrade.
 
Ottoman settlement developed around tomb
On Selim II’s orders, a tomb was built at the site where Suleyman was believed to have died and where his internal organs were thought to have been buried.
As the tomb developed into an important pilgrimage site, a mosque, dervish lodge, guesthouse and guard barracks were constructed nearby.
The complex was protected by a wooden palisade and other defensive structures, while a civilian settlement gradually emerged around it.
Known as Turbek, the settlement was destroyed as Ottoman rule in the region ended. Its exact location was eventually forgotten after the buildings disappeared and the land was converted into vineyards and gardens.
Scientific research locates long-lost tomb
Modern efforts to locate Suleyman’s tomb began after the Turkish Cooperation and Coordination Agency and the Municipality of Szigetvar signed an agreement in 2012.
An interdisciplinary team led by Professor Norbert Pap of the University of Pecs studied historical documents, maps and land records, as well as a plan of the tomb complex drawn in 1664.
The researchers concluded that the original tomb complex stood on Vineyard Hill in the Turbek-Zsibot area, about 4.2 kilometers northeast of Szigetvar Castle.
Excavations launched in 2015 uncovered a square building that researchers identified as the tomb constructed in Suleyman’s honor.
Subsequent work revealed traces of a mosque, dervish lodge, guesthouse, guard barracks, wooden palisade and civilian buildings.
 
Discoveries offer glimpse of daily life
During the 2024-2025 research period, Turkish and Hungarian researchers led by the University of Pecs used modern surveying equipment to conduct surface studies and geophysical surveys across the wider area surrounding the tomb complex.
Everyday objects, ceramics, coins, jewelry and examples of Ottoman metalwork were discovered around buildings, some of which were constructed of brick and covered with roof tiles.
Archaeologists also uncovered a well and large storage pits containing traces of grain, terracotta pieces from heating systems, footed bowls, fragments of porcelain cups and pieces of painted glass vessels.
Other finds included a rare 16th-century gold coin, a silver coin from the Crimean Khanate, pieces of Ottoman tableware, rings, decorated buckles and horse-harness ornaments.
Researchers said the findings point to the existence of an extensive Ottoman settlement beyond the central tomb complex and suggest that some of its residents and visitors were affluent by the standards of the period.

U.S. contacts with Ukraine and the Russian Federation have thawed the negotiation process, but there has been no breakthrough so far, says a political scientist
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:51:46 EEST
23:51:46 KST

U.S. contacts with Ukraine and the Russian Federation have thawed the negotiation process, but there has been no breakthrough so far, says a political scientist
Kyiv • UNN
According to the expert, it was important for Washington to receive positive signals from both sides, and in his assessment, this became the main result of the visits.
American negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Russia and Ukraine on September 5 and 6. A journalist from UNN spoke with Oleksii Buriachenko, president of the International Institute for Security Studies, about what to expect after the negotiation process and whether it produced any real results.
Details
Oleksii Buriachenko noted that the very emergence of a new contact between the parties is already a certain result. However, one should not expect these meetings to bring a swift end to the war for now, because, according to him, the main participants in the process have different interests.
I would not call what happened full-fledged negotiations. It was more an attempt to "revive" the negotiation process, which had been blocked by the Russian Federation, because for six months no meetings had taken place in any format. Thawing the negotiation process is better than a complete absence of such dialogue. This is probably a certain positive development that should be noted following the communications between the two special representatives of the President of the United States of America—Witkoff and Kushner
The expert also believes that the resumption of negotiations was particularly important for the Donald Trump administration. The US president promised to end the Russian-Ukrainian war during the election campaign, and now, in the political analyst's view, this issue also has domestic political significance for the White House.
Trump had already promised to end the Russian-Ukrainian war during the election campaign. This is the only foreign policy issue that was incorporated into his inaugural address, meaning it was, to a certain extent, legally recorded. Now, ahead of the midterm elections, the Democrats are actively attacking Trump and the Republican Party specifically over this issue. Therefore, this story, which is disadvantageous for Trump, had to be somehow rebooted
That is why, according to the political analyst, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were primarily carrying out a tactical task—namely, establishing contacts with both Kyiv and Moscow. Oleksii Buriachenko notes that it was important for Washington to receive positive signals from both sides, and in his assessment, this became the main result of the visits.

At the same time, the political analyst sees a long-term goal of the US administration as well. There is a maximum plan—to achieve, by the midterm elections, at least a first approximation of what Trump promised, and then a second approximation approximately six months later, as Kushner said. That is, ultimately, to end the Russian-Ukrainian war. But it seems to me that they may also remain with the minimum plan and continue consultations if they realize that, for a whole range of reasons, it will not be possible to move toward quick results. This is the degree of flexibility that suits the American side as of today
The expert also believes that the current situation does not indicate Russia's readiness to quickly agree to peace. He points to the lack of sufficient pressure from the United States and Europe. Meanwhile, Ukraine's long-range strikes remain one of the few factors that genuinely influence Russia.

In the expert's opinion, Ukraine, the United States, Russia, and the European states are currently pursuing different goals. Thousands turn out in Serbia for funeral of  'Butcher of Bosnia' Ratko Mladić
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:50:50 BST
23:50:50 KST

Thousands turn out in Serbia for funeral of 'Butcher of Bosnia' Ratko Mladić
- Published
Thousands of people have turned out in Serbia's capital, Belgrade, to attend the funeral of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić.
Widely known as the Butcher of Bosnia, Mladić died at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence in the UN prison in The Hague, the Netherlands.
He was found guilty of genocide by a UN war crimes tribunal for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when around 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed. It was described as Europe's worst atrocity since World War Two.
A Serbian government minister had initially said that Mladić would be given a state funeral but those plans were changed after objections from some European leaders. On Monday, the EU denounced Mladić's "glorification".
"Ratko Mladić was a convicted war criminal who had committed war crimes, genocide, and crimes against humanity," the EU said in a statement.
"Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries," the statement said.
Serbia has been a candidate to join the EU since 2012, even though membership talks have recently stalled.
Ratko Mladić commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s against the Bosnian Croat and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) armies.
During the 1992-1995 Bosnian war, his troops committed what became known as "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a bid to expel the non-Serbian population by force. They besieged the capital city of Sarajevo, with the deaths of more than 10,000 people.
Mladić was arrested in 2011, 16 years after he was first indicted, and sentenced to life in prison in 2021 after a nine-year trial.
Despite his conviction for genocide, Mladić remains a national figure perceived by many Serbs as a heroic defender of the nation.
Many Serb nationalists see him as a hero and protector, particularly in the Bosnian Serb entity of Republika Srpska, where his death sparked vigils.
Several Serbian government ministers joined the crowds paying tribute outside the church where Mladić lay in state before the burial, including the Defence Minister Bratislav Gašić, and the Minister of Justice Nenad Vujić, local media reported.
The funeral service was led by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije, who said Mladić's name would remain "deeply etched in the memory and prayers of the majority of our Serbian Orthodox people, who feel and nurture a deep sense of gratitude towards him".
Early in the day, long queues formed outside the small St Luka church, as people waited to go in and pay their respects to the coffin. Many of those in the crowds were army veterans and some men were draped in flags printed with his picture on.
Crowds arrived several hours before the funeral began to light candles outside the church, accompanied by a choir on a loudspeaker in the sunshine.
Inside the church, Mladić's coffin was guarded by several men, mainly war veterans, while his wife, son, and grandchildren stood inside receiving condolences.
In a sign of the reverence held for the former general, his coffin was flown back to Serbia last week on a government plane, and was carried from the plane by six soldiers and draped in flags.
Free bus services were organised from Bosnia and most towns in Serbia for anyone who wanted to pay their respects.
On Sunday night, fans of the Serbian football club Red Star Belgrade unveiled a display of Mladic before their derby win over Partizan Belgrade.
For others, the funeral has rekindled painful memories of the war.
A woman in Sarajevo called Zdravka Gvozdjar - whose nine-year-old son was killed by Mladić-led forces during the siege of the city - told Reuters news agency it was "really horrible" that the funeral was taking place in Belgrade.
Mladić "deserved to be erased from memory for good, not to be... promoted as a hero," she said.
"He should be remembered only as a butcher."
Thousands attended the funeral because he "remains a figure of national pride and defiance," said Daniella Peled, Editor at the Institute of War and Peace Reporting NGO - who covered Mladić's war crimes trial in detail.
The war crimes tribunal "provided an incredibly detailed historical record of Mladić's crimes," she told the BBC, but the Serbian media and education system "has not reflected the true scale of his crimes or the perspectives of victims and survivors."
Pro-government Serbian media "depict him as a loyal soldier who simply carried out his duties," Peled said.
"It's extremely challenging for post-conflict societies to undertake a national reckoning or acknowledge responsibility for the crimes of the past."

EXPLAINER - How Germany’s AfD surged in Saxony-Anhalt but missed a majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:50:28 UTC
23:50:28 KST

- German voters put economic problems first, surveys show, as AfD mobilized non-voters and peeled support from conservatives
- Anger at Chancellor Merz ran deep; a survey found 75% of voters in the state believe he damaged CDU’s regional performance
- AfD won a record 43.8% vote but only 39 of 83 seats; coalition talks now hinge on the left-populist BSW’s kingmaker role
Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany scored its strongest result in any state election on Sunday, winning 43.8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt and shaking the political establishment.
The ballot was regional, in a state with less than 3% of Germany’s nationwide electorate. Even so, the outcome increased pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right-led coalition government in Berlin.
For the first time in a German state, a party classified by the state’s domestic intelligence agency as a “proven right-wing extremist” won by such a wide margin and came close to assuming power, despite Merz’s earlier pledges that his government would halt the AfD’s rise by solving people’s problems.
The vote was a particular blow to Merz. His Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which had governed the former East German state for decades in changing coalitions, slumped to a historic low of 17.2% in preliminary official results. 
Why voters swung so hard to the AfD
Surveys point to widespread concern about the economy, anger at Merz’s federal record and the CDU’s failure to field a more popular candidate. Public broadcaster ZDF found that 75% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt believe Merz damaged the CDU’s regional performance. Some 88% said if Merz’s government had pursued better policies, the AfD would not have grown so strong in Saxony-Anhalt.
The AfD also owed its victory to a highly popular lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, 35, who reached beyond the party’s traditional base through a strong social media campaign and close contact with voters. The party more than doubled its 20.8% share from 2021.
Polls show the surge stretched far beyond a hardcore right-wing base. Of about 1.7 million eligible voters, the largest net gain came from people who stayed home in 2021 — about 170,000 — according to infratest dimap. Another roughly 82,000 switched from the CDU, reversing the flow of five years earlier. A smaller net of about 19,000 came from the Free Democrats.
Asked what problems mattered most for their vote, statewide respondents put the economic situation first at 21%, followed by schools and education at 17% and migration at 16%. Infrastructure and doctor shortages were cited by 14%, and the same share named jobs as their top concern.
Saxony-Anhalt has some of Germany’s lowest average wages and one of its highest unemployment rates, at about 8%. About 61% of workers voted for the AfD. 
No majority, and no easy way to govern
The AfD’s record vote, however, did not produce a firm grip on power. It won 39 of 83 seats in the Magdeburg state parliament — three short of the 42 needed to govern alone. Every other major party except the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) has ruled out a formal coalition or cooperation with the AfD, leaving Saxony-Anhalt heading into weeks of uncertainty.
The new parliament is highly fragmented. The CDU holds 15 seats, while the Social Democrats finished third with 9.3% and eight seats. The Greens took 8.9% and the Left Party 8.6%, with eight seats each. The BSW scraped in with 5.3% and five seats. The Free Democrats, partners in the outgoing government, missed the 5% threshold with 2.6%.
An AfD-led government is one possible path, but only with outside help. The most direct route would be BSW support. Party founder Sahra Wagenknecht is not endorsing a coalition with the AfD. Unlike the other parties, however, she has not ruled out cooperation in principle and spoke of a “political new beginning” in Saxony-Anhalt.
“Hopefully there are now majorities in the Magdeburg state parliament for a change of course in energy policy, an end to the sanctions on Russia and better education,” Wagenknecht said.
Several BSW figures repeated on election night that they favor a technocratic premier who governs with shifting majorities, potentially including AfD votes. AfD lead candidate Siegmund, by contrast, has repeatedly said he wants to govern only with an outright majority, arguing that even a margin of two or three seats would be too fragile.
Another option being discussed is that the AfD could try to form a government with support from individual lawmakers in other parties, such as conservatives who decide to back the AfD or even switch sides. Speaking to the news portal Nius, Siegmund said he was stretching out a hand to everyone, adding: “That does not necessarily always apply only to whole parties. It can also apply to individual lawmakers.”
According to Die Welt, AfD politicians have long claimed — without naming names or providing evidence — that they held private talks with CDU state deputies about a possible switch. Any defector, however, would face intense public pressure.
A third option, a government formed against the AfD, would require almost everyone else to work together, from the CDU through the SPD, Greens and Left Party to the BSW. That camp would hold 44 seats.
However, political observers are pointing out that this five-party alliance would be highly unusual and hard to hold together.
The CDU has ruled out a coalition or cooperation not only with the AfD but also with the socialist Left Party. It says it could accept informal cooperation to keep the AfD from power, but only in exchange for policy concessions.
The BSW, which campaigned to drive the CDU from office, opposes Premier Sven Schulze or any other CDU figure staying in charge. It wants a nonpartisan executive led by an independent figure acceptable to the parties in the state parliament.

Ukraine's Prosecutor General says he won't resign amid major scandal unless Zelensky asks
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said on Sept. 7 that he has no plans to resign amid a major scandal and would do so at the request of his colleagues, the president, or parliament, public broadcaster Suspilne reported.
The statement came after Kravchenko denied any connection to a criminal organization running protection for scam call centers to launder millions of hryvnias, allegedly involving a senior official in the Prosecutor General's office.
The alleged criminal scheme was uncovered by Ukraine's two chief anti-corruption bodies — Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) — on Sept. 4.
Kravchenko said he has not made a decision to step down as of now. He said seven prosecutors could be dismissed.
"I'm not clinging to my position, and I never will. I always say: the team comes first, and then there’s me," he told reporters.
The Prosecutor General heads the overall system of court prosecutions in Ukraine and is appointed directly by the president.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has not commented on the scandal. The President’s Office did not respond to a request for comment on Kravchenko's future by the time of publication.
NABU detained, Serhii Kropyva, deputy head of the office's international cooperation department, suspected of laundering assets worth more than Hr 89 million ($2 million).
Ukraine's High Anti-Corruption Court on Sept. 7 remanded Kropyva in custody until Nov. 2 and set his bail at Hr 120 million ($2.7 million). Kropyva has been suspended from his duties.
As part of the investigation, searches were also conducted in Kravchenko's office.
According to investigators, the official created the group in mid-2025, recruiting serving prosecutors and associates outside the Prosecutor General's Office. The group allegedly received systematic bribes in exchange for allowing scam call centers to operate without interference. The call centers targeted both Ukrainian citizens and foreigners, investigators said.
Previously, Kravchenko announced that all staff working on cases involving illegal call centers would now have to undergo polygraph testing.
However, Kravchenko may have been implicated in the alleged scheme.
Recordings released by NABU refer to someone identified as the "boss" who protected the group Kropyva is thought to have led, who had the patronymic "Andriiovych," and who previously led the State Tax Service.
Kravchenko served as head of Ukraine's State Tax Service from December 2024 to June 2025.
An earlier Telegram post by the Prosecutor General's Office confirms that the investigation understands the term "boss" as referring to Kravchenko.
At a Sept. 6 court hearing, a SAPO prosecutor also mentioned the close relationship between Kropyva and Kravchenko. Case materials allege Kropyva arranged repair work at a house in Kozyn, an an elite residential area south of Kyiv where Kravchenko lives.
Kravchenko later confirmed that his family rents the house and said it needed some finishing work and equipment to be installed. He promised to declare the property.
"My position does not exempt me from scrutiny. But it also does not waive the requirement to substantiate accusations with facts," Kravchenko said.

UN's Albanese: Gaza rubble removal could erase atrocity evidence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:46:35 UTC
23:46:35 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza rubble removal risks erasing evidence of alleged crimes, UN expert Albanese says
A UN expert warned Monday that large-scale rubble removal in parts of Gaza under Israeli control risked erasing traces of "atrocity crimes", and preventing the recovery and identification of human remains.
Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the Palestinian territories, warned in a statement that the implications of Israel's "ongoing removal, crushing and relocation of rubble in Gaza" were "profound".
"Gaza's rubble contains human remains and physical evidence relevant to the investigation of alleged international crimes, including genocide," she said, pointing to estimates from Palestinian authorities that more than 10,000 people remain buried under the debris in the war-ravaged Palestinian enclave.
The Italian-born independent expert has faced harsh criticism from Israel and some of its allies over her long-standing accusations that Israel is committing genocide and other war crimes against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Albanese, who was appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022 but who does not speak on behalf of the United Nations, said she had received credible information from multiple sources last month of "deliberate and widespread removal, crushing and transport of rubble".
In the devastated, Israeli-occupied Palestinian territory, "rubble is not just construction waste", the expert insisted.
"It is part of a crime scene, a graveyard, and the material record of what happened during a brutal and senseless bombing campaign that lasted two years.
'Illegal'
Israel's full-scale war on Gaza reduced much of the Palestinian territory to rubble.
The relentless Israeli bombardment and ground offensive has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, including more than 1,330 since a ceasefire agreed last October, according to Gaza's health ministry.
Hamas's October 7 attack resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to Israeli figures.
Many of the Palestinians killed in Gaza are children.
Albanese insisted on Monday that the possibility of recovering human remains in Gaza was far from theoretical.
She pointing to the burial last month of 112 members of one extended civilian family whose remains were recovered from under Gaza City buildings destroyed by Israel in November 2023.
"The remains of 41 others killed in the same strike were never located," her statement said.
"It is vital that before decisions are made on displacement or crushing by the occupying army or its allies, the recovery and dignified identification of human remains, systematic documentation of sites and materials, preservation of potentially relevant evidence, and an unbroken chain of custody under independent oversight must take place," Albanese said.
The expert called for international criminal investigators to oversee the evidence gathering, and to warn countries and companies involved in any removal that they "could incur international criminal responsibility" if they destroyed evidence of international crimes.
"Destroying evidence of atrocity crimes is illegal," she stressed.
"It is unacceptable that the reconstruction of Gaza is conditioned upon the erasure of its past and the evidence required to secure justice for its victims."
The United States, a major ally of Israel, imposed sanctions on Albanese after she criticised Washington's policy on Gaza.

Syrian nuclear site destroyed by IDF in 2007 was useful for weapon production, IAEA chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:46:22 UTC
23:46:22 KST

The nuclear reactor Syria had nearly completed in 2007 when Israeli jets destroyed it was of a type that could quickly produce fissile material usable in nuclear weapons, International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director-General Rafael Grossi said on Monday.
The United Nations nuclear watchdog has described its recent investigation into secret nuclear activities under the Assad family's rule as a " historic breakthrough. The investigation uncovered around 73 metric tons of natural uranium metal, mainly in the form of reactor fuel.
In a report to member states seen by Reuters, the IAEA confirmed its previous finding that the bombed site in Syria's eastern province of Deir al-Zor was a nuclear reactor under construction, and that fuel for it had been made in Syria, all of which should have been declared at the time to the agency.
"This is a reactor that is very efficient in the production of fissile material that could be used directly for the fabrication of nuclear weapons," Grossi told a press conference, adding that it was "almost completed."
"That was a very serious proliferation concern," he said, while cautioning that the then-authorities' intentions "cannot be judged."
Syria's new government committed to working with IAEA on nuclear issues
Since the ouster of former president Bashar al-Assad in late 2024, Syria's new authorities have committed to working with the IAEA to answer questions relating to so-called nuclear safeguards - the process of accounting for and monitoring nuclear material.
"Having received the necessary access and information from Syria, ...the agency has been able to clarify and resolve the agency's questions concerning the outstanding safeguards issues related to Syria's past nuclear activities," Grossi said in a speech to the IAEA's 35-nation board.
"I welcome Syria's transparency and cooperation with the agency, which facilitates the resolution of the outstanding safeguards issues related to Syria's past nuclear activities," he added.

A majority of Israelis fear that an October 7-style terrorist attack may originate from the West Bank, according to findings released by the Jerusalem Center for Foreign Affairs and Security (JCFA) on Monday.
The findings show that 77% of Israelis, including 86% of Jewish Israelis, are afraid that Palestinian Authority security forces could conduct a large-scale attack much like Hamas did on October 7, 2023.
The study further found that 75% of Jewish Israelis, among 67% of all Israelis, oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state along the 1967 lines.
Earlier on Monday, Defense Minister Israel Katz announced that, should Israel identify a plan to launch an "October-7 style" attack, he and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have directed the IDF to target senior PA officials in an "all-out war" on terrorism in the West Bank.
"If the security apparatuses of the Palestinian Authority and the bodies associated with them launch, or we know for certain that they are about to launch, an October 7-style terrorist attack against forces and Jewish settlements, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and I instructed the IDF to prepare to launch an all-out war against senior officials and mechanisms of the [Palestinian] Authority, the bodies associated with them, and against all terrorist infrastructure in Judea and Samaria - in order to quickly bring about their complete defeat," said Katz.
JCFA warns of potential for Oct. 7-style attack by PA in West Bank
The release of the findings follows the “turning the guns” warning issued by the JCFA on July 15, when a study by Lt.-Col. (res.) Maurice Hirsch noted the buildup of the PA's military capabilities.
According to Hirsch's findings, the PA security forces have grown to a size 133% larger than that permitted by the Oslo Accords, reaching a total of about 70,000 personnel, 40,000 more than the number allowed by the agreement.
The study noted that, in the West Bank, the over 50,000 armed PA personnel breach the permitted amount by approximately 400%, with their arms including rocket-propelled grenades (RPGs) and shoulder-launched missiles.
Four potential routes, each totaling around 22 kilometers in length, were identified by the study through which the forces could reach Israeli civilians in a relatively short period of time.
The poll was conducted in cooperation between JCFA and Lazar Research, surveying a representative sample of 703 respondents between September 2 and 4.
Miriam Sela-Eitam contributed to this report.

Saudi Arabia set to grant IAEA more investigative powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:46:11 UTC
23:46:11 KST

A planned US-Saudi atomic deal does not include Riyadh signing the Additional Protocol, which gives the UN nuclear watchdog sweeping inspection powers, but something close to it on some points is in the works, the agency's chief said Monday.
The US and Saudi Arabia reached an agreement on civil nuclear power cooperation in July that would let Riyadh enrich uranium and build nuclear reactors using US technology.
Non-proliferation groups, such as the Arms Control Association, have criticized the planned "123 agreement" for not including the Additional Protocol, which grants the International Atomic Energy Agency extra powers such as the ability to carry out snap inspections at undeclared locations.
Iran implemented the Additional Protocol from 2016 to 2021 under a nuclear deal with major powers that unraveled after the US pulled out in 2018.
Saudi's prepare to go beyond its core obligations
IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said that while the Additional Protocol would be the "ideal setup," Riyadh was preparing to go beyond its core obligations under its Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement governing relations with the IAEA.
"What is important is that in the consultations, in the preparation process, it has been possible to introduce a number of provisions to the bilateral agreement that will give the agency additional verification and monitoring authorizations," he told a press conference.
Those would relate to activities such as uranium enrichment and the step preceding it, known as uranium conversion, as well as reprocessing, which can separate plutonium from spent reactor fuel.
"These are sensitive activities, as we all know. So for those we are going to have authorizations and capacities which are very, very similar to those that you may find in an Additional Protocol," he said, without elaborating.
Once the details are finalized, the bilateral agreement between the IAEA and Saudi Arabia will be presented to the IAEA's 35-nation Board of Governors, Grossi said.

Education Minister Kisch asks High Court to preserve proportional funding for haredi schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:46:08 UTC
23:46:08 KST

Education Minister Yoav Kisch asked the High Court of Justice to preserve a system that funds party-affiliated haredi (ultra-Orthodox) schools according to the amount of core curriculum they teach, placing him directly at odds with the attorney-general.
On Sunday, Kisch asked the court to cancel an order requiring the government to justify the system and to reject a petition filed by religious freedom advocacy group Hiddush.
The dispute concerns hundreds of schools operated by the Independent Education Center and Ma’ayan Hahinuch Hatorani Bnei Yosef, which are affiliated with United Torah Judaism and Shas, respectively.
The schools are recognized by the state but are not part of the state school system. A special legal provision allows the two networks to receive funding on the same basis as state schools. Other recognized but unofficial schools generally receive 75% of equivalent state-school funding.
Hiddush argues that the networks are entitled to full funding only if they teach the full core curriculum, including mathematics, English, and science. It claims that schools have continued to receive funding despite failing to meet those requirements and that the Education Ministry’s supervision has not provided an accurate picture of what is taught.
Kisch disputes that interpretation. He defended the ministry’s practice of adjusting each school’s funding according to the proportion of the core curriculum it teaches. Under that system, a school assessed as teaching 85% of the required program may receive funding at a similar rate.
Kisch warns all-or-nothing rule could drive schools from state oversight
The minister argued that the system has encouraged schools to expand their core studies. An “all-or-nothing” rule could instead push schools out of the networks and into educational frameworks subject to fewer state requirements, he said.
Kisch also argued that previous attorneys-general and court rulings had accepted proportional funding. The attorney-general’s position is that the arrangement was, at most, temporary and never provided a permanent legal basis for funding network schools that do not meet their full obligations.
The disagreement led Kisch to obtain separate legal representation rather than join the state’s response filed on behalf of the Education and Finance ministries.
The court first sought additional information after a January 5 hearing at which the state hadn’t filed a preliminary response addressing the substance of the petition.
On January 8, Justices Dafna Barak-Erez, David Mintz, and Ruth Ronnen ordered the state to provide information already held by the Education Ministry. The court asked what core studies the schools must teach, how compliance is calculated, how teacher qualifications and external examinations are considered, and how the schools are supervised.
Court questions funding rules and oversight of haredi schools
After receiving a supplemental filing, the court issued a conditional order on February 17, requiring the government to justify its policy before the court reaches a final decision.
The court asked why each school’s funding should not depend on teaching the full core curriculum, employing suitably trained teachers, and participating in external assessment exams at rates comparable to state schools.
It also asked why the ministries should not establish school-by-school supervision that does not rely solely on self-reporting or visits arranged in advance, and why schools that fail to meet the conditions should not be removed from the networks.
Kisch’s Monday response said Education Ministry data showed substantial improvement. According to the filing, 498 of the networks’ 517 schools taught between 96% and 100% of the required core curriculum during the 2025-26 school year. Of those, 476 were assessed as teaching the full program.
Those figures are disputed. The attorney-general’s response said the ministry’s calculation method could conceal gaps in individual subjects.
Shortcomings in teacher training
ACCORDING TO the state, schools that did not teach English or mathematics in entire grades could still be classified as teaching more than 95% of the program because the ministry calculated total hours across subjects and age groups.
The state also identified shortcomings in teacher training, external testing, and enforcement.
Kisch acknowledged a shortage of trained teachers but argued that similar shortages exist in state schools. He also said teacher qualifications had not previously been treated as a direct condition for funding a school.
His filing presented different qualification rates for each subject, ranging from 4.6% for middle-school science teachers to 24.5% for general elementary-school teaching. Kisch said the ministry had introduced a multiyear training program intended to improve those figures.
The minister also said the ministry strengthened inspections and enforcement, saying that removal notices were sent to 22 schools, and two Independent Education Center schools were subsequently transferred out of the network.
Under the transition proposed by Attorney-General Gali Baharav Miara, a school that does not teach the full curriculum during the 2026-27 school year could continue receiving reduced funding only if it commits to full compliance the following year. A school that refuses would face removal from the network.
Kisch also argued that the court should exercise restraint because Israel is approaching an election and haredi education funding is politically disputed.
Hiddush rejected that position. Dr. Yifat Solel, the organization’s deputy director and the lawyer who filed the petition, accused Kisch of seeking to preserve public funding without ensuring that the schools provide the education for which the money was allocated.
The High Court must now decide whether the responses justify the existing arrangement or whether to make its order final.

Reporter's Notebook: The two faces of General Ratko Mladic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:46:02 UTC
23:46:02 KST

BANJA LUKA, Republika Srpska – In the center of Banja Luka, at a memorial dedicated to those killed in the wars accompanying the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, a smaller memorial had appeared. It showed the photo of a man decked in military garb and was accompanied by floral wreaths. It was for Gen. Ratko Mladic.
The former commander of the Bosnian Serb Army died on August 27 at the age of 84. He was serving a life sentence imposed by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY).
Yet in Republika Srpska, the Serb-majority entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the reaction encountered by The Jerusalem Post was often far removed from the international condemnation that followed his death.
“Mladic defended us when we were under attack,” a Banja Luka resident told the Post. “He fought for Serb rights.”
Others who spoke with the Post during a visit to the city similarly described Mladic as a hero, reflecting the extraordinary divide that continues to surround his legacy more than three decades after the end of the Bosnian War.
Those feelings, often buried in the hope of looking to the future, rose to the surface again when Mladic died last week. They were visible again on Monday, when thousands gathered outside a Serbian Orthodox church in Belgrade ahead of his burial.
Mourners carried Serbian flags and photographs of the former military leader, while free buses were provided from towns in Serbia and from Bosnia for those wishing to attend. His coffin was displayed inside the church as his family received condolences.
The reverence is juxtaposed alongside a judicial record that is among the most serious to emerge from the wars that accompanied the breakup of Yugoslavia.
Mladic's genocide conviction
In 2017, the ICTY convicted Mladic of genocide over the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, as well as persecution, extermination, murder, deportation, and forcible transfer. An estimated 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed following the fall of the town of Srebrenica in July 1995.
Mladic was also convicted of crimes connected to the campaign of sniping and shelling against civilians during the siege of Sarajevo and the taking hostage of UN personnel. His life sentence was upheld on appeal in 2021.
Mladic was, alongside former Bosnian Serb political leader Radovan Karadazic, the highest-ranking Bosnian Serb official to be convicted by the Hague tribunal. Former Serbian and Yugoslav president Slobodan Milosevic died in custody in 2006 before a verdict could be reached in his war-crimes trial.
President Milorad Dodik, the longtime dominant political figure in Republika Srpska, made little attempt to disguise the depth of the divide during an interview with the Post in Banja Luka last week.
“What the West and the Muslims have done is turn Gen. Mladic into an icon of identification for the Serbs, whatever anyone may think about him,” he said.
Attempts to criminalize the glorification of convicted war criminals in Bosnia have strengthened rather than diminished Mladic’s standing among some Serbs, Dodik said.
“You can prohibit someone from saying something publicly, but you cannot prohibit people from saying what they want in private conversations,” he told the Post.
Mladic's reputation as a defender of the Serbs has survived into a new generation
What particularly concerned Dodik, though, was that the phenomenon was no longer restricted to the generation that fought or lived through the war: The fierce Serb nationalism of the 1990s has taken root among today’s youth.
“Today, these people – young people born after the war – are going into the streets and paying tribute to Gen. Mladic,” he said. “Excuse me, how am I supposed to prohibit that? Should I use force?”
The conversations the Post had in Banja Luka suggested that whatever the reasons, Mladic’s reputation as a defender of the Serbs has survived into a generation with little or no personal memory of the conflict.
Many of the people who spoke to the Post – Bosnian citizens who identify first and foremost as Serbs – expressed deep contempt for the Bosnian state and distrust of Sarajevo; politically and culturally, their eyes remain firmly turned toward Belgrade.
Dodik also rejected the international narrative surrounding Mladic’s responsibility, saying he had been made into a symbol of what many Serbs regard as the unequal treatment of the different sides in the Bosnian War.
“A myth has been created around Mladic – the image of a beast that certain liberal circles needed in order to portray him that way,” Dodik said.
This view was also expressed by others who spoke with the Post. They did not necessarily deny that crimes had been committed by Bosnian Serb forces, but they repeatedly returned to what they regarded as the unequal judgment of the war: that crimes were committed by all sides, while the Serbs alone have come to be defined by them.
Mladic’s death has once again exposed divisions that have never fully disappeared since the 1992-1995 war.
Before his death, Mladic had personally requested to be buried in Belgrade alongside his daughter, Ana, who died in 1994.
“During his lifetime, he asked to be buried in the cemetery where his daughter is buried,” Dodik said. “Among us Christians, Orthodox Christians, that is a definitive and irrevocable decision, and we cannot change it.”
Serbian-European relations suffer tension following Mladic's death
The Serbian government’s treatment of Mladic following his death has meanwhile produced a new confrontation with Europe. EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a planned visit to Serbia last week, saying the glorification of convicted war criminals was incompatible with the principles of reconciliation and respect for victims expected of countries seeking EU membership.
Dodik characterized the criticism surrounding the funeral as “hysteria,” saying it would only reinforce the sense among Serbs that Mladic and, by extension, themselves were being treated unjustly.
“I think all of this would have passed much more peacefully if the Muslims had not started this hysteria,” he said. “Then the Serbs react in defense of their dignity.”
That sense of grievance helps to understand what was visible in Banja Luka in the days following Mladic’s death.
The legal judgment regarding Ratko Mladic was delivered long ago. His final appeal failed five years before his death, leaving in place a life sentence for genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes.
But judicial judgments and collective memory do not necessarily travel together.
Three decades after Srebrenica, the memorial in central Banja Luka, the conversations with residents, and now the thousands who turned out in Belgrade for his funeral demonstrate that for many Serbs, Mladic remains something very different from the man described in the judgments of The Hague.
For one resident who spoke with the Post, at least, there was little ambiguity.
“He defended us,” he said.

Swiss geothermal drilling could resume in St Gallen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:45:57 UTC
23:45:57 KST

Swiss geothermal drilling could resume in St Gallen
A study to assess the potential for exploiting deep geothermal energy in the Swiss canton of St Gallen concludes that the region is “geothermally attractive”.
Buchs, Ebnat-Kappel and Widnau/Diepoldsau are among the locations mentioned as potential sites for drilling.
Thirteen years after the failure of the geothermal project in the city of St Gallen, there could soon be a new push in the canton to harness deep geothermal energy.
At the time, an earthquake brought an end to the cantonal capital’s pioneering role in harnessing energy from great depths. All that remained as a reminder was a 4,400-metre-deep borehole.
More
Can deep geothermal projects help secure Swiss energy independence?
That marked the end of the momentum for such ambitious large-scale projects – not just in St Gallen. Since then, there have been no major projects anywhere in eastern Switzerland.
+ St Gallen geothermal power project abandoned
In Thurgau, the legal framework was still being drawn up. But after that, not much happened. For example, a project by Geo-Energie Suisse in Etzwilen, Thurgau, has been ‘on hold’ for many years.
The company is instead pushing ahead with a geothermal project in Haute-Sorne in the canton of Jura.
Geothermal potential
This standstill in eastern Switzerland is not set to continue. The groundwork for a fresh start is already in place. The cantonal government commissioned a specialist consultancy to carry out extensive investigations.
The result is the 178-page final report “Potential of medium-depth and deep geothermal energy in the canton of St Gallen”, which can be found on the canton’s website.
One of the conclusions is that the area studied can be classified as “geothermally attractive”. This is due to “gravel deposits in the glacial channels”. In addition, there are large fault and fracture zones that are potentially permeable and aquiferous.
More
Heat from the ground, it’s there for the taking
The greatest chances of success lie where fracture or fault zones can be drilled through. During the last ice ages, channels around 300 to 600 metres deep were formed – for example in the Rhine Valley – which were filled with unconsolidated rock.
200 gigawatt-hour potential
If only the four most promising sites in the canton were developed, the estimated annual heat output could exceed 200 gigawatt-hours. This would cover around one-fifth of the target set out in the cantonal energy strategy for the production of renewable energy.
The study recommends a step-by-step approach. Due to drilling costs rising sharply with increasing depth, as well as the growing risks involved, testing should first be carried out in a ‘shallow play’. The term ‘play’ refers to an area with geothermal potential.
With drilling at great depths, knowledge of the subsurface remains limited. Although there are numerous boreholes in the canton of St Gallen, these are only for geothermal probes reaching depths of 200 to 300 metres.
The exception is the project in the city of St Gallen, which was ultimately halted. At the time, an area of 300 square kilometres between Gossau and Rorschach was surveyed using ‘3D seismic’ techniques.
According to the report, the greatest fears amongst the public centre on earthquakes that could be triggered by drilling. Risk analyses and adapted procedures are therefore essential.
Communication must be “early and open”. The project in Haute-Sorne should now demonstrate that a geothermal project can be implemented without any noticeable earthquakes.
From the perspective of the report’s authors, the next step should be a “geothermal exploration strategy”. To this end, “specific sites, drilling targets, tests and investigations” should be defined.
The report lists particularly suitable sites. These include Buchs. The municipality lies both on the “western edge of the deep Quaternary Rhine Valley trough” and within the zone of the “scaled Helvetic”, to use the technical terminology of geologists.
What makes this site particularly interesting is the possibility of “storing thermal energy underground”.
In Benken, various deeper potential areas are being considered for exploration. These involve depths of more than 4.5 kilometres. In Ebnat-Kappel, the deeper “plays” at depths of over four kilometres are also suitable.
Other potential sites include Wildhaus, Walenstadt, Sargans/Mels and Widnau/Diepoldsau. How promising these opportunities actually are “can only be quantified through test drilling”, the report concludes.
More
Technical problems put Swiss geothermal project on ice

US Air Force widow initially denied benefits because Iran conflict ‘not technically a war’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
