Libby Klinner, the widow of 33-year-old Air Force Maj. Alex Klinner, will receive at least some of the payment she is entitled to after she was initially told that combat-related benefits were unavailable to her family because the conflict with Iran “is not technically a war,” prompting a frustrated social media post that went viral.
Maj. Klinner is one of 18 US servicemen who have lost their lives since the war against Iran started in February. He was on board the KC-135 refueling aircraft that crashed in Iraq in March.
In addition to Klinner of Alabama, Ariana Savino, 31, of Washington; Ashley Pruitt, 34, of Kentucky; Seth Koval, 38, of Indiana; Curtis Angst, 30, of Ohio; and Tyler Simmons, 28, of Ohio lost their lives in the crash.
Klinner told the Associated Press, “My husband lost his life because we’re in a war, and then I was told that because it’s not technically a war, we lose out on something… It all comes down to principle.”
After Klinner said she was told she was ineligible for some benefits, the Air Force told her that her husband’s final paycheck would include hazard pay and combat-related tax breaks.
The incident grabbed the attention of US Vice President JD Vance, who promised to look into her case when asked about it during a White House briefing on Thursday.
“We want to be as helpful as we can and ensure she gets everything that she is entitled to,” Vance said. “My message to her would be, ‘We love ya, we’re grateful for the sacrifice, and we very much take very seriously our commitment to get you what you need to get.’”
Vice President Vance rejects using the word 'war'
Despite thanking Klinner for her sacrifice, Vance went on to reject using the word “war” as a characterization of the current conflict, arguing there was “no active shooting.” The US military has conducted multiple rounds of strikes on Iran this past week, and the Islamic regime has continued to fire at Gulf states.
The Air Force acknowledged that Klinner had been provided with inaccurate information on Thursday, Klinner said, adding that she was told that her husband’s paycheck had already included, but had incorrectly itemized, the combat-related hazard pay and tax breaks.
Combat pay in the US military amounts to an additional $225 per month and is not conditioned on a formal war declaration but just that the service member be in an area where there is “grave danger of physical injury” or be “killed, injured, or wounded by a hostile fire event,” according to First Command Financial Services, a private, financial services company that provides services to members of the US forces, veterans, and their families.
In addition to his wife, Maj. Klinner left behind three children. A GoFundMe for the bereaved family, launched in the days after Maj. Klinner’s death, has raised more than $1.5 million.
Klinner has not yet responded to The Jerusalem Post’s contact request.

The chair of the UK government’s “moonshot” science and technology research unit has been forced to stand down after taking a job with the San Francisco AI firm Anthropic, in a move senior MPs called a “clear conflict of interest”.
Matt Clifford announced last week that he was taking a full-time job working for the company behind the Claude chatbot, “leading its engagement” with governments outside the US – including the UK. But he retained his leadership at the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (Aria), which funds frontier science and tech projects.
The move sparked concern, with Chi Onwurah, the Labour chair of the Commons science, innovation and technology committee, calling it a “clear conflict of interest” and outlining her disquiet in a letter to the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan.
At the time Clifford’s new employer said he would recuse himself from any Anthropic-related business at Aria in an arrangement that had been agreed with the government.
Clifford announced on Monday: “I have decided to step down to ensure my new role at Anthropic doesn’t become a distraction from Aria’s incredible work.” He said he would stay in place until 6 November “with appropriate safeguards against potential conflicts in place”.
Onwurah welcomed the move but said questions remained, including “how this situation arose, what conflict of interest assessments were undertaken and what safeguards are in place to protect confidence in Aria’s governance.”
Beeban Kidron, a crossbench peer and prominent critic of government AI policy, welcomed Clifford’s resignation. “If we are to rebuild trust in the government, we need to see a clear line between tech interests and those of citizens and the nation,” she said.
Clifford’s full-time Anthropic role highlighted a revolving door between the government and AI companies. The former prime minister Rishi Sunak has taken jobs with Anthropic and Microsoft, and the former chancellor George Osborne works for OpenAI. They followed Nick Clegg, who held a senior role with Meta until 2025.
Tom Brake, the chief executive of Unlock Democracy, a not-for-profit campaign group, had said taking extensive knowledge about a policy as sensitive as AI to a private sector company shortly after leaving government could weaken the government’s hand when pushing for a precautionary approach towards AI development.
On Monday the risks of the race to ever more powerful AIs were again highlighted by the AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton, who gave a statement supporting a private member’s bill being introduced on Tuesday in the UK parliament to prohibit the creation of artificial superintelligence, warning: “Losing control over AI smarter than ourselves … could even lead to human extinction.”
Clifford was appointed Keir Starmer’s AI adviser in January 2025 but stepped down for personal reasons after six months in the role.
The 40-year-old made his career in the private sector as the co-founder of the venture capital outfit Entrepreneurs First, becoming a pivotal figure in the UK tech scene. As well taking the chair of Aria in 2022, he became a key adviser to Sunak and played a prominent role in organising the 2023 AI safety summit in the UK. He also helped create the organisation that later became the world-leading AI Security Institute.

The discussions follow recent accusations from Germany targeting Russian intelligence services over the August 5 Leipzig Airport incident. Trial begins in Finland over alleged sexual offences against 361 children
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
17:40:23 EEST
23:40:23 KST

A 28-year-old man has gone on trial in Tampere accused of sexual offences involving 361 boys across Finland, in a case prosecutors say involved contact with children through Snapchat over several years. Police estimate the number of possible victims at about 900, although hundreds have not been identified.
Pirkanmaa District Court opened proceedings on Monday with a public presentation of the case.
The main hearings will continue behind closed doors from Tuesday because the charges concern minors and sexual offences.
The court has reserved about 45 hearing days through the end of the year. A judgment is expected in early 2027.
The defendant faces charges including aggravated sexual abuse of a child, sexual abuse of a child and aggravated distribution of an image depicting a child in a sexually offensive manner. The alleged offences took place between 2019 and 2022, when the defendant was aged between 21 and 24.
Prosecutors say all 361 identified complainants were boys aged between nine and 15 and lived in different parts of Finland.
Police believe the defendant had contact with about 900 possible victims. Prosecutors said around 530 people seen in material recovered during the investigation remain unidentified.
According to the prosecution, the defendant approached children on Snapchat while presenting himself as a girl, at times using the name Emilia and related usernames. He allegedly sent sexual images and videos before asking boys to send similar material.
The prosecution says he also gave instructions about what should appear in videos and secretly recorded material sent through Snapchat. The children believed much of the content would disappear through the application’s normal messaging functions.
Investigators recovered more than 4,200 images and videos connected to identified complainants. Ilta-Sanomat reported that 3,225 of the 4,223 files contained sexual material.
The alleged offences took place online. Prosecutors have not accused the defendant of meeting the children for the acts covered by the current charges.
Some of the boys were already known to him through sport or his work as a substitute teacher.
Yle reported that the defendant had played floorball at Finland’s highest league level and had taken part in junior coaching and youth camps.
Lawyer Jyri Kilpi, who represents 77 complainants, told the court that sport had provided a link to many of his clients. He said 70 of those he represents had participated in team sports, while the remaining seven had friends who did.
The defendant joined Monday’s hearing by video link from Kanta-Häme District Court rather than appearing in the Tampere courtroom. Images from the hearing showed him covering much of his face.
His legal representative told the court that the defendant regrets his actions and has largely accepted the prosecution’s description of events. According to the defence, about 90 per cent of the alleged acts have been admitted. Disputes concern cases in which details were not clearly remembered during the police investigation.
The investigation began after police seized the defendant’s phone during a separate criminal case in late 2022. Officers found large quantities of material involving children, prompting an investigation that lasted several years.
Police spent about two years identifying children shown in the files. Investigators interviewed each identified child and also questioned their guardians.
The defendant was previously convicted in 2023 of aggravated sexual abuse of a child and sentenced to three years in prison. That case concerned a 14-year-old pupil whom he knew while working as a substitute teacher.
Material found during that earlier investigation led police to the wider case now before Pirkanmaa District Court.

Australia to let social media users switch off Big Tech algorithms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:37:08 UTC
23:37:08 KST

Faisal Mahmud
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Australia is preparing legislation that would allow social media users to switch off algorithms that determine what appears in their feeds, in what would be a world-first attempt to give users greater control over content recommended by Big Tech.
Under the proposed Digital Duty of Care legislation, platforms would be required to regularly display pop-up messages asking users whether they want to continue with an algorithmically curated feed or see only posts from accounts they follow, ABC News reported.
The draft legislation is expected to be unveiled by the federal government this week.
It would also shift responsibility to social media companies to identify and mitigate risks on their platforms and prevent harmful content from reaching users, with additional protections covering several categories of psychosocial harm for people under 18.
Companies could face fines exceeding A$100 million ($66 million) for breaches.
Australia's eSafety commissioner and registered independent researchers would also be empowered to use accounts posing as children to investigate what platforms' algorithms recommend to young users.
Opposition leader Angus Taylor has expressed concern that the proposal could facilitate government censorship, while the Greens have called for tougher rules under which algorithmic feeds would be opt-in rather than opt-out.
The legislation follows Australia's restrictions on social media access for children under 16.

Ukrainian drones struck several Russian oil refineries, along with a storage and launch site for strike drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky reported, saying the strikes were part of Ukraine’s continued response to Russian attacks.
“A refinery was hit in the Ryazan region. Our long-range forces were used against oil refineries in the Perm region and Tatarstan, and against a storage and launch site for strike drones in the Kursk region,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Ryazan refinery is one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities, producing gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation kerosene, and other petroleum products, including supplies for the Russian military.
On Sunday, Sept. 6, Ukrainian drones struck the refinery’s primary oil-processing facilities. The plant has a reported annual processing capacity of about 8.5 million tons.
Ukrainian forces also struck the facility in late July. Fires were subsequently reported at the refinery and a Wildberries warehouse in Ryazan, with the regional governor confirming fires at industrial facilities.
Zelensky also said Ukrainian forces had struck a Russian target in the Black Sea.
The General Staff of Ukraine separately reported strikes on Russian military targets on Sept. 6 and overnight into Sept. 7, including a railway bridge, ammunition depot, and command posts.
FACT CHECK: Was Putin Telling the Truth About Some More Big Russian Victories in Ukraine?
“In the Vladyslavivka area, in occupied Crimea, a railway bridge over the North Crimean Canal was hit,” the General Staff said. The bridge is used by Russian forces for military logistics.
Ukrainian forces also struck Russian command posts in Nizhny Naholchyk and Dovzhansky in the Luhansk region, as well as Azovsky in the Zaporizhzhia region.
In Perekop, Crimea, Ukrainian forces hit an automated technical reconnaissance post known as “Grenadier.” A Russian ammunition depot was also struck in the Teply district of the Luhansk region.
“The extent of the damage is being clarified. Work on key enemy military targets continues,” the General Staff added.
One killed in the Perm region
Meanwhile, Perm Governor Dmitry Makhonin said Russian air defenses and mobile fire groups had shot down 27 Ukrainian drones over the region overnight.
“Today, air defense forces and mobile fire groups repelled a massive attack by enemy drones. According to operational data, 27 unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) were shot down in the sky over the Perm region. Emergency services are working at the site of the debris,” Makhonin wrote on Telegram.
He said the attack damaged an apartment building, killing one person and injuring four others.
Possible fire at Sochi oil depot
The Russian outlet Astra initially reported that an oil depot in Sochi, which had been targeted by a drone attack on Sept. 4, may have caught fire again late on Sunday, Sept. 6.
The report was based on a video published by the Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channel Supernova+.
Astra later cited its own OSINT analysis as indicating a possible re-ignition at the Adler oil depot operated by Rosneft-Kubannefteprodukt. The depot is located in Sochi’s Adler district near Sochi International Airport, storing and supplying petroleum products.
Local authorities did not officially report a fire at the facility. The reports came from Telegram channels, including Supernova+, and there was no official confirmation that the depot was burning. There were also no reports of a drone attack or air raid alert in the area before the fire was reported.
Nevertheless, the Russian defense ministry said its forces had intercepted and destroyed 306 Ukrainian UAVs overnight.

Three Italian artists and two South Korean artists are the protagonists of the third Italian Pavilion at the 2026 Gwangju Biennale with the exhibition “The Look is A Li(k)e,” curated by Irene Campolmi and promoted by the Italian Cultural Institute in Seoul in collaboration with the Italian Embassy.

China to issue $44.2B in special bonds to support state financial firms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:32:53 UTC
23:32:53 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
China plans to issue $44.25 billion in special treasury bonds to support eight state-owned financial enterprises in replenishing their core Tier One capital, the country's Finance Ministry announces on Monday.
The Chinese Ministry of Finance said it will issue 300 billion yuan ($44.25 billion) in special treasury bonds to strengthen these institutions' operational capacity and resilience to risks, Xinhua reported.
The ministry released a circular stating that this move will provide stronger support for the country's steady and sound economic growth.
The eight institutions include two major state-owned commercial banks, the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) and the Agricultural Bank of China (ABC), alongside the Export-Import Bank of China and the China Export and Credit Insurance Corporation.
The list also features four state-owned commercial insurers, including the People's Insurance Company of China, China Life Insurance Company, China Taiping Insurance Group and China Reinsurance Corporation.
The circular noted that the capital replenishment will help listed enterprises create greater value for investors and deliver stable long-term returns.
The ministry added that the eight institutions currently operate steadily with stable asset quality and major regulatory indicators remaining within safe ranges.
The announcement followed specific plans unveiled by the eight firms on Sunday to strengthen their core Tier One capital by raising or receiving a combined 360 billion yuan ($53.1 billion).
ABC and ICBC plan to raise up to 260 billion yuan ($38.35 billion) of this total through A-share issuances to designated investors.
Financial institutions use core Tier One capital as the highest-quality form of capital to absorb losses and serve as a key buffer against financial risks.
A stronger core Tier One capital position generally provides banks with more room to expand lending while maintaining regulatory capital ratios.

World Insights: From labs to life, Chinese tech redefines innovation at IFA Berlin 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:32:31 CST
23:32:31 KST

BERLIN, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- From robots stepping into kitchens to living rooms that anticipate daily routines and jewelry that connects partners across distances, this year's IFA Berlin, one of the world's largest trade fairs for consumer electronics and home appliances, offers a glimpse into a near future increasingly shaped by Chinese innovation.
Of the more than 1,900 exhibitors at the five-day trade show, nearly half are from China, making their presence across the event hard to miss. More significant than their scale, however, was a broader shift in how they innovate -- moving technologies more quickly from lab prototypes to commercial applications, building interconnected home ecosystems, and developing personalized consumer tech.
ROBOTS ENTERING REAL LIFE
Humanoid robots offered perhaps the most vivid sign of that shift. At the booth of Unitree Robotics, several humanoids moved in formation to the beat of music, while another took on a far more ordinary task: making a sandwich. It picked up slices of bread, added lettuce and neatly stacked the layers. The futuristic technology suddenly felt unexpectedly familiar. Nearby, Dobot Robotics' panda-shaped robots danced from side to side, drawing visitors with its playful moves.
At PrimeBOT's booth, an 88-centimeter-tall PrimeBOT Q1 humanoid stood out with a fluid sequence of martial arts moves. Its flexible joints carried it smoothly through punches, turns and a crisp finishing stance. Beside it, the PrimeBOT T1 demonstrated a different capability: within seconds, it shifted from a two-legged humanoid posture into a four-legged configuration, drawing surprised reactions from onlookers.
Beyond the spectacle, the real test is whether these eye-catching demonstrations can translate into real-world applications
"China is moving robots rapidly from products in the laboratory into real industrial and consumer markets," Zou Jiyuan, chief marketing officer for international markets at PrimeBOT, told Xinhua.
Zou attributed that speed in part to China's extensive manufacturing base and well-developed supply chains. "With strong support across key components such as motors, sensors, batteries and chips, robotics companies can shorten development cycles, bring down costs and iterate products more quickly," he said.
FROM PRODUCTS TO LIFESTYLES
The efforts to bring technology closer to everyday life extended well beyond robotics. In the home appliance sector, Chinese companies are presenting not just smarter products, but entire living environments built around them.
TCL turned its booth into a glimpse of future living. Large-screen televisions anchored the space, while AR glasses brought digital content directly into view. Nearby, an AI-enabled air conditioner adjusted indoor comfort based on room conditions, while a smart washing machine could sense factors such as load size and fabric type and tailor the wash accordingly. Walking through the space felt more like stepping into a home where technology worked as part of a single, connected experience.
"What we are presenting here is more than a collection of smart products. It is a vision of how people may live in the AI era, with different devices working together around real-life needs," Daniel Sun, CTO of TCL Industries, told Xinhua in an exclusive interview.
He noted that the move from individual products to scenario-based experiences reflects a broader evolution in China's home appliance industry. "Companies are now combining pure manufacturing scale with design, software, and system integration to build complete home ecosystems."
Hisense echoed that approach with an AI-powered home system linking televisions, refrigerators, air conditioners, and other devices. In one demonstration, a simple request to "watch the game tonight" prompted the system to coordinate lighting, room temperature, and a food-delivery reminder, illustrating how appliances are being designed to work within a shared living environment.
"Chinese companies are showcasing more than a wider range of products and faster iteration," said Yan Ronghua, head of overseas portfolio operations at Hisense Global Commercial Center. "They are actively defining how technology can reshape everyday lifestyles, a shift that emerged as a clear hallmark at this year's IFA."
INNOVATION GETTING PERSONAL
Beyond robots and connected homes, Chinese companies were also pushing into more specialized corners of consumer technology.
At the booth of smart jewelry brand TOTWOO, Chinese innovation found a more intimate expression in bracelets and necklaces. Connected via Bluetooth to a mobile app, the smart pieces turn a simple touch into a signal that can travel across distance: tap one, and its paired piece lights up and vibrates in response. Intangible emotions -- longing, companionship and connection -- are soon translated into a soft glow and a subtle pulse.
For TOTWOO founder and CEO Wang Jieming, bringing technology into such delicate spaces is part of a broader trend. As he told Xinhua, Chinese tech firms are expanding into specialized, high-emotion markets.
"Backed by mature hardware supply chains and advances in AI and smart interaction, Chinese brands are moving beyond high-profile categories like smartphones, appliances, and robotics," Wang said. "We are entering niche areas like smart jewelry, where personalization and emotional experience take center stage."
The move into new product categories also reflects a broader change in how Chinese companies are expanding overseas. "Chinese companies are moving from simply selling products abroad to building brands and establishing a long-term presence in global markets," said Ye Can, head of Europe at WeBranding Global, which helps Chinese companies expand internationally.
Ye said the competitiveness of Chinese companies comes from a combination of supply-chain strength, technological innovation and operational efficiency. "As new sectors such as AI hardware and smart homes grow, Chinese firms are playing a bigger role in shaping new products and technologies for global markets." ■

Healey says debt interest now bigger than Defence
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:32:12 BST
23:32:12 KST

Chancellor John Healey has said the government is spending £1 in every £10 on debt interest, arguing that the bill is now larger than spending on Defence, the Home Office and Justice combined as he set out a new drive for economic growth.
Speaking at the Manufacturing Technology Centre today, Healey placed fiscal discipline alongside investment, innovation and devolution at the centre of his economic programme, saying Britain needed stronger growth to reduce the pressure created by high borrowing and debt costs.
Healey said: “There’s nothing progressive about the government spending £1 in every £10 on debt interest.
“If debt interest were a government department, it would be the second biggest in Whitehall, after Health – bigger than Defence, the Home Office and Justice put together.”
He said controlling government spending remained necessary despite the administration’s wider ambitions, adding: “That’s why staying true to our values means being honest about the need to control government spending.”
Healey said fiscal discipline had been his first priority on entering the Treasury and that he and the Prime Minister were committed to meeting the government’s fiscal rules at the upcoming Budget.
He said: “The Prime Minister and I are in lockstep in our commitment to meeting the fiscal rules at the upcoming Budget:
“To balancing the books, with a buffer to protect against uncertainty,
“To controlling borrowing to bear down on inflation,
“And reducing long term pressures on our public finances.”
The Chancellor also set growth as the central objective of his tenure, describing the UK as strong in areas including defence technology, life sciences, financial services and advanced manufacturing.
Healey said: “And while Britains growth trajectory has been weak this now must change. This is essential, it is possible, it is central to my purpose as Chancellor.”
He added: “I dedicate myself to this mission as Chancellor, to make Great Britain, Growth Britain again – with more investment, more innovation and more jobs.”
Among the measures announced was a planned roadmap to fiscal devolution at the Budget, including greater retention of business rates by local authorities and a share of local income tax for mayoral strategic authorities from 2028.
Healey said: “That is why at the Budget I will set out a roadmap to fiscal devolution – a permanent transfer of power and resources from Whitehall to our regions,
“With greater business rates retention for local councils and strategic authorities…
“…grants from central government replaced by a share of local income tax for every Mayoral Strategic Authority beginning in 2028.”
He also announced £150 million through the British Business Bank for scale-up companies in the North and said South Yorkshire, Liverpool City Region, North-East England and Cardiff Capital Region would become strategic partners of the National Wealth Fund.
Changes to government investment appraisal are also planned, with the Treasury Green Book discount rate due to fall from 3.5 per cent to 3 per cent. Healey said the change would give greater weight to projects with longer-term economic potential. The Chancellor also promised to reduce the regulatory burden on business by 25 per cent by the end of Parliament and extend reforms to judicial review beyond energy infrastructure.
He said: “And I can today announce that we will extend our reforms of judicial review from energy to all major infrastructure so that vexatious legislation and vexatious litigation cannot block economic growth.”
Healey added: “So I will end the consultation culture at the Treasury and beyond – supported by new guidance from the Attorney General today that legal risk is not the be-all and end-all of ministerial decisions.”
Defence also featured in his plans for growing British technology companies. Healey set an ambition to double the number of UK unicorn companies and said government could act as an early customer to help promising firms scale.
He said: “Together, with Johnny Reynolds I will identify the next wave of unicorns, with the state as an early first customer to ensure they have the necessary backing to scale. I did this at Defence, I announced this for Sovereign AI last week, we’re doing it with today’s scale-up fund for the North.”
Healey also linked industrial capacity with national security, arguing that the UK had become increasingly dependent on external sources in strategically important areas. He said the country had been “deindustrialised, as the cost to make anything, to build anything here soared, and our dependence on unreliable sources grew including in areas critical to our national security and sovereignty.”
On artificial intelligence, the Chancellor said the government wanted to exploit its economic potential while retaining oversight of risks to national and business security, pointing to the AI Security Institute and AI Economics Institute as part of that approach.
Healey closed by saying: “We will not deliver all this tomorrow. But we’re delivering the start of it today.”

====================================================================================================

Israeli, Chinese, French scientists reveal hidden process behind cracks, earthquakes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
22:32:00 CST
23:32:00 KST

JERUSALEM, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Israeli, Chinese, and French scientists have uncovered a hidden process that takes place before materials suddenly break, a finding that could help explain how earthquakes begin, the Hebrew University of Jerusalem said in a statement Monday.
In their new study, published in Physical Review Letters, the researchers found that cracks do not always appear and spread suddenly. Instead, they can begin as tiny, two-dimensional damaged areas that slowly grow inside a material.
Through experiments and high-speed cameras, the team found that these small damaged areas can grow extremely slowly, at speeds ranging from microns to millimeters per second, making up at least 75 percent of the entire breaking process.
The major change occurs when the damaged area extends through the material's full thickness and forms a larger crack, causing the material to break in a fraction of a second.
The researchers said the same basic process may also occur when surfaces suddenly slide against each other, as happens during earthquakes, therefore helping scientists better understand how fractures and earthquakes begin. ■

BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- China's foreign exchange reserves totaled 3.4383 trillion U.S. dollars at the end of August 2026, up by 19.5 billion U.S. dollars, or 0.57 percent, compared to the end of July, official data showed Monday.
The combined effects of currency translation and asset price changes led to the increase in China's foreign exchange reserves in August, the State Administration of Foreign Exchange said in a statement.
The statement also noted that China's economy has remained generally stable and made solid progress, with its resilience and vitality supporting the stability of the country's foreign exchange reserves.
While commenting on the latest data, Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank, said that the rise in China's foreign exchange reserves last month came as the U.S. dollar index fell 0.5 percent in August to 99.4, with the dollar's weakness contributing to a positive valuation effect on China's foreign exchange reserves.
He said that China's exports are also expected to maintain strong resilience going forward, which will continuously consolidate the foundation of China's balance of payments. He explained that the global manufacturing upswing driven by AI-related capital expenditure is set to continue, providing a strong impetus for export growth.
Meanwhile, various foreign trade business entities are steadily expanding into diversified overseas markets, constantly tapping into new drivers of trade growth, he noted.
China's foreign trade sustained steady growth momentum in July, buoyed by robust exports of innovative and high-tech products. The General Administration of Customs is scheduled to release the latest foreign trade data for August on Tuesday. ■

EU pledges $232M in Greenland investments amid Trump pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:31:00 UTC
23:31:00 KST

EU chief Ursula von der Leyen unveiled plans on Monday for some 200 million euros ($232 million) in Greenland investments amid a push for closer ties with the Danish Arctic territory, which U.S. President Donald Trump had earlier insisted should belong to the United States.
Von der Leyen arrived in Greenland on Sunday for a two-day visit serving as a show of support for the governments of Greenland and Denmark, which have strongly rebuffed Trump’s campaign to acquire the world’s largest island.
The head of the 27-nation European Union's executive body said the EU money would focus on sectors including critical minerals, satellite communications and renewable energy in Greenland, a semi-autonomous part of the Danish realm.
"The EU stands in full solidarity with the Kingdom of Denmark and the people of Greenland," von der Leyen told a news conference.
"We will continue to do so."
Von der Leyen's visit reflects the increasing geopolitical importance of the Arctic to major powers, such as the U.S., Russia, China and Europe, as melting ice opens new shipping routes to make the region’s mineral wealth more accessible.
The European Commission chief, who took a boat trip on Sunday in a fjord scattered with chunks of ice, had earlier posted on X how she was struck by Greenland's stunning landscapes, but aware of the "visible scars of climate change."
"As the ice melts, a new reality is taking shape," she wrote.
U.S. President Trump sparked a crisis in U.S.-European ties and turmoil within the transatlantic NATO military alliance this year when he stepped up his demands for the U.S. to control Greenland, arguing that fellow NATO member Denmark could not defend it.
European officials stressed Greenland is part of NATO territory, meaning it is covered by the alliance’s mutual defense pact, and that the U.S. already has the right to increase its military presence there under a long-standing treaty.
Tensions lowered after Trump and NATO boss Mark Rutte agreed in Davos in January that the U.S., Denmark and Greenland would begin talks to resolve their differences and NATO would step up its role in Arctic security.
However, the trilateral talks have yet to yield an agreement and at a NATO summit in Türkiye in July, Trump restated his insistence that the U.S. should control Greenland.
Von der Leyen said Greenland's future was for the people of Greenland and Denmark to decide and no one else.
"The Arctic has become one of the places where the tectonic plates of geopolitics collide. We have a direct stake in what happens here," she said, adding that her Commission would set out a new EU Arctic strategy in the coming months.
While Denmark is a member of the EU, Greenland left the bloc in 1985. But its people, as Danish citizens, are also citizens of the EU.
The EU has long provided funding to Greenland, mainly to pay for fishing rights and support its education system. The €200 million package represents not only a big increase in funding but a broadening of the sectors that will receive EU cash, according to EU officials.
The Commission has also proposed more than doubling EU funding for Greenland from 225 million euros in its current seven-year budget to 530 million euros for the period between 2028 and 2034.

Europe’s largest carbon capture facility opens in the Netherlands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

Europe’s largest carbon capture facility opens in the Netherlands
AMSTERDAM – The largest carbon capture facility in Europe opened in the Netherlands on Sept 7, developed by Norwegian fertiliser company Yara International.
The carbon capture and storage (CCS) facility in Sluiskil, in the southern Dutch province of Zeeland, will cut emissions at one of Europe’s largest fertiliser production sites and transport captured carbon to Norway, Yara said.
From 2026, Yara Sluiskil will capture and liquefy up to 800,000 tonnes of CO2 a year. The carbon will be transported and stored 2.6km beneath the seabed on the Norwegian continental shelf by transport and storage operator Northern Lights.
Over 15 years, Yara expects to remove about 12 million tons of CO2 from the site.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere said the Sluiskil project offers a solution that is both scientifically advanced and commercially viable.
“Our climate challenge lies in industry because that’s where we find the combination of labour, capital and technology. And of course energy is all around it. So being modern energy nations, the Netherlands is first among them, is the way to go,” Stoere said.
The European Union plans to use carbon capture technology to help meet its 2050 net-zero emissions target, particularly for industrial processes such as chemical manufacturing, where low-carbon alternatives are not yet available.
But the technology has struggled for decades in Europe because of questions over commercial viability and opposition from environmental campaigners and some governments. Critics say CCS can allow companies to continue producing oil and gas while promising to capture emissions in the future. REUTERS

Europe ramps up gas injection into UGS for winter at high prices in early September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:28:50 UTC
23:28:50 KST

MOSCOW, September 7. /TASS/. Europe decided to ramp up gas injection into underground gas storage (UGS) facilities ahead of winter at prices reaching four-year highs in late August and early September 2026 amid historically low levels of its UGS reserves, according to TASS calculations based on Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE) data.
In early September the average rate of gas injection into EU UGS facilities has been at one of the highest levels seen in recent years. That said, gas prices at European hubs have been approaching the highs of late 2022, which demonstrates the European Union’s drive to fill its UGS facilities ahead of winter even at high prices.
As of September 5, Europe’s underground gas storage facilities were 66.59% full (16.58 percentage points below the five-year average for this date), compared to 79% in the previous year. This is the lowest level for this date since records began in 2011. Europe’s UGS facilities hold roughly 72.9 bln cubic meters of gas, which is 14 bln cubic meters lower than last year’s levels, and the lowest since 2013.
The European Commission requests EU members to make sure their UGS facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 of each year. Moreover, 10% flexibility is allowed in the event of difficult UGS filling conditions. Thus, net injection into European storage facilities by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter period must reach at least 68 bcm to meet the filling standard. Since the beginning of April, Europe has managed to inject a total of 62% of the volumes needed for the upcoming winter, or 42 bln cubic meters, into its UGS facilities.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday refused to give the expert panel examining the definition and protection of the Aravalli Hills another six months to submit its final report, telling it to "work day and night" and complete the exercise by November 30.A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana rejected the high-powered committee's request to extend the deadline till February 28, 2027. The court also warned that it would reconstitute the panel if it failed to submit the report within the next two months, news agency PTI reported."Let the panel work day and night to submit a report on the Aravalli issue. If they are unable to do that in two months, we will reconstitute the whole panel," the CJI observed.The court also directed the committee to submit issue-specific interim reports, allowing it to address urgent aspects of the contentious Aravalli definition without waiting for its comprehensive final report.The CJI appeared particularly unimpressed with the timing of the extension request, observing that the committee had sought more time "with the first stroke of the pen" and appeared to be waiting for his retirement.
The court further directed the panel to hear all stakeholders, including tribal communities in Rajasthan and Gujarat, before finalising its recommendations. The matter will next be heard on December 2.The committee had sought six additional months, saying it needed more time to undertake a “comprehensive and defensible” assessment of the Aravalli range. Its deadline for submitting the final report was August 31.In its compliance report filed on August 31, the panel said its assessment required the integration of spatial, ecological, geological, hydrological and socio-economic evidence, besides inputs from stakeholders.It said additional time was needed for geospatial assessment, sensitivity analysis, expert examination, field verification and stakeholder validation.
The committee also argued that the Aravalli issue could not be resolved through a “single terrain-based criterion or a single source of evidence”.The urgency around the exercise stems from a controversy over how the Aravallis should be defined for regulatory purposes, particularly mining.'Unfortunately & inexplicably': Congress reactsThe Congress expressed disappointment over the Supreme Court’s decision to reject the High Powered Committee’s request for a six-month extension to submit its final report on the Aravallis.Calling the decision “unfortunate and inexplicable”, party leader Jairam Ramesh said the committee’s request for an extension beyond August 31, 2026, was “most justifiable”. Congress maintained that the additional time was necessary for the committee to complete its work and submit a comprehensive report on the ecologically sensitive Aravalli range.

UAE refuses to be 'held hostage' by Iran war, pushes for security self-reliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:28:32 UTC
23:28:32 KST

The United Arab Emirates is building alternative routes for its energy exports and trade to ensure they are not "held hostage" by the ongoing US-Iran war, UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said, adding that the partnership with the US is essential, but the current conflict underscored the importance of national security capabilities.
The conflict has had a significant impact on Gulf Arab states, including the UAE, after Tehran fired missiles at the country and attacked its oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for US-Israeli attacks.
"Our energy exports will not be held hostage, nor will our trade and economic activity," Gargash told the Hili Forum in Abu Dhabi on Monday.
The UAE has been expanding port capacity along its eastern coast, as well as developing pipelines, railways and trade routes for alternative corridors, he said.
While acknowledging that relations with Iran could eventually recover, Gargash warned that rebuilding trust after the attacks could take decades.
‘Unified strategy’ 
He also criticised Gulf Arab states for failing to mount a coordinated response to Iran, saying they had been unable to translate shared concerns into a unified strategy.
Earlier, Qatar's foreign ministry spokesperson echoed similar concerns at the policymakers' forum, saying Gulf Arab countries should not rely solely on their strategic partnership with the US for security.
Gargash argued that while the partnership with the US is essential, the current conflict has exposed the importance of national capabilities.
"Our security is our priority. When we depend entirely on others, we cannot always assume it will be their priority," he said.
Hormuz remains a central obstacle in negotiations between Washington and Tehran, mediated by Qatar and Pakistan, with Iran claiming the strait belongs to Iran and Oman, a position Gulf states broadly reject.
"Freedom of navigation is not a concession to be granted, nor a principle to be renegotiated under pressure," Gargash said, adding that any long-term resolution must include credible guarantees against further Iranian attacks on Gulf Arab states.
The conflict, sparked by US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, remains deadlocked. A preliminary ceasefire reached in June has unravelled, and little progress has been made in efforts to revive the peace process.

"It was the German authorities who, once again, provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations," the Foreign Ministry said, adding Berlin "bears full and complete responsibility" for the consequences.
Russia also earlier ordered the closure of all Goethe-Institut branches on Russian territory, with Goethe-Institut staff having to leave the country by September 13.
Goethe-Institut is a center that promotes German language and culture. Goethe-Institut is largely financed by the German government.
Germany, Russia trade barbs over Leipzig drone attack

Russia Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejected Germany's allegations, calling them "the beginning of a real war."

Speaking in Berlin on Monday, the German chancellor said he saw a society "longing for disruption" and "fundamental change."
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has expressed his shock after the far-right AfD party stormed to victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election over the weekend.
Merz appeared before the press in Berlin on Monday, together with the CDU's lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Sven Schulze, to address the outcome of the vote.
"Yesterday's result has changed not only Saxony-Anhalt, but Germany as a whole," Merz said following Sunday's state election results. "We are all profoundly shocked. We did not expect it to turn out like this."
The anti-immigration AfD party won the election by a landslide, taking 43.8% of the vote. The CDU came in a distant second with 17.2%.
Compared with the 2021 state election, the AfD more than doubled its vote share, while the CDU saw its share halved.
Almost 60% of voters had chosen parties that call democracy into question, the chancellor said, adding that it was "the most severe electoral defeat" the CDU has suffered in years.
"There will have to be consequences," he added.
'Longing for disruption'
For months, Merz has been sliding from one polling low to the next.
Most recently, 78% of respondents felt he was doing a worse job as chancellor than they had expected.
That is according to the "trendbarometer" survey by RTL and n-tv. The poll also showed that 59% of CDU/CSU voters were disappointed with Merz's performance as chancellor. The survey was carried out by the polling institute Forsa.
Despite his poor approval ratings and the electoral defeat in Saxony-Anhalt, Merz is sticking to his course "without wavering."
"Our country needs fundamental reforms," he said.
Merz sees one of the reasons for the public's dissatisfaction as the government's failure to communicate policies in a sufficiently emotive and compelling way.
In future, the CDU, together with the SPD, wants to create a better "narrative" to achieve this.
Merz said he also wanted to "personally do justice" to the election result in the coming weeks and that he saw a society "longing for disruption" and "fundamental change."
The need for compromise must, he argued, be emphasised more strongly.
Little room for AfD on migration policy
The chancellor also sought to reassure the public following the election defeat.
In general, the AfD would in many areas have to follow the line set by the federal government. That also applies to policy on foreign nationals and migration. There is a principle of "federal loyalty".
Schulze, the CDU's lead candidate, minister-president of Saxony-Anhalt and chair of the CDU in the state, also wants to draw lessons from the election result, although he did not provide specifics.
It comes as calls for Schulze to step down have grown louder. The Young Union (JU) in Saxony-Anhalt has demanded that the entire CDU leadership in the state resign, as the magazine "Stern" reported, quoting a resolution adopted by the JU Saxony-Anhalt.
It reportedly stated: "The CDU in Saxony-Anhalt needs a comprehensive fresh start. We therefore call for the resignation and the prompt re-election of the entire state leadership - from the state chair to the full executive board."
Schulze: No defections from the CDU to the AfD
Schulze again stressed that the mandate to form a government now lies with the AfD.
"Overall, this is a day that has shaken us deeply, not only in Saxony-Anhalt," he said.
In his own constituency, he added, his result was twice as good as the CDU's statewide performance.
As the AfD announced in a press release on Monday, it is now seeking to form a government despite lacking an absolute majority.
Previously, the AfD's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund had ruled that out. To achieve this, the AfD wants to win over parliamentary groups or individual MPs. Only then would Siegmund seek to be elected minister-president.
Asked about this, Schulze said there would be no defections from the CDU, adding that he was sure that members of the BSW would try to help Siegmund become minister-president.

Von der Leyen tries to counter Trump with €200 million investment in Greenland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:26:46 UTC
23:26:46 KST

Ursula von der Leyen backed Greenland's territorial integrity as she unveiled a €200 million investment package to counter pressure from Donald Trump, who has repeatedly threatened to annex the mineral-rich island.
The European Union will invest an additional €200 million in Greenland over the next two years to deepen economic ties and extract raw materials, Ursula von der Leyen announced on Monday during an official visit to the vast Arctic island.
"We know that the Arctic has become one of the places where the tectonic plates of geopolitics collide, so we have a direct stake in what happens here," the president of the European Commission said in Nuuk.
The financial package aims to expand the bloc's presence in the semi-autonomous territory, which has long been in US President Donald Trump's sights.
Trump has rattled the transatlantic alliance with his push to seize Greenland from the Kingdom of Denmark. Tensions peaked in January, when he threatened to impose steep tariffs to pressure Denmark into relinquishing the territory. He later backed down amid backlash.
But in July, Trump suddenly revived his ambition to annex the island, indicating the subject was still top of his mind. On Monday, he posted a map of the world that showed Greenland under American control.
Von der Leyen used her trip to Nuuk to underline European support amid what she called "enormous pressure", though she did not mention Trump by name.
"The European Union stands in full solidarity with the Kingdom of Denmark and the people of Greenland. We will continue to do so. And we want to be very clear and repeat again here that Greenland's future is for the people of Greenland and Denmark to decide. No one else," she said in remarks to the press.
"Territorial integrity, sovereignty, the inviolability of borders. These are fundamental principles of international law."
Standing by her side, Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen thanked von der Leyen for her words.
"Greenland needs the European Union, and the European Union needs Greenland," Nielsen said. "I firmly believe this to be true. We need each other."
"Your voice has been very clear the last couple of years. We needed that, and we need it now, so thank you for that," Frederiksen told von der Leyen.
Frederiksen said Denmark was open to working "closer" with both the US and Europe on security and defence matters related to the Arctic, a region that climate change is making increasingly attractive to world powers.
The €200 million investment package will spread across three key areas: digital connectivity, including subsea cables and satellite infrastructure; clean energy, with a particular focus on hydropower; and sustainable mining of critical raw materials.
Greenland holds 25 of the 34 minerals that Brussels considers crucial for the homegrown development of renewable energy systems and cutting-edge technology. The sector is monopolised by China, leaving the EU at the mercy of Beijing's export controls.
Mining on the island, however, remains well below its potential due to harsh glacial conditions that discourage investors from undertaking expensive projects.
Minerals were among the reasons Trump cited to justify his threat to take over Greenland, though he told the New York Times it was ultimately a question of ownership. He has also complained that allies have failed to invest enough in the region.
Europeans have since tried to counter Trump's narrative by doubling down on their commitments to Greenland. Over the next two weeks, soldiers from 10 countries will take part in NATO's Arctic Shield exercise.
Meanwhile, the Commission is working to update its Arctic strategy and has earmarked €530 million specifically for Greenland in its proposal for the next EU budget.

US Navy certifies Rolls-Royce engines for autonomous ships
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:26:29 BST
23:26:29 KST

The US Navy has certified Rolls-Royce mtu Series 4000 and Series 2000 marine engines for use aboard autonomous naval vessels following reliability testing designed to demonstrate that they can operate for extended periods without human maintenance, Rolls-Royce has announced.
The certification allows Series 4000 engines to be used in autonomous applications providing up to 4,300kW of propulsion power and 3,000kWe of electrical generation. The engine is available in V8, V12, V16 and V20 configurations.
Rolls-Royce said the Series 4000 passed two 720-hour durability tests before receiving approval. The Series 2000 was certified following component testing and thousands of hours of operational experience, with the platform capable of providing up to 1,939kW for propulsion in V10, V12 and V16 configurations.
The testing is intended to demonstrate that propulsion systems can support an unmanned vessel during a 30-day deployment without preventive or corrective maintenance to its main propulsion, fuel or oil systems.
Scott Hanson, Vice President of Governmental Sales at Rolls-Royce Power Systems in North America, said: “The certification of our engines for unmanned operations further demonstrates the reliability and advanced technology of our mtu Series 4000 and 2000 marine propulsion systems. For decades, mtu engines have been trusted to provide reliable, mission-ready power for our crews at sea.”
He added: “As autonomous missions become increasingly important to naval strategy, we are proving that we can deliver the power systems, long-endurance capability and technology required for the new operational demands of unmanned vessels.”
The certification comes as the US Navy expands its use of unmanned surface vessels as part of efforts to increase fleet capacity and operate platforms for longer periods without putting sailors aboard them.
One of the Navy’s best-known autonomous vessels, Sea Hunter, is already powered by two mtu 12V 2000 engines. Rolls-Royce said the vessel has accumulated tens of thousands of operational hours since its christening in 2016.
Sea Hunter and the related Seahawk were operationally deployed earlier this year as part of the US Navy’s first division of unmanned surface vessels, according to the company.
Certification of propulsion systems is one element of the wider process required before autonomous vessels can be routinely deployed. Rolls-Royce said US Navy requirements also place emphasis on control systems, cybersecurity and safety-critical functions as unmanned systems become more prominent across maritime operations.

Plans for a large reorganisation of local government have been put on hold after the government received new legal advice that suggested they might not comply with the law.

The reorganisation plans, announced in December 2024, proposed the abolition of the current two-tier system of districts and counties in favour of a smaller number of unitary authorities – or “mega-councils” – covering large areas.
At least eight councils had launched legal challenges or were considering doing so owing to opposition to the government’s choice of boundaries for new councils.
Reform UK-led Kent county council is to consider a judicial review at a meeting on Tuesday after it did not receive a response from the government to a letter setting out concerns.
Plans for reorganisation in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn in the light of new legal advice.
Councils in Essex launched legal action in June after it emerged that its own preferred option to create three unitary councils in the county was backed by senior government officials but rejected by the then communities secretary, Steve Reed.
There has been little appetite for the proposals within local government, with many councils regarding the changes as expensive and time-consuming, and offering little in the way of cost savings that would ease local authorities’ dire financial crisis.
Decisions on 14 further areas will be reviewed and paused alongside the cases of Cambridgeshire-Peterborough and West Sussex, which are yet to have a decision confirmed.
The government will also confirm that local elections in May 2027 will go ahead on existing council boundaries, saying it remains committed to effective and sustainable local government and simplifying these structures.
The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, is expected to tell parliament on Monday: “As we are now more determined than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent, it’s only right that as a new secretary of state I make sure that everything we do is working towards that plan to change Britain, without delay.
“The prime minister told the house last week he was ‘prepared to look at local government reorganisation’ and he asked me as his communities secretary to ‘do that’.
“In that context, in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law.
“And, secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new prime minister, and any additional considerations.
“I do not take this lightly. I recognise the huge amount of work that has already gone into progressing reorganisation in each of these areas and I am very grateful for it.”
MHCLG said reorganisation in Surrey would not be affected by the review and the two new unitary authorities, East and West Surrey, would go live in April 2027.
Cllr Sean Matthews, chair-elect of the County Councils Network, said: “Many of our members will be relieved that the decisions they viewed as damaging to local services and financially unsustainable have been withdrawn or are being reviewed. For our councils that do want to proceed with reorganisation in their area, we will support them in their next steps and we will be seeking further clarity from government in the coming days.
“With the government clearly listening to our concerns, we now stand ready to work with ministers. Where reorganisation is desired, this review must ensure a robust, legally compliant process in line with the original criteria. This should include establishing realistic implementation timescales and ensuring that any further decisions only create sustainable new unitary councils capable of improving local services.”
Jonathan Carr-West, chief executive of the Local Government Information Unit (LGIU), said: “What began as the most ambitious change to local government in a generation now looks in danger of becoming a colossal white elephant – a huge drain on time, resources and goodwill. Those councils undergoing local government reorganisation have been trying to implement a massively complex project, under intense pressure and to very challenging timescales. Our overriding concern is that local government leaders, staff and councillors have strained every sinew to meet the deadlines set by MHCLG. Today’s announcement – whatever the reasons behind it – rides roughshod over 1,000s of hours of work.
“If the prime minister is serious about his ambitions to rewire the state, then lessons must be learned from this debacle and learned fast.”

Germany Makes Naval History With First Warship-Launched Ballistic Missile in Signal to Russia

Germany Makes Naval History With First Warship-Launched Ballistic Missile in Signal to Russia
Germany has successfully launched an Israeli-made LORA ballistic missile from a German Navy warship during a live-fire test in the North Atlantic, demonstrating a new long-range strike capability for its fleet.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the UK Defence Journal on September 6, two German frigates deployed to waters between Ireland and Iceland for the trial, which had not been publicly disclosed before its completion. A containerized LORA launcher was installed on the deck of one of the vessels.
The outlet described the previously undisclosed test as a direct signal to Moscow, pointing to European efforts to develop longer-range strike capabilities. NATO also presented the launch as part of a broader shift toward greater European responsibility for deterrence.
NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum subsequently confirmed the test, saying the launch had been conducted secretly before being publicly revealed.
“Kept secret. Now revealed. The German Navy just tested the Israeli LORA ballistic missile from a German frigate in the North Atlantic—quietly, deliberately and with a range of 500+ km,” the command said.
Vice Admiral Jan Christian Kaack, Inspector of the German Navy, described the launch as a milestone for Germany’s naval forces. “With the successful launch of a ballistic missile last night in the North Atlantic, we made naval history. I am extremely satisfied with this achievement,” Kaack said.
He added that the weapon “can be successfully deployed from our units, and the potential range exceeds anything we have known before.”
The missile used in the trial was the LORA, or Long-Range Artillery Weapon System, developed by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI). The company lists the missile with a range of approximately 400 kilometers and an accuracy of within 10 meters, while NATO described the weapon tested by Germany as having a range exceeding 500 kilometers.
According to IAI, the LORA was fired from an operational German vessel equipped with a command trailer and launcher. The missile completed its planned flight path and successfully struck its designated target, with the company saying the system met the objectives established for the trial.
The launch was conducted under the German Navy’s OPEX initiative, which allows new weapons, technologies, and operational concepts to be tested rapidly under conditions designed to approximate operational deployment. The program forms part of Germany’s broader Marine 2035 and Beyond modernization effort.
Earlier, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Germany’s accusations against Moscow over the attempted explosive-drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport marked “the start of a real war,” while also accusing Chancellor Friedrich Merz of “declaring war” on Russia.

Russian Military Intelligence Soldier Says 70% of His Company Was Wiped Out—Then He Chose to Surrender

- Category

Russian Military Intelligence Soldier Says 70% of His Company Was Wiped Out—Then He Chose to Surrender
A Russian military intelligence special forces soldier voluntarily surrendered to Ukraine after an assault in which he says roughly 70% of his company was killed, an experience that convinced him his supposedly elite unit had simply been sent to die.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) released the serviceman’s account through the state-run I Want to Live project, which facilitates voluntary surrenders by Russian troops on September 7.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to HUR, the prisoner served in a special operations unit subordinate to the Main Directorate of the Russian General Staff, commonly known by its former acronym GRU. Ukrainian intelligence described his surrender as unusual, saying personnel connected to Russian intelligence services are rarely taken prisoner voluntarily.
The serviceman said he joined the unit after signing a military contract and received training in weapons, tactics, engineering, explosives, topography, communications, and other disciplines.
But he said the reputation surrounding Russian special forces no longer matches their reality.
“The training there is better than in ordinary units, but expectations of these special forces are greatly exaggerated. Now they take many people in and filter them out afterward,” he said.
The prisoner also said he initially believed Russian state propaganda and regarded the war as a legitimate cause.
“I thought I was taking part in something big. Now I understand that the propaganda simply worked very well. If the state does something, you get used to thinking that it must be right,” he said.
The turning point, according to his account, came during an assault on a Ukrainian village.
His company was ordered forward and ultimately completed its assigned objective, he said, but most of the unit was killed in the process.
“We completed the task, but at the cost of terrible losses. About 70% of the company died. When I saw the settlement for which so many people had been sacrificed, I realized it made absolutely no sense. It looked more like some kind of hidden genocide of Russia’s male population,” the prisoner said.
What he found inside the village further changed his perception of the war, he said.
“We entered houses, and family photographs were still hanging there. This was someone’s home, where people had created a comfortable life. And now the Russian army leaves only ruins behind. I didn’t see anything there that needed to be ‘liberated,’” he stated.
After the operation, the serviceman began searching for a way to avoid returning to combat.
He described his options as increasingly narrow: being killed, being transferred into another assault formation, or surrendering.
The solution eventually appeared on TikTok. While watching videos from Ukrainian soldiers and interviews with Russian prisoners, he came across information about the I Want to Live project.
“I saw a link to the I Want to Live chatbot and wrote to them. Then the coordinator and I discussed the extraction plan in detail. I explained that I no longer wanted to participate in the occupation and that I understood I was taking away someone else’s home,” he said.
He ultimately surrendered voluntarily through the program. The prisoner said the project offers an alternative for Russian soldiers who no longer want to participate in the invasion.
“It is very good that such an opportunity exists. For people who have regained sound judgment, it is a chance to stop taking part in this lawlessness, lay down their weapons, and stay alive,” he said.
Earlier, reports emerged that twenty Russian soldiers are currently held in Ukrainian captivity after surrendering to the Ukrainian Defense Forces for a second time following prisoner exchanges.
Russian commanders sent these servicemen back to active duty after they returned home in swaps, leading them to surrender again when sent back to the front line.

Swiss labour market remains strong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:23:09 UTC
23:23:09 KST

Swiss labour market remains strong
The Swiss labour market continues to show signs of strength against a backdrop of geopolitical and economic uncertainties.
This was stated by Jérôme Cosandey, head of the labour division at the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), while commenting via teleconference on the unemployment figures (3% in August).
The only significant increase was among young people aged between 15 and 24, with the unemployment rate rising to 3.4% in the eighth month of the year. This was an increase of 0.6 percentage points compared with July, with 2,400 more people out of work (bringing the total to 14,700).
More
Why unemployment in Switzerland is increasing more than elsewhere in Europe
According to Cosandey, however, this is a perfectly normal seasonal phenomenon as every summer, thousands of young people who have finished school, vocational training or university enter the labour market and have not yet found a job.
Unemployment in this age group usually peaks in August. The number of unemployed under-20s then falls rapidly as autumn approaches, while for 20–25-year-olds the situation improves significantly at the start of the following year. “It should happen this time too,” he said.
The figure also confirms a structural difference: young people are more at risk of being unemployed, but find new jobs much more quickly than older age groups.
On average, it takes just over three months for those under 25 to come off the unemployment register, while for the over-55s it takes more than nine months.
There are also positive signs from short-time working: this scheme, which allows companies to temporarily reduce working hours without making redundancies, is being used less and less, confirming the resilience of Switzerland’s manufacturing sector, concludes Cosandey.

Will Trump succeed in restarting Russia-Ukraine peace talks?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:22:58 UTC
23:22:58 KST

Will Trump succeed in restarting Russia-Ukraine peace talks?
The Witkoff-Kushner visit to Moscow and Kyiv did not produce a breakthrough, but can help begin a new process.
The visit by White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv has left more questions than answers. Details of what was discussed in both meetings are scant, but all participants seem to describe them as “positive”.
It is indeed a positive development that US President Donald Trump is trying to jump start negotiations at this point. The biggest problem he faces is that Russia’s position has only hardened.
Russia wants Ukraine to be genuinely neutral, with no Western military presence, open or clandestine. It wants to keep previously occupied territories and it insists that Ukraine withdraw from the small part of Donbas that remains in its hands.
Moscow demands a cap on the size of the Ukrainian army and on the types of weapons it may possess. It also wants far-right units and paramilitary groups disbanded and outlawed, the legislation limiting the use of the Russian language cancelled and elections to be held in which Russia-friendly parties could compete freely with the pro-Western ones.
For Ukraine and its European backers, this would be a hard pill to swallow, all the more so after spending the summer trying to convince the European public and Trump that the “tide is turning” in the war.
As evidence, Ukrainian and Western officials have repeatedly pointed to the Russian offensive slowing down and Ukraine intensifying strikes deep within Russian territory, targeting oil facilities and causing fuel shortages across the country.
The campaign against Russian energy infrastructure was meant to coerce Russian President Vladimir Putin into accepting peace on conditions more favourable to Ukraine.
But the opposite has happened. Russia’s negotiating position is now even less open to compromise. The land swap, once eyed as a way to compensate Ukraine for its withdrawal from the Donbas region, is now out of the question.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin has launched its own devastating campaign of strikes aimed at collapsing Ukraine’s economy. In addition to shutting down exports of Ukraine’s main commodities, grain and ore, through Odesa ports, Russia is also methodically destroying logistical hubs and warehouses owned by large retailers as well as large-scale industry, from metallurgical plants to beverage factories.
This is the point when Trump’s peacemaking duo resurfaced on the Russo-Ukrainian front after a protracted absence. The very fact that Kushner and Witkoff embarked on this trip and were received by Putin personally signals a change of tack in Washington.
A week before their arrival, CIA director John Ratcliffe mysteriously appeared in Moscow. Ratcliffe was effectively snubbed by Putin, who refused an audience when the CIA chief’s convoy reached the Kremlin. Instead, Ratcliffe had meetings with the heads of Russian security agencies, FSB and SVR, before heading home.
Nothing emerged from this meeting, apart from media speculation based on dubious sourcing. Hawkish media outlets claimed that Ratcliffe arrived with a stern warning against Russia attacking East European NATO members.
Others claimed Ratcliffe was trying to convey the “tide is turning” narrative to Putin and push for new negotiations based on that. The Atlantic magazine claimed last month that it was the CIA director who planted the idea that Russia was beginning to lose into Trump’s head during golf games.
Russian emigre outlet Agentstvo confirmed, quoting a Kremlin source, that Putin cancelled the meeting after hearing what Ratcliffe had been telling his subordinates and concluding that he was delusional.
Whether that is true or not, it is quite telling that Ratcliffe, who is a more senior US official than Kushner and Witkoff, was turned away, while they received a warm welcome in Moscow and spent a considerable time with Putin. Clearly, Trump’s envoys did not make the long trip to repeat what the Russian president sees as Western propaganda.
Whether Kushner and Witkoff’s mission has added anything substantial to the peace process is another question. They expressed cautious optimism regarding their progress. They said that no immediate breakthrough was foreseen but were eyeing direct trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US.
What is remarkable about the Witkoff-Kushner mission is the sheer number of commentators who were all too keen to claim that it was doomed from the outset. This is a reflection of the power pro-war circles continue to wield, despite growing war fatigue in Western societies.
The pro-war party simply wants any talks with Russia to be doomed, like they wanted the Istanbul talks to be doomed in the spring of 2022 and Minsk agreements to be ditched before that.
In trying to jump-start the peace talks, Trump will also have to face off with this party, which includes, European governments, NATO leadership and parts of the political establishment in his own country.
He would be keen to achieve some progress in peace talks prior to midterm elections and pressure Putin into limiting his military cooperation with Iran, but that’s impossible to achieve while the US plays a crucial role in helping Ukraine target infrastructure in Russia’s own territory.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s resilience is increasingly under question amid continuing brutal bombardment by the Russian army. As winter approaches, the targeting of energy and water infrastructure could severely worsen living conditions in the country.
Kyiv is already shaken by a political crisis, aggravated by corruption scandals involving top officials close to Zelenskyy, as well as a turf war between security agencies. There is also a $26bn gap in the Ukrainian defence budget, which needs to be covered by Western aid that’s not necessarily forthcoming.
There is no limit to warmongers pressuring Ukraine into fighting a suicidal war with a far stronger rival, but there is a limit to how long Ukrainians would be willing to die for an agenda that’s increasingly at odds with their national and personal interests.

EU unveils $232M investment package for Greenland as Brussels deepens strategic partnership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:22:48 UTC
23:22:48 KST

Melike Pala
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
The European Union announced a €200 million ($232 million) investment package for Greenland on Monday, targeting digital connectivity, clean energy, critical raw materials, and projects aimed at improving local living standards as Brussels seeks to deepen its economic and strategic engagement in the Arctic.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the package during a visit to Nuuk, where she joined Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen for the signing of a new joint declaration on EU–Greenland relations.
The package will finance investments in Greenland over the next two years, with the EU identifying digital connectivity, clean energy, and critical raw materials as its primary strategic priorities. Von der Leyen noted that these investments are intended not only to strengthen Europe’s presence in Greenland, but also to drive local job creation, economic growth, and opportunity.
As part of the initiative, the EU is providing approximately €9.1 million over five years—co-financed by Denmark—to support satellite-based internet services in East and North Greenland. The project is expected to improve the speed, reliability, and resilience of internet access in remote settlements, schools, and businesses.
Additionally, the EU and Greenland plan to advance sustainable mining projects linked to European industry. EU support will include technical analysis and investor matchmaking to help build more resilient supply chains. Von der Leyen specifically highlighted the Malmbjerg molybdenum mining project, noting it could become one of Greenland’s largest ventures and generate up to €90 million a year in added value for the country if successfully developed.
This investment push comes as Greenland's strategic importance grows amid escalating geopolitical tension in the Arctic. Von der Leyen stated that the EU aims to be "more present and more engaged" in the region, adding that Brussels is preparing a new EU Arctic strategy to be presented in the autumn.
She also reiterated the EU's support for Denmark and Greenland, emphasizing that Greenland's future should be determined solely by its people. An autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, Greenland holds immense strategic value due to its Arctic location and vast mineral and energy resources.
Former U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly called for U.S. control of Greenland during his presidency, calling it a historical and strategic necessity. However, both Danish and Greenlandic leaders firmly rejected the proposal, maintaining that Greenland "is not for sale."
