Syrian nuclear reactor could have been useful for weapons, IAEA chief says
VIENNA, Sept 7 - The nuclear reactor Syria had nearly completed in 2007 when Israeli jets destroyed it was of a type that could quickly produce fissile material usable in nuclear weapons, U.N. nuclear watchdog chief Rafael Grossi said on Monday.
The International Atomic Energy Agency has described as a "historic breakthrough" its recent investigation into secret nuclear activities under the Assad family's rule. The investigation uncovered around 73 metric tons of natural uranium metal, mainly in the form of reactor fuel.
In a report to member states seen by Reuters, the IAEA confirmed its previous finding that the bombed site in Syria's eastern province of Deir al-Zor was a nuclear reactor under construction, and that fuel for it had been made in Syria, all of which should have been declared at the time to the agency.
"This is a reactor that is very efficient in the production of fissile material that could be used directly for the fabrication of nuclear weapons," Grossi told a press conference, adding that it was "almost completed".
"That was a very serious proliferation concern," he said, while cautioning that the then-authorities' intentions "cannot be judged".
Since the ouster of President Bashar al-Assad in late 2024, Syria's new authorities have committed to working with the IAEA to answer questions relating to so-called nuclear safeguards - the process of accounting for and monitoring nuclear material.
"Having received the necessary access and information from Syria, ... the Agency has been able to clarify and resolve the Agency's questions concerning the outstanding safeguards issues related to Syria's past nuclear activities," Grossi said in a speech to the IAEA's 35-nation board.
"I welcome Syria's transparency and cooperation with the Agency which facilitates the resolution of the outstanding safeguards issues related to Syria's past nuclear activities," he added. REUTERS

National day of mourning in Nepal for mudslide victims

Nepal held a national day of mourning with candlelight vigils on Monday for victims of devastating glacial floods, as families of missing hydropower workers feared trapped in tunnels prayed rescuers might yet find them alive.
The August 26 glacial and mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,399 people, with more than 5,500 missing, including around 800 foreigners.
Flags flew at half-mast and hundreds of people gathered for the vigils in the Nepali capital Kathmandu, as the nation marked the 13th day after death in line with Hindu mourning rituals.
Hundreds of hydropower workers are among the missing, but the rescue of three of them from deep inside tunnels – two Nepalis on Friday and a Chinese man on Saturday – have buoyed hopes that more could still be alive.
Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet said rescue efforts were continuing at "the same tempo" to make sure "that no one is still stranded".
Entire communities have been swept away, with roads destroyed and homes demolished.
But families of some of the missing workers who gathered in Kathmandu said the government must move faster.
"We have a lot of hope," said Reena Amatya Shrestha, whose brother is among the missing.
"They say they are doing rescue. If the rescue is there, where's the result? We need the result."
Australian tunnel rescue expert Arnold Dix, who is advising Nepali teams, said the operation presented an unprecedented challenge.
"We are facing something I have never faced before," said Dix, president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, in a post on social media.
"Not one rescue, but multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties, and lives that may still be saved."
Foreign experts, including from China, India and South Korea, are aiding Nepali teams in rescue efforts.
"We are measured not only by the lives we save, but by the lives we refuse to abandon," said Dix.
Nepal President Ram Chandra Paudel visited relief camps in Nuwakot, speaking to those left homeless by the disaster.
"Today the entire nation is mourning this horrific disaster," he said in a statement.
"To everyone waiting for news of family members and friends, I want to assure you that search and rescue operations will continue."
With mortuaries overflowing, Nepal has buried hundreds of bodies in mass graves after taking DNA samples for future identification, according to police.
Despite the gloom, there have been remarkable tales of survival.
Chandika Shrestha, a 64-year-old Nepali woman, was pulled out alive from her mud-covered home in Bidur on Saturday.
Her family had already held a symbolic funeral ceremony, believing her dead.
"Chandika has got a new life," her neighbour Buddhi Lal Dongol told AFP. "It would be so good if the others who are missing also came back."
Several families held last-rite ceremonies in Nuwakot to mark the 13th day of mourning, while Buddhist monks held prayers for the dead.
"I have had to hold myself together a lot," 63-year-old Kula Priya Nepal, whose son was killed at a hydroelectric project, told AFP.
Rescuers have retrieved 1,356 bodies in Nepal, while around 4,994 people are missing, according to the disaster agency.
The toll in China stands at 43 dead and 519 missing. (AFP)

Trump administration attacks UK plans to boost traditional media on social platforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:20:12 UTC
23:20:12 KST

The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force YouTube and other digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”.
In a pointed intervention, the US government said the proposals to boost traditional media outlets in social media algorithms could “establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content”.
It also warned it could undermine “independent journalists” and amount to “extraterritorial censorship of protected speech by Americans online”.
The statement, made via the US embassy in London, raises the stakes in the plans to give the likes of the BBC, ITV and other established media more visibility on increasingly dominant digital platforms.
Ministers, regulators and public service broadcasters have suggested new rules are needed to counter growing misinformation online as people increasingly turn to less regulated online platforms such as X, YouTube and TikTok.
In a consultation this year, the UK government said it would consider legislating should the platforms not act to prioritise trustworthy content. However, Washington claimed such a plan risked effectively removing the content of “independent journalists” over established outlets.
“Preserving a free, open internet and protecting freedom of expression online are top priorities for the Trump administration,” it said. “A framework that empowers governments to influence which sources receive preferential visibility risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship.
“If the UK compels platforms to boost government-preferred media in algorithmic feeds, the effect on a government-disfavoured speaker or media source’s reach is not meaningfully different than outright removal. The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship.”
The administration has asked what safeguards will be in place to ensure “any biases and preferences of UK government officials and third-party organisations” do not influence the plan in ways that disadvantage “independent or minority-viewpoint journalism”.
A spokesperson for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said: “We welcome engagement and responses to our media green paper. We believe strongly in free expression and fair competition, and any action we take will ensure these are protected.”
Insiders say any measures would only affect the UK. The US complaint highlights its readiness to fight for the largely US-based tech companies that run the world’s largest digital platforms.
Donald Trump also has a long record of attacking and bypassing the established media, regularly accusing major outlets of “fake news” and biased coverage. He often tries to reach supporters online.
The US president is still engaged in his lawsuit with the BBC over an episode of Panorama in which it spliced together one of his speeches. The BBC has apologised for the edit, but stated the show did not defame Trump.
Social media companies have previously been sceptical about artificially boosting the prominence of traditional media, arguing that it goes against the principle of creator content.
Online content creators have compared the proposals to state control and fear their content would be pushed down the rankings as a result.
Simon Squibb, a UK YouTube creator, said he was encouraged that his concerns were shared by an “entity that I think politicians will listen to”.
“This is a very dangerous potential direction for the UK to go in,” he said. “I’m happy that the USA has stepped in.”
Supporters of the enforced prominence plans have couched them as a way of dealing with misinformation and preserving culturally British content.
However, the government has also been clear that it wants to help public service broadcasters survive the economic turmoil created by the rise of digital platforms, which all media companies are confronting.

Ursula von der Leyen, Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Mette Frederiksen hold a press conference in Nuuk, Greenland on Sept. 7, 2026. | Mads Claus Rasmussen/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP via Getty Images
Greenland is making a “clear choice” to strengthen ties with the EU, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Monday, as Brussels unveiled a €200 million investment package and moved to deepen its political, economic and security footprint in the Arctic.
Speaking in Nuuk alongside Greenlandic Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, von der Leyen cast the relationship as a two-way partnership.
The renewed EU-Greenland declaration, she said, “reflects a clear choice expressed by Greenland to strengthen ties with the European Union,” while also demonstrating Europe’s own decision “to be more present” and more engaged in Greenland and across the Arctic.
Advertisement
U.S. President Donald Trump has made repeated threats to take over Greenland. In July, he said that “Greenland … should be controlled by the United States, not by Denmark” at the outset of a NATO summit in Turkey.
The Arctic has rapidly climbed up Brussels’ geopolitical agenda. Von der Leyen said the region had become a place “where the tectonic plates of geopolitics collide,” adding that the EU has a direct stake in developments there and is preparing a new Arctic strategy for presentation this fall.
The Arctic is also expected to feature prominently in von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech next week, as Brussels prepares the revamped strategy.
She also reiterated that Greenland’s future is for the people of Greenland and Denmark to decide.
The two-day visit, which began Sunday, was aimed at turning the political message into concrete projects. A Commission official said the trip had been months in the making but was postponed at Frederiksen’s request due to Danish elections in March.
Von der Leyen signed a renewed joint declaration with Greenland and Denmark and unveiled a €200 million EU partnership package for this year and next.
Advertisement
At Greenlandic telecom operator Tusass, she launched a satellite connectivity project designed to improve internet access in remote communities. Brussels will also support hydropower development and work with Greenland on mining projects intended to more closely link the island’s raw materials to European industry.
The broader declaration expands cooperation into education, infrastructure, fisheries, tourism, housing, research, climate action, civil protection, cybersecurity and Arctic resilience.
Von der Leyen also pointed to the longer-term relationship, saying the Commission has proposed more than doubling EU funding for Greenland to €530 million through 2034.

Search continues for hundreds trapped in hydro-plant after Nepal floods

Search for 900 missing hydro-plant workers continues in Nepal
In short :
More than 100 hydro-power workers are feared trapped in tunnels almost two weeks after floods ripped through the Himalayan site.
A total of 900 people are still missing from the hydro-electric tunnels in Nepal.
What's next?
Rescuers are working with specialised equipment to free people they believe may have air pockets inside the vast tunnel systems.
Nepali rescuers have searched for more than 100 hydropower workers feared trapped in tunnels days after four miracle rescues from the wreckage of catastrophic floods that laid waste to towns and villages on the Himalayan border with China.
The rescues on Monday have offered a glimmer of hope as Nepal marked the 13th day after the disaster, traditionally the final day of mourning in Hindu rites, for the hundreds killed in the floods.
About 121 of a total 900 people missing from the hydro-electric projects could have been trapped in these tunnels, army rescuers said.
Others may have been working elsewhere at the power plants but not inside the vast network of tunnels.
Among those whom rescuers were trying to find on Monday were four out of six people missing at the Chilime hydropower project in the hard-hit Rasuwa district who could still be alive, Shri Ram Neupane, a lawmaker involved in rescue efforts, told Reuters.
Authorities had obtained specialised equipment and identified techniques needed for the Chilime operation, Mr Neupane said.
Rescuers believe that there could be survivors trapped inside tunnels because many have air pockets, as well as spaces and rooms for people to stay, they said last week.
In recent days, search teams in Nepal have rescued four people, including a Chinese national who was pulled from a tunnel on Saturday.
The others were two hydropower workers rescued from another tunnel on Friday and a Nepali woman pulled out from her buried house on Saturday.
Government offices in the Hindu majority country and at missions abroad would fly the national flag at half-mast to mark the 13th day after death, the home ministry said in a statement.
The day is considered the final day of mourning by the faithful, who commemorate it with rituals and food offerings.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said in a statement last week, the Australian government would deploy a team of specialist drone operators to contribute to Nepal's search and rescue efforts.
"The team, including members of Fire and Rescue New South Wales and the Queensland Fire Department, will depart in the coming days as part of a 15-person Disaster Assistance Response Team," the statement read.
"They will use advanced drone technology to provide rapid mapping and imaging to support Nepali authorities' search operations."
At least 1,380 people have been killed by the mudslide. More than 5,500 are missing in Nepal and Tibet, among them 35 Australians.
The disaster was triggered on August 26 when a huge mass of mud and rock, following the collapse of part of a glacier, crashed into a river along the border between Nepal and China's Tibet region.
The resulting floods washed away towns and villages and buried roads and highways under mud and debris.
Chinese officials said on Sunday that workers had recovered 12 more bodies as the search continued for hundreds still missing in Tibet.
"The Chinese side will continue to make every effort to conduct search-and-rescue operations and handle post-disaster matters," foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a press briefing.
China has faced pressure from some families of foreign visitors missing in Tibet, who say they have struggled to obtain information on missing relatives.
Mr Mao said Beijing would promptly release "updated information on the disaster situation and rescue activities."
On Sunday, China for the first time invited journalists from eight foreign media outlets, including Reuters, to visit the core affected areas.
With search teams still looking for survivors, Nepal's government has not planned any wider events for the final day of mourning.
"There are no government programmes organised as the rescue and search operation is still going on in the flood-hit areas," Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC) told Reuters.
President Ram Chandra Paudel, the ceremonial head of state, was touring flood-hit areas on Monday and would survey damage caused by the disaster, his aide said.
Security personnel at the district jail in Nuwakot, one of the two worst affected districts, saved 923 prisoners by shifting them to a building in a higher location before flood waters entered their low-lying building on August 26, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a social media post.
Authorities also captured 50 prisoners who had broken the prison wall and gates as flooding began, and had fled barely 100 metres, Shah said on Monday.

white stainless-steel cylinders form coral-like swing installation on chinese coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:15:41 UTC
23:15:41 KST

Twelve Cylinders Form a Coral-Inspired Coastal Installation
Composed of twelve oversized white cylinders, Coral is a swing installation that transforms the coastline of Yantai, China, into an inhabitable underwater world. The work, created by XBTW Office, stands at the northwest corner of West Park at Longfor Puti peninsula. Facing tidal flats and the sea, the site is shaped by the daily rhythm of tides, sea breeze, and sunsets, which together form its most distinctive landscape. Visitors wander between shifting frames of sea and sky or swing toward the sunset, experiencing the tides and sea breeze through movement. The form of the installation is inspired by the repetition and aggregation of similar units found in coral colonies. The design uses twelve white stainless-steel cylinders as basic units, arranged into two groups above and below. A thin horizontal roof plane passes through the composition, with two west-facing swings suspended beneath it. The cylinders, positioned at different heights and orientations, overlap and shift against one another, creating an inhabitable space for people to enter, move through, and pause.
Perforated Cylinders Frame the Coast and Shift with the Light
Viewed from a distance, the white forms emerge along the open coastline as an unfamiliar presence, resembling a group of marine organisms. As visitors approach, the spaces between the cylinders gradually reveal fragments of tidal flats, sea, and sky, transforming the continuous landscape into a series of constantly changing frames. Upon entering the installation, the relationship between body and scale begins to shift. The oversized cylinders surround the body, making the familiar coastline temporarily feel unfamiliar, as if entering an underwater world. Visitors can move through the structure or sit on the west-facing swings, experiencing the sea breeze, tides, and sunset through gentle movement.
The perforated patterns on the cylinders are inspired by variations in the density of deep-sea fish schools. Each cylinder contains approximately 2,000 to 4,000 perforations of different sizes, ranging from 4 to 25 millimeters in diameter. Variations in the density and scale of the openings create a gradient texture on the white stainless-steel surfaces, evoking the gathering and dispersal of fish schools. Among these openings, a small number of larger perforations take the forms of marine creatures, including starfish, octopuses, and seashells, adding another layer of detail to the surface. After sunset, light emerges through the perforations, transforming the previously quiet white forms into another state. The installation by creative practice XBTW Office gradually appears like a group of slowly breathing marine organisms.

Estonia has 5th-highest obesity rate in Europe, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:14:00 UTC
23:14:00 KST

Estonia has 5th-highest obesity rate in Europe, data shows
Estonia has the fifth‑highest share of obese adults in Europe, with 22.0 percent of the population aged 18 and over classified as obese, according to 2025 Eurostat data.
The EU average stood at 16.3 percent, with the highest rates posted in Malta (26.6 percent), followed by Estonia's immediate neighbors to the south and north: Latvia (which saw 24.6 percent of the population classified as obese) and Finland (at 23.2 percent). Ireland at (22.1 percent was fractionally ahead of Estonia. The lowest proportions were seen in Romania (12.9 percent), Greece (12.8 percent) and Italy (7.0 percent).
In addition, 35.4 percent of Europe's population was classified as overweight, or pre‑obese, with a Body Mass Index (BMI) between 25 and 30. Overall, more than half of Europe's population was either obese or pre‑obese/overweight.
Men were more likely to be overweight than women, on the whole. The obesity rate among men was 17.4 percent, compared with 15.3 percent among women EU-wide. Meanwhile, 41.9 percent of men were pre‑obese, compared with 29.3 percent of women. Also, rates of being underweight were nearly three times higher among women (at 2.9 percent) compared with men (at 1.0 percent).
According to Eurostat, 46.4 percent of European adults were at a normal and healthy weight: 39.8 percent of men and 52.5 percent of women.
In Estonia alone, the situation is even more pronounced. ERR's science portal Novaator reported in July, citing a study by the National Institute for Health Development (TAI), which found more than 60 percent of Estonian adults were overweight as of last year, and with 26 percent classified as obese.
The TAI study also found that excess weight imposes significant additional costs on society, affecting healthcare, productivity and overall economic well‑being.
The obesity rate is calculated using body mass index (BMI), which is determined by dividing body weight in kilograms by the square of height in meters. A BMI of 30 or higher is classified as obese, while a BMI between 25 and 30 is considered pre‑obese.

Türkiye aims to reach single-digit inflation with 3-year economic plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:12:31 UTC
23:12:31 KST

Serhat Tutak and Emir Yildirim
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Türkiye’s new Medium-Term Program (MTP) aims to resolve persistently high inflation and reach single-digit levels through the disinflation process.
The economic plan covering 2027-2029 aims to break inflationary inertia and achieve price stability by reducing the inflation rate to single-digit levels through the uninterrupted continuation of the disinflation process.
Türkiye’s annual consumer inflation rate is at 31.51% as of August, prompting Ankara to prioritize the disinflation process driven by coordination of monetary, fiscal, and revenue policies to be maintained throughout the three-year period.
The economic roadmap projects annual consumer inflation to end this year at 28.4% before falling to 21% in 2027, 13.5% in 2028, and 9% by the end of 2029.
Türkiye’s Central Bank (CBRT) will maintain its framework targeting inflation and a floating exchange rate regime to allow free market supply and demand to dictate currency values.
The plan is to utilize all monetary tools to cool domestic demand while strengthening supply policies to promote broader market competition.
The program aims to change how businesses set their prices by urging them to base their expectations on future government targets instead of adjusting prices to match past inflation, in an attempt to break the cycle of continuous retail hikes.
The plan also outlines that state purchase prices for crops will be determined by their impact on public finances and market dynamics to prevent indexation to past inflation rates, while specially tailoring agricultural production to seize regional potential to ensure long-term food security.
Communication channels will be strengthened to anchor inflation expectations within targets, while public awareness of a website for viewing prices at supermarket chains will be raised to increase transparency.

The Ministry of Defense explained what representatives of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers can and cannot do during an air raid alert
Kyiv • UNN
Representatives of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers have no right to stop or detain people heading to a shelter. Document checks in the shelter are not separately prohibited.
Representatives of the territorial recruitment and social support centers (TCCs and SСs) are not authorized to stop, hold or detain citizens in public places or prevent them from proceeding to a shelter during an air raid. This is stated in the response of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine to Oleksii Honcharenko, Head of the Verkhovna Rada's Temporary Investigative Commission, which UNN has reviewed.
At the same time, the legislation does not separately require TCC personnel to immediately stop notification efforts or the verification of military registration documents once inside shelters.
Details
The Ministry of Defense noted that the procedure for actions by TCC and SS notification groups during the "Air Raid Alert" signal is regulated by legislation in the areas of civil protection, military service and the performance of service duties by military personnel. At the same time, there are no separate regulatory acts of the Ministry of Defense, orders or directives of the Ministry of Defense or the General Staff that would establish a special algorithm for the conduct of TCC notification groups in public places directly during an air raid.
The ministry reminded that, in accordance with the Code of Civil Protection of Ukraine, ensuring citizens' safety and protecting people from the consequences of emergencies, military actions or an air attack is a priority duty.
"The implementation of protective measures in response to civil protection signals is mandatory for all persons located on the territory of Ukraine," the Defense Ministry's response states.
The ministry separately emphasized that military personnel who are members of TCC and SS notification groups are not authorized to prevent people from proceeding to a safe place.
"The legislation does not grant military personnel who are members of TCC and SS notification groups the authority to stop, hold or detain citizens in public places or prevent them from proceeding to a shelter while the \"Air Raid Alert\" signal is in effect," the relevant ministry stated.
At the same time, the ministry drew attention to another legal detail: the current legislation contains no special provision requiring TCC and SS representatives, after an alert is announced, to immediately stop notifying citizens or checking military registration documents if such actions are already taking place inside a shelter or another protective structure.
It follows that the work of notification groups during an air raid must be carried out in compliance with the requirements of legislation in the areas of civil protection, military service and mobilization, while the protection of people's lives and health and compliance with established safety rules must remain the priority.
We remind you
As UNN reported, due to Russian strikes on TCCs and SSs, their work will be reformatted to ensure the safety of personnel and visitors. Possible options include dispersing recruitment office personnel, remote services and expanded digitalization.

Carbon capture tech exists. Scaling it up is the hard part
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:12:00 UTC
23:12:00 KST

Carbon capture tech exists. Scaling it up is the hard part
September 7, 2026
For years there has been talk of capturing and storing the carbon dioxide generated by burning fossil fuels as one way to keep the planet from overheating. In fact, the United Nations' climate science body envisions somewhere between 350 to 1,200 gigatons of CO2 storage within the century to avoid the worst effects of climate change.
But is it really happening? Yes and no.
Carbon capture and storage, or CCS, is an effort to trap CO2 at what's called a point source. This might be a smokestack or at an ammonia factory — in other words, a single, concentrated spot where the planet-heating greenhouse gas is emitted.
After being captured, it is compressed and transported, usually using pipelines or trains, before being stored geologically — in aquifers or old oil reservoirs, for example.
CCS is related to, but distinct from, carbon dioxide removal (CDR), which involves pulling CO2 out of the atmosphere after it's already been emitted. That CO2 is often stored similarly to CCS, but uses very different technologies for capturing.
"Given the legacy of emissions in the atmosphere, given where we are in terms of emissions reductions, we're going to need these approaches," said Wil Burns, co-director of the Institute for Carbon Removal Law & Policy at American University.
"We just have to figure out how to use them thoughtfully and still keep our eye on the prize of decarbonizing."
The technology works, but scaling is another matter
The feasibility of CCS and CDR is a subject of much debate among scientists and climate campaigners.
Advocates for scaling up the technology as a key pillar of decarbonization say the main hurdle is getting more plants built, which would require government subsidies and policy intervention.
Without governments putting a price on carbon or offering tax credits, experts say it's hard to imagine investors shelling out for these expensive commercial projects. Renewable energy, by contrast, has become so cheap over time that it's often commercially viable on its own.
"It's ready to go, technologically. We know how to do this process," said Susan Hovorka, a geoscientist at the University of Texas-Austin, researching CCS since 1998.
How CCS began
CCS traces its roots back to the 1960s, when oil companies began piping natural CO2 into oil fields for enhanced oil recovery — that's where captured CO2 is injected into old oil fields to help push more oil out of the ground. It wasn't until 1996 that the first large-scale CCS project designed to reduce emissions went online in Norway.
Progress since then has been slowly ramping up. In 2020, there were 26 operational commercial CCS facilities around the world. As of last summer, the number has nearly tripled.
But others say the technology remains in its infancy, and our real-world capabilities lag far behind our technical knowhow.
"What is not well-established and basically doesn't exist at scale is the commercial experience doing this," said Danny Cullenward, an economist at the University of Pennsylvania's Kleinman Center for Energy Policy. "And proving that it works; that it's easy, that it's cost-effective, that it can be deployed at large scale, that it works in lots of different places."
Researchers from the University of Texas-Austin recently revealedthat though small-scale pilot projects have been successful in injecting CO2 into the ground, many of the world's large-scale CCS initiatives are pumping far less into storage sites than promised.
And they are not unlimited. While previous estimates put the Earth's CO2 storage capacity somewhere between 10,000 and 40,000 gigatons, a new study foundthe number is just about 1,460 gigatons, meaning most CCS-reliant climate scenarios would breach the planetary limit for storage over the next 250 years.
Climate models bet heavy on new technology
Starting this week, the European fertilizer giant Yara will open what it calls Europe's largest carbon capture project. It will harvest excess CO2 at its factory in Sluiskil Netherlands, liquefy it, and ship it to Norway's Atlantic coast to be stored in an underground rock formation, some 2,600 meters below the seabed.
That plant will only be able to capture 800,000 metric tons of CO2 annually. To meet that 350 gigaton threshold — the lower end of the UN's climate scenarios used to inform climate policy — would require about 5,800 more Yara-size plants to open tomorrow.
The International Energy Agency, another intergovernmental body that models climate data, projected7.6 gigatons of carbon will be captured every year by 2050, with almost all of it stored. Right now, the world's 77 operating plants are capable of capturing 64 million tons annually. That output would need to be multiplied by 119 over the next quarter-century to reach the IEA number.
"The scale of what's being called for in those scenarios is astronomically beyond any real activity that exists today," Cullenward said.
He says climate models tend to underestimate renewables and lean too hard on "gee-whiz" technologies.
That's because models basically have three ways to hit an ambitious climate target: add more renewables, use less energy, or bet on some new technology that solves the problem without forcing society to change much.
"If you tell a model to solve an impossible problem, it's like pouring water down a flight of stairs — it's going to find the fastest way to get to the bottom," Cullenward said.
A license to keep drilling?
One of the most contentious arguments about CCS is whether it represents a legitimate decarbonization solution or is a tactic from oil and gas companies to justify and prolong more fossil fuel extraction.
In 2023, about 80% of the world's CCS capacity was used for enhanced oil recovery, according to research and advocacy group, Oil Change International — ultimately increasing emissions and defeating CCS's climate benefit.
Some researchers also argue that CCS poses a moral hazard, or a situation where having a form of protection allows for more risk-taking.
On the other hand, advocates for the technology often talk of reserving CCS for what's called "hard-to-abate" industries, like cement.
"I don't think we're going to get to five or 10 or 20 gigatons a year of carbon removal," Cullenward said. "But we may need to get as much as we can and to me that's a reason to be more engaged rather than less engaged."

US approves sale of over 10,000 bombs to Saudi Arabia
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:10:17 BST
23:10:17 KST

The United States has approved a possible $5 billion Foreign Military Sale to Saudi Arabia covering more than 10,000 JDAM guidance kits, more than 10,000 general-purpose bombs and associated equipment, the US Department of State has announced.
The proposed sale, notified to Congress under Transmittal 26-35, covers Joint Direct Attack Munition – Extended Range equipment for the Royal Saudi Armed Forces and remains a potential Foreign Military Sale rather than a completed procurement contract.
Saudi Arabia has requested 5,004 KMU-572 JDAM guidance kits and 5,000 KMU-556 guidance kits. The package also includes 5,004 BLU-111 500lb general-purpose bombs and 5,000 BLU-117 2,000lb general-purpose bombs.
Together, the requested quantities amount to 10,004 JDAM guidance kits and 10,004 bomb bodies. JDAM kits are used to turn compatible general-purpose bombs into precision-guided weapons by adding a guidance and control system. The wider package would include FMU-139 fuze systems, DSU-38 and DSU-40 target detectors, containers and support equipment, spare parts, consumables and accessories, repair and return support, and US Government and contractor engineering, technical and logistics services.
The State Department said: “This proposed sale will support the foreign policy goals and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a Major non-NATO Ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf Region.”
Washington said the package is intended to strengthen Saudi Arabia’s ability to respond to regional threats and operate alongside American and other Gulf forces.
The department stated: “The proposed sale will improve Saudi Arabia’s airborne defense capability to counter current and future regional threats, strengthen its homeland defense, and improve interoperability with systems operated by U.S. forces and other Gulf Region partners. The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia will have no difficulty absorbing these articles and services into its armed forces.”
It added: “The proposed sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military balance in the region.”
Boeing, based in Arlington, Virginia, has been identified as the principal contractor. The US Government said it was not currently aware of an offset agreement connected with the proposed sale, with any such arrangements to be negotiated separately between Saudi Arabia and the contractor. The deal would not require additional US Government or contractor representatives to be permanently assigned to Saudi Arabia for implementation, according to the notification. The State Department also said: “There will be no adverse impact on U.S. defense readiness because of this proposed sale.”
The approval represents the US Government’s authorisation for the proposed Foreign Military Sale to proceed through the congressional notification process. The final value and quantities could change if Saudi Arabia ultimately concludes an agreement for the equipment.

Potential end of US aid to Peshmerga could mark 'transitional phase' in US-KRG relations, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:09:39 UTC
23:09:39 KST

- 'Withdrawal of coalition forces will impact KRG security more than the end of the aid, at least in the immediate term': Paul Iddon, Erbil-based journalist specializing in Mideast affairs, history and politics
 
 Experts say the potential end of US financial assistance to Peshmerga forces in northern Iraq’s Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) would raise concerns in the KRG leadership, but could also represent another “transitional phase” in US-KRG relations, with the sides potentially in the future operating under a new security framework.
According to reports by the BBC and local media in the KRG, US support, including up to $61 million in annual financial assistance to Peshmerga forces, is expected to end on Sept. 30.
The reported date for the potential end of assistance also coincides with the expected conclusion of the mission in Iraq of the US-led Global Coalition Against ISIS (Daesh).
Experts who spoke to Anadolu said the potential end of aid could affect both the security of the KRG, which has been targeted by numerous drone and missile attacks this year during the US/Israel-Iran war, as well as relations between Washington and Erbil, the KRG regional capital.
 
‘Would make KRG more vulnerable to attacks’
Omar Al-Nidawi, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, said the possible end of US assistance to the Peshmerga would likely increase concerns in Erbil about Washington’s direction as an ally.
As an example, Al-Nidawi pointed to what Iraqi Kurdish leaders viewed as developments during 2025-2026 conflicts in which the US appeared to abandon Syrian Kurds in favor of strengthening Syria’s post-Assad central government.
He said the most urgent security concern for Iraqi Kurds is acquiring air defense capabilities that could protect the KRG against drone and missile attacks by Iran and allied militias.
"Combined with the loss of US systems as the US pulls its last remaining troops, ending the aid program would make the KRG more vulnerable to attacks," he said.
Al-Nidawi also said the KRG could face growing pressure to meet Iranian demands on issues such as the presence of Kurdish opposition groups in the region.
 
Aid assistance 'was never a long-term setup'
Hamzeh Hadad, a fellow with the Middle East Security Program at the Washington-based Center for a New American Security (CNAS), said he did not believe relations between the US and the KRG would fundamentally change.
"At the end of the day, the Kurdish parties in Iraq need the US more than the US needs them," he said.
Hadad said US assistance to the Peshmerga had “never been a long-term setup” in terms of security.
The possible end of the aid, he said, could "force the KRG to take security reform more seriously" and require greater coordination with security forces led by Iraq’s central government in Baghdad.
"US presence and support hasn’t prevented attacks from Iran and armed groups in Iraq, (so) with less US involvement then there will be less of an excuse for KRG to be a target," he added.
 
KRG to become more dependent on Baghdad to finance Peshmerga
Journalist Paul Iddon, who covers the Mideast with a particular focus on the KRG, said the impact of ending assistance to the Peshmerga would not necessarily be negative.
"From the start, this aid was provided under the framework of the anti-ISIS mission that’s now ending and was never going to be permanent, he said.
Iddon said KRG officials had also acknowledged this in recent weeks, noting that the coalition’s combat mission officially ended in December 2021 and so this should not come as a surprise.
"At the same time, the timing is a little worrying for Erbil, which has long struggled to pay most civil servant salaries on time and will become even more dependent on Baghdad to fund these Peshmerga troops employed by the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs," he added.
 
Coalition withdrawal may have greater impact on KRG security
"The withdrawal of coalition forces will impact KRG security more than the end of the aid, at least in the immediate term," said Iddon.
American and British air defense systems provided significant practical protection for Erbil against drones and missiles during the continuing US/Israel-Iran war, he said, although most of those systems are now being withdrawn.
Nevertheless, Iddon stressed that the systems “never provided a strategic defense for the KRG,” noting that Peshmerga members were killed in missile strikes during the war and that the residences of KRG leaders were repeatedly targeted by drones.
He also said coalition forces either “could not or did not” defend Erbil against missile attacks carried out by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in 2022 and 2024.
"There is a small chance the US withdrawal may see a reduction in Iran and Iraqi militia attacks against the KRG, but I wouldn’t count on it," he added.
"I think after the withdrawal, you will still see US/coalition fighter jets flying from bases outside Iraq occasionally shooting down Iraqi militia and Iranian drones targeting the region; we’ve already seen that in recent months," Iddon said.
 
New security framework possible between US and KRG
Iddon said the current developments likely represent another “'transitional phase” in US-KRG relations and that the two sides will most likely operate under a new security framework in the future.
"US officials keep pointing to the fact that the largest American consulate was just built here in Erbil as a testament to continued ties. Still, a potential power vacuum in Iraq is worrying for KRG," he said.

The death of ‘hello’: how gen Z – and scammers – put paid to the greeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:08:36 UTC
23:08:36 KST

Name: Hello.
Age: 200 years old.
Status: Under threat of extinction.
That’s ridiculous – we’ve been saying hello to each other for millions of years. Well, that isn’t true. As I just mentioned, the word appeared in print a couple of hundred years ago. But it’s a deviation of “holla”, “hollo”, “halloo” or “hillo”, all of which were used in English as attention-grabbing noises since at least the 16th century.
But we use it all the time now. Only because of the telephone. After the phone’s invention by Alexander Graham Bell in 1876, Thomas Edison decided that a new standardised greeting needed to be invented.
Why? Because previously people tended to greet each other with time-based salutations, such as “good morning” or “good evening”. But the telephone could instantly cross time zones, which made these redundant.
But why hello? Because Edison preferred it to Bell’s favoured “Ahoy-hoy”.
Shame. I know. Anyway, forget all that, because nobody says hello any more.
But I like hello. Too late. Technology has marched on again: everyone has a smartphone with caller ID now. Why go through the charade of a “hello?” when you already know who’s calling you?
I don’t know, basic politeness? Tell that to gen Z. The New York Times has reported on the death of hello, stating that young people now prefer to answer the phone with “Hi”, “What’s up?” or “Yeah?”.
This sounds spurious. It isn’t. A survey last year revealed that 40% of 18-24 year-olds feel that it is acceptable to answer the phone without any form of greeting whatsoever.
Isn’t that a bit weird? It sort of makes sense, though. Conversations have become free-form things spread across multiple formats. If you’ve just been texting, or DMing, or emailing with someone, a phone call is just a continuation and arguably doesn’t require anything as formal as a hello.
Still, it’s nice. Only if you love AI scammers.
What the hell? Where did that come from? You didn’t hear about this? Apparently scammers can now replicate your voice with AI, cloning it from your telephone greeting, and use it to beg your loved ones for money. This is a real thing that has been covered by the consumer watchdog Which?, the BBC and the Guardian.
This is genuinely nightmarish. Guess what the best way to beat it is.
I’ll guess rudeness. Correct! If you’re called by an unidentified number, the advice is to remain silent until you are sure that a friendly human being is on the other end of the line. Not saying hello first could save you a whole heap of trouble.
Well, it looks like this is goodbye to hello. Don’t say goodbye. Say au revoir.
Because it’s romantic? No, because the terrifying hordes of robot scammers might clone you into a French person, and your family would be confused.
Do say: “Hello is becoming obsolete.”
Don’t say: “Ahoy-hoy!”

Exclusive: Iraqi factions reject September weapons deadline
Unknown

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Iraqi factions reject September deadline to hand over weapons
Two prominent Iran-aligned Iraqi armed factions have told The New Arab they will not hand over their weapons by a government-imposed deadline at the end of September unless Baghdad meets a series of conditions, including the withdrawal of US and Turkish forces from the country.
In exclusive comments to The New Arab, spokesmen for the Sayyid al-Shuhada Brigades and the Nujaba Movement said they did not consider the 30 September deadline binding and would not disarm in return for promises that failed to guarantee Iraq's security and sovereignty.
Sheikh Kadhim al-Fartousi, spokesman for the Sayyid al-Shuhada Brigades, said the group would not hand over its weapons within the government-set deadline unless conditions previously communicated to negotiating parties affiliated with the Coordination Framework were met.
Speaking to The New Arab in Baghdad on Monday, around three weeks before the deadline, Al-Fartousi said the group's position had been made clear during talks between armed factions and Coordination Framework representatives over the previous two days.
"The Brigades refuse to hand over their weapons within the deadline set by the Iraqi government unless the conditions it previously announced are met," he said.
"This position was clearly conveyed to the negotiating parties affiliated with the Coordination Framework during the talks held with armed factions over the past two days."
Al-Fartousi said the Brigades and other armed factions within the "Axis of Resistance" continued to "insist on the need for a vision that guarantees Iraq's security and sovereignty".
"We affirm that strengthening the authority of the state and placing weapons under the control of its institutions cannot be achieved separately from addressing the challenges and threats that the factions believe still exist," he said.
Al-Fartousi said the factions supported strengthening state authority and regulating weapons but argued that their conditions must first be met to ensure Iraq could defend itself against external threats.
He also said the factions did not trust promises that US forces would fully withdraw from Iraq, arguing that previous withdrawal announcements had not ended the presence or movement of US forces in the country.
"The position of the Brigades and the other factions is not based on rejecting the strengthening of the state's authority, but rather on the need to provide conditions that guarantee the state can exercise its sovereignty and its ability to protect its territory and airspace," he said.
The factions' main demands include the withdrawal of US and Turkish forces from Iraq, an end to what they describe as Washington's "political and financial tutelage", the dismantling of the Peshmerga and deployment of federal forces in the Kurdistan Region, and the provision of missile and air defence systems capable of protecting Iraqi airspace.
Mehdi al-Kaabi, a leader in the Nujaba Movement, separately told The New Arab that his group also "does not regard the government deadline for handing over weapons as binding".
"Any talk of handing over weapons before the conditions previously announced by the factions are met is meaningless," Al-Kaabi said.
He said the factions rejected what he described as a unilateral process in which they would be required to relinquish their weapons without guarantees that Iraq could protect its territory and sovereignty.
"Weapons are not the problem in themselves, but rather the problem is Iraq remaining exposed to foreign forces and external attacks," he said.
Al-Kaabi said any process to regulate weapons must be preceded by the withdrawal of US and Turkish forces and measures to strengthen the state's ability to protect its territory and airspace.
He said the factions "will not accept handing over their weapons in exchange for promises or unsecured timetables", arguing that placing weapons under state control must be accompanied by guarantees that foreign forces cannot operate in Iraqi territory or airspace without approval.
"The factions support a strong state that possesses its security and military decision-making," Al-Kaabi said, but "will not be a party to arrangements that weaken Iraq's deterrence capabilities or strip it of its means of defence".
The Sayyid al-Shuhada Brigades and Nujaba are among several armed factions resisting the government's timetable, alongside Hezbollah Brigades and al-Awfiya.
The Iraqi government set 30 September as the deadline for bringing weapons outside official institutions under state control, warning that "any weapons remaining outside state authority after this date will be subject to legal action".
The government has said it wants to resolve the issue through dialogue rather than confrontation and maintains that the remaining disagreement centres largely on how and when weapons are brought under state control.

Russia closes German consulate in St Petersburg after drone spat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:06:59 UTC
23:06:59 KST

Russia closes German consulate in St Petersburg after drone spat
MOSCOW, Sept 7 - Russia said on Monday it was closing down the German Consulate-General in St. Petersburg in retaliation for Berlin's decision to close the Russian consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural centre in Berlin.
Germany took its own measures after accusing Moscow of an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, an allegation Russia called an absurd fabrication.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said in a statement that the German consulate in St. Petersburg must cease operations no later than September 18.
It also confirmed that Germany's Goethe-Institut cultural centres in Russia must cease their activities, with staff ordered to leave the country by September 13 at the latest.
"It was the German authorities who, once again, provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations. The German government bears full and complete responsibility for the consequences," Russia's Foreign Ministry said. REUTERS

Implications of Saxony-Anhalt state election for German political dynamics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:06:28 UTC
23:06:28 KST

M. Erkut Ayvaz is research director at the Berlin office of the Foundation for Political, Economic and Social Research (SETA), a Turkish-based think tank.
On Sept. 6, a major state parliamentary election took place in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt. Voter turnout jumped from 60.3% in 2021 to a record high of 77.8%. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, classified by the Saxony-Anhalt state office for the German intelligence agency the BND as a “confirmed far-right organization,” finished first in the election by a significant margin, with a record 43.8% of the vote, according to preliminary official results. [1] The AfD has managed to outpace other political parties with its rhetoric, which capitalizes on social discontent, and its extreme policy promises. Meanwhile, Saxony-Anhalt's incumbent state premier from Germany’s ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the three-party state government suffered a major setback. The CDU lost roughly half of its vote share from the 2021 state election, dropping to 17.2% to finish in second place. Among the coalition parties, the Social Democratic Party (SPD) secured 9.3% of the vote, while the Free Democratic Party (FDP) failed to clear the 5% electoral threshold. The Left Party got 8.6% and the Greens 8.9%. With 5.3% of the vote, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) has likely emerged as a key player in the government formation process. Although the BSW has rejected cooperation with the AfD, it may take a more neutral stance, particularly during the state premier election process. This stance could lead to an AfD member becoming state premier for the first time in a potential round three of the state parliament’s election for state premier.
The Saxony-Anhalt state parliament has 83 seats, so at least 42 seats are needed to secure an absolute majority. Although the AfD finished first in the election with a significant margin, it was unable to secure an absolute majority on its own with 39 seats. In the run-up to the election, the AfD leadership in Saxony-Anhalt indicated that it was not open to the idea of forming a government without an absolute majority. On the other hand, the fact that the party’s federal leadership holds a more flexible view and claims that the authority to form a government lies with them could complicate the process.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s party, the CDU, along with other parties, continues to adhere to the principle of not cooperating with the AfD at both the federal and state levels. Although state-level party organizations have occasionally taken a more moderate approach, a shift toward cooperation with the AfD is not widely expected. On the other hand, the sustainability of the CDU’s principle of non-cooperation with the AfD—often described as a “firewall”—is also being questioned. In principle, it is mathematically possible for the five parties in the state parliament to come together to form a majority against the AfD and form a government. However, two potential obstacles stand in the way of such a scenario. First, it must be borne in mind that it would be extremely difficult for the CDU to cooperate with the Left Party. Moreover, the BSW has stated that it will not support the incumbent CDU state premier and is proposing a non-partisan figure for the post. In the coming days and weeks, other, more complex and challenging options may also come into play. For example, from the perspective of parliamentary arithmetic, there is the possibility of five parties joining forces against the AfD to form a coalition government, the Left Party and the BSW supporting a minority government, or even the BSW tolerating a minority government that includes the AfD.
The AfD’s latest success is likely to have an impact on the state elections scheduled for Sept. 20 in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. As for its short- and medium-term effects on federal politics, the parties face challenging times in the coming days and weeks. Calls for revisions to current policy priorities and personnel changes may come to the forefront. As SPD Co-Chair Lars Klingbeil said, the way the results serve as a “signal to Berlin” [2] could open up debate over the Merz government’s legislative plans, particularly for pension reform. It should also be remembered that the three CDU state premiers in eastern Germany have previously opposed this reform.
Merz’s position is not, for now, being called into question by his party. Moreover, it is, for now, unlikely that alternative candidates will seek to step forward given the current stage and dynamics of the situation. However, it can be said that Merz, whose popularity in the polls has fallen significantly, is being directly linked to the failure in the state legislative election. It should be noted that as the chancellor made headlines for a number of negative incidents over the summer, he was not prominently featured in the election campaign in Saxony-Anhalt. It is also likely that criticism of the federal leadership of the coalition partner, the SPD, and calls for leadership changes will grow louder.
Ultimately, the state parliament election in Saxony-Anhalt is expected to have significant and lasting effects on German politics. These results, which could be characterized as a political crisis, will also have significant implications for federal politics. Saxony-Anhalt lags far behind other states in terms of economic size. Furthermore, it represents only about 2.5% of the country’s population. Nevertheless, it is possible to identify specific and realistic examples of how a potential AfD state premier could influence federal politics, including security and foreign policy.
Although the AfD, classified as a “confirmed far-right organization” by the Saxony-Anhalt office of the German intel agency the BND, secured 39 of the 83 seats in the state parliament, it did not capture an absolute majority on its own. The principle adopted by the five other parties that surpassed the 5% electoral threshold to refuse cooperation with the AfD signals the start of a particularly challenging process in the state. The stance taken by the BSW is expected to play a critical role in determining the new state premier. If the BSW provides direct or indirect support to the AfD, the AfD’s lead candidate could be elected state premier in a potential third round of the state parliament’s election for premier.
On the other hand, provided they can reach an agreement among themselves, it is also possible for a CDU state premier to be elected if the CDU, SPD, Greens, Left Party, and BSW can find common ground. However, aside from the fact that the CDU has suffered such a critical and serious election defeat, it should not be forgotten that it has continued to adhere to its principle of not cooperating with the Left Party. Although some politicians have sent more conciliatory messages on this issue, the CDU’s uncompromising stance prior to the election could further complicate the process in the days ahead. Furthermore, Merz made notable statements opposing cooperation with the Left Party during the election campaign. Consequently, any potential concessions made to the Left Party and the BSW in the coming days could further erode the CDU’s credibility in the eyes of the public. It will also become clear in the coming days in what form these five parties, including the BSW, despite their differing policy preferences, can cooperate against the AfD, such as whether they will support a minority government. This state legislative election, viewed as a critical turning point in Germany, marks a new phase in the process of normalizing the AfD. This situation, however, leaves political parties purported to be centrist facing a serious representation problem.
It appears that Chancellor Merz’s promises to curb the AfD failed to resonate in Saxony-Anhalt; on the contrary, the party captured a greater vote share to the point where it neared the threshold for an absolute majority. The fact that the AfD is currently leading the CDU/CSU in national polls will continue to exert significant pressure on Berlin. Consequently, the election results are expected to have serious implications for the future of German politics.

FIA chief says F1 drivers won’t be put ‘at risk’ in Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:05:41 UTC
23:05:41 KST

Breadcrumb
FIA President Ben Sulayem says F1 drivers and teams won't be put 'at risk' over Middle East events
FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem has defended the wait for clarity over how this year's Formula 1 season will end amid uncertainty over the Middle East security situation- stating that drivers and team staff will not be put “at risk.”
Speaking to news agency The Associated Press, the F1 season is still scheduled to end Qatar Grand Prix on Nov. 29 and the season finale in Abu Dhabi on December 6, but F1 has been examining potential alternative venues. A replacement finale at the Imola circuit in Italy is widely considered the likeliest option.
Ben Sulayem told the AP it remains “business as usual. We are not changing anything unless we have to,” and said he's in regular communication with F1 chief executive Stefano Domenicali.
“Being from that part of the world, we can’t jump the gun and just say, that’s it, we are canceling and then cancel,” he added. “Are we going to allow our people, our staff, the drivers or the teams to go at risk? No, of course not. We will not. But we’ll have also to listen to the governments and to the local promoter there.”
F1 sets its own calendar and agreements with host venues, but as the governing body, the FIA must approve the schedule and any changes.
Saudi Arabian Grand Prix was called off and Bahrain moved 
Iran has previously targeted Qatar and the UAE, which includes Abu Dhabi, as part of its response to U.S. airstrikes and F1 called off the other two Middle East rounds earlier in the season — in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia.
The Bahrain Grand Prix was rescheduled in Malaysia for October 4, still with Bahrain branding.
“Do I feel disappointed? I think human lives are more important than motor sport,” said Ben Sulayem, who is from the United Arab Emirates, when asked about the impact on his home region of losing its events.
“And the well-being of my family being there and the UAE nationals and everyone that lives there comes as a priority.”
Ben Sulayem added that “for the time being, there is no emergency” in deciding a calendar for the 2027 season.
Imola could mean another party in Italy for Antonelli 
If the season does end in Imola, it would mean that Kimi Antonelli’s quest to become F1’s youngest champion could now end with the party of a lifetime, just down the road from his home city of Bologna.
When Antonelli raced there last year, he invited his family and his whole school class to see him at the track.
The 20-year-old Antonelli moved 66 points clear in the title race with a statement victory at the Italian Grand Prix on Sunday, after an epic fightback from the back of the grid.

LUCKNOW: Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath has written a letter to the people of Uttar Pradesh on the occasion of Teacher’s Day and ahead of International Literacy Day, stressing the need to combine traditional education with modern technology and skills.In his letter, Yogi said teachers are “the lamps who spread the light of knowledge” and play a key role in shaping future generations. Referring to the ancient Gurukul tradition, he said holistic education should remain the foundation of the modern education system.The chief minister said rapid technological changes had made AI literacy as important as digital literacy. He said AI, deep-tech and emerging technologies were opening opportunities in education, healthcare, agriculture, industry and employment. He added that the AI City in Lucknow and the developing drone and UAV technology ecosystem in Kanpur were laying the foundation for new technological possibilities in Uttar Pradesh.
Yogi highlighted Operation Kayakalp, Mission Prerna, Mukhyamantri Abhyudaya Yojana and skill development programmes, saying the state government had focused on improving education quality and school facilities, preparing students for competitive examinations and developing youth skills.He said these efforts had helped achieve significant success in minimising the school dropout rate across the state, with more children joining the mainstream of education.Calling teachers the most important link in the education journey, Yogi said they instil values, curiosity, discipline, self-confidence and a sense of responsibility among students while connecting India’s knowledge tradition with modern knowledge and innovation.
Ahead of International Literacy Day on September 8, Yogi appealed to people to help those around them who remain deprived of literacy. He said even a small effort to teach someone to read and write could open new avenues of knowledge, confidence and opportunities.The chief minister urged people to resolve that every child reaches school, every student receives quality education, every youth connects with skills and innovation, and every citizen becomes not only literate but also aware of digital knowledge and AI.

Ukraine's prosecutor general defends delay in letting anti-corruption raid proceed, reveals what was seized – video
Ukraine's Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko has explained that security staff initially did not let the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) detectives into the Prosecutor General's Office (OPG) building to carry out searches, because they did not disclose which specific offices they planned to search.
Source: Kravchenko at a press conference on 7 September
Details: Responding to questions about the searches at the OPG, Kravchenko said that officers from the State Guard Directorate initially did not let NABU detectives in, because the detectives did not want to show them the search warrants or say exactly which offices they were heading to.
Quote from Kravchenko: "The officers had search warrants for my office and my deputy's office, but at first they refused to show them, because they didn't want us to know where they came to search.
At around midnight, I spoke with the heads of both NABU and SAPO [the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office – ed.]. I called and asked what was going on. They said they had authorisation to search my office and were going to carry it out.
I said: 'Okay, everything will be opened for you – the office, the room, the safes.' I gave the order, the investigators were let in, and they carried out all the searches."
More details: Kravchenko said he also asked the heads of the anti-corruption bodies whether he should expect a search of his home.
Quote from Kravchenko: "I was told I'd find out about everything through the proper channels. Then I got a signal that an investigator was near my house. I asked them not to break down the door or the locks and to wait for my wife, who was already on her way and would open everything for them. The investigators waited, and my wife showed them everything."
More details: Kravchenko also revealed exactly what detectives seized during the search of his office.
Quote from Kravchenko: "Not much was taken from me: some new empty envelopes, four gift vouchers worth UAH50,000 (US$1,125) each from the Canali store, which I can easily afford to buy on my salary.
They also seized an identification code and other data from my personal file in the reception area."
More details: Kravchenko said that during the searches, NABU detectives also gained access to case files featuring, among others, employees of anti-corruption bodies.
Quote from Kravchenko: "There was nothing in my office, but my staff reported to me that their offices contained files relating to NABU employees, as well as files relating to employees of other law enforcement agencies. And NABU investigators gained access to these materials.
But I can't disclose what these files are, because I'm not the prosecutor assigned to those proceedings and I haven't been given permission to disclose them."
Background:
- On 4 September, Ukrainska Pravda reported that NABU and SAPO were conducting searches at the premises of Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, his deputy Mariia Vdovychenko and Oleh Kiper, Head of Odesa Oblast Military Administration. The Prosecutor General's Office initially denied that a search had been conducted at Kravchenko's home or office.
- On the evening of 4 September, it was reported that NABU and SAPO were conducting investigative actions at the Prosecutor General's Office as part of a special operation to expose a criminal organisation.
- On 5 September, the Ukrainian Prosecutor General's Office confirmed that detectives from NABU carried out searches at offices used by Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko.
- According to Ukrainska Pravda sources in business circles, NABU and SAPO detained Serhii Kropyva, Deputy Head of the International Legal Cooperation Department of the Prosecutor General's Office.
- On 5 September, NABU and SAPO announced that they uncovered a criminal organisation which investigators say was headed by the head of a department at the Prosecutor General's Office. Members of the organisation are suspected of regularly taking bribes from scam call centres and laundering. According to Ukrainska Pravda sources, this refers to Serhii Kropyva.
- On 6 September, a court imposed a pre-trial restraint of remand in custody on Serhii Kropyva, with the alternative of bail set at UAH 120 million (US$2.7 million).
- On 7 September, the High Anti-Corruption Court imposed a pre-trial restriction on 24-year-old Yelyzaveta Ivakhnenko, a suspect in NABU's Carthage operation concerning protection of fraudulent call centres, ordering 60 days' detention with the alternative of bail set at UAH 20 million (US$450,000).
- The court has also remanded Serhii Kutsyi, driver for Serhii Kropyva, in custody with bail set at UAH 3 million (US$67,500).

Why is the far-right AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next in German politics?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:04:23 UTC
23:04:23 KST

Germany is reeling from the biggest far-right victory in a state election since the Nazi period after voters in Saxony-Anhalt in the former communist east gave the anti-immigration, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party a thumping first-place finish of 44%, just short of an absolute majority.
What happened and why is it significant?
For the first time since the second world war, a German state is on the brink of electing a far-right government after a big win in Saxony-Anhalt, described by the news magazine Der Spiegel as a magnitude 9.0 “political earthquake”.
Coming in nearly 27 points ahead of the co-ruling Christian Democrats (CDU), the conservative party of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, the AfD pulled off a coup whose aftershocks will ripple across Germany and beyond its borders. The AfD will have broad powers over education, culture and domestic security if it manages to take power in the state. Among other policies, it has promised to start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools, and halt the building of new windfarms. It now has a strong wind at its back for the two state elections yet to come this month.
Its triumph also raised doubts whether the unpopular Merz could hold on in the face of such a clear rejection of his policies and leadership after just 16 months in power. The AfD co-leader Alice Weidel told reporters in Berlin that her party was targeting a 40% result at the next general election, scheduled for 2029. It is currently polling in first place at 28%.
Alice Weidel (right, with Ulrich Siegmund, centre, and her AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, left) said the AfD was targeting a 40% vote at the next general election. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA
What might happen next?
The AfD’s national leaders and the chief candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, the media-savvy former fragrance salesman Ulrich Siegmund, said the state’s voters had given the party a clear mandate to govern. However, without an absolute majority in the state parliament, the party would need partners or supporters to either join a coalition or “tolerate” a minority government. Siegmund said repeatedly before the vote he would only stand for election as premier with a clear majority. The remaining parties ruled out playing kingmaker to Siegmund by lending formal support. However, the BSW, a small “left-conservative” populist party which narrowly cleared the 5% hurdle to representation, has hinted at tacit cooperation.
Prior to the election, some Christian Democrats in the state openly questioned the “firewall” policy. Siegmund indicated he would spend the coming days and weeks “with an outstretched hand”, testing the hitherto resolute opposition to helping the AfD into power. If Siegmund fails to build a coalition, he suggested holding a new election, something that would require a two-thirds majority in the state legislature.
What does the result say about the firewall approach?
The stunning outcome in Saxony-Anhalt has underscored doubts about the viability of the policy of mainstream parties to exclude the AfD from power. The only other time the AfD won in a state, in neighbouring Thuringia in 2024, its victory was less decisive, allowing the remaining parties to cobble together an ideologically awkward, cross-spectrum coalition. Given the AfD’s margin of victory in Saxony-Anhalt, it is difficult to imagine how the humiliated CDU could form such a “Frankenstein” alliance of disparate parties this time. The state premier, Sven Schulze, acknowledged the party no longer had a mandate to try.
Siegmund has suggested a new election if he fails to build a coalition. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA
What does the result mean for the CDU and Friedrich Merz?
Sunday’s election amounted to a stinging rebuke of Merz and his CDU. The stony-faced chancellor admitted he was “deeply shocked” by the result. Exit polls showed voters were furious about his broken promises to revive the economy and shore up fiscal discipline. Energy prices, stoked by inflation and the Iran war, have hit voters hard in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany’s poorest state. Cost of living issues appeared to far outweigh immigration, the AfD’s trademark call to arms, as a mobilising issue. Although support for the AfD has been strongest in the ex-communist east, the party also made strong gains in two elections in western states earlier this year amid fears over deindustrialisation.
The Social Democratic party (SPD), a junior partner in Merz’s alliance, indicated on Monday it would be willing to water down planned changes to Germany’s costly and creaking social welfare system in order to placate disgruntled voters. Merz insisted the measures to shore up the healthcare and pension systems were necessary and vowed to remain and fight for them “in the interest of our children and grandchildren”.
Friedrich Merz has been ‘deeply shocked’ by the result. Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA
What about the next two state elections?
Voters in the German capital, Berlin, and the Baltic coast state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, two of Germany’s 16 länder, will go to the polls on 20 September. The obvious momentum for the AfD, as well as widespread German dissatisfaction with Merz and his right-left government with the SPD, mean those polls are also fraught with risk for the parties in the federal coalition. The AfD currently has a narrow lead ahead of the co-ruling SPD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but for now looks unlikely to win an absolute majority. The situation in Berlin – once divided between east and west – looks muddled, with the CDU, far-left Linke and the AfD all jockeying for first place. Even if the CDU managed to hold on to its lead on election day, it would struggle to form an ideologically coherent coalition, dealing Merz and his party another stinging blow that could further destabilise his government.
