Struggling to find “the one”? A new psychology study says the problem might be your underlying motivation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:00:25 UTC
22:00:25 KST

A new study finds that the reasons single people want a relationship shape both the type of partnership they seek and whether they achieve their dating goals. Individuals driven by a genuine desire for connection tend to focus on relationship quality, while those driven by social pressure or a need for validation often prioritize simply finding a partner, which can hinder their progress. The research was published in Social Psychological and Personality Science.
Self-determination theory is a psychological framework for understanding human motivation. It suggests that our reasons for doing things exist on a spectrum, ranging from actions we take for pure enjoyment to actions we take because we feel forced or pressured. Historically, psychological research has shown that the internal drive behind our actions matters just as much as the actions themselves. For instance, a 2004 study demonstrated that why someone chases an objective and what that objective actually is are two distinct forces that shape their overall well-being.
Building on this idea, a 2008 study found that people tend to make far more headway on goals they truly care about than on goals driven by guilt or social pressure. Recently, scientists began applying this concept specifically to single people and dating. In fact, a 2025 study introduced a framework to measure internal versus external motivations for dating, noting that a person’s inner drive makes them more likely to find a partner. This framework aligns with a study covered by PsyPost in 2026, which found that emotional fulfillment strongly motivates the pursuit of long-term relationships.
The new study builds on this lineage to see how singles’ core motivations dictate the exact goals they set and whether they achieve them over time. “Previous work suggests that the average single person desires to partner, but it was unclear to us what exactly it is that single people desire from these relationships, if they desire one at all,” said study author Laura Hawkins, a second-year PhD student in psychology at the University of Toronto.
“In other words, what are their goals for romantic partnership?” The research uses this motivational framework to categorize why single people might want a relationship.
These categories include intrinsic motivation, which means enjoying relationships for what they are, and identified motivation, which means personally valuing partnership. They also include introjected motivation, which involves acting to avoid guilt or to boost self-worth, and external motivation, which involves acting due to social pressure. Finally, the researchers measured amotivation, which refers to a complete lack of desire or intention to seek a partner.
To understand how these motivations operate in the real world, the researchers recruited 4,019 single adults between the ages of 18 and 39. Participants completed a baseline survey that measured their motivations for wanting a romantic relationship. They were also asked to write out up to three personal relationship goals for the upcoming six months.
The research team read through the roughly 12,000 written goals and categorized them into 41 distinct themes. These themes included things like going on dates, improving finances, remaining single, or building intimacy. Six months later, 3,176 of the original participants returned for a follow-up survey. They reviewed the goals they had written down previously and rated their progress on a scale from zero to 100 percent. On average, participants reported a 41.7 percent completion rate across their goals.
The results indicate that singles who were intrinsically motivated or had identified motivation set goals focused on high-quality connections. Intrinsically motivated singles had a higher likelihood of setting goals to have fun, build emotional intimacy, and enter a healthy relationship. Identified motivation was linked to seeking committed, long-term partnerships. Both of these groups were far less likely to say their main goal was to remain single.
People driven by a need for self-affirmation or a fear of failure displayed a very different pattern. Singles with this introjected motivation focused more on securing a relationship than on the quality of that connection. They were more likely to set goals to go on dates, have sex, socialize, or improve their physical attractiveness and self-confidence.
At the same time, introjected singles were less likely to prioritize building intimacy, sharing a home, or having a healthy relationship. Interestingly, introjected motivation was also linked to making less progress on relationship goals over the six-month period.
“You would think that entering a relationship is easier than entering a quality relationship,” Hawkins said. “But one finding that surprised me was that singles who simply wanted to enter a relationship (irrespective of quality) actually made less progress on this goal.”
“Although we can’t be sure, we think part of the reason this may be is because these singles are fundamentally pursuing partnership to improve their self-image, which may hinder their ability to build a romantic connection,” she continued. “So, in an ironic twist of fate, the reason they want a relationship may actually be driving potential partners away.”
External motivation, or dating to appease others, was mainly linked to the goal of going on dates. Amotivation was strongly associated with a desire to remain single or setting no relationship goals at all. When evaluating their success six months later, amotivated singles reported the highest amount of progress among all the groups.
“Not every single wants to partner!” Hawkins pointed out. “In fact, our data suggests singles who did not want to partner were not necessarily relationally avoidant, but rather, actively pursuing singlehood.”
These findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost last year. That earlier study, which looked at whether singles actually entered a relationship rather than the specific goals they set, similarly found that autonomous motives support positive romantic outcomes while introjected motives and a lack of motivation do not.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The researchers did not test whether these patterns look different depending on a person’s age, gender, sexual orientation, or cultural background, which could change how people approach dating. The measurement of goal progress also relied entirely on self-reports, which might contain subjective biases.
Additionally, the structural nature of the goals varied wildly from person to person. For example, staying single is an objective a person can accomplish all on their own. Finding a healthy, long-term romantic relationship requires the cooperation of another person. Because of this, the high reported success rate of amotivated singles might simply reflect that it is easier to achieve the goal of staying single than the goal of finding a compatible partner.
“As a singlehood researcher I often get asked ‘how do I find “the one”?'” Hawkins noted. “Our data suggests that answer might lie inwards. Simply put, why you want to become partnered shapes the quality (or lack thereof) of the romantic relationship you seek.”
The study, “Does Why You Want Partnership Shape What You Want? A Self-Determination Perspective on Singles’ Relationship Goals,” was authored by Laura Hawkins, Serena Thapar, Will Ryan, and Geoff MacDonald.

Ukraine's PM and European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity discuss three issues concerning EU financial aid for Ukraine
Following a video conference between European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity Valdis Dombrovskis and Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi on 7 September, the European Commission said it was too early to name a specific amount for Ukraine's financial needs in 2026-2027, and that work to determine it would continue at the technical level.
Source: European Commission spokesperson Balázs Ujvári following the meeting, as reported by European Pravda from Brussels
Details: The European Commission has not yet finalised its assessment of Ukraine's financial needs for 2026 and 2027.
Ujvári said that Dombrovskis and Koretskyi discussed three main issues.
"So they discussed the financing needs of Ukraine for 2026 and 2027. That's one. Second, they looked at the implementation of the reforms which are needed in order to unlock the funding under the €90 billion loan programme. And thirdly, they looked at the preparations for Ukraine's 2027 financing strategy," Ujvári said.
He recalled that to gain access to the funds under the €90 billion loan, Ukraine must prepare financial strategies for both 2026, which has already been prepared and approved, and 2027.
According to Ujvári, "the two sides also agreed that it is important for other international partners to step up to the plate and put forward assistance, be it in the budgetary field or in the field of defence, on top of what the EU has committed".
Ujvári cited Norway as an example, noting that it had recently committed to providing Ukraine with US$9 billion in 2027.
"So this is a good example. This is the path. And we expect other partners as well to step up to the plate," he said.
Meanwhile, the European Commission stressed that the specific scale of Ukraine's financial needs still needs to be determined.
"I think what you need to do first is to get a clear picture of what the budgetary or financial situation is. That is step number one. And then as a potential step number two, you can look at ways of addressing it," Balázs Ujvári explained.
He said that Dombrovskis and Koretskyi's conversation focused specifically on the first stage – assessing the situation and obtaining information from the Ukrainian side.
"So before we can establish a concrete figure, more discussions will be needed. And that's exactly what we'll be doing in the coming days and weeks," he said.
On 8 September, Dombrovskis is also due to meet with Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund. According to the spokesperson, the sides will discuss the results of the IMF mission that worked in Ukraine last week.
"The macro financial assistance programme of the EU is highly linked to the IMF programme, which is being rolled out in the country. The common goal there is to get Ukraine to advance reforms which strengthen the country's economic resilience," Balázs Ujvári stressed.
Background:
- The EU previously recalled that the €90 billion in assistance would cover only two-thirds of Ukraine's needs in 2026-2027.
- The EU recently said that Ukraine had not submitted a formal request to the European Commission asking for part of the €90 billion loan planned for 2027 to be disbursed ahead of schedule in 2026 in order to cover Ukraine's €27 billion defence budget shortfall this year.
- On 24 August, the European Commission approved €6.1 billion in defence procurement for Ukraine as part of the EU's €90 billion loan.
- The EU is expected to disburse around €20 billion to Ukraine by the end of 2026, with new tranches potentially arriving in the coming weeks.

Taiz again emerges as battlefield of choice in Yemen renewed war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:58:59 UTC
21:58:59 KST

Breadcrumb
Taiz again emerges as battlefield of choice in Yemen renewed war
The latest fighting around Taiz has revived fears of another major battle for one of Yemen's biggest cities.
But military analysts say the Houthis may have little interest in actually storming it.
Instead, they argue, the group's more achievable objective is to cut the roads keeping Taiz connected to the rest of government-held Yemen - and gradually make the city harder to sustain.
"The real danger does not lie in a direct attack, but in the Houthis succeeding in cutting the supply arteries and turning the siege into a permanent reality," military and security affairs researcher Assem al-Mujahid told The New Arab.
"Accordingly, the western front remains the key to the battle for Taiz: if the supply routes remain open and the forces retain the ability to manoeuvre, the strangulation project will remain obstructed, while cutting this corridor would mean subjugating the city without the need for a comprehensive assault."
That helps explain the pattern of the latest escalation.
The Houthis have launched intense attacks west of Taiz, using ballistic missiles and drones and temporarily breaking through government lines. But around the city itself, their strategy has largely involved pressure on roads and supply routes rather than an attempt to seize its densely populated neighbourhoods.
Al-Mujahid said: "The forces defending the city have accumulated extensive field experience in urban and mountain warfare, which has pushed the Houthis to favour a strategy of strangulation and attrition rather than entering a direct battle to storm the city."
Why Taiz matters
Taiz is Yemen's most populous governorate, with close to four million inhabitants.
Its importance is also strategic. To the west lie the port of Mocha and the approaches to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes.
Control of the governorate is divided among several anti-Houthi forces as well as the Houthis.
The internationally recognised government controls much of Taiz city and large parts of the governorate. On the western coast, the National Resistance forces of Tariq Saleh - an anti-Houthi commander who sits on Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council - control Mocha and other coastal districts.
The Houthis control much of the north and east, including the economically important al-Hawban area north-east of the city.
Al-Hawban contains major factories, trading companies and markets, giving the Houthis access to substantial revenues while most of densely populated Taiz city remains under their opponents' administration.
That makes the current division of the city economically useful to the group: it can extract revenue without assuming the full cost of governing Taiz.
The battle for the roads
The latest offensive began early last Thursday after the Houthis fired 14 ballistic missiles as well as drones, followed by fighting that lasted around 15 hours.
They temporarily reached strategic positions including Jabal Nu'man in Jabal Habashi district, before government and allied forces counter-attacked and recovered many of them.
At al-Kadha, an important link between Taiz and the western coast, anti-Houthi forces also repelled the attack.
Reinforcements have since arrived from the Giants Brigades, a powerful southern anti-Houthi force, and Nation's Shield, another military force aligned with Yemen's internationally recognised authorities.
The significance of the fighting lies in two crucial roads.
One connects Taiz with Mocha and the western coast. Another runs south-west towards Aden, the interim seat of Yemen's government.
For residents, they are not simply military supply routes. They are among the main arteries carrying civilians, food and commercial goods into and out of the city.
The Houthis have also targeted al-Wazi'iyah bridge, an important route between Taiz and the western coast.
"The Houthis understand that controlling the supply routes would give them the ability to gradually strangle the city and recreate the siege model of the early years of the war," al-Mujahid said.
"The Houthi objective at the current stage is focused on exhausting Taiz until it reaches a point where it loses its ability to withstand pressure, with the aim of draining the government and blackmailing it politically and militarily."
The consequences of cutting those routes could include higher prices, disruption to trade and further displacement among a population that has already endured years of war.
It could also give the Houthis greater leverage in future political negotiations.
Why not simply capture the city?
Taking Taiz would be extremely difficult.
The city consists of densely packed neighbourhoods surrounded by mountainous terrain, including Jabal Sabir, which provides defenders with a powerful natural position.
Government forces and local fighters have also accumulated more than a decade of experience in urban and mountain warfare.
Al-Mujahid said: "Taiz's rugged geography, the high ground surrounding it, and the complex nature of fighting inside residential areas make any large-scale attack a military adventure with uncertain results."
Military analyst Colonel Sarhan al-Muhaya argues that years of fortification have made the city's defences significantly stronger.
"The positions of the National Army inside Taiz have become literally impregnable, thanks to strong engineering fortifications combined with the rugged geography and innovative obstacles, alongside the precise implementation of concealment and camouflage principles. All of this has created a firm conviction among the Houthis that achieving any breakthrough is impossible, regardless of how long the war lasts or the intensity of firepower, meaning that the attacks result in human and material losses for them."
Even a successful assault would carry substantial costs.
The Houthis would have to fight through a hostile and heavily damaged city, then take responsibility for services and infrastructure serving a large civilian population.
By contrast, their current position around Taiz allows them to retain economic influence and military pressure without bearing those costs.
"The Houthis' dreams of controlling the al-Dhabab road and the Taiz-Mocha road, and closing the remaining corridors under the control of government forces, are unattainable, and Houthi forces will not be able to achieve them."
He added: "It has been proven theoretically and practically that the Houthi forces are unable to retake any territory they have lost in Taiz governorate despite their repeated attempts."
Fakhr al-Azb is a Yemeni journalist based in Taiz. Writes for Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, The New Arab's Arabic-language sister edition.

Oxford University museum to return human remains to Naga people

Oxford University museum to return human remains to Naga people in India
- Oxford University’s Pitt Rivers Museum will return 39 human remains to the Naga community in north-east India, collected during Britain’s colonial era.
- The repatriation is part of a wider movement to return artefacts and remains taken by Western institutions during colonial times.
- The museum is coordinating with the Naga community for a handover ceremony, highlighting the importance of memory and heritage restoration.
AI generated
LONDON – Oxford University’s Pitt Rivers Museum will return the remains of 39 people taken during Britain’s colonial era to the Naga community in north-east India, the museum said on Sept 7.
The museum, which holds the world’s largest collection of Naga artefacts, confirmed it was preparing the repatriation after the university approved a restitution request by the Forum for Naga Reconciliation (FNR).
The remains “have been away from their homeland for far too long”, museum director Laura Van Broekhoven said in a statement.
The human remains were collected in the early 20th century by British colonial administrators, and some remained on public display until 2020.
“Repatriation, for the Nagas, is not simply about bones and ancestral remains finding their way back to the land but importantly about memory returning to where it belongs,” the FNR and other Naga organisations said in a statement, welcoming the agreement.
The request covered 40 sets of human remains, Pitt Rivers Museum said.
Oxford University approved the return of 39 of them on July 13, concluding that one specimen “does not have a clear provenance as Naga”.
The museum said it was “working closely” with the Naga community to agree on a date for a handover ceremony, which has not been set yet.
The agreement forms part of a wider international movement to repatriate artefacts and human remains acquired by Western institutions during the colonial era.
In 2022, London’s Horniman Museum returned 72 artefacts to Nigeria, including 12 Benin bronze artefacts, and earlier in 2026 the University of Edinburgh returned the skulls of six people to a Native American group.
Greece has for decades demanded the return from Britain of the Parthenon Marbles, saying they were looted in the early 19th century by Lord Elgin, British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire.
London insists they were legally acquired and successive British governments have noted that the decision rests with the British Museum, where they are kept. AFP

The curfew in Kyiv will be shortened to 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. amid intensified Russian aerial attacks on the Ukrainian capital, the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, announced on Sept. 7.
The changes will take effect at midnight on Sept. 10, and the public transportation services in Kyiv will also be extended by an hour, according to Klitschko. He said that the working hours of restaurants, cafes, shopping malls, and other venues would remain unaffected.
The curfew reduction comes as the security situation in Kyiv deteriorates, with air raid alerts going off regularly and restricting movements within the city. Round-the-clock Russian drone attacks have targeted Kyiv for over a week, from the end of August to the beginning of September, leaving the city's residents to worry about what awaits them in the upcoming winter.
At the same time, all entertainment and sports events in open air locations or facilities without shelters will be temporarily prohibited in Kyiv, said Klitschko.
Facing a severe shortage of air defense missiles, Ukraine is increasingly strained in its efforts to protect cities, including Kyiv, from heavy Russian missile and drone attacks.
With trains often arriving in the city late, the city will organize four bus routes during curfew so people can get home from Kyiv's central railway station, Klitschko said.
Most restaurants and bars work until 11 p.m. in Kyiv, and the metro currently operates from around 5:30 a.m. to 11 p.m.
Earlier in September, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine will change how air raid alerts operate and introduce red and yellow levels, a change from the previous single air raid alert.
The yellow level corresponds to incoming drones, whereas the red level indicates threats from missiles, including ballistic missiles, and massive combined attacks, according to Zelensky.

John Healey backs growth but says Labour must be honest on spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:54:05 UTC
21:54:05 KST

John Healey has said boosting economic growth will be his defining mission as chancellor as he warned Labour had to “be honest” about the need to control public spending at next month’s budget.
In his first big speech since taking the job in July, Healey said the top priority for his 28 October budget would be to support stronger growth across the UK while sticking firmly to the government’s fiscal rules.
“I want to be the chancellor that gets things done and I want to see growth driven from more places across the UK,” he said.
Against a backdrop of jittery global financial markets, the chancellor said he and Andy Burnham were “in lockstep” in their commitment to meeting the government’s self-imposed target to balance day-to-day spending with tax receipts by 2029-30.
With the public finances under pressure from soaring long-term bond yields, which hit an 18-year high last week, Healey argued that stronger growth was the most sustainable way to balance the books. However, he also signalled that his budget would require Labour “being honest about the need to control government spending”.
Economists have warned the chancellor could be forced to increase taxes or cut spending in response to rising spending pressures and the economic fallout from the war in Iran triggering turmoil in global bond markets.
The UK’s 10-year borrowing costs rose slightly on Monday amid pressure on governments worldwide, as fears over the impact of the war pushed the price of oil closer to $100 a barrel.
Aiming to soothe concerns in a speech to business leaders at a manufacturing centre in Coventry, Healey said Britain was continuing to pay a “Truss penalty” almost four years since the former Conservative prime minister’s ill-fated mini-budget triggered a meltdown in the UK government bond market.
With Labour under pressure amid questions over Burnham’s tax and spending priorities and as the UK carmaker Jaguar Land Rover – headquartered down the road from the venue for his speech – announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs, Healey said maintaining fiscal discipline was important in an uncertain and volatile world.
“It makes our task in government harder. It makes the task of every business looking to invest much harder, too,” he added.
Business groups said they welcomed the chancellor’s pro-growth message, including pledges to devolve tax and spending powers to regional mayors and also his promise to “take an axe” to regulations he said were holding back business investment.
Louise Hellem, the chief economist at the Confederation of British Industry, said: “Firms will welcome the positive signals of intent from the chancellor and will now be looking ahead to the budget to see whether the government can match its ambition with decisive action to cut business costs and give firms the headroom they need to invest.”
The chancellor’s critics said his speech was light on detail despite the mounting pressure on the economy.
Andrew Griffith, the Conservative shadow chancellor, said: “John Healey sounds increasingly like continuity Rachel Reeves. Warm words about growth will not make growth a reality, or cover up the enormous damage Labour have done to businesses and family finances.”
Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s Treasury spokesperson, said: “On the day 4,000 people are losing their jobs, Healey gave a dire and dreary speech that will change absolutely nothing.”
Refusing to be drawn on the details of his tax and spending plans less than two months before the budget, Healey promised to stick to Labour’s manifesto commitments not to raise taxes on working people. However, he signalled the government could look at finding savings from the welfare bill by tackling youth unemployment.
“As the prime minister has said, there is a need to bring down welfare costs. And most importantly for me we have to get more of Britain working again,” he said.
The chancellor ducked questions on whether taxes would need to rise and also a suggestion from the British Chambers of Commerce that the government should scrap the pensions triple lock to fund a cut in employer national insurance contributions to help support youth jobs.
The government is awaiting the findings of a highly anticipated review into youth worklessness by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which Healey said would “address this scar of youth unemployment”.
Healey said there was a “moral duty” and a “fiscal duty” to supporting young people to find work.
“A person coming off benefits and into work saves the taxpayer money. And that becomes a win-win when those people start paying tax themselves,” he said.

21:54:03 KST

25 years after Sept. 11 attacks, Taliban rules Afghanistan again, but now with $7 billion in U.S. firepower
Kabul — As Americans reflect this week on the 25 years that have passed since the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, CBS News has returned to Afghanistan, where the war those attacks triggered ended five years ago with the Taliban's stunning return to power.
When the last U.S. and allied soldiers left after a brutal two-decade war, the Taliban's fighters seized billions of dollars worth of American-purchased military hardware. President Trump, whose first administration negotiated the deal to end the war with the Taliban, has accused the Biden administration of "totally botching" the withdrawal.
Five years later, the hardware of America's longest-ever war is still easy to spot on the streets of Kabul. Taliban fighters patrol in armored vehicles once supplied to Afghan forces, wearing American tactical gear and carrying American weapons.
CBS News saw one Humvee in the Afghan capital still adorned with a faded Green Bay Packers decal — a remnant from its past operators.
President Trump has been fiercely critical of the former Biden administration, accusing his predecessor of allowing the U.S. military to abandon billions of dollars in military hardware. Mr. Trump has demanded that the Taliban hand it back.
But the Taliban has proudly shown off its American-funded arsenal, even staging military parades through Kabul's streets.
Pentagon figures released last year show some $7 billion in hardware and weaponry fell into the group's hands when the Afghan National Army collapsed.
Shortly after the 2021 withdrawal, CBS News filmed as "Badri 313," an elite Taliban special forces battalion, patrolled in their American vehicles, American commando gear and with their American weapons.
Asked about President Trump's determination to reclaim the equipment, Taliban Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi told CBS News the hardware now belongs to "the state of Afghanistan, and we are not in the business of doing transactions and deals on the assets of the state of Afghanistan."
When it was pointed out that American taxpayers purchased the equipment, Balkhi said: "The Americans did a lot of things. Americans killed a lot of people, destroyed the majority of the country. Should they not be paying for that first?"
The Taliban waged a vicious insurgency during a war that killed more than 2,400 U.S. service members and tens of thousands of innocent Afghans.
But critics of the Biden administration's handling of the U.S. withdrawal say it's allowed the Taliban to transform from insurgents into a state military force armed with billions of dollars in American-funded firepower.
They have used those weapons to impose a draconian interpretation of Islamic rule on Afghanistan's people, almost completely depriving women and girls of the right to work and study, and restricting life for everyone in the country in ways that some analysts say are even harsher than during the group's previous reign.
Biden has offered little public commentary on the Afghanistan withdrawal, but he said in September 2021, a month after the Taliban took back control, that he "was not going to extend this 'forever war,' and I was not extending a 'forever exit.'"
"If anything, the developments of the past week reinforce that ending U.S. military involvement in Afghanistan now was the right decision," said the then-president in August 2021, as the Taliban reasserted their rule 20 years after being ousted by the U.S.-led military campaign. "American troops cannot and should not be fighting in a war and dying in a war that Afghan forces are not willing to fight for themselves."
In 2023, the Biden White House released a 12-page summary of a classified review of the Afghanistan exit that largely blamed the Trump administration for the deal it struck with the Taliban to withdraw U.S. forces from the country by May 2021.
The so-called Doha Agreement brokered by the first Trump administration laid out a series of conditions for the Taliban to fulfill in order for U.S. forces to leave. Another report partially declassified and released by the State Department in 2023 faulted both the Trump and Biden administrations for "insufficient" planning surrounding the withdrawal.

Qom: A province of ancient beacons along historic routes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

Qom: A province of ancient beacons along historic routes
TEHRAN - Scattered across the mountains, plains and historic routes of Qom province, a group of ancient Meels, standalone beacon towers once used to guide travelers and caravans, offers a distinctive glimpse into the history of travel and communication in central Iran.
Often standing on elevated ground overlooking old roads and passes, the structures are among the lesser-known heritage sites of Qom. Their locations, architecture and relationship with ancient routes could make them compelling destinations for travelers, historians, architects and enthusiasts of Iran’s cultural heritage.
Speaking to ISNA, historian and researcher Hossein Sadeqi says Qom is unusual in having a relatively large concentration of historic Meels, with the structures spread across different parts of the province. Based on existing roads, the distance between some of them is estimated at around 50 kilometers.
The term Meel historically referred to a standalone beacon or light-bearing structure. Such towers were built beside important roads and routes, particularly in periods before and during the Islamic era, to help travelers and caravans navigate difficult terrain. Fires were traditionally lit at their upper sections, allowing people to identify the route during darkness or in fog.
Unlike minarets attached to mosques or other religious buildings, these structures were originally independent ones. According to Sadeqi, their functions included guiding travelers as well as communication and signaling. Their elaborate architectural features in some cases, however, have led researchers to consider whether certain examples served additional purposes.
Most surviving historic Meels in Iran date from the fourth to sixth centuries AH, although examples attributed to earlier periods also exist. Many were equipped with stairways leading to their upper sections, with some featuring separate spiral staircases.
Aliabad Meel
The stone Meel of Aliabad stands about 50 kilometers along the Qom-Tehran road, beside the historic stone castle of Aliabad. Built on an elevated hill, it is believed to have served as a landmark for caravans.
The tower is about 11 meters high and has an arched entrance approximately 1.5 meters wide. Spiral stairs lead toward the upper section. Stone and sarooj, a traditional Iranian waterproof mortar, were used in its construction.
Several rows of what appear to be reed pipes can be seen in the structure at a height of about three meters. Sadeqi suggests that these may have been incorporated to reduce the effects of ground vibrations.
The cylindrical structure has a base diameter of about 4.33 meters. Its association with the nearby Seljuk-era caravanserai and its construction style have led researchers to attribute it to the Seljuk period.
Imamzadeh Abdullah Meel
Another historic beacon stands outside the city of Qom along the old Qom-Isfahan road, near Cheshmeh Ali village. Located on high ground, the structure has a conical form and was once accompanied by a protective enclosure, of which only walls remain.
The Meel rises about 6.4 meters and has a base diameter of approximately 5.5 meters. Its exterior is built of rubble stone and gypsum mortar. The structure stands around 200 meters above the surrounding plain.
Its form and construction suggest that it dates from the Seljuk period.
Babak Meel
Babak Meel occupies one of the highest peaks of the northern mountain range overlooking the valley. From the tower, the surrounding valleys can be seen clearly.
Only about 3.7 meters of the northern section of Babak Meel survives. Its exterior consists of rubble stone and gypsum and sarooj mortar.
Chahak Meel
Chahak Meel lies in the Khalajestan district, east of Chahak village and north of the Vezva River, on high ground overlooking the surrounding plain.
Pottery from both the Sasanian and Islamic periods has been found in the area. Its masonry and architectural form have been compared with a Sasanian-era Chahar-Taq, leading to an attribution to the Sasanian period.
The surviving structure is about 4.6 meters high at its highest point and has a base diameter of roughly 5.1 meters. Its exterior is circular, while its interior follows a cross-shaped plan, recalling the architecture of Sasanian Chahar-taqs, or four-arched structures.
Shahrestan Meel
Shahrestan Meel stands in central Qom province, and it is attributed to the Sasanian period and is thought to have stood within the ancient settlement known as Shahrestan.
The area, now called Mazraeh Shahrestan, is believed to have been a fortified site in antiquity and a village by the fourth century AH.
The tower has been heavily affected by erosion and now resembles a cone-shaped structure. It stands about 7.5 meters high and was built of mud brick.
Safarali Meel
Safarali Meel rises on a mountain opposite Mount Sepor-e Rostam, west of Kaj village. The site commands extensive views over the surrounding settlements and plains.
The structure is about 6.8 meters high, with a base diameter of approximately seven meters. Its exterior is made of rubble stone and sarooj, while the interior was constructed without mortar.
Much of its interior is filled with rubble stone, while a circular chamber survives above it. The chamber has a floor diameter of about 3.45 meters and walls approximately 1.7 meters thick.
An opening on the eastern side faces Kaj village. The tower's elevated position provides views toward Mohammadabad, Korgol, Aliabad, Bayer Kalhar, Malek Qaleh and surrounding seasonal settlements.
Pottery found around the site includes prehistoric material as well as pottery associated with the Seljuk period. The latter has contributed to the attribution of the surviving Meel to that era.
Maghbulabad Meel
In Khalajestan, southwest of Maghbulabad village, another Meel survives at an elevation of about 1,893 meters above sea level and approximately 65 meters above the surrounding plain.
Its architectural style is attributed to the Seljuk period. The tower was constructed from local rubble stone and gypsum mortar and originally had a cylindrical form.
Only about 2.7 meters of its height survives today. Its strategic position is particularly notable: the tower stands at a point from which it could have served travelers using the historic routes connecting Saveh, Tafresh and Qom.
Although it has little decorative ornamentation, the arrangement of its masonry remains of architectural interest.
Meem Meel
Meem Meel, located in the village of Meem in Kahak district, resembles Safarali Meel but is smaller.
The structure stands roughly 85 to 90 meters above the surrounding plain and is about nine meters high. Its base diameter is approximately 4.62 meters.
Built of rubble stone and gypsum mortar, it has a conical exterior and an enclosed chamber inside. Its architectural similarities with other Qom beacons have led researchers to attribute it to the Seljuk period.
Rahjerd Meel
The stone Meel of Rahjerd stands near Dizijan village on the heights of Mount Zanbureh, overlooking a gorge and the Zavvarian passage in the Rahjerd area.
Approximately 4.25 meters of the structure survives. Its base diameter is about 6.3 meters, and it rises roughly 60 meters above the surrounding plain.
Its rubble-stone construction and gypsum mortar are similar to those used in other Seljuk-period Meels in Qom province.
Taken together, these structures form a scattered network of architectural landmarks that reflects the importance of movement across central Iran long before modern roads transformed the landscape. Their locations on high ground, near passes and along historic routes reveal a practical relationship between architecture and travel.
For modern visitors, the appeal of Qom's Meels lies partly in their isolation. Unlike major monuments located in urban centers, many of these towers survive amid mountains, plains and old travel corridors. Reaching them can therefore offer not only an encounter with historic architecture but also a sense of the landscapes through which merchants, pilgrims and caravans once moved.

Chris Horton launches Taiwan edition of ‘Ghost Nation’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:53:07 UTC
21:53:07 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — On Saturday night in Taipei, down a quiet alley in the city’s Wanhua District, just a couple of blocks from the glowing screen-lit concourses of Ximending, a small bookshop rooted in the Xi-era Hong Kong and China diasporas hosted a capacity crowd for an event with an American writer.
Chris Horton, a journalist based in Taiwan for over a decade, had come to Nowhere Books to give a talk for the release of the Mandarin edition of his book “Ghost Nation: The Story of Taiwan and Its Struggle for Survival” (幽影之國：台灣的故事與其奮鬥求生的400年). Over the past year, he has traveled around Asia, Europe, and North America promoting it.
Horton has written on Taiwan for a long list of international publications, including The New York Times, The Atlantic, Nikkei Asia, and Bloomberg, where he was a staff writer. Before moving to Taiwan, he lived for many years in China followed by a stint in Hong Kong.
Although long known to people who follow English-language news about Taiwan, Horton’s profile has risen with the book’s publication, with the likes of Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) even photographed handing out copies to visiting lawmakers.
The following draws on Horton’s talk and written responses to questions from Taiwan News.
On the relevance of the Mandarin edition of Ghost Nation
“I have been very lucky to have interviewed a lot of the people who have shaped modern Taiwan,” Horton wrote to Taiwan News. “That includes the last interviews given by both Lee Teng-hui and Su Beng, as well as the first interview with Tsai Ing-wen after she stepped down as president.”
“I also had the good fortune to interview Lin Fei-fan shortly before he was appointed to the National Security Council — he really opened up about his political journey, starting with when his father would take him to protests as a kid. I think Kolas Yotaka's words describing the subtle and less-subtle types of discrimination faced by Indigenous Taiwanese might offer food for thought for non-Indigenous Taiwanese.”
“I also know how difficult it can be to explain Taiwan to foreigners. I hope the book can be useful to Taiwanese people who want their foreign partners, family, and friends to better understand their homeland so that they can have more substantial discussions of Taiwan's past, present, and future.”
On Chinese namefare over Taiwan
“Taiwan isn’t seen even when it is seen,” Horton told the audience at his event. “When you win a gold medal in the Olympics, you have this ridiculous flag, this Olympic flag with the plum blossom and the KMT emblem in the center, and nobody in the world knows what that is.”
“Actually, that KMT emblem is very appropriate because it was the KMT who negotiated the whole Zhonghua Taibei (中華台北, Chinese Taipei) silliness in 1981,” he explained.
He went on to note that Beijing has pressured journalists to refer to Tibet by the Chinese name Xizang (西藏), while East Turkestan becomes Xinjiang (新疆), meaning “new frontier” or “new territory”; Inner Mongolia becomes Beijiang (北疆), or “northern frontier”; and even Manchuria, homeland of the Manchus whose loose and overextended Qing Empire provides the historical basis for many of China’s expansive territorial claims, is simply Dongbei (東北), or “the northeast,” in contemporary CCP parlance.
“That’s what awaits Taiwan if it becomes part of China,” he said.
On historical misconceptions about Taiwan
“I lived in China for 13 years and Hong Kong for two before ever visiting Taiwan,” Horton wrote in an email. “I'd absorbed much more of the CCP line on Taiwan than I thought I had.”
“I didn't realize the Dutch were the first outsiders to colonize Taiwan. I didn't realize just how big Japan's influence on modern Taiwanese identity was and still is. I had no idea about 228 — not only the atrocities committed by the KMT, but also how the United States provided material support and political cover for the massacres of March 1947.”
“When I first arrived in Taiwan, most international coverage of Taiwan was done by China-based reporters who wrote about Taiwan from a Chinese perspective, often only including Chinese and KMT commentators. I didn't know at the time that the four years between 1945 and 1949 were the only four years in all of human history that a Chinese-identifying government based in China controlled all of Taiwan. Perhaps the biggest surprise was that Taiwan controlled territory across the strait in Kinmen and Matsu.”
On whether Taiwan has become less of a ghost in recent years
“I started writing the book in 2022. In the four-plus years since then, I would say the world sees and understands Taiwan much better than before. While there is much room for improvement of international media coverage of Taiwan, it is being covered with more breadth and depth than ever before, although starting from a relatively low bar,” he wrote.
“Regarding Taiwan's global visibility, it is worth noting that China does not control this; it is the rest of the world's countries who actually control how visible Taiwan is, and most of them tend to pretend Taiwan and their relations with Taiwan don't exist in order to avoid offending Beijing. The CCP knows this, which is why it attempts to disrupt or suppress any display of Taiwan's sovereignty or international solidarity with Taiwan anywhere on the planet.”
“It is the complicity of the world's largest and most powerful democracies in Taiwan's international isolation that I find most hypocritical. That said, as with international journalism, I would say that this has improved noticeably in recent years, and the diplomatic corps in Taipei is bigger than it's ever been since Taiwan's democratization in the 1990s, and Taipei-based diplomats have been more vocal than ever in speaking up for Taiwan, both here on the ground and when reporting back to their capitals.”
On whether he is more concerned about Taiwan than before
“Certainly more,” Horton wrote. “While I don't think an attack by China is likely this year or the next, I do see the next presidential election being likely to precipitate a crisis.”
“Should Lai win, then Xi may abandon hope of the KMT ever returning to power and decide to increase pressure. Should the KMT win, the government would in all likelihood move closer to Beijing, leading to social unrest.”
“Meanwhile as the PLA continues to upgrade its capabilities, especially in drones and robots, I worry that Taiwan's ability to deter is being weakened by the KMT-TPP coalition that currently controls the Legislative Yuan. With the PLA leadership whittled down by Xi's ongoing purge, Taiwan has a golden opportunity right now to build up its domestic defense industry, especially drones.”
“But for Taiwanese companies to make large long-term investments, there must be signalling from the government that it is committed to procurement going forward. The KMT and TPP stripped that signalling from Lai's special defense budget, resulting in the stunting of the drone industry's development here, and just as crucially, wasted time as Xi works to get his military in order.”
Green shoots and room to maneuver
“Taiwan’s visibility is not determined by Taiwan, and it’s not determined by China; it’s determined by the outside world,” Horton said to the crowd as the evening wore on. Regarding the Gwangju Biennale in South Korea, where China recently failed to pressure organizers to keep Taiwanese artists out of a major art world event, he said, “That was Taiwan winning one. China took its ball and went home. And that doesn’t happen very often.”
“What was the key?” he said. “Local solidarity. The communists aren’t good at what they do. They’re just relentless.”
He reminded the largely Taiwanese audience that Taiwan has leverage too: last year, a threat to restrict semiconductor exports to South Africa after the country downgraded Taiwan’s representative offices and sought to force its Pretoria office to relocate to Johannesburg marked a more assertive turn in Taiwanese diplomacy.
Toward the close of the event, Horton asked, “If everyone starts calling Taiwan a country, what’s Beijing going to do? Blow up the whole world?”
The line drew a burst of uneasy laughter from the audience. Soon afterward, attendees began lining up for the book signing.

Taiwan Chemicals Administration warns cat owners over insecticides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:52:43 UTC
21:52:43 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Chemicals Administration urged cat owners on Monday to keep their pets away from areas where insecticides are being used, according to a press release.
The agency said some bug sprays contain pyrethrins, which are more toxic to cats than to humans and most other mammals. It issued a public reminder telling owners to protect their cats from direct and second-hand exposure.
The agency said cats are less able to metabolize the chemicals and are therefore more likely to develop severe symptoms after exposure. It warned owners not to spray insecticides directly on their cats and instead use approved veterinary flea treatments according to a veterinarian’s instructions.
The agency decided with experts and vendors to add warning labels. Existing products will not be subject to a mandatory recall, though retailers are encouraged to provide additional warnings at points of sale.
The agency recommended that owners keep cats away after spraying and sufficiently ventilate treated areas until the chemicals have dried to minimize exposure.
According to the Ministry of Agriculture, Taiwan had an estimated 1.74 million pet cats in 2025, a 32.8% increase from 1.31 million in 2023. The number of households owning two or more cats has also increased.

Saudi Arabia preparing to grant IAEA more intrusive powers, Grossi says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Saudi Arabia preparing to grant IAEA more intrusive powers, Grossi says
VIENNA, Sept 7 - A planned U.S.-Saudi atomic deal does not include Riyadh signing the Additional Protocol that gives the U.N. nuclear watchdog sweeping inspection powers, but something close to it on some points is in the works, the agency's chief said on Monday.
The U.S. and Saudi Arabia reached an agreement on civil nuclear power cooperation in July that would let Riyadh enrich uranium and build nuclear reactors using U.S. technology.
Non-proliferation groups, such as the Arms Control Association, have criticised the planned "123 agreement" for not including the Additional Protocol, which grants the International Atomic Energy Agency extra powers such as the ability to carry out snap inspections at undeclared locations.
Iran implemented the Additional Protocol from 2016 to 2021 under a nuclear deal with major powers that unravelled after the U.S. pulled out in 2018.
IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said while the Additional Protocol would be the "ideal setup", Riyadh was preparing to go beyond its core obligations under its Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement governing relations with the IAEA.
"What is important is that in the consultations, in the preparation process, it has been possible to introduce a number of provisions to the bilateral agreement that will give the agency additional verification and monitoring authorisations," he told a press conference.
Those would be in relation to activities such as uranium enrichment and the step preceding it known as uranium conversion, as well as reprocessing, which can separate plutonium from spent reactor fuel.
"These are sensitive activities, as we all know. So for those we are going to have authorisations and capacities which are very, very similar to those that you may find in an Additional Protocol," he said, without elaborating.
Once the details are finalised, the bilateral agreement between the IAEA and Saudi Arabia will be presented to the IAEA's 35-nation Board of Governors, Grossi said. REUTERS

UN rapporteur says Israeli rubble-clearing in Gaza could erase 'atrocity crimes' evidence
The United Nations special rapporteur on Palestinian territories Francesca Albanese warned Monday that large-scale rubble removal in parts of Gaza under Israeli control could risk erasing "evidence relevant to the investigation of alleged international crimes". Israel's bombardment and ground offensive on Gaza has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza's health ministry.
Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the Palestinian territories, warned in a statement Monday that the implications of Israel's "ongoing removal, crushing and relocation of rubble in Gaza" risked erasing traces of "atrocity crimes", and preventing the recovery and identification of human remains.
"Gaza's rubble contains human remains and physical evidence relevant to the investigation of alleged international crimes, including genocide," she said, pointing to estimates from Palestinian authorities that more than 10,000 people remain buried under the debris in the war-ravaged Palestinian enclave.

The Italian-born independent expert has faced harsh criticism from Israel and some of its allies over her long-standing accusations that Israel is committing genocide and other war crimes against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Albanese, who was appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022 but who does not speak on behalf of the United Nations, said she had received credible information from multiple sources last month of "deliberate and widespread removal, crushing and transport of rubble".
In the devastated, Israeli-occupied Palestinian territory, "rubble is not just construction waste", the expert insisted.
"It is part of a crime scene, a graveyard, and the material record of what happened during a brutal and senseless bombing campaign that lasted two years."

"It is vital that before decisions are made on displacement or crushing by the occupying army or its allies, the recovery and dignified identification of human remains, systematic documentation of sites and materials, preservation of potentially relevant evidence, and an unbroken chain of custody under independent oversight must take place," Albanese said.

China releases 5-year development plan for information, communications sector
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
20:50:10 CST
21:50:10 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has issued a development plan for the information and communications industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) to promote the high-quality development of this sector.
By 2030, a new-generation communications network with comprehensive coverage and leading performance is expected to be fully established, according to the plan, which has called for efforts to accelerate the development of a technologically advanced, secure and controllable information and communications industrial system.
Meanwhile, an agile and efficient governance system integrating technology and management is expected to be effectively established, and network and data security capabilities featuring all-domain coordination and practical application will be significantly enhanced, the plan said.
The industry's empowerment level and degree of globalization will be further improved, laying a solid foundation for basically achieving modernization of the information and communications sector by 2035, the plan added.
The plan also outlines 13 key indicators, including achieving information and communications industry revenue of 4.1 trillion yuan (about 604.8 billion U.S. dollars) by 2030, cumulative investment of 3.8 trillion yuan in information infrastructure, and an average annual growth rate of 7 percent in total telecommunications business volume.
By 2030, there will be 50 5G (including 5G-A) base stations per 10,000 people, intelligent computing power will reach 9,800 EFLOPS, and the 5G user penetration rate will reach 95 percent, the ministry said.
EFLOPS, or ExaFLOPS, is a unit of computing performance, with each unit representing 1 quintillion floating-point operations per second.
The plan lays out 26 key tasks across six major areas including information infrastructure construction as well as network and data security assurance. Among these, it specifically highlights the need to initiate 6G commercial services at an appropriate time and to accelerate the establishment of a nationwide integrated computing power network.
Specific measures also include building an industry anti‑fraud laboratory and supporting enterprises to deeply promote the integration of artificial intelligence and manufacturing, the plan said.
China has established the world's largest information infrastructure. Gigabit optical network access is available in every county, while 5G networks covers all towns and more than 95 percent of administrative villages.
The country is pushing ahead with its Digital China initiative, aiming to raise the added value of the core industries of the digital economy to 12.5 percent of GDP by 2030, according to the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030). ■

Economic Watch: From VR dinosaurs to beer index, China's tourism offers novel experience

TIANJIN, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- At an exhibition booth, visitors used game consoles to control cartoon dinosaurs racing across prehistoric landscapes in an immersive virtual world.
This was one of China Dinosaur Park's programs displayed at the 2026 China Culture & Tourism Industries Expo in north China's Tianjin last week.
The interactive experience was one example of how tourist attractions in China are turning to technology to reinvent the visitor experience.
The dinosaur park, one of the world's largest, sits in eastern China's Changzhou city. It has in recent years introduced virtual reality (VR) and mixed reality (MR) headsets, allowing guests to enter digital prehistoric worlds and interact with lifelike dinosaurs.
Traditional culture is also presented in an innovative way to appeal to modern consumers.
At the booth for Dong'e Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) Culture and Tourism Area, shelves were filled with ejiao (donkey-hide gelatin) products, incense, accessories and souvenirs.
In Dong'e County, east China's Shandong Province, attractions have been built around the centuries-old craft of making ejiao, which has been recognized as a national intangible cultural heritage item. This culture and tourism area now boasts museums, an experience factory, TCM study tours, wellness programs and heritage workshops.
"Visitors can tour the museums, learn how ejiao is made, and experience blended Chinese incense-making," said Chen Xiaoming, a booth staff member.
In 2025, the Dong'e TCM-themed tourist attractions recorded 1.07 million visits and more than 100 million yuan (about 14.8 million U.S. dollars) in operating revenue.
According to China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism, Chinese residents made 3.46 billion domestic trips in the first half of 2026, up 5.4 percent year on year, while their domestic tourism spending rose 2 percent to 3.21 trillion yuan.
Cross-industry integration is reshaping the tourism sector and blurring boundaries between tourism and other forms of consumption.
Experts at the Tianjin exhibition, which attracted over 2,500 culture and tourism enterprises from 20 countries and regions, noted that demand for high-quality cultural and tourism products, immersive experiences and diversified consumption scenarios continues to rise.
The Chinese government approved a five-year consumption promotion plan in July, calling for fostering new forms, models and scenarios of consumption.
At the expo, Beijing-based recreational vehicle (RV) firm Xingchengyao displayed Class C motorhomes, pickup campers and camper vans.
"We want the vehicles themselves to become part of the travel experience," said Wang Li, the company's operations director. "We have vehicles that can provide mobile stages for performances in scenic areas, and pickup campers that can be paired with camping or desert tours."
In 2025, Xingchengyao signed agreements with automotive and tourism partners to develop a new RV-tourism ecosystem, with plans to procure 20,000 vehicles over the next three years at a contract value of 2.2 billion yuan.
Another attraction at the expo was a beer exhibition featuring a giant screen displaying a stock market scenario, where beer prices fluctuated in real time based on sales. At the "beer exchange," visitors could buy beer as if trading shares.
On the expo's opening day, a total of 1,200 half-liter cups and 220 1.5-liter bottles were sold.
The combination of beer and tourism has already gained traction in Qingdao, a coastal city in Shandong known for its brewing heritage. A similar beer exchange opened there in May 2025, attracting an average of more than 10,000 visitors daily, with single-day sales this summer vacation exceeding 1,200 liters.
"Competition among tourism products has entered a new stage," said Ge Lei, secretary-general of the China Tourism Association. "It is now centered on content, experience and creativity." ■

Interview: Long-term thinking key to building global brand, says CUKTECH executive
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
20:49:39 CST
21:49:39 KST

BERLIN, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) - As technological change reshapes the global consumer-electronics landscape, competition is increasingly moving beyond raw specifications toward more sophisticated engineering, more intuitive interaction and new applications of existing technologies. At IFA Berlin 2026, this evolution is visible in the growing emphasis on how technological advances can translate into better products and new possibilities for everyday use.
For Eric Wang, chief marketing officer of Chinese charging-technology firm CUKTECH and head of its design center, good product design should combine performance with visual restraint. The company's devices, he said in a recent interview with Xinhua, should look "cool" while conveying a sense of quality and performance, yet should not become "the loudest voice in the environment."
Wang also believes a strong design language should carry across generations of products. His aim is to create devices that remain relevant over time, with each iteration retaining enough common details to make the brand immediately recognizable. Such continuity, he said, comes from deliberate refinement rather than change for its own sake.
Underlying this philosophy is CUKTECH's long-term focus on R&D in charging and portable power. Wang sees sustained investment in engineering as essential to improving efficiency, power density and the overall user experience. As Chinese technology companies build on strong engineering and manufacturing capabilities, he believes that building a global brand also requires trust built over time.
This technological base is also allowing CUKTECH to explore new areas. At IFA, the company unveiled a prototype lower-limb exoskeleton powered by its portable power banks, applying its accumulated expertise in battery systems and power management to wearable robotics.
Wang said the use of portable, swappable power banks gives the prototype greater flexibility across different scenarios and showcases how the company's existing expertise can provide a competitive edge. The company is still exploring where the concept may lead, with the aim of seeing whether technologies built up over years in power management can translate into real value in a new field.
As technology matures, Wang also sees room for products to respond to needs beyond pure functionality. Some CUKTECH products combine visible charging information with interactive elements designed to add what he calls "sentimental value," reflecting his view that advanced technology can also have warmth and personality.
CUKTECH products are now sold in more than 40 countries and regions, and the company is making its first appearance at IFA this year as it seeks to expand further in Europe. Wang described Germany as an important market, citing strong demand for premium charging products and consumers' close attention to engineering and product performance.
Looking ahead, Wang believes that CUKTECH will continue to build on its core technologies while exploring where those capabilities can be applied next. Whether in established charging products or emerging areas such as wearable robotics, sustained R&D, enduring design and trust built over time, in his view, form part of the same long-term process of building a global technology brand. ■

How rules operate differently for foreign, Indian MBBS graduates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:49:21 UTC
21:49:21 KST

NEET-PG aspirants arrive at an examination centre to appear for the medical entrance exam on August 30
NEW DELHI: The National Board of Examinations (NBE) has ruled out lowering the pass percentage for foreign medical graduates (FMGs), saying that “qualifying standards cannot be diluted”.However, when it comes to NEET-PG, the centralised entrance exam taken by almost all Indian medical graduates, the qualifying cut-off has been significantly reduced over the past five years.In NEET PG, percentile cut-off is used, whereas to qualify in FMGE,candidates have to score 50%.The initial cut-off for NEET PG in each of these years has been 50th percentile for the general category, which has been equivalent to roughly 35% marks, and 40th percentile for reserved category, equivalent to about 30%.However, for the sake of filling vacant seats, the cut-off percentile has been reduced every year.It was dropped to zero percentile in 2023 for all categories, which meant that everyone who wrote the exam was deemed qualified including those with negative marks.In 2024, it was dropped to 5th percentile for all, but the equivalent percentage score cannot be calculated because the data on marks was not made public that year.
If 50% marks was the cut off for NEET PG, only about 25% of those who appeared would have qualified in the last five years.The proposed single licensing-cum-entrance exam for post graduate seats in India, which would be common for FMGs and for Indian medical graduates, called National Exit Test or NExT, has been postponed indefinitely.NEET PG results raise the question: What share of Indian graduates would be able to qualify in such an exam with 50% and not 50th percentile as the qualifying cut off ?NBE points out that the difference between the FMG screening test and NEET PG is that one is for qualifying to get a licence to practise while NEET PG exam is to rank Indian medical graduates, who have already passed final year MBBS exams, for getting post-graduate seats.Final year MBBS exams are held in the medical colleges where the students have been taught and trained with the inherent vulnerability of institutional bias to boost pass percentages.FMGE was introduced in 2002 by the erstwhile Medical Council of India ostensibly to ensure that doctors trained abroad meet the same standards as those trained in India.
NEET-PG cut-offs and the share of candidates qualifying after revised cut-offs from 2020 to 2025
The 2002 regulation also made it mandatory for FMGs to complete one-year internship from an institution approved by the MCI after clearing FMGE to get a licence to practise.From Nov 2021, the National Medical Commission, which succeeded the MCI, has mandated that all FMGs, after passing the final year MBBS exam in whichever country have they trained in, have to obtain a licence to practise in that country before they appear for FMGE.While the criteria for an FMG to get a licence to practice in India has been progressively tightened, the opposite has been happening to medical education in India.The infrastructure and faculty norms, and the regulatory oversight for starting new medical colleges in India has been progressively relaxed or diluted to help rapid expansion of MBBS seats.Between 2014 and 2026, the number of medical colleges has jumped from 387 to 818 and the number of MBBS seats from over 51,300 to about 1.3 lakh with complaints piling up of colleges being run without adequate faculty, infrastructure or patient load.
Though every candidate appearing for NEET PG is supposed to have passed MBBS with minimum 40% in each subject and 50% overall, candidates scoring single digit, zero or even negative marks in NEET PG puts a question mark over the quality of graduates being churned out from medical colleges in India.It also raises the question, can India have different criteria/double standards for screening FMGs and its own medical graduates given the highly uneven standards of medical education here.

 Weightlifting will also attract significant attention. The Iranian lineup includes established names such as Mostafa Javadi, Ali Aalipour and Ali Davoudi, alongside two female lifters. Yet the competition will be fierce, with Asia’s traditional weightlifting powers leaving little room for error.
 
 Athletics is another discipline carrying high expectations. A target of 10 medals has been discussed, although achieving that figure will be challenging given the gap between some Iranian athletes and the continent’s leading performances.
 
 In canoeing, nine Iranian athletes will compete, with hopes of ending a 16-year wait for an Asian Games gold medal.
 
 In team sports, Iran’s volleyball team remain one of the continent’s leading contenders. Basketball, football and several other teams, however, face tougher challenges. Iran’s U23 football team, in particular, have been drawn alongside China, North Korea and the United Arab Emirates, while limited preparation and a lack of sufficient friendly matches remain concerns.
 
 Beyond the established medal hopefuls, Nagoya 2026 could also provide a valuable platform for Iran’s younger generation. For some, this may be their first major international experience, potentially marking the beginning of a journey toward future success.
 
 With a blend of proven champions and emerging talent, Iran head to Japan with genuine hopes of producing a strong medal haul. From wrestling and taekwondo to shooting, weightlifting, volleyball, athletics and canoeing, the expectation is clear: Iran want to make their presence felt across Asia.
 
 The 20th Asian Games will be held from Sept. 19 to Oct. 4, 2026, in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. As the continent’s best athletes gather for two weeks of competition, millions of Iranians will be watching their national delegation with hope and pride, dreaming of gold, silver and bronze medals and the sight of the Iranian flag rising above the podium in Nagoya.

Overcoming financial, logistical hurdles: path to Iran-Vietnam trade expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

Overcoming financial, logistical hurdles: path to Iran-Vietnam trade expansion
TEHRAN- Despite significant potential in petrochemicals, agriculture, and industry, Iran and Vietnam have yet to reach their desired trade levels. Overcoming financial, logistical, and intermediary obstacles is essential for a leap in bilateral exchanges, reports Mehr News correspondent.
Vietnam has emerged as a major production and trade hub in Southeast Asia, while Iran—with its strong petrochemical, mineral, agricultural, and chemical sectors—can supply many of this export-driven economy's needs. Yet sanctions, payment transfer issues, reliance on third countries, logistics costs, and limited Iranian business awareness of the Vietnamese market have left much of this potential untapped.
UN Comtrade data shows Iran's exports to Vietnam at about $67.84 million in 2022, with imports around $38.64 million—totaling roughly $106.5 million, well below targets. However, signs of renewed momentum are emerging. In March 2026, Vietnam's ambassador reported bilateral trade reached about $109 million over eight months, with goods like rubber, coffee, and tea flowing to Iran, while petrochemicals, IT products, and construction materials moved to Vietnam. He projected 7–10% annual growth and hoped for a 50% increase over five years.
Vietnam's total foreign trade hit a record $930.05 billion in 2025, with exports of $475.04 billion and 8.02% GDP growth—making it a far larger market than current Iran-Vietnam figures suggest.
Mostafa Mousavi, head of the Iran-Vietnam Joint Chamber, reports fresh Vietnamese requests for petrochemical and agricultural purchases, with barter deals under consideration. In some cases, Vietnam has shown readiness to buy directly and even offered to send its own ships for cargo pickup.
A key challenge has been the indirect nature of much trade, often routed through third countries like the UAE. This inflates costs, lengthens transit times, and raises sanctions-related risks. Direct trade is seen as a crucial competitiveness booster. Barter and alternative financial channels are being explored, alongside leveraging Vietnam's 2015 preferential trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union—which Iran joined in 2023—as a complementary access route.
Direct air links are also improving. The Tehran–Ho Chi Minh City route launched on August 31, 2026, with Tehran–Hanoi to follow soon. Trade attaché Mohsen Rezaeipour called this a game-changer for business travel, investment, and high-value, time-sensitive cargo, complementing sea freight.
In agriculture, a Vietnamese delegation recently toured apple production and packaging facilities in West Azarbaijan, with quarantine hurdles largely resolved—opening a new market beyond traditional destinations. Beyond apples, Iran can export dried fruits, processed foods, and horticultural products, while Vietnam offers coffee, rice, tea, seafood, and consumer goods.
Petrochemicals remain Iran's strongest export advantage, with some non-official estimates placing chemical exports to Vietnam in the hundreds of millions for 2025, though data discrepancies exist. Meanwhile, Iran could import electronics, machinery, and rubber products, suggesting a balanced, diversified trade basket is achievable.
Vietnam's $930 billion foreign trade landscape means Iran's $109 million share is still marginal. Yet recent steps—direct flights, quarantine progress, and interest in barter—signal a shift from "potential" to "practical pathways." If stable financial mechanisms, reduced intermediation, and better logistics take root, Vietnam could become a key Iranian market in Southeast Asia, offering not only off-take for petrochemicals and agriculture but also a gateway to broader ASEAN supply chains.

Indian IT firm to build $7.4 bn data center campus for AI training

Indian IT firm to build $7.4 bn data center campus for AI training
Indian IT services company Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) plans to build a $7.4 billion data center campus, exploiting the opportunities offered by the white-hot global demand for artificial intelligence as it seeks to move away from the traditional outsourcing model. 
The 1-gigawatt (GW) facility will cater to AI companies and large cloud providers, known as hyperscalers, offering support for AI training, inference, and other advanced workloads, TCS said on Saturday. 
TCS unit HyperVault will build the campus – expected to be among the country’s biggest – in the southern city of Hyderabad. The buildout will happen in phases, based on customer demand and technology requirements, the Mumbai-based company said in a statement.  
TCS CEO K. Krithivasan said the project is part of the company’s “infrastructure-to-intelligence” strategy. 
“AI demand is increasingly becoming infrastructure demand,” Sohom Banerjee, a technology analyst at the think tank CUTS International, told RT. He said TCS’s move should be viewed as some IT companies “moving vertically down the AI stack.” 
TCS, which reported about $30 billion in revenue in the financial year ended March, last month signed a $1.5 billion deal with German luxury carmaker Porsche to ride the AI-led transformation in the auto industry. 
The data center investment comes as AI rapidly reshapes India’s labor-intensive, billing hours-based IT services industry – whose boom drove the country’s economic growth in the last two decades. The IT and business process management industry in India is currently valued at more than $300 billion by revenue.
Banerjee noted that while AI is putting pressure on parts of the IT consultants’ traditional business model, it is also simultaneously creating demand for a new layer of services around data centers, computing capacity, cloud platforms, AI models, and enterprise applications.
Large domestic AI data center investments move India from “being primarily a user and integrator of AI toward becoming an important location for AI compute,” he said.
Demand for such capacity is already rising. Property consultancy JLL estimates India’s data center capacity will grow from around 1.6 GW in mid-2026 to 6 GW by 2029. Hyderabad is emerging as one of the hubs for gigawatt-scale investment.
Local officials have said the project could generate up to 7,000 direct and indirect jobs across technology, construction, engineering, and operations.

Estonian tennis player Mark Lajal gets death threats after tournament loss
Estonia's top tennis player Mark Lajal received abusive messages and death threats, some to his own phone, following a tournament defeat Delfi reported.
The messages came following his semifinals loss at the ATP Challenger 75 tournament in Manacor, Spain, held at the Rafa Nadal Academy on Mallorca, and the player said they were from sports bettors unhappy about losing money.
Lajal, currently ranked 152nd in the world, shared screenshots of messages he had received aftermath of his semi-final defeat, including from those who had obtained his personal phone number.
The screenshots were in English and included the message:"I really but really hope you will get cancer including your family as well. I hope you will see then [sic] suffer."
Another screenshot Lajal posted read "Look, you son of a b*tch, you're a f*cking loser. I hate you and you must die. You must die, you f*cking son of a b*tch. You and your family must die. You b*stard. I want to kill you."
"Know, we are going to talk, you know what you are doing and you are not dumb as you want people to know you, that's why I'm going to kill all your family," a third message stated.
Lajal, 23, said the abusive and threatening messages had come primarily from disgruntled sports bettors who had lost money on the outcome, and added while he would not normally post on the topic, the messages had gone too far.
"Sometimes these days happen, you lose, but then you get on your phone and somehow people have gotten your number and are calling and texting death threats," he explained, noting the threats and abuse had been directed against his family as well as personally against him after losing.
The player noted abuse like this is the lot of many top players, but questioned the trade-off between this and the big money that sports betting involves: "At the end of the day, ATP keeps accepting all this money from betting platforms, but at what cost?" he noted.
"Gambling addiction is a real issue and I hope these people find and get the help they need," Lajal concluded.
Lajal went through qualifying at the Mallorca event, and defeated Nicolai Budkov Kjaer, a Norwegian player with Estonian roots, 6-3, 6-1 The next round, the quarterfinals, saw him defeat Spanish player Alejo Sanchez Quileze again in straight sets, 6-2, 6-3.
The winning streak came to an end however with a 7-6 (7), 5-7 defeat to France's Felix Balshaw (ATP 252) in the semi final, despite the Estonian initially leading the second set 4-1.
The entire encounter lasted two hours and 10 minutes and Balshaw, 20, will face Spanish player Inaki Montes-De La Torre (ATP 274) in the final.
Other top tennis players who have recently reported receiving death threats and abusive messages include Italy's Matteo Berettini and Panna Udvardy of Hungary.
