BRUSSELS — The Irish Council presidency welcomed “consensus” among governments to introduce new EU-wide levies on foreign polluters and electronic waste to finance the bloc’s next seven-year budget, according to a document seen by POLITICO.
The EU’s 27 countries are narrowing down a list of potential new taxes, or own resources, to fund the bloc’s common cash pot as negotiations enter their crunch phase.
Introducing new EU-wide levies is crucial to lay the groundwork for a budget agreement by the end of the year, before national elections in France, Spain and Italy in 2027 threaten to disrupt the negotiations.
Advertisement
The president of the European Council, António Costa, urged national leaders to home in on several potential taxes during their next gathering in Brussels on Oct. 15. Supporters argue that own resources are essential to generate more revenue and reduce national contributions to the EU from 2028 to 2034.
With less than four months to go until the informal deadline, the bloc's governments have shown openness towards a tax on foreign carbon imports, officially known as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and a separate levy on non-collected electronic waste.
“Of the Commission’s proposals for new Own Resources, the most consensual among Member States is CBAM, with many open to increasing the call rate further,” the Irish Council presidency, which is steering discussions, wrote in a note to EU governments seen by POLITICO.
Under current rules, capitals must funnel 75 percent of CBAM revenues to the EU budget, and retain 25 percent for their domestic budgets.
CBAM is expected to generate, on average, €1.644 billion per year, roughly adding up to €11.5 billion for the whole budget cycle, according to an updated estimate by the European Commission seen by POLITICO.
The Irish presidency also noted “a broad degree of support” among governments towards the electronic waste tax, which is expected to generate €17.9 billion per year. They added that criticism towards the levy largely focuses on statistical issues.
Advertisement
More EU taxes
France is leading the charge to introduce more EU taxes to generate extra revenue and further reduce national contributions to Brussels.
Last year, the Commission proposed five new levies — targeting carbon imports, emissions trading scheme (ETS), non-collected electronic waste, corporate profits and tobacco products — worth €66 billion per year.
But most of the ideas — which must be approved unanimously by EU members — have been met with resistance from national governments.
António Costa arrives for a summit in Brussels on March 19, 2026. | Marco Tacca/Getty Images
The Irish presidency noted that “a group of Member States remain opposed to ETS.” The group includes highly polluting Eastern countries, such as Poland and Hungary, who want to retain the ETS revenues for their domestic budgets.
It also wrote that many governments criticized the tobacco tax and a majority opposed the corporate levy because it will undermine competitiveness.
In a bid to break the deadlock, the European Parliament last spring proposed new levies on online gambling, crypto firms and digital giants.
Advertisement
However, the Irish presidency threw cold water on these suggestions, noting that “most Member States were opposed to or doubted the ability for the EP proposals to be implemented by 2028.”
They added that few countries showed openness toward the digital levy, but others warned against “geo-political concerns” such as the threat of retaliation by the U.S.
Finally, Ireland noted that governments are divided around the idea of postponing repayments of the bloc's post-Covid recovery fund, which are expected to cost €25 billion per year.

Kyiv stockpiles food and water as Russia’s new aerial tactics threaten a brutal winter

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

Kyiv is building reserves of food and drinking water to help residents during prolonged power outages and other emergencies, the Kyiv City Council said on 7 September.
The preparations come as Russia continues to target Ukraine’s critical infrastructure and food supply chains, while Ukrainian officials warn that water systems could also come under attack. Kyiv is therefore preparing for a broader range of disruptions this winter, not just power outages.
The city is preparing the reserves ahead of the 2026–2027 fall and winter season, with priority given to low-income residents and people facing difficult circumstances.
The supplies will also be available at Points of Invincibility, emergency support centers set up to provide basic services during prolonged blackouts, for people affected by emergencies, and for workers involved in emergency and other urgent response operations.
Kyiv prepares for attacks on food and water supplies as Russia makes air attacks harder to stop
Russia has increasingly targeted infrastructure connected to Ukraine’s food supply in recent months. Russian strikes have hit food warehouses and distribution facilities around Kyiv, contributing to shortages and periods of empty supermarket shelves in the capital and other parts of the country.
Ukrainian officials have also warned that Russia could target water infrastructure as part of its attacks on critical civilian systems, raising concerns about access to drinking water during prolonged disruptions.
This year, the threat is particularly acute as Russia has expanded its use of ballistic missiles and introduced faster, jet-powered Geran drones that are harder for Ukraine to intercept. Ballistic missiles can only be reliably intercepted by a limited number of air defense systems, while the faster drones reduce the time available to detect and engage them.
Russia has destroyed 90% of Ukraine’s modern commercial storage capacity. Retail logistics are being reshaped
Kyiv prepares for another difficult winter
Russia's strikes have repeatedly targeted Ukraine's energy infrastructure during previous winters, causing extended blackouts and disruptions to heating and other essential services.
Kyiv is now preparing for the possibility that attacks could again leave residents without electricity or access to essential supplies for extended periods.
Kyiv says food supply remains stable, for now
Oleh Kuіavskyi, deputy head of the Kyiv City State Administration, said the city's preparations are focused not only on accumulating supplies but also on ensuring they can quickly reach people who need them.
“Food security in the capital is not only about having the necessary reserves, but also a clear system for their distribution and delivery to those who need help most,” Kuіavskyi said, according to the Kyiv City Council.
He said Kyiv's consumer market remains stable and predictable, while the city continues to hold agricultural food fairs across its districts to help maintain access to basic food products.
Reserves could feed 25,000 people
According to the city council, Kyiv has already formed and is maintaining reserves of key food products for use if the energy system comes under severe strain.
With support from charitable and civic organizations, the city can organize hot meals for up to 25,000 people, officials said.
The city's Department of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development also plans to purchase another 20,000 food packages for use during emergencies.
The reserves are being coordinated through Kyiv's Humanitarian Headquarters, established in February 2022. The body coordinates the city administration, district administrations, municipal companies, charities, and donors, including the accounting and distribution of emergency resources.

Chinook helicopters have been operating at low level as part of Exercise Kukri Dawn, a training deployment that has taken the aircraft over Fife, Edinburgh and Glasgow.
RAF Lossiemouth set out the detail in a flying notice issued on 25 August, confirming that Chinooks from 28 (AC) Squadron would be operating out of Leuchars Aerodrome from the first of September, and that the exercise would end by the twentieth.
The notice told residents what to expect and how the aircraft would be flown. “The aircraft may be seen operating around Leuchars, Fife, and surrounding areas for the duration of the exercise. Low-level circuits (50-100ft) over rural landscapes will be conducted as part of the aircrew’s training – farms and villages will be avoided at all times,” it said.
Horse riders were given specific advice, the station saying: “We advise horse riders to wear hi-viz during hacks (rider and horse!) so the pilots can see you and divert accordingly during low-level sorties.” Explaining the purpose of the flying, it added: “These training flights ensure Chinook aircrew are ready to secure the skies, no matter the flying conditions.”
A separate Ministry of Defence alert circulated in north east Fife on 24 August had already warned of an increase in day, and occasional early evening, flying between 1 and 18 September, saying that training would take place across Scotland as part of Exercise Kukri Dawn and that activity would be particularly noticeable in areas around Leuchars Station. That notice said: “The ability to operate effectively at low level is essential for Military helicopters in their role supporting troops on the ground. Realistic low-level training is therefore a vital part of preparing aircrew for operational duties.” It also stated that military helicopters would avoid overflying horse riders wherever possible, provided riders can be identified in sufficient time and it is safe to do so.
28 (Army Cooperation) Squadron is the Royal Air Force’s support helicopter training unit, based at RAF Benson in Oxfordshire, where it prepares Chinook and Puma crews before they join front-line squadrons. Deploying students away from their home station for the final phase of that training is a deliberate part of the design, since it obliges the squadron to operate as it would when deployed and puts crews into terrain and weather closer to what they will meet on operations.
Sorties this month have covered a good deal of ground too, one Chinook operating under the callsign KUKRI1 was tracked this morning leaving the Leuchars area and running south west across Fife by way of Cupar and Kinross, before crossing the Forth at South Queensferry and continuing over Edinburgh and the eastern edge of the Pentland Hills. From there it worked west into Lanarkshire and around the southern and eastern fringes of Glasgow, taking in Larkhall, East Kilbride, Rutherglen and Cumbernauld, before turning back north with further orbits recorded near Stirling and Alloa.
Low-level rotary flying over built-up areas of this kind is, of course, less common than the rural circuits described in the flying notice, and it tends to generate a good deal of public interest.
We have asked the RAF for more information.

Can women solve Ukraine's manpower problem?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:25:33 UTC
21:25:33 KST

Can women solve Ukraine's manpower problem?
(L-R) Maryna, 23, call sign Vesna, Tetiana, 22, call sign Titan, Daria, 35, a commander of the crew with a call sign Hilka, Viktoriia, 26, call sign Karma, and Oleksandra, 24, call sign Smakolyk, members of the all-women UAV crew recently created as part of the Typhoon special forces unit of the National Guard of Ukraine, in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 6, 2025. (Oksana Parafeniuk / The Washington Post via Getty Images)
During a routine assignment in Mykolaiv Oblast in 2022, Nataliia Lishchyshena suffered an injury that would change her life. Jumping out of a vehicle, she landed hard, badly bruising her chest.
At first, Lishchyshena thought little of the injury, aggravated by body armor designed without women's bodies in mind. But doctors later linked it, along with stress and hormonal changes, to the development of a benign tumor. The condition ultimately led to a mastectomy. A military medical commission later concluded the illness was directly related to her service.
"We conducted a survey with the women's movement Veteranka, and we were shocked by the results," Lishchyshena told the Kyiv Independent. "About 85% of women in the military have problems with their breasts, and there are very many cases of cancer."
Conditions for women in the Ukrainian military remain challenging — from a lack of properly fitted equipment, which can lead to serious health problems, to unwelcoming and, at times, dangerous attitudes from male colleagues. Nonetheless, recent comments from prominent political figures have revived the debate over mobilizing women.
Former Defense Minister Oleksii Reznikov brought the question to media attention in an interview with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) on Aug. 20, when he said that military service should be mandatory for both men and women.
Reznikov argued that requiring women to serve in the military would "immediately double the mobilization pool."
But doubling the pool on paper does not necessarily mean doubling the size of the military in practice, raising broader questions about the proposal's practical necessity and whether political considerations may also be at play.
"Reznikov's idea is logical in theory, but in practice it has significant limitations," Viktor Kevliuk, a reserve colonel and analyst at the Center for Defense Strategies, told the Kyiv Independent.
U.S. Special Envoy for Ukraine Keith Kellogg intensified the controversy in an interview with the Naspravdi MAX YouTube channel published on Aug. 24. "So do I believe women should be mobilized into the army? My answer is yes, because they fight no worse than men," Kellogg said.
Hours after Kellogg's remarks, the Ukrainian parliament issued a statement clarifying that the mobilization of women "is not being carried out, prepared, or considered."
Military service for women in Ukraine remains voluntary, and Reznikov's position sharply contrasted with President Volodymyr Zelensky's 2023 stance that he would never sign a law mandating the mobilization of women.
Reality behind the numbers
More than 75,000 women currently serve in Ukraine's Armed Forces, according to the General Staff. About 55,000 serve as military personnel, while the rest hold civilian positions. Their ranks have nearly doubled since the start of the full-scale invasion. Military registration is mandatory only for women with medical or pharmaceutical training.
Most women serve in medicine, logistics and support, analysis, and drone operations rather than in front-line infantry and assault units. That is where the military's most acute personnel shortage remains, Kevliuk said, with those positions carrying significantly greater physical and psychological demands.
"Massive recruitment of women into such roles is unlikely to bring a qualitative breakthrough in the short term," the analyst added.
Reznikov suggested that bringing more women into the military could have a knock-on effect: with women taking up more positions in the rear, more men could potentially be moved closer to the front.
"Many men in rear positions have health limitations, and under the law, they cannot be sent to combat units because of their health conditions," Kevliuk said.
Some "rotation effect" is possible, Kevliuk added, but not overnight or at scale, and only with changes to staffing structures, additional training for women, and a broader rethinking of how units are staffed.
Fight to be seen
The growing presence of women in Ukraine's military dates back to 2014, when Russia occupied Crimea and began its war in Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts. There were no serious efforts at the time to develop standard-issue uniforms for women, while those serving in combat roles were often officially registered as cooks or other rear personnel.
Legal restrictions on women holding combat positions were lifted in 2018, but the military took years to adapt its equipment to the growing number of women in its ranks.
The first standard-issue summer uniform designed for women was introduced only in 2023. There is still no standard-issue winter uniform for women. When it came to body armor, the gap was even more striking: the State Rear Operator (DOT) made its first purchase of women-specific body armor only in July 2026, with just 2,000 units for around 55,000 women serving in military positions.
While men in the military also face shortages and often have to cover their own equipment needs, women's access to essential gear remains more limited.
Kseniia Drahaniuk, co-founder of Zemliachky, a Ukrainian nonprofit that helps equip women serving at the front, said Ukraine has made significant progress in recent years — even if that progress is not always immediately visible.
The U.S. military spent five decades discussing the need for women-specific uniforms, Drahaniuk said, and the issue remains unresolved for many of Ukraine's European partners. Ukrainian forces, meanwhile, have had to adapt to battlefield conditions in real time.
"Every bureaucratic process, every approval takes a very long time. The country cannot respond as quickly as the civilian sector can," Drahaniuk said, adding that "years" can pass between the purchase of equipment and the moment it reaches a servicewoman.
Demand for women's equipment has grown as more women join, she said, and positions once considered relatively removed from the front line, such as air defense operators, have become more dangerous with increased Russian attacks.
An electronic warfare operator who goes by the call sign "Strada" told the Kyiv Independent that attitudes toward women in the military have improved significantly over her two years of service. But she said state-provided equipment and support still have a long way to go.
"Strada" also said that while seeing women in Ukraine's military is no longer "unusual," skepticism toward them has not disappeared but simply taken different forms.
"When a woman is asked, 'Are you sure you can handle it?' or 'Why do you need this?' or is told, 'It will be difficult for you,' it really diminishes you," she said, adding that women often face a kind of overprotectiveness that is neither necessary nor helpful.
"I'm for judging people in the military by their results. If you can do the job, do it. If you can't, that's a question of professional ability, not gender."
Another sensitive issue rarely discussed publicly is sexual harassment.
The servicewomen and female veterans interviewed by the Kyiv Independent said they had not experienced sexual harassment while serving. But they also stressed that their experiences do not mean such cases do not occur.
A law signed by Zelensky on March 16 established principles of equality and non-discrimination and introduced mechanisms to protect military personnel from discrimination and sexual harassment.
Oksana Hryhorieva, gender adviser to the General Staff, said at a press conference on March 24 that the number of such cases in the military had decreased. At the same time, she acknowledged how difficult it can be to prove that harassment occurred.
"Basically, it's one person's word against another's. There is still no evidence because witnesses will not testify about it," Hryhorieva said.
Why is women's mobilization being discussed now?
According to political analyst Ihor Reiterovych, Kellogg's remarks may have been more of a coincidence and a sharing of personal experience, given that his wife and daughter served in the military. Reznikov's statement, though, was "not his own initiative," Reiterovych said.
"I think there was a certain request from the Presidential Office to divert attention from other issues by making such statements," Reiterovych said.
Reznikov's remarks came as Zelensky's team was dealing with yet another corruption scandal involving Iryna Mudra, a former presidential deputy chief of staff. The president was also still recovering from a political crisis triggered by the unexpected dismissal of then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov without clear justification on July 15, followed by Fedorov's calls for elections to be held during martial law, and nationwide protests.
"So, as of now, (the mobilization of women) is nothing more than a trigger issue that attracts attention, gets good views, but it is futile," Reiterovych said. "I cannot imagine how the Ukrainian parliament would vote for something like this."
Reiterovych said the government might seriously consider mobilizing women only if Ukraine faced a "catastrophic shortage of people" liable for military service. That manpower shortage has not yet been reached, he argued, noting that an estimated 2.5 million to 3 million men in Ukraine have not updated their military registration data.
Other options remain, he added, from reconsidering the criteria for limited or full exemption from military service to allowing civilians willing to support the military in rear positions to do so without formally joining the armed forces.
The servicewomen and female veterans interviewed by the Kyiv Independent also questioned the need to debate women's mobilization now, saying the government should first improve conditions for women willing to serve voluntarily.
Yuliia Mykytenko, a reserve officer and active member of the women's movement Veteranka, said she was not opposed to women joining the military, but raised concerns about the need for mass mobilization of women.
"At the beginning of the full-scale war, we had an almost million-strong army of motivated soldiers, where one was worth ten. How was this resource squandered to the point where we are now talking about mobilizing women?" Mykytenko said.
For the reserve officer, the problem lies deeper than the size of the mobilization pool. Mykytenko said the military's combat effectiveness is being undermined by failures to respect service members' rights, a lack of clear communication about battlefield objectives, and unresolved questions over economic exemptions from mobilization and those evading service.
Bringing women into the mobilization pool would not fix those problems but instead signal that the military had been pushed to a critical limit, she added.
"If it really comes to the point where women are mobilized, I will automatically consider that our country has lost," Mykytenko said.

Volkswagen, Israeli firm agree on sale of Osnabrueck plant

Oliver Towfigh Nia
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Volkswagen agreed to sell its Osnabrueck plant to Israeli private equity firm Aurelius and the state of Lower Saxony, the German automaker said Monday.
Under the deal, air defense systems from the Israeli Iron Dome manufacturer Rafael are to be produced at the factory.
“Aurelius and the State of Lower Saxony intend to develop the site over the coming years into a competence center for security and defense solutions.
"As an initial anchor project, Aurelius and the State of Lower Saxony are planning to cooperate with Rafael Advanced Defense Systems,” VW said in a statement.
The plant is expected to manufacture systems and components for air defense systems for Germany and Europe, he said.
The cooperation is also intended to pave the way for further partnerships and projects, VW said.
Two years ago, the carmaker decided to phase out vehicle production at the Osnabrueck site by the summer of 2027.
As part of the plans, Aurelius will acquire a majority stake in the plant, while the state of Lower Saxony will take a minority stake.
The details of the deal are to be negotiated in the coming months.
VW facing major criticism
Volkswagen has been grappling in recent years with sluggish demand, persistently high production costs in Germany, the negative impact of trade tensions with the US, and fierce competition from Chinese electric-vehicle makers.
Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume had said in March that the company will stop manufacturing Volkswagen Group vehicles at Osnabruck starting in 2027 and confirmed talks with several defense firms about shifting the plant for military vehicles production.
The proposal, since then, has sparked significant controversy within Germany.
Volkswagen employees, peace activists and opposition politicians have criticized the plan, arguing the automaker should focus exclusively on civilian production.
The Osnabruck Peace Initiative (OFRI) has also organized multiple protests urging Volkswagen to abandon any defense contracts.
Germany’s opposition Left Party called Volkswagen’s planned cooperation with Israel’s state-owned Rafael Advanced Defense Systems “unacceptable,” citing the Netanyahu government’s war crimes and genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Rafael, meanwhile, has been expanding its European footprint as governments across the continent boost defense spending and procurement following the war in Ukraine.

Türkiye’s 3-year roadmap outlines new incentives for domestic production, investment strategy

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:25:18 UTC
21:25:18 KST

Ayse Bocuoglu Bodur and Emir Yildirim
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Türkiye is preparing to launch new programs to facilitate the development and production of critical products and technologies through domestic means to enhance the competitive edge of the country’s production in foreign markets.
Ankara’s Medium-Term Program (MTP) covering 2027-2029 will feature targeted industrial policies on sectoral priorities to support high-value-added transformation in industry, as well as other measures to expand the scope of programs serving as a catalyst for domestic production.
The High-Tech Investment Program (HIT-30) will facilitate large-scale investments in priority tech sectors via project-based and customized mechanisms.
The new advance credit program based on investment commitments will be implemented alongside the existing investment incentive system to contribute to exports in productive sectors and promote high-value-added product groups, while a new application area covering high-quality but relatively smaller manufacturing industry investments will be developed.
Türkiye’s new strategic initiative program will contribute to investments ensuring supply security, reducing foreign dependency, and offering high research and development (R&D) content aligned with twin transformation goals.
The transformative roadmap also includes the allocation of state aid to the production of critical components for developing competitive manufacturing in priority sectors through domestic capabilities. The economic aid will be tightly regulated to prioritize companies demonstrating tangible increases in energy efficiency, job creation, and export volume.
The overarching investment incentive system will transition to a project-oriented framework to target specific regional development needs.
Ankara will also encourage agricultural investments to convert farming byproducts into profitable goods to strengthen the ties between rural agriculture and urban industry.
The local development initiative program will provide funding for private-sector projects addressing regional challenges with technological upgrades and localized job creation.
Türkiye’s future roadmap also includes other efforts to subsidize branding, certification, and e-commerce infrastructure to commercialize local products for global export markets.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said Monday that Beirut supports renewing the mandate of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) and welcomed a French-Italian initiative for an international presence after the UN mission ends, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA).
“Lebanon supports the renewal of the international force in the south, and we are working with (French) President (Emmanuel) Macron to facilitate the renewal,” Aoun said during a meeting with French Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin, NNA reported.
He also welcomed the French-Italian initiative to form a European force to fill the vacuum following UNIFIL’s withdrawal.
Aoun said he will visit Paris next week to join Macron at the opening of a preparatory meeting for an international conference to support the Lebanese army and Internal Security Forces and to discuss the future of the international presence in southern Lebanon.
France and Italy announced an initiative in June to launch an international coalition, in coordination with the EU and UN, aimed at developing a mechanism for the post-UNIFIL period and preventing a security vacuum in southern Lebanon.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani later said Rome could contribute troops to an international post-UNIFIL mission, while stressing that any deployment would require a multilateral agreement.
Separately, the EU is planning a mission to advise and train the Lebanese armed forces, including in border and maritime security. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said last week that the initiative is not intended to replace UNIFIL but to strengthen Lebanon’s ability to provide its own security.
Aoun also condemned Israel’s continuing attacks on Lebanon, including the killing of civilians and destruction of homes and property.

Darmanin, for his part, praised reforms undertaken by Lebanon and said Beirut could “always count on France,” according to NNA.
Lebanon and Israel signed a US-brokered framework agreement on June 26 following negotiations in Washington. The deal calls for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of armed groups.
Israel has continued its attacks on Lebanon despite the agreement. According to figures released by the Lebanese Health Ministry in late August, Israeli attacks since March 2 have killed more than 4,000 people and injured over 12,000.
UNIFIL has operated in southern Lebanon since 1978. Its mandate is set to expire at the end of 2026, prompting discussions over security arrangements for the post-UNIFIL period. Lebanon has repeatedly said it prefers the mission to remain but is open to an alternative international presence if its mandate cannot be extended.

Putin’s ‘Battlefield Fiction’ Could Take Russia Until 2032 to Seize Donetsk, ISW Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:24:19 UTC
21:24:19 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin is doubling down on a fictional picture of the battlefield that he defines as “reality” and using it to justify Russia’s refusal to make meaningful compromises in peace negotiations with Ukraine, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said.
Putin reiterated Russia’s commitment to achieving all of its war aims through military means during his Saturday meeting with US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff and former senior adviser to President Donald Trump Jared Kushner, according to Russian Presidential Aide Yuriy Ushakov.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ushakov said on Sunday that Putin gave the US envoys a comprehensive assessment of Russia’s “significant advances” along the frontline – a claim ISW said was exaggerated and did not match the realities on the ground.
A person close to the Kremlin told Reuters before Witkoff and Kushner’s visit that there would be no peace agreement until Russian forces seize the remainder of the Donetsk region.
The source said Putin is confident his forces can capture the entire region by the end of 2026 – the Kremlin’s latest deadline for achieving the goal.
ISW said that belief is being reinforced by Russia’s own military leadership.
“The Russian military systematically misinforms Putin about the state of the front line,” the think tank said, pointing to the pervasive culture of lying within the Russian armed forces that Russian milbloggers refer to as “beautiful reports.”
‘I Can’t Mislead People’: Ukraine’s Spy Chief Warns Russia Can Fight Through 2028
Senior Russian commanders routinely exaggerate battlefield gains as part of what ISW described as a systematic cognitive warfare effort designed to portray Russian forces as making sweeping advances while Ukrainian defenses are collapsing.
Those distortions are likely leading Putin to further harden his belief that Russia can achieve its objectives in Donetsk region by the end of 2026 – and therefore that he has no reason to compromise in peace negotiations.
Russia keeps missing Putin’s deadlines
Putin has reportedly set at least 15 deadlines for the seizure of Donetsk region since February 2022. Russian forces have failed to meet not even one.
They will also fail to meet his latest deadline of Dec. 31, 2026, ISW assessed.
Russian forces have been fighting for Kostiantynivka since October 2025 and have still not seized it after 11 months of fighting.
They have not reached, let alone entered or captured, the other key cities of Ukraine’s Fortress Belt – Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, and Druzhkivka.
ISW said Russian forces will not be able to capture all three within the four months remaining in 2026, given that they have failed to complete the seizure of even one Fortress Belt city in nearly a year.
“Putin’s battlefield fiction remains divorced from the reality of Ukraine’s defensive abilities, Russia’s own degraded offensive capabilities, and the difficult and expansive terrain Russian forces must still fight through to achieve Putin’s strategic goal in the region,” ISW said.
Putin’s repeated deadlines also serve a domestic political purpose, the think tank said. He needs to provide Russians with a significant informational victory after promising them victory in exchange for enduring the burdens of war without placing Russian society on a full wartime footing.
At the current pace, Donetsk falls in 2032
Russia’s actual rate of advance makes Putin’s 2026 deadline even more unrealistic.
Russian forces advanced across the entire theater of operations at an average rate of 2.91 square kilometers (719 acres) per day in August 2026, a slight increase compared with recent months.
But their advance in their priority effort in Donetsk region was slower – just 2.36 square kilometers (583 acres) per day.
At that rate, Russia would need until Oct. 2, 2032 to seize the remaining 19% of Donetsk region, ISW calculated.
That would be more than a year after Russia’s next State Duma elections, which are likely to be held in September 2031.
But ISW stressed that even this calculation should not be interpreted as a prediction that Russia will eventually capture the region.
The think tank said Russian forces must first fight through attritional urban battles in the Fortress Belt before attempting to advance across open fields – terrain where Russian troops have historically struggled to make progress.
Russia’s rate of advance has also slowed significantly across the battlefield since 2025, when it had already begun to decline.
Ukraine has demonstrated that it can contest the tactical initiative in several sectors of the frontline and disrupt Russian logistics in 2026, while Russia has struggled to counter those efforts.
“Neither the trajectory nor any likely dynamics of the current conflict suggest that Russian forces will be able soon to accelerate their rate of advance dramatically,” ISW said, provided Western support for Ukraine continues at roughly current levels.

Key player at bankrupt East Flemish chip manufacturer held for spying for China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:23:32 UTC
21:23:32 KST

A former key employee of the bankrupt chip manufacturer BelGaN in Oudenaarde (East Flanders) is in custody on suspicion of spying for China Francophone broadcaster RTBF and Flemish daily De Standaard have reported. The Federal Public Prosecutor’s Office has confirmed the news. The suspect is alleged to have passed on trade secrets concerning the production of so-called gallium nitride chips to a front company in China.
Key player at bankrupt East Flemish chip manufacturer held for spying for China
On 10 May, H.L. was detained at Brussels Airport just as he was about to fly back to the Chinese capital Beijing. The 52-year-old, who holds both Belgian and Chinese nationality, has been in custody ever since.
The allegations against him are serious: espionage, participation in a criminal organisation, misuse of company assets, and the unlawful disclosure of trade secrets.
The story begins with the bankruptcy of BelGaN in the summer of 2024. “New investors were sought. Various avenues were explored, but unfortunately without success,” was what was said at the time. 440 employees of the once-thriving chip company found themselves out of work.
However, the bankruptcy aroused suspicion and an investigation was launched. BelGaN had been taken over by Chinese investors a few years earlier. Investigators suspect that their aim was not to get the company back on track, but to get hold of its trade secrets.
A long track record
The site in Oudenaarde was established over 40 years ago and called MIETEC. It went on to become a flagship of Flemish technology. The company – the last industrial chip manufacturer in Belgium – specialised primarily in innovative gallium nitride chips. This technology is mainly used in electric vehicles, aerospace and the military sector.
When the company ran into financial difficulties, in February 2022 it was taken over by a consortium of Chinese investors. BelGaN’s new CEO, Alan Zhou Zhen, announced that he “saw an opportunity to launch a GaN valley in Europe”.
A few months after the takeover, Gankool was established in the Chinese province of Fujian. It is a company producing exactly the same technology as BelGaN. Gankool was financed by a Chinese investment fund.
Suspect, H.L., held a “senior research position” at BelGaN and is therefore believed to have held a senior position at the Chinese company as well.
Investigators suspect that H.L. therefore transferred BelGaN’s knowledge and know-how to Gankool. “The investigation may point to the unlawful transfer of specialised intellectual property and trade secrets relating to the production of gallium nitride chips abroad.”
“There are indications that the individual in question, who held a senior research position, was simultaneously serving as a director of a Chinese company engaged in a similar manufacturing activity,” the Belgian public prosecutor’s office says.
Investigators are also still searching for a second suspect in this case. According to the RTBF and De Standaard, that person is former CEO Alan Zhen Zhou.
The tactics of ‘front companies’
The Belgian intelligence services are familiar with the tactics of using so-called front companies to achieve industrial espionage. The latest annual report from the Belgian State Security Service explicitly warns against this.
“China realises that in some very specific areas it still lags behind Europe and the US in terms of technology. Closing that gap – and building a strategic lead – is the absolute top priority for the Chinese regime,” the report states.
One way of doing this is through ‘mirror companies’. “Chinese companies invest in Belgian companies, research centres or spin-offs, preferably in smaller entities that are developing promising technologies but are struggling with insufficient funding. In this way, they gain access to a particular technology. They then set up a mirror company in China that will produce the same technology on a larger scale. The parent company is subsequently sold off again, if possible, at a profit.”

Nausėda says AfD victory in German state election is disappointing and worrying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:20:00 UTC
21:20:00 KST

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda on Monday described the strong showing by Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, in a state election as disappointing and said the growing strength of populist forces was a cause for concern.
“I view it as a disappointment,” Nausėda told reporters at the Lithuanian parliament. “Unfortunately, it was probably a disappointment that could have been predicted, given the opinion polls and the mood in Germany.”
He said the result showed that foreign policy is far from the only factor influencing voters when they cast their ballots.
“The strengthening and entrenchment of populist forces in some German states is worrying,” Nausėda said. “And, without a doubt, it could also shift some of the political weight centres in national German politics in the coming years.”
The far-right AfD won a landslide victory Sunday in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt but fell short of the majority needed to form Germany’s first far-right state government since World War Two.
The result was also a major setback for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which had governed Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years.
Nausėda said he hoped Germany’s policy toward Lithuania would remain friendly and constructive.
“Merz and his government’s foreign policy has been very clearly recognisable,” Nausėda said. “It has been very consistent, with great empathy and support for Ukraine in its war against the aggressor Russia.”
He added that Germany’s policy toward Lithuania “has been, and I hope will remain in the future, very friendly and very constructive”.
Lithuania also expects Germany and Lithuania to honour commitments they have made to each other, Nausėda said.
Migration and EU finances
Nausėda said the rise of populist forces could lead to changes in Germany’s national political balance, but some of those changes could be positive.
He said he hoped the result would strengthen support for a tougher European migration policy and make discussions on migration more constructive within the European Council and other EU institutions.
But he warned that other consequences could be less welcome, including stronger opposition in Germany to increasing its contribution to the European Union’s next long-term budget.
“I am afraid that after these elections, voices arguing that Germany should contribute less to the common European finances could become stronger,” Nausėda said. “Let’s simply be realistic.”
He said Lithuania would continue working to secure an ambitious EU budget, although that would become more difficult.
The AfD, which has repeatedly campaigned against immigration and is widely viewed as sympathetic to Russia, won 44% of the vote in Sunday’s election. It fell three seats short of an absolute majority.
Forming the first state government in the party’s 13-year history would represent its biggest political achievement. The result came amid widespread dissatisfaction with Germany’s national government and continuing concerns about the country’s sluggish economy.

From rainwater to figs: Estahban’s tradition of sustainable cultivation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:19:54 UTC
21:19:54 KST

From rainwater to figs: Estahban’s tradition of sustainable cultivation
Fars province in southern Iran, home to more than 75% of the country’s fig cultivars and around 17% of the world’s, is one of the most important centers of rainfed fig production.
Among its key regions, Estahban holds a special place, with approximately 2.6 million fig trees cultivated across 25,950 hectares, making it one of the world’s leading centers for rainfed fig production.
For more than 250 years, Estahban’s gardeners have passed down their knowledge and experience from one generation to the next. Their expertise in traditional fig cultivation, combined with innovative water-management practices, has helped sustain the region’s orchards in a challenging, water-scarce environment.
Their unique methods for capturing and efficiently using rainwater not only improve water use but also help protect the soil, reduce erosion, and maintain the long-term sustainability of the orchards.
These traditional yet sustainable practices show the important contribution of Estahban’s gardeners to preserving and continuing the development of rainfed fig production, both in Iran and around the world.
Rainfed fig cultivation plays a vital economic and social role in the region, providing livelihoods for thousands of families, directly and indirectly, and even providing food for both domestic and wild animals. Communities from the county’s main city regularly spend a month or more in the fig gardens each year, helping to pick the fruit.

Evaluation: Finnfund and Finnpartnership play a key role in delivering Finland’s international goals
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
15:19:51 EEST
21:19:51 KST

Evaluation: Finnfund and Finnpartnership play a key role in delivering Finland’s international goals
According to a recently published independent evaluation, the Finnish development financier and impact investor Finnfund and the Finnpartnership programme are key instruments for advancing Finland's development policy objectives and international economic relations. They also support Finnish companies in entering and expanding in emerging markets. The evaluation concludes that maintaining their impact will require adequate public funding and continued development.
Finnfund is a state-owned development finance institution, which invests in responsible companies operating in developing countries. Finnpartnership is a business partnership programme funded by the Ministry for Foreign Affairs and managed by Finnfund. The programme connects Finnish companies with actors in developing countries and promotes long-term, sustainable business operations. Covering the period 2019–2025, the evaluation examines the effectiveness and performance of the activities of Finnfund and Finnpartnership and how well they align with policy objectives.
A unique and effective financier
The evaluation shows that Finnfund is a unique actor for the Finnish government: it effectively finances sustainable business in developing countries, attracts private investments and operates on a financially self-sustaining basis. During this government term the State’s ownership policy has guided Finnfund to strengthen cooperation between Finnish companies and actors in emerging markets. Finnfund has introduced new operating models to advance this objective, such as matching its investee companies’ needs with Finnish companies’ offering.
Finnfund is regarded as a reliable and respected partner, whose strength lies in its strong focus on sustainability and responsible business practices. However, the growth of its operations is constrained by the relatively low level of state funding and its high level of indebtedness. The evaluation recommends that the Finnish government strengthen Finnfund’s capital base. It also recommends placing a stronger emphasis on profitability, in line with the State’s ownership policy and the company’s strategy. In recent years, guarantees provided by the EU have proved to be an important tool for Finnfund to fulfil its development impact mandate. These guarantees have allowed Finnfund to take on greater risk while maintaining the financial sustainability of its operations.
The Finnpartnership Business Partnership Programme is an important instrument especially for SMEs seeking to expand internationally. There is strong demand for the programme's services and a need to expand the programme, according to the evaluation. Opportunities related to the reconstruction of Ukraine have increased companies’ interest in the programme. The evaluation also highlights areas for improvement: application processes should be significantly simplified and accelerated, and funding targeted more clearly towards companies with strong growth potential.
Cooperation has intensified, yet a gap remains in the financing chain
According to the evaluation, Finnfund and Finnpartnership have intensified their cooperation. Despite this, a significant financing gap remains: Finnpartnership supports the early stages of projects, whereas Finnfund's investment volume is many times larger.
Both instruments have a key role in the Team Finland network and in implementing the EU's Global Gateway initiative. This offers opportunities to further enhance Finland’s international impact and role in promoting sustainable business globally.
“This evaluation shows that Finnish actors play a prominent role in promoting sustainable business and development impacts in emerging markets. However, we must ensure that the financing and support systems better aid Finnish companies in growing and expanding their business abroad,” says Juha Savolainen, Director General of the Department for Development Policy.
“We will use the recommendations to better align these instruments with the needs of companies. We are currently reforming the Act on Finnfund. The Government proposal on the Act will proceed to Parliament for consideration,” Savolainen says.

American nuclear attack submarine arrives in Scotland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:12:39 BST
21:12:39 KST

US Navy submarine spotted arriving at Faslane in Scotland for a routine port visit.
A United States Navy Virginia class attack submarine was spotted running on the surface in the Firth of Clyde on the morning of Monday 7 September.
Sightings of this kind are a familiar part of daily life on both sides of the firth. His Majesty’s Naval Base Clyde at Faslane, on the Gare Loch, is the home of the Royal Navy’s submarine service, and the associated armaments depot at Coulport sits on Loch Long a short distance away. Boats entering or leaving the base must pass down the Gare Loch and out through the firth, which brings them within clear view of Dunoon, Gourock, Cloch Point and the surrounding coastline for a considerable stretch of the transit.
The Virginia class is the backbone of the United States Navy’s attack submarine force, a nuclear-powered design built for anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare, land attack with the Tomahawk cruise missile, special operations support and intelligence gathering. Boats of the class have visited the Clyde on a high number of occasions in recent years, and the base is one of a small number of locations in Europe capable of supporting visiting American nuclear submarines alongside.
Surface transits are the norm in these confined and comparatively shallow waters, and the routing takes submarines past some of the most heavily populated coastline in the west of Scotland. As readers will know, that combination has made the Clyde one of the most productive stretches of water in the country for anyone with an interest in naval movements, and community pages in Dunoon, Helensburgh and Inverclyde routinely carry photographs and video of departures and arrivals taken from front windows and hillside paths.
Visits by allied submarines to Faslane are not announced in advance, and neither the Royal Navy nor the United States Navy routinely comments on the movements of individual boats. Port calls of this kind allow for maintenance, stores and crew rest, and they also form part of the wider pattern of American submarine operations in the eastern Atlantic and the waters to the north of Scotland, an area that has drawn steadily greater attention from NATO navies over the past decade.
Movements through the firth are supported by Royal Navy police and Ministry of Defence marine units, and small craft are frequently seen accompanying boats on passage. The waters around the base and the approaches to it are subject to restrictions on the approach of other vessels, and mariners operating in the area are advised of movements through the usual navigational channels.
Work has continued in recent years to expand and modernise the facilities at Faslane under the programme to consolidate the submarine flotilla on the Clyde, covering waterfront infrastructure, engineering support and accommodation, and the base remains one of the largest single employment sites in Scotland.

Curfew hours in Kyiv will be reduced by an hour starting at midnight on Thursday, Sept. 10, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Klitschko wrote on Monday that public transportation will also run an extra hour to accommodate the new schedule.
“These changes will come into effect from 00:00 on September 10. Accordingly, the working hours of public transport in the capital will be extended by 1 hour,” Klitschko wrote in his Telegram update.

Preserving the past: Kyrgyzstan's World Nomad Games continues as new village brings history to life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:10:01 UTC
21:10:01 KST

Kyrgyzstan's World Nomad Games have brought the past firmly into the present with its plans to make permanent a village dedicated to its traditional arts and crafts.
The World Nomad Games may be over for another year but the impact of the event is likely to echo throughout Central Asia for some time.
After the grand opening at Kyrgyzstan's Bishkek Arena, the games and more than 3,000 athletes from 110 nations moved to a lake-side venue in the Isyk Kul region, a popular tourist destination.
Traditional equestrian and archery skills filled every corner of the Kyrchyn Gorge, as competitors pitted their wits and strengths against each other, giving visitors a lookback in time travelling experience at an ancient style settlement.
Village people
Each region of the Kyrgyz Republic built their own village by erecting age-old nomadic dwellings and yurts, all traditionally decorated.
Yurts - tent-like structures with wooden framework covered with felt, animal skins and heavy canvas - have been used by Asian nomadic tribes for millennia. A yurt houses a single nuclear family who can assemble and disassemble it in about half an hour, making it suitable for nomadic lifestyle.
Among the decorated yurts, people from all parts of Kyrgyzstan, dressed in traditional colourful costumes, displayed their works of folk art, alongside handicraft like embroidery and carpet-weaving.
During the first two days, more than 150,000 visitors were treated to traditional songs and folk tunes and offered the chance to taste national dishes often prepared right on the spot.
The attraction, named “The Universe of Nomads”, was opened with a theatrical performance on a hillside that included a dramatic village raid where horsemen and women amazed the crowds by showing off extremely impressive defensive riding skills.
At the opening, Kyrgyz Prime Minister Adylbek Kasymaliyev, said that the village would not be a one-off. The plan is for it to remain open as a tourist attraction and help educate visitors about the country's past.
“We do not preserve the heritage of our ancestors only behind the museum glass – we are bringing it back into the people’s lives. We build yurts today – that is a living heritage," said Kasymaliyev.
"We are raising shyrdaks, smelting metal, making horse tack – that is a living heritage. The craftsmanship of the father passes onto the son, the skills of the mother to the daughter,” he added.
Bone crush bonaza
Opposite the village, a reconstruction of an ancient fort houses a bazaar where one can enjoy the atmosphere of an ancient town bustling with activity and acrobats performing high jinks.
Right next to the fort, Nomad games athletes were engaged in archery and strength games, such as tug of war and arm-wrestling and the more unusual sport of bone crushing.
In this Mongolian and Central Asian popular game participants show their strength by breaking the back bones of animals (not live ones). It is frequent sight at festivals and folk fairs. This year, the Mongolian world champion managed to defend his title with 58 bones crushed in a minute.
Whille the World Nomad Games aim to promote nomadic heritage, culture and influence on different civilisations, they are usually accompanied by scientific and cultural events. This year, the highlight among dozens of such events was the International Scientific Conference “Nomadic Civilisations: Heritage, Paradigms and Prospects”.
“Nomadic civilisation represents a vast body of humanity’s historical experience, knowledge and cultural practices," said Gylzat Isamatova, Kyrgystan's Minister of High Education. "Today, its study is particularly relevant in the context of climate change, environmental challenges, the sustainable use of natural resources and the preservation of cultural heritage.”

Bolsonaro son to hold rallies as Brazil court crisis offers opening against Lula
SAO PAULO, Sept 7 - Brazil's opposition is set to take to the streets on Independence Day on Monday, as right-wing presidential hopeful Senator Flavio Bolsonaro seeks to capitalize on a crisis engulfing the country's Supreme Court to bolster his campaign against President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva ahead of next month's election.
Organizers have cast the rally as a protest against Lula's government and Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, whose aggressive pursuit of former President Jair Bolsonaro, the senator's father, over a coup plot that led to the former president's conviction has made him one of Brazil's most polarizing figures.
The main protest on Paulista Avenue, Sao Paulo's most traditional stage for political demonstrations, comes at a politically sensitive moment as opinion polls show the senator running neck and neck with leftist Lula.
"We have a commitment to Brazil. Out Lula! Out Moraes! Independence and our freedom must be defended," Senator Bolsonaro said in a social media post calling supporters to Paulista Avenue.
"We are the last obstacle preventing Brazil from becoming a dictatorship," he added in a separate post.
FOLLOWING IN HIS FATHER'S FOOTSTEPS
The senator is following in his father's footsteps, frequently invoking Independence Day and other patriotic symbols to rally support for what he portrays as a struggle against a corrupt political establishment.
The senator has so far struggled to mobilize the tens of thousands his father used to attract in his defense, but this time the demonstration follows an unprecedented conflict between justices that has engulfed Brazil's Supreme Court and raised difficult questions about Moraes' conduct.
The feud erupted after Justice Andre Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee, disclosed a report raising questions about alleged contacts between Moraes and a banker accused of leading a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme, prompting calls for an investigation of the justice.
Moraes responded by seeking an investigation into Mendonca for alleged abuse of authority.
A large turnout on Monday could strengthen calls for investigations into Moraes.
The controversy could also provide a boost to Flavio Bolsonaro, who has argued that his father, currently under house arrest and barred from running for office, is the victim of political persecution by Moraes.
"Brazil has a unique opportunity to remove Alexandre de Moraes from the Supreme Court," said former lawmaker Eduardo Bolsonaro, the senator's brother.
Lula, meanwhile, is expected to attend the annual Independence Day military parade in Brasilia, maintaining a tradition observed by Brazilian presidents. REUTERS

"Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries," a spokesperson for the bloc said in a statement.

Inside the 'academic apartheid' silencing Palestinians in Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:06:24 UTC
21:06:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Inside the 'academic apartheid' silencing Palestinian students in Israel
Palestinian citizens of Israel studying at Israeli universities are being pushed to self-censor and, in some cases, abandon their studies after being punished for expressions of Palestinian identity and opposition to Israel's genocide in Gaza, a lawyer who represented many of the students has told The New Arab.
Lubna Tuma, an attorney with Palestinian rights group Adalah, said universities had subjected Palestinian students to disciplinary proceedings in which they were effectively treated as supporters of "terrorism" unless they could prove otherwise, while similar restrictions were not imposed on Jewish-Israeli students.
"Freedom of expression is supposed to be a foundational, universal principle of academic life, for all students," Tuma, who co-authored a new report on the crackdown, told The New Arab.
"In Israeli academia, it plays quite the opposite role: institutions have turned themselves into bodies policing private political expression, deciding which expressions of identity, religion, solidarity, and criticism are legitimate, and which are not."
Adalah's report, Apartheid in Israeli Academia: Palestinian Students After 7 October 2023, found that Israeli universities and colleges had effectively established two disciplinary systems based on students' ethno-national identity, which the rights group says amounts to apartheid within higher education.
The group received 132 inquiries from Palestinian students at around 40 institutions and provided legal representation or advice in 100 cases after universities began taking action over social media posts following the 7 October 2023 attacks and the start of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
More than 60% of those who approached Adalah were suspended before any determination of wrongdoing, while 20 students were either permanently expelled or suspended for between one and five years. Of 78 disciplinary cases examined, 52 resulted in convictions.
The posts targeted were not limited to statements about the 7 October attacks. Criticism of Israel's government, military or war on Gaza, prayers and Quranic verses, images of Palestinian identity and expressions of concern about Gaza's humanitarian catastrophe all triggered proceedings.
In some cases, merely "liking" a post, displaying the Palestinian flag or the word "Palestine", sharing a news report or posting a prayer for Palestinians in Gaza was enough to prompt a complaint.
"What that produces isn't just individual punishment, it's a chilling effect across the whole Palestinian student population," Tuma said.
‘Humiliation by design’
Tuma, who represented many of the students before disciplinary committees, described the hearings as "humiliation by design", saying students entered them treated as if they were "a traitor or enemy from the outset".
"These processes carried a deep personal, emotional, and psychological cost," Tuma said. "The committees' starting assumption was often that the student supported terrorism and required the student to actively disprove it."
The report documented cases in which students were not shown the posts behind complaints, universities relied on automatic translations of Arabic prayers and Quranic verses, and students were required to defend themselves against content they had not published.
Adalah said the result was a reversal of the usual burden of proof, with Palestinian students forced to demonstrate that their speech did not amount to support for "terror". In some cases, university proceedings continued and ended in convictions even when law enforcement authorities found no basis to pursue criminal charges.
Tuma described the proceedings as "sham processes from start to finish", saying some students chose not to appeal because of the anxiety caused by the process, while others abandoned their studies in Israel and pursued education abroad.
Some universities also reported their own Palestinian students to Israeli police, leading in certain cases to criminal investigations and arrests. Tuma said the University of Haifa was the first to suspend at least one Palestinian student after 7 October and filed a criminal complaint against one student.
The crackdown was encouraged by the Israeli government. Days after the 7 October attacks, the education minister demanded universities suspend students, report them to the Council for Higher Education and police, and expedite disciplinary proceedings. Jewish-Israeli student unions, campus political groups and outside organisations also monitored Palestinian students' social media posts and reported them to university administrations.
‘A completely different set of rules’
Adalah found a starkly different approach towards Jewish-Israeli students. Universities largely preserved protections for their political expression, including in cases involving extreme speech, while the report said institutions ignored widespread calls for the annihilation and genocide of Palestinians in Gaza and racist posts targeting Palestinian citizens and students.
For Palestinian students, by contrast, universities expanded their disciplinary reach beyond campus and into private political expression, according to the report.
"This is why we speak of apartheid. It is a completely different set of rules, applied on the basis of students' ethno-national identity," Tuma said.
"This can't be addressed case by case. Freedom of speech is an absolute precondition of academic life, not a privilege granted to some students and withheld from others."
Adalah said the crackdown has consequences beyond those formally disciplined, creating a "chilling effect" in which Palestinian students increasingly censor themselves and feel less secure or welcome on Israeli campuses.

North Korea Commissions Kang Kon Destroyer That Capsized During 2025 Launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:05:48 UTC
21:05:48 KST

North Korea has commissioned the Kang Kon destroyer into its navy, following its capsizing during an unsuccessful launch attempt last year.
The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported on this.
The commissioning ceremony took place on September 6 at the port of Wonsan on North Korea’s east coast. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attended the event.
The destroyer is the second Choe Hyon-class warship and is going to join the Korean People’s Navy East Sea Fleet.
Despite being officially commissioned only now, the ship has already been used to demonstrate its combat capabilities. In early July 2026, it carried out a mass missile launch.
In addition to the missile launches, North Korean state media showed the ship’s onboard artillery systems firing.
In May 2025, during the ceremony to launch the ship from the slipway, the destroyer lost stability and tipped onto its side, damaging its hull.
The accident was captured in satellite imagery. North Korean state media also confirmed it.
Kim Jong Un, who attended the launch ceremony, said the accident was caused by negligence and irresponsibility that could be regarded as a criminal act.
He ordered the ship’s restoration to be completed by the June plenary meeting of the Workers’ Party of Korea and those responsible for shortcomings in its design and construction to be held accountable.
Following the failed launch, North Korean authorities arrested four officials, including the chief engineer, construction manager, and project administrative manager. They also detained Ri Hyong-son, a member of the Central Military Commission, whom the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) identified as one of the officials primarily responsible for the accident.
As early as June 2, 2025, satellite imagery captured the ship being raised while in an upright position.
On June 5, the destroyer was successfully launched and sent to a shipyard in Rajin for repairs. On June 8, the ship was moved into a dry dock to complete the restoration work.
The 5,000-ton Choe Hyon-class warships are multi-purpose missile destroyers of the Korean People’s Army Navy. They are equipped with two types of vertical launch systems: larger for strike weapons and smaller for air defense missiles. The ships have a total of 74 launch cells.
The ship’s artillery armament includes a 127 mm automatic gun, as well as a close-in weapon system that visually resembles the Soviet 30 mm AK-230 and AK-630 systems.
A North Korean anti-aircraft gun system located at the stern provides the ship’s air defense. Its appearance resembles that of the Russian Pantsir-M.
The anti-ship and strike weapons are housed in transport-launch containers on both sides of the ship. They likely include eight Hwasal-2 cruise missiles capable of engaging moving targets. In addition, each side is equipped with four launchers for a North Korean equivalent of the Spike ER/NLOS missiles.
Militarnyi previously reported that North Korean authorities had instructed shipbuilders to construct a new Choe Hyon-class destroyer within one year.

EXCLUSIVE: Nigerian government and Boko Haram strike secret ceasefire deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:02:33 UTC
21:02:33 KST

Share & more
A ceasefire agreement with the jihadist group Boko Haram has been in effect for the past three months and is expected to be extended, but has not been previously reported publicly, The New Humanitarian has learned.
The agreement is linked to hostage negotiations that secured the release in June of 360 civilians abducted by the group from Ngoshe village, in the foothills of the Mandara mountains on the border with Cameroon. The mass kidnapping occurred in March during a Boko Haram attack on a nearby army base.
Three people with contacts among Boko Haram members, some of them senior figures, independently told The New Humanitarian that a truce had been in effect since June and was likely to be extended for a further 40 days. Communities in the Ngoshe area – regular victims of Boko Haram predation – say attacks have stopped since the ceasefire, according to two of the sources.
The deal that freed the villagers also reportedly included a ransom payment of five billion naira ($3.7 million) by the government, a transaction Abuja has denied amid controversy over the alleged misappropriation of some of the money.
The New Humanitarian reached out to spokespeople for the government, defence headquarters, and the army to verify reports of a ceasefire, but received no reply prior to publishing.
What remains unclear is the longer-term significance of any agreement. “It could be just a temporary, tactical ceasefire that benefits both sides, but doesn’t really affect the trajectory of the war,” said conflict researcher Malik Samuel. “I don’t think it’s a step towards a sustainable peace settlement.”
The deal does not involve so-called Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), an offshoot and rival to Boko Haram, based on the islands of Lake Chad and a rural swathe of northeastern Borno State. Clashes have continued between the two groups.
After 17 years of a war that has indirectly cost close to 350,000 civilian lives, the idea of negotiations with Boko Haram – officially Jama’at Ahl al Sunna li Da’wa wal Jihad (JAS) – and other armed groups sharply divides Nigerians. Those living closest to the conflict tend to be far more supportive of dialogue than the rest of the country.
However, the government’s public position is an emphatic rejection of talks with a group legally proscribed as a terrorist organisation.
President Bola Tinubu has instead announced the beefing up of an overstretched army – an initiative related to elections early next year in which public safety will be a key issue. The promised 30,000 new recruits and four extra divisions will provide the “teeth that are needed to defeat terrorism and banditry”, Tinubu said in July.
Nevertheless, behind the scenes, “the government seems very interested in having a dialogue with Boko Haram, perhaps realising a military response alone is inadequate to resolving the problem,” noted Samuel.
“Both sides believe a settlement is possible”
Since the Boko Haram insurgency began in 2009, there has been a long if faltering history of under the radar dialogue approaches, according to security officials, diplomats, and mediators, who spoke to The New Humanitarian on the condition of anonymity so they could talk freely.
“Both sides believe a settlement is possible,” a diplomat with knowledge of the chronology of contacts told The New Humanitarian. “For all parties, a non-kinetic [military] approach is intellectually acceptable. But they still believe that by improving their military situations they can influence those negotiations.”
Those talks have been led on the government’s side by the Office of the National Security Advisor and the spy agency, the Department of State Services. They have repeatedly failed, typically scuppered by spoilers within the government and military, forcing the parties to rebuild confidence each time.
Historically, “we’ve negotiated a couple of ceasefires but they couldn’t be maintained,” said a government security official with knowledge of the dialogue process. “The last hudna [armistice] was in the 2022/2023 period but it also collapsed.”
The current agreement may suffer the same fate. Two sources who told The New Humanitarian about the deal warned that Boko Haram may be using the ceasefire to strengthen its position, potentially by moving “equipment” into the Mandera mountains.
Who’s who
Boko Haram is headed by Ibrahim Bakura Doro, the overall commander and imam (religious leader), based on the islands on the northern section of Lake Chad, on the Niger Republic border.
Boko Haram has three factions, all of which have sworn allegiance to Bakura: Darul Gazwa, operating in southeastern Borno and headed by Alhai Kale; the Sadiku group of Abubakar Sadiku Saidu, active around north-central Nigeria; and the Ali Ngulde faction, which carried out the Ngoshe kidnappings.
The success of the ceasefire depends on whether Bakura, from his Lake Chad base thousands of kilometres away, can yoke the three other Boko Haram commanders into a sustainable deal.
Rival ISWAP is operationally and organisationally distinct from Boko Haram, its jihadist cousin. While Boko Haram survives on looting and extorting civilians – a practice known as ghanima – plundering is banned by ISWAP.
Boko Haram is also more locally focused whereas ISWAP – among the most active of so-called Islamic State-Central’s franchises – is loyal to the transnational “caliphate”, which effectively hands IS-Central veto power over any dialogue initiative, according to people familiar with the group.
“ISWAP needs buy-in from IS. They make the final decision,” a rehabilitated former ISWAP commander told The New Humanitarian. “But Bakura needs money, you can make a deal with him.”
Money is not just an inducement but also a practical requirement. “Any arrangement involves a payment, otherwise how would they eat as there would be no ghanima?” explained the Abuja-based security official.
Buying off opponents has also been the traditional approach of the Nigerian political establishment, from ending the insurgency in the oil-rich Delta in 2009, to ongoing attempts to try and contain bandit violence in the northwest.
However, such a transactional arrangement can be a negative incentive, creating a demand for more. “If you give them money, that doesn’t guarantee peace,” cautioned a former Boko Haram hostage negotiator.
“Do a deal with one, to fight the other”
Yet the scenario the security establishment would most welcome – and see as tantalisingly plausible – is if dialogue could then lead to an alliance with Bakura against ISWAP: “To do a deal with one, to fight the other.”
ISWAP is the most lethal of the jihadi insurgents. It is centralised, bureaucratic, and well-funded, with a tax base that far outstrips the revenue Borno State earns.
It has also proven tactically adaptable, technologically advanced, and its combat successes have attracted experienced fighters and instructors from across the Sahel and North African Maghreb.
The failure of the Nigerian navy to undertake a meaningful lake-based offensive – which would involve navigating through a complex and changing ecology of swamps, channels, and islands – means ISWAP’s bases are relatively safe.
“They are only nervous about the [air force] bombing, but every house has a shelter,” said Abu Jabir, a farmer who lives in ISWAP-controlled territory but comes to Maiduguri to buy fishing gear.
Bakura, however, is seen as a persistent danger to ISWAP. “Bakura people are always attacking: They are powerful, they know how to fight on the water,” he explained.
Bakura holds a particular animosity towards ISWAP. When Boko Haram split in 2016 (see timeline), he remained loyal to the group’s then leader and imam, Abubaker Shekau, who rewarded him with significant autonomy.
But in 2021, ISWAP managed to overrun Shekau’s Sambisa Forest base in southern Borno, and Shekau detonated a suicide vest.
“For Bakura, it’s personal,” said Samuel. “Former Bakura fighters have told me that he prefers to attack ISWAP rather than the military. Even if he attacks military bases, it's to get weapons to attack ISWAP.”

Ratko Mladic buried in Serbia with no state honors (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

Mass Serbian public demonstrations mark Ratko Mladic burial (VIDEOS)
Thousands of people gathered in Belgrade on Monday to pay their respects to former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic before his burial, which took place without formal state or military honors.
Supporters carrying Serbian flags and photographs of Mladic gathered outside the Church of St. Luke, where his coffin was displayed ahead of the funeral service. He was later buried beside his daughter at a nearby cemetery.
Mladic commanded Bosnian Serb forces during the 1992-1995 war that broke up Yugoslavia. In 2017, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) convicted him of genocide for targeting Bosnian Muslims, Croats and other groups.
Mladic died in The Hague on August 27 at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence.
His remains were returned to Serbia last week on a government plane. Serbian soldiers carried the coffin from the aircraft, which was then escorted through Belgrade. A separate commemoration was held on Saturday at the House of the Serbian Army.
Despite the convictions, Mladic has remained a respected figure among some Serbs, who view him as a wartime defender of the Bosnian Serb population. Many also share longstanding complaints that international courts have treated crimes against Serbs differently from those committed by Serb forces during the Yugoslav wars.
Public tributes to Mladic have also spread to football stadiums. The normally fierce rivalry between Crvena Zvezda (Red Star) and Partizan Belgrade was set aside at the Serbian capital’s derby over the weekend as both sets of fans chanted Mladic’s name, before a giant tifo bearing his image was unveiled. Crvena Zvezda fans also chanted in Mladic’s honor during a Europa League match last month, prompting UEFA to fine the club €90,000 ($105,000). Bosnia’s FK Borac Banjaluka was also fined €39,500 over similar chants and other fan offenses.
🫡
🔴⚪️ #fkczpic.twitter.com/n0IwG1NDTu
Justice Minister Nenad Vujic had initially suggested that Mladic would receive state honors, however, the final funeral arrangements included no artillery salute, ceremonial military presence, or attendance by senior Serbian officials.
The commemorations have nevertheless prompted strong criticism from Brussels. EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a planned visit to Serbia, saying the “glorification” surrounding Mladic’s death was “incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built.” She also warned that Belgrade’s handling of the funeral could affect Serbia’s membership bid.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic rejected the criticism, arguing that Brussels had failed to identify any concrete act of “glorification” by the Serbian authorities, and called Kos’ statement “stupid, as usual.”
“I suppose we should ban people from showing up, ban the funeral,” he said.
Vucic had earlier said Serbia would help Mladic’s family arrange a “dignified” burial and criticized The Hague for refusing repeated Serbian requests to allow the former general to return home as his health deteriorated.
The president did not attend Monday’s funeral, citing a previously scheduled visit by Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.
