====================================================================================================

Germany's shocking far-right surge rattles Europe's political foundations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
11:58:49 UTC
20:58:49 KST

AfD's landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt could be the prelude to far-right forces governing alone across Europe. Germany's 'grand coalition' model, and the centrist alliance underpinning EU politics, are starting to crack.
The radical-right Alternative for Germany's landslide victory in the Saxony-Anhalt region election may be the first real crack in the power structure that has held European politics together since the Second World War.
On Sunday, Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a resounding victory in the eastern German region, taking 43.8% of the vote. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which leads the governing coalition in Berlin, collapsed to 17.2%, while its junior coalition partner, the Social Democrats (SPD), managed just 9.3%.
For the first time since the Nazi period, a German region could be led by a far-right force, as local leader Ulrich Siegmund could become president if the far-left party BSW decides to support him or to abstain in the election.
Beyond dealing a further blow to an already deeply unpopular government in Berlin, the results drew mixed reactions across Europe, with far-right forces eager to capitalise as key EU states head to the polls next year.
"This result is not an outlier - it is a signal to the rest of Germany and to Europe," René Aust, the head of the AfD delegation to the European Parliament, told Euronews.
"We are on course to become the country's leading governing party, and I am convinced that at the next European elections we will return to the European Parliament with more than twice our current strength," Aust said.
European repercussions
"The region Saxony-Anhalt is a small part of Germany. 1 out of 16 regions," Andreas Schwab (Germany/EPP) said, playing down the impact of the vote. "The [AfD] party has no real power in Berlin, where the great coalition has a clear majority."
For Schwab, the vote's impact in Brussels will likely be limited to reinforcing the EU's simplification agenda — cutting red tape, including for farmers — and pushing for a more nationally oriented EU budget.
Svenja Hahn (Germany/Renew) echoed that view. "We can only hold up a democratic majority in 2029 by finally delivering on economic growth and prosperity and taking the regulatory burden off of people and businesses," she said.
Still, the result is bound to raise alarm bells across Europe, not just for its impact on German domestic politics, butbecause Germany’s grand-coalition tradition provided a foundation for the political consensus at the heart of European integration for much of the postwar era.
The centre-right European People's Party (EPP) and centre-left Socialists and Democrats (S&D) have been the linchpin of Brussels politics since the European Parliament was created, at times with the support of the centrist Renew Europe group.
But the rise of extremist parties and the steady erosion of the political centre is now calling that approach — born in Germany, exported to Brussels — into question. Last month, Europe Elects projected that the three centrist forces would, for the first time, fail to secure an absolute majority if European Parliament elections were held today.
"It is no more about who can speak with whom and how different factions of democratic society can unite. It is about how to get their joint share larger, not by stealing the electorate from one another, but by convincing those who are disappointed by all of us, democrats," MEP Sergey Lagodinsky (Germany/Greens-EFA) told Euronews.
Far-right into power
The AfD's growing electoral gains across Europe have raised the prospect that far-right parties could enter government outright. In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD fell short of a majority to govern alone but could reach one in coalition with the BSW.
How much power-sharing traditional parties allow has depended on national context, and on whether mainstream forces are willing to ally with the far right.
In Italy, for instance, Giorgia Meloni has steered her coalition government towards the centre, making her European party, the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR), increasingly mainstream. As a result, she now faces competition from a new far-right force led by Roberto Vannacci (Italy/ESN), a former army general turned MEP.
In Spain, the centre-right Popular Party has partnered with the hard-right Vox to govern several regions, including Andalusia and Castilla y León, a model some would like to see exported to Brussels.
"In each country, it really depends on how radical the far right is and how much there can be any kind of collaboration. But, in general, collaboration with the far right was not good for us. We have stayed weak," MEP Hildegard Bentele (Germany/EPP) told Euronews.
Within the European Parliament, the EPP group led by the Bavarian Manfred Weber has throughout this legislative term kept a flexible approach to forming variable majorities, at times seeking support from hard-right parties over specific files.
While Weber's strategy has strengthened the EPP's negotiating hand and drawn the ire of other centrist forces, moving from case-by-case alignment to a more structural alliance would entail a fundamental reshaping of power-sharing at the EU level.
As of now, Weber has always excluded structured cooperation with far-right forces, while some parties forming the EPP have often wished for it.
Elections loom
In 2027, voters in France, Italy, Poland, Spain, Estonia, Greece, Finland, Malta and Slovenia will all go to the polls in high-stakes national elections. In France, in particular, far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen is projected to win against any other candidate in the run-off.
These upcoming elections will reshape Europe's political landscape ahead of the next EU elections in 2029, which, if current trends hold, could be the first not to hand mainstream parties a governing majority.
"[The Saxony-Anhalt election] It's a very strong warning signal, but we have three years ahead of elections, so we have a lot of time to become stronger again. The warning signal is out. We have to work on our own strengths," Bentele said.
Bentele drew two main lessons from the results: the need to mobilise people who had not voted in the last elections — the main driver of the AfD's surge — and the need to choose better-suited candidates.
Meanwhile, Aust noted that only voters over 70 kept the AfD from securing an absolute majority at the regional level, which he considers clear evidence that the future belongs to patriotic forces and that the CDU will soon become "the party of yesterday," as was the case for Democrazia Cristiana in Italy.
For Lagodinsky, the challenge ahead is nothing less than restoring disappointed voters' faith in liberal democracy. "If we don't get our act together on that, our democracy is doomed," he concluded.

China Focus: China's top court sets rules for AI deepfakes and other disputes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
19:58:48 CST
20:58:48 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- A familiar face on a video call may not be what it seems. Artificial intelligence (AI) can now replicate people's faces and voices with startling realism, creating new challenges for the law. China's top court on Monday issued guidelines spelling out when such AI-generated content can lead to legal liability.
The guidelines, released by the Supreme People's Court (SPC), address a range of emerging disputes, including AI deepfakes and voice cloning, algorithmic price discrimination and AI-generated false information.
They make clear that people cannot use AI to create or distribute recognizable digital replicas of others without their consent, including cloned faces and voices. Such use constitutes an infringement of individuals' rights, while using AI-generated faces or voices to spread false claims or damage someone's reputation can also result in legal liability.
China has already addressed such issues in court. In April 2024, the Beijing Internet Court ruled in the country's first AI-generated voice infringement case that using AI to recreate a person's identifiable voice without their consent can infringe upon their rights.
The new rules come as AI-generated impersonation becomes increasingly easy to create and difficult to distinguish from authentic content. A handful of photographs or a short voice recording can provide enough material to produce a convincing digital replica.
The guidelines also address algorithmic discrimination against consumers. Businesses that use algorithms to offer different prices or other transaction terms for the same goods or services without reasonable justification may be held liable if the practice causes harm to consumers.
"We cannot expect every consumer to become an expert at spotting deception. The law must step in promptly to protect consumers' legitimate rights and interests," said Zhou Jiahai, head of the research office of the SPC.
Another challenge is that generative AI systems can produce false or inaccurate information, commonly known as "AI hallucinations."
AI service providers can be held liable if they are notified that their systems have generated content that infringes a person's rights but fail to take timely action.
Users, too, can be held responsible for how they use AI. Anyone who deliberately uses prompts or other methods to induce an AI system to generate infringing content that harms others can be held liable.
The guidelines also provide a way for people to seek swift protection when AI-generated content threatens to cause serious and irreversible harm. For example, someone whose face has been digitally altered and used to spread false and defamatory sexual claims may ask a court for an injunction if waiting to act could cause harm that would be difficult to repair later.
As AI advances, governments worldwide are grappling with the challenge of encouraging innovation while also protecting people from potential harm.
China has taken a series of steps to address the challenges posed by AI. In September 2025, it put into effect measures governing the labeling of AI-generated and synthesized content. The SPC's latest guidelines set out how courts should handle AI-related disputes, adding to China's evolving legal framework for AI. ■

PARIS, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- France's wine production in 2026 is estimated at nearly 34 million hectoliters, down 6 percent from 2025 and 17 percent from the 2021-2025 average, according to the estimates released Monday by the French Ministry of Agriculture.
The decline is attributed to both a reduction in the area under vine production and lower yields affected by weather conditions, particularly drought and heatwaves during the summer, the Agriculture Ministry's statistics service Agreste said.
According to Agreste, the situation varies significantly across wine-growing regions. In Champagne in northeastern France, production is expected to fall by half from 2025 and the 2021-2025 average. In Languedoc-Roussillon in southern France, the harvest is forecast to increase by 5 percent from 2025, but remain 8 percent below the 2021-2025 average.
The pressure on vineyards is part of a broader impact of extreme weather on French agriculture and the economy. At a crisis meeting devoted to drought on Aug. 12, French Minister for Ecological Transition Monique Barbut said this summer's heatwaves could cost the French economy between 10 billion and 15 billion euros (11.6 billion to 17.5 billion U.S. dollars).
On September 2, France's Ministry of Economy and Finance said that heatwaves and drought in France were expected to shave 0.1 percentage point off France's gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 2026 due to lower agricultural production. ■

Pacific island nation Nauru opens embassy in Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
11:57:56 UTC
20:57:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Pacific island nation Nauru opens embassy in Jerusalem
The tiny Pacific island nation of Nauru opened its embassy in Jerusalem on Monday, joining a small group of countries taking the symbolic step of backing Israeli sovereignty in the contested city.
"We see opening an embassy here in Jerusalem not only as a strengthening of our ties with Israel, but also as a message to the world of where we stand," said Nauru's vice president and foreign minister Lionel Aingimea.
Most countries have kept their embassies in Tel Aviv on the grounds that the status of Jerusalem will be settled in a final resolution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
President Donald Trump shattered that consensus in 2018 during his first term by moving the US embassy to Jerusalem, which is home to Israel's parliament, prime minister and most other major governmental institutions.
Since Trump's move, only a handful of small, US-aligned countries have followed suit: Fiji, Guatemala, Honduras, Papua New Guinea and Paraguay.
Kosovo and Somaliland, which are not member-states of the United Nations, have also opened what they consider their embassies in Jerusalem.
At Monday's inauguration ceremony, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called Nauru "one of Israel's greatest friends".
He said other countries would soon follow Nauru in opening embassies in Jerusalem, noting that Colombia was expected to do so in early October.
Bogota has yet to confirm a date, but Colombia's new hard-right President Abelardo de la Espriella announced such a move in July.
The Democratic Republic of Congo said last week it would move its embassy in Israel to Jerusalem.
Argentine President Javier Milei, an outspoken supporter of Israel, has also promised to move his country's embassy to the holy city.
The status of Jerusalem is one of the thorniest issues in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Israel occupied east Jerusalem and annexed it in 1967, in a move not recognised by the vast majority of the international community- as it is recognised under international law as occupied Palestinian territory.
Rights groups, including Israeli legal rights organisation Adalah, have previously condemned plans to construct a permanent embassy on land taken from Palestinians in Jerusalem, saying it "deliberately enshrines a profound historical injustice" and violates the city's international legal status.
Israel claims Jerusalem as its eternal and undivided capital, while the Palestinian Authority seeks East Jerusalem, including the Old City, as the capital of a future Palestinian state.

French wine yields drop to new historic low after searing summer heat
French wine production is expected to suffer its worst harvest in some 70 years with the agriculture ministry on Monday forecasting a 6 percent drop in output after a summer of scorching temperatures, heatwaves and drought. France last week announced more than €1 billion in emergency support for farmers.
French wine production this year is expected to fall 6 percent from 2025 after a summer of unprecedented heatwaves and drought, the agriculture ministry said on Monday, predicting the most paltry harvest for some 70 years.
France, the world's second-largest wine producer after Italy, is expected to produce less than 34 million hectolitres in 2026, according to estimates released by the agriculture ministry.
According to the International Organisation of Vine and Wine (OIV), which tracks global wine production and consumption, the 2025 figure was already a historic low, marking the lowest production in France since 1957.
The decline expected in 2026, which is 17 percent below the average seen between 2021 and 2025, is due both to shrinking vineyards and lower yields caused by drought and summer heatwaves, according to the ministry's statistics service.
Read moreClimate crisis pushes French winemakers to bet on warmer future in Brittany and Normandy
As of September 1, production was estimated at nearly 33.9 million hectolitres, compared with 35.9 million hectolitres last year. A hectolitre is the equivalent of 100 litres.
The service noted, however, significant differences between regions.
In Champagne, output is expected to be cut by half compared with both 2025 and the five-year average.
But in the southern region of Languedoc-Roussillon, the harvest is expected to rise 5 percent from the 2025 weak crop thanks to improved yields, although it would still remain 8 percent below the 2021-2025 average.
France last week announced more than one billion euros in emergency support for farmers, but agricultural groups said the package fell short of needs.

Taiwanese defence minister says exchanges with the US are ‘even more extensive than you might imagine’
According to the budget plan, which still needs legislative approval, the programme would focus on “proactive cyber threat hunting”, moving the military beyond conventional defences, such as firewalls and post-attack remediation, towards actively searching networks for hidden threats.
Taiwan’s defence ministry did not identify where the foreign instructors would come from, but local media reports suggest they would mainly be from the United States. The instructors are expected to introduce realistic adversarial training comparable to the US military’s Cyber Flag exercises, according to the Taipei-based Liberty Times.
Like detectives following clues, team members would be trained to search military networks and critical infrastructure during peacetime for hostile hackers bypassing existing defences and concealing themselves inside systems, the outlet said.
The Information, Communications and Electronic Force Command is an independent branch of Taiwan’s military specialising in digital warfare, with responsibilities that include cyber operations, electronic warfare, military communications resilience and the protection of critical infrastructure.
The planned threat-hunting team would identify and eliminate hidden intruders and back doors before an adversary launched an attack, while bringing Taiwan’s cyber capabilities more in line with international practices, according to the report.
The plan comes as Taipei and Washington expand military exchanges well beyond arms sales, with American military personnel, civilian defence officials and contractors increasingly involved in advising, training and observing forces from the island.

Eight outbreaks have been identified in the villages of Butyrki and Koty, according to Leonid Frolov, the district’s head, who said the suspected cause was the illegal import of sheep and goats. Local media reported that lumpy skin disease was detected in at least 96 head of cattle.
Authorities have promised compensation for the seized animals: 224 rubles per kilogram for cattle, 307 rubles for sheep and goats, and 190 rubles for pigs.
The Russian Telegram news channel Ostorozhno Novosti published a video showing Butyrki residents telling government officials at a meeting that the compensation offered won’t cover their losses. They are demanding full compensation for the value of the seized animals.
The Russian news outlet 7×7 also reported that residents objected to having the livestock destroyed near their homes.
Mass livestock seizures from farmers have occurred repeatedly over the past year. On August 12, authorities in the Tyumen region began seizing pigs from farmers and killing them, citing an unknown but “very dangerous” disease. In the spring, authorities in the Kemerovo region began the mass slaughter of cattle, which they attributed to lumpy skin disease. In February, authorities seized livestock from farmers in the Novosibirsk region; the cause was later determined to be foot-and-mouth disease.

Kyiv metro, Pivdenny bridge traffic to run unrestricted under yellow-level threat – mayor
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:53:26 EEST
20:53:26 KST

Kyiv's Syretsko-Pecherska metro line will operate without restrictions during a yellow-level threat, with trains continuing to run across the Pivdenny (Southern) bridge, while car traffic on the bridge will also be allowed without restrictions during air raid alerts, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
"During a yellow-level threat, the Syretsko-Pecherska line (green metro line) will operate without restrictions, with trains running and carrying passengers across the Pivdenny bridge (from the left to the right bank and back)," Klitschko wrote on Telegram.
Car traffic on the Pivdenny bridge during air raid alerts will also be allowed without restrictions, with only a 30-minute technical closure after an alert is declared and another 30 minutes after the all-clear.
Access to the Pivdenny bridge from Saperno-Slobidska and Mykhaila Boichuka streets will be closed during air raid alerts, however.
Under a red-level threat, service on the green metro line will be restricted, with trains running only between Syrets and Vydubychi stations and between Slavutych and Chervony Khutir stations.
"The Sviatoshynsko-Brovarska line (red line) will continue operating as before, in a limited mode, carrying passengers on the underground section from Akademmistechko station to Arsenalna," the mayor said.
Other bridges across the Dnipro — the Darnytskyi bridge, the Paton bridge, the Metro bridge and the Pivnichny (Northern) bridge — will continue operating without changes.
The Podilsko-Voskresensky bridge crossing will have a 30-minute technical closure after an air raid alert is declared and another 30 minutes after the all-clear, with traffic organization also changed there to introduce reversible lanes.
Surface public transport will continue operating without restrictions.
Kyiv has also organized an additional bus route that duplicates the red metro line, running continuously from Palats Sportu metro station via Arsenalna station to Lisova metro station, Klitschko said.

Narayanan said India’s space programme was about 64-65 years old and that 56 space assets were currently operating in orbit to serve the country.He said the scale of India’s requirements meant that the number of space activities and launches would have to increase substantially.
Recalling the space sector reforms introduced six years ago, Narayanan said the government’s approach was to support private companies and startups and expand the overall space ecosystem.“Since the space sector reforms were rolled out six years ago, as per that, we are supposed to hand-hold the private sector, startup companies, and grow the space ecosystem,” he said.He also said Indian industry already had a substantial role in Isro’s launch programmes.“In fact, whenever a PSLV or a GSLV is lifting off, almost 80 per cent budget is invested in Indian industries. Mustafa Foundation launches blockchain platform for global scientific support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
11:51:49 UTC
20:51:49 KST

Mustafa Foundation launches blockchain platform for global scientific support
TEHRAN – Mustafa Science and Technology Foundation unveiled a new platform powered by blockchain technology on Saturday to enable Muslims around the world to participate more easily in programs and projects of the Foundation.
The platform uses cryptocurrencies, smart contracts and innovative financing mechanisms to enable transparent, rapid and international participation in supporting the Mustafa Prize and other scientific and technological initiatives.
“Many Muslims and businesspeople who, as a result of technological developments in recent years, have converted part of their assets into cryptocurrencies have faced the question of how to put those assets to work in real, clearly defined projects,” Ali-Akbar Salehi, the chairman of the board of trustees of the Mustafa Science and Technology Foundation, said.
“This is where the idea of creating a platform to connect crypto assets with real investment opportunities and tangible projects emerged.”
He highlighted the ability to set precise conditions governing the use of funds as one of the technology’s most important features.
“For example, a patron can specify that their contribution or financial participation should only be released after a particular event or outcome has been achieved. A smart contract then automatically executes the process according to the rules defined in advance,” he explained.
“This reduces the possibility of intervention outside the agreed framework and increases transparency throughout the process.”
Global network for supporting science and innovation
Salehi has proposed the establishment of a “Global Network of Patrons of Science” alongside the network of scientists that the foundation has worked to build over the years.
“Just as the Foundation has spent years working to build a network of scientists across the Muslim world, we should now establish a global network of patrons of science alongside it,” Salehi said.
“I have said many times that knowledge and ideas cannot be confined to a particular geography, and scientific progress cannot take place without interaction and exchange among scientists. The Mustafa Prize was established from the outset with precisely this vision in mind: to connect the scientific capacities of the Muslim world with the international scientific community.”
“If the production and exchange of knowledge can be global, why shouldn’t support for science be global as well?” he added. “Alongside a network of scientists, we can create a network of people who want to contribute to scientific progress.”
The key question, Salehi said, is how to make it easier for an individual anywhere in the world to support science by contributing to a young scientist or a specific research project.
New financial technologies and digital assets, he noted, can help reduce some of the geographical barriers to international participation. “We want to put these capabilities at the service of science,” he said.
 
 “Imagine a credible project in areas such as cancer treatment, water, energy, artificial intelligence, or other cutting-edge technologies that needs funding. Instead of simply making a payment to an institution, an individual could know exactly what problem they are supporting, which research team is working on it, and what the intended objective is.”
Salehi described the initial motivation behind the initiative as supporting defined scientific projects involving Muslim countries through financial contributions from individuals around the world.
“If this happens, the financing of science itself could become a tool for building networks and advancing scientific diplomacy,” he said.

UN rights chief warns how AI could pose ‘existential risk to humanity’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
11:50:53 UTC
20:50:53 KST

Volker Türk has called for urgent global safeguards, independent checks and agreed limits on advanced artificial intelligence.
The United Nations human rights chief has warned that advanced artificial intelligence could pose an “existential risk to humanity”, calling for immediate action to make the technology safer.
Addressing the UN Human Rights Council on Monday, Volker Türk said people faced “unfamiliar, even unprecedented” threats to their rights.
"The need for AI governance is widely acknowledged, but where is the action?" he asked, warning that "delay only benefits the massive tech companies, their owners and enablers".
Türk said that “a handful of men has almost unlimited power over AI, which we are repeatedly told has unimaginable computing capacity”.
“They talk about freedom, but on closer inspection, this turns out to be little more than the freedom to exploit our data,” he said.
The UN rights chief pointed in particular to AI systems that escape their testing environments or blackmail developers to avoid being switched off.
According to AFP, Turk warned in particular that "AI that escapes its testing environment or blackmails developers to prevent itself from being turned off, is AI that is too powerful".
His comments appeared to refer partly to revelations in July that OpenAI agents had escaped supposedly controlled environments and gained access to servers belonging to Hugging Face, a widely used platform where developers share AI software.
OpenAI later said the agents had executed code on dozens of Hugging Face servers and gained full access to one of them.
The incident renewed calls for tighter oversight of advanced AI systems.
Anthropic, Meta and other technology companies have reported similar incidents involving agents during testing.
“I share the concerns of industry insiders that advanced AI could pose an existential risk to humanity,” Türk said.
“I am calling here, today, for an all-out effort to put cast-iron guarantees in place around the safety and security of AI, before it is too late.”
Calls for international safeguards
The UN rights chief said he would write to AI companies in the coming days, urging them to take immediate steps to reduce the risks within their control.
At a minimum, he said, "we need countries hosting AI and those involved in its supply chains to come together around agreed red lines".
“We need independent verification, and much stronger collaboration on security within the industry,” Türk added.
"We also need to consider the human rights impacts of AI on employment practices, on fundamental principles of democracy, and on our environment," he said.
In the European Union, the AI Act provides a legal framework for AI.
Under the law, high-risk systems have to meet strict requirements before they can enter the EU market, while uses considered an unacceptable threat to people’s safety or rights are banned.
The law prohibits AI designed to manipulate or exploit people, score them based on their behaviour, predict whether an individual will commit a crime, or indiscriminately collect images to build facial-recognition databases.
It also prohibits emotion recognition at work and in schools, some forms of biometric profiling and most real-time police facial recognition in public places, while a ban on AI-generated sexual images made without consent and child sexual abuse material takes effect in December 2026.

Bhattacharya said."Here, goat meat is offered as an offering to Maa Kali," he added.
BJP leader backs Bengal’s food traditions
Bhattacharya said eating 'luchi' (puris) on Ashtami and goat meat on Navami has long been part of Bengali tradition during Durga Puja. He said there was no question of abandoning these practices because of Shastri’s appeal."We generally eat 'luchi' on Ashtami and goat meat on Navami.
We will continue to do that. Nobody can tell the people of West Bengal what they should eat," he said.While saying that he respected Shastri as a religious figure, Bhattacharya argued that his personal views should not be treated as rules for Bengali society."A saint or a doctor may have the right to advise people to become vegetarian. But nobody coming from outside can sit in Bengal and decide who will eat what and who will wear what," he said.He also stressed that Shastri's remarks represented his personal views.The issue has sparked a wider debate in West Bengal, where fish and meat are closely associated with traditional Bengali food and religious practices vary across communities and regions. The practice of offering goat meat to Goddess Kali at several temples has also been cited in the debate.
Shastri’s visit takes on political overtones
The controversy comes days after Shastri made his appeal during his visit to West Bengal. His visit has also attracted political attention after he was able to hold religious programmes across the state under the BJP government, despite allegations that he had faced difficulties in obtaining permission during the previous Trinamool Congress regime.Bhattacharya’s comments indicate that the BJP’s West Bengal unit does not support any attempt to impose a blanket vegetarian prescription on the state’s population during Durga Puja.The BJP has been trying to expand its presence in West Bengal by combining its Hindutva politics with an appeal to Bengali cultural identity. Shastri’s remarks have highlighted the challenge of balancing religious messaging with the state’s distinct food and cultural traditions.
Bhattacharya also commented on a separate controversy involving a West Bengal government advertisement that showed Goddess Durga with 11 hands.He advised against turning what he described as a "possible technical or printing error by the advertising agency" into a political issue and said the mistake should simply be corrected.The BJP leader’s response to both controversies reflects an attempt by the state unit to distinguish religious beliefs from Bengal’s established cultural practices, particularly when it comes to food during Durga Puja.

Akhilesh's 'chavanni' jab: Can Jayant Chaudhary be BJP’s trump card in western UP?
Pallavi / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Sep 07, 2026, 19:08 IST

Akhilesh's 'chavanni' jibe: Is Jayant Chaudhary the game-changer BJP needs in Jatland?
Akhilesh Yadav may have intended "chavanni" as a put-down, but in Uttar Pradesh politics, old coins have a habit of changing hands and sometimes gaining value in the process. Three years after Jayant Chaudhary insisted he was no "chavanni" to be flipped, the coin metaphor has made a comeback, this time from his former ally, just as the RLD chief prepares for another electoral test in western UP.The row began when Akhilesh, without naming Jayant, said: "Humne chavanni ka rupya bana diya tha, tab bhi humein chhod kar chale gaye wo" — we turned a 25-paise coin into a rupee, yet they left us. The remark was widely seen as a jibe at the RLD chief, who had once used the same "chavanni" metaphor while rejecting speculation that he could switch sides.
Jayant's response was swift. "Siyasat ki ladai mein kuch saste shabd bolne hi the, to mera naam lekar bol dete, koi baat nahi thi," he said. He accused Akhilesh of targeting the Jat community and added: "Main is ahankar ko dekh chuka hoon kareeb se aur maanta hoon aisa aacharan sirf patan laata hai" — I have seen this arrogance from close quarters and believe such conduct only leads to downfall.Meanwhile, Uttar Pradesh CM Yogi Adityanath also jumped in and hit back at Akhilesh, saying the language used against political opponents was making a "mockery of democracy" while describing the remark as an insult to Jayant, the legacy of Chaudhary Charan Singh and the farming community.
Throwback to what Jayant Chaudhary said on alliance before 2022 polls.
The exchange may look like little more than pre-election sparring. But it points to a bigger question: why is Jayant Chaudhary important enough for both sides to keep talking about him?Jayant is no longer merely a smaller ally being wooed by rival camps. He is a Union minister, heads a party that won both Lok Sabha seats it contested in 2024 and carries the Chaudhary family name into a region where Jats and farmers remain central to the political arithmetic.So, ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly election, the real question is less about whether Akhilesh turned a "chavanni" into a rupee and more about how much political currency that rupee can buy in western UP.
Akhilesh Yadav took a swipe at Jayant Chaudhary without naming him.
The 'coin' that changed hands
In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, Jayant's RLD posted a 100% strike rate, winning both seats it contested while in alliance with the BJP.But the picture was very different in the assembly elections.In 2017, the party was reduced to a marginal force in Uttar Pradesh, winning just one seat with around 1.5% of the vote share.However, in 2022, as it entered an alliance with the Samajwadi Party, the RLD contested 33 seats and won eight, with its vote share rising to nearly 3%.But the revival was not entirely an SP creation.Jayant had already begun rebuilding his political base, and the 2020-21 farmers' protests gave him an opportunity to re-establish himself as one of western UP's prominent political faces. Through kisan panchayats and sustained attacks on the NDA government over the farm laws and sugarcane dues, he reconnected with sections of a Jat electorate that had moved towards the BJP after the communal polarisation following the 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots.The SP-RLD alliance therefore worked both ways. The SP provided the RLD electoral space and organisational support, while Jayant offered the SP access to a Jat political network in a region where the BJP had built a formidable base.The numbers underline both the limits and value of that alliance. The RLD won eight of the 33 seats it contested in 2022, but the BJP won all 25 seats that the RLD lost.The RLD had regained relevance in pockets of western UP, but it was nowhere close to being a statewide challenger.
Jayant Chaudhary's comeback after Akhilesh's 'chavanni' swipe.
Akhilesh may therefore have a point when he says the SP helped turn the RLD's "chavanni" into a rupee. But that is only half the transaction.Jayant brought the SP something that could not be created simply through seat-sharing - a political bridge to sections of the Jat electorate and the symbolic capital of the Chaudhary family.
How BJP 'won' RLD chief's heart
In February 2024, the BJP and RLD announced their alliance, with the BJP offering the smaller party two Lok Sabha seats and a Rajya Sabha berth.The announcement came shortly after the Centre conferred the Bharat Ratna on former prime minister Chaudhary Charan Singh, a move Jayant publicly welcomed.He immediately posted on X: "Dil jeet liya" - won the heart.
When asked whether the post meant the RLD would join the BJP, Jayant replied: "Koi kasar rehti hai? Aaj main kis muh se inkaar karoon aapke sawalon ko?" - Is there anything left? How can I deny your questions today?The RLD then contested Baghpat and Bijnor in the 2024 Lok Sabha election and won both.For the BJP, however, the bigger prize was a political intermediary who could speak to sections of the Jat electorate on behalf of the NDA while carrying the Chaudhary name.The BJP's relationship with Jayant Chaudhary's party and family had also undergone a dramatic reversal.In 2014, the BJP swept western Uttar Pradesh, defeating then-RLD chief Ajit Singh in Baghpat and his son Jayant in Mathura. Five years later, the father-son duo suffered another setback, losing in Muzaffarnagar and Baghpat respectively.But the saffron party subsequently lost some ground among Jats amid the farmers' protests and the long-running demand for reservation.Jayant's entry into the NDA therefore gave the BJP a recognised Jat face at a time when the opposition was trying to rebuild a broader farmer-minority coalition in the region.
Why Jats matter in western UP
There is no recent official caste census providing a definitive figure for the Jat population in Uttar Pradesh. Estimates commonly put Jats at around 2% of the state's population, but their concentration in western UP gives them much greater political weight in the region. Estimates have put their share at roughly 17-18% in the area often described as "Jatland".They heavily sway the electoral outcomes of roughly 40 to 45 assembly seats and about 10 to 12 Lok Sabha (parliamentary) seats in western UP.There is also a historical reason the Jat vote matters.
The legacy of Chaudhary Charan Singh.
Before the 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots, the politics of Chaudhary Charan Singh and later Ajit Singh rested in part on a cross-community farmer coalition involving Jats and Muslims. The riots fractured that relationship and pushed many Jats towards the BJP.The farmers' movement briefly reopened the possibility of a Jat-Muslim political convergence that the SP-RLD alliance tried to convert into votes in 2022.Jayant's subsequent move to the NDA, however, made that opposition combination considerably harder to sustain.For the BJP, therefore, Jayant may be useful not simply because he can attract Jats, but because his presence can also complicate the social coalition Akhilesh is trying to build.
The Jayant question in Akhilesh's PDA strategy
That brings the RLD directly into Akhilesh's larger PDA strategy — Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak — which seeks to bring backward classes, Dalits and minorities together while reducing the SP's dependence on its traditional Yadav base.The 2024 Lok Sabha election demonstrated the potential of that strategy, with the SP emerging as the largest party in Uttar Pradesh.
The 'Jatland' of UP.
For the BJP, the challenge ahead of 2027 will be to prevent that coalition from consolidating, particularly in regions where the party faces a more competitive opposition.Jayant is one piece of that counter-strategy.The RLD, meanwhile, appears keen to expand beyond its traditional Jat base. Its outreach has included Gurjars and other communities, while party leaders have spoken of a broader AJGR formula - Ahir, Jat, Gurjar and Rajput - along with efforts to reach Dalits and Muslims.
Why September 3 rally matters
That is why the RLD's September 3 'Swabhiman Rally' in Saharanpur mattered beyond its immediate spat with Akhilesh.The rally was an attempt to demonstrate that Jayant can still mobilise on his own political terms rather than functioning merely as a BJP ally.And Jayant used the "chavanni" controversy to turn criticism into an argument for relevance."Jo abhi gaaliyan de rahe hain, abhi to sun lo... sahi samay par nipat lenge," he said — those abusing us should listen for now; they will be dealt with at the appropriate time. He then added that the fact that opposition leaders kept mentioning the RLD showed that the party was working in the "right place and in the right direction."But the more significant part of his pitch was directed at farmers, the community most closely associated with the Chaudhary family's political legacy.
Calling on farmers to identify their "true supporters" and choose a strong political advocate, Jayant said: "Farmers are in a majority and governments are made and unmade on their strength, but the hard reality is that the farmers’ lobby is weak in political corridors. Therefore, farmers need to choose a strong advocate for their cause."This could be seen as more than a regular rallying cry. It was a reminder of what Jayant believes his political value rests on: being the voice of a region and a community larger than the RLD's current electoral footprint.
The 2027 seat-sharing exercise could be the clearest measure yet of Jayant's political "worth".A meaningful allocation of seats would suggest that the BJP believes the RLD's organisation can add value across western UP. A sharply limited share, on the other hand, would indicate that the BJP sees little reason to give Jayant enough room to build an independent base.Jayant also has something to prove.The RLD's two Lok Sabha victories in 2024 demonstrated that the party could convert its alliance with the BJP into electoral success. The next test is whether it can build enough support beyond those two constituencies to negotiate from a position of strength.Now, ahead of the 2027 elections, the question is whether Jayant can convert that symbolic capital into enough independent political influence to remain indispensable to the BJP.

Saxony-Anhalt election delivers a blow to Merz and a warning to Europe

Unknown Publisher

Saxony-Anhalt election delivers a blow to Merz and a warning to Europe
BERLIN, Sept 7 - The far-right AfD's triumph in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt marks a defeat for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and sends a warning to other European leaders battling the same mixture of slow growth and disillusion with mainstream politics.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD), just short of an absolute majority in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament after Sunday's vote, has become the face of opposition to the consensus-based political system that has governed Germany since World War Two.
Thorsten Frei, the parliamentary leader for Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), called it "a watershed for our country".
In an increasingly polarized political system, Merz, whose personal approval ratings have sunk to record lows, was one of the main targets of voter ire over the cost of living, pensions and economic insecurity.
A survey by Infratest dimap for ARD public television found 87% of voters in the state were unhappy with his government. A separate survey for ZDF public television found three quarters of people, including almost half of CDU supporters, believed Merz had hurt the party's result.
In his first reported comments on the election outcome, Merz on Monday told the CDU's executive board the result had shaken his party "to its very foundations", but he also again ruled out cooperating with the AfD, according to the Bild newspaper.
The AfD has said it sees victory in Saxony-Anhalt as a first step towards winning federal elections due in 2029 but there was no immediate sign of any internal revolt against Merz in the party committees that met on Monday, CDU sources said.
One member who was present said discussions had been "open and frank" but added: "Everybody knows we have to continue with our policy."
GLOBAL 'POPULIST WAVE'
While far-right parties have governed in several European countries, the AfD's best performance so far in a state election in Germany carries an urgent warning to other nations facing elections in coming months.
In France, where opinion polls suggest the far-right National Rally could win next year's presidential election, Finance Minister Roland Lescure said the outcome of the election in Saxony-Anhalt was a "very, very worrying signal".
"It shows we face a major challenge from a populist wave that is now global," he told RTL radio.
Saxony-Anhalt, a largely rural state of some 2.1 million inhabitants in the formerly communist east, is one of the smaller German states, which has lost around a quarter of its population since Germany reunified in 1990.
Sunday's result can be partly explained by the unhealed divisions between east and west Germany nearly four decades after reunification.
And yet over the past 10 to 15 years it has staged a steady recovery from the shock of reunification in 1990, when its industry largely collapsed. Its unemployment rate is not far above the national average at 8% and it has rebuilt its chemicals industry and developed new sectors including logistics and green energy.
However, voters disregarded warnings from business groups and economists, as well as Merz himself, that a vote for the anti-immigrant AfD would put much needed foreign investment at risk and discourage the skilled workers the state sorely needs.
Amid unusually heavy voter turnout, workers, male voters and the young all voted in large numbers for the party.
Under its 35-year-old candidate Ulrich Siegmund, a TikTok adept who attracted thousands to election rallies and meetings, promising to bring back "our good, old, safe Germany", the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt brushed off its classification by the domestic security service as "extremist" right-wing.
'VERY SIGNIFICANT CHALLENGES'
"The AfD is now a highly visible political force which is far more effective at getting its message across than other parties manage to do," said Thorsten Faas, a political scientist at Berlin's Free University.
"And this is not set to change in the short term, which poses very significant challenges for the federal government in its attempts to paint a positive picture of the country and its future," he said.
For Merz, confronted with a deep-seated crisis in Germany's industrial base and battling to push through pension reforms that have proved particularly unpopular in eastern Germany, there appear to be no easy answers.
Volkswagen AG's announcement last week of a radical restructuring plan, which could see 50,000 job cuts worldwide and the closure of major factories in Germany, underlined the grim picture facing Europe's largest economy, struggling to emerge from years of stagnation.
High energy costs, fuelled in part by the wars in Ukraine and Iran, offered an easy attack point for the AfD, which found a ready audience for its argument that German support for Kyiv had needlessly antagonized Moscow and driven up oil and gas prices.
Merz came to power in 2025, pledging tough reforms to revive the economy. He abandoned decades of fiscal caution by promising to borrow hundreds of billions of euros to restore Germany's withered military and rebuild infrastructure.
But voters, particularly in eastern Germany, have given him no credit for the plans, which have so far produced few visible results.
By big majorities, voters favoured the AfD to address their main concerns around social insecurity, peace in Europe and their own economic situation, the Infratest dimap poll showed.
Before the vote, Eva von Angern, the main candidate of the far-left Left party, expressed some sympathy for Merz, saying, "He's not responsible for everything."
But she added that on the campaign trail, he was "Hate figure number one" for voters. "He's the reason why people don't want to vote for the CDU and all the other established parties." REUTERS

MOSCOW, September 7. /TASS/. The governments of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) and Russia will strive for new results in developing cooperation, living up to expectations of the two countries’ peoples who seek shared prosperity, said North Korean Prime Minister Pak Thae Song.
The ceremony marking the completion of construction of a road bridge across the Tumannaya River on the border between the two countries took place earlier on Monday. Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and Pak Thae Song launched traffic on the bridge via video link.
"On the basis of valuable success and experience gained as the road bridge across the Tumannaya River was constructed, the governments of the two countries, the DPRK and Russia, will strive for further practical results in cooperation, which fulfills the hopes and aspirations of the peoples of both countries as they seek shared development and prosperity," the North Korean premier said.

The total length of the bridge crossing is almost 5 km, with the bridge itself spanning around 1 km. Two traffic lanes are available for vehicles. Russia Moves Oreshnik-Equipped Missile Units Into Belarus, Ukraine’s Spy Chief Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Moves Oreshnik-Equipped Missile Units Into Belarus, Ukraine’s Spy Chief Says
Russia has stationed elements of its 101st Missile Brigade in Belarus, a formation equipped with the Oreshnik intermediate-range missile system, according to Ukraine’s military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko on September 7.
Ivashchenko told Ukrinform that Ukrainian intelligence currently sees no evidence that Belarus itself is preparing to directly enter Russia’s war against Ukraine. Kyiv assesses the immediate military threat from the Belarusian direction as low.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
However, Russia’s growing use of Belarusian territory for missile and drone-related infrastructure remains a significant concern.
“However, we are concerned that Belarus has permitted the deployment on its territory of radio-signal relay stations that guide Russian Shahed-type strike UAVs toward Ukrainian civilian targets and critical infrastructure,” Ivashchenko said.
He added: “We also note the deployment in Belarus of units of the 101st Missile Brigade of the Russian Armed Forces, which is equipped with the Oreshnik intermediate-range missile system.”
The deployment gives Russia another potential platform for positioning long-range missile capabilities closer to Ukraine and NATO’s eastern flank, even as Minsk stops short of directly committing its own forces to the war.
Ivashchenko also raised a broader question over how much control Belarusian authorities retain over Russian military activity inside the country.
“If Belarus did not grant such permission, then this indicates that Minsk no longer controls Russia’s activities on its own territory,” he said.
Ukraine has monitored Belarus closely throughout the full-scale war because Russian forces used Belarusian territory during the initial invasion in February 2022, and Moscow has continued maintaining military infrastructure and personnel there.
In general terms, the “Oreshnik” is an intermediate-range ballistic missile with nuclear capability that travels through the stratosphere, making it extremely difficult to intercept.
It is equipped with a multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle (MIRV) system, meaning a single missile can carry several warheads that separate in flight to strike different targets, though they are not independently guided after release.
For now, Ukrainian intelligence does not assess Belarusian forces themselves as preparing for a new offensive against Ukraine.
Previously, Belarusian Deputy Foreign Minister Igor Sekreta has claimed that Minsk would use its “entire arsenal” if Ukrainian forces crossed Belarus' state border, a statement that comes amid renewed rhetoric from Belarusian officials over alleged threats from Ukraine.

University of Hong Kong suspends professor over past sexual misconduct in Canada
University of Hong Kong confirms that Peter Tanuseputro was asked to work from home after it became aware of professional misconduct ruling against him
A professor at Hong Kong’s oldest medical school has been suspended from clinical work and face-to-face teaching after the university discovered he was temporarily disqualified from practising in Canada following past sexual harassment allegations.
The University of Hong Kong (HKU) confirmed on Monday that Peter Tanuseputro, a clinical professor in the department of family medicine and primary care, was asked to work from home after the university became aware of a professional misconduct ruling against him.
“After learning of the incident, HKU’s faculty of medicine immediately suspended all of the professor’s clinical work and face-to-face teaching activities, and arranged for him to work from home,” the university said in response to an inquiry from the South China Morning Post following a whistle-blower’s complaint.
Tanuseputro, who obtained his medical practice certificate from the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario in 2010 and joined HKU in 2024, was found by the Ontario Physicians and Surgeons Discipline Tribunal on April 8 to have “constituted conduct that was disgraceful, dishonourable or unprofessional and conduct unbecoming a physician”.
He was reprimanded, and his certificate of registration in Canada was suspended for eight months from April 9. He was also ordered to pay C$6,000 (US$4,335) in costs to the college.
The tribunal heard that in 2018, while working for the University of Ottawa and holding two research positions at hospitals, Tanuseputro made sexual comments to a female research assistant after a social gathering and engaged in unwanted touching.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Russia Turns to Foreign Recruits From Over 40 Countries to Replenish Forces in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
11:45:34 UTC
20:45:34 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Turns to Foreign Recruits From Over 40 Countries to Replenish Forces in Ukraine
Russia is recruiting foreign nationals from more than 40 countries to fight against Ukraine as Moscow seeks additional manpower to replace battlefield losses and expand its forces, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) chief Oleh Ivashchenko said in an interview with Ukrinform on September 7.
Ivashchenko said Russia needs to simultaneously compensate for personnel losses and increase the size of its forces if it intends to pursue further military objectives, prompting Moscow to look for additional recruits beyond its borders.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Today, Russia is using foreign nationals from more than 40 countries, including countries in Central Asia, Africa, and Latin America. They are primarily deployed in assault units. In intercepted communications, the Russians themselves call them ‘allies’ and often send them ahead of their own troops,” he stated.
Some foreign nationals are recruited through deception, according to the HUR chief. They travel to Russia seeking employment and subsequently sign contracts, in some cases without fully understanding what they are agreeing to.
Ivashchenko said Ukrainian forces have captured foreign nationals serving with the Russian military, allowing Ukrainian intelligence to assess the recruitment practice not only through documents and intercepted communications, but also through testimony from prisoners of war.
“We are working separately with countries whose citizens Russia is attempting to recruit in order to reduce the scale of such recruitment and prevent Russia from freely using this manpower in its war against Ukraine. However, foreign nationals cannot solve Russia’s manpower problem. They can only partially compensate for its losses,” HUR chief added.
The growing presence of foreign recruits has also been documented on the battlefield. On September 2, Ukraine’s 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade reported that Ukrainian forces had killed foreign nationals from Colombia and Zimbabwe serving with Russian troops on the Lyman front, where foreigners account for around 30% of personnel in newly deployed Russian units.
The brigade said the Colombian and Zimbabwean fighters were killed by troops from its 3rd Mechanized Battalion “Fireflies” and the “Siverska Sich” Motorized Infantry Battalion.
Overall, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence has identified more than 28,000 foreign nationals who have signed contracts with the Russian military, with the number continuing to rise.

Russia’s Budget Deficit Surges to $82 Billion as Ukrainian Strikes Hammer War Economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
11:45:18 UTC
20:45:18 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Budget Deficit Surges to $82 Billion as Ukrainian Strikes Hammer War Economy
Ukraine’s strikes against targets deep inside Russia are increasingly damaging Moscow’s ability to sustain its war effort and contributing to a federal budget deficit that has reached $82 billion.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In an interview with Ukrinform published on September 7, Chief of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Oleh Ivashchenko said Ukrainian strikes are forcing Russia to halt production, repair damaged facilities, alter logistics, redeploy air defense systems, and spend additional resources.
“Our strikes are contributing to the growth of the Russian Federation’s budget deficit, which today stands at $82 billion,” Ivashchenko said.
He described the impact of Ukrainian attacks on Russia as “very critical,” saying Ukraine is targeting energy infrastructure that supplies Russian forces with fuel, logistics hubs, and facilities supporting the country’s military-industrial complex.
Ivashchenko said the broader objective of the campaign is not simply to demonstrate how far Ukrainian weapons can reach, but to reduce Russia’s capacity to manufacture weapons, supply its forces, and continue the war.
Russia’s finances have come under increasing pressure as the war continues. On September 3, Russian leader Vladimir Putin acknowledged that the country’s budget deficit was growing but insisted it remained manageable. Russia’s deficit reached 2.8% of GDP in January through July, while the government’s official target for the full year remains 1.6%.
Ivashchenko also said Russia is now significantly weaker economically than it was at the beginning of the full-scale invasion, pointing to labor shortages, the expanding federal budget deficit, and worsening conditions in the banking sector.
Despite those pressures, Ukrainian intelligence assesses that Moscow still possesses enough resources to continue its war against Ukraine, potentially through 2027 and 2028.
Ivashchenko said further pressure—including Ukrainian strikes, sanctions, and efforts to restrict Russia’s access to foreign components, technologies, and industrial equipment—would be needed to further erode Moscow’s ability to finance and sustain the war.
Earlier, Russia’s central bank gold reserves fell to their lowest level in more than six years as Moscow increasingly relied on liquid reserve assets to meet rising budget demands.

Russia Preparing to Mobilize Up to 600,000 More Troops Through 2027, Ukrainian Intelligence Says

Russia Preparing to Mobilize Up to 600,000 More Troops Through 2027, Ukrainian Intelligence Says
Russia is preparing for a new wave of mobilization that could bring up to 600,000 additional people into its military through 2027 as Moscow struggles to replace battlefield losses while seeking enough manpower for further offensive operations in Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko in an interview with Ukrinform published on September 7, Russian military planners are considering mobilizing approximately 300,000 people in 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027.
“We see such preparations,” Ivashchenko said, adding that Ukraine bases its assessment on intelligence rather than public statements from Russian leader Vladimir Putin denying plans for additional mobilization.
Ivashchenko said the mobilization could intensify after Russia’s upcoming State Duma elections and may be conducted without a major public announcement, particularly in remote regions, allowing the Kremlin to avoid creating additional tensions in large population centers such as Moscow and St. Petersburg.
Without additional mobilization, Russia is currently able primarily to replace its losses and maintain the size of its forces fighting against Ukraine, according to Ivashchenko.
However, he said additional manpower would be required if Moscow intends to expand its operations and pursue further military objectives, including the full occupation of Ukraine’s Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
Russia is also facing growing problems with its existing contract recruitment model. Ivashchenko said regional budgets are increasingly unable to finance payments offered to new recruits, while Russian battlefield losses continue to rise.
He estimated Russia’s average daily losses at between 1,200 and 1,400 killed and seriously wounded, with the figure sometimes reaching 1,500.
Earlier, reports of forced military recruitment emerged from at least 17 Russian regions, with rights groups describing detentions, threats, and coercion into signing Defense Ministry contracts as Moscow struggled to attract enough voluntary recruits.

As CFO, Ian will join the NAD Group Executive Committee and play a crucial role in how the NAD Group delivers the Defence Investment Plan (DIP), reacting to Defence’s new capability priorities. Under his leadership, the Group’s finance professionals will support the NAD Group teams responsible for developing, delivering, sustaining, housing and harbouring the UK’s ‘national arsenal’ and defence estate.
Ian has a history of crafting smart financial strategies and improving performance in both FTSE 100 and private international companies, and has helped solve financial business challenges for FTSE 100 firms.
Commenting on his appointment, Ian Brimicombe said:
  I’m delighted to be joining the National Armaments Director Group as Chief Financial Officer. Having spent my career in the private sector, I’m excited by the opportunity to bring that experience to the Ministry of Defence at such an important time for the organisation, for defence and for the UK. I look forward to working with the team to build on its foundations and support its future growth and success.
On graduating from King’s College London, Ian completed his accountancy and tax qualifications at Coopers and Lybrand (now PWC). After building a strong technical foundation across audit, tax and corporate finance, he moved into the pharmaceutical industry, joining what later became AstraZeneca, where he spent over 20 years in increasingly senior leadership roles.
Ian subsequently joined the British fashion house, Burberry, where he spent nearly seven years supporting finance and business transformation, including navigating the organisation through the COVID-19 pandemic and leading refinancing activities. Most recently he was CFO at Abercrombie & Kent Group.
Rupert Pearce, National Armaments Director, said:
  I am delighted to welcome Ian to the NAD Group. He brings with him a wealth of experience from the high-tech world of pharmaceuticals and the fast-paced retail arena. As UK Defence continues its transformation, and we look to drive greater efficiency into our systems, these are skills we really value.
David Johnson, who retires this Autumn, leaves an exceptional legacy as our first Group Finance Director. He has been a stalwart member of the MOD for 37 years. His professionalism, rigour and sharp eye for detail have helped make our armed forces and country more secure. We wish him all the best for his retirement.
Ian will join the NAD Group on 7 September 2026, succeeding David who retires at the end of November.

Germany asks ICJ to dismiss Nicaragua-backed case against Israel arms export
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
11:44:05 UTC
20:44:05 KST

Germany asked the International Court of Justice on Monday to throw out a 2024 case brought by Nicaragua, which accuses Berlin of violating the 1948 Genocide Convention because it supplies arms to Israel.
Berlin suspended weapons exports to Israel for a few months in 2025, but it has since resumed. A US-backed ceasefire that took effect in October 2025 halted large-scale fighting that had devastated Gaza, but it has not ended Israeli strikes.
Nicaragua and Germany are both signatories of the Genocide Convention, which includes an obligation on states to act to prevent possible genocides - but it is unusual for the court to hear cases where neither party is directly involved in the conflict at the heart of it.
Israel rejects genocide allegations as politically motivated and says its military campaign has targeted the militant group Hamas, whose attack on Israel triggered the war in October 2023.
Nicaragua's claim builds on the case South Africa brought against Israel for allegedly committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Argument over jurisdiction
In an interim ruling in 2024, the ICJ said it was plausible Israel violated some rights guaranteed under the Genocide Convention during its assault on Gaza.
Israel opposes the case and says it respects international law and has a right to defend itself. The main genocide case is not expected to be heard in full until late 2029.
Germany told the ICJ, also known as the World Court, on Monday that Nicaragua had not taken the proper steps before turning to the court and that much of the claim falls outside the jurisdiction it has under the genocide treaty.
"Germany respectfully requests the court to reject Nicaragua's claims," Julia Monar, legal adviser of the German foreign ministry, told the judges.
Nicaragua, which broke off diplomatic relations with Israel in 2024 over the war in Gaza, will have a chance on Tuesday to argue why the case should move forward.
A ruling on Germany's objection to jurisdiction is expected later this year. Even if the case can continue, it is expected to take years before a final ruling on the merits.
The ICJ is the United Nations' top court, which deals with disputes between states and alleged violations of numerous international treaties. Its rulings are final and without appeal.

Republicans defend US House majority as 50 competitive races loom ahead of 2026 midterms

Only about 50 of the 435 races for the House of Representatives are expected to be competitive on the November 3 US midterm ballot, but they could decide whether Democrats gain the three seats needed to reclaim control of the chamber from Republicans.
Here is a look at some of the races that will determine the outcome:
Arizona
This battleground state includes two of the most competitive House districts in the country.
In Phoenix's northern suburbs, Democrat Amish Shah, a former state representative and emergency-room doctor, and Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker, face off for an open seat.
In a Tucson-based district, Democrat JoAnna Mendoza, a retired Marine drill instructor, is taking on Republican Representative Juan Ciscomani, a moderate.
California
At the urging of US President Donald Trump, several Republican-led states have redrawn their district maps to boost their chances of retaining control of the House, in a departure from the usual practice of setting those boundaries once a decade to reflect population shifts.
Democratic-led California pushed through a redistricting of its own last year in response to the moves by Republican-led states, which analysts say could allow them to pick up five more of the state's 52 seats from Republicans.
Among the most endangered Republicans is Representative David Valadao, a centrist who has survived previous close elections in this Central Valley seat. He faces Democrat Randy Villegas, a school board member.
Republican Darrell Issa opted to retire rather than run for reelection in a less hospitable seat. Republican San Diego County Supervisor Jim Desmond and Democratic San Diego City Council member Marni von Wilpert are competing to take his place.
Democrats are on defense east of San Francisco, where incumbent Representative Adam Gray, who won his last race by 187 votes, will try to hold off Republican Kevin Lincoln, a former mayor of Stockton.
Colorado
Republican Representative Gabe Evans won his 2024 race by less than a percentage point. He faces Democrat Manny Rutinel, a state representative. Trump's immigration crackdown has been a major issue in this district north of Denver, which is 40% Hispanic.
Florida
Florida's Republican-led redistricting could leave the state with a House delegation of 24 Republicans and four Democrats.
Democratic Representative Kathy Castor now must run for reelection in a Tampa-based district that includes more Republican-leaning areas. She will face Republican Mike Beltran, a former state representative.
Democratic Representative Jared Moskowitz moved to a new district along the Atlantic coast north of Miami. He will face Republican Scott Singer, the former mayor of Boca Raton.
And in a redrawn district that stretches from Palm Beach to the Gulf Coast, voters will choose between Democrat Pia Dandiya, an educator, and Republican Casey Askar, a veteran.
Iowa
Though Iowa has trended steadily Republican over the past decade, concerns over Trump's tariffs and higher fuel and fertilizer costs stemming from the US-Israeli war with Iran have put a range of races across the farm state in play.
Three of the state's four House districts will be competitive this year.
In the southeast corner of the state, Democrat Christina Bohannan is challenging Republican Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks for a third time, after losing by 799 votes in 2024.
The state's northeast corner hosts a matchup for an open seat between Democratic state Representative Lindsay James, a Presbyterian minister, and former Republican state Representative Joe Mitchell.
Democrats are running another member of the clergy, Lutheran pastor Sarah Trone Garriott, to take on Republican Representative Zach Nunn in a Des Moines-based district.
Michigan
Republican Representative Tom Barrett, narrowly elected in 2024, faces Democrat William Lawrence, a progressive climate activist, in this Lansing-area district.
New Jersey
Republican US Representative Tom Kean Jr., son of a former governor, has faced scrutiny for an extended absence from the House. Kean later said he was receiving treatment for depression. Navy pilot Rebecca Bennett is the Democratic nominee.
New York
Democrat Cait Conley, a former national security official, is challenging Representative Mike Lawler, one of the more moderate House Republicans, in this Hudson Valley district.
Ohio
Republican redistricting could complicate the reelection prospects of Democrat Marcy Kaptur, who first won office in 1982. She faces a rematch with Republican Derek Merrin, a former state representative.
Pennsylvania
Three Republican incumbents in Pennsylvania will face tough reelection battles this year.
In an Allentown-based district, Representative Ryan Mackenzie, who is finishing up his first term, faces Democrat Bob Brooks, a firefighter union leader who is emphasizing his blue-collar background.
In a neighboring district that covers the northeastern corner of the state, Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti is challenging another freshman, Republican Representative Rob Bresnahan.
Republican Representative Scott Perry faces former news anchor Janelle Stelson in a rematch in Pennsylvania's Harrisburg-area district after narrowly defeating her in 2024.
Texas
Republican-led Texas imposed a new congressional map that could help the party pick up as many as five House seats. But three districts in the south of the state are shaping up as competitive races.
In a district that runs along the border with Mexico, Republican Tano Tijerina, the top elected official in Webb County, is trying to unseat Democratic Representative Henry Cuellar.
Along the southern Gulf Coast, Republican Eric Flores, a former federal prosecutor, is challenging Democratic Representative Vicente Gonzalez.
In a neighboring inland district, Democrats have recruited a Tejano musician, Bobby Pulido, to take on Republican Representative Monica De La Cruz.
Virginia
In the Virginia Beach-area district, Republican Representative Jen Kiggans will again face Democrat Elaine Luria, whom she defeated in 2022.
Wisconsin
In western Wisconsin, Democrat Rebecca Cooke is hoping voter unhappiness with rising farm costs will help her unseat Republican Representative Derrick Van Orden.

UN rights chief urges states to refer Myanmar situation to ICC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
11:40:22 UTC
20:40:22 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
The UN human rights chief on Monday urged member states to refer the situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court (ICC), warning that years of international efforts have failed to resolve the country's worsening human rights crisis.
 
Speaking at the 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, Volker Turk also called on states to end transfers of arms, ammunition, jet fuel, and dual-use items to Myanmar "where there is a clear risk they could facilitate violations of international human rights and humanitarian law."
 
Credible sources verified the killing of more than 1,200 civilians during the reporting period, while open sources indicate the actual figure could exceed 3,000, Turk said. Airstrikes remained the leading cause of civilian deaths.
 
He also highlighted the "catastrophic" situation of Rohingya in Rakhine, saying they face "widespread and systematic" violations and abuses, including arbitrary arrests, torture, sexual and gender-based violence, enforced disappearance, forced labor and recruitment by both the military and the Arakan Army.
 
Turk warned against efforts to normalize relations with Myanmar's military without evidence that it is complying with its obligations under international law.
 
“We need more than so-called ‘calibrated engagement’; we need human-rights-based engagement,” he said, adding that any engagement should be conditioned on ending violence, allowing humanitarian access and releasing those arbitrarily detained.
 
Turk also warned there could be “no question” of returning Rohingya and other refugees amid current insecurity, saying such returns would constitute a “flagrant breach” of the non-refoulement principle.
 
"And I call for all States to support the people of Myanmar politically and financially, in their demands for democracy, justice, and human rights," he concluded.
 
'Serious' int'l crimes committed frequently
 
Nicholas Koumjian, chief of the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar, meanwhile, also told the UN Human Rights Council that "serious" international crimes were being committed with "greater frequency and intensity."
 
He said investigators had identified military units involved in aerial attacks and the airbases from which they operate, while also documenting an increase in "double-tap" strikes in which second attacks hit first responders and people assisting the wounded.
 
The mechanism has also collected evidence from more than 1,600 sources and over 750 witness testimonies as part of efforts to identify those responsible for international crimes.
 
He noted that the International Court of Justice held hearings concerning Myanmar’s obligations under the Genocide Convention earlier this year, and the mechanism provided much of the evidence before the judges in that case.

The cognitive domain is the operational space or dimension in which human thinking, perception of reality, beliefs, emotions and social attitudes are shaped. The term is used in military affairs, geopolitics and strategic communications. Unlike traditional physical domains (land, sea, air) or technological ones (space, cyberspace), the cognitive domain encompasses the human mind and the information environment that shapes it.

Tight security around Putin in Vladivostok
Security measures were visibly reinforced during Putin’s visit to the forum.

The unusual escort came amid Ukraine’s expanding drone operations inside Russia and concerns that small unmanned aircraft could bypass conventional security measures.
