Israeli researchers find startling clue to black-eye disease in cats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:59:37 UTC
19:59:37 KST

It's an uncertain world but there's one thing you can bet the bank on: Mittens will resist being medicated. Signs of a pet cat suffering can be taken as indicative that you will too.
Persians, Himalayans and other brachycephalic "pug" breeds may seem fluffy and docile, but they have fangs and claws, and sadly, they're also particularly prone to a mysterious condition called feline corneal sequestra, or "black eye lesion" disease.
The condition also occurs in other predisposed breeds, including the Sphynx, even though its face isn't brachycephalic – it isn't pushed in.
Now a discovery by Israeli researchers sheds new light on this strange disease, which appears as a dark, spreading stain in the cat's eye. Iron and bromine were detected in the diseased part of corneas but not in the normal control corneas analyzed, Oren Pe'er, Lionel Sebbag and Ron Ofri reported last month in the journal Veterinary Ophthalmology.
Though their paper is called "The Role of Trace Elements in the Formation of Feline Corneal Sequestra," the researchers do not purport to know exactly what that role is. The study does not establish whether iron and bromine cause the lesion, contribute to its development or accumulate because of tissue damage.
So the cause of black eye remains unknown; the study merely identifies iron and bromine's presence in sequestral tissue and raises questions about their possible involvement in the disease process.
Cat owners need to know about this condition because it's usually painful and, if untreated, the lesion may progressively deepen within the cornea. Some cats develop sequestra in both eyes, either simultaneously or at different times, and advanced lesions may leave your cat blind as a bat.
What should the kitty owner be on the lookout for? A discoloration of the eye ranging in color from reddish to light brown to ebon black. "We don't know what gives the color," Pe'er says. Previous studies have investigated several possible sources of this pigmentation, including iron, melanin and porphyrins, but the exact origin remains unresolved, he adds.
Feline herpesvirus-1 has been proposed as one of several possible factors associated with corneal sequestra, alongside chronic corneal irritation, genetic predisposition and abnormalities to the tear film – the eye's super-thin liquid outer layer. But the exact cause remains unclear.
"The new findings raise the possibility that iron- and bromine-associated biochemical processes may be involved in the tissue changes seen in sequestra, including oxidative damage and stromal degeneration," Pe'er says. "Whether these elements contribute to the disease or accumulate as a consequence of tissue injury remains unknown."
Absent knowledge on causation, the key treatment for black eye remains surgical removal of the dead tissue, Sebbag says.
He adds that possibly more than one cause or compound may underlie the disease, which is exactly the sort to give cat owners the nightmare of dilemma. Which is – take him or her to the vet, causing suffering and pain to everybody involved but hopefully help; or steer clear of the vet to spare the stress but possibly causing the little darling more suffering. Might the condition pass on its own?
No, not normally. In isolated cases, the eye heals itself, sloughing off the necrotic tissue spontaneously. The process, if it happens at all, can take months. But in the meantime, Mittens is hurting. "The lesion can get deeper and harder," Sebbag notes.
So at what point should we take our furry friend to the vet? Basically, when we see the lesion, but it isn't a drop-everything-and-rush situation, Sebbag says. "The condition progresses slowly. It won't progress to perforation of the eye or blindness within 24 hours," he advises, but you definitely want to take your friend to the doctor within a week.
Note that not all cats clearly demonstrate suffering. Some may rock on for a while, but you don't want the lesion to get worse.
Why are brachycephalic cats more prone? Pe'er and Sebbag note that one reason could be that pushed-in facial structure. Persian and Himalayan cats were bred for prominent eyes and relatively large eyelid openings, which unhappily increases the risk to their corneas. Abnormalities of the tear film and reduced corneal sensitivity may further compromise the eye's surface.
Why some cats heal and some don't remains unknown. Future studies will be needed to determine where iron and bromine are located within the lesion and whether they contribute to tissue damage or are a consequence of it.
Ultimately, understanding these mechanisms could help identify new therapeutic approaches beyond surgery, Pe'er says.
Ahead of developing, one day, eyedrops or some less invasive treatment, how does the operation go? Gingerly. The feline cornea is about half a millimeter thick, and the vets operate under a microscope, removing the sequestrum while preserving as much healthy corneal tissue as possible. When a sequestrum extends deep, its removal may leave a substantial defect that requires additional structural support, using a graft or another reconstructive technique for the cornea.
The study included nine cats with corneal sequestra, representing 11 affected eyes because two cats had it on both sides, as well as four control cats with clinically normal corneas collected postmortem, Pe'er says. In the samples analyzed, neither bromine nor iron was detected in the control corneas, whereas both elements were detected in sequestral tissue.
Is that a big enough sample size? Pe'er acknowledges that the sample was small, reflecting the difficulty of obtaining surgically excised corneal tissue suitable for analysis, but statistically significant differences were identified for both iron and bromine. So, yes.
The bottom line is that the findings don't show cause but raise important questions about the biology of the disease. What can you do in the meantime? If you notice a new brown or black spot in Mittens' eye, don't wait for any caterwauling but human up and take the cute little beast to the vet.

Russian Airlines Face Superjet Fleet Loss Without State Engine Subsidies
Russian airlines will face a gradual loss of their Sukhoi Superjet 100 (SSJ-100) fleets because they cannot afford to replace the aircraft’s foreign-made engines with domestic ones without significant government subsidies, Aeroflot CEO Sergei Alexandrovsky warned, The Moscow Times reported on September 7.
Speaking to the Russian state media outlet, Alexandrovsky stated that installing the import-substituted engines is only feasible “with certain measures of state support,” The Moscow Times wrote. He cautioned that a lack of government subsidization for the re-engining process would inevitably lead to “a gradual phase-out of the fleet for all companies operating the SSJ-100.”
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The struggle to replace domestic engines is part of a larger technical crisis facing Russia’s commercial aviation sector under Western sanctions. Between 2023 and 2025, Russian authorities suspended the operations of over 480 aircraft, nearly half of the country’s entire commercial fleet.
This happened due to severe technical defects and falsified maintenance records. Safety regulators found widespread non-compliance with flight fitness requirements driven by airlines' inability to access authorized repairs and spare parts.
While Alexandrovsky did not specify the exact volume of state funding required, he noted that airlines will be forced to compensate for the retiring planes by redistributing flight hours across their remaining fleets and relying on the introduction of new MS-21 aircraft, according to The Moscow Times.
The financial and economic viability of re-engining the SSJ-100 has been a pressing crisis for the Russian aviation industry since 2022. That year, the French aerospace company Safran withdrew from its joint venture with Russia’s United Engine Corporation (UEC), The Moscow Times noted. Safran was previously responsible for manufacturing and servicing the hot section of the Superjet’s original SaM-146 engines.
Industry sources estimated the cost of replacing the SaM-146 engines with Russia’s domestic PD-8 engines at 2.1 to 2.3 billion rubles (24.2$ million to 26.5$ million) per aircraft, The Moscow Times reported.
However, some insiders warned that this figure is likely an underestimate, pointing out that the production cost of a single PD-8 already exceeded 1 billion rubles (11.5$ million) in 2024 and has continued to rise. While some hope the price will drop once serial assembly begins, lingering doubts remain over whether UEC can actually manufacture the PD-8 engines in sufficient quantities.
The re-engineering process is also highly complex. According to The Moscow Times, the SSJ-100 manufacturer acknowledged in 2023 that the overhaul requires state support because it involves far more than simply swapping the engines; engineers must also replace engine nacelles and extensively modify wing pylons, the wing box, onboard cable networks, and auxiliary power unit systems.
Due to expiring engine lifespans, UEC previously forecasted the retirement of nearly the entire existing SSJ-100 fleet by 2030, The Moscow Times reported. Russian airlines currently operate around 160 of the aircraft, with 78 flying for Rossiya Airlines, a subsidiary of the Aeroflot Group.
During operator meetings at the United Aircraft Corporation (UAC), industry representatives concluded that it only makes economic sense to replace engines on approximately 50 aircraft due to severe lifespan limitations on other critical components, according to The Moscow Times.
However, UAC head Vadim Badeha later offered a conflicting assessment, claiming that engines could be replaced on 50 to 100 aircraft. Contradicting the Aeroflot CEO’s warnings, Badeha asserted that the cost to airlines would not be prohibitive and that state assistance would not be required.
In a separate legal development regarding Russian aviation, Canada’s Federal Court recently upheld Ottawa’s refusal to lift sanctions against Russian cargo operator Volga-Dnepr Airlines. The ruling maintains the sanctions and serves as a test of Canada’s enforcement framework, which allows for the seizure and forfeiture of sanctioned assets.
The decision keeps Volga-Dnepr’s Antonov An-124 cargo aircraft grounded at Toronto Pearson Airport, where it was seized following the 2022 invasion. The Canadian government has indicated that if the aircraft is permanently forfeited, its value could be redistributed as direct support for Ukraine.

The Oreshnik is a Russian intermediate-range ballistic missile system that Moscow has presented as a new weapon capable of striking targets deep inside Europe. Russia first used an Oreshnik missile against Ukraine in November 2024, striking the city of Dnipro.
Oreshnik has been stationed in Belarus
Russia has maintained Oreshnik missile systems in Belarus since at least December 2025, when Belarusian leader Aliaksandr Lukashenka said an Oreshnik system had been placed on combat duty there as part of expanded military cooperation with Moscow.
The system is capable of carrying nuclear warheads, although Russia has used Oreshnik against Ukraine in a non-nuclear strike. Ukrainian intelligence has previously said the deployment is aimed in part at increasing pressure on Europe and NATO by shortening the missile's flight time to European targets.
The Oreshnik systems in Belarus remain under Russian control rather than Belarusian command, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
Nuclear-capable but carrying concrete: Expert explains Russia’s Oreshnik is psychological weapon, not military one
Belarus allows Russia to use its territory to guide drone strikes
Ivashchenko also said Belarus has allowed Russia to deploy radio-signal repeaters that help guide Russian Shahed-type attack drones toward Ukrainian civilian and critical infrastructure targets.
“If Belarus did not give such permission, this indicates that Minsk no longer controls Russia’s activities on its own territory,” he said, according to Ukrinform.
The use of Belarusian territory to support Russian attacks has stopped short of Belarusian forces directly entering the war, but it demonstrates Minsk's growing role in enabling Russia's military operations.
That cooperation makes the prospect of Russia using Belarusian territory for additional military capabilities less remote, particularly as Moscow expands its forces and intensifies attacks on Kyiv from the northern direction.
Renewed concern over a northern Russian offensive
The comments come as Russian strikes on Kyiv have intensified in recent weeks, while Ukrainian officials have increasingly warned about the possibility of another Russian offensive from the north toward Kyiv and Chernihiv.
There is no reported Russian ground offensive from Belarus underway. But the northern direction remains a major concern for Ukraine because of the precedent set in 2022, when Russian forces crossed from Belarus and advanced toward Kyiv before withdrawing in early April.
For now, Ivashchenko assesses the military threat from Belarus as low. The deployment of Russian missile forces nevertheless adds another significant Russian weapons capability to Belarus, while leaving open questions about how Moscow could use the territory in a future escalation.

US airman's widow denied benefits as Iran conflict 'not a war'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:55:59 UTC
19:55:59 KST

Breadcrumb
US military denied widow benefits because Iran conflict 'not a war'
The widow of a US airman killed while taking part in logistical operations during the war on Iran has criticised the US Air Force after she was initially told her husband was not eligible for some combat-related benefits because Washington was not technically “at war”.
Major John Alexander “Alex” Klinner, 33, was one of six US service members killed when a KC-135 refuelling aircraft crashed in western Iraq on 12 March while supporting operations against Iran.
The dispute comes more than six months into the US war with Iran, which has killed at least 18 US service members and wounded 790, according to the Associated Press.
Despite the toll and continuing exchanges of fire, the Trump administration has resisted describing the conflict as a war.
US forces struck targets in Iran twice this week, while Tehran retaliated against US allies in the Gulf as well as tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
Klinner’s widow, Libby Klinner, said the Air Force contacted her this week to clarify that her husband’s final pay did include combat-related hazard pay and tax benefits.
The move came after a social media post in which she said she had previously been told by a military official that her husband was not eligible for some benefits because the United States “was not at war”.
“My husband lost his life because we’re in a war, and then I was told that because it’s not technically a war, we lose out on something,” Klinner told the Associated Press. “It all comes down to principle.”
Her post gained widespread attention in the United States and prompted Vice President JD Vance to promise to look into the case after being questioned about it at a White House briefing.
“We want to be as helpful as we can and ensure she gets everything that she is entitled to,” Vance said.
“My message to her would be, ‘We love ya, we’re grateful for the sacrifice and we very much take very seriously our commitment to get you what you need to get.’”
But when asked separately about the US military campaign against Iran, Vance rejected the term “war”, saying there was “no active shooting”.
His comments came despite the continued exchanges between the two sides, including the US strikes on Iran that week.
President Donald Trump defended Vance’s remarks on Friday, describing the US strikes as “intermittent”.
“I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
The dispute over terminology also comes as Washington has altered the way it records casualties from the confrontation with Iran.
In late July, the Trump administration created a separate category in the Pentagon’s casualty tracking system for those killed and wounded in renewed US-Iran fighting.
Pentagon officials said the change came after “Operation Epic Fury”, the original name for US combat operations against Tehran, had ended.
Since 7 July, all US casualties in the Middle East have instead been recorded under the category “Overseas Operations”.
Klinner said Air Force officials later acknowledged that she had initially been given inaccurate information.
She said officials told her that her husband’s final pay had already included combat-related hazard pay and tax exemptions, but that the payments had been incorrectly itemised, causing confusion.
The Air Force said it had spoken to Klinner to ensure all her questions were addressed and confirmed that all eligible combat-theatre benefits had been included in her husband’s pay.
Combat-related hazard pay is worth $225 a month and does not require a formal declaration of war. Eligibility is instead based on serving in an area where troops face a serious risk of physical injury or hostile fire.

Ukrainian drone blitz hits 3 Russian oil refineries, Zelensky confirms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:54:15 UTC
19:54:15 KST

Ukrainian long-range drones targeted three oil refineries across Russia, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 7.
"Our soldiers continue to respond fairly to Russian strikes on Ukraine. An oil refinery was hit in the Ryazan region. Our long-range force was used against oil refineries in the Perm region and Tatarstan," Zelensky said in a post on social media.
Ukrainian drones also struck a launch and storage site for strike drones in Russia's Kursk Oblast and "a target" in the Black Sea, he added without providing further details, though he did attach a video of highlights.
Zelensky's statement came as Telegram reports, some of which included geolocated details, said that Ukrainian drones struck the LUKOIL-Permnefteorgsintez refinery, one of Russia's largest oil refineries in Perm, located more than 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukraine.
Videos shared by the Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ purportedly show Ukrainian long-range drones flying over Perm and smoke rising from the oil refinery amid explosions.
Independent Russian outlet Astra had earlier said on Sept. 6 that Ryazan Oil Refinery Plant, part of Russia's state-controlled oil giant Rosneft, was struck again, following attacks in May and July. With a capacity to process about 17 million tons of oil per year, it produces a wide range of oil products, including automobile gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation kerosene, fuel oil, and liquefied gases. The facility is located about 500 kilometers (310 miles) from Ukraine.
Elsewhere in Russia, NASA's FIRMS detected a thermal anomaly at the Taganrog-Central military airfield in Taganrog, near Rostov-on-Don in Rostov Oblast, Militarnyi reported. FIRMS uses satellite instruments to detect thermal anomalies and active fires on Earth's surface. Exilenova+ reported that local residents had reported an attack on Taganrog earlier on Sept. 7.
The Kyiv Independent cannot verify the claims or the extent of the damage caused. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attacks.
Without acknowledging any of the reported attacks, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed on Sept. 7 that it downed or intercepted 306 Ukrainian drones overnight, including over Perm Krai, Rostov Oblast, and Kursk Oblast. It didn't mention Ryazan Oblast in its report. 
The new reported strikesagainst Perm's oil refinery are the latest in a series of attacks that temporarily suspended operations at the site in August. The facility processes more than 13 million metric tons of crude oil annually and produces gasoline, diesel fuel, jet fuel, and lubricating oils.
Ukrainian forces had previously struck the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery on July 29 as part of Ukraine's broader missile and drone campaign against Russian energy and oil infrastructure far from Ukraine. 
On Sept. 5, a pro-Ukraine partisan force, Atesh, announced that it had recruited a defector from the Russian military who then destroyed a communications tower near Perm, hindering coordination between security forces in the area. The sabotage reportedly cleared the way for Ukrainian drones to again strike the refinery on Aug. 21. 
In Taganrog, Ukrainian forces previously struck a Russian defense industry facility on April 19. The targeted site was the Atlant-Aero plant, which develops and manufactures strike and reconnaissance drones for the Russian military. A fire broke out at the facility following the strike.

Russia and North Korea Open First Road Bridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:52:49 UTC
19:52:49 KST

Russia and North Korea opened the first road bridge linking the two countries on Monday, coming after months of construction delays.
Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song presided over a ceremony via video link to mark the official launch of traffic along the two-lane bridge, which stretches one kilometer (0.6 miles) over the Tumen River.
Mishustin hailed bilateral relations as being at an “unprecedentedly high level of comprehensive strategic partnership,” adding that the bridge, which cost 9 billion rubles ($104 million), would boost trade and tourism.
A rail bridge, built in the 1950s, already connects the two countries.
The new road bridge is named after Yakov Novichenko, a Soviet officer who saved North Korean founder Kim Il Sung by shielding him from a grenade explosion in Pyongyang in 1946.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed the formal construction agreement during a 2024 summit in Pyongyang.
Work on the bridge began in April 2025. North Korea completed its section ahead of a planned June 19, 2026 deadline, while construction delays on the Russian side pushed the opening back by several months.
According to news agency Interfax, the bridge and its newly constructed border checkpoint, which connects the Far East Primorye region with North Korea, are designed to process up to 300 vehicles and 2,300 people daily.
Some observers have said that the bridge will provide Russia and North Korea an additional route through which they can discreetly move military cargo and personnel.
In 2025, North Korea’s shipments of rocket artillery, shells and short-range ballistic missiles to Russia were estimated to be between $7 billion and $13.8 billion, according to the Institute for National Security Strategy, a government-funded research institute in South Korea.
Russia and North Korea have deepened military ties since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. In 2024, the two countries signed a mutual defense treaty that requires them to provide military support if either is attacked.

What AfD's election victory in Germany's Saxony-Anhalt could mean for Jewish life - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:52:29 UTC
19:52:29 KST

MAGDEBURG – The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has scored a historic victory in Saxony-Anhalt, falling just three seats short of an absolute majority. Its rise could reshape Holocaust education and remembrance policy, while a small party critical of Israel may now hold the balance of power.
The AfD scored a historic victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, winning 43,8% of the vote – over twice as much as the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which received 17,2%. However, victory does not yet mean power: The party won 39 of the 83 seats in the state parliament, three more seats needed to secure an absolute majority.
The face of this success is 35-year-old Ulrich Siegmund. He called the election result a “mandate to govern.” Legally, however, no such mandate exists: The minister-president will be whoever can secure the necessary majority in the state parliament.
Siegmund has succeeded in giving the radical party a friendly, modern image. He smiles for the camera, films videos for social media, shares family celebrations, and poses for photos with voters. One of the symbols of his campaign has been mass rides on Simson mopeds.
But Simson was founded by a Jewish family whose property was confiscated under the Nazis. The founders’ descendants protested the AfD’s use of the brand, saying that its political appropriation was a mockery of their family’s history. Siegmund, however, continued to use the mopeds as a symbol of East German pride.
Concept of 'remigration' for 'insufficiently assimilated'
In November 2023, Siegmund attended a meeting of AfD representatives and right-wing extremists near Potsdam, where Austrian far-right activist Martin Sellner presented his concept of “remigration.”
The concept applied not only to asylum seekers but also to German citizens of immigrant origin who were deemed insufficiently “assimilated.”
At the same meeting, Siegmund presented his Vision 2026 – a plan for the AfD to come to power in Saxony-Anhalt. Following the publication of an investigative report, he was removed as chair of the state parliament’s committee on social affairs, though this did not hinder his political career.
SIEGMUND HAS also faced criticism over his attitude toward Germany’s Nazi past.
In a 2025 interview, he was asked whether he considered the Holocaust the most horrific crime in human history. Siegmund refused to give a direct answer, saying that he did not consider himself qualified to rank crimes in history. Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, called the response a relativization of the Shoah.
At Siegmund’s events, the host would shout “Sieg,” and the audience would respond with “Mund.” In the German context, the association with the Nazi slogan is obvious. Siegmund dismissed the criticism, asking what was wrong with supporters chanting his last name.
Following the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, Siegmund also stopped short of directly condemning Hamas or expressing solidarity with Israel in comments reported by German public broadcaster MDR.
Instead, he said that the state parliament was not in a position to change the geopolitical situation and that the main task was to prevent “the conflicts of this world” from spilling over into Germany.
In the run-up to the election, the Union of Jewish Students in Germany ran a campaign in Saxony-Anhalt under the slogan “Demokratiefeinde ANHALTen.” In videos published by the organization, some AfD supporters express support for Hitler’s policies. Other videos from AfD events, filmed by independent bloggers, show people performing the Nazi salute or denying the Holocaust.
At the same time, some Jewish voters themselves support the AfD, primarily because of the party’s hardline stance on migration and political Islam. There is even a small organization in Germany called “Jews in the AfD” (Juden in der AfD), whose chairman said in 2025 that it had 22 full members.
After October 7, this argument gained additional weight. Antisemitic incidents in Germany increased sharply, and the AfD regularly presents itself as a defender of Jews against so-called “imported antisemitism.”
Yet a state government cannot close Germany’s borders, independently determine federal migration policy, or shape Germany’s foreign policy. It does, however, have direct influence over schools and Holocaust education, cultural policy, the police, state-level domestic intelligence, and the allocation of public funds.
After the election results were announced, Schuster said he was personally appalled by the AfD’s result and singled out education policy in particular.
He said that education plays a central role in combating antisemitism, and the damage caused by an AfD government could be enormous.
The AfD wants to strengthen the state government’s influence over standardized teaching materials. The party also intends to abolish the State Center for Political Education (Landeszentrale für politische Bildung) in its current form and replace it with an institute for “civic and political education and cultural identity.” The current center focuses on political education and funds external projects, including initiatives against racism and extremism.
AfD platform criticized German 'guilt complex'
In its platform, the AfD argues that Germany’s approach to its historical responsibility has created a persistent “guilt complex,” weakened national pride, and hindered the formation of a stable national identity.
THE PARTY also calls for a different approach to commemorating German soldiers who served during World War II, emphasizing their courage and sacrifice for their country. Kai Langer, director of the Saxony-Anhalt Memorial Foundation, has warned that the AfD does not directly deny the Holocaust or the Wehrmacht’s war crimes but pushes them into the past as issues that have already been “settled,” while seeking to establish a more positive national historical narrative.
The AfD also wants to cut funding for school trips to memorial sites dedicated to victims of National Socialism while devoting greater attention to the maintenance of war memorials.
One of the party’s specific targets is the German Lost Art Foundation (Deutsches Zentrum Kulturgutverluste) in Magdeburg. It funds provenance research into cultural property, including works of art seized from Jews and other victims of Nazi persecution.
The AfD promises to completely eliminate Saxony-Anhalt’s funding for the foundation.
The party’s platform states that provenance research places museum collections under unjustified suspicion and that research conducted without an existing, specific restitution claim artificially perpetuates a sense of German guilt.
The German Lost Art Foundation itself has warned that the AfD’s plans would primarily affect victims of Nazi persecution and extermination and call into question a research-based culture of remembrance.
It remains unclear whether the AfD will be able to implement this program. The party holds 39 of 83 seats. The CDU, SPD, Greens, and the Left Party (Die Linke) together also have 39 lawmakers. Another five seats went to the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), a party founded in 2024 by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht that combines left-wing economic policies with a hardline stance on migration and opposes arms deliveries to Ukraine while advocating closer ties with Russia.
BSW has ruled out a formal coalition with the AfD but is open to cooperation on specific issues. Even individual votes from its lawmakers could therefore prove decisive.
The party has also taken a sharply critical stance toward Israel. BSW has repeatedly called for a German arms embargo on Israel, while its Saxony-Anhalt election platform calls for an end to German arms deliveries to Israel, recognition of a Palestinian state, an end to the Israeli occupation, and the suspension of the EU-Israel Association Agreement.
In 2024, Wagenknecht and other BSW lawmakers also introduced a motion in the Bundestag calling on the German government to revoke arms export licenses for Israel and impose an arms embargo over the war in Gaza.
Wagenknecht’s clashes over Israel predate the current war by many years.
In January 2010, Israeli president Shimon Peres addressed the Bundestag on International Holocaust Remembrance Day. After his speech, the parliament gave him a standing ovation, but Wagenknecht and two other lawmakers from the Left Party remained seated.
Wagenknecht later explained that she had stood during the commemoration of Holocaust victims but refused to join the ovation for Peres because of the Israeli government’s policies.
The results of the September 6 election have not yet brought the AfD to power. Yet nearly 44% of voters have turned a party that seeks to reshape Holocaust education and Germany’s culture of remembrance into the largest parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt.

Fighting increases in Yemen as Houthis look to al-Mandab Strait as potential pressure point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:52:20 UTC
19:52:20 KST

Reports in Yemen suggest that Yemen’s government forces have made some limited gains against the Houthis.
The Houthis have dominated a swath of Yemen since 2015. Over the past decade, they have consolidated control and launched attacks against Saudi Arabia, Israel, and other countries.
They are backed by Iran, which now has fewer funds to support them. This could cause setbacks.
Nevertheless, the Houthis could seek to threaten Bab el-Mandeb, a key strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. They could do this to try to reduce pressure on Iran.
Both the Houthis and government forces have been increasing their attacks, but it is still not clear how much the conflict has escalated.
Government continues combating Houthi attacks, targeting Houthi fighters
Yemeni government forces had taken full control of the Hays district in Hodeidah province and made gains in Taiz and Al-Jawf, as Houthi forces fired three ballistic missiles at Taiz city, according to Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), Syria’s official news agency, and Saudi-based news channel Al Arabiya.
SANA cited Yemen’s Saba News Agency, which itself quoted a Yemeni military source as “saying government forces secured the remaining rural areas of Hays on Saturday evening. Hays city was already under government control.”
“Government forces had begun operations in neighboring Al-Jarrahi district and advanced toward Houthi positions,” the report said. “The military reported Houthi casualties but gave no figures.”
Meanwhile, clashes broke out along a front line in Taiz province. The clashes have taken place in numerous areas. Jawf is close to Saudi Arabia in northern Yemen, whereas Taiz is in the mountains closer to Mocha and the Red Sea.
“Government forces said they captured several positions on the Hayfan front during clashes with Houthi forces,” SANA reported.
The Houthis fired ballistic missiles that targeted Taiz, the report said.
“The attack came a day after a Houthi ballistic missile struck a civilian gathering in Taiz province, killing four people and [wounding] nine others, according to [Saba News Agency],” SANA reported.
IN AL-JAWF, Yemeni Armed Forces spokesperson Col. Majed al-Nuzaili said government forces had targeted Houthi fighters, the report said. Government forces reported shooting down several Houthi drones on other fronts, including one east of Al-Hazm.
“Fighting continues in Hodeidah, Taiz, and Al-Jawf between government forces and the Houthis,” SANA reported.
Al Arabiya reported: “Yemeni armed forces gained control of Jabal Koura in the Kadha area, west of Taiz, after a bloody night of fighting against the militias.”
“A military source told Al Arabiya/Al Hadath that the forces had taken control of Jabal al-Koura and a security point that belonged to the Houthis, while clashes were taking place on the hills of Al-Hanaya and the vicinity of Jabal Ghubari, west of Al-Kadha,” the report said.
The government forces also launched several other raids in various areas, Al Arabiya reported.
“The Yemeni Armed Forces Media Center reported that warplanes carried out a series of raids targeting a command and control room, a thermal sensor system, and Houthi gatherings on the top of Mount Nasa in the Maris front in Al-Dhale’ Province,” the report said.
It was not clear what types of air assets the government of Yemen has. “Yemeni forces announced they had taken control of the city of Hays, southeast of Hodeidah,” Al Arabiya reported.
The battles are taking place within the context of a Houthi offensive aimed at cutting off access to the coastal city of Mocha. This area has been under attack for a month.
A military source in the internationally recognized government, based in the southern city of Aden, confirmed that “the armed forces were able to consolidate their positions north of Hays after advancing in the area,” Al Arabiya reported.
The Houthi advance could threaten the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. This would give an Iranian-backed group more ways to pressure the international community.
The overall picture suggests escalation in Yemen. There have been clashes over the past month in which Saudi Arabia was accused of targeting Sanaa International Airport because Iran was trying to reopen an air corridor to the airport. The Houthis then attacked Saudi Arabia.
“These battles came in the context of the recent renewed escalation in the region between Iran and America, and since last July, Yemen has returned to the forefront of regional tension, with renewed attacks and threats by the Houthis against cargo ships and maritime traffic,” Al Arabiya reported.
The reports indicate that there is fighting at several fronts over key areas of Yemen, near the coast, and near Saudi Arabia. The Yemen government is trying to use its limited air power in strikes in the governorates of Al-Bayda and Al-Jawf, as well as in Ma’rib and Taiz.
The Houthis “attempted to advance towards government-held areas near the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait,” Al Arabiya reported. “However, Yemeni forces repelled these attacks and made territorial gains, particularly west of Taiz and in Al-Jawf. They captured Jabal al-Koura, while clashes continued on the hills.”

Israel must implement its commitments under the Gaza peace roadmap for the process to move forward, Nickolay Mladenov, High Representative for Gaza at the Board of Peace, said on Monday.
Speaking at the third Hili Forum in Abu Dhabi, Mladenov said progress had been made compared to a year ago, but the situation remained far from what was needed to achieve a political solution.
“We are still at the point at which we need to make sure that what has been agreed is going to be implemented and is going to change significantly the lives of the people in Gaza,” he said.
“Unfortunately, we’re not there yet,” he added, saying discussions were continuing with Israel on “the implementation of their part of the commitments” required to move the process forward, referring to its withdrawal in exchange for disarmament of Hamas and reconstruction to begin in the Palestinian enclave.
Mladenov pointed to seven months of negotiations with Hamas on disarmament, describing them as “very intense, very difficult discussions,” and praised the mediation efforts of Türkiye, Egypt and Qatar, as well as support from the UAE and other regional countries.
He said the people in Gaza continued to live in “terrible conditions” and could not face another winter under the current circumstances.
Mladenov outlined three possible paths: maintaining the current situation, expanding Israeli military operations and reoccupying Gaza, or implementing the Board of Peace roadmap.
He described the third option as the “reasonable” one, saying it requires disarmament by agreement, an agreed Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction with international and regional support.
Mladenov warned that failure to advance the roadmap could make the two-state solution “practically impossible.”
“The only way that we can build back to that is if we have transitional governance, if we have decommissioning of weapons, if we have withdrawal in Gaza,” he said.

He said the crisis had caused “massive emotional, political, human suffering” for Israelis, besides the humanitarian tragedy in Gaza, and argued that a longer-term perspective was needed despite the short-term political pressures of an election campaign.
“Neither Palestinians nor Israelis are going anywhere. Nobody is going to leave their homes,” he said, stressing the need to restore political dialogue and find a way for the two peoples to coexist.
The Board of Peace was established in January as part of US President Donald Trump’s broader plan for Gaza, with Trump serving as its chairman. The initiative, backed by UN Security Council Resolution 2803, is tasked with overseeing Gaza’s transition, including governance, security and reconstruction.
A Palestinian technocratic body, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, was also established to assume responsibility for civilian administration, restoring public services and rebuilding institutions in the enclave.
The Board of Peace issued a roadmap on July 31 for implementing the next phase of the Gaza plan, including Hamas’ disarmament, a phased Israeli withdrawal, transfer of administration to the Palestinian technocratic committee, deployment of an international stabilization force and reconstruction.
The third Hili Forum is being held in Abu Dhabi under the theme “Gulf at Crossroads: Conflict, Consequences and Course Correction.” It is co-organized by the Emirates Center for Strategic Studies and Research and the Anwar Gargash Diplomatic Academy.

Cutting support for Haredi families would weaken Israel’s demographic resilience, economy - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:52:01 UTC
19:52:01 KST

Israel enters the final stretch of its election campaign against a turbulent backdrop. Israel’s war with Iran has yet to yield an agreement preventing Tehran from developing nuclear weapons, the arrangement on the northern border still faces serious obstacles, and Hamas’ demilitarization is hardly around the corner.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Yet for many politicians, the campaign’s defining issue is not these security and diplomatic challenges, but the “Haredi question.” The conflict over conscripting yeshiva students has prompted a broader reassessment of the relationship between Haredi society and the state.
In this atmosphere, a policy paper presented by the Israel Democracy Institute at the 2026 Eli Hurvitz Conference on Economy and Society proposes reducing public support for Haredi families according to the number of their children.
It suggests conditioning child allowances, day care subsidies, housing assistance, and child-related tax credits on maximizing earning capacity or civic participation.
The paper distinguishes between protecting children’s basic needs and publicly funding what it calls a “high-fertility pattern.”
Proposal a step backward
This proposal is a step backward. It threatens one of Israel’s unique economic strengths while overlooking the real long-term danger: Not an excess of births, but a shortage.
The demographic crisis is no longer a distant forecast. Fertility in the European Union has fallen to roughly 1.4 children per woman, well below the replacement level of 2.1. In Italy and Spain, it is near 1.2, while South Korea’s rate has fallen below one. These countries face aging populations, labor shortages, growing pressure on pension and health care systems, and diminishing prospects for long-term growth.
Population decline can create a feedback loop. As populations shrink, the burden on younger generations grows, making it harder for young couples to raise families. Governments have tried to reverse the trend with little success.
Many countries have turned to immigration as a stopgap. Yet immigration offers only a temporary solution, as immigrants tend over time to adopt the lower fertility rates of their host countries. It can also produce integration difficulties, tensions over national and religious identity, and political polarization.
Israel's high fertility rate a boon
Europe is discovering that immigration may fill immediate labor shortages but cannot restore the social cohesion and intergenerational confidence weakened by family decline.
Japan has chosen to limit immigration to preserve social cohesion but pays a heavy economic price as its population falls by hundreds of thousands each year.
Against this backdrop, Israel is an anomaly. Its fertility rate remains close to three children per woman, making it the only Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development country safely above replacement level.
This is not a structural weakness of the Israeli economy. It is a singular strategic advantage.

Russia and North Korea Open First Road Bridge Across Shared Border

Russia and North Korea opened the first road bridge linking the two countries on Monday, coming after months of construction delays.
Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song presided over a ceremony via video link to mark the official launch of traffic along the two-lane bridge, which stretches one kilometer (0.6 miles) over the Tumen River.
Mishustin hailed bilateral relations as being at an “unprecedentedly high level of comprehensive strategic partnership,” adding that the bridge, which cost 9 billion rubles ($104 million), would boost trade and tourism.
A rail bridge, built in the 1950s, already connects the two countries.
The new road bridge is named after Yakov Novichenko, a Soviet officer who saved North Korean founder Kim Il Sung by shielding him from a grenade explosion in Pyongyang in 1946.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed the formal construction agreement during a 2024 summit in Pyongyang.
Work on the bridge began in April 2025. North Korea completed its section ahead of a planned June 19, 2026 deadline, while construction delays on the Russian side pushed the opening back by several months.
According to news agency Interfax, the bridge and its newly constructed border checkpoint, which connects the Far East Primorye region with North Korea, are designed to process up to 300 vehicles and 2,300 people daily.
Some observers have said that the bridge will provide Russia and North Korea an additional route through which they can discreetly move military cargo and personnel.
In 2025, North Korea’s shipments of rocket artillery, shells and short-range ballistic missiles to Russia were estimated to be between $7 billion and $13.8 billion, according to the Institute for National Security Strategy, a government-funded research institute in South Korea.
Russia and North Korea have deepened military ties since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. In 2024, the two countries signed a mutual defense treaty that requires them to provide military support if either is attacked.

AIIMS Delhi displays live population count of India: How does it get data on newly born babies?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:51:58 UTC
19:51:58 KST

AIIMS Delhi displays live population count of India: How does it get data on newly born babies?
TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Sep 07, 2026, 16:21 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
AIIMS population display (Instagram)
A digital clock is going viral in Delhi. Well, it’s not an ordinary clock. It’s a population counter clock which is displayed at All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS Delhi). It has recently attracted attention online, with the number on the screen changing continuously and appearing to show India’s population growing every second. Now, this viral display has also raised an important question: if the number increases every few seconds, is AIIMS actually receiving information every time a baby is born somewhere in India?So the answer is NO.It’s a population clock and it is an estimate based on demographic data and population projections. It’s not a nationwide live birth-tracking system. The distinction is important because India does have official systems for recording births and deaths. These systems do not work like a real-time national counter.A population clock, not a birth register
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare’s National Health Profile identifies the Census, registration of vital events, population surveys, population projections and the Sample Registration System (SRS) among the sources used for demographic information.
The Civil Registration System (CRS), maintained through the registration machinery of the government, is responsible for the continuous recording of vital events such as births and deaths. The Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner describes civil registration as the continuous, permanent and compulsory recording of the occurrence and characteristics of vital events.But this does not mean that a national population display receives an electronic notification every time a birth takes place in India.So why the number keeps changingNow this is where population estimation comes in. A population clock takes a known or estimated population at a particular reference point and applies demographic rates to project how that population changes over time.If the estimated population is expected to rise by a certain number over a year, the annual change can be mathematically distributed across months, days, hours, minutes and seconds. A digital display can therefore make the number appear to be changing in real time.If the display increases by one, it does not necessarily mean that a particular baby has just been born somewhere in India. It represents a calculated movement in the estimated population total.India's last completed population Census
A population clock (Instagram)
India's last completed population Census was conducted in 2011, when the country's population was recorded at about 121.1 crore. The National Health Profile notes that India's population was projected to increase from 121.1 crore in 2011 to 152.2 crore by 2036, an increase of about 25% over 25 years.The United Nations follows a similar demographic approach. Its World Population Prospects 2024 provides population estimates and projections based on analyses of historical demographic trends for countries and territories around the world.What about babies born at AIIMS?The fact that the clock is located at AIIMS can easily create another misconception that AIIMS might somehow be using its maternity records to calculate India's population.Instead, births are recorded through the country's civil registration framework, while demographic agencies use registration data, surveys and statistical methods to understand population trends.Why does the clock look so precise?That is perhaps the most fascinating part of the viral display.A computer can calculate an estimated population to several decimal places and refresh the display every second. That does not mean demographers know the exact number of people alive in India at that precise second.The changing digits are essentially a visualisation of a statistical model. It is similar to a countdown or a continuously updated financial index: the display can change every second even though the underlying information is based on data collected over a longer period.
The viral AIIMS population clock is therefore best understood as a demographic awareness tool, not as a nationwide surveillance mechanism for births.India's population is certainly changing continuously. Babies are being born, people are dying and migration changes the distribution of people across regions. So, the next time the AIIMS population clock ticks upward, it does not mean that a computer has just received the birth certificate of another Indian baby.

Israel's SpearUAV announces 1,000 suicide drones ready to deploy around the world

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:51:46 UTC
19:51:46 KST

SpearUAV, an Israeli defense tech company based in Tel Aviv, has close to 1,000 Viper 300 loitering munitions (LM) ready to deliver to customers around the world, the company has announced on Linkedin.
According to the company, the Viper 300 is an artificial intelligence (AI) based suicide drone that was designed for armored divisions, specialized ground forces, and tactical squads carrying out various missions - from reconnaissance and surveillance, asymmetric warfare, border patrol, homeland security, and even “the elimination of high-value targets.”
Weighing 2.8 kilograms, including capsule and payload, the suicide drone can be folded into a capsule or backpack. It has a range of five kilometers, an endurance of 20 minutes, and troops can launch the LM while on foot or from a platform.
The Viper 300’s design allows it to hover in place, and using its AI tools, provide immediate target acquisition for precise attacks. Operators can use the system after a short training period.
While the company didn’t disclose the end-users or the contracts involved, the company wrote in a LinkedIn post that “this significant milestone reflects the trust of our growing international customer base, which recognizes the operational value of SPEAR UAVs armed VIPER 300 system and its ability to deliver precise, mission-ready, and easy-to-use capability - on time and ready for use by any soldier, mounted or dismounted. Hundreds of systems a month - and counting.”
Combat proven
The company’s unique encapsulated weapons systems can be launched from the air, ground, and from the depth of the sea from submarines.
The Viper 300 is part of a broader group of systems, including the Viper 750 for naval use, and the Viper 1, which acts as an interceptor rather than striking targets. All are battle-proven, having been used across IDF corps and other militaries.
In June, Rafael and Spear announced a collaboration for another compact interceptor called the Iron Wasp, which can be launched from combat vehicles.
Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post has understood that the Viper 300 was developed with lessons learned from various combat zones, including the war in Ukraine.
“From conflict zones like Eastern Ukraine to border regions, the VIPER 300 is an invaluable tool for capturing real-time, high-resolution intelligence without tipping off adversaries,” the company wrote on its website.
The platform’s capabilities were designed to address operational requirements that have become increasingly relevant in modern battlefield environments and provide troops with a combination of real-time intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), and precision strike capabilities, while maintaining a low operational signature.
SpearUAV was founded in 2017 in the garage of co-founder and CTO Gadi Kuperman, and CEO Yiftach Kleinman. Former Mossad chief Yossi Cohen serves as chairman of the company’s advisory committee.

The US federal government will begin incorporating artificial intelligence into the interview and hiring process for some new employees in the coming days, CBS reported on Monday, citing US officials.
The government will test the technology using the platform CodeSignal on the "Tech Force," an initiative started eight months ago to recruit private-sector tech experts into two-year government posts, according to one official.
The federal government employs 1.9 million workers and has fallen behind the private sector in using AI interviewing tools as the first screening layer for large employers, CBS wrote.
AI is already used regularly in the Office of Personnel Management, the government's HR unit, with administrative staff having access to programs including Microsoft's Copilot, Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's ChatGPT, and Google's Gemini on their government computers. OPM also began using an AI tool to prepare job descriptions earlier this year.
OPM urges agencies to use AI
The personnel office issued guidance encouraging agencies to use AI in their hiring process with human oversight, especially in certain crucial personnel decisions.
Office director Scott Kupor has pushed to make the federal hiring process more efficient and has encouraged agency heads to hire at least a third of new hires from early-career professionals as the federal workforce continues to age, according to CBS.
CodeSignal will provide AI-powered tools to screen job applications in early rounds of the hiring process in the Tech Force hiring pilot program, with virtual AI agents handling interviews with phone, audio, and text-based options. Hiring managers will be sent transcribed recordings of candidates.
AI is likely to grow more common in the federal government hiring process, several officials told CBS.

07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Large-scale rubble removal in areas of Gaza under Israeli military control could erase evidence of atrocity crimes and hinder the recovery of human remains, UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territory Francesca Albanese warned Monday.
“The ongoing removal, crushing and relocation of rubble in Gaza must not destroy evidence of international crimes or prevent the recovery and identification of human remains in the besieged enclave,” Albanese said in a statement.
She stressed that Gaza's rubble contains human remains and physical evidence relevant to investigations into alleged international crimes, including genocide.
Palestinian authorities estimate more than 10,000 people remain buried under the debris.
Albanese said recovery and identification of human remains, systematic documentation, and preservation of potential evidence should take place before rubble is moved or crushed, calling for international criminal investigators to oversee evidence gathering.
She also warned states and companies involved in rubble removal that destroying evidence of international crimes could expose them to international criminal responsibility.
“Any removal must happen in the context of a plan designed by Palestinians and supported by actors who have the trust of Palestinians,” Albanese said.
“Destroying evidence of atrocity crimes is illegal,” she added, arguing that Gaza's reconstruction must not be "conditioned upon the erasure of its past and the evidence required to secure justice for its victims."

====================================================================================================

what kind of life should housing make possible? 33 projects offer answers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:50:09 UTC
19:50:09 KST

housing is not a fixed product: laura traub on how we live now
What should housing make possible today? In HOUSING — 33 Answers to the Housing Question, editors Jeanette Kunsmann and Laura Traub bring together projects from across Europe that approach this increasingly urgent question from different directions. The book looks beyond housing as a matter of units, square meters, and supply, examining social and cooperative housing, low-cost construction, shared living, renovation, and adaptive reuse.
For Laura Traub, one of the most significant changes is a shift in how we understand the home itself. ‘Home has become much more than simply a place where we live,’ she tells designboom. ‘It has become the center of our everyday lives and often also of our working lives.’ As households, careers, and care arrangements become less predictable, the model of housing as a fixed product increasingly struggles to accommodate the ways people actually live.
Across its 408 pages, HOUSING — 33 Answers to the Housing Question suggests that housing may need to become more adaptable, more connected to its surroundings, and more attentive to the existing structures and social systems shaping everyday life.
Council Apartments in Barcelona by Narch + Maira Arquitectes | image © Adrià Goula
WHEN HOME HAS TO ACCOMMODATE EVERYTHING
During the pandemic, domestic spaces had to absorb work, education, family life, leisure, and retreat, often simultaneously, the expanding role of the home particularly visible. ‘The way we live is much less static,’ Traub says. ‘Families change, we work differently, we move, we age, and our needs evolve throughout our lives.’
This instability challenges the assumption that a home can be designed as a finished and permanent answer. One project included in the book, by Buchner Bründler in Zurich, offers a broader way of thinking about the question, considering housing as part of a larger residential environment that combines different forms of dwelling with shared spaces and a relationship to its surroundings. ‘Perhaps this is the fundamental shift,’ Laura Traub reflects. ‘We need to think of housing less as a fixed product and more as something that evolves with the people who live in it.’
That distinction runs through the publication. The book is organized around three chapters — Social and Community Housing, Building Simply, and Renovate, Adapt and Build New — bringing together projects from Portugal to Bosnia and from Oslo to Basel. Their methods differ, but the larger question remains consistent: what happens when housing begins with changing conditions rather than a standardized idea of domestic life?
Council Apartments in Barcelona by Narch + Maira Arquitectes | image © Adrià Goula
THERE IS NO SINGLE ANSWER TO THE HOUSING QUESTION
The diversity of the projects featured in the book is central to its argument. Some address affordability and collective living and others work with limited resources or existing structures. What connects them, Traub suggests, is not a common formal language but a shared refusal of standardization.‘They question the idea that there is one standard answer to housing,’ the editor explains. ‘They come from very different contexts and work with very different means, but they all ask what people actually need and what can be achieved with the resources available.’
Kuku23 in Vienna illustrates this expanded understanding of residential architecture. The development combines around 430 subsidized apartments with ateliers, workshops, cultural uses, and shared spaces, connecting housing to work and neighborhood life. ‘The lesson is not that one of these projects should become a universal model. ‘For us, the lesson of the 33 projects is not that we need one new model,’ Traub shares with us, ‘but that we need a greater diversity of solutions that respond to their particular context and to the people who live there.’
Council Apartments in Barcelona by Narch + Maira Arquitectes | image © Adrià Goula
THE HOME DOES NOT END AT THE FRONT DOOR
Housing is shaped by far more than the architecture of an apartment. Public space, schools, transport, shops, and social infrastructure all influence how a place is experienced. Yet Traub is careful not to assign architecture more power than it possesses. ‘We see this relationship as very strong, but also more complex than simply saying that better architecture creates better communities,’ she observes. ‘A beautifully designed communal space does not automatically create social relationships.’
The observation is important in a field where shared spaces are often presented as inherently social. Architecture can provide opportunities for encounter, but it cannot prescribe community. Nor should it eliminate the need for privacy.
‘A home also needs to offer privacy and retreat,’ Traub continues. ‘The role of architecture is not to prescribe how people should live together, but to create the conditions for different forms of everyday life.’
Housing Complex Auenweide near Vienna by einszueins architektur | image by Hertha Hurnaus
HOUSING, CARE, AND THE TIME OF EVERYDAY LIFE
Affordability and supply remain fundamental concerns, but Traub argues that the conversation must also address the organization of everyday life. ‘We also need to ask what kind of homes and neighborhoods support a good life.’
Care is one of the questions that becomes visible through this broader lens. Who looks after children, older people, or people who need support? And can housing reduce some of the pressure placed on the individual household?
The House for Five Women in Bosnia, included in the book, was developed around the needs of five women and combines private rooms with generous shared spaces. For Traub, the project demonstrates how housing can support both independence and social connection without presenting collective life as an obligation.
The question also concerns time. ‘The location and organization of housing influence how much time we spend travelling, working, caring and managing everyday life,’ she highlights. ‘Perhaps the housing crisis is therefore not only about a shortage of homes, but also about how we organise everyday life.’
Housing Complex Auenweide near Vienna by einszueins architektur | photo by Hertha Hurnaus
THE MOST IMPORTANT BUILDING MAY ALREADY EXIST
Among the forms of experimentation gathered in the book, Laura Traub sees particular potential in working with what is already built. As the ecological and material costs of new construction become increasingly difficult to ignore, renovation, conversion, and adaptation are likely to become as important as new housing. ‘Given the amount of housing and infrastructure that already exists, renovation, conversion, and adaptation will be at least as important as new construction in the future,’ she argues.
The Felix-Platter-Spital in Basel, a former hospital that was transformed into around 135 apartments while retaining much of its existing structure and character, demonstrates this approach. ‘The project does not simply preserve an existing building,’ she suggests. ‘It adapts it to new needs and gives it a new role.’
This position reframes experimentation in housing. Innovation does not necessarily require a spectacular new typology or an entirely new building. It can emerge from the slower work of understanding what already exists and finding ways to make it useful again. ‘For us, this is where experimentation becomes meaningful: not when it produces the most spectacular new building, but when it finds an intelligent way of using what already exists.’ Laura Traub adds.
Collective Living near Paris by Plan Común | image by Javier Agustín Rojas
33 POSSIBILITIES FOR HOW WE MIGHT LIVE
The 33 selected projects form what Edition DETAIL describes as an atlas of possible strategies, with plans, sections, construction drawings, photographs, and interviews making different architectural positions available for comparison. For Traub, the larger takeaway is to understand housing as more than a commodity or a collection of square meters. ‘Housing shapes how we live our everyday lives, how we relate to others and how connected we feel to the places we live in,’ she reflects.
There is no universal model for a good home, she emphasizes. ‘The right answer depends on people, places and circumstances, and these change over time.’
HOUSING — 33 Answers to the Housing Question therefore leaves the housing question deliberately open, assembling different responses and asking readers to consider what domestic architecture should actually support. ‘So perhaps the question is not simply how much housing we need, or how much we can afford, but what kind of life we want our homes to make possible,’ Traub concludes. ‘For us, that is the real value of the book: it reminds us that housing is ultimately not just about places to live, but about how we want to live.’
Collective Living near Paris by Plan Común | photo by Javier Agustín Rojas

Far-right AfD win in Germany is ‘grave moment’ for Europe, politicians warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:49:51 UTC
19:49:51 KST

Mainstream politicians around Europe have expressed alarm after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) swept to a historic state election victory in Germany, while nationalist figures cheered the result as a mandate for change.
While falling just short of an absolute majority, the AfD surged into first place in the Saxony-Anhalt state election on Sunday, exit polls showed, putting the far right within reach of power at the state level for the first time since the second world war.
Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, told a party gathering in Madrid on Monday that the result showed that “the extremist threat, largely thanks to the surrender of the traditional right, is gaining ground in Europe and in the world”.
France’s finance minister, Roland Lescure, said it “clearly sends out a very, very worrying signal … This shows that we face a major challenge in the face of a populist wave which is spreading around the world today and which we must resist.”
Lescure’s comments echoed similar remarks on Sunday evening by France’s European affairs minister, Benjamin Haddad, who posted on social media: “To see the far right prevail in the German regional election marks a very grave moment for Europe.”
Haddad added: “We must listen with humility to the anger, fears and worries and duly respond to these concerns. But nationalism and xenophobia will never be the answer. We cannot forget our history.”
Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, said on Monday the AfD’s win was “a very worrying sign”. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, said on Sunday night in Poland: “Only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD in Germany.”
Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, described the election result as “terrible news … because it concerns a political force that is antithetical to liberal and western values”.
The reaction was not limited to Europe. Elon Musk congratulated the far-right party on its election victory with a “Well done!” on his social media platform X, prompting Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, to thank the nativist US tech billionaire for his support.
“If we take on responsibility here, I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation,” Siegmund wrote. “Germany would then once again be a place worth investing in. Best regards from Saxony-Anhalt!”
The US president, Donald Trump, whose White House has made no secret of its support for Europe’s nationalist far-right parties, posted a screenshot of the projected election result on his Truth Social platform without any comment.
Kirill Dmitriev, Russia’s presidential envoy, took a screen grab of Trump’s post and praised a “historic win for the pragmatic AfD”. The AfD is pro-Kremlin, has called for an end to aid for Ukraine and to refugee status for Ukrainians.
The former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán, who was heavily defeated in elections earlier this year, celebrated AfD’s win, describing it as “a huge night for Germany and Europe” and adding: “Buckle up. This is just the beginning!”
Far-right leaders in Spain and Portugal also hailed the AfD’s win. Santiago Abascal, of the Spanish Vox party, called it a “spectacular result that represents great hope for Germany and Europe”, while André Ventura, of the Chega party in Portugal, praised a “historic victory”.
Italy’s far-right deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, also congratulated the AfD’s co-leader Alice Weidel on X, describing the party’s victory as a “resounding success that highlights the strong demand for change, security, and jobs”.
Salvini, who serves in Giorgia Meloni’s radical rightwing coalition alongside Tajani, taunted “those on the left who stoked fears and catastrophic scenarios”, adding: “Fear? Terror? Danger? No, it’s called DEMOCRACY. Another Europe is possible.”
The leader of the far-right Dutch Freedom party (PVV), Geert Wilders, posted his congratulations, while in the UK, the leader of Restore Britain, Rupert Lowe, said the AfD’s victory was “an inspiration” for what his nativist party could achieve.
Not all of Europe’s far-right parties were pleased. France’s National Rally (RN), which two years ago expelled the AfD from its European parliamentary group, has made clear that it finds the German party’s rhetoric and policies too extreme.
The two parties’ rift followed comments by a leading AfD figure, Maximilian Krah, downplaying the crimes of the Nazi SS by suggesting they were “not all criminals” – and revelations that the AfD backed mass deportations of immigrants.
The RN’s president, Jordan Bardella, confirmed on Saturday that his party, whose figurehead, Marine Le Pen, is comfortably ahead in the polls in the run-up to next year’s French presidential elections, had no plans to resume an alliance with the AfD.
While keeping his distance from the party, however, Bardella noted that “electoral pressure exerted by the AfD in Germany” was contributing to policy shifts within the German government, pointing to Berlin’s re-establishment of border controls.
AfD won 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin. That was far ahead of Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union, which polled 17.2% – losing about half its support.
The centre-left Social Democrats scored 9.3%, the Greens 8.9% and the Left party 8.6%, winning eight seats apiece. However, the AfD fell three seats short of an absolute majority, with 39 lawmakers in an 83-member state parliament.

Glowworms shine again in North Yorkshire after larvae reared in garden shed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:49:40 UTC
19:49:40 KST

The bioluminescent beams of “fairy folk” are shining again from a nature reserve in North Yorkshire for the first time in a century after the successful reintroduction of endangered glowworms.
Female glowworms were spotted over multiple weeks at Nosterfield nature reserve this summer following a no-frills, almost zero-budget reintroduction of the much-loved invertebrates, which have vanished from the British countryside in recent decades and are notoriously difficult to re-establish.
The reintroduction by volunteer “glow-getters” and the independent ecologist Pete Cooper involved the authorised collecting of a small number of glowworms from a local donor site, breeding them in captivity and rearing hundreds of snail-eating glowworm larvae in a garden shed in Bristol.
Larvae were transported north and first released at Nosterfield in 2024 but because glowworms take two years to reach the adult stage of their life cycle – where the flightless female glows to attract feeble-flying, beamless males – it was not until this summer that the first signs of success emerged.
Volunteers for the Lower Ure Conservation Trust counted up to 12 glowing females over successive weeks this summer, which was a “huge relief” for Cooper, who has spent six years mastering the complexities of breeding and releasing glowworms.
“It’s a really great first indicator of initial success,” said Cooper, who gave his time to the project for free. “We know that glowworms can live out their full life cycle at this site – there is great food and plenty of mating opportunity, and it makes all that time and effort worthwhile.”
Cooper is developing formal standards and guidance for glowworm breeding and release, as well as appropriate habitat management to ensure sites are suitable for glowworms to thrive.
A profusion of glowworms in 1909 were hailed at Nosterfield by the writer Edmund Bogg as “wont to hang out their fieldstar lamps … as if lit by the hands of fairy folk”.
But here, as elsewhere across Britain, the much-celebrated beetles and their “love torches” – as Samuel Taylor Coleridge put it – have been extinguished because of more intensive farming, development, electric lights and the cult of tidiness which has removed the rough and varied grassland they require.
In Nosterfield, quarrying led to the glowworm’s disappearance but, since 1997, when the Lower Ure Conservation Trust bought its first 72 acres of disused quarry, swaths of land have gradually returned to species-rich wetland and grassland on magnesian limestone. The charity will soon be managing nearly 600 acres of former quarry for wildlife, with booming bitterns and marsh harriers now making their home on the site.
Simon Warwick, the director of the conservation trust, said the project was a credit to “the raw passion and enthusiasm” of Cooper and his willingness to freely volunteer his time, as well as the 80 volunteers at the nature reserve who had tweaked habitat management for the glowworms and monitored their emergence.
“We are very fortunate to have a lot of really knowledgable volunteers alongside our brilliant staff who are managing the land that allows the glowworms to re-establish itself in this landscape after an absence of more than 100 years,” said Warwick. “They are incredibly rare in the region and I can’t tell you how excited the volunteers have been about it.”
This year, helped by glow-getter volunteers at Westbury Wildlife Park Foundation, Cooper has bred another 1,900 glowworm larvae which will be released at Nosterfield later this year.
According to Cooper, they will not be certain that the reserve has a self-sustaining population of glowworms until 2030, when the offspring of this year’s wild adult glowworms will reach maturity and shine their lights.
Ceilidhs for wildlife organised by Cooper and friends have raised enough money to upgrade the breeding facilities at Westbury to ensure it is easier to captive-breed more glowworms, with growing interest from other conservation groups in glowworm translocations and reintroductions. The UK glowworm survey is also helping by collecting sightings of glowworms nationally to help conservationists assess where translocations would be helpful and where hidden populations of glowworms may still endure.
“It will be wonderful to see this project grow bigger than me,” said Cooper.
