UN urges ‘accountability’ after 23 die in US immigration custody in 2026
- The UN rights chief reported 23 deaths in US immigration custody in 2026 and demanded accountability for these fatalities.
- The UN urged the US to stop deportations to dangerous locations like Haiti and to ensure due process for removals to third countries.
- Concerns were raised about ICE's plan to buy electric shock gloves, which may increase violence during enforcement operations.
AI generated
Geneva – The United Nations rights chief on Sept 7 demanded accountability for swelling numbers of deaths in US immigration custody, and urged Washington to halt deportations to places where people face “irreparable harm”.
Speaking before the UN Human Rights Council, Volker Turk highlighted that “four more people have died in US immigration custody since my last update to this council” in June.
That meant there had been “a total of 23 deaths in 2026 alone”, he said, insisting that “there needs to be accountability for these deaths”.
US President Donald Trump has made combating illegal immigration a top priority of his second term, with the authorities rounding up thousands of people and expanding detention centres.
A joint report by Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights in June said the rate of people dying in ICE custody has reached its highest level in over a decade amid the crackdown.
The UN rights chief on Sept 7 also called out a range of other US immigration enforcement practices, including forcing migrant returns to dangerous places and to countries they had no connection to.
“I urge the United States to halt the return of people to places where they could suffer irreparable harm, including Haiti, and to ensure due process for all removals to third countries,” he told the council.
Turk also voiced alarm at the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency’s reported plans to “equip immigration agents with electric shock gloves”, warning this would “increase the violence associated with their operations”.
The plan to purchase the shock gloves, which was first reported by The Associated Press, calls for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the ICE parent agency, to spend US$10 million to US$20 million (S$12.6 to S$25.3 million) on what are described as “distraction and de-escalation” devices.
ICE has been criticised for a series of fatal shootings during enforcement operations, including those of two American citizens in Minnesota in January who were involved in anti-ICE protests.
Critics have focused on the forceful tactics used by ICE agents in rounding up migrants and on an alleged lowering of the standards of training for new recruits. AFP

Hainan’s resort city of Sanya to strengthen environmental measures under new Chinese code
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:08:55 UTC
19:08:55 KST

HAIKOU, China, September 7. /TASS/. The southern Chinese resort city of Sanya on the coast of Hainan Island plans to strengthen its environmental measures in accordance with China's new Environmental Code, the Hainan Daily newspaper reported.
The newspaper noted that the legislation took effect on August 15. It is expected to provide an important boost to Sanya's high-quality development. The new measures could help restore natural vegetation, expand mangrove forests, and increase populations of various local wildlife species. Another key objective is to develop modern environmentally friendly infrastructure, including a more extensive network of electric vehicle charging stations and convenient cycling routes.
The article noted that Sanya is a city with excellent environmental conditions, surrounded by tropical forests and boasting pristine beaches and numerous bodies of water. One of the goals is not only to create even more favorable living conditions, but also to harness the city's green potential to develop new modern industries and advance promising business projects.
To successfully achieve these goals, Sanya plans to continuously strengthen its legal and regulatory framework, carefully work out the details of the relevant measures and improve their effectiveness. Such efforts, the article stressed, are aimed at creating a "calm and orderly urban environment," which it compared to an "invisible but extremely important form of soft power." In practice, this will include tougher measures to combat noise pollution, stronger monitoring of residential conditions, and the introduction of "precise, intelligent, and systematic methods." These measures are expected to reduce the environmental impact of construction sites, as well as industrial and commercial activities.
The new strategy includes fines for violations and sets deadlines for remedying environmental damage. At the same time, continuous real-time monitoring mechanisms using smart technologies will be strengthened. Local cafes and restaurants will also face more effective oversight of their equipment to prevent smoke and unpleasant odors. To this end, officials from the relevant government agencies are expected to provide businesses with tailored recommendations, helping them properly install kitchen exhaust systems and lay pipelines in accordance with official standards.
At the same time, the modernization is intended to avoid imposing excessive costs or obstacles on businesses, while encouraging the expertise sharing and improvements in service quality. Air, water, and soil pollution will also be punishable through criminal prosecution and court proceedings. Meanwhile, to ensure that the legal provisions are put into practice and reach beyond "a limited audience," the authorities plan to raise legal awareness among ordinary residents and tourists – both urban and rural – through a series of specific measures, including special lectures and notifications on social media.

Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon says her pro-Palestine stance is still costing her film roles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:08:28 UTC
19:08:28 KST

Oscar-winning US actor Susan Sarandon said she continues to lose film roles because of her outspoken support for Palestinians, with some talent agencies still discouraging filmmakers from hiring her.
Sarandon made the remarks at the Venice Film Festival on Sunday, where she was promoting her latest film, The Echo Chamber.
“I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still,” she told a news conference.
“But that’s the power structure. I think among people, certainly internationally, I feel welcome,” she added.
The 79-year-old actor said she believed public understanding of Palestine and the relationship between Israel and the US had changed significantly since Israel’s war on Gaza began in 2023.
“I think that the narrative has completely changed in terms of the historical relevance of Palestine and the ties of Zionists with America and our politics,” she said.
“That has been a major revelation for people, how much money the United States gives to Israel. Nobody really understood that.”
Sarandon said reluctance to hire people who publicly criticise Israel remained particularly strong among major studios.
She thanked The Echo Chamber director Andrea Pallaoro for casting her despite what she described as warnings from within the industry.
“In terms of doing this film, I thank Andrea for that, because he didn’t listen to the warnings,” she said.
Sarandon was dropped by talent agency United Talent Agency in 2023 following remarks she made at a pro-Palestinian rally in New York.
Directed by Pallaoro, The Echo Chamber is an Italian-Belgian production starring Sarandon, Luca Marinelli and Alicia Vikander. The film is competing for the festival’s top prize, the Golden Lion.
Sarandon won the Academy Award for Best Actress for her performance in the 1995 film Dead Man Walking. Her other prominent films include The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Bull Durham and Thelma & Louise.

Russia will not enter into agreements that fail to balance interests — Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

19:08:03 KST

MOSCOW, September 7. /TASS/. Russia is not prepared to enter into agreements that fail to ensure a balance of interests, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said during a meeting with students and faculty at MGIMO University.
"Whenever we reach an agreement with someone, it is based on pragmatism. On our side, there are still some emotions, given our strong character - we love fairy tales, fables and Russian literature in general, which teaches humanism," Lavrov said.
"But pragmatism is certainly present. Without pragmatism and a balance of interests, we will not enter into any agreements," he emphasized.
Lavrov also questioned the sincerity of the other side, noting that Russia has been cheated many times throughout its history.

Macklemore backs Palestine at Ed Sheeran shows, prompting removal petition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:07:25 UTC
19:07:25 KST

US rapper Macklemore used his opening performances for Ed Sheeran in New Jersey to deliver a forceful pro-Palestinian message, prompting an Israeli-American organisation to call for his removal from the remaining dates of Sheeran’s tour.
Performing before crowds of more than 80,000 at MetLife Stadium on Friday and Saturday, Macklemore wore a keffiyeh and performed his 2024 song “Hind’s Hall” as images from Gaza and the occupied West Bank appeared on screens around the venue.
“I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them,” he told the crowd during Friday’s performance.
He also spoke about the broader principle behind his message, saying everyone should have the right to “freedom,” safety and peace.
‘Free Palestine’ message draws backlash
Macklemore repeated his message during Saturday’s show, again wearing a keffiyeh and leading the crowd in chants of “Free Palestine” before performing “Hind’s Hall.”
He also called for freedom for Palestine, Cuba, Congo, Sudan and Iran and described US Immigration and Customs Enforcement as a “terrorist organisation.”
Addressing Jewish members of the audience, Macklemore said opposition to Israeli policies should not be equated with hostility toward Jewish people.
“To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is criticism of you,” he said.
He added that his message was about “peace, love” and ensuring people are treated with dignity, respect and equality.
At least one message shown on the stadium screens read: “Holocaust survivor says stop the genocide in Gaza.”
Following the performances, the Israeli-American Council launched a petition urging Sheeran and organisers of his Loop Tour to remove Macklemore from his remaining appearances.
The organisation argued that the concert was intended as a musical event rather than a political rally and accused Macklemore of using the platform to promote what it described as a “one-sided political agenda.”
The petition also asked organisers to clarify whether Macklemore’s remarks, visuals and performance had been approved beforehand and called for clearer rules governing political messages during future shows.
The story behind ‘Hind’s Hall’
Released in 2024, “Hind’s Hall” takes its name from Hamilton Hall at Columbia University, which was occupied by pro-Palestinian student protesters and renamed in memory of Hind Rajab, a Palestinian child killed in Gaza in January 2024.
The song became one of Macklemore’s most prominent political statements, with the rapper using his music to criticise US support for Israel and express solidarity with Palestinians.
His appearances at MetLife Stadium extend that activism to one of the world’s largest concert stages, putting the Israeli war on Gaza and Palestinian rights at the centre of a major US music event.

Twenty-five years after 9/11, Americans still live with its legacy
Unknown

25 years after 9/11, Americans still live with its legacy
- Scott Larsen, whose firefighter father died on 9/11, followed in his footsteps and became a firefighter for the New York City Fire Department himself.
- Michael Crane has dedicated the past 25 years to treating the tens of thousands of responders suffering from severe 9/11-related illnesses.
- Michael Tuohey, an airline agent who unknowingly assisted two hijackers, reflects on missed instincts and the profound changes in US security after the attacks.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Scott Larsen was four years old when his dad, the New York City firefighter he was named after, was killed when the World Trade Center collapsed on Sept 11, 2001.
His father, then 35, had recently been temporarily assigned to Lower Manhattan from his normal firehouse in Woodside, in the borough of Queens, when a pair of jets hijacked by Al-Qaeda Islamist militants crashed into the Twin Towers.
He was one of 343 members of the New York City Fire Department (FDNY) who died in the attack 25 years ago.
The two jets, as well as a third piloted into the Pentagon and a fourth downed in Pennsylvania, killed about 3,000 people in an unprecedented attack that left behind tens of thousands of grieving spouses, parents and children and stunned the world.
The events of Sept 11, early in President George W. Bush’s first term, profoundly reshaped US national security policy and led to decades-long wars in which more than 900,000 died, primarily in Iraq and Afghanistan.
They also changed the course of individual lives, inspiring some children of victims to follow their parents into emergency service, steering others toward military, medical or public-service careers, and leaving survivors, responders and millions of Americans still reckoning with the legacy of that day.
These are the stories of three of them.
‘His memory comes up every day’
Larsen followed in his father’s footsteps. He joined the New York City Fire Department, seeking and securing an assignment to the same Woodside firehouse where his dad served.
“It was something in me. I just always wanted to go here,” Larsen, now 29, said during an interview at the firehouse.
He is far from alone – 58 children of FDNY firefighters who died on 9/11 have done the same, according to data collected by the International Association of Firefighters.
At the firehouse, Larsen is surrounded by reminders of his father, whose name is engraved on a memorial plaque and painted on a fire truck. Photographs of him hang in the kitchen and break room.
“His memory comes up every day, honestly,” he said. “There is never a day I come here and I don’t look at him.”
Larsen is the third generation of firefighters in his family. His younger brother, born two days after 9/11, has passed the entrance exam and hopes to join the FDNY in 2027.
“Hopefully, when I have a son or a daughter, either one, they’ll continue on the legacy,” Larsen said.
‘This was personal’
Michael Crane never stopped helping rescue workers.
As devastating as the initial death toll was, it was not the end of the story. Tens of thousands of police, firefighters, utility workers and construction workers responded to the wreckage in downtown New York.
Known as “the pile”, it towered about five stories high, and the search for survivors, and later remains, continued for months beneath lingering clouds of dust.
As medical director at New York electric utility Con Edison, Crane’s job was to protect the rescue and clean-up workers, including making sure each had a properly fitted respirator.
Getting the respirators to the crews turned out to be the easy part – once in use, they quickly clogged with dust. Many simply tossed their respirators aside.
In the early days of the recovery effort, a young man showed up at Crane’s office with a severe cough after working on the Ground Zero pile. When Crane told him to take a few days off and get treatment, the man refused.
A member of the young man’s family was buried somewhere beneath the rubble, Crane recalled in an interview at Mount Sinai Hospital, where he now serves as medical director of the World Trade Center Health Program.
“At that moment, I realised this was not just some type of national thing or state thing. This was personal,” Crane, 74, said. “This was personal to a lot of these guys who had lost people down there.”
The government-funded World Trade Center Health Program provides health care for 9/11-related illnesses to more than 150,000 responders involved in rescue-and-recovery efforts and survivors who lived, worked or studied in the disaster area, according to data collected through June 30 by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
As of June 30, people in the programme had received roughly 85,000 certifications for World Trade Center-related health conditions.
About half were linked to inhaling or swallowing toxic dust and about 30 per cent were for cancer. More than 9,000 responders tracked by the programme have died since 9/11, though officials say it is difficult to determine the role that 9/11 played in their deaths.
A quarter-century after the attacks, Crane is still deeply affected by the recovery workers.
“You fall in love with these people,” he said. “They are amazing, just resilient, funny, a little bit crazy. And even, despite what they’ve been through, really mentally tough and proud of what they did.”
‘I didn’t listen to my gut’
Like so many affected by 9/11, Michael Tuohey lives with unanswerable questions.
As an airline customer service agent, Tuohey helped two of the hijackers check into their flights at Portland International Jetport in Maine, the starting point of a journey that ended in American Airlines Flight 11 crashing into the North Tower of the World Trade Center.
Mohammad Atta and Abdul Aziz al Omari arrived just a half hour before their flight.
Tuohey scanned the men’s paper tickets to see whether they had been recently purchased or paid for in cash, which would have raised red flags even by pre-9/11 standards. But the tickets had been bought weeks in advance, paid for with credit cards, and were for first class.
“I was getting a vibe from the older, shorter guy that he didn’t like being there,” Tuohey said, referring to Atta. “And I’m thinking: it’s 5.30 in the morning. Nobody wants to get up at 5.30 in the morning.”
Later, in the aftermath of the attacks, US intelligence failures that missed the Al-Qaeda plot would be widely dissected. The Department of Homeland Security would be created, safety procedures at airports revamped and the nation ushered in a web of new security laws.
But as the first glimmers of sunlight warmed the eastern skies over Portland that crisp fall morning, Tuohey had no way of knowing the horrors the morning would bring.
“My gut instinct was good but there were laws, there were laws against profiling people,” said Tuohey, now 80 and retired. “I didn’t listen to my gut. And it turned out to be an awful thing. But it wasn’t that I was right. It’s just that it could have changed something. Not that it would have, but it could have. Who knows?” REUTERS

Russian Agribusiness Giant’s Profit Collapses 99% as Grain Piles Up at Home

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Agribusiness Giant’s Profit Collapses 99% as Grain Piles Up at Home
Russia is struggling to export grain from its new harvest as disruptions to port logistics create a growing domestic surplus, pushing agricultural prices lower and increasing pressure on producers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) on September 6, Russian grain exports fell 2.5-fold between August 1 and 20 to 1.4 million metric tons, while wheat shipments declined 2.6-fold over the same period.
The agency said wheat exports could fall by a further 52.1% to 62.5% in September, reaching between 1.8 million and 2.3 million tons. If confirmed, that would mark Russia’s lowest September wheat export volume since 2010.
The slowdown has contributed to an accumulation of agricultural products inside Russia. Prices for wheat, barley, sunflower seeds, and soybeans declined by between 3.3% and 8.5% in a single week and are now more than 40% lower than a year earlier, according to the SZRU.
The pressure is particularly visible in the Rostov region, which accounts for nearly 10% of Russia’s grain harvest. Regional authorities introduced a state of emergency on August 28 amid difficulties exporting agricultural products.
Russia’s government is considering measures including state purchases, subsidized loans, subsidies, and lending secured against unsold crops, the Ukrainian intelligence agency reported. Authorities are also considering eliminating the grain export duty and compensating producers for the higher cost of transporting shipments to alternative ports.
However, rerouting exports presents additional logistical and financial constraints. Up to 70% of Russia’s grain exports previously moved through southern ports, while alternative routes lack comparable capacity, according to the SZRU.
Transporting grain to Baltic Sea ports adds an estimated $30 to $50 per ton to shipping costs, further reducing the profitability of Russian exports.
The effects are also being reflected in the financial results of major agricultural companies. Rusagro, one of Russia’s largest agribusiness groups, saw its net profit fall by 99% in the first half of 2026—from 4.8 billion rubles (about $59 million) to 55.88 million rubles (about $690,000), according to figures cited by the SZRU.
Earlier, Russian grain exports through the Azov-Black Sea basin nearly ground to a halt after drone strikes forced major terminals in Novorossiysk and Taman to suspend operations, while navigation through the Kerch Strait was also restricted.

Kushner made the remarks alongside Steve Witkoff during talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy after the US envoys traveled to Kyiv following meetings in Moscow. He stressed that the initiative was intended to go beyond simply stopping the fighting and establish a settlement capable of lasting.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“What President Trump’s task, you know, Steve and I are doing, is really creating a peace package,” Kushner stated. He added that Washington was working closely with European partners and examining what Ukraine, Russia, and the wider international community could gain from a durable settlement.

Ukrainian Defense Forces destroyed two launchers of a Russian S-300 air defense system and a Pantsir air defense system of an unidentified modification near Sochi.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This was reported by the Telegram channel “Absolutely Reliable Source” on September 6, citing satellite imagery of the strike.

Chinese State Firm Secretly Sent Russia 46 Tons of Carbon-Fiber Materials for Strike Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:06:41 UTC
19:06:41 KST

- Category
- World
Chinese State Firm Secretly Sent Russia 46 Tons of Carbon-Fiber Materials for Strike Drones
A Chinese state-owned company supplied Russia with materials needed to manufacture hundreds of strike drones, according to internal Russian shipping records obtained by POLITICO on September 4.
The documents, which have also been reviewed by Western governments, offer evidence to date that a Chinese state-controlled company has continued supplying a sanctioned enterprise linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Shipping and customs records show that earlier this year, the Chinese company sent 46 metric tons of carbon-fiber-related chemicals to a subsidiary of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom. According to POLITICO, the shipment was declared under a customs classification typically used for materials such as nylon and polyester.
The Rosatom subsidiary develops critical components for strike drones used by Russia in attacks against Ukraine, including a strike on a shopping mall in central Ukraine in August that killed at least 16 people.
Chinese-made components have previously been found in Russian drones recovered after attacks on Ukraine. However, the newly obtained records reportedly provide the first detailed evidence of a Chinese state-owned company directly exporting essential drone-production materials to Russia.
The Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre (USCC), a Kyiv-based think tank, uncovered the documents through Russian sources and subsequently shared them with the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States.
David Albright, founder and president of the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security, said the records could provide grounds for the US State Department to sanction the Chinese supplier, as they document shipments to the Rosatom subsidiary after it had been sanctioned by several Western countries.
“Rosatom and its enterprises operate in full compliance with applicable laws and regulatory requirements,” said a spokesperson for the Russian state firm. “Any claim to the contrary is false and demonstrates a lack of understanding of how Russia’s customs authorities operate.”
The reported shipments come amid growing scrutiny of Chinese companies accused of supporting Russia’s war effort. The European Union’s diplomatic service has been seeking sanctions against four Chinese companies over their alleged involvement in supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The companies were expected to be included in the EU’s next sanctions package. Officials said their alleged activities included supporting Russia’s shadow fleet, supplying chemicals used by the Russian military, and providing components for the production of attack drones.
The proposed measures were outlined in a May 21 document and formed part of a smaller sanctions package that two EU officials said was expected to be approved by foreign ministers at a meeting in Luxembourg on June 15.

CGTN: We noted that a delegation from the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) visited China and inspected facilities for the disposal of Japan’s abandoned chemical weapons (ACWs). Could you please provide more information on the visit?
Mao Ning: From August 31 to September 5, the Director-General of the OPCW, the Chairperson of the Executive Council, as well as permanent representatives and senior diplomats from 12 countries to the OPCW, visited China upon invitation. During the visit, they travelled to Hunchun, Dunhua and Haerbaling in Jilin Province to inspect the excavation, recovery and destruction of Japan’s ACWs.
The delegation’s visit coincided with China’s annual commemoration of the victory of the Chinese People’s War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War. Japan’s militarist aggression inflicted immense humanitarian catastrophes on China and left behind the menace of ACWs. Through the visit, the delegation gained a deeper understanding of the grave harm posed by Japan’s ACWs to the lives and property of the Chinese people and to the country’s ecological environment, and expressed support for the OPCW, in accordance with the Chemical Weapons Convention, in urging the Japanese side to earnestly fulfill its obligations by completely and thoroughly destroying its ACWs in China without further delay, so as to restore a safe habitat for the Chinese people at an early date and realize the noble goal of a world free of chemical weapons as envisaged by the Convention.

Mao Ning: Cooperation between China and Venezuela is under the protection of international law and laws of both countries. It has nothing to do with any third party and should not be disrupted by any third party. China’s lawful rights and interests in Venezuela must be protected.

Mao Ning: China and the U.S. maintain communication on AI.

What’s China’s take on this election result? Will China enhance communication with the AfD?
Mao Ning: Regional elections in Germany are its domestic affair. China will not comment on that. China’s position on developing its relations with Germany is consistent.

Mao Ning: The mudslide in Gyirong has drawn close attention from the international media, who hope to enter the area for reporting and interviews. China will continue its all-out search and rescue efforts to deal with the aftermath. We will provide timely updates on the situation on the ground and rescue operations.

Ukraine Hits Taganrog Aviation Hub Keeping Moscow’s Scarce A-50U AWACS Fleet Alive

Ukraine Hits Taganrog Aviation Hub Keeping Moscow’s Scarce A-50U AWACS Fleet Alive
Ukrainian drones struck a Russian military airfield in Taganrog overnight on September 6-7, with satellite monitoring detecting a fire in the aircraft parking area, according to Militarnyi, citing data from NASA’s FIRMS fire-monitoring system.
The thermal anomaly was recorded at approximately 2:44 am on the grounds of the military airfield.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Located roughly 40 kilometers, or 25 miles, from Ukraine’s border, the facility is actively used by the Russian military and forms part of a larger aviation-industrial complex in Taganrog.
The airfield hosts Russia’s 325th Aircraft Repair Plant, which specializes in maintaining military transport aircraft and components used by the Il-76.
The Taganrog aviation plant also shares the airfield with a military unit belonging to Russia’s 5th Aviation Group.
Its proximity to Ukraine and its role in supporting Russian military aviation have made the site a recurring target of Ukrainian long-range strikes.
Another strategically important aviation facility lies immediately south of the airfield: the factory airfield of the Beriev Taganrog Aviation Scientific and Technical Complex.
The Beriev facility repairs and modernizes Russia’s A-50U airborne early-warning and control aircraft, as well as servicing Il-76 transport aircraft and Il-38 maritime patrol planes.
A-50U aircraft are among Russia’s most valuable airborne surveillance platforms, providing long-range radar coverage and helping coordinate military aviation and air-defense operations.
Ukrainian open-source intelligence project CyberBoroshno identified the change after analyzing more than 1,600 aviation-related reports recorded between June and August.
The A-50U is one of Russia’s key airborne early warning and command aircraft used in the war against Ukraine. It does not carry out strikes itself but uses its long-range radar to detect aircraft, drones, and low-flying cruise missiles beyond the reach of ground-based radar systems.
The aircraft can transmit targeting data to Russian fighter jets, air defense units, and command posts, helping coordinate interceptions and track Ukrainian aerial attacks.

Zelenskyy Says Donbas Goes Beyond Territory in a War for “Survival and Endurance”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:06:22 UTC
19:06:22 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Zelenskyy Says Donbas Goes Beyond Territory in a War for “Survival and Endurance”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy framed the fate of Donbas as central to the outcome of Russia's war, responding to a question about the region during talks with US President Donald Trump's envoys, according to a UNITED24 Media correspondent in Kyiv on September 6.
He made the remarks as envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Kyiv to negotiate an end to the war. Asked about Donbas, Zelenskyy stressed that the issue reached beyond the territory.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The question of Donbas is not only a question of Donbas," he stated, describing the war with Russia as a matter of survival and endurance.
He tied Ukraine's diplomatic options directly to its standing on the front. "Without a strong position on the battlefield ... there will be only ultimatums," Zelenskyy warned.
The president argued that Ukrainian forces had stabilized the front, creating the conditions for negotiation. Diplomacy was possible today only because of that position, he indicated.
Zelenskyy identified the east as the decisive theater, where Russia has concentrated additional troops. He anticipated that Moscow would launch a fresh wave of mobilization after its elections, directed at that front.
Ukraine had grown stronger over the past 10 to 12 months, he assessed, though he cautioned that winter presented a serious challenge.
Financing ran through his broader concerns. Zelenskyy described funding for the military, humanitarian needs, and domestic defense production as pressing and interconnected.
Witkoff, appearing alongside Kushner after the Kyiv talks, pointed to momentum in the negotiations. He reported progress from the delegation's meeting in Moscow and raised the prospect of a three-way meeting.
"You heard President Zelenskyy talk about a trilateral that we're hopeful will be announced in short order," Witkoff noted. He described collaboration among the parties as critical, citing the presence of national security advisers from the E3—France, Germany, and the United Kingdom —in Kyiv.
Witkoff acknowledged that any settlement would demand concessions from both sides. "It's going to take both sides to make some compromises and narrow the issues between them," he added, expressing hope for a peaceful diplomatic resolution.
The diplomatic push has moved quickly in recent days. On September 5, Witkoff and Kushner held talks with the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, for 3 hours and 10 minutes in Moscow before traveling to Kyiv. The Moscow meeting focused on approaches to ending the war and preceded a temporary arrangement under which Russia was to halt strikes on Kyiv for three days.
Even so, Russian forces continued aerial attacks on September 5, launching 167 drones alongside ballistic missiles despite Kyiv's proposed reciprocal air truce.

'Jubilation and pain': German far right marches to victory in key state election

PRESS REVIEW – Monday, September 7: The far right marches to victory in a German state election: what does this mean for the future of Germany and Europe at large? Also: the Daily Telegraph publishes an exclusive interview with the sons of former Pakistani PM Imran Khan about his imprisonment conditions in Pakistan. Plus the US Open descends into chaos after influencers, weed and disruptions stir controversy.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has won a crucial state election but fallen just short of winning an outright majority. The AfD – an anti-immigrant, populist, far-right party – was hoping for a majority in the Saxony-Anhalt election, which would have allowed it to govern alone and overcome mainstream parties' refusal to work with it. It fell short, but its resounding victory – and thumping loss for Chancellor Frederich Merz's CDU party – is a win in itself. German tabloid Bild headlines with a play on words: "Jubel und Schmerz" – "Jubilation and pain" – pain for Chancellor Friedrich Merz and jubilation for Ulrich Siegmund, head of the AfD list in the state. The Berliner Zeitung says he gets "the last laugh today" and calls him the most dangerous man in Germany, reprising a recent headline from Der Spiegel.
Die Zeit evokes an "historic turning point for German democracy." In an article entitled the "blue storm", the daily reminds us that the AfD continues its political dominance, after becoming the main opposition party in Germany in federal elections last year. While there are more right-wing parties in power, Die Zeit says many have become more moderate in their governance, taking the example of Italy's Giorgia Meloni. However, it warns that the AfD is going in the opposite direction, becoming more radical. In another article, Die Zeit argues that this vote is also an indictment of Merz. He has lost popularity and authority in the country. To surmount this defeat, the paper suggests looking to the historical roots of the CDU party – a union, not a party, born in reaction to Nazi Germany. Its then-leader Konrad Adenauer, himself persecuted by the Nazis, became the first chancellor of Germany.
Across Europe, the press is reacting to the AfD's election win in Saxony-Anhalt. Spain's El Pais calls it an "overwhelming victory". Here in France, the left-wing daily Libération evokes the "fascist shock in Germany." There are also lots of reactions in Italy. La Republicca says that an obscurity has fallen in Berlin, noting bitterly that the EU is confronted with Nazi-era nostalgia. Left-leaning Il Fatto Quotidiano accuses Merz of handing this victory to the AfD. The right-wing paper Il Giornale is thrilled about the victory of the "euroright" but expresses caution about the AfD's manifesto, which contains themes dear to the Nazis.
In other news, the Daily Telegraph has published an exclusive interview with the sons of former Pakistani leader Imran Khan about his health. Sulaiman and Kassim Khan warn that their father's health is declining while imprisoned in Pakistan. They say the former Pakistani prime minister is living in quarters so cramped that they are usually reserved for death row inmates. The water is fetid, he has no reading material and is kept in solitary confinement for 23 hours a day. Khan, a former Pakistan cricket captain turned prime minister was thrown into prison four years ago – a coup orchestrated, he says, by his enemies. The Khan sons also accuse the British government of "being the opposite of helpful", despite the Khan family's strong roots to the country.
Finally, there's uproar at this year's US Open, which has descended into chaos. ESPN reports that the US Open organisers have accredited more influencers this year in a bid to add hype to the event. The problem is that play has been interrupted several times due to noise during points and selfies taken with spotlights. In addition, the strong odour of cannabis has been present in recent editions – cannabis is legal in New York – and the tournament feels more like a music festival than a sporting event. Wimbledon, known for its strict court etiquette, has already vowed not to allow influencers into next year's edition. You can forget about smoking – the only grass in Wimbledon is on court!

‘Germany’s most dangerous man’ leads AfD landslide as rivals scramble to keep far right out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:04:27 UTC
19:04:27 KST

The far-right Alternative for Germany party’s landslide victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt has triggered a political earthquake whose effects are being felt far beyond Germany.
Near-final results showed the AfD winning 43.8% of the vote, more than doubling its previous support and securing 39 of the 83 seats in the state parliament. It fell just short of the 42 seats needed for an outright majority, making it difficult for the party to form a government because most other parties have ruled out working with it.
Even so, the result is an extraordinary breakthrough for a party founded only 13 years ago and represents a particularly painful defeat for Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose center-right Christian Democratic Union, or CDU, has seen public support fall sharply since he took office last year.
The CDU, which had controlled Saxony-Anhalt’s state government for 24 years, won only 17.2% of the vote and 15 seats, roughly halving its support. The center-left Social Democrats received 9.3%, the Greens 8.9% and the Left Party 8.6%. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, or BSW, narrowly cleared the 5% electoral threshold and secured five seats.
The result leaves Germany confronting a question that would have been almost unimaginable only a few years ago: whether a far-right party could eventually take control of a state government for the first time since the end of Nazi rule in 1945.
The ‘firewall’ leaves AfD short of power
Most German parties have long maintained what is known as the “firewall,” a refusal to cooperate with the AfD in forming governments. That barrier previously kept the party out of power after another state election victory in neighboring Thuringia.
All the parties elected to the Saxony-Anhalt parliament except BSW have again ruled out cooperation with the AfD, leaving the formation of a government extremely complicated.
BSW opposes the idea of a blanket firewall and has said it could cooperate with the AfD on specific issues, although it has indicated that it would prefer an outside candidate for state premier rather than one of the existing party leaders.
Ulrich Siegmund, the 35-year-old AfD leader in Saxony-Anhalt and the party’s candidate to head the state government, signaled that he would not accept political maneuvering that required his party to abandon its principles.
“If necessary, we’ll simply have new elections, and then we’ll get 50 or 55%,” he said after the victory, while also saying his party remained open to cooperation with others.
The result is nevertheless being viewed as a turning point for the AfD. The party entered Germany’s federal parliament, the Bundestag, for the first time only in 2017. It finished second in the February 2025 federal election with more than 20% of the vote and is now the largest opposition party in Berlin.
Its rise was initially concentrated in the poorer eastern states of the former East Germany, but support has increasingly spread into wealthier western regions as frustration has grown over mass immigration, economic stagnation and dissatisfaction with mainstream parties.
Current polling ahead of Germany’s next federal election, expected in 2029, places the AfD at around 28%, roughly eight points ahead of Merz’s CDU.
Anti-immigration platform and ties to Russia
The AfD has built much of its identity around opposition to immigration, particularly Muslim immigration into Europe. It advocates what it calls “remigration,” a policy aimed at returning migrants to their countries of origin, and has proposed separating refugee children from German children in schools.
It also holds strongly pro-Russian positions. Senior party figures maintained close contacts with Moscow throughout the war in Ukraine, have called for restoring relations with the Kremlin and want Germany to stop sending financial support to Kyiv, arguing that the money should instead be spent on Germans.
The AfD is Euroskeptic and has called for Germany, Europe’s largest economy, to leave the euro currency system. It also opposes major elements of green climate policy and has embraced the kind of culture-war politics increasingly associated with populist right-wing movements elsewhere.
Critics accuse the party of providing a political home for neo-Nazis and of attempting to minimize Germany’s Nazi past as part of its campaign to restore pride in German national identity. One of its slogans is “Germany for Germans.”
The AfD rejects those accusations and says its opponents are using state institutions to exclude it from legitimate democratic politics. In Saxony-Anhalt, domestic intelligence authorities have classified the party’s state branch as a confirmed far-right extremist organization, allowing it to be subjected to enhanced surveillance.
Party officials have also proposed banning Pride flags from schools while requiring German flags to be flown, establishing civilian patrols to help fight crime and reforming public broadcasting, which Siegmund accuses of spreading “disinformation.”
‘The people want change’
The scale of the AfD victory also reflects widespread frustration with Merz’s federal government. Surveys in Saxony-Anhalt showed that 87% of residents were dissatisfied with the national government.
Merz has struggled to fulfill promises to revive Germany’s sluggish economy and reduce illegal immigration, and the scale of the CDU’s defeat has intensified discussion over whether he can remain the party’s candidate for chancellor at the next federal election.
Germany’s ARD public broadcaster said the question now being asked was “how long he will survive” politically.
The CDU nevertheless reiterated that it would not cooperate with the AfD.
“It is a far-right party. It wants to leave the euro, which would be an economic disaster. It works closely with Russia, and it wants a completely different social model,” CDU Secretary-General Franziska Hoffmann said. “We will not work with them.”
The AfD’s success, however, cannot be explained solely by anger at Berlin. Much of the result is also being attributed to Siegmund, a charismatic local leader who drew thousands of supporters to rallies and used social media effectively to soften the party’s image despite the accusations surrounding it.
Der Spiegel has described him as “the most dangerous man in Germany” because of his ability to give the party a more positive public image.
“We made history,” Siegmund said after projections showed an even stronger result than polls had predicted. “The people sent an absolutely clear message that they finally want political change, and above all they showed that they want that change with us.”
One AfD voter told the BBC that while other parties merely promised improvement, he believed Siegmund could actually deliver it.
“This man gives us something no one else can give,” he said. “This is a party for working people. It is the alternative for Germany.”
Another voter said people in eastern Germany increasingly felt that things were going wrong.
“It has to get better for us, for my family. I have three children,” he said. “I’m afraid, I’m genuinely afraid that security is being eroded more and more.”
Trump, Musk and Kremlin figures react
Although the vote was a state election, the scale of the AfD victory drew reactions from across Europe, the United States and Russia.
Italian Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, leader of the right-wing League party, said “another Europe is possible.” Former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán also celebrated the result, calling it “a huge night for Germany and Europe” and adding: “Buckle up. This is just the beginning.”
Elon Musk, a prominent supporter of right-wing movements in both the United States and Europe, responded to a post by national AfD leader Alice Weidel with the German phrase “Gut gemacht,” meaning “well done.”
U.S. President Donald Trump, whose Vice President JD Vance publicly challenged Germany’s exclusion of the AfD ahead of last year’s federal election, shared a graphic of the Saxony-Anhalt results on Truth Social without adding a comment.
Russia also welcomed the result. Kirill Dmitriev, a special envoy for President Vladimir Putin, shared Trump’s post and described the AfD victory as a “humiliation” for what he called the arrogance, warmongering, incompetence and hypocrisy of Germany’s governing coalition.
At the other end of Europe’s political spectrum, the reaction was markedly different.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “in Poland, only idiots and traitors could rejoice” over an AfD victory in Germany. French officials also expressed concern, with France itself approaching a presidential election in which the far right is expected to be a major force.
Jewish leaders warn of danger
The result has also caused deep unease in Germany’s Jewish community.
A senior Israeli official told ynet anonymously that the outcome was a “real alarm” and posed a serious threat to German Jews.
“They are not for us, and they are also in favor of stopping aid to Ukraine,” the official said. “On the other hand, the far left is also strengthening. It is very troubling.”
The AfD presents itself as strongly supportive of Israel and argues that its opposition to illegal immigration, particularly from Muslim countries, helps protect Germany’s Jewish community. But senior party figures have also faced accusations of minimizing or attempting to rewrite aspects of Germany’s Nazi history, while others have been criticized over the use of Nazi symbols.
On Israel, positions within the party have also varied. Some AfD figures have opposed weapons shipments to countries involved in active wars, while others have stressed the importance of maintaining defense cooperation with Israel.
For many German Jews, however, the party’s rise remains deeply alarming.
Charlotte Knobloch, the 93-year-old Holocaust survivor who has long led the Jewish community in Munich and Bavaria, said the election result frightened her.
“On days like this, I find it hard to recognize my homeland anymore,” she said, urging Germany’s mainstream political parties not to stand aside and allow what she described as the country’s continuing political deterioration.

Russia drops aerial bombs on central Kramatorsk: apartment blocks hit, two people killed – photos
Russian forces dropped four aerial bombs on Kramatorsk in Donetsk Oblast on 7 September morning, hitting apartment blocks and killing two people.
Source: Kramatorsk City Council
Quote: "Today, 7 September, at dawn, Russian forces carried out a massive airstrike on the Kramatorsk hromada A hromada is an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories . Between 05:34 and 05:52, Russian forces carried out four strikes using FAB-250 aerial bombs with unified gliding and correction modules."
Details: Two strikes hit multi-storey residential buildings in the central part of the city, while another struck a bridge structure in the settlement of Yasnohirka.
An unexploded munition was found near an apartment block in the city centre.
Three apartment blocks in the central part of Kramatorsk are also reported to have been damaged.
Two men, aged 67 and 46, were killed as a result of the Russian attack.
Four more Kramatorsk residents were injured: a man aged 60 and three women aged 61, 58 and 79.
"The appropriate services are working at the sites of the strikes. The consequences of the attack and the extent of the damage are being assessed," the city council stated.

Russia and North Korea Open Bridge to Facilitate Military Cargo Transfers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:03:30 UTC
19:03:30 KST

A road bridge over the Tumen River has been opened on the Russia–North Korea border, along with the Khasan border crossing.
Russian outlet Interfax reported on this.
The new two-lane 1-kilometer-long bridge and the 10-lane border crossing will significantly expand land connection between the two countries.
Such infrastructure creates a direct road transport lane for the rapid transfer and logistics of military cargo and ammunition between North Korea and Russia.
With the access road connecting to the federal Ussuri Highway, Russia will be able to transport North Korean military aid across the country.
The two countries were previously connected only by a railway bridge and air links, which significantly limited the speed of cargo flows.
Construction of the bridge started in spring 2025 under the strategic partnership agreement signed by Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong Un.

Ukraine lost over US$1 billion on defence procurement in one year – NYT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:03:00 EEST
19:03:00 KST

Ukraine lost over US$1bn on defence procurement in one year – NYT
Ukraine lost around US$1.2 billion in 2024 alone due to fraud, waste and mismanagement in defence procurement. Meanwhile, the country continued to award contracts to unreliable suppliers.
Source: The New York Times, citing classified findings from government audits for 2024 and 2025
Details: The newspaper examined three striking examples of defence procurement fraud identified in the audit reports.
In 2024, the Pavlohrad Chemical Plant supplied the military with thousands of defective mortar shells. Its director, Leonid Shyman, was eventually arrested in one of the most high-profile cases of alleged fraud in Ukraine's wartime defence industry.
However, even after it became clear that the shells were defective, government audit findings show that the Defence Procurement Agency (DPA) continued to award new contracts to Shyman.
For example, the government awarded a US$280 million contract while he was out on bail on corruption charges.
Overall, seven of Ukraine's 10 largest arms manufacturers received new contracts despite ongoing criminal investigations into fraud, failures to fulfil previous contracts or the arrests of executives on corruption charges.
Audit documents indicate that warning signs in procurement were disregarded and that overcharging or failures to fulfil delivery obligations rarely resulted in consequences.
Some companies were also awarded contracts without demonstrating that they were capable of supplying the weapons or without holding the necessary licences to do so. Auditors identified 18 companies that were awarded deals despite failing to fulfil previous contracts. Six of them had not successfully completed a single contract.
Around US$126 million was lost as a result of lower bids being disregarded and weapons being purchased at inflated prices. Auditors said the contracts had been awarded without a legal basis.
Second example
Another case involved a 2024 DPA tender to purchase rocket artillery ammunition worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Three companies submitted bids. The first said it could supply the rockets for the equivalent of about US$4,200 each. Another asked for US$4,600 per rocket, while the third quoted US$5,100.
All of the rockets were identical – manufactured at the same factory by the same company in Türkiye – and the only difference was the price. The Turkish manufacturer, Arca Defense, offered the lowest price through a direct sale from its factory.
However, the contract was awarded to the company that submitted the highest bid – a subsidiary of the Czechoslovak Group, a major Czech holding company. Rather than buying directly from the manufacturer, the government paid the Czech company to act as an intermediary.
The decision added around US$130 million to Ukraine's bill for the rockets. The reports said auditors found no justification for the decision.
Despite the auditors' concerns, Ukraine considered another deal with the company, this time to replace its stock of Kalashnikov rifles with a Czech-designed NATO-calibre model. No agreement has been reported as having been concluded.
Third example
Also in 2024, the DPA sought to purchase Soviet-designed rockets from a Serbian manufacturer. Given Serbia's pro-Russian policies, Ukraine used a chain of intermediaries to obtain the rockets.
The government awarded the contract to Spetstechnoexport, a Ukrainian state-owned arms intermediary with a history of failing to fulfil contracts.
Spetstechnoexport also lacked a Serbian export licence for the rockets. Instead, the company provided a "letter of guarantee" from Ukraine's Defence Intelligence, auditors found.
The company then subcontracted the deal to US arms company Regulus. Rustem Umierov, Ukraine's defence minister at the time, wanted to remove intermediaries from Ukraine's wartime arms procurement.
He asked Regulus to negotiate directly with the state procurement agency, effectively cutting Spetstechnoexport out of the deal. The agreement subsequently fell through.
As a result, the Ukrainian government sued Spetstechnoexport to recover late-payment penalties and interest. Spetstechnoexport, in turn, sought money from Regulus.
Background: In May, the DPA contracted a record quantity of long-range 155mm artillery rounds, with competition helping to save 16% of the initial amount.

The Gymnastics Academy changed my prepaid booking but said ‘no’ to a refund
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:02:45 UTC
19:02:45 KST

I booked my daughter for three sessions during the school summer holidays at The Gymnastics Academy. The reservation was made and paid for last November because of a promotional offer.
In June, I received emails from The Gymnastics Academy, confirming a session for a venue I had not booked. I was concerned my account had been hacked.
I emailed the company and was told the venue I had booked had since closed, and my booking had been moved to a different site. One of the dates I’d chosen had also been changed. I had not been notified of this.
The new venue was too difficult to reach and the substituted date wasn’t suitable. I asked for a refund and was refused.
CH, Leeds
The email you received from The Gymnastics Academy customer services team acknowledged the changes to your booking had caused “frustration and inconvenience” and apologised for “any confusion”. It concluded, however, that you do not meet the criteria for a refund, citing its booking terms.
You say you signed an online form, including terms and conditions, when you booked, but have been unable to access it since. The T&Cs on the Academy’s website make no mention of entitlements if it changes the date or venue on a booking.
In any case, a clause that rules out refunds if that happens may be unlawful under the Consumer Rights Act 2025, according to consumer expert Gary Rycroft of Joseph A Jones & Co Solicitors. “It is likely to be unfair for a trader to be able to unilaterally change fundamental aspects of the delivery of the contract, including dates and venues,” he says.
“Just because a term and condition is there does not make it enforceable if it is inherently unfair on the consumer.”
The Gymnastics Academy, through its lawyers, told me your account of your experience is “untrue, inaccurate and ultimately misleading”.
It said that you had entered a contract with a “separate legal entity” which owned the now closed venue.
It declined to specify which legal entity. It also said that you had signed T&Cs with the “relevant operating company which clearly contained provisions governing the operating company’s right to change dates, times and venues”.
Of the enforceability of its terms, it said it “maintains a Primary Authority Partnership with Trading Standards, and its current terms and conditions have been vetted/approved through this relationship”.
Since you paid by debit card, you were able to make a chargeback claim via your bank, which re-credited the payment while it investigated. It warned you that if the company disputed your claim, it may take the money back.
It appears The Gymnastics Academy did not, so you are no longer out of pocket, although you were left trying to find and fund holiday childcare at late notice for three of your working days.
We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us at consumer.champions@theguardian.com or write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject to our terms and conditions.

“If that’s the case, then it’s over…” – MEP comments on shooting down drones in Latvia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:02:44 UTC
19:02:44 KST

“Are we going to shoot down every drone with fighter jets from now on? If that’s the case, then it’s over – we’re in serious trouble,” MEP Ivars Ijabs, deputy chairman of the board of the For Latvia’s Development party, said on TV24 programme Runāsim atklāti! (“Let’s Speak Openly!”).
Speaking about Latvia’s security and defence, one of the current issues is tunnels dug by migrants. According to independent MP of the 14th Saeima and reserve colonel of the National Armed Forces (NBS) Igors Rajevs, the tunnels being discovered along the border are a new phenomenon in Latvia, although they are nothing new or surprising in other countries.
“Poland had such tunnels two or three years ago,” he said. “The Border Guard is working there and monitoring the situation, and let’s be honest – it wasn’t Minister Dombrava who found that tunnel! These things cannot be handled as one-off campaigns; there must be systematic action. It is clear that the new government wants to demonstrate results quickly, which explains all this activity.”
To safeguard national security, MP of the 14th Saeima, former Defence Minister and candidate in the 15th Saeima elections Andris Sprūds (PRO) stresses that many measures have already been implemented,
including the construction of a border fence, although, as he himself acknowledges,
“the fence is not a panacea – what matters most is how institutions coordinate with one another.”
“One of the important solutions that must be implemented as quickly as possible – and which was started but has nevertheless encountered some difficulties – is the installation of sensors so that we are technologically capable of responding when a border violation occurs.”
Asked by the programme host whether there is really as long a waiting list for procuring sensors as there is for air defence systems, Sprūds replied that the issue involves more than sensors alone.
“We are talking about 450 kilometres. Obviously, cables also have to be installed. Yes, years have passed, but first the fence had to be built. I think the previous government faced problems, and this government and the next one will face them as well for as long as the pressure continues. There will be no single silver bullet that solves everything.”
Continuing the discussion on security, the participants turned to the issue of drones. Sprūds and Rajevs said that although Latvia has interceptor drones, drones are currently being shot down only by NATO fighter jets.
“All drones that have been shot down so far were taken down by NATO fighter jets, not by counter-drone systems,”
Rajevs explained.
Ijabs expressed concern about this approach: “Is the idea really that from now on we are basically going to shoot down every drone with fighter jets? If that’s the case, then it’s over – we’re in serious trouble.”
Meanwhile, Jānis Urbanovičs, chairman of the board of the Harmony party and a candidate in the 15th Saeima elections, recalled events in Rēzekne in May this year, when a drone crashed.
“Those drones were flying there and – bang! – they fell. First one came down, then another, but we were told there was only one. Fine, we can’t shoot them all down, but perhaps we could at least detect them?”

Freddie Mercury’s 80th birthday celebrated in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:02:14 UTC
19:02:14 KST

Freddie Mercury’s 80th birthday celebrated in Switzerland
Thousands of Freddie Mercury fans travelled to Montreux to celebrate the former Queen singer's 80th birthday in front of his statue.
The town, where the Queen frontman spent the final years of his life, has been hosting ‘Freddie Days’ since 2003.
To mark this significant anniversary, many people had donned outfits just as extravagant as those Mercury used to wear during his lifetime. The British singer had spent the last years of his life in Montreux before dying in 1991, aged 45, from complications of AIDS.
More
Don’t stop me now: Freddie Mercury and Montreux
Since 2003, ‘Freddie Days’ have been celebrated in Montreux to mark Mercury’s birthday. To mark this milestone birthday this year, concerts and panel discussions were held from Wednesday to Sunday. On Saturday evening, Mercury’s sister, Kashmira Bulsara, cut a birthday cake.
“There are people who come every year. I wouldn’t call it a community of fans; it’s more like a family,” said Lucien Muller, who organises these celebrations on a voluntary basis. “We’re trying to honour Freddie Mercury’s legacy in a town that meant a great deal to him.”
Mercury’s band, Queen, had a studio at the Montreux Casino, where they recorded six albums. The venue now houses an exhibition where fans can have a go at the mixing desk.
Erected in Montreux in 1996 and depicting Mercury in a triumphant pose, the bronze statue was entirely covered in balloons, flowers and messages left by fans from all over the world. “It’s a special anniversary, so we have to make the effort to come and celebrate everything to do with Freddie,” said a woman who had travelled from Canberra, Australia.
The 2018 Oscar-winning film Bohemian Rhapsody also helped introduce Mercury to a younger generation. “There are so many people here who aren’t old enough to have seen Queen in concert. It’s fantastic, because it helps keep Freddie’s memory alive,” said Julie Criddle, who took part in the filming of the music video for the hit We Are the Champions in 1977.
Composer Mike Moran, who co-wrote the tracks on the album Barcelona with Mercury, said the singer would probably have been surprised to see so many people gathered on his birthday. “He would have loved it – he loved being adored – but he would have hated turning 80.”

Russia slams US despatch of missile system to Norway as another blow to idea of arms talks
MOSCOW, Sept 7 - Russia on Monday condemned the U.S. deployment of an advanced missile system to Norway, saying the move dealt a further blow to the prospect of U.S.-Russia talks on strategic nuclear stability.
Russia's Foreign Ministry said in a statement that the deployment in Norway of a missile system based on Mk-41 launchers which can be used to fire a range of missiles, includingTomahawk cruise missiles, posed a threat because missiles fired from them would be capable of reaching a substantial part of European Russia, including Moscow.
"Steps such as the deployment in Europe of U.S. ground-based intermediate range missiles that pose a threat to the Russian Federation 'reset to zero' - to put it mildly - the conditions for constructive dialogue with the US on strategic issues," the ministry said.
It added that Russia would pay "particular attention" to the deployment sites and command-and-control centres of U.S. missile systems and that they would become targets in the event of a military conflict.
U.S. media reports suggested Washington had delivered the new missile launch system to Norway in August.
The Foreign Ministry said dialogue on strategic stability between Moscow and Washington had been curtailed under the previous U.S. administration and described plans by the current administration to pursue multilateral negotiations involving China as "unrealistic." REUTERS

H2EU+Store hydrogen consortium targets EUR 500 mln Phase 1 approval by 2028 – RAG Austria CEO
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
13:01:31 EEST
19:01:31 KST

The consortium behind the H2EU+Store RAG project to produce "green" hydrogen in western Ukraine using solar and wind power for subsequent delivery to Europe, initiated by RAG Austria AG and Eco-Optima LLC, is expected to be ready in 2028, RAG Austria CEO Markus Mitteregger said.
"The first step of EUR 500 million must be resolved by 2028. Already in 2029, there should be a first flow of hydrogen mixed with the flow of natural gas," he said during the "Rebuilding Together with Ukraine: Turning Ambitions into Concrete Action" panel at the European Forum Alpbach, an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent reports.
Mitteregger recalled that RAG Austria is Europe's fourth-largest natural gas storage company and that, amid the reduction in gas supplies from Russia, it became interested in the idea of producing gas (hydrogen) from solar energy and subsequently transporting it through pipelines for delivery to combined-cycle power plants to produce heat and electricity. The availability of favorable conditions for building solar and wind power plants in western Ukraine, developed infrastructure there and a partner such as Eco-Optima, one of the largest operators in the region, led to the creation of a consortium to implement this idea, which has continued to develop the project.
"Now we are at the stage where we need to do detailed engineering. We have completed the feasibility study, we have done the basic engineering, and the next step will be to carry out all the detailed engineering for wind and solar power. We have already started the work," the Austrian company's CEO described the situation.
He added that the consortium had established business relations with Ukrainian gas storage operator NJSC Naftogaz Ukrainy and Ukrainian gas transmission system operator GTSOU, Slovak gas transmission system operator Eustream, Austrian gas transmission system operator Gas Connect Austria, as well as Bavaria-based bayernets.
"So everything is ready, and we also have three contracts with customers from the Bavarian chemical industry, as well as from Austrian industry, who need hydrogen instead of natural gas," Mitteregger said.
According to him, the project has received support from Ukraine, and another major market operator is ready to join it.
The RAG Austria CEO added that Raiffeisen Bank, the largest foreign bank in Ukraine, is ready to take "the next big steps" with the consortium.
"I hope that by 2028 we will be celebrating the final investment decision," Mitteregger stressed again, noting that a dedicated hydrogen pipeline is planned to be built by 2032.
Regarding the steps required to implement the project according to the plan, he highlighted risk-coverage instruments, mutual certification and guarantees that natural gas and hydrogen can be blended.
The RAG Austria CEO explained that when green energy is produced and converted into hydrogen, RFNBO certification is required to confirm that it is indeed "green" hydrogen that can be fed into the gas network, and that this certification must be recognized by all countries to which the hydrogen is supplied.
"It sounds simple, but it is not easy. We have already been negotiating with the German government for three years," Mitteregger said, citing an example. According to him, blending, in this case, 2-4% hydrogen in natural gas, is another issue being discussed in Brussels, and it should also be discussed between Austria and Ukraine.
He said that until these issues are resolved, there will be no final investment decision because it will not be possible to attract bank and other financing for the project.
At the same time, the RAG Austria CEO noted that the project also cannot be postponed until the war is over, because the consortium is not the only party looking for suitable sites for solar and wind power plants, and, as warned by Eco-Optima, which has already built many such plants, it will be too late later.
Rainer Schnabl, a member of the Management Board of Raiffeisen Bank International AG, confirmed that the implementation of the project had been discussed with the consortium at a bilateral meeting, as well as the conditions required for this.
In his opinion, H2EU+Store could also attract funds from the European Union's recently established flagship investment fund, amounting to EUR500 million in equity.
As reported, the project's participants also include Open Grid Europe (OGE) (Germany), Bayerngas (Germany), NAFTA (Slovakia) and MND (the Czech Republic).
The H2EU+Store website notes that the project is structured in three phases, with corresponding development of new photovoltaic, wind and electrolyzer capacities in Ukraine and conversion of transport infrastructure and storage facilities in Central Europe. Currently, the first project under Phase 1 is being prepared to produce approximately 9,000 tonnes of hydrogen per year, with production expected to reach 62,000 tonnes by 2032.

The planet is… up to something

During the Artemis II crewed mission around the Moon in April 2026, the NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman took a series of photographs capturing the nightside of Earth illuminated by moonlight. After the photographs were released to the public, a Redditor combined several of them to create a dynamic image. In this video essay, the popular US YouTuber Hank Green makes the case that – like the famed ‘Earthrise’ photo, the ‘Pale Blue Dot’ image popularised by Carl Sagan, and the Hubble Deep Field pictures containing thousands of galaxies – watching this brief timelapse is an awe-inspiring experience, even if it doesn’t necessarily convey any new information. However, unlike those earlier images, its message isn’t one of our extraordinary smallness. Instead, with its dance of naturally occurring and human-made phenomena, the story it tells is one of our growing significance – for better and for worse.

UN approves true-size Africa map with sole dissent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
10:00:54 UTC
19:00:54 KST

UN approves true-size Africa map with sole dissent
The UN General Assembly has adopted a nonbinding resolution promoting world maps that show Africa at its true relative size, following longstanding objections that the 16th-century Mercator projection makes the continent appear disproportionately small.
The “Correct the Map” resolution, sponsored by Togo on behalf of the African Group, passed on Friday by 164 votes. The US voted against it, while Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia, and Ukraine abstained.
The measure encourages governments, schools, publishers, international institutions, and digital platforms to use Equal Earth or other equal-area projections when comparing the size of countries and continents. It neither bans Mercator nor establishes a single official UN map. The resolution also states that it does not affect international borders or territorial claims.
Togolese Foreign Minister Robert Dussey said correcting the map would restore an accurate understanding of the continent’s true dimensions. “A more faithful representation can help better cover Africa’s real wealth and potential, particularly in global economy and commercial dynamics,” Dussey told reporters.
Created by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569, the old projection preserves angles and was designed for maritime navigation. However, it increasingly enlarges landmasses closer to the poles. Greenland consequently appears comparable in size to Africa, although the continent is about 14 times larger.
Equal Earth, introduced in 2018, preserves relative land area but, like every flat representation of a spherical planet, still distorts some shapes, distances, or directions. France backed the resolution but said it would use another equal-area projection, Eckert IV.
The vote followed the launch of the Correct the Map campaign by Africa No Filter and Speak Up Africa in April 2025. The initiative described Mercator’s continued dominance as “cartographic colonialism,” arguing that making Africa appear smaller influences education, identity, and perceptions of the continent’s global importance. Those wider social effects remain an argument advanced by campaigners rather than a feature of the projection itself.
Washington said the resolution “mocks the work and purpose” of the UN and promotes an “ideological agenda.” Ukraine objected to maps on the Equal Earth website depicting Crimea as politically separate from the rest of the country.
African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf welcomed the resolution and urged international institutions, schools, publishers and digital platforms to progressively adopt maps that accurately reflect land areas. “Africa must be represented as it truly is: in its true dimensions and in its rightful place in the world,” he said.
Russia also backed the measure, saying the widespread use of Mercator maps had entrenched a misleading perception of Africa’s size. Deputy Permanent Representative Maria Zabolotskaya said the resolution sought to “correct a long-entrenched disproportion” associated with the “heavy historical legacy of colonialism,” under which Africa’s “place and significance were diminished.”
#CorrectTheMap
