Gongwin canine cancer drug set to enter Taiwan market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:23:40 UTC
18:23:40 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Gongwin Biopharm Holdings Co.’s new animal cancer drug has received marketing approval from the Ministry of Agriculture to treat melanoma in dogs, Liberty Times reported Saturday.
Melanoma develops from pigment-producing cells and is one of the most common cancers in dogs. It can occur on the skin, toes, and in the mouth, with oral melanoma accounting for more than 80% of cases and being particularly aggressive, according to SBM.
Gongwin’s Gwa103 uses a mechanism called intratumoral drug ablation to destroy cancer cells. The drug selectively enters malignant cells, helping reduce damage to surrounding healthy tissue, according to Anue.
Current treatment relies mainly on surgery and chemotherapy. Because canine melanoma often develops in the mouth and limbs and can affect large areas, surgery may require the removal of additional tissue.
Gongwin has signed letters of intent to collaborate on the drug with more than 100 animal hospitals across Taiwan. The drug can be used as a standalone treatment or in combination with other cancer therapies, according to UDN Money.
After completing labeling, supply chain arrangements, and hospital onboarding, the company plans to begin supplying the drug in stages in accordance with regulatory requirements. It will also provide clinical training for veterinary teams.
Gwa103 is also eligible for conditional marketing approval in the US, where Gongwin has obtained authorization to conduct clinical trials. The company also plans to expand into other major pet markets, including Australia, Japan, China, and Hong Kong.
Fortune Business Insights said the global veterinary oncology market was worth NT$91.9 billion (US$2.9 billion) in 2025. It estimates the market will grow at a compound annual growth rate of 10.7% from 2026 to reach NT$225 billion by 2034.

Chi Mei to feature 8 rare string instruments in Kaohsiung concert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:23:35 UTC
18:23:35 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — This year’s Chi Mei Music Festival will culminate Nov. 14 with a concert featuring eight rare string instruments from the Chi Mei Museum collection at the National Kaohsiung Center for the Arts, also known as Weiwuying, per a press release.
The concert, titled “Mountains and Waters, Rain and Storms: A Feast of Masterpieces by Brahms and Dvorak,” will feature pianist Liu Meng-chieh (劉孟捷), French conductor Victorien Vanoosten, music director of the Toulon Opera, and the National Taiwan Symphony Orchestra (NTSO).
Liu, who specializes in the works of Brahms and received an Avery Fisher Career Grant, will perform Brahms’ Piano Concerto No. 1 in D minor. Vanoosten will conduct Dvorak’s Symphony No. 8 in G major with the NTSO, according to the museum.
One of the most notable instruments will be a 1674 viola by Austrian luthier Jacob Stainer featuring a lion-head design. The museum described it as one of only four surviving Stainer lion-head violas in the world. The NTSO’s principal players will use the eight instruments during the concert, adding depth to the orchestra’s middle and lower registers.
This year’s festival is centered on Johannes Brahms (1833–1897). Brahms was a major figure of the Romantic era who combined the formal structures of the Classical period with the emotional language of 19th-century Romantic music, per the press release.
The festival program covers different periods of Brahms’ musical career and places his works alongside those of composers who influenced him or were his contemporaries, including Beethoven, Schubert, Robert Schumann, Liszt, and Wagner, as well as Dvorak.
The festival is curated by Chiao Yuan-pu (焦元溥), a writer and producer who holds a doctorate in musicology from King’s College London. The museum said this year’s festival features 13 instruments from the Chi Mei collection across its concerts, including works by Stradivari and Guadagnini and examples from the German and Austrian violin-making traditions.

"A Royal Navy of Oman (RNO) vessel provided logistical support to the tanker's 25-member crew and evacuated 16 crew members," the Oman MSC said.
Last Wednesday, Saudi Arabia said the attack on the tanker, owned by national shipping company Bahri, had killed two Filipino seafarers.
The status of the seven not accounted for yet is not immediately known.
Germany urges UN's top court to quash Israel genocide case
Germany's top legal representative has told the UN's top court that a genocide case over weapons sales to Israel, should be thrown out.
The matter was brought by Nicaragua and Germany's top lawyer, Julia Monar, said the judges at the International Court of Justice lacked the jurisdiction to rule on the case , dismissing Nicaragua's allegations of Berlin "facilitating genocide" as "inaccurate and distorted."
Nicaragua argues that Germany's backing of Israel, notably in terms of arms exports, contravenes the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.
"Nicaragua’s conduct indicates that it was not interested in hearing Germany’s view on its allegations, but simply in bringing Germany before this court," Monar, told the judges.
Monar said that Nicaragua failed to properly notify the German government and gave her country less than a month to reply before launching proceedings.
It's typically expected that countries attempt to resolve disputes before bringing them to the court.
Monar pointed out that Berlin scrutinizes all exports of military equipment in accordance with international law.
"Germany has not, since 2024, authorized an export of weapons of war, with final destination in Israel that can be used in the Gaza conflict,” she said.
The German government operates what it calls a "case by case" approval process of arms sales to Israel, with the stated goal of avoiding anything that might be used in Gaza, where at least 73,000 Palestinians were killed between the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks on Israeli civlians and late August of this year.
However, Germany only instituted this policy in 2025, and continued to ship defensive equipment worth hundreds of millions of euros this year.
Iran issues warning as South Korea mulls Hormuz contribution
Iran's Foreign Ministry issued a warning against any country participating in security operations in the Strait of Hormuz.
"Any military deployment or participation in operations by other countries in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz can only be regarded as direct support for the party responsible for that aggression and will have serious consequences," Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X.
Baqaei noted Tehran's diplomatic relationship with Seoul, saying that Iran "places great importance on its friendly relations with the Republic of Korea."
The comments come after South Korea's presidency on Friday said it had not reached a decision on sending forces to the Strait of Hormuz to help ensure free navigation of the waterway.
South Korea has been facing pressure from the Trump administration to make military contributions relating to Iran and has been accused of turning down any request for assistance.
"We are closely communicating with the international community, including relevant countries, to help restore peace and stability in the Middle East as soon as possible and to ensure the free passage of all vessels, including those of our country, through the Strait of Hormuz," Yonhap news agency cited South Korea's Foreign Ministry as saying in a statement.
Shipping traffic in Strait of Hormuz drops following US-Iran strikes
Maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has dropped to the lowest level since May , according to data analytics platform Kpler.
According to its latest figures, an average of 10 commodity vessels, transited the vital shipping route over the past 10 days.
Kpler recorded the number on Sunday, which was down from the 15 vessels on Friday and the 13 seen on Saturday.
The drop in maritime traffic comes amid strikes targeting tankers by the US and Iran.
On Saturday, US forces hit three Iranian oil tankers, following Iranian attacks on US warships in the region.
In retaliation, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it has targeted three oil tankers travelling what it said ewas an unathorized route in the strait.
The strikes over the weekend represented a "major escalation in maritime conflict," the Reuters news agency cited maritime intelligence firm Marisks as saying.
"Commercial tankers are now being deliberately used as instruments of reciprocal economic pressure, substantially weakening the previous distinction between military confrontation and commercial shipping," Marisks noted.
"Risk is therefore assessed as extreme for Iranian/Iran-linked tonnage and materially elevated for US-linked or US-escorted shipping throughout the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman," the firm said

Thousands gather in Belgrade for funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:22:05 UTC
18:22:05 KST

Funeral of convicted war criminal Mladic draws thousands, opens old wounds
BELGRADE, Sept 7 - Thousands of people gathered in Belgrade on Monday for the funeral of the former Bosnian Serb General Ratko Mladic, who died last week while serving a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Crowds carrying Serbian flags and pictures of Mladic wearing a traditional Serbian military cap gathered outside the church in a Belgrade suburb where the head of the country's Orthodox church, Serbian Patriarch Porfirije, presided over the service.
Mladic's coffin, surrounded by armed soldiers in fatigues and accompanied by a brass band, was then paraded through streets thronged with onlookers, who chanted his name. He was buried at a nearby cemetery next to his daughter, who died in 1994.
It was one of the biggest public funerals in Serbia since the fall of communism in 1990 and showed how revered Mladic remains among many in Serbia and in Bosnia's autonomous Serb Republic, despite his convictions linked to his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre and in the siege of Sarajevo - two of the bloodiest events in post-war Europe.
"He is a hero," Djordje, a 34-year-old man who came from Prijepolje to pay respects to Mladic, said. "He was a great military strategist."
CONFLICTS TRIGGERED BY BREAK-UP OF YUGOSLAVIA
Mladic's death has stirred up strong feelings linking back to the break-up of Yugoslavia and the ethnic conflicts that ensued in the Balkans.
Mladic was found guilty by the United Nations International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia of genocide for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which about 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed after Bosnian Serb forces overran the U.N.-designated enclave.
He was also convicted over the 43-month siege of Sarajevo, during which about 10,000 people were killed.
Last week, EU enlargement commissioner Marta Kos postponed her visit to Serbia, which is a candidate country to join the bloc, because of what she said was the "glorification" of Mladic after his death, including the use of a government plane to return him to Serbia.
"The Western Balkan armed conflicts of the 1990s were among Europe’s darkest moments in its recent history," an EU spokesperson said in a statement on Monday.
"Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries."
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, who dismissed Kos' statement last week, did not attend the funeral. However, his son Danilo attended, along with Defence Minister Bratislav Gasic and Justice Minister Nenad Vujic.
PAINFUL REMINDER FOR THOUSANDS
In Sarajevo, meanwhile, the funeral rekindled painful memories of the war. Telecom companies in Bosnia's Bosniak-Croat federation blocked the signal of the two Bosnian Serb TV stations that carried live broadcast of the funeral and procession.
Bosnia's Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic said the country will withdraw all staff from its embassy in Belgrade except for the ambassador and consul in protest at Serbia's handling of the funeral, including the military escort of the body and the attendance of government officials.
"It is really horrible that this is taking place there (in Belgrade) because I know there are normal people who are against it," said Zdravka Gvozdjar, a retired pharmacist whose 9-year-old son was killed during the Sarajevo siege by a grenade fired by the Mladic-led forces, one among more than 1,000 children killed in the city.
"Mladic ... only deserved to be erased from memory for good, not to be ... promoted as a hero," she said. "He should be remembered only as a butcher." REUTERS

Cricket Australia green lights BBL privatisation, defying power states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:22:03 UTC
18:22:03 KST

Cricket Australia is set to proceed with the partial privatisation of the Big Bash League despite opposition from New South Wales and Queensland.
States will be allowed to explore sell-offs of 49 per cent stakes in their BBL franchises.
What's next?
A formal announcement is expected to be made by Cricket Australia on Tuesday in concert with several of Australia's cricket stars.
The Big Bash League will be partially privatised, in what looms as one of the most significant shake-ups of Australian cricket in decades.
Cricket Australia will defy heavyweight states New South Wales and Queensland to forge ahead with plans to allow states to explore sell-offs of 49 per cent stakes in their BBL franchises.
The decision to proceed was effectively made at a Cricket Australia board meeting last week, and will be officially green lit on Monday night.
It is understood a formal announcement will be made by Cricket Australia on Tuesday, in concert with several superstars of Australian cricket — a coup, given some initial pushback from the Australian Cricketers' Association.
However, there remains several details to be ironed out between the ACA and the CA, which has argued, amongst other things, for a greater share of revenue for its players.
The ACA insists it's supportive of privatisation as long as the long-term interests of the game are protected.
The players' union will continue to negotiate with Cricket Australia over, among other things, just how big a slice of the pie the players will receive.
This will form part of a new memorandum of understanding between the two parties.
Tasmania, Victoria and Western Australia are in support of the decision, that will allow states to undertake a market sounding process for the sale of 49 per cent stakes in their teams.
But power states New South Wales and Queensland remain opposed to the plan and will undoubtedly be rankled by Cricket Australia's decision to press ahead without them fully on board.
South Australia remains lukewarm on the concept but is more open to the idea than New South Wales or Queensland.
New South Wales has long believed an injection of private equity would largely amount to a sugar hit, and broader structural reform is needed to ensure Cricket Australia's financial viability into the future.
Cricket New South Wales has been contacted for comment.
In contrast, Cricket Australia believe that privatisation of the BBL will allow the league to keep pace with rival competitions around the world, with proceeds to be spread throughout the broader Australian cricket ecosystem.
Transactions could be complete before the start of next season.
It is likely that prospective international team owners will be courted across the upcoming summer, with potential buyers expected to be in Australia to cast their eye over this year's BBL tournament.
In June, the privatisation process was accelerated when Cricket Victoria pre-emptively made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades, while retaining the Melbourne Stars licence.
Several state CEOs recently travelled to India and the UK to connect with prospective buyers, ahead of being given formal approval to commence a sell-off process by Cricket Australia.

"Russia's imperial ambitions will not end with Ukraine," Finnish defence minister says
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:20:46 EEST
18:20:46 KST

Finland must respond to the threat from Russia calmly, but also firmly and decisively, Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen (NCP) said on Monday.
Häkkänen made the remarks during his opening address at the 257th National Defence Course, which brings together leaders from government, the media and academia to discuss national security issues.
"Russia's imperial ambitions will not end with Ukraine," Häkkänen said. He added that Moscow is seeking to restore at least the spheres of influence it had during the Soviet era.
Häkkänen described the Russian threat as long-term and unpredictable, with his remarks coming as Finland completes its eastern border fence.
"The time to strengthen Finland's national defence is now," Häkkänen said, noting that the impact of Europe's increased defence spending will only become visible in practice in the 2030s.
Finland is also investing in counter-drone capabilities together with Sweden.
"This is a significant and historic step in closer Finnish-Swedish cooperation. It is also a testament to the Nordic countries taking responsibility for their own defence," Häkkänen said.
The defence minister also welcomed the growth in Finnish defence exports. Last year, 479 export licences were granted, while the value of completed exports was around 700 million euros.
Eastern border fence completed
Finland has completed a 200-kilometre barrier along its eastern border with Russia this autumn.
The project affected thousands of Finns, with around one thousand landowners receiving compensation. The fence is designed to prevent unauthorised entry. Construction began after the asylum seeker situation in 2023, when thousands of migrants crossed the border, prompting Finland to close its eastern border crossings.
The Finnish government still considers it possible that the threat of instrumentalised migration could return.
The project cost 356 million euros, with maintenance expected to cost a further 1.5 million euros a year.

Iran’s withdrawal has significant implications for IWBF
TEHRAN – International Wheelchair Basketball Federation (IWBF) has announced that Iran’s withdrawal at this very late stage of the 2026 IWBF World Championships has significant implications for the organization and integrity of the World Championship.
Iran were forced to pull out of the Championships after four members of its delegation were denied visas.
IWBF issued a public announcement on Sunday addressing the incident:
IWBF was informed by the Iran Sports Federation for the Disabled that the Iranian men's national wheelchair basketball team, who are due to compete at the 2026 IWBF World Championships, will not travel to Ottawa to participate in the event.
The Iranian Federation made this decision due to the fact visas remain outstanding for four members of its delegation, including the head coach and assistant coach.
All 12 players and four other members of staff have received their visas.
IWBF and the Local Organizing Committee have worked closely with the Iranian Federation and provided all possible support regarding the outstanding applications, including maintaining regular communication with the relevant Canadian authorities. However, visa decisions and processing timelines are the responsibility of the relevant authorities and remain outside our control.
IWBF recognizes the difficult circumstances facing the Iranian Federation. At the same time, a withdrawal at this very late stage has significant implications for the organization and integrity of the World Championship. Consequently, our immediate priority is to focus on delivering the event, address the areas affected and work closely with our partners to mitigate the impact. Updated schedules and further information will be released in due course.
The longer-term implications of the withdrawal will be considered separately by the IWBF Executive Council in accordance with the applicable IWBF regulations and procedures.

US Envoys Say Putin Talks Were “Very Constructive,” Sees Opening for Trilateral Format
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:18:14 UTC
18:18:14 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
US Envoys Say Putin Talks Were “Very Constructive,” Sees Opening for Trilateral Format
US President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, outlining a pathway toward renewed peace talks and expressing hope for a trilateral format soon.
The two envoys outlined their assessment during remarks in Kyiv, a day after meeting the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, in Moscow, according to a UNITED24 Media correspondent on September 6.
Kushner told reporters that Washington had consulted both sides about reviving three-way negotiations. "One thing Steve and I really thought would be productive is to go back to the trilateral format," he explained. "We've spoken with both parties, and so hopefully we'll have progress on that very soon."
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Witkoff stated that Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio had dispatched the pair to reopen talks. "The President asked Jared and me to come here and to restart conversations, negotiations, because this is so important to him," he noted.
Kushner characterized the Moscow talks as constructive and substantive, with both delegations posing questions about the elements of a durable settlement.
Witkoff, who has made about eight visits to the Russian capital to meet Putin, emphasized the role of personal ties in ending the war. He and Kushner have traveled there together at least three times. "Relationships are critical in terms of solving conflicts like this," Witkoff declared.
The envoys met Putin first to gauge Moscow's position and briefed Zelenskyy's team on the discussion. Witkoff stated that their task is to bring the two sides together, narrow the issues between them, and build reliable communication channels.
He described the previous 48 hours as a constructive start and expressed confidence in an eventual resolution.
The Kyiv visit was the envoys' first trip to the Ukrainian capital, which they reached by train after their aircraft landed in Poland. Ukraine had readied its airports to receive the delegation by air, but Russian strikes ruled out a direct landing.
At the railway station, they were met by senior Ukrainian officials, including presidential office chief Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy Serhii Kyslytsia, and parliamentary faction leader Davyd Arakhamia.
The timing carries added weight as winter nears, with Moscow calculating that Ukrainian resolve will weaken through the cold months and that Putin's willingness to negotiate will fade until the season ends in mid-March.
The Kyiv talks followed directly from a marathon session in Moscow the previous day. There, Witkoff and Kushner spent more than three hours with Putin—three hours and 10 minutes in all—focused primarily on approaches to ending the war in Ukraine.
Officials on both sides framed the exchange as substantive and unusually frank, and the delegation was reported to have arrived with a range of settlement proposals. The discussions extended beyond Ukraine to potential large-scale US-Russian economic projects.
The Moscow visit unfolded under a temporary arrangement on strikes. Putin had ordered Russian forces to refrain from hitting Kyiv for three days from midnight on September 5, and Zelenskyy signaled Ukraine's readiness to observe a matching halt on cities tied to the negotiations.

Ukraine Strikes Deep Into Russia, Hitting Airfield, Major Oil Refinery and Air Defenses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:18:01 UTC
18:18:01 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Strikes Deep Into Russia, Hitting Airfield, Major Oil Refinery and Air Defenses
Ukrainian forces struck the Rostov-on-Don airfield, the Ryazan Oil Refinery, and three Russian air defense assets during an overnight operation in Russia on September 6, with fires reported at both the airfield and refinery.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on September 6, Ukrainian forces targeted the Ryazan Oil Refinery in Russia’s Ryazan region. A fire was recorded at the facility, which the General Staff said is involved in supplying the Russian armed forces.
The Ryazan refinery is one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities, with a design capacity of around 17 million metric tons of crude per year. It produces gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation kerosene, and other petroleum products.
Fire Point, a Ukrainian defense manufacturer, said its FP-1 drones struck equipment at two major primary crude-processing units at the refinery.
The company reported hits on the distillation columns of the ELOU-AVT-6 unit, the refinery’s largest primary processing unit with an annual capacity of 8.5 million metric tons, as well as equipment at the AVT-3 unit, which has a capacity of 3.1 million tons per year.
Together, the two units account for more than 77% of the refinery’s primary oil-processing capacity, according to Fire Point.
Separately, Ukrainian forces struck the Rostov-on-Don airfield in Russia’s Rostov region. The General Staff reported a fire in the area of the facility but said the extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Three Russian air defense assets were also hit in the Rostov region—a Podlet radar station and two Pantsir-S1 surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery systems.
The Podlet radar is designed to detect low-altitude and small aerial targets, including drones and cruise missiles. The Pantsir-S1 is a short-range air defense system combining surface-to-air missiles with 30 mm automatic cannons to engage aircraft, helicopters, drones, and precision-guided weapons.
The strikes were part of a broader overnight Ukrainian drone operation that targeted at least 14 Russian regions, as well as temporarily occupied Crimea and areas over the Black and Azov seas. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed 258 Ukrainian drones were intercepted, while Moscow and the surrounding region were left untouched under a temporary airspace arrangement during US envoy visits.

Kathmandu goes after social media abuse of Nepal-China flash floods as death toll climbs to 1,398
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:17:59 UTC
18:17:59 KST

Aamir Latif
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
The death toll from devastating flash floods and mudslides at the Nepal-China border has climbed to 1,398, with over 5,500 people remaining missing, official statistics showed on Monday.
Of those missing, 850 are foreigners, according to official figures from Nepal and China.
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said that 1,355 bodies have been recovered so far, while around 5,000 people, including 589 foreigners, remain missing.
More than 13,000 people have been rescued from the flood-hit areas.
Chinese authorities said at least 43 people have been confirmed dead, while 519 others, including 261 foreigners, remain missing in the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet.
Nepal’s Cyber Bureau has launched an investigation into social media abuse targeting people affected by last month’s river floods, local English daily Kathmandu Post reported.
Following a warning from Prime Minister Balendra Shah, the bureau formed a 10-member team to investigate social media users accused of posting abusive and hateful comments against those affected.
Shah warned in a Facebook post that those who mocked or harassed people suffering in the aftermath of the disaster would face consequences, adding that the government would take a tough line against such behavior.
Authorities said they are compiling profiles of people who have posted insensitive comments about flood survivors.
Many families searching for relatives who went missing in the floods are using social media to appeal for help. Their posts, however, have been met with a slew of hostile and demeaning comments.
“People who make unnecessary remarks, belittle those in pain or seek to cause them further suffering at this sensitive time are criminals,” Shah wrote. “The government will show no leniency towards them.”
The abuse continues despite the prime minister’s warning.
 
At least one person has been arrested for posting hateful comments on social media against those affected by the floods.
According to local law, those found guilty can be fined up to Rs100,000 or sentenced to up to five years in prison, or both.

Belgium detains Chinese man on suspicion of semiconductor espionage
BRUSSELS – Prosecutors in Belgium said they have held a man with dual Chinese and Belgian nationality in pre-trial detention since May on suspicion of espionage in a case involving semiconductor technology.
The prosecutors said the 52-year-old man used to hold a senior position at Belgian microchip maker Belgan, a specialised producer of gallium nitride semiconductors which was declared bankrupt in July 2024.
The man was suspected of simultaneously acting as a director of a Chinese company that made the same kind of chips, which had been established only a few months after he joined Belgan and which was financed by a Chinese investment fund.
In that position, he is suspected of illegally transferring specialised intellectual property and trade secrets abroad, all relating to the production of gallium nitride chips used in electric vehicles, aerospace and the military, the prosecutors said.
The man lives in Belgium and was arrested in May at Zaventem airport, where he was planning to take a flight to Beijing.
Prosecutors said the man remained in detention, and that a second suspect in the investigation remained at large.
The Chinese embassy in Belgium was not immediately available for comment. REUTERS

Rapper Macklemore voices support for Palestine at Ed Sheeran concerts, faces removal petition

Unknown Publisher

Dilara Hamit
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
US rapper Macklemore voiced support for Palestinians during two opening performances for Ed Sheeran at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium, leading an Israeli-American organization to petition for his removal from the remaining tour dates.
Wearing a keffiyeh before a crowd of more than 80,000 people, Macklemore performed his pro-Palestinian song Hind’s Hall as footage from Gaza and the occupied West Bank was displayed on screens around the stadium.
“I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them,” he told the audience during Friday’s concert.
“I believe that every human being walking this earth deserves the exact same freedom, to know safety and peace before knowing the sounds of violence, and to know the sound of laughter on the playground before planes and bombs,” he added.
Macklemore also called for freedom for Palestine, Cuba, Congo, Sudan and Iran and described US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as a “terrorist organization.”
He repeated his pro-Palestinian message during Saturday’s second concert at MetLife, again wearing a keffiyeh, chanting “Free Palestine” and performing Hind’s Hall.
Macklemore also directly addressed Jewish members of the audience.
“To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is criticism of you,” he said.
“My message is for peace, love and for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.”
At least one message displayed on the stadium screens read: “Holocaust survivor says stop the genocide in Gaza.”
Following the performances, the Israeli-American Council launched a petition urging Sheeran and the organizers of his Loop Tour to remove Macklemore from his remaining scheduled appearances.
“This was an Ed Sheeran concert, not a political rally, not a protest and not an activist event,” the petition said.
The organization accused Macklemore of using the concert to promote what it called a “one-sided political agenda” and asked tour organizers to clarify whether his speech, visual material and performance of Hind’s Hall had been approved in advance.
It also called for organizers to establish clearer rules governing political messages during the tour.
Hind’s Hall, released in 2024, takes its name from Hamilton Hall at Columbia University, which pro-Palestinian student protesters occupied and renamed in memory of Hind Rajab, a Palestinian child killed in Gaza in January 2024.

Years ago, Russia entered its all-out war against Ukraine with a commanding navy and treated the Black Sea as its own. A country left with almost no warships has since answered with cheap robot boats, turning expendable machines into the tool that now contests that sea.
More than 500 sorties to hunt one small drone group

Biggest Magura sea drone doesn’t ram ships. It carries other drones and stays out seven days
The commander split the unit's rise into three stages: victory at sea, an end to Russian air dominance over the water, and now strikes on land from the sea. The bar set in 2023 and 2024 is unrealistic to hold in the Black Sea today, he said, because there are no ship targets left, and what remains is harder to reach. A struck S-400 air-defense system does not pay off like a sunk warship, he added.
The bill for Russia

He pointed to the Syrian Express, Russia's sea supply line to Syria. It once ran a short route and now goes through the Baltic Sea, and the whole bill runs into the millions, he said.
The unit's capabilities came together in a strike on the Ivan Khurs, a Russian reconnaissance ship, its first target. The later sinking of the missile boat Ivanovets killed 40 Russian crew in minutes, the commander recalled. He expects the unit to be remembered as revolutionaries, likening its sea drones to the first tanks more than a century ago.

Germany seeks to dismiss Nicaragua's Gaza genocide case at top UN court
Germany is set to ask the International Court of Justice on Monday to dismiss a case accusing Berlin of "facilitating genocide" in Gaza by supporting Israel after the deadly October 7, 2023 attacks by Hamas militants. The details of the case, filed by Nicaragua in 2024, have not yet been made public.
Germany will Monday ask the top United Nations court to toss out a case brought against it by Nicaragua, which has accused Berlin of "facilitating genocide" with its support of Israel.
Lawyers for Germany will kick off four days of hearings at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the court based in The Hague that rules on disputes between countries.
Read moreGermany denies aiding 'genocide' in Gaza, says Israeli security at 'core' of foreign policy
The case dates back to 2024, following the start of Israel's offensive in Gaza. Nicaragua urged ICJ judges to impose emergency measures to force Berlin to halt all aid to Israel, in particular military equipment.
The court threw out Nicaragua's request in April of that year, saying "the circumstances, as they now present themselves" did not justify emergency orders.
The case is nevertheless ongoing and Germany is now seeking to have it removed, either by persuading judges they do not have the power to rule in the case or that Nicaragua's argument does not stack up.
Berlin has filed so-called "preliminary objections to the jurisdiction of the Court and to the admissibility of certain claims" presented by Nicaragua, according to an ICJ statement.
The detail of Berlin's case has not yet been made public.
Genocide claim
After Germany presents its case on Monday, Nicaragua will respond before both countries get another chance to address the court on Wednesday and Thursday.
It takes on average six months for the court to hand down a ruling in such cases.
The court could either side with Germany and throw out the case completely or rule against Berlin, meaning the case would then be considered "on the merits" in more detail.
During hearings at the court in April 2024, Nicaragua said Germany was "pathetic" to provide aid to Gaza while also simultaneously furnishing Israel with weapons.
Nicaragua's ambassador to the Netherlands, Carlos Jose Arguello Gomez, told the court: "Germany seems not to be able to differentiate between self-defence and genocide."
Germany retorted that Nicaragua's case was "grossly biased", strongly denying the accusations that it was in breach of the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.
Read moreWhy is it so hard to talk about Palestine in Germany?
Israel launched its offensive in Gaza in response to the deadly October 7, 2023 attacks against it by Hamas militants.
Due to its Nazi past, Germany has placed Israel's security "at the core" of its foreign policy, its representative told the court in the 2024 hearings.
Germany said its arms trade with Israel was subject to "detailed scrutiny ... that far exceeds the requirements of international law".
This procedure is separate from a high-profile case also before the ICJ, in which South Africa has accused Israel of perpetrating genocide in Gaza, which Israel denies.
The ICJ's rulings are binding but it has no power to enforce them.
For example, it has ordered Russia to stop its invasion of Ukraine, a demand that has fallen on deaf ears in the Kremlin.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Nepal holds day of mourning for more than 1,300 killed in floods
Nepal flags fly at half-mast to mark a day of mourning after catastrophic Himalayan floods kill more than 1,300.
Nepal is holding a national day of mourning to remember more than 1,300 people who died in last month’s catastrophic floods.
Government offices in Nepal and missions abroad are flying the national flag at half-mast on Monday, the 13th day since the floods, the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement.

In the Hindu tradition, it is the final day of the mourning period, during which close family members stay at home and relatives visit to pay their respects. On the final day, rituals are held to pray for those who died.
The government has not planned any wider events for this day of mourning because search teams are still looking for survivors and resources are limited.
“There are no government programmes organised as the rescue and search operation is still going on in the flood-hit areas,” Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Center (NEOC) told the Reuters news agency.
A huge wall of mud and rock, triggered by a glacier breaking off, collapsed into a river on the Himalayan border of Nepal and China’s Tibet region on August 26, causing flooding that killed at least 1,380 people and left more than 5,500 missing.
In recent days, search teams in Nepal have rescued four people, including a Chinese national who was pulled from a tunnel at a hydropower site on Saturday. The others rescued were two hydropower workers from another tunnel on Friday, as well as a Nepali woman pulled out from her buried house on Saturday.
President Ram Chandra Paudel, the ceremonial head of state, is touring flood-hit areas on Monday and will survey damage caused by the disaster, his aide said.
In Kathmandu, family members gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the speeding up of the search for the hundreds of people who were working on hydropower projects and were either swept away by the rushing Bhotekoshi River or buried by the debris.
Sumana Shrestha stood with her family members holding a poster with the photo of her 55-year-old husband, who has not been heard from since the day of the flood.
Her husband, a consulting geologist, was supposed to return home after his shift at the project office for the Trishuli hydropower plant on the day of the flood. The two-and-a-half-storey office was buried by debris.
“We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said. “The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle.”
Another protester, Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, held a photograph of his brother Niraj Shrestha, a 52-year-old engineer who worked at the same site.
He said authorities sent only a small excavator by helicopter on the sixth or seventh day after the disaster, adding: “They should have ordered big helicopters from places like China or India to fly in equipment.”
Rescue efforts have focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said.
Specialised rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects.

At 22, Russian design student Julia Molchanova met Jeffrey Epstein by chance on the street. She spent years trapped in his ‘cult.’

Unknown Publisher

At 22, Russian design student Julia Molchanova met Jeffrey Epstein by chance on the street. She spent years trapped in his ‘cult.’
The Wall Street Journal has published a major new investigation into the crimes of Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier and sex offender who died in 2019. The article’s central figure is Julia Molchanova, a 37-year-old born in Russia. She spoke to journalists for the first time about her complicated relationship with Epstein, the abuse she suffered at his hands, and her role in a class-action lawsuit against Bank of America filed by women who were harmed by the financier. Meduza summarizes the key points of the Wall Street Journal’s report.
Who is Julia Molchanova, and how did she meet Epstein
The Wall Street Journal does not detail Molchanova’s life before she met the disgraced financier, saying only that the two met in December 2011 in New York. Molchanova was 22 at the time, living in Russia and studying design at a university; she had come to the United States on a trip and spoke little English.
Epstein spotted her outside the Barneys department store on Madison Avenue, Molchanova said, complimented her — he “said something about her blue eyes,” she recalled — and pointed out his townhouse nearby as if it were a tourist attraction.
Using another young Russian-speaking woman as a translator, Epstein invited his new acquaintance to breakfast the next morning, where he peppered her with questions: “What did she want [in life]? What did she dream of doing?”
Molchanova told him she was interested in fashion design, and Epstein offered to help her get into the prestigious Fashion Institute of Technology (FIT) in New York — “that was the hook,” she said, that the American used to reel her in. Back home, she signed up for additional sewing courses to prepare for the FIT program, and Epstein paid for them.
In January 2012, Epstein invited Molchanova back to New York, ostensibly to show her FIT, and put her up in an apartment where he housed many other women who had suffered abuse at his hands. During that trip, Molchanova was sexually abused for the first time. When she told Epstein she was unhappy with what he had done, he told her that sexual openness was part of American culture and that she would have to change to fit in, she told the Wall Street Journal.
The following month, Molchanova fell even more firmly under the financier’s control. She traveled to Paris with her boyfriend, who assaulted her during an argument, and, frightened, wrote to Epstein, who happened to be in the French capital as well. He helped her get away, paying for a plane ticket back to Russia.
How Molchanova ended up in Epstein’s “cult” and got pulled into his financial schemes
Growing increasingly attached to Epstein, Molchanova eventually moved to New York for good and began following the advice of her “mentor” in hopes of breaking into fashion design. But he never actually helped her get into FIT.
Instead, Epstein set out to groom Molchanova as his “assistant,” tightening his control over her life. She recalled that he expected her to thank him constantly, act cheerful, and be friendly with everyone. “It was like a cult,” Molchanova now says.
Epstein regularly coerced Molchanova and other women who had become dependent on him into sex, and he expected them to bring him new potential victims. Molchanova says she refused to take part in this kind of procuring, and his attitude toward her worsened as a result. He constantly demanded that she explain how she could be useful to him and often isolated her from the outside world.
Epstein also monitored her spending, Molchanova said, giving her less than $3,000 a month, though the amount varied. He dictated what she wore, how long her hair should be, which doctors she could see, and who she could spend time with. In 2013, he even arranged a sham marriage for Molchanova to another woman. He is known to have used this tactic more than once within his “cult.”
In 2014, Epstein’s lawyer, Darren Indyke, registered a company called JSC Interiors in Molchanova’s name — she said that Epstein presented it as a way to launch her design business. In reality, she carried out only a handful of design-related tasks, such as putting together flower arrangements, while Epstein kept JSC Interiors under his own control, using it to move money and carry out other transactions without the knowledge of its nominal founder.
Molchanova says she only learned about this years later. Bank of America, where the company held its account, clearly turned a blind eye to actions Epstein allegedly took in her name, she says, and she later became the lead plaintiff in a collective lawsuit against the bank brought by women harmed by the financier. A court recently approved a settlement in the case, under which Bank of America agreed to pay a total of $72.5 million to dozens of plaintiffs. The bank denies facilitating crimes related to human trafficking for the purposes of sexual abuse.
Indyke and Epstein’s accountant, Richard Kahn, also deny any wrongdoing. Their representatives told the Wall Street Journal that Molchanova never told them she had been abused and “appeared to be one of Epstein’s assistants working through an LLC that Epstein set up for interior design purposes.” Indyke and Kahn deny knowing that their employer had arranged a sham marriage for Molchanova or used accounts registered in her name.
How Molchanova angered Epstein, and what helped her escape the trap
Epstein never helped Molchanova build a career in design, but he did try to place her in other jobs, including at Next Management, the modeling agency run by well-known businesswoman Faith Kates.
In a May 2015 email, Kates told Epstein that Molchanova had said in a job interview that she did not want to sit at a desk all day and had never worked in an office before. Epstein reprimanded her for turning down a receptionist job. ”[I] am angry,” he wrote.
Next Management told reporters it never had any relationship with Epstein. “Faith Kates’ multi-decade long, personal relationship with Jeffrey Epstein was completely and absolutely unknown to Next Management and its top executives,” the company stated in a statement. Kates did not respond to requests for comment. She left Next Management in late 2025, after the U.S. Justice Department published part of her correspondence with Epstein.
Epstein also arranged internships for Molchanova through his friends, including, she said, one with publicist Peggy Siegal in 2016. Molchanova said she felt out of place there, hampered by her poor English. “If he really wanted to help, he would have sent me to learn English,” she said. Siegal did not respond to requests for comment. She has previously said she did not know about Epstein’s “nefarious behavior” and that associating with him was a mistake.
Years of total dependence on Epstein took a severe toll on Molchanova’s physical and mental health. Her weight fluctuated, and Epstein criticized her for it, calling her fat. At her lowest point, she said, she thought about suicide, and Epstein would not let her see a therapist. Her mental health deteriorated further after a tabloid published photos of her with Epstein in 2016: “I remember thinking that I’m trapped forever, and my life is over.”
In 2017, Epstein’s lawyer drew up paperwork so Molchanova could dissolve her sham marriage. She describes the years that followed as an attempt to break free from what she calls a “cult.” She got a boyfriend she hoped to marry as a way out, but Epstein kept calling her back and the abuse continued. She never told her boyfriend what was happening, and the two eventually broke up.
Molchanova did not tell a friend about her dire situation until early 2019, and the friend helped her come up with a plan to fight back. That March, she emailed Kahn, Epstein’s accountant, asking why her credit history showed credit cards she had never opened. She also demanded to see her tax returns and be removed as a founder of JSC Interiors. Kahn replied that she could hire someone else to handle the tax returns but promised to send her the paperwork to leave JSC Interiors.
Around the same time, Molchanova sent Epstein an email accusing him directly. He responded by inviting her to Palm Beach, but she did not go. “I thought for sure, at that moment, someone would find me on the bottom of his pool if I go,” she said. Lesley Groff, Epstein’s longtime assistant, tried to persuade her to call him, and another young woman from his circle called her as well. Despite the pressure, she never returned to the “cult.”
In her interview with the Wall Street Journal, Molchanova recalled that she had nicknamed Epstein “little bear.” In June 2019, she painted a picture depicting the arrest and beheading of a bear, with no way of knowing that Epstein would be taken into custody on July 6, and that weeks later he would be found dead in his cell at a federal jail in New York.

Future pension – the result of today’s choices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:09:17 UTC
18:09:17 KST

By Evija Dundure, Head of the Insurance and Pension Supervision Department at Latvijas Banka.
We still too often think of a pension as something the state will pay us in the future. However, Latvia’s pension system already works differently. Part of our social security contributions is invested in financial markets, and our future pension depends not only on how much we have contributed, but also on how much our money has earned.
The figures clearly illustrate the scale of these funds. More than €11 billion has already been accumulated in Latvia’s second-pillar pension system. Investments generated €556 million in returns in 2025 and as much as €891 million in the first half of 2026. Naturally, financial markets will experience both rises and falls, and we cannot expect such growth to continue uninterrupted or in a straight line. However, over a period of several decades, this is precisely the purpose of the second pension pillar – the money we contribute is invested so that it can generate returns and increase our future pension capital. Recent years have demonstrated that investment returns make a significant contribution.
This is also where the principle of “money making money”, or the effect of compound interest, comes into play. During the first years of saving, most of the accumulated capital consists of our own contributions. Over time, however, investment returns become increasingly important – the money earned is reinvested and continues to generate further returns. The true power of this effect becomes apparent in the third and fourth decades of saving. This is why time is one of the most valuable resources when building pension savings, particularly for younger people.
The importance of the second pension pillar will only increase. It is expected that in approximately 20 years it will account for at least 30% of newly granted old-age pensions. This means that how a person’s second-pillar pension capital is invested today will have an increasingly significant impact on their income in retirement. From the perspective of pension system supervision, one of the most important questions is therefore seemingly simple: is people’s money being invested in a way that makes the best possible use of the long period remaining until retirement?
Only a few years ago, too many young people were enrolled in pension plans that were excessively conservative for their age. Many had originally been placed in these plans automatically and had not reviewed their choice for years. Their money was less exposed to financial market fluctuations, but it also had less potential to generate long-term returns.
The situation has changed dramatically in recent years. Since pension fund managers began more actively informing clients about whether their chosen plans were appropriate for their age two years ago, people have been switching pension plans almost 50% more frequently than before. People aged between 25 and 40 have been the most active in reviewing their choices.
These changes are already visible in the pension plans themselves. More and more young people are choosing plans with a higher proportion of investments in equities, thereby giving their money greater potential to grow over the long term. Nevertheless, more than one in ten second-pillar participants under the age of 45 are still in a pension plan that is too conservative for their age. Two years ago, this was almost one in seven. Considerable progress has been made, but these figures also clearly show that there is still work to be done: some people have several decades remaining until retirement, yet their money is not making full use of that time.
As retirement approaches, however, the situation is reversed. Protecting accumulated capital from sharp financial market fluctuations becomes increasingly important. There is therefore no single pension plan that is best throughout a person’s entire working life. A good pension plan at the age of 30 is not the same as a good pension plan at the age of 60.
This brings us to one of the most important conclusions about the pension system. A well-functioning system is not simply one that offers people a wide range of pension plans. Fund managers need to manage people’s money professionally, costs must be reasonable, competition must work effectively, and investment risk must correspond to the time remaining until retirement. But that alone is not enough. People must also understand the options available to them and be able to make use of them.
Another figure illustrates this well. In Latvia, people can determine what happens to their second-pillar pension savings if they die before reaching retirement age. However, only 43% of second-pillar participants have indicated their choice. This means that more than half have yet to make this decision. Of those who have made a choice, 98% want their savings to pass to their heirs rather than be transferred to the state special pension budget. These figures reveal more than simply a desire to leave money as an inheritance. They demonstrate the gap between the opportunities the pension system provides and the opportunities people actually use. I encourage everyone who has not yet done so to log in to the Latvia.gov.lv portal and indicate their choice regarding the inheritance of their accumulated pension capital.
I see an even greater challenge in voluntary savings. Only around 200,000 people in Latvia regularly make additional savings for retirement. This is insufficient. The first and second pension pillars provide the foundation for retirement income, but for people who want to maintain a standard of living in retirement comparable to that of their working years, this may not be enough.
Here too, time is the best ally. Starting earlier with a relatively small amount can be far more effective than trying to make up for lost time ten years before retirement. The same principle applies: money makes money, and the longer the saving period, the greater the importance not only of the contributions themselves but also of the returns those contributions have had time to generate.
In my view, this is precisely the next stage in the development of Latvia’s pension system. In recent years, we have done a great deal to improve the system itself – expanding investment opportunities, reducing costs and encouraging people to choose plans that are more appropriate for their age. Now, an increasingly important question is whether people know how to make use of these opportunities. The data from the past two years provide grounds for cautious optimism: when people are clearly shown how their choices can affect their future pension, they take action.
It is precisely with this objective that Latvijas Banka has taken over and completely redesigned Manapensija.lv. Our aim is not to create yet another website filled with pension tables and figures. Information has value when it helps people understand their options and make decisions.
On Manapensija.lv, everyone can learn how to use the opportunities offered by the pension system to their advantage, compare pension plans and other forms of savings, including their costs and performance, and choose the most suitable solution for building greater savings for the future.
The website also provides answers to practical questions that arise at different stages of life. What should you do if financial markets fall sharply? Should you switch pension plans at such a time? What should you do with pension capital accumulated in Latvia if you live abroad? When should you begin reducing investment risk? How should you build additional savings? And what must you do to ensure that your second-pillar pension savings pass to your heirs in the event of your death?
As the supervisory authority, Latvijas Banka’s responsibility is to ensure that the pension system is safe and efficient, that people’s savings are professionally managed and that costs are reasonable. However, individuals’ own choices also matter – and when it comes to pension savings, it is particularly important not to postpone them.
Time is one of the most valuable resources in building a pension. The longer money remains invested, the longer it has the opportunity to generate returns not only on the contributions made but also on the returns already earned. This means that even relatively small differences in the choices we make today can lead to significantly different outcomes several decades from now.
A future pension will not be determined by a single decision made shortly before retirement. We are building it today – through choices whose value can be multiplied by time.
Source: bank.lv

Leaked text reveals Australia's $980 million commitment to Solomon Islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:08:27 UTC
18:08:27 KST

Australia strikes in-principle agreement with Solomon Islands for new treaty
In short:
Australia is set to tip more than $980 million into Solomon Islands as part of a new treaty, a leaked text message says.
The two countries have been negotiating over the new deal for some time.
What's next?
Sources have told the ABC that negotiations have all but concluded, with the treaty potentially to be signed in coming weeks.
Australia and Solomon Islands have reached an in-principle agreement on a landmark new treaty, with a leaked text message revealing the federal government has promised to plough more than $980 million in additional funding into the Pacific nation as it tries to lock in the pact.
The federal government is racing to get the treaty signed in the coming weeks after Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale successfully warded off a leadership challenge on Monday.
Mr Wale was forced to scramble back to Solomon Islands last week just hours after landing in Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) leaders meeting when his Home Affairs Minister, Manasseh Maelanga, launched a motion of no confidence, accusing the prime minister of making major decisions without consulting cabinet.
A message from Australia's High Commissioner to Solomon Islands, Jeffrey Roach, to the deputy prime minister Francis Sade last week, which is verified by ABC News and now circulating in political circles, reveals the details of the deal, and shows how Australia was keen to buttress Mr Wale's position as he fought for his political survival.
Mr Roach writes that there had been "terrific progress" on the treaty negotiations, and that Australia was willing to contribute an additional $280 million into the Pacific nation over the next two years under the deal and a further $700 million after that.
He says that will include 820 million Solomon Islands dollars ($142 million) in funding for Mr Wale's signature "free education" policy and SI$275 million ($47.8 million) to provide "visa improvements" and deal with "security requests from Solomon Islands".
Australia also looks set to ramp up support for a sometimes-contentious scheme which funnels money directly to MPs to spend on their constituencies as part of the comprehensive treaty.
The message says Australia would contribute SI$5 million ($870,000) to every constituency for MPs' "development priorities" before the end of this year, along with a further SI$3 million ($500,000) per constituency for 2027 and a further $500,000 per constituency in 2028.
Solomon Islands parliament has 50 seats, so it would see Australia funnelling a total of some $43 million into constituencies before the end of this year, along with a further $25 million in the following two years.
The message reflects Australian government anxieties that the treaty could be endangered if the prime minister was toppled and replaced by Mr Maelanga or another candidate more sceptical towards Australia, like former leader Manasseh Sogavare.
"I very much hope both countries can hold steady to seize this opportunity and lock this in ahead of the November budget session," he writes.
Text could spark political tension
While Mr Roach never directly endorses Mr Wale in his text, the message could still be politically contentious given it was sent in the midst of wrangling over the top job in Solomon Islands.
Opposition leader Manasseh Sogavare has repeatedly accused Australia of foreign interference in Solomon Islands, including when he was prime minister.
Mr Sade told the ABC there was nothing "political" about the message from the Australian High Commission.
"This was simply an update regarding the progress of the treaty discussions; it was never intended for political expediency," he said.
"I routinely receive these briefings to stay informed about the Community Partnerships Program."
The leak comes the day after Mr Wale managed to see off the challenge to his leadership, with the GREAT coalition winning back several defectors and recruiting additional opposition MPs to join their side.
On Sunday, Mr Maelanga announced he would withdraw his challenge, effectively acknowledging the prime minister still had the numbers.
Mr Wale told parliament on Monday morning that he wanted to "thank those that stood firm" behind him, as well as his new supporters, while praising Mr Maelanga for backing down.
"I would like to thank the member for withdrawing the motion … and bring[ing] down the temperature, both in the house, but also in the public mind," he said.
"What is clear, Mr Speaker, is that the public, not just in Honiara but right across the country … want to see the government be given adequate, reasonable opportunity to be able to deliver on its vision."
The prime minister also acknowledged that he had moved at breakneck pace since taking office, saying "many things are changing fast", adding that he had learned lessons from the whole episode.
Canberra moves to seize pro-Australia sentiment
His clear political victory will cause relief in Canberra, which was worried by the prospect of the prime minister being ousted.
Mr Wale only seized power in May, but has tacked sharply towards Australia and the US since then, signing a new agreement with the US Coast Guard and making it clear that he was deeply sceptical of China's attempts to embed itself as a security partner for the Pacific nation.
Australia has also been racing to complete negotiations on the new treaty with Solomon Islands while Mr Wale retains power, with the government keenly conscious that Solomon Islands politics remains inherently fluid and unpredictable.
The Pacific Minister Pat Conroy and senior Australian officials held multiple discussions on the treaty with Solomon Islands Foreign Minister Rick Hou and minister Peter Kenilorea Jr on the sidelines of the PIF leaders meeting last week.
In a statement, Mr Wale's office said the discussions "covered key national priorities including education, health, infrastructure, energy, agriculture, skills development, natural resource management and economic growth".
"A key focus was how Australia's development assistance can be better aligned with Solomon Islands' national priorities and contribute to tangible and measurable outcomes for communities," they said.
Treaty negotiations 'substantively concluded'
The talks came just a week or so after the Foreign Minister Penny Wong also held talks on the treaty with Mr Hou and a host of other Solomon Islands cabinet ministers in Adelaide.
While negotiations are officially ongoing, the ABC has been told that talks are rapidly coming to a close, with one source saying they are "substantively concluded."
An official from the Solomon Islands also said that the two countries had reached a "bilateral understanding" on the treaty.
Mr Conroy would not be drawn on exactly when the treaty would be signed, saying negotiations were "underway".
"Consistent with all of Australia's bilateral treaty negotiations, we will not comment on the details of the negotiations until the treaty is signed," he said.
The government has previously signalled it wanted to sign the pact before the end of the year, but the rapid progress meant the government was beginning to eye possible signing dates within the coming weeks.
Anthony Albanese and Mr Wale are both expected to attend several high-profile global gatherings, including the September United Nations General Assembly in September and possibly the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda in early November.
The former Australian High Commissioner to Solomon Islands, Lachlan Strahan, said while the idea of a treaty was not new, the major commitments being made by Australia were "significant".
"If that's all new money then that's a step change in the amount of funding," he said.
James Batley from the Australian National University said Australia's decision to tip much more money into the constituency funds showed it was willing to do "whatever it takes" to get the deal over the line.
But he said while the risks around corruption and transparency connected to constituency funds were very real, they were manageable.
"I can't imagine that Australia would just tip in money and say go for it. I imagine there would be standards of transparency and accountability that they will insist on," he said.
"There's no question that it's a strongly held bipartisan view in Solomon Islands that MPs understand their constituencies best and should have a role promoting development in their constituencies."
Dr Strahan said that Australia had already been ramping up the quantities of money it was funnelling directly into local constituencies in Solomon Islands over several years.
"This is actually a fairly effective way of getting money out into constituencies and local communities. The main issue is making sure it's spent well, and ensuring it isn't used simply to prop up incumbents," he said.
However Tess Newton Cain, Associate Professor at the Griffith Asia Institute, said she was worried that Australia was trying to "pick winners" by throwing cash behind Mr Wale, which could backfire.
"It's not very strategically smart, because this is Melanesia and the politics are fluid and he's got elections on the horizon … if he's seen as Australia's man, that can have blowback," she said.
Dr Newton-Cain also said she would "need to be convinced" that the constituency funds were the best way to drive development in Solomon Islands.
"We've seen other attempts to make these funds more accountable and transparent and better governed, but they haven't really had much success," she said.
Mr Conroy did not confirm the increase in funding, but said Australian development projects would always maintain high standards.
"All Australian official development assistance is provided in line with Australia's high-quality development programming guidelines, and OECD eligibility criteria for Official Development Assistance," he said.

New Medium-Term Program focuses on maintaining disinflation momentum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:07:09 UTC
18:07:09 KST

Türkiye aims to break inflation inertia and bring consumer inflation back to single-digit levels during the new Medium-Term Program (OVP) period, according to the government’s 2027-2029 economic roadmap.
The program foresees the continuation of the disinflation process following annual consumer inflation of 31.51 percent recorded in August.
Under the OVP targets, annual consumer inflation is projected to reach 28.4 percent by the end of 2026, before declining to 21 percent in 2027, 13.5 percent in 2028 and 9 percent by the end of 2029, returning to single-digit levels.
The program identifies the sustained and uninterrupted continuation of disinflation as a key objective, aiming to restore price stability during the program period.
To support this goal, monetary, fiscal and income policies will continue to be implemented in close coordination, while domestic demand conditions will be guided along a non-inflationary path.
The contribution of aggregate demand conditions to lower inflation will be supported by more favorable cost conditions, while enhanced competition in product markets and stronger supply-side policies will help raise the economy’s production potential.
The Central Bank will continue to use all available policy instruments effectively until price stability is permanently secured, according to the program.
Türkiye will also maintain its inflation-targeting framework and floating exchange rate regime, with currency rates continuing to be determined by market supply and demand conditions.
Communication channels will be strengthened to anchor inflation expectations in line with official targets.
Through a comprehensive policy framework, pricing decisions will be increasingly guided by inflation expectations rather than past inflation, reducing price stickiness and helping to overcome inflation inertia. Administered and regulated prices will be aligned more closely with inflation forecasts and targets.
Authorities will monitor short- and long-term changes in the supply, demand, imports and exports of food and agricultural products through an early-warning approach. Production planning for strategic agricultural goods will continue, taking into account supply-demand balances, self-sufficiency levels, water constraints and regional production potential in order to strengthen food security.

Traffic accidents up 40% in Rapla County year-over-year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:07:00 UTC
18:07:00 KST

Traffic accidents up 40% in Rapla County year-over-year
The number of traffic accidents has increased in almost every region, with Rapla County standing out in particular. There have been 40 percent more accidents there than last year.
Something appears to be going on in Rapla County as traffic accident statistics make the county a clear record holder. There were 324 traffic accidents there in the first half of this year, compared with 228 during the same period last year, an increase of more than 40 percent.
"Rapla County really stands out because, if we look at the accidents that have occurred there, drivers in Rapla County are twice as likely to hit objects — roadside posts, guardrails and possibly fences," said Tuuli Pärenson, chair of the board of the Estonian Motor Insurance Bureau.
The bureau cannot say what specifically may be behind the high number of accidents, but extensive roadwork related to the construction of Rail Baltica is currently underway in the county.
"Any major road construction project, detour or change in traffic management — if something is changed or a traffic light is installed where there wasn't one before — always temporarily increases the number of accidents because drivers misjudge the situation," Pärenson said.
At the same time, the number of people injured in traffic accidents has fallen. Last year, 36 people were injured in crashes in Rapla County, compared with 23 this year.
In a written response, police said that while extensive construction work has made traffic conditions more difficult in parts of Rapla County and requires drivers to pay greater attention, speeds are lower in those areas, meaning accidents also tend to have less serious consequences.
Setting aside the Rapla County anomaly, 40 percent of accidents occur in parking lots, 17 percent are rear-end collisions and 13 percent are collisions between vehicles at intersections.
Driving instructor Aldis Alus said the most common cause of traffic accidents is failure to follow a basic rule.
"As we know, the right-hand rule applies in parking lots when there is no yield sign. Many drivers look at it and think, 'I'm on what looks like the through road, so I can just keep going.' But in fact, they don't have the right of way," Alus said.
According to the driving instructor, many people drive from memory rather than paying attention to traffic signs, even when traffic arrangements were changed as much as a year ago.
As an instructor, he would give Estonia's driving culture a grade of 3+ or 4-. Some things on the roads have improved, but there is still a widespread lack of consideration for other road users.

Kaşif Kozinoğlu's funeral (AA Photo)
Authorities on Sept. 7 ordered the detention of 11 prison officials over the 2011 death of a former intelligence officer, Kaşif Kozinoğlu, whose case was recently reopened.
Kozinoğlu, a former senior official at Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization (MİT), was arrested in 2011 as part of the Ergenekon investigation.
The Ergenekon trial was based on fabricated evidence and accusations by FETÖ members trying to purge the military officers by accusing them of planning a coup.
Kozinoğlu died in prison on Nov. 12, 2011, in the eighth month of his detention, shortly before he was due to give testimony in the case.
His death was officially attributed to a heart attack. However, questions were raised over whether he had received timely and proper medical intervention, while allegations that he may have been poisoned also became a subject of controversy.
The case file also revealed contradictory statements from prison guards and medical staff regarding how Kozinoğlu was transferred from the prison to the hospital.
The case into Kozinoğlu’s death was recently reopened after the Justice Ministry established a special unit to investigate unsolved cases that have generated significant public attention.
In the investigation conducted by the Silivri Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office, detention warrants were issued for 11 people who were working at the prison at the time of Kozinoğlu’s death.
Ten of the suspects were detained, while one was reported to be a fugitive abroad.
In a written statement on Sept. 7, Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said a special team was conducting the investigation and that a confidentiality order was imposed on the case.
Recalling that the initial investigation launched following Kozinoğlu’s death resulted in a decision not to prosecute on April 10, 2012, Gürlek said the non-prosecution decision was lifted on Aug. 26.
“Comprehensive efforts have been launched to shed light on the incident in all its aspects,” Gürlek said.
The minister said the suspect being sought as a fugitive abroad was also a FETÖ fugitive, adding that efforts were continuing to identify those responsible and ensure that they were brought to justice.
Kozinoğlu was the former head of MİT’s Department of Foreign Operations.
While serving in the military as a major at the Special Warfare Department, Kozinoğlu was responsible for Central Asia.
He also served in Syria, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Afghanistan. In September 2010, he was appointed to the Asian region as a “chief adviser” on the instructions of then-MİT leader Hakan Fidan.
