25 years ago, two strangers met in the twin towers and escaped on 9/11. What happened next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:00:30 UTC
18:00:30 KST

He has told the story hundreds of times, but it never seems to fade. If anything, it only becomes more vivid. “Oh, gosh,” exclaims Stanley Praimnath, his voice cracking with an “ooooooh!” as if bearing a weight. “It’s like reliving that day.”
Nearly 3,000 people died in the terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DC on September 11 2001. But Praimnath and another office worker, Brian Clark, were two of only four individuals known to have survived from above the impact zone in either tower of the World Trade Center. The two strangers met in the smoke and fire of the 81st floor of the south tower, and walked down 1,620 steps into the rest of their lives.
Their split-second decisions that day made all the difference. Over the next 25 years, both men moved from middle age into old age and retirement. Both enjoyed family weddings and watched children and grandchildren grow. Both saw US presidents come and go as old wars ended and new wars began. They remained friends through it all.
They also told their story – countless times – in churches, schools, TV studios and elsewhere. “It could be 800, 1,200, a number like that,” Clark estimates.
Praimnath, in a separate interview, muses: “People refer to me as ‘the 9/11 guy’. It doesn’t feel repetitive. It is like unloading baggage from my shoulder, like washing my soul with tears. It is comforting to know that people out there still want to hear.”
A cry for help
Clark is now 79, living in retirement in northern New Jersey with his wife; he has 11 grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. Praimnath, a decade younger, lives in Valley Stream, Long Island; he is a pastor, grandfather and empty-nester who speaks of his survival not as luck, but as an act of God’s grace.
Their recollections of 9/11 are still as clear as the cloudless sky over Manhattan on that September morning. Clark, a Canadian who was executive vice-president at the financial brokerage firm Euro Brokers, arrived at his office on the 84th floor around 7.15am. Down on the 81st floor, the Guyanese-born Praimnath had settled into his desk at Fuji Bank, where he worked as a loan officer.
At 8.46am, the peace was shattered by a deafening double boom as the hijacked American Airlines Flight 11 slammed into the north tower. Clark recalls: “The lights above me flickered and I spun around in my chair and my peripheral vision caught flames against the window. It was surreal. Two or three seconds later, the flames dissipated and the airspace was filled with singed paper.”
Having volunteered as a floor fire warden after the 1993 World Trade Center truck bombing, Clark sprang into action. He retrieved an official torch marked “WTC fire safety team” from an overhead cabinet and began shepherding staff toward the building’s central corridor.
Co-workers crowded against the north-facing windows, gazing up nine stories at the raging “ring of fire” consuming their twin building. Thinking the emergency was confined next door, Clark phoned his wife at home and his father in Toronto, reassuring them that he was safe.
Three floors below, Praimnath was on the telephone with a colleague in Chicago who had witnessed the north tower explosion on television and begged him to evacuate. He was looking towards the Statue of Liberty when he spotted another plane – so close that he could make out the “U” on the tail of United Airlines Flight 175.
“On a given day, it was normal for a plane to zoom by a half a mile to a mile away,” he recalls. “But this plane is coming towards me. I made eye contact. I dropped the phone and screamed and said, ‘Lord, I can’t do this. You take over’. I don’t know why I said that – but thank God I said that.”
Praimnath dived under his desk in the foetal position, weeping and praying as the Boeing 767 bore down on his window. “With the most thunderous sound, the plane came and crashed into the building,” he says.
The aircraft struck diagonally at 9.03am, cutting through the 77th to 85th floors. The impact flattened entire walls, severed electrical wiring and sent a shock wave of jet fuel and debris through Fuji Bank’s offices.
Praimnath says: “That big orange glow that you see there – I’m stuck in the middle of it. Upon impact, it looks like a demolition crew came with a big giant wrecking ball and ripped the entire office. Every wall is flattened. I remember a large chunk of the plane was broken off and stuck in the office doorway.
“I remember flames all around me, as if somebody took a giant bag of cement, threw it in the air and I can’t breathe. The floor above me collapsed and it’s hovering over the desk and I’m like, ‘Oh, my God, I’m going to die. It’s gonna totally collapse, crush me to death, or I’m gonna get sucked out by the air pressure.’ You can hear the sound.”
At the memory, he sets his teeth and blows down the phone to recreate the terrifying whoosh.
Three floors higher, Clark was standing on the west side of the 84th floor when the aircraft sliced into the building’s eastern trading floor. “Our room exploded,” he says. “Everything came out of the ceiling – air conditioning ducts, lighting, the whole works. For five seconds the building swayed to the west and then it swayed back to vertical. For those 10 seconds I was quite terrified, thinking the building was going to roll over. But it didn’t.”
When the tower steadied, Clark gathered a group of six or seven colleagues and led them toward the central core. The impact had demolished stairwells B and C, but stairwell A, tucked furthest away on the north-west side, somehow remained open.
The group began descending stairwell A. On the 81st floor landing, they were halted by a man and woman coming up the stairs. “She was insistent we not go down,” Clark says. “‘No, no, no. You can’t go down,’ she said and, because she stopped us, it allowed me to hear a call for help from within the 81st floor, a muffled cry: ‘Help, I’m buried. I can’t breathe.’”
Brothers for life
Clark squeezed through an opening where the door frame had been ripped from the drywall and stepped into the dark 81st floor, guided by Praimnath’s desperate shouts.
Inside the office, Praimnath prayed for rescue. “I can still remember the flames encroaching and I’m screaming, ‘Lord, send somebody, I don’t want to die.’ I’m crawling away from the flames, dodging all the cables that were hanging in the ceiling, short-circuiting because the sprinkler system came on,” he recalls.
“I’m like, ‘Oh my God, I’m gonna die.’ Somebody had a flashlight on the other end of the floor. The person’s saying, ‘I’ll wait for you’, but I couldn’t hear because I got temporarily deaf when the plane hit the building. As I’m crawling away, the flames are coming closer, licking up the office space.
“I got to the wall. The person’s saying, ‘Bang on the wall, I know where you are’. I hit the wall and the person says, ‘Climb over there.’ It had a hollow ceiling, a 10-foot sheetrock wall, a drywall. I remember that so vividly.”
Clark’s torchlight had picked out a hand protruding from a hole in the 10-foot sheetrock wall. He grasped Praimnath’s hands and hauled him over the partition. The desk beneath Clark gave way, and both men crashed to the floor in a heap.
Clark recalls: “We fell and he gave me a big kiss. I said, ‘What’s going on, what are you doing?’ I stuck out my hand and said, ‘I’m Brian Clark.’ He says, ‘I’m Stanley Praimnath; we’ll be brothers for life.’ I said, ‘Well, I don’t have any siblings.’”
Clark noticed that Praimnath had a puncture wound on his palm, while his own hand was cut and bleeding from moving debris. Clark recalls his instinctive gesture of solidarity: “I smooshed our hands together and said, ‘In fact, we’ll be blood brothers for life. Come on, buddy. Let’s go home.’”
When they returned to the stairwell, Clark made the critical decision to ignore the warning of the woman on the landing. Pointing his torch down the staircase, he saw no flames. Clark and Praimnath turned downward. Most of the colleagues who had been with Clark, however, chose to head upward, believing safety lay on the roof. They died in the collapse. At Euro Brokers, 61 of Clark’s colleagues perished.
Lives intertwined
When Clark and Praimnath finally emerged on to the street, police and emergency workers yelled at them to run. Minutes later, the south tower collapsed in a cascade of steel and concrete, sending a rolling cloud of debris surging through lower Manhattan. The two men dived inside 42 Broadway to escape the choking dust.
In the chaos, Praimnath reached into his pocket and handed Clark a business card from a small home business he and his wife operated. Separated in the confusion, Clark used the number on that card to reach Praimnath late that evening, confirming that both had made it home.
While Clark suffered remarkably little long-term psychological distress – describing his lack of post-traumatic stress as an unearned “gift” – Praimnath’s return to the living was fraught.
Arriving home on Long Island on the evening of 9/11, Praimnath says he suffered profound memory loss. “I wanted to know what this strange woman was doing in our house with two children, not going home. I refused to go to bed because this strange woman was in that room.”
His wife, Jennifer, quietly cared for him without judgment. “She would hobble me into the bathroom, fill the tub with warm water and Epsom salts, and tell me to soak,” he says. “Then she would put me on the couch. Every day, she would leave an apple, a sandwich, a bottle of water and a notepad. I don’t know how long I was in that state. All I know is that one day, I got up, looked at her, recognised her and snapped out of it.”
When Praimnath returned to work in October at a temporary office in Jersey City, he still could not navigate on his own. “I had to draw out my commute on a map and color-code it,” he recalls. “When I got to work, people would say, ‘Stan, can you please sign this?’ I didn’t have a clue what I was signing. But they were kind, patient managers. Gradually, the pieces came back.”
In the quarter-century since that Tuesday morning, the lives of Clark and Praimnath have remained intertwined. They shared family milestones, celebrated at each other’s daughters’ weddings and phoned one another regularly.
When Clark’s eldest daughter married, Praimnath and his wife were seated at the head table. Praimnath says: “Brian introduced me to all his friends and family as his blood brother. You could see people looking around, thinking, ‘Something doesn’t quite fit the picture!’ But Brian didn’t care. That’s who he is. He is the big brother I never had.”
For Praimnath, surviving 9/11 opened a deep spiritual vocation. In 2006, he became a pastor, joining the staff of the church where his father-in-law was senior minister. Over the past two decades, he has travelled to churches, military bases and schools worldwide, delivering his testimony as a sermon on redemption.
“On 9/11, I was crying out to the Lord under that desk, ‘Lord, let me live to walk my daughters down the aisle,’ and God answered. I walked Stephanie and Caitlin down the aisle. I’ve lived to see my grandchildren, Hannah and Ezra. They don’t call me Papa – they call me ‘Papaya’. Stephanie even bought me a shirt that says ‘Papaya’.”
Yet Praimnath’s resilience has been tested repeatedly. In 1993, he narrowly escaped the first truck bombing at the World Trade Center. He was diagnosed with leukaemia and a severe bout of Covid-19 scarred his lungs with bilateral pneumonia. Then, after a trip to Europe with his wife, doctors discovered that his four coronary arteries were severely blocked, requiring emergency quadruple bypass surgery.
“My question has always been: how many times do you try to kill one man?” asks Praimnath, who retired from the Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation two years ago. “I’m living by grace. I still travel. I still do exactly what I used to do before.”
Blood brothers
He and Clark know they have more years behind them than lie ahead. On the 25th anniversary, Clark will attend a memorial service at his local town square in New Jersey, beginning at 8.45am, before spending the day quietly with his wife. Praimnath will be at a church in Virginia, telling his story once again, with gratitude.
Both men find themselves speaking to a generation for whom 9/11 is not a living memory, but history. Clark, who retired in 2006, says: “I don’t have to teach history anymore – the textbooks have that covered. What textbooks don’t have is the emotional reality, the optimism that life carries on despite terrible evil. But whenever I speak at schools, 98% of the time, the very first question the kids ask is: ‘Are you still in touch with Stanley?’”
Praimnath experiences the exact same phenomenon. Just recently, he addressed 700 students over Zoom at a Christian school in Tampa, Florida. “These children weren’t even alive when the towers fell,” Praimnath says. “Yet when you describe the roar of the jet engine and the wing slicing through the office, you can hear the audible gasp in the auditorium. It becomes real to them.”
The blood brothers look out at the contemporary US with a mixture of sorrow and perplexity. Clark has become an outspoken pacifist, dismayed by the decades of overseas conflict that followed the attacks.
He says: “With 25 years of time to think about it, I realise more and more the utter futility of war. I think of Germany, Italy, and Japan being our greatest allies today. What on earth are we doing to ourselves? Dropping bombs on residential areas in Ukraine, Russia, Gaza – what a senseless waste of energy and human life.”
Clark’s aversion to vengeance ran so deep that he was repulsed by the street celebrations following the killing of al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden in 2011. “I was disgusted when people were driving around in pickup trucks chanting ‘USA!’ and cheering for another human being’s death. Capture him, interrogate him, lock him away – fine. But taking lives and celebrating it? No. That is not who we should be.”
Praimnath recalls the profound but fleeting sense of unity that blossomed after 9/11. “After that infamous day, the entire nation rallied around each other,” he reflects. “All the churches were packed. A month later, everything went back to normal.
“But I still believe we are a resilient people. We may have our political differences but at the end of the day we know that, when tragedy strikes, the labels fall away. On the 81st floor, there were no Republicans or Democrats, no Black or white. We were just brothers trying to find the way out.”

I had an amazing experience as a disabled person at school in the 70s. Since then, discrimination has got far worse | Mik Scarlet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:00:29 UTC
18:00:29 KST

As a disabled person, you’re forced to repeatedly explain your medical history – but for this article, I think it’s important. I was born with a very rare type of cancer called a neuroblastoma. In 1965, it was pretty much a death sentence. Luckily, I took part in a clinical trial and, with only days to live, I had major surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy with a new drug. Despite being given no more than five years to live, on my last birthday I celebrated hitting 60. I doubt anyone in 1965 would have imagined how attitudes towards disabled people would improve as I grew up. It is devastating to see how those same attitudes have reversed in the past decade or two.
The cancer left me with a paralysed right leg, so I wore a leg brace, but otherwise I was a pretty normal kid. I was lucky to be starting school in 1970 when the Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act came into force, which made it possible for disabled children to attend mainstream schools, if they could manage it. My parents moved across Luton to be near the only school that would accept me on a trial run and then as a pupil. When I was a child, if you could manage living like non-disabled people then you were allowed to do so. Not the fully inclusive practice I later campaigned for, but an acknowledgment that disabled people shouldn’t be written off.
At 15, my spine collapsed and crushed the nerves to both legs, an unforeseen side effect of chemo. After months in hospital I came home a full-time wheelchair user. I was lucky our town centre in Luton was very wheelchair accessible and, during my time in hospital, my high school put in some serious adaptations to ensure I could return. Accessible toilets and a lift meant I could take my exams without any real difficulty, thanks to Putteridge high school and the then headteacher, Mr Price. At Luton sixth form college, adaptations were made again, this time under my guidance. Through the course of my childhood ideas around disability had changed from “if they can, let them try” to “what can we do to help them succeed?” and even “what do they want us to do?”
That was the overarching attitude I encountered for the next 20 years. Some viewed being disabled as a tragedy, others as part of life. Most people saw any help that we received as important and something a healthy society should be offering. The exception was the workplace. I tried two jobs, both of which ended in me being sacked because I took a couple of days off. One was because I broke my foot in a lift that was too small for my wheelchair, the other was following a car accident. Both times, taking sick leave was seen as proof that disabled people couldn’t manage the world of work. So I focused on my hobby, music, and was soon touring the UK and Europe playing in bands. This led to my discovery by a TV producer. I ended up on the BBC, ITV and Channel 4, where my show Beat That won an Emmy. My media career, as one of the first disabled celebrities, lasted more than 15 years and only ended during a period of ill health.
In the late 90s and early 00s, I found attitudes became twisted towards an angrier, almost jealous view of disabled people. My Motability vehicle was vandalised repeatedly, because local people were upset about my “free car”. This morphed into “free car, free house and loads of benefits” as Tony Blair’s government, from 1998 onwards, implemented cuts to the benefits bill that scapegoated disabled people. I was attacked twice, my car was vandalised every week and my wife was beaten to a pulp by three people wearing masks. When they threatened to burn our flat down, we packed up and left our fully adapted home to rent somewhere that was safe from violence but totally unsuitable. The police? Useless.
My own brother even once spouted that it was “all right for you with your free car, free house and benefits cash”. It was especially galling as I had worked most of my adult life, paying taxes. The only time I stopped work was when I was very ill. My wife cared for me during this time, and we went from earning about £50,000 in joint income to being paid £15,000 in benefits to cover everything, including our rent. Luckily I got well again, retrained and went back to work as an access consultant.
But those toxic narratives seem to be getting worse, and have become embedded in the national psyche. Successive governments and the media have continued to tell the public lies, such as the much repeated accusations of huge amounts of fraud within the so-called “disability benefits” system that has led to terrifying levels of anger. Only a week ago I was punched in the street for being a “scrounger”.
I call them lies because that’s what they are. Motability is not a free car. It is a vehicle that is leased for a set fee over a three- or five-year period. We don’t get a free Mercedes or BMW. We make a huge upfront payment and it costs the same per week as a tiny little car. And personal independence payment (Pip) is not an out-of-work benefit. It is paid to support independent living, based on people’s ability and support needs. No one is getting it for tennis elbow. In fact, Pip and its forerunners allowed me to work, and my Motability vehicle lets me travel the UK working as co-CEO of the national charity Phab. The access to work scheme saves employers money by paying towards the adaptations and support a disabled worker might need. It brings in £1.48 for every £1 paid out, with the wider economy benefiting by £3.86, according to research carried out by the Royal National Institute of Blind People.
As we mark 31 years since the Disability Discrimination Act and 16 since that was superseded by the Equality Act, please don’t believe the hype around disabled people. Try to imagine a day walking in our shoes, or pushing our wheels. Before you allow the hype around “the freebies” we get, do some research. My wheelchair alone cost me £6,500, for example. No support; that was all out of my pocket.
As I visit the clubs and events Phab supports I meet many disabled people who can only dream of having a life like mine. But shouldn’t all disabled people have the chance to shine? When I was young I had hoped that the future would allow disabled people to fulfil their potential, and let them lead the discussion around making society more accessible and inclusive for everyone. An accessible, inclusive society helps us all. Take the lift, the ability to text and voice-to-text software. All designed to help disabled people, but now a boon to us all. If disabled people are listened to, everyone benefits.
I doubt many of us considered that things would get worse, but if disabled people are allowed to tell the reality of our lives maybe we can get back to a positive place. One where being disabled is just part of daily life. Not sad or tragic, or a licence for free government handouts. Just normal.
- 
  Mik Scarlet is co-CEO of the national charity Phab, a campaigner and a music journalist for Blitzed magazine

SCMP partners with top Kazakh university to deepen Hong Kong’s Central Asia ties
Memorandum of understanding with Nazarbayev University signed ahead of SCMP’s China Conference: Central Asia 2026 in Astana
The South China Morning Post has signed an agreement with a leading university in Kazakhstan to foster the exchange of knowledge between East and Central Asia while extending Hong Kong’s media presence in the region.
The memorandum of understanding (MOU) was signed on Monday in Astana, just ahead of the SCMP’s China Conference: Central Asia 2026, a flagship event making its debut in the region.
According to the agreement, the strategic partnership formalises links between the SCMP and Nazarbayev University – Central Asia’s top-ranked higher education institution – by fostering academic dialogue and knowledge-sharing as well as “connecting the city’s capital and media reach with the region’s tech and resource ecosystem”.
SCMP publisher Tammy Tam said the agreement represented a vital bridge between leading academic research and global media excellence.
“As a premier voice on China and Asia, the South China Morning Post is proud to collaborate with Kazakhstan’s flagship university to elevate cross-border storytelling, foster deeper cultural and educational exchange, and illuminate Eurasia’s critical role in shaping the future of global connectivity and building a talent pool for the region,” she said.
Professor Waqar Ahmad, president of Nazarbayev University, said the partnership would bring the institution’s academic expertise and research to a much wider international audience, adding its studies could also provide the newspaper with new perspectives on the region.
“The partnership also creates new opportunities for our students to access knowledge and perspectives from a leading international media organisation, while bringing our academic communities closer together,” he said.

Chinese firms’ green-tech expansion hinges on Hong Kong, senior bankers say
Offshore yuan liquidity makes city a ‘superconnector’, but finding projects with strong returns is now the challenge, senior bankers say
Hong Kong is poised to play a bigger role in financing Chinese green-technology companies’ expansion into emerging markets, as geopolitical fragmentation and high funding costs reshape how capital is deployed in the global energy transition, according to senior banking executives.
The city’s deep sustainable-finance market and offshore yuan liquidity could help channel capital into green and climate-resilience projects across developing economies, executives from Bank of China (Hong Kong), DBS, HSBC and Standard Chartered said during a panel discussion at a forum on Monday.
The annual forum organised by the Hong Kong Green Finance Association and the Greater Bay Area Green Finance Alliance brought together policymakers, financiers and industry leaders to discuss sustainable investment amid rising geopolitical, trade and economic uncertainty.
Chinese companies in solar power, wind energy, batteries and other green technologies are increasingly taking their solutions overseas, particularly to the Global South, and Hong Kong could play a larger role in financing these companies as they expand into developing markets, said Wang Huabin, deputy CEO of Bank of China (Hong Kong).
“Hong Kong has also led Asia in sustainable finance for years … [and it] is well positioned as a bridge for Chinese green technology going global,” Wang said, adding that the city’s sustainable-finance market, offshore yuan liquidity and professional services could be combined to provide financing and professional support for Chinese companies investing abroad.
Natalie Blyth, HSBC’s global head of sustainable finance and transition, said that mainland Chinese companies have some of the “most dynamic low-carbon technologies” globally.

A Clockwork Orange to come to stage in eerily prescient adaptation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

A Clockwork Orange comes to stage in first Belvoir St Theatre season since fire
When Margaret Thanos read A Clockwork Orange for the first time last year, she was struck by the similarities between the dystopia of the novel and society today.
"I couldn't help but feel Burgess was not describing some horrific imagined future, but the world I and my female friends feel like we live in right now," the director says.
Written by English author Anthony Burgess in 1962, in the shadow of World War II, A Clockwork Orange follows teenager Alex, who, with his gang of "droogs", inflicts "ultraviolence" on other people living in their near-future society.
When Alex is caught and convicted of the murder of an elderly woman, he is subjected to an experimental rehabilitation program, designed to make him severely ill at the thought of violence.
A Clockwork Orange was made into a movie by Stanley Kubrick in 1971 and will be adapted into a new play by Sydney's Belvoir St Theatre in 2027.
"I do feel like it's getting worse actually — that we're seeing a regression into a culture that not only condones but rewards behaviour of this kind: misogyny, racism, right-wing extremism," Thanos says.
In her early 20s, Thanos worked in feminist activist spaces, including as an advocate for girls' equality non-profit Plan International, but found herself feeling despondent.
"I didn't really matter what we did inside of the feminist movement if we couldn't address the challenges inside of 'boys' club' culture," she says. "The internet was making the problem worse. It was encouraging us to stop thinking for ourselves."
That lack of thinking is something Thanos saw in Burgess's novel.
"[He] makes the central question about choice and free will and whether anyone is really choosing to be good," Thanos says.
"If we're not guided by a true sense of obligation to another human being standing in front of us, then we are more easily swayed by the structures of society around us to behave in whatever way we are told to behave."
Tom Wright, who Thanos approached to adapt A Clockwork Orange, was drawn to the story as a kind of fable.
"It's not a story of profound psychology," Wright says. "It's a story about a society and about how a society deals with its demons."
Wright was also excited by the chance to work with the made-up language Alex and his droogs speak to one another: the Russian-influenced "Nadsat".
"What leapt out was the quality of that spoken language and just how theatrically inventive it is," he says. "It's the language of an alienated class, but it also has a celebratory quality.
"Somehow Alex and his droogs have found a way to be almost more energetic and more exuberant than the society they belong to — they dress and speak more flamboyantly; their imaginative inner lives seem stronger than those of the people around them.
"[It's] almost as if their violent, antisocial behaviour is a legitimate response to an uncaring society."
Cross-generational collaboration
The collaboration between Thanos and Wright exemplifies the way Belvoir forges connections between artists of different generations and acts as a training ground for emerging theatre-makers.
"In theatre terms, Margaret and I are like two generations apart," Wright says. "That's a really useful collaboration.
"She can call upon my experience and I can call upon her ambition."
It's a theme of the season, which also sees Belvoir's artistic director Eamon Flack assistant-directing the debut play from Kalkadoon writer-director Abbie-lee Lewis, Dirty Diamonds, about two Aboriginal women — played by Logie winner Lila McGuire (Goolagong) and Ruby Henaway — hitting the road to escape one of their exes.
Other young artists coming to the fore at Belvoir in 2027 are Ayah Tayeh and Mehhma Malhi, co-directors of Wish You Were Here, by Pulitzer Prize-winning Iranian American writer Sanaz Toossi (English); director Hannah Goodwin, and writer Grace Chapple, who are collaborating on The Landlord, Chapple's horror-comedy about intergenerational inequity, set in a pair of Sydney terrace houses.
"The only way a new generation can learn the sort of secret lore of [theatre] is for it to get passed on from one person to another," Flack says.
Arts community banding together
Belvoir's 2027 season is the company's first since its workshop and warehouse were destroyed by fire in June.
"We're through that initial stage of 'How the f*** do we keep going?', and we're now in the 'How do we rebuild?' stage," Flack says.
Thanks to the sheer willpower and efforts of Belvoir's production team — and the support of audiences through donations — The Jungle and the Sea and The Book of Everything opened as scheduled.
The former's sets had been destroyed in the fire and were re-created from scratch in just 10 days, while the latter's had already been lost after a previous tour and were painstakingly remade by both Belvoir staff and external contractors.
"We didn't have to miss an hour of [Jungle and the Sea] rehearsals because of the commitment and cunning and heart with which our production team just swung into action," Flack says.
"You could call it a miracle, but it's the people and the spirit of, 'let's get on with it'."
The support of the arts community, including Sydney Theatre Company and Opera Australia offering space and equipment, is an example of how local companies are working together at a time when it is increasingly difficult to make theatre.
While the cost-of-living crisis is impacting audiences and artists alike, theatre companies are grappling with rising production costs, changing audience behaviours and a lack of funding.
"There's a vicious cycle going on," Flack says. "The material challenge of living the life of a theatre artist is excruciatingly difficult for so many people, and at the same time, so many companies are in such tight financial circumstances they're having to hire fewer artists."
So, companies are collaborating through co-productions and transfers, which not only extend the lives of shows, but keep artists, many of whom survive contract to contract, employed for longer periods.
Belvoir's 2027 season includes two co-productions, Stereophonic by David Adjmi, with Melbourne Theatre Company (MTC) and Queensland Theatre Company, and Dirty Diamonds, with MTC and in association with Yirra Yaakin Theatre Company in Perth.
It also includes two transfers, with Megan Wilding's Game. Set. Match. coming to Sydney from Melbourne's Malthouse, a decade after the Gamilaroi writer and actor first started to develop the play with Belvoir, and one-woman show The Lark, starring Noni Hazlehurst, opening after seasons in cities and regional centres around Australia.
"We're nothing on our own at Belvoir," Flack says.
"Sharing resources and giving shows future lives, letting them grow and become better and be seen by more communities across more parts of the country, that's the only strategy left."

Plastics Companies Are Writing Lesson Plans. What Could Go Wrong?

18:00:00 KST

This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
This fall, 54 million K-12 students are headed back to the classroom for another year of lessons in all the classic subjects: math, English, history, biology. But there’s another subject that’s been sneaking into school curricula: plastics.
A new report from the nonprofit Plastic Pollution Coalition documents the many ways the plastics industry has been inserting its agenda into classrooms across the US—including through lesson plans and worksheets, hands-on science experiments, and a program called “PlastiVan” that travels from city to city teaching students about “the contribution plastics make to modern life.”
Industry interests offer these resources to teachers for free or for cheap, according to the report. The materials tend to highlight the necessity of plastics while downplaying their significant downsides to human health and the environment.
“When that information is provided to kids, it obfuscates the true impacts of plastic pollution,” said Madison Dennis, senior policy and advocacy manager for Plastic Pollution Coalition and one of the report’s main authors. Besides harming marine life, plastics can expose people to hazardous chemicals, clog storm drains and contribute to flooding, and release planet-warming greenhouse gases. The Plastic Pollution Coalition is calling for stricter school policies against the use of industry-sponsored learning materials.
The report lays out four case studies of plastics industry “propaganda” for schoolkids. One involves the Society of Plastics Engineers, or SPE, a trade group that recently became a division of the Plastics Industry Association. SPE’s lesson plans include activities like a “plastic scavenger hunt,” which aims for students to “understand that plastics are ubiquitous and their importance to society and their personal life.” A video titled “Your Bottle Means Jobs” explains how plastics recycling supports local employment.
Another case study highlights the American Association of Chemistry Teachers, an initiative of the Dow Chemical Company. One of the association’s lesson plans teaches elementary and middle school students how to compare the strength of various types of plastic bags that can be found in a grocery store. After a brief experiment, the lesson invites them to “pretend [they] are an employee for Dow Chemical Company” and are designing a plastic bag for a customer.
While many of the materials claim to support STEM learning objectives, they do so while promoting familiar industry talking points, emphasizing the affordability and safety of plastics. Some acknowledge plastic pollution as a serious problem, but they blame irresponsible consumer behaviors and, instead of recommending less plastic be produced, propose more recycling as the primary way to address it.
In reality, only 9 percent of all plastics are recycled worldwide, and scientists have repeatedly warned that recycling will be unable to keep up with projected growth in plastic production. Investigative reporting has shown that industry groups knew this decades ago, but promoted recycling anyway in order to defuse growing concern over plastic pollution.
Wendy Johnson, a science education specialist at the National Center for Science Education, said the industry’s lesson plans and worksheets don’t reflect good pedagogy. Materials claiming to be aligned with state-level STEM standards don’t say which standards they support, or how they’re aligned. Lesson plans instruct students to read teachers’ notes, or list industry-specific vocab terms like “stretch blow molding” or “thermosetting.”
“By using all of these technical terms, it’s tricking people into thinking … that they’re doing science,” Johnson told Grist. What the materials really teach, she said, is “ideological perspectives about the economy,” like the desirability of cheap consumer goods.
“It’s so clear that the purpose isn’t to make really clear, easy-to-use materials,” Johnson added. “The idea isn’t to teach,” but to get industry talking points into classrooms. The report documents plastics propaganda finding its way into schools since at least the 2000s. Between 2009 and 2011, for example, a plastics trade group lobbied the California Department of Education to add a section on “The Advantages of Shopping Bags” to the state’s high school textbooks. The PlastiVan initiative has been ongoing since 2011, and SPE claims it’s reached over 132,000 students in total.
Plastic Pollution Coalition suggests that the problem is particularly significant in schools located near petrochemical facilities. In Beaver County, Pennsylvania, for example, Shell operates a 386-acre plastics production complex and has invested millions of dollars in the development of plastics-related curricula and recycling programs, both for grade schoolers and for community college students. It has also donated hundreds of backpacks filled with school supplies, and bought one school a basketball court—seemingly in exchange for incorporating plastics recycling into the curriculum.
Shell didn’t respond to Grist’s request for comment. Neither did SPE, the American Association of Chemistry Teachers, nor the school district in Beaver County.
The report hints at a broader problem with STEM education in US public schools. Teachers often lack the time and money needed to design their own curricula, or to buy high-quality materials and lesson plans needed for in-class labs or science projects. When vested interests come along offering support—whether it’s the tobacco industry, the junk food industry, the pesticide industry, or the fossil fuel industry—it can be hard to say no.
“As a teacher, I’m always looking for free stuff,” said Suzie Hicks, a K-8 environmental educator in California who consulted on the Plastic Pollution Coalition report. Hicks said their education and background make them comfortable vetting materials for greenwashing—but that’s likely not the case with most teachers.
Dennis recommended that school boards adopt policies banning educational materials sponsored by the chemical, fossil fuel, and plastics industries. She also emphasized the need for better school funding more generally, so that teachers and districts aren’t so desperate for ready-made learning materials.
One way to achieve this would be to eliminate tax breaks for petrochemical processing and plastics production facilities, which deprive communities of much-needed cash.
Katie Allen, executive director of Algalita, a California-based environmental nonprofit that develops educational materials on plastic pollution, pushed back against the idea that schools should ban all industry-sponsored content.
“Once you start banning one thing, where does it end? What I want to do is give educators the benefit of the doubt and allow them to make their own decisions,” she told Grist. She argued that teachers should be trusted to properly contextualize industry materials—and that they could even use them to teach critical-thinking skills.
That said, there are plenty of educational materials on plastics that are developed by nonindustry sources. Algalita, for instance, offers free lesson plans on topics like plastic garbage patches in the oceans and biomagnification—the phenomenon where plastics build up inside sea creatures as you move up the food chain. The Story of Stuff, another nonprofit, offers a broader high school curriculum focused on the costs and consequences of producing consumer goods—including those made from plastics.
Those learning materials still come from organizations with an agenda. But Hicks argued they’re more trustworthy, since nonprofits usually aren’t trying to sell something.
Another option is for teachers to simply design their own curricula. That’s what Jacqueline Omania, a recently retired elementary school teacher in Berkeley, California, did in 2015. She turned her classroom into a zero-waste laboratory, and each year for 11 years, Omania and her students developed a set of zero-waste classroom agreements, vowing to minimize their plastics use—by swapping individual glue sticks for a communal tub of glue, for example—while also advocating for more systemic change, like by campaigning for a policy requiring Berkeley restaurants to stop giving out single-use plastic foodware.
“There are so many challenges in the world, but plastic is something tangible,” Omania said. “It’s right there in front of them, and they can see the difference that they’re actually making through their actions.”

Trump’s ‘small potatoes’ conflict is now a big bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:59:23 UTC
17:59:23 KST

Donald Trump has used an expression for America's war against Iran that, perhaps more than anything, reflects his effort to downplay a reality that is taking on ever-larger dimensions by the day: "small potatoes." It is a term used in English political and everyday language for a matter that is insignificant and marginal. But if the war with Iran is truly "small potatoes," why has the United States, after seven months, still not been able to close the file on it?
This very contradiction is one of the most important signs of the gap between the White House's political narrative and the strategic reality of the war. A war that, in Washington's initial calculations, was supposed to be short, limited, and decisive has now become a multilayered crisis whose effects have extended beyond the military battlefield into energy, the economy, budgets, regional security, and even US domestic politics.
From the beginning, Trump has invested in a specific calculation: that intense military pressure could force Iran to accept Washington's demands within a short period. This calculation, of course, was not only a mistake about Iran's military capability; the bigger mistake was the incorrect understanding of Tehran's political will to continue resisting.
Contrary to the war planners' assumptions, Iran did not become an actor that would quickly retreat from its positions as pressure increased. This very issue caused the equation that was supposed to end with a military strike to enter a process of attrition; a process that, the longer it lasts, the more its costs increase for the United States. This is where the phrase "small potatoes" comes into contradiction with reality.
A war cannot be measured solely by the number of military operations or the amount of damage inflicted on the opposing side. A war demonstrates its strategic importance when it can affect the economic and security order surrounding it. The Iran–US war has become a major crisis precisely from this point. The most important example is energy.
The Strait of Hormuz is of exceptional importance to the global economy and energy markets. Any sustained disruption to the passage of ships through this waterway is not just a military issue between Iran and the United States; it directly affects energy prices, transportation costs, industrial production, and ultimately the cost of living for people in various countries. For the United States, too, this issue is of particular importance. Rising fuel prices, at a time when American households are already facing cost-of-living pressures, can quickly turn from a foreign issue into a domestic political problem.
This is why Trump has repeatedly been compelled to speak about the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the openness of shipping routes. If the war were truly a marginal matter, reopening and normalizing traffic through one of the world's most important energy waterways should not have become one of the main concerns of the US president. The problem, of course, is not only fuel prices.
Months of military operations mean massive consumption of munitions, wear and tear on equipment, the cost of moving forces, repairing and rebuilding damaged facilities, and increased operational costs. These costs are not visible at the moment a missile is fired, but they show up in the government budget and the financial bill of the war.
On the other hand, the cost of war does not drop to zero with the end of the conflict. Replacing equipment and munitions, rebuilding military infrastructure, paying costs related to injured personnel, and restoring the military's operational capacities to prewar levels could continue for years.
Forbes, in a report published on Saturday, also emphasized this very issue, warning that the end of the war does not necessarily mean the end of its costs for the United States and that the financial consequences of this conflict could last for decades. This point is highly significant from a political perspective; because Trump cannot erase the war's bill simply by declaring the end of operations.
In fact, perhaps Trump's greatest challenge is to connect the "military victory" he speaks of in his political rhetoric to a "strategic achievement" that is tangible for the American public.
The American voter will ultimately face a simple question: What did this war bring me?
If the answer is rising fuel prices, a higher cost of living, pressure on the public budget, and continued economic uncertainty, the victory narrative will not be sustainable for long.
This issue becomes even more significant given that, according to a recent poll published by the Financial Times, satisfaction with Trump's performance has fallen to 33 percent, with 64 percent of Americans dissatisfied with his performance. Even among Republicans, satisfaction with his economic performance is reported at only 53 percent. The Iran war is thus gaining a third dimension: US domestic politics.
Trump may be able to present his desired narrative about the military results of the war, but he cannot easily manage the economic experience of millions of Americans. People do not compare the price of gasoline, the cost of food, and the state of their bank accounts with White House statements; they see the result in their daily lives.
From this perspective, downplaying the war may be less a communication strategy and more a sign of concern about its consequences. The more the costs rise, the greater the US government's need will be to present a low-cost image of the war.
But the problem is that reality cannot be forever shrunk with words. Trump may be able to call the war "small potatoes," but seven months of war, the Strait of Hormuz, military costs, energy pressure, and declining public satisfaction present a completely different picture.
Ultimately, the measure of a war's success lies not in the president's description, but in the result it leaves behind. If the United States, after months of war, is still struggling to normalize traffic through Hormuz, contain economic costs, and explain the real achievements of this conflict, it is difficult to consider this war a small matter. Perhaps the real issue for Trump is that what he today calls "small potatoes" is turning into one of the largest foreign policy bills of his presidency; a bill whose most important part may be paid not in the Middle East, but inside the United States.
MNA

BERLIN, September 7. /TASS/. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says he does not feel a need to step down amid his Christian Democrat Union (CDU) party's loss in Sunday’s election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
"I am thinking non-stop about how we can return to working successfully across party lines. Giving up is not an option for me," Merz said at a news conference in Berlin, fielding questions about his potential resignation in the wake of the outcome of the Saxony-Anhalt election. Merz explained that he sees it as his duty, as well as the federal government's, to "open up opportunities for the next generation."
"Our responsibility, including my personal responsibility, is exactly to make sure our children and grandchildren have the same opportunity to live in a country such as Germany in an atmosphere of freedom, peace and prosperity. This is our responsibility. And I do not dodge this responsibility," the German leader said.
The Saxony-Anhalt state parliament election was held on September 6. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a decisive victory with 43.8% of the vote, according to early official results. This was the AfD’s best-ever result in any German state, doubling its share of the vote from the previous state election five years ago. Merz’s CDU came in second, losing more than half of its vote share compared with 2021. The Christian Democrats received just 17.2% of the vote, the CDU’s worst-ever result in Saxony-Anhalt. The Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD) scored third with 9.3% of the vote. The Greens received 8.9% and the Left Party 8.6%. The BSW (formerly the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance -- Reason and Justice) also cleared the threshold to enter the Landtag with 5.3%.
Experts suggest that CDU's defeat reflects disillusionment that has grown in Germany for Merz's policy course, including toward Russia.

Kyiv is preparing reserves of water and food in case of emergencies
Kyiv • UNN
The capital is building up reserves of water and food in case of outages and emergencies. Hot meals will be available to 25,000 people.
The capital is creating reserves of food and drinking water in case of prolonged power outages and other emergencies. The city is primarily preparing to provide assistance to low-income Kyiv residents and people who have found themselves in difficult life circumstances. This was reported by Oleh Kuiavskyi, Deputy Head of the Kyiv City State Administration for the Exercise of Self-Governing Powers, writes UNN.
Details
According to him, as part of preparations for the autumn-winter period of 2026–2027, Kyiv has formed and continues to maintain the necessary reserves of the main groups of food products. This will make it possible to promptly provide low-income residents with essential food supplies if the operation of the energy system becomes more difficult.
These reserves can also be used:
-  at Points of Invincibility – during prolonged power outages; 
-  to assist people affected by emergencies; 
-  to provide for employees involved in emergency rescue and other urgent work. 
For this purpose, with the support of charitable and civic organizations, the city can arrange hot meals for 25,000 people. The Kyiv City State Administration's Department of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development also plans to purchase an additional 20,000 food packages, which can be used in the event of emergencies.
The Kyiv Humanitarian Headquarters, established in February 2022, is responsible for preparing and distributing the reserves. It coordinates cooperation among the city authorities, district administrations, municipal enterprises, charitable organizations, and donors. The headquarters also monitors resource accounting and organizes their prompt delivery in the event of a worsening security situation or urgent needs.

Bosnian Serb War Criminal Ratko Mladic Gets Hero's Funeral In Belgrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:51:34 UTC
17:51:34 KST

BELGRADE -- Former Bosnian Serb Army commander Ratko Mladic, who was convicted by The Hague tribunal for war crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina, has been buried with state honors in Belgrade on September 7 despite international condemnation.
In the presence of members of the Serbian Army, Serbian officials, and the political leadership of the Republika Srpska entity, many of those gathered at the Belgrade cemetery chanted Mladic's name and greeted the arrival of his coffin with applause.
Mladic, who died at the age of 84 on August 27 in The Hague while serving a life sentence for genocide and crimes against humanity, had lain in state at the Church of St. Luke in the Serbian capital.
During the ceremony, the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Porfirije, said the Hague convict's name "will remain deeply embedded in the memory and prayers of the majority of the Serbian and Orthodox people."
Mladic was honored on September 7 by numerous officials from Serbia, Republika Srpska, and Montenegro, despite warnings from the United States and the European Union that glorifying convicted war criminals was unacceptable.
During the funeral service, a prayer was offered that "General Ratko be forgiven for his voluntary and involuntary sins" as an honor guard from the Serbian armed forces stood watch. Veterans from the former Bosnian Serb Army are taking turns to stand beside the coffin.
Thousands of people waited in lines outside the church to pay their respects, with some wearing T-shirts with Mladic's image or symbols related to the 1992-95 Bosnian War.
Four buses carrying demobilized members of the former Bosnian Serb Army traveled to Belgrade from Banja Luka, the administrative center of Bosnia's Serb-majority Republika Srpska, for the funeral. The transportation was organized by the Republika Srpska Veterans Organization.
Politicians from Serbia attending the funeral, included Culture Minister Nikola Selakovic and Public Investment Minister Darko Glisic. Defense Minister Bratislav Gasic and Justice Minister Nenad Vujic also paid tribute to Mladic.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said he could not attend because the president of Uzbekistan, Shavkat Mirziyoev, was visiting Belgrade. The ceremony was also attended by Zeljka Cvijanovic, the Serb member of Bosnia's Presidency, and former Republika Srspka leader Milorad Dodik.
Russian Ambassador to Serbia Aleksandr Botsan-Kharchenko also led a delegation to the funeral.
Reporters from RFE/RL's Balkan Service say numerous media crews were outside the church during the ceremony but were not allowed to enter the cordoned-off area or the site itself.
Nearby streets were closed to traffic ahead of the funeral, and police patrolled the area.
'A Mirror Of Serbia'
Mladic took command of the Bosnian Serb Army in 1992 and led a campaign that seized large parts of Bosnia. His forces laid siege to Sarajevo and carried out the 1995 Srebrenica massacre killing more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys.
In 2017, the UN-backed International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia convicted Mladic of genocide, crimes against humanity, and violations of the laws or customs of war.
Speaking to RFE/RL's Balkan Service, Fazila Efendic, president of the Mothers of Srebrenica association that represents families of victims, lamented that Mladic had been buried "as if he were a statesman."
"This is terrible for me. But there it is. This is a mirror of Serbia, let the whole world see," said Efendic, who lost her son, husband, and 22 other family members in the massacre.
Earlier, the association had said the funeral "threatens to become the largest fascist gathering in Europe in the past 70 years."
US lawmaker Joe Wilson (Republican-South Carolina) wrote on social media that the funeral was "a rogue's gallery of anti-American Vucic and Russian regime figures."
Bosnia's foreign minister, Elmedin Konakovic, announced on September 7 that the country was downgrading its diplomatic relations with Serbia and recalling a majority of the diplomatic staff from the embassy in Belgrade.
He justified the decision by citing developments in Serbia following Mladic's death, including the funeral, the commemoration, and the public messages that emerged.
"If I could, I would sever diplomatic relations with Serbia today. What I can do, I will work on reducing relations to the absolute minimum," Konakovic said.
In the days since Mladic's death, tributes have been held across Serbia and Republika Srpska. A banner describing Mladic as a "hero" has been put up on a wall near the Church of St. Luke. A post on X shared by the Red Star Belgrade soccer team showed fans unfurling a tifo with a portrait of Mladic next to a banner with the words "Direction Potocari."
Potocari, a village just outside Srebrenica, was the site of the Dutch UN base where thousands of civilians fled in July 1995 and where Bosnian Serb forces separated men and boys from women and children. It is now home to the Srebrenica Genocide Memorial.
On August 27, Denis Becirovic, chairman of Bosnia's presidency, issued an official statement saying the Hague judgment placed Mladic among the most brutal killers of the 20th century.
In a statement on September 4, Becirovic condemned the granting of Serbian state and military honors to Mladic, saying they represented an "unacceptable act of institutional glorification" of a convicted war criminal and constituted an insult to the victims of the Srebrenica genocide.
Politicians in the United States and Europe joined in the condemnation of the public glorification of Mladic in Serbia.
Ahead of the funeral, US Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Chuck Grassley, and Keith Self released a joint statement, calling on the authorities in Republika Srpska and Serbia to distance themselves from Mladic's funeral.
"It is deeply concerning that Serbia has announced Mladic will be buried with state and military honors. The coming days will be a test of whether Serbia and RS are ready to break with the past and move toward European Union membership and Euro-Atlantic integration," the statement reads.
On September 4, EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a planned visit to Serbia after a government plane flew Mladic's body to Belgrade, where soldiers carried his Serbian flag-draped coffin from the aircraft.
The US Embassy in Bosnia said two US representatives, Greg Murphy (Republican-North Carolina) and Marc Veasey (Democrat-Texas), "traveled to Srebrenica to honor the victims of the 1995 genocide."
In a statement, the diplomatic service of the European Union said, "Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial, and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries."
Serbia is an official candidate for membership of the EU.

Russian authorities report more deaths in Ukrainian attacks
Russian authorities have reported further deaths from Ukrainian attacks, including two people killed in Russian-annexed Crimea, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed strikes on targets deep inside Russia.
The latest reports expand on earlier accounts of deadly drone attacks in Russia's Perm and Belgorod regions.
In Sevastopol, the Moscow-appointed governor, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said a man and a teenage girl were killed in a Ukrainian attack. Eight apartment buildings were also damaged, he said.
Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine in 2014. Kyiv has repeatedly targeted the peninsula, which Russia uses as a military staging and supply base.
Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukrainian forces had attacked a number of targets in Russia.
He said a refinery in the Ryazan region had been damaged, while refineries in the Perm region and the Republic of Tatarstan had also been targeted.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces had additionally struck targets in the Kursk region and the Black Sea.
UN rights chief urges ban on fully autonomous weapons
The UN human rights chief has called for an urgent ban on weapons that can kill without human involvement, citing reports that fully autonomous drones have already caused deaths in Ukraine.
Volker Türk said he was "horrified" by reports that Russian forces used a fully autonomous drone to kill three Ukrainians last month, while also noting reports that Ukraine had field-tested similar systems.
The New York Times reported last month that a Russian drone guided entirely by artificial intelligence killed three civilians in Zaporizhzhia in southeastern Ukraine on July 6.
According to the report, human operators had programmed the drone to travel toward a particular petrol station, but the system itself selected the precise target, thought to have been propane tanks.
Türk, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, also highlighted reports that Ukraine had tested autonomous weapons.
There has been growing pressure from international organizations and NGOs to regulate so-called lethal autonomous weapons, sometimes referred to as "killer robots."
"I join calls for the urgent prohibition of weapons that can take lives without human involvement," Türk told the UN Human Rights Council.
After years of debate, 128 countries agreed at the UN on Saturday on a definition of autonomous weapons.
NGOs have accused the United States and Russia in particular of trying to weaken the agreed language.
Zelenskyy says Russian drone targeted SBU chief's office
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that a Russian drone which struck the headquarters of Ukraine's SBU security service in Kyiv on Friday had been aimed directly at the office of the agency's chief.
The revelation adds to the significance of one of the most high-profile Russian strikes on a Ukrainian government building since the start of the full-scale invasion.
SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad was not there at the time and was unharmed.
Zelenskyy said he had instructed the SBU to prepare an "appropriate, tangible response" and suggested Ukraine could retaliate in a similar manner.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the strike a "major escalation."
Black smoke was seen rising from the SBU building, close to the UNESCO-listed St. Sophia Cathedral.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least 12 people were wounded in the wider attack on the capital, although it was not immediately clear whether any of them were injured at the SBU headquarters.
The strike also damaged nearby buildings and shattered windows in the area.
It was the first time the SBU headquarters had been hit since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
The SBU plays a central role in Ukraine's war effort and has carried out long-range and covert operations against Russian military targets. It was behind Operation Spiderweb in 2025, when drones targeted Russian strategic bombers at air bases deep inside Russia, as well as the 2022 bombing of the bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.
Russia, North Korea open first road bridge
Russia and North Korea have opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River, expanding transport links as political, economic and military ties between Moscow and Pyongyang deepen.

Attacks with drones killed at least two people and injured several others in Russia, regional authorities have said.
One person was killed and four others were injured in Russia's Perm region after a drone attack damaged a residential building, regional Governor Dmitry Makhonin said.
He said local air defense units had shot down 27 Ukranian drones over the region, which lies deep inside Russia.
In the Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, one person was killed and another injured in a separate Ukrainian drone attack, according to local authorities.
Reuters said it could not independently verify the reports. There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.
No end in sight after diplomatic effort, says Zelenskyy
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the war with Russia currently appears likely to continue into the winter, after talks with visiting US envoys in Kyiv.
The talks produced upbeat assessments from both sides but no announced breakthrough in efforts to end the war.
"We very much hope that we will be able to reach agreements with our American partners, and we are counting on the support of our European partners if the war continues in winter — and this is how it appears at the moment," Zelenskyy said.
He also said Ukraine would hold talks with the US, France and Germany, without giving further details.
Zelenskyy again argued that the most difficult territorial issues could only be resolved in a meeting between leaders.
US envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, had traveled to Kyiv a day after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
Putin had announced a three-day pause in attacks on Kyiv for the duration of the US negotiators' visit. Ukraine, in turn, refrained from attacking Moscow during the same period.
Zelenskyy joked that the presence of Witkoff and Kushner had "worked better than the Patriot air defense systems."
It was Witkoff and Kushner’s first visit to the Ukrainian capital, a repeated target of Russian strikes since the start of Moscow's full-scale invasion. The pair have made several visits to Moscow.
While Witkoff and Zelenskyy both described Sunday's talks positively, neither side announced a concrete breakthrough.

EU watchdog probes handling of undisclosed financial support to pro-Israel Swedish lawmaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:48:11 UTC
17:48:11 KST

Melike Pala
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
The European Ombudsman has opened an inquiry into the European Parliament’s handling of documents concerning undisclosed financial support received by Swedish lawmaker Alice Teodorescu Mawe, investigative journalism platform Follow the Money reported Monday.
Teodorescu Mawe, a member of Sweden’s Christian Democrats and the European People’s Party group in the European Parliament, declared earlier this year that she receives “ongoing financial support from a private donor related to personal security arrangements.”
She has not disclosed the donor’s identity or the amount of financial support, according to documents cited by Follow the Money.
The inquiry follows a complaint filed by Follow the Money after the European Parliament refused to release correspondence between Teodorescu Mawe’s office and its Advisory Committee on the Conduct of Members.
The parliament reportedly cited privacy concerns and the need to protect the internal process through which lawmakers receive advice on ethical matters.
Follow the Money argued that access to the correspondence was necessary to determine how parliament applied its rules and whether the financial arrangement complied with its Code of Conduct.
The inquiry will also examine the parliament’s practice of sending decisions on access-to-documents requests by physical mail, according to the investigative outlet.
Teodorescu Mawe has emerged as a prominent pro-Israel voice in the European Parliament and Swedish political debate.
The Times of Israel has described her as Israel’s “most outspoken European ally,” while other reports have highlighted her positions on Israel.
She has also faced scrutiny over other activities, including reported investments in German arms manufacturers and meetings with US technology company Palantir while serving on the European Parliament’s Security and Defence Committee, according to Follow the Money.
The Christian Democrats’ party secretary has previously said there was no conflict of interest in Teodorescu Mawe receiving the financial support and that the European Parliament had approved the arrangement, according to Follow the Money.
However, the precise details of what parliament approved are among the issues at the center of the transparency dispute.
Neither the European Parliament nor Teodorescu Mawe responded to requests for comment from Follow the Money, according to the investigative outlet.
The European Ombudsman’s recommendations are not legally binding, although EU institutions generally follow them.

Asia outperforms US, European markets as AI demand fuels tech rally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:48:06 UTC
17:48:06 KST

Tunahan Kukurt and Emir Yildirim
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
- High interest rates and sticky inflation affect real estate and consumer stocks across all regions
The massive surge in the information technology sector drove the Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) Asia Index to outperform global markets in the first eight months of the year, rising 23.01%.
The Asian benchmark of global index provider MSCI outpaced the US index’s 12.21% rise and the European index’s 8.87% increase during the same period.
Asia’s regional rally was driven by a whopping 70.51% year-to-date surge in its information technology sector.
Strong artificial intelligence (AI) demand and data center investments, as well as positive earnings by tech giants like Nvidia, eased short-term concerns over chipmaking competition in the region.
Nvidia’s better-than-expected financial results and strong revenue forecast eased concerns that AI and data center investments might slow down, while the chipmaker’s shares rose 6.8%.
Reports that China was producing homegrown deep ultraviolet lithography machines eased selling pressure on chip equipment stocks ahead of August, but competition concerns were also alleviated as production of the state-of-the-art machines would reportedly remain limited in the initial phase.
Salesforce and CrowdStrike raised their expectations, supporting tech stocks, while strong chip and AI demand from China, Japan and South Korea also contributed to the tech rally in the region.
The US and European tech sectors posted more modest year-to-date gains of 22.96% and 31.63%, respectively.
Meanwhile, the communications services index rose 4.07% in Europe in August, while falling 0.71% in the US and 1.17% in Asia, indicating that the rise in information technology stocks was not reflected to the same extent in communications services.
At the same time, the US market dominated the energy sector with a 41.42% increase, led by Brent crude oil surpassing $91 a barrel in August due to escalating Middle East risks and concerns over Russian supply, compared with Europe’s 32.06% rise and Asia’s 1.64% decline.
Additionally, the materials sector grew across all three regions last month, led by a 7.85% gain in Asia, while growth in materials was further supported by expectations of US tariffs on refined copper and a four-year high in eurozone manufacturing activity.
The price of three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange rose to $14,343 per metric ton, approaching a record high of $14,527.5. Low inventories at the exchange also drove zinc prices to a four-year high.
The eurozone’s manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) reached its highest level in over four years at 52.8, bolstering demand expectations for industrial metals, according to preliminary data. The final reading came in at 52.7.
The real estate sector fell 4.18% in Europe, 2.65% in Asia and 1.83% in the US last month amid high bond yields due to persistent inflation concerns worldwide.
The utilities index fell 5.25% in the US and 1.22% in Europe, while rising 0.4% in Asia.
Concerns over inflation and public debt kept bond yields high, pressuring interest-rate-sensitive sectors.
US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s recent hawkish statements increased expectations of a September rate hike from 35% to 60%, driving up borrowing costs.
The US two-year Treasury bond yield rose 11 basis points to 4.34%.
High borrowing costs affected financing-sensitive real estate firms, while the rise in bond yields reduced the appeal of utility stocks, which are often deemed alternatives to bonds due to their regular dividend payments.
At the same time, Asia led the other regions in the healthcare sector with a 6.86% gain in August, followed by a 4.49% rise in the US due to improved profitability expectations and increased mergers, and a 0.29% decline in Europe.
Consumer stocks were the weakest link across the three regions, with mixed or negative results.
The MSCI Consumer Discretionary Index rose 0.73% in Europe, while falling 0.11% in the US and 0.56% in Asia.
The core consumption index rose 0.04% in Asia, while falling 0.8% in the US and 2.82% in Europe.
US retail sales dropped 0.6%, and persistently high gas prices fueled concerns over shrinking disposable income, affecting consumer discretionary and core consumption indexes across the globe.

Herzog to visit Cyprus for talks on ‘deepening cooperation’ amid tensions with Turkey
The Israeli president’s one-day visit comes as Israel, Cyprus and Greece expand strategic ties in the increasingly contested Eastern Mediterranean
President Isaac Herzog will travel to Cyprus on September 10 for a one-day diplomatic visit focused on “deepening cooperation” and strengthening ties between the two countries, his office announced.
Herzog will visit at the invitation of Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides, who will receive him at the Presidential Palace. The two leaders will hold private talks before leading a bilateral meeting attended by Israeli and Cypriot delegations.
Although Herzog’s office did not identify Turkey as a formal subject of the talks, the visit comes amid growing friction involving Ankara and the expanding strategic relationship between Israel, Cyprus and Greece.
Cooperation among the three countries has grown to include defense, energy and regional security. That alignment has drawn scrutiny from Turkey, which has long-standing disputes with Cyprus and Greece over maritime boundaries, energy resources and sovereignty in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Cyprus has remained divided since 1974, with the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus controlling the south and a Turkish Cypriot administration governing the north. Turkey, the only country that recognizes the breakaway northern state, maintains troops on the island.
Tensions rose further after Cyprus acquired the Israeli-made Barak MX air-defense system. Turkey warned that the deployment could destabilize the divided island, while Cyprus has argued that upgrading its defenses is necessary amid mounting regional threats.
Israel has also strengthened defense cooperation with Greece, recently signing a €3 billion agreement to help construct a multilayered Greek air-defense network. The partnership has developed against the backdrop of Greek-Turkish rivalry and wider concerns over Turkey’s regional influence.
Herzog’s trip therefore carries broader regional significance, even if its official agenda remains centered on bilateral cooperation.
The visit continues the working relationship between Herzog and Christodoulides. The Cypriot president traveled to Israel in December 2025 and met Herzog at the President’s Residence in Jerusalem.
