====================================================================================================

Unfilled state comptroller seat stalls Israel's whistleblower protections and campaign oversight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:30:52 UTC
17:30:52 KST

When a public employee who says he was fired for reporting wrongdoing sought emergency protection from Israel’s state comptroller, the office had no authorized head to consider his case. He turned instead to the labor court, spending nearly 90,000 shekels - about $30,000 - on legal action, according to an attorney who advised him.
Israel has had no state comptroller since the term of the outgoing comptroller, Matanyahu Englman, expired on July 5. The vacancy has interrupted a central avenue for protecting public-sector whistleblowers and left parts of Israel’s campaign-finance oversight without the official empowered to act.
The vacancy followed a disputed vote in the Knesset to choose Englman’s successor. The state comptroller is elected by lawmakers through a secret ballot, but several members recorded or otherwise revealed their votes during the second round of the process. On July 2, the High Court of Justice invalidated the election of attorney Michael Rabello and instructed the Knesset to conduct another vote between the two candidates who had already been presented.
The court did not rule on a separate conflict-of-interest argument raised against Rabello. Attorney Rachel El-Shai Rosenfeld of the Movement for Quality Government in Israel said Rabello had represented Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Likud, including in matters involving coalition agreements that could later fall within the comptroller’s scrutiny. She described the compromised ballot as unlawful and a case of improper administration, while stopping short of defining it as corruption in the criminal sense.
Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana has not convened the renewed vote. According to reports, Ohana said the Knesset had already expressed its position and indicated it did not intend to hold another election. The Knesset’s legal adviser, Sagit Afik, reportedly advised that the Knesset was required to comply with the ruling and that its dissolution did not prevent it from voting for a comptroller.
Law does not provide for assumption of comptroller functions during vacancy
Opposition parties have not mounted a sustained effort to force another vote either. Israeli reports said that some of the parties connected with the original court challenge had not asked the High Court to enforce its ruling, set a firm deadline, or consider contempt proceedings.
Dr. Guy Lurie, a research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, told The Media Line that the petitioners could request a clarification specifying when and how the Knesset speaker must carry out the decision.
In an earlier dispute involving a speaker who delayed compliance with a court order, the justices issued further instructions governing the process. Such an application could move quickly, Lurie said, although he declined to speculate about why it had not been filed.
He noted that the law does not provide for an official who automatically assumes all of the comptroller’s functions during a vacancy. Although the office continues to employ investigators and other professional staff, the statutory powers belong to the comptroller personally.
Work approved by Englman before his departure may continue, but no comptroller is available to initiate new examinations, make required decisions, or approve completed reports for publication.
“You don’t have an actual state comptroller who can fulfill the powers of the state comptroller,” Lurie said. “It’s a very substantial weakening of the institution at a crucial time in this institution’s role, namely the election process.”
That role is narrower than policing every disputed campaign activity. Questions involving election propaganda generally fall under the chair of the Central Elections Committee, while suspected crimes may be referred to the police. The comptroller’s election responsibilities include auditing the finances of political parties and primary candidates, examining the work of the elections committee, and supervising outside organizations whose activities fall under Israel’s rules for entities active in elections.
Much of that enforcement occurs after voting is over. The comptroller reviews income, donations, and expenditures, publishes findings, and may reduce a party's public funding if violations are found. Reports may also produce information that leads to a criminal investigation. During the campaign, the comptroller can request records and advise parties, candidates, and outside groups on whether proposed financial activity complies with the law.
Lurie did not argue that the vacancy, by itself, invalidates the coming election. He said Israel’s campaign-finance supervision was already limited by its reliance on reviews conducted after the fact. The absence of a comptroller, however, may give parties or private individuals additional room to circumvent donation and spending rules, particularly because there is no officeholder able to demand information or update guidance as questions arise.
The most immediate consequences are being felt outside party politics. The state comptroller also serves as Israel’s ombudsman and can issue temporary or permanent orders when a public employee faces retaliation after reporting corruption. Those orders can stop a dismissal or reduction in salary, return an employee to work, provide compensation, or arrange a transfer to another suitable position.
Rosenfeld, who heads the Movement for Quality Government’s Whistleblower Protection Unit, said that the procedure was designed to be faster and more accessible than litigation. Applicants do not generally need an attorney, and the process is not bound by the same evidentiary and procedural rules as a labor-court case. She said police and correctional officers are in an especially precarious position because they cannot use the labor-court route available to other public employees.
The difference is not limited to cost and waiting time. Rosenfeld said an employee who files a labor court case may be questioned under oath by lawyers representing the employer, who can argue that the dismissal resulted from poor performance rather than retaliation. The ombudsman’s examination is conducted by professional staff and does not require the whistleblower to confront the employer in court.
Rosenfeld said her unit had received substantially more requests for assistance during the current government, but she had not yet identified an increase specifically connected with the election campaign. The movement is preparing for possible cases as voting approaches, she said, but the available information does not establish that the campaign itself has produced more whistleblower complaints.
“There is now a void,” Rosenfeld told The Media Line. Existing investigations have been stopped, and new requests are being rejected without an examination, she said. In one case, documented in a July 9 letter from the movement, the comptroller’s office informed a whistleblower whose complaint was already under review that the process had been halted because no authorized official could decide it.
The movement said it had verified the account but withheld the employee’s identity and the details of the complaint to prevent further retaliation.
Broader hearing not held
The movement’s first letter to the Knesset State Control Committee, sent July 8, proposed appointing an acting comptroller under Section 29 of the State Comptroller Law. It cited a 1978 case in which the committee named Yaakov Hirsch, then director-general of the comptroller’s office, to serve temporarily while State Comptroller Yitzhak Nebenzahl was ill.
The movement asked the committee to use that authority at least for the ombudsman’s whistleblower-protection powers.
Rosenfeld said the committee rejected that interpretation, concluding that Section 29 applies when a serving comptroller is temporarily unable to perform the job, not when the position is vacant.
The committee also did not hold the broader hearing requested by the movement, which wanted officials to explain how many complaints had been halted, whether emergency applications were pending, and what information was being given to new applicants.
The movement’s follow-up letter argued that even if the professional staff cannot issue protection orders, it could continue to collect documents, interview the parties, and prepare cases for a decision once an authorized officeholder is appointed.
A complete suspension creates additional legal uncertainty because whistleblower claims are subject to limitation periods. It is unclear whether cases already under examination will resume from the point at which they stopped, or whether the intervening months will count against applicants.
Rosenfeld was not confident that another court ruling would resolve a dispute already rooted in the refusal to implement the first one. The movement could file another petition, she said, but it has previously had to seek contempt proceedings when government officials did not carry out judicial decisions.
For whistleblowers facing dismissal now, the choice cannot always wait for that legal process. They can spend tens of thousands of shekels and enter the labor courts, or remain without an enforceable protection order until the Knesset elects a comptroller.
Once an employee chooses litigation, Rosenfeld said, the ombudsman will generally not reopen the matter later. “You’re stuck there,” she said.

Germany Plans Counter-Drone Units Across Nine Cities to Defend Against Russian Hybrid Attacks
Germany is preparing to deploy specialized counter-drone police units across nine strategically important cities. The move is part of a broader security plan aimed at protecting the country from Russian hybrid attacks, sabotage, cyberattacks, and espionage.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Bild on September 6, the plan developed by Germany’s Federal Interior Ministry would establish rapidly deployable federal police units equipped with helicopters and specialized vehicles. They would operate in Berlin, Munich, Hamburg, Stuttgart, Düsseldorf, Frankfurt am Main, Leipzig, Hanover, and Cologne.
The units would protect airports, railway stations, major transport hubs, critical infrastructure, and Berlin’s government district. Their responsibilities would extend beyond detecting and intercepting unauthorized drones to neutralizing unmanned aircraft carrying explosives and dealing with explosive devices.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt confirmed the planned measures, describing Russian hybrid activity as an increasingly persistent security challenge.
“Russia’s hybrid attacks—drones carrying explosives against airports, agents in our cities, cyberattacks on our networks and sabotage against our infrastructure—have become an everyday reality. These attacks will intensify, but we can defend ourselves and ensure security,” Dobrindt said, according to Bild.
The plan would also expand the ability to counter drones beyond federal police and other government agencies. Operators of critical infrastructure—including energy facilities, water utilities, and defense companies—could receive additional legal authority to respond directly to hostile or suspicious drones around their facilities.
Germany also plans to expand the use of artificial intelligence, facial recognition, biometric identification, and video surveillance to detect suspected spies, saboteurs, weapons, and potentially dangerous behavior, Bild reported. In parallel, authorities developing a national “Cyberdome,” a network of digital sensors designed to detect and block cyberattacks.
The measures follow a series of suspected sabotage and drone incidents. Since the beginning of 2026, German authorities have recorded 165 suspected sabotage cases and 747 incidents involving suspicious drones near military sites and critical infrastructure.
Germany formally blamed Russia for the Leipzig/Halle Airport incident, where an explosive-laden drone was found near a Ukrainian An-124 transport aircraft, and later announced the closure of Russia’s consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin.

Main takeaways from Witkoff’s and Kushner’s Appearance in Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:28:08 UTC
17:28:08 KST

The latest Moscow-Kyiv peace effort from Kushner and Witkoff ended with an incredibly revealing press conference which laid bare the problem with the Trump peace effort in Ukraine.
Most telling were Kushner’s comments suggesting that he saw the peace process as some kind of business deal and that, as in a business deal, what is “simply” needed is to find a “win-win.” If anything demonstrated that Kushner has zero understanding of this war – or as Putin says the fundamental causes of this war – it was this comment.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
For Kushner et al. it’s just about territory. That Putin just wants to keep Crimea and to be given the rest of Donbas, and then if Ukraine can be assured as to its long-term security, then that’s the win-win and that both states can go forth and prosper, and that the Trump administration can then take a big commission for cutting the deal with minerals deals et al. with Russia and Ukraine.
But for Putin it’s not just about territory, it’s about the subjugation of the whole of Ukraine. He even said as much in the long-winded essay Putin wrote in mid-2021 laying out his justification for war. In that Putin denies the very right of a truly independent and sovereign Ukraine to exist.
That’s the fundamental cause of this war – that for Putin if Ukraine is to exist as a state, then it has to be within Russia’s sphere of influence and to bow to Russia.
Witkoff and Kushner Get Confronted in Kyiv
He annexed Crimea in 2014, first invaded Donbas back in the same year and then launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 because with the Euromaidan it was clear Ukrainians wanted a different path, and wanted to look West, to Europe. That they wanted to truly break free from the Kremlin’s shackles.
There is no win–win peace solution here when it’s actually a zero-sum game as Putin wants the destruction of an independent Ukraine, and actually the erasure of Ukrainian identity which is an affront to him personally. Ukrainians are fighting for their very identity.
Obviously, Kushner et al. just cannot grasp this simple and obvious concept or don’t want to understand that.
But not all business deals end up as win wins. Think here back to the US’s own history of the robber barons, or of vulture funds, black knights, there are plenty of them. The weak are typically exploited to the full by the more powerful as the nature of the game.
And I guess Trump himself has plenty of history in business of zero or near zero-sum outcomes. I doubt many of the business deals Trump has conducted in his career were nice win-win outcomes. It’s a myth. Look at the Gaza deal, is that really a win-win as it stands today?
In this war Ukraine was the weaker party, but because it had no choice as Ukrainians were fighting for their very survival and have used that survival instinct plus immense bravery and innovation to transform a very weak position into one where they now have leverage and “cards.” But there is still no win-win when the other side – Putin – still wants to end your very survival.
But as said, Kushner, Witkoff and Trump just do not get the above. And remarkable that after eight “pilgrimages” to Moscow by Witkoff he still has no clue how to read Putin – he is too busy with platitudes.
One other notable take out here is that ultimately this is all about power, and perhaps Trump, Witkoff et al. don’t understand the power they have in their hands – actually the power to bring about a peace.
In this respect it is clear from Putin and Zelensky in their messaging around this peace process that they both understand the power of the US. Both are going overboard to keep the messaging about Trump and his peace effort positive, despite I think fundamental concerns about the character of Trump.
Putin understands that if he misplays Trump the US president could perhaps go all in in support for Ukraine – maximizing weapons supplies to Ukraine and sanctions on Russia. In that scenario the momentum in this war could turn quickly against Moscow and it could face a catastrophic defeat in Ukraine which would have ramifications for the survival both of the Putin regime but the Russian Federation itself.
And similarly Zelensky knows that the US could pull even the moderate munitions supplies it currently provides to Ukraine, paid for by the Europeans, and that could be similarly catastrophic for Ukraine in this war. Further, the US could threaten Europe with sanctions or tariffs unless they pull support from Ukraine to get Kyiv to back literally any peace deal Trump proposes.
Note the bad deal for Ukraine (loss of territory which would likely then cause a political and social explosion inside the country then setting off centrifugal forces) would be existential for its survival – it would likely fight on, and Europe might decide to continue to back Ukraine because stopping Putin is now existential for Europe.
So Zelensky is playing along with Trump, respecting US power, not that he is willing to accept any peace deal imposed by Trump, but he knows that if the US support is pulled the war just gets much worse for Ukraine, with many more Ukrainians dying.
But Trump does not realize that Putin respects power. He understands the might of the US and does not want to get into a conventional war with NATO – that’s partly why he has not used nuclear weapons in Ukraine. If faced with the prospect of accepting a deal short of his ambitions, or risking the US maxing out support for Ukraine, and then a catastrophic defeat for Russia I think Putin would choose survival.
Accepting a deal short of Putin’s maximalist demands would not be as catastrophic for Russia as a bad deal would be for Ukraine – Putin can sell almost any deal at home as a win as he controls the PR narrative. Zelensky cannot as Ukraine is a democracy, and he lacks the tools of control over society, unlike Putin.
But Putin is not being forced to accept that choice by a weak POTUS who does not really understand the power he has in these negotiations. Trump has power over Putin – to accept a peace deal short of his maximalist demands – but Trump does not understand the power the US has over Putin and Russia or is too scared to use that power.
For whatever reason Trump always fails to wield any power – sanctions et al. – against Moscow. But if Trump wants peace in Ukraine, and his Nobel peace prize, he has to wield that power against Russia.
The only deal that could stick here is freeze the frontlines as is and then give Ukraine a cast iron guarantee to supply the full range of conventional weapons to defend itself, plus EU membership to assure the prosperity it needs to fund its own defense and ensure long term social and political stability.
We have gone beyond NATO membership as NATO itself is now dysfunctional and its very future is in doubt given differences in interests and values across the transatlantic divide. The alternative now to Trump using his power to impose the above peace is never ending war.

Kyiv Builds Food and Water Reserves Ahead of Winter Amid Risk of Blackouts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:27:17 UTC
17:27:17 KST

Kyiv is building up reserves of food and drinking water to prepare for prolonged power outages and other emergencies during the upcoming winter, the Kyiv City State Administration said on Monday, Sept. 7.
The city will prioritize assistance for low-income residents and people facing difficult circumstances, according to Oleh Kuiavskyi, deputy head of the Kyiv City State Administration.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kyiv has already established reserves of essential food products as part of preparations for the 2026-27 fall and winter season. The supplies are intended to ensure residents can receive basic food if disruptions to the energy system affect the city.
The reserves will also be used at Points of Invincibility during prolonged blackouts, to assist people affected by emergencies and to provide food for workers involved in emergency response and other urgent operations.
With support from charitable and civic organizations, Kyiv can organize hot meals for up to 25,000 people, the administration said.
The city also plans to purchase another 20,000 food packages that can be distributed if an emergency occurs.
The preparations are being coordinated through Kyiv’s Humanitarian Headquarters, established in February 2022 to coordinate the city administration, district authorities, municipal companies, charities, and international donors.
The headquarters is responsible for tracking and distributing resources and organizing emergency assistance if the security situation deteriorates or critical needs arise.

“Food security in the capital is not only about having the necessary reserves, but also a clear system for distributing and delivering them to those who need help most,” Kuiavskyi said.
He added that the city was strengthening its reserves ahead of potential challenges during the fall and winter and continuing to hold agricultural farmers’ markets across Kyiv.
The announcement comes as Ukraine prepares for another winter under Russia’s ongoing war, with the country’s energy infrastructure remaining a key target of Russian attacks.

UK house prices fall for first time since 2023, led by London and south-east
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:27:12 UTC
17:27:12 KST

UK house prices have fallen for the first time in almost three years, as prospective buyers were squeezed by higher mortgage rates, geopolitical uncertainty and stretched affordability.
Prices have dropped by 0.4% compared with a year ago, the first year-on-year decrease since November 2023, according to the lender Lloyds. That came in below expectations of a 0.2% annual rise, according to a poll of economists by Reuters.
The average property cost £298,468 in August, falling 0.2% or £685 compared with July, the bank’s monthly index found.
Andrew Asaam, a director at Lloyds, said the UK’s housing market was “subdued” in the face of higher inflation, borrowing costs and geopolitical tensions.
“What we’re not seeing is a rush of homeowners cutting prices,” he said. “But more are choosing to sit tight, with sellers reluctant to accept offers they feel are too low, while some buyers are waiting to see how conditions develop.”
He added that the market is forecast to “remain fairly subdued in the months ahead, but this will likely only have a limited impact on house prices”.
Tensions in the Middle East have stoked fears around inflation this year, feeding expectations of further interest rate rises.
Property buyers looking for a mortgage deal have faced months of heightened volatility, with the average interest rate for a two-year fixed residential mortgage at 5.63% on Monday, according to the market tracker Moneyfacts, while the average five-year deal was 5.68%. Both were below 5% at the start of the year.
Mortgage approvals were at their lowest level since the start of 2024, Lloyds said.
Jeremy Leaf, an estate agent in north London, said the slowdown in the market reflected a “standoff” between nervous buyers and sellers who believe they have already reduced their prices by as much as they can.
“There is more movement when sellers set realistic asking prices from the outset and appreciate after a period of marketing that even a cheeky offer is worth considering,” he said.
“Activity is picking up now that the main holiday season is over, which is helping to improve confidence a little.”
Northern Ireland was still the best performer for house price growth across the UK, with the average home rising by 6.9% year on year to £231,245.
Prices in Scotland rose by 3.5% to an average of £223,437, while in Wales prices grew by 0.6% to an average of £230,282.
In England, there was a stark divide between the north and south, with the north-east and north-west recording growth of 2.7% and 2% respectively, with averages of £184,370 and £248,675.
Meanwhile the south-east reported the biggest drop in house prices across the UK, down by 1.6% to an average of £381,729. In greater London, prices dropped 1.5% to £534,177.
An RBC Capital Markets analyst, Anthony Codling, said the Lloyds figures paint “a picture of a market under meaningful pressure from multiple directions: elevated mortgage rates, geopolitical uncertainty pushing up energy prices, and a consumer that is both cautious and increasingly stretched.
“Sellers are not panicking and cutting prices aggressively; they are simply sitting tight. Buyers, meanwhile, are waiting for clarity on the path of interest rates.”

Sierra Space secures national security cargo for its spaceplane’s first flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:27:09 UTC
17:27:09 KST

- Sierra Space secured national security and commercial payload contracts for the first flight of its Dream Chaser spaceplane, which will launch from Kennedy Space Center and land at Vandenberg Space Force Base.
- The mission was revised in 2025 to fly as an independent orbital demonstration rather than dock with the International Space Station, following years of delays.
Sierra Space has signed contracts with undisclosed national security and commercial customers to fly payloads aboard the first mission of its Dream Chaser spaceplane, the company announced, adding new passengers to a debut flight that has already been delayed for years.
Dream Chaser is a reusable, uncrewed spacecraft designed to land on a runway like an airplane rather than splash down in the ocean or parachute onto land the way most cargo capsules do. Sierra Space has completed environmental testing, command and telemetry validation, and rehearsals for recovering the vehicle after landing, according to the company. The debut flight will launch from Kennedy Space Center in Florida and land on a runway at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.
The mission was originally supposed to dock with the International Space Station under a NASA cargo contract Sierra Space won in 2016, which required the company to fly at least seven resupply missions. After years of technical delays tied to Dream Chaser’s propulsion system, NASA and Sierra Space agreed in September 2025 to revise that contract. Instead of docking with the station on its first flight, Dream Chaser will fly as an independent “free flyer,” demonstrating its capabilities in orbit before NASA commits to ordering resupply missions. The flight is expected to conduct multiday orbital operations before returning to Earth.
“As the space domain has become increasingly contested, Dream Chaser has evolved into exactly what America needs, a strategic national capability built on commercial innovation and investment,” said Dan Jablonsky, CEO of Sierra Space. “We’re establishing a new operational model in which the same platform serves national security, civil, and commercial customers on a single mission. We’re not just talking about the multi-use space economy, we’re operating it. Dream Chaser is truly America’s Spaceplane.”
Sierra Space said this now makes Dream Chaser’s inaugural flight the first mission to combine national security, commercial and civil payloads, including NASA cargo under its Cargo Resupply Services program, on a single spacecraft.
“We spent years solving the hardest engineering challenges: deployable wings so we could maximize our payload capacity in a standard rocket fairing, hypersonic flight control providing unparalleled maneuverability and mission flexibility, autonomous reentry, and less than 1.5g runway landing,” said Dan Polis, senior vice president of engineering and Dream Chaser at Sierra Space. “The result is a multi-use space transportation system with operational capabilities no other vehicle offers.”
Dream Chaser folds its wings to fit inside a rocket’s payload fairing at launch, then unfolds them in orbit. The spacecraft is designed to be reused up to 15 times and can carry cargo with only partial space certification rather than full environmental qualification, which Sierra Space says lowers costs and speeds up development for customers building hardware to fly on it. The vehicle, named Tenacity, will launch aboard a United Launch Alliance Vulcan Centaur rocket. If successful, it would mark the first orbital flight of a winged spacecraft since NASA’s Space Shuttle program ended in 2011.
Sierra Space said it is still finalizing the full manifest of defense, civil and commercial payloads for the flight and has not disclosed the identities of the national security or commercial customers, the specific cargo involved, or a firm launch date.

Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:27:08 UTC
17:27:08 KST

Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people.
Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing.
This is the seventh typhoon to affect China this year, and Saudel arrived shortly after Typhoon Narra dumped heavy rain on Guangdong, Hainan and Guangxi late last month.
The South African Weather Service implemented several thunderstorm warnings late last week, covering a large swathe of the northern and western provinces. Disruptive rainfall, damaging winds, excessive lightning and hail were all reported, with rainfall totals expected to have reached at least 75-100mm for parts of the Northern Cape and North West provinces over the weekend. In Johannesburg, eight families were evacuated from an apartment building after strong winds tore off a significant part of its roof.
Oppressive heat in the US affected states across the central-southern plains and the Mississippi valley this weekend, with maximum temperatures easily reaching the high 30s celsius (high 90s fahrenheit). However, with high humidities, the heat indices in this region have been closer to 40-43C (105–110F). The unrelenting temperatures will continue across the midwest and southern US this week, with maximum temperatures continuing to reach the high 30s.

Sweden election race tightens as Liberals make parliament threshold, poll shows
STOCKHOLM, Sept 7 - Sweden's ruling right-wing bloc has closed in further on the centre-left opposition ahead of Sunday's general election, according to a fresh opinion poll by Novus that shows the Liberals party making parliament's 4% threshold for the first time in years.
While earlier polls have pointed to near-certain victory for the opposition headed by Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson, the latest surveys show that the government of Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, in office since 2022, may still win.
The Novus poll, published on Monday by commercial broadcaster TV4, indicated 50.3% backing for the four centre-left parties while the three-party government and its support party, the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, stood at 47.9%.
The gap between the blocs was 0.2 percentage points smaller than in Novus' previous poll.
Junior coalition party the Liberals rose to 4.3% from 3.3%, clearing the threshold needed to win seats and easing fears the party could lose its 16 seats and the coalition its majority.
Three weeks ago the centre-left held a lead of 10 percentage points in a poll by a different agency, which political scientists at the time said was a near-insurmountable gap to bridge before election day.
Novus polled 2,888 voters between September 1 and September 5. REUTERS

German far-right scores big win in regional elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:24:59 UTC
17:24:59 KST

Germany’s far-right has scored its biggest regional victory since World War II, bringing the Alternative for Germany (AfD) closer to a realistic chance of winning power for the first time, Politico reports.
The state elections are seen as a key test of whether the anti-immigration, pro-Russia AfD, which has become the most popular party in Europe’s largest economy, can turn its popularity into a government. The party has made no secret of its view of the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt as the foundation for its national ambitions, using the slogan “It begins here.”
Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s candidate for prime minister in Saxony-Anhalt, said in a statement that the party had made history and would reclaim Germany, starting with Saxony-Anhalt. On the evening of the 6th of September, when almost all the votes had been counted, the AfD had received 44% of the vote, giving it 39 seats in the federal state parliament, just three short of the 42 seats that would provide a solid majority.
Now the political bargaining for the chance to gain power will likely hinge on whether the AfD can reach an agreement with the populist left-wing party BSW, founded by a former member of the East German Communist Party. Another option would be to convince members of other parties to switch political affiliations.
The results are devastating for Germany’s Christian Democratic Party, represented by current German Chancellor
Friedrich Merz. It won just 18% of the vote (in Saxony-Anhalt, the Christian Democrats had 37.1% of voters in 2021). The AfD’s victory in the state elections has also sparked talk of a possible change of chancellor. Siegmund said his party’s victory was a clear signal to Merz. He said that every day that Merz spends as chancellor is a day too many.
However, the question remains whether the AfD will succeed in coming to power. One of the party’s leaders, Alice Weidel, immediately welcomed the historic victory and said that the AfD had been given a clear mandate to lead the regional government. Siegmund will now have to figure out whether he can muster enough support to win a 42-seat majority. Weidel said her party is always open to working with coalition partners.
The most likely partner is the populist BSW of Sahra Wagenknecht, which has previously condemned the “firewall” of the big parties against the far right, calling it anti-democratic. The BSWW could win four seats in the regional parliament.
The AfD has also called on Christian Democrat members to leave their party and join forces with the far right.
The outcome of the Saxony-Anhalt election is unpleasant for the Christian Democrats, who have been in power in the state for 24 years. The party’s general secretary, Franziska Hoppermann, called the result very difficult and described it as a defeat overall.
The fact that four out of ten voters in Saxony-Anhalt supported the AfD, despite the fact that the state security services have included the party’s branch in the list of right-wing extremist organizations, highlights the widespread distrust in the east of Germany of the big parties, the media and public institutions.
The party has had its best showing since its founding in 2013, promising to deport migrants, build closer ties with Moscow (including reviving exchange programs in schools), remove rainbow flags from schools and offer 2,000 euros in support for the first two children and 4,000 euros for each additional child in a family.
However, the AfD’s success seems to have less to do with the party’s promises and more to do with growing distrust of the major parties, especially Merck and his conservative bloc.
Saxony-Anhalt is among the lowest-income federal states, and economic anxiety was a major factor. Some 70% of those polled said they were very worried that rising prices would make it impossible to pay all their bills, and 58% feared they would not be able to maintain their living standards.

Free delivery less common in Swiss online shops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:24:12 UTC
17:24:12 KST

Free delivery less common in Swiss online shops
Unconditional free delivery is increasingly becoming the exception among Switzerland’s largest online shops.
At the same time, more and more retailers are delivering orders the very next day.
This is according to the latest analysis by the e-commerce consultancy Carpathia.
Of the 49 highest-turnover B2C online shops surveyed, 12.2% still offer free delivery regardless of the order value, according to a press release issued at the weekend. Last year, the figure stood at 15%.
In 2023, 20% of shops still offered free delivery. For just under two-thirds of the shops, free delivery is currently only available for orders above a certain value, whilst 22.5% always charge delivery charges.
Retailers have, however, become significantly faster at delivering goods. Twenty-four of the 49 shops surveyed now offer next-day delivery. This means the number has more than doubled since 2023, when there were only 11 providers.
For 15 shops – or 31% – next-day delivery is now standard at no extra cost. A further nine charge an additional fee for this service. In 2023, only 19% offered standard next-day delivery.
As for the other terms and conditions, however, little has changed. The cheapest standard delivery charges average CHF6.45, down from CHF6.65 the previous year. The average returns period is 42 days, whilst the median remains unchanged at 30 days.
Just under half of the shops also offer click-and-collect.

UK government condemns 'thuggish' anti-migrant protests in Portsmouth

UK government condemns anti-migrant protests
September 7, 2026
British minister Emma Reynolds on Monday slammed "thuggish" anti-migrant protests that blocked roads in the English coastal city of Portsmouth.
Hundreds of protesters gathered in Portsmouth on Sunday following the arrival of about 140 migrants who had crossed the English Channel from France, UK media reported.
"This is thuggish and intimidating behavior," Reynolds, who is Chief Secretary to the Treasury, told Sky News, adding that the police brought the Portsmouth protest under control.
The demonstration came a day after masked protesters disrupted traffic at Dover terminal, blocking routes to the busy ferry port.
Masked protesters in Dover
On Saturday, hundreds of masked people blocked traffic at England's port of Dover as part of an anti-migrant protest, halting ferry traffic between France and the UK.
Video footage showed demonstrators, reportedly backed by far-right groups, in balaclavas chanting "stop the boats," in a reference to refugees and migrants who attempt the dangerous English Channel crossing in a bid to reach Great Britain.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Labour Party government said that "the right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behavior in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused."
The Dover demonstration caused a traffic jam of about four miles (6.4 km) and temporarily halted traffic into and out of the port.
Britain has struggled for years to curb small-boat crossings from France, although Reynolds said arrivals were down 43% from last year to about 17,000 so far this year.

Billionaire Adani’s firm to make ammo for Indian-made Kalashnikovs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:21:49 UTC
17:21:49 KST

Billionaire Adani’s firm to make ammo for Indian-made Kalashnikovs
The defense firm owned by Indian billionaire Gautam Adani has signed an agreement with Indo-Russian Rifles Private Limited (IRRPL) to supply locally made ammunition for AK-203 assault rifles. 
Under the deal, Adani Defence will supply 7.62 mm ammunition to IRRPL, which is making the Russian-designed rifles for the Indian armed forces at a facility in Korwa in the northern Uttar Pradesh state. 
“Adani Defence will supply the small-caliber ammunition required for the AK-203 programme for five years, providing an Indian source of supply,” reports cited the company as saying. The ammunition will be made at Adani Defence’s facility in Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh, where the company already produces small-caliber rounds. 
The financial terms of the deal, the number of rounds to be supplied and the delivery schedule were not disclosed. 
Gautam Adani became Asia’s richest man in June, ahead of Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani and SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son. He hails from Gujarat, the home state of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and has businesses in energy, transport, infrastructure, defense, and minerals and mining. A US court recently dismissed a criminal case against Adani brought by the Department of Justice under former President Joe Biden.
IRRPL was established in 2019 under an intergovernmental agreement between India and Russia. Its Indian shareholders are state-owned Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited and Munitions India Limited, while Russia is represented by Kalashnikov Concern and state arms exporter Rosoboronexport.
India’s Defense Ministry signed a contract with the venture in December 2021 for 601,427 AK-203 rifles, valued at 51.2 billion rupees (about $542 million).
The ammunition deal comes as IRRPL is increasingly localizing the rifle’s components, in line with Modi’s Make-in-India initiative. The company recently manufactured and test-fired its first AK-203 made entirely from Indian components and input materials, named ‘Sher’. Around 70,000 AK-203s have so far been delivered from the Korwa plant to Indian security forces, according to the Times of India.

Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz under pressure after far-right election triumph
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:20:58 UTC
17:20:58 KST

The ballot box triumph put the pro-Trump and Moscow-friendly AfD, officially listed as "right-wing extremist" by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, within reach of running its first-ever state government.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will huddle with his CDU party on Monday to discuss and digest their thumping defeat at the hands of the far-right AfD party in a state election in the ex-communist east.
The anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) scored its biggest win yet on Sunday with 44% of the vote in the Saxony-Anhalt, against around 18% for the centre-right CDU, according to broadcasters' projections.
The visibly dejected CDU state premier Sven Schulze said his campaign was not always helped by national government policies, saying that "we often faced headwinds, and that wasn't always easy."
The ballot box triumph put the pro-Trump and Moscow-friendly AfD, officially listed as "right-wing extremist" by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, within reach of running its first-ever state government.
However, it appeared to have fallen just short of an absolute majority, setting the stage for lengthy haggling before a new government is formed in the state assembly in Magdeburg.
Nonetheless, the result sent shock waves through Germany, which in the post-war era had so far managed to keep far-right parties at bay.
"For the first time since the end of World War II, the AfD, a party whose state branch is classified as right-wing extremist, is close to securing an absolute majority," said Daniel Guenther, the CDU premier of Schleswig-Holstein state. "This is a shocking moment for our country."
AfD winner mocks Merz
For Merz, who watched the results come in from Berlin party headquarters late on Sunday but did not speak in public, the result is another blow at a time when his approval ratings have dipped sharply.
The AfD's triumphant lead candidate in the state election, 35-year-old Ulrich Siegmund, took pleasure in mocking 70-year-old Merz, calling him "a very good campaigner" for the AfD.
Siegmund said his party had "made history" and that voters had sent "a signal to Berlin." Every day with Merz in the chancellery was "one day too many," he added.
AfD national co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla urged the state branch to seek to take over the government, viewing it as a blueprint for national elections in 2029.
According to projections by German public broadcasters, the AfD fell just three seats short of an absolute majority of 42 seats in the regional parliament.
In the other camp, but also without a clear majority, is a grouping of parties opposed to the AfD; the CDU, centre-left SPD, Greens and the far-left Die Linke.
One option would be for the tiny BSW, a leftist party that veers hard-right on immigration, to act as kingmaker, provided it manages to cross the five-percent hurdle to enter parliament.
The AfD could also try to poach lawmakers from other parties who might want to defect and join its ranks.
Siegmund said his party stood ready to "extend a hand to all forces that want to bring about a fundamental political shift with us."
'Watershed moment'
Rumblings of discontent meanwhile came from within the CDU, which is ruling Germany in coalition with centre-left Social Democrats.
Dennis Radtke, chairman of the CDU's employee wing, called Sunday's vote a "watershed moment" and said that "the usual platitudes about a 'bitter evening' and the need for analysis won't cut it."
Thorsten Frei, leader of the centre-right parliamentary group, called for calm and noted that the chancellor was elected for a four-year term.
He therefore warned against drawing "wrong conclusions" from the result in Saxony-Anhalt.
Political scientist Oliver Lembcke of Ruhr University Bochum agreed however that the election result is "more than a severe electoral defeat for the CDU."
"We are witnessing a tectonic shift in the party system," he said.
"A protest and opposition party is transforming, at least in parts of east Germany, into a party with a realistic prospect of holding power."
The AfD, founded in 2013 as a eurosceptic protest party, soon transformed into an Islamophobic and anti-immigration party, railing against the open-door policy of former CDU chancellor Angela Merkel.
Merz has vowed to return the CDU to its conservative roots and launched a crackdown on irregular immigration while trying to reboot a stagnant economy.
Lembcke recalled that last year Merz "took office with the promise of pushing back the AfD, yet instead, the party has grown even stronger, despite the Union's shift to a more conservative course."
"This confronts Merz with a question of renewed urgency: what strategy can the CDU use to reverse this trend?"

Can the new EU rules save you hundreds on broken appliances? Take our poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:20:26 UTC
17:20:26 KST

Broken toaster? Dead vacuum? Faulty fridge? For most Europeans, the answer is not repair but replacement. And that convenience comes with a large price tag: almost €12 billion a year.
Eurostat estimates that consumer goods thrown away prematurely generate close to 35 million tonnes of waste annually across the EU. Although most discard their devices when broken, a Eurobarometer survey showed that 77 percent of Europeans would prefer repairing their appliances to replacing them. But professional repair services are often expensive, and parts are made inaccessible by the companies that provide them.
The EU wants to stop this cycle of premature replacements through the Right to Repair Directive and an accompanying set of Ecodesign regulations.
Amongst other things, the new laws ask manufacturers to design appliances with standard screws instead of glue, so that consumers can easily dismantle them with basic tools. The law also bans the software locks used by some companies to block independent technicians.
Companies will have to supply repairs, affordable parts, and repair manuals for up to 10 years, even after the warranty expires. They have to ensure post-warranty repairs and provide an automatic 12-month warranty extension for appliances repaired during their initial coverage period. If a repair takes too long, consumers will be entitled to a temporary loaner device.
Would you be more likely to fix a fridge or vacuum cleaner if repair costs were lower than replacing it? Is the process strict enough? Our poll is anonymous and takes only a few seconds to complete. The results will be featured across XL's EU-wide coverage, including videos, articles and newsletters, and will help shape our reporting as we examine how Europe can secure its position in the age of artificial intelligence.

The sender said the alleged attacks were motivated by opposition to fossil-fuel power generation.

Nepal mourns flood victims as hopes persist for workers trapped in tunnels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:18:08 UTC
17:18:08 KST

Nepal held a national day of mourning on Monday for victims of devastating glacial floods, as families of missing hydropower workers feared trapped in tunnels prayed rescuers might yet find them alive.
The August 26 glacial and mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,398 people, with more than 5,500 missing, including around 800 foreigners.
Flags flew at half-mast, with candlelight vigils planned later in the day, following traditional Hindu mourning rituals on the 13th day after death.
Hundreds of hydropower workers are among the missing, but the rescue of three of them from deep inside tunnels, two Nepalis on Friday and a Chinese man on Saturday, have buoyed hopes that more could still be alive.
Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP on Monday that rescue efforts were continuing "with the same tempo we had on day one".
"Our focus is on search and rescue at three levels, on ground, by air, and in the tunnels," he said.
"We are making sure that no one is still stranded."
Entire communities have been swept away, roads destroyed, and homes demolished.
'Hope'
But families of some of the missing workers who gathered in the capital Kathmandu said the government must move faster.
"We have a lot of hope," said Reena Amatya Shrestha, whose brother is among the missing.
"They say they are doing rescue. If the rescue is there, where's the result? We need the result."
Australian tunnel rescue expert Arnold Dix, who is advising Nepali teams, said the operation presented an unprecedented challenge.
"We are facing something I have never faced before," said Dix, president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, in a post on social media.
"Not one rescue, but multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties, and lives that may still be saved."
Foreign experts, including from China, India and South Korea, are aiding Nepali teams in rescue efforts.
"We are measured not only by the lives we save, but by the lives we refuse to abandon," said Dix, a key adviser during the Indian rescue of 41 men trapped for 17 days inside the collapsed Silkyara tunnel in Uttarakhand state in 2023.
"Silkyara taught me never to confuse unlikely with impossible," he said.
'Help Nepal'
With mortuaries overflowing, Nepal has buried hundreds of bodies in mass graves after taking DNA samples for future identification, according to police.
Only around 100 bodies have been identified and handed over to families.
While the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate crisis is accelerating glacial melting worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.
Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people that has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming, says reconstruction could cost billions of dollars.
Its economy is already under pressure, with limited resources to respond to a disaster of this scale.
The disaster has come just ahead of the anniversary of last year's September 8-9 mass anti-corruption protests that toppled the government, and the young government now faces the enormous task of rebuilding communities and critical infrastructure.
A UN preliminary assessment estimated building damage from Nepal's floods at $158 million alone, warning that total losses, including damage to roads and bridges, agricultural land and humanitarian costs, would be far higher.
The United Nations has appealed for $50 million to help more than 84,000 people.
"My plea to the international community is, this is the time to help Nepal," UN country chief Lila Pieters Yahia told AFP.
In Nepal, rescuers have retrieved 1,355 bodies, while around 4,996 people are missing, according to the disaster agency.
In China, the toll is 43 dead and 519 missing, according to state media.

Chinese State-Owned Company Supplies Russia With Raw Materials for Geran Drones – Politico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:14:13 UTC
17:14:13 KST

China’s state-owned company Jilin Chemical Fiber Group supplied Russia’s military industry with raw materials used to manufacture attack drones.
The information is based on internal shipping and customs documents obtained by Politico journalists.
The Ukrainian Center for Security and Cooperation (USCC) collected and analyzed the documents. They have since been verified and shared with the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom. Representatives of the U.S. House Select Committee on China and Ukrainian government officials also independently confirmed the authenticity of the documents.
According to the documents, Jilin Chemical Fiber Group shipped two 40-foot containers containing 46 tons of polyacrylonitrile precursor, a chemical material used in manufacturing, to the Russian company Alabuga-Volokno.
The delivery address listed in the documents belongs to a Rosatom subsidiary located in the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Russia’s Tatarstan region.
The material is a critical precursor in the production of high-strength carbon fiber, which is used in the fabrication of the airframes and internal structural components of Geran loitering munitions. According to estimates, the quantity of precursor material supplied would be sufficient to produce carbon-fiber materials for approximately 1,300 strike UAVs.
To circumvent international export controls, the shipment was declared under a civilian customs classification typically applied to conventional nylon or polyester materials. This classification effectively obscured the transfer of dual-use materials that are subject to international export restrictions.
The Russian company Alabuga-Volokno has been under sanctions imposed by the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and Ukraine since 2023. According to USCC estimates, by 2030, as much as 89% of the company’s total output is expected to be directed toward the needs of Russia’s military industry.
Journalists note that the Chinese manufacturer Jilin Chemical Fiber Group is not currently subject to Western sanctions. USCC analysts have identified at least eight similar tenders for containerized shipments of the material from China to Tatarstan since 2022.
The U.S. Department of the Treasury and Department of State said they take reports of sanctions violations seriously and have the authority to impose additional restrictions on the networks identified in the investigation. The UK Foreign Office has also reviewed the documents provided.
China remains the primary source of critical components for Russia’s defense sector. According to the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, China accounts for more than 60% of the imported parts and materials required for the operation of Russia’s military industry.
In return for military assistance, Russia is supplying China with its own technologies to enhance and modernize its defense capabilities.

L3Harris finishes first F-16 shield systems for allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:13:59 UTC
17:13:59 KST

- L3Harris completed the first 35 Viper Shield electronic warfare systems for F-16 jets, with eight allied nations now ordering 233 units total.
- The $1 billion program, funded by foreign partners including Peru, Poland and Taiwan, could let the U.S. Air Force join later without paying upfront development costs.
L3Harris Technologies has finished building the first 35 units of an electronic warfare system designed to protect F-16 fighter jets from radar-guided missiles and other threats, the company announced, marking the start of full production after years of development.
The system, called Viper Shield and officially designated the AN/ALQ-254(V)1, detects and jams enemy radar signals to help F-16 pilots avoid being tracked or hit. L3Harris builds it in two forms: mounted inside the aircraft or carried as an external pod, and the company said it also assembled its first pod using the same production line. Eight allied nations have now ordered the system, and L3Harris is ramping up toward full-rate production to fill a combined order of 233 units.
Lockheed Martin and the U.S. Air Force selected L3Harris in 2021 to build Viper Shield specifically for the newest version of the F-16, the Block 70/72, which Lockheed sells primarily to foreign buyers rather than the U.S. military. The system pairs a digital radar warning receiver with a jamming technique known as digital radio frequency memory, which can mimic and confuse enemy radar signals, and it’s built to work with the F-16’s newer APG-83 radar as well as older F-16 models already in service.
Confirmed Viper Shield customers include Bahrain, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Morocco, Taiwan and Poland, along with Peru, which selected the system in August for a fleet of 12 new F-16 Block 70 jets that will replace its aging Mirage 2000s and Russian-made MiG-29s. L3Harris has not named the eighth country in the program.
“The $1 billion shared investment by countries operating F-16s means the U.S. Air Force and National Guard could benefit from joining the program,” said Chris Aebli, president of Communications & Spectrum Dominance at L3Harris. “The foreign investment is funding development, lab testing, flight testing and current production of Viper Shield systems, which presents the United States with a savings opportunity to avoid upfront costs.”
That $1 billion figure reflects the combined value of orders placed by the eight partner nations so far, and L3Harris has said it’s in discussions with additional countries that could add another $1.5 billion in demand. Because those foreign orders are already funding the system’s development and manufacturing line, the U.S. Air Force could potentially adopt Viper Shield later without covering the upfront research and testing costs itself, something L3Harris has pointed to as a selling point for eventual American use.

In Egypt, a court sentenced 12 people, including popular TV presenter Sarah Khalifa, to death in a major drug manufacturing and trafficking case.
In Egypt, well-known television presenter Sarah Khalifa has been sentenced to death along with 11 others in a major case involving drug manufacture and trafficking.
According to reports carried in the state-run press on Saturday, the 39-year-old Khalifa was known for her programme Mission Impossible, which covered security and crime issues.
State-affiliated newspaper Al-Ahram reported that a court in Cairo convicted Khalifa and the 11 other defendants of offences including "forming an organised criminal group to procure substances used in drug manufacture for the purpose of trafficking, and possessing and transporting unlicensed firearms and ammunition", and handed them death sentences.
The verdict was announced after consultation with Egypt's Grand Mufti for a religious opinion, in line with the procedures laid down in Egyptian law for capital cases. The court's ruling can be appealed.
State media outlet Akhbar El-Yom said that Khalifa, who also owns a cosmetic clinic and an events company, and the other defendants were accused of "importing raw materials used in production from abroad to manufacture synthetic drugs and trade in them".
El-Ahram said law enforcement officers seized more than 750 kilogrammes of drugs and raw materials during the raids, as well as two flats used as laboratories and numerous unlicensed firearms and rounds of ammunition.
The court also sentenced Khalifa and some of the defendants to five years in prison each in a separate case over the abduction and assault of a young man.
In Egypt, the death penalty is applied in cases of premeditated murder, terrorism, certain sexual assault offences and drug trafficking. According to figures from the Egyptian Rights and Freedoms Commission, 541 death sentences were handed down in the country in 2025.

‘I refused this marriage’: Meet West African women who fought for their right to education
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

17:12:42 KST

In West Africa, many girls will be missing when the new school term begins because they will have been married during the holidays.
Child marriage can be both a cause and a consequence of girls’ lack of access to education. They may drop out of school because they are forced to marry, or they may be married off because they do not have the opportunity to attend school.
According to UNICEF, West and Central Africa have the highest prevalence of child marriage in the world. In this region, four out of 10 girls are married before the age of 18.
Absétou* from Côte d’Ivoire, Aubierge from Benin and Bibata from Burkina Faso all dreamt of continuing their education. Through resistance, activism, and resilience, they tell their stories.
“From the moment I refused to get married, I was beaten everyday”
Absétou*, from Côte d’Ivoire, resisted the marriage her father tried to force upon her when she was still just a teenager. Now aged 29, she wants to marry a man of her own choosing.
“When I was 14, my father wanted to marry me off to a cousin who was in his thirties. He’d started making arrangements for the wedding behind my back; I realized he’d already bought the fabric to have the wedding clothes made.
I refused to go through with the marriage, telling my father that I wanted to continue my studies. I knew my rights because we were taught about them at school. At 14, I already had plans to become a midwife. From the moment I refused to get married, my father would send people to find me on my way to school, beat me, and drag me back home by force. I was beaten every day, and sometimes I wasn’t given anything to eat.
At the start of the following school year, my father didn’t pay my school fees. My mother said she couldn’t afford to help me; she was desperate. In our family, the mother has no say. I was suffering and crying every day.
My father can no longer stand in my way.
Survivor of early and forced marriage Absétou*
I went to see my English teacher to explain my situation, and he put me in touch with the people at Amnesty. I went to ask them for help. When they came to see my father, he refused to see them. In the end, my father threw me out of the house. Thanks to the support of Amnesty and the Ministry of Education, I was able to attend secondary school and, after my final examination, I went to live with a mentor and I trained as a midwife.
Even today, my relationship with my father is not good. When I visit him, we say hello but we don’t speak beyond that. I’m going to choose my own husband and organize my own wedding; that’s what I want, and my father can no longer stand in my way.
My little sister also refused the marriage our father wanted to force upon her, and he kicked her out of the house too, so she came to live with me. I ran a small business to pay for her school fees. My father no longer speaks to her at all.
I have been working as a state-registered midwife for three years now, and I am proud of my profession. As part of my work, I meet women who have been victims of violence. Some have been forced into marriage, others have undergone female genital mutilation; they tell me about their problems. I take the time to listen to these women and give them advice. Sometimes, when I think about them and what I’ve been through, I cry.
Early marriage is not a good thing. We need to raise awareness amongst parents and ask young girls what they want for their future. I encourage them to fight for themselves.”
*Name has been changed
“I decided to campaign for the right to education”
Aubierge, 22, a business student in Parakou, in northern Benin, has been campaigning for the right to education since the age of 15. Named a ‘Human Rights Star’ by Amnesty International Benin in 2024, she runs awareness-raising sessions in her community.
“When I was 14, my parents were talking about marrying me off. They didn’t tell me outright that they wouldn’t pay for my schooling any longer, but I realized I couldn’t expect anything from them and that I had to work to stay in school. I started doing small jobs, such as selling liquid soap and fabric, to pay for my school supplies.
I stopped asking my parents for anything, and they saw that I was determined, so they stopped talking about marrying me off. My sisters also fought to be able to study.
Once married, many girls were abused by their husbands.
Beninese activist Aubierge
That’s how it is in our community. I’ve often heard parents tell their 12-, 13- or 14-year-old daughters that they could no longer continue their education and that they had to get married. This happened to many of my classmates. Once married, many were abused by their husbands. My cousins, too, were married off at a young age, and some are in dire straits today. These girls were far too young when they were married; they knew nothing about marriage… Some were unable to stay with their husbands; they now farm, run small businesses and beg to make ends meet.
Faced with this, I told myself I couldn’t just stand by and do nothing. I decided to campaign for the right to education. I didn’t want to go through that myself, and I wanted to put an end to it.
Raising parents’ awareness of the harmful effects of early marriage is by no means easy. Sometimes, they take what we tell them the wrong way. It’s as if we were taking food out of their mouths or stripping them of their privileges. Parents often say that a child is there to help their parents. For them, a young girl must go to live with a man and provide for her parents, so when we raise awareness, it’s as if we’re calling all that into question.
I’ve fought hard to get where I am. It’s really difficult, but I’m staying the course. I speak out on behalf of vulnerable children.”
‘I won’t let that happen again’
Believing that she could continue her studies, Bibata got married when she was 22 and left her home country, Burkina Faso, to go and live in Côte d’Ivoire with her husband. Now aged 27, the Burkinabè woman has had to return to her home country.
“When I was at secondary school, my parents told me they could no longer afford to pay for my education. A young man told me he would pay for it if I agreed to marry him. I accepted his proposal because it would allow me to go back to school, and that was very important to me!
When I left with my husband for Côte d’Ivoire, I took all my schoolbooks with me. But once we’d settled in, he never mentioned school again. I realized he’d lied to me.
He didn’t look after me, even when I was ill. For two years, I spent my days doing housework and at night I couldn’t sleep because my legs hurt so much. I was very ill, I lost a lot of weight… I decided to leave before I lost my life there.
I didn’t have any money to get back to Burkina Faso, but one of my former classmates who’d settled in Abidjan helped me out, and I was finally able to return to my parents’ home.
Now I know that, in a relationship, you need communication and honesty right from the start; each person needs to understand the other’s expectations. My husband may have had problems, but he didn’t talk about them and made me pay the price. After what I’ve been through, I won’t let that happen again.
I haven’t been able to go back to my studies yet. For the time being, I’m helping my parents in the fields. What I’d like to see is women being helped to set up businesses so they can earn an income. When women work, they can get by even without their husbands’ support. Women need to take matters into their own hands.”
Amnesty International is working with partner organizations and communities to put an end to early and forced marriage in West Africa. Through a human rights education programme implemented since 2017 in Burkina Faso, Senegal and Sierra Leone, the organization is working to combat gender-based violence, including female genital mutilation and early and forced marriage. In Benin and Côte d’Ivoire, the human rights organization campaigns to advance girls’ rights and carries out awareness-raising and educational activities about early and forced marriage at community level.

IDF moves to widen combat eligibility as manpower shortages deepen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:12:38 UTC
17:12:38 KST

The IDF is expected to introduce a new medical profile, 70, which will allow more recruits to be considered for combat positions. The new profile will be positioned between profiles 64 and 72, and would allow prospective recruits who previously received a profile limiting them to rear-echelon positions to undergo screening for combat units.
According to the military, the goal is to make better use of the potential of new recruits. Staff work examining the issue is underway in the Medical Corps and the Personnel Directorate and is expected soon to move into the initial screening stage, known as the first draft notice, as part of determining each prospective recruit’s military medical profile.
Previously, the lowest profile a soldier could have and still serve in any combat role was 72 out of 100. They will still be prevented from serving in infantry units.
The IDF Spokesperson’s Unit said in response: “The IDF is currently conducting staff work to examine a new medical profile that would allow service members who in the past were designated only for rear-echelon positions to serve in a range of combat and combat-support roles, in accordance with their medical condition and the fitness level determined by the Medical Corps.
“This move will make it possible to expand the ranks of those serving, improve placement matching and broaden opportunities for individuals to serve as combat soldiers. The staff work is being conducted jointly by the Medical Corps and the Personnel Directorate. Once it is completed and finalized, the details will be presented to the public and communicated to prospective recruits.
“The IDF will continue working to maximize manpower potential and expand the pool of those serving, while maintaining strict attention to the health of those entering its ranks and tailoring solutions to their needs and the needs of the military.”

France heat wave persists as temperatures approach 40C in south
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:12:16 UTC
17:12:16 KST

Melike Pala
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
A heat wave continued to grip southern France on Monday, with six departments under an orange heat wave warning and temperatures forecast to reach 39C (102.2F), according to Meteo-France, cited by broadcaster BFMTV.
The departments of Aude, Herault, Gard, Vaucluse, Drome and Ardeche remained under the orange alert as temperatures stayed above 20C across much of the southern half of the country early Monday.
Temperatures reached 26C in Nice, while Montpellier recorded 23C and Nimes and Montelimar 21C, according to the national weather service.
Daytime temperatures were expected to rise to between 35C and 38C across the southeast, with some areas forecast to reach 39C.
Meteo-France said temperatures would ease slightly Tuesday before falling significantly Wednesday as a band of rain and thunderstorms moves across the region.
The orange heat wave warning is scheduled to be lifted across all affected departments Tuesday morning.
Several locations recorded unprecedented September temperatures Sunday.
Albi in the Tarn department reached 39.2C, Auch in Gers 38.4C, Toulouse-Blagnac 37.9C, Marseille-Marignane 36.8C and Aurillac 34C.
In Durban-Corbieres, in the Aude department, temperatures climbed to 40.8C, setting a new national record for the month of September.
The latest heat wave is part of a series of intense heat events recorded in France this year.
One episode in late June reached record intensity, while another, extending from late July into August, lasted 23 days and matched France's longest heat wave on record, set in 1983.

Russia and North Korea open first road bridge between the two countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:12:12 UTC
17:12:12 KST

Russia and North Korea open first road bridge between the two countries
A new road bridge over the Tumen River linking Russia and North Korea has opened to traffic.
Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korean Cabinet Premier Pak Thae Song took part remotely in the ceremony marking the bridge’s opening.
It is the first road bridge between Russia and North Korea; previously, the two countries were connected overland only by rail, across the Friendship Bridge.
The new bridge is just over 1 kilometer (0.6 miles) long, and construction began in late April 2025.
The bridge is named for Red Army officer Yakov Tikhonovich Novichenko, who saved North Korean leader Kim Il Sung from an assassination attempt in March 1946. Novichenko threw himself over a grenade hurled at Kim during a rally in Pyongyang, shielding him with his own body. He was severely wounded but survived, and North Korean authorities later awarded him the country’s highest state title, Hero of Labor.
At the opening ceremony, a red Zaporozhets that once belonged to Novichenko led the column of vehicles on the Russian side.
Russia and North Korea signed the agreement to build the bridge over the Tumen River in June 2024, during a visit to North Korea by Russian President Vladimir Putin. The two countries signed a treaty on comprehensive strategic partnership at the same time. That treaty later became the basis for sending North Korean soldiers to Russia to fight in the war against Ukraine.

Hormuz traffic dips to lowest since May after US strikes on ships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
08:10:51 UTC
17:10:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Hormuz traffic dips to lowest since May after US, Iranian strikes on ships
An average of 10 commodity ships transited the Strait of Hormuz per day over the past 10 days, the lowest since May, according to shipping data on Monday, after US and Iranian strikes on tankers.
The 10-day moving average was 10 on Sunday, down from more than 15 on Friday and nearly 13 on Saturday, data from analytics firm Kpler found.
Only two vessels passed through the strait on Saturday while six went through on Sunday, mostly using the Iranian route.
US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday, US Central Command said, including one off Kharg Island, Iran's key oil export hub, following attacks by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on US warships in the region.
In retaliation, the IRGC navy said on Saturday it targeted three oil tankers travelling unauthorized routes in the strait as well as three additional US vessels in other areas.
The three Iranian tankers were Downy, Stark I and Kylo, also known as Noxen, maritime intelligence firm Marisks said in a note.
The Saturday attacks represented a "major escalation in the maritime conflict", Marisks said.
"Commercial tankers are now being deliberately used as instruments of reciprocal economic pressure, substantially weakening the previous distinction between military confrontation and commercial shipping," it added.
"Risk is therefore assessed as extreme for Iranian/Iran-linked tonnage and materially elevated for U.S.-linked or US-escorted shipping throughout the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman."
There have been 27 projectile strike incidents since July 6, resulting in damage to vessels operating in and around the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said in its weekly report.
On Sunday, one very large crude carrier and three bulk carriers laden with metals, grains or oilseeds entered the strait, Kpler data showed.
A tanker carrying refined products loaded from a Saudi port attempted to exit but was turned back, data from LSEG showed.
There has been no VLCC exiting the strait since Wednesday, according to Kpler data.

Thousands of mourners gather in Belgrade for war criminal Mladic's funeral
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
