From grey skies to heatwaves: climate drives Swiss abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

From grey skies to heatwaves: climate drives Swiss abroad
Every year, many Swiss choose to settle abroad for a better climate. In the past the main motivation was often to escape the country’s long grey winters. But increasingly severe heatwaves, such as that of summer 2026, may encourage more Swiss citizens to leave.
“I live on the central coast of California. When someone asks us why we chose to live here, we always say there are three reasons: the climate, the climate, the climate. No, I’ll never go back to Switzerland,” says Gabrielle Robbins-Essig, as part of a debate launched among Swissinfo readers across our platforms.
More
In the past, people fled the grey weather
For many years, the typical Swiss emigrant was someone fed up with the long winters and damp weather of the Swiss Plateau, in search of a pleasant, predictable climate all year round.
“We emigrated to Southern California ten years ago because we’d had enough of the bad weather in Switzerland. San Diego has one of the best climates in the world, with glorious sunshine for over 300 days a year,” writes Mike Vetter.
Also based in Southern California, Marianne Shintaku did not leave her home country for climatic reasons. But she admits it has now become one of the main reasons she chooses to stay: “I hate the damp and the cold, so the Californian climate has clearly become the reason I stay here.”
In Costa Rica, Agnès Vetsch is delighted with the decision she made 20 years ago: “I’m never cold anymore. And I don’t regret my choice.” “I don’t miss the fog and winter slush of the Aargau plateau,” adds Pascal Leutwyler, who now lives in Ontario, Canada.
Heat as a new reason for leaving
Escaping the grey Swiss weather may soon no longer be the primary motivation for all those seeking a more pleasant climate. With Switzerland ranking among the ten countries in the world that are warming the fastest, rising temperatures could well become a major reason for emigration within a few years.
For Norbert Roth, this is already a reality. Climate change is one of the main reasons that prompted him to leave Switzerland: “The heat, the frequent thunderstorms, the heavy hailstorms…” He now lives on the North Sea coast.
Andrea Wildi has come to the same conclusion. Unable to bear the summer temperatures in Switzerland any longer, she chose to settle in Ireland. “I moved to a more temperate climate. I only go to Switzerland during the summer months if it’s absolutely necessary,” she says.
More
Why Switzerland is among the ten fastest-warming countries in the world
Countries better equipped
Paradoxically, some people living in parts of the world where temperatures are significantly higher say they cope better with the heat than they did in Switzerland, largely thanks to suitable infrastructure.
“In Florida, we’re used to the heat, but also to air conditioning. It surprises me a bit to see how much people complain about the summer heat in Switzerland, which seems perfectly bearable,” says Ruth Härri.
In Sicily, a region that has nevertheless been hit hard by climate change, Monique Staehli has no plans to leave either: “Sicily is suffering greatly from climate change (wildfires, water shortages)… But here, I have the sea on my doorstep and we’ll soon have air conditioning in every room, powered by solar panels. We also have a shaded garden. In Switzerland, it would be difficult for me to put such solutions in place and I’d suffer more from the heat,” she explains.
Retiring to a warm country where the cost of living is cheaper undoubtedly enables some Swiss Abroad to better protect themselves against periods of extreme heat. This allows them to invest in suitable equipment and facilities – a level of comfort they might not otherwise afford in Switzerland.
Some regions are more affected than others
Of the approximately 840,000 Swiss Abroad, nearly two-thirds live in Europe, a continent particularly affected by global warming. However, this does not yet seem to be having a massive impact on the lifestyle choices of the Swiss Abroad worldwide.
Speaking from Canada, Kati Lyon-Villiger puts the scale of the phenomenon into perspective: “Climate change is much less noticeable here than in Switzerland. The snow simply takes a bit longer to arrive.”
The weather isn’t everything
Despite the appeal of a milder climate, nostalgia and family ties sometimes matter more than the weather.
“I emigrated to Australia 28 years ago to escape the fog and the grey, dreary winters. Climate-wise, it was an excellent decision: the climate in Western Australia is exceptional. But as the years go by, I miss my brothers and sisters more and more,” says Verena Edmondson-Siegenthaler.

Israeli air attacks kill at least 12 people in southern Lebanon
Lebanon’s president asserts step up in Israeli attacks intended to undermine US-backed ceasefire framework.
Israeli air attacks in southern Lebanon have killed at least 12 people, including children and medics.
Israeli warplanes hit a residential building early on Monday in the town of Kfar Reman in southern Lebanon, killing 11 people – including two children – and wounding five others, Lebanon’s Health Ministry said.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Israeli drones drop bombs on southern Lebanon’s Mansouri
- list 2 of 4Israel claims control of Lebanon’s key Ali al-Taher ridge: What that means
- list 3 of 4Nearly 9,000 killed in Israeli attacks on Lebanon since 2023
- list 4 of 4Israeli air attacks on Lebanon kill at least four
A separate Israeli drone attack on a civilian vehicle in the town in Nabatieh province killed at least one medic, Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency reported.
Israel has stepped up its attacks on southern Lebanon over the past three days, killing at least 27 people and injuring 69, according to the ministry. Lebanon’s president has asserted that the rise in hostilities is part of an Israeli bid to undermine the United States-brokered framework agreement to end the conflict.
The Israeli military also struck a residential area in the town of Deir al-Zahrani in southern Lebanon overnight after it issued a forced evacuation order. The army says it targeted a building near a Hezbollah facility, which it claims was used to launch an explosive drone.
The attacks come a day after at least seven people were killed and 20 others were wounded in Israeli air raids on the nearby town of Arab Salim, also in the Nabatieh district.
Attacks have continued despite the framework agreement, which was signed by Israel and Lebanon in June.
That plan includes a “pilot zone” plan, which are meant to act as a test area for the Lebanese army to disarm Hezbollah and for the Israelis to withdraw. However, Israel still occupies dozens of villages in southern Lebanon and has refused further withdrawals, leading to a “stalled” diplomatic process, notes Al Jazeera’s Zeina Khodr.
Reporting from Kfar Reman, Khodr said “uncertainty and fear” are now the prevailing feelings in southern Lebanon, as people had started returning to the region and rebuilding their homes with the hope that attacks would stop after the Lebanon-Israel deal was signed in June.
“The feeling here is that Israel is trying to impose or establish new rules of engagement,” Khodr said. “People just do not know what is next. There’s been a wave of Israeli attacks over the past 48 hours. Civilians are being killed. Residential homes are being destroyed.”
“Recovery efforts by civil defence workers are continuing. They’ve been here throughout the night, but it’s no longer a rescue operation,” Khodr added. “It’s a recovery operation.”
Israeli strikes on Lebanon have killed more than 4,350 people and wounded over 12,300 since the conflict escalated in early March, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry.
The ministry said in a report on Wednesday that there had been 179 Israeli attacks on Lebanese ambulance crews since March 2, killing 135 healthcare workers.
Though the US-brokered deal between Lebanon and Israel saw violence decrease, Israeli forces have continued razing villages in its so-called “security zone” in southern Lebanon, carrying out air strikes both within the zone and to its north, mostly without forced evacuation orders.
Alongside the strikes, Israel has continued to carry out demolitions across southern Lebanon.
“Massive explosions” were reported in the town of al-Mansouri on Monday by the National News Agency, which said almost two-thirds of houses in town have been destroyed, while the remaining third are uninhabitable.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun insisted on Monday that the attacks and other destructive activities being carried out by Israel are intended to undermine the US-backed deal aimed at a ceasefire.
“These attacks target the framework agreement process and undermine all efforts to halt the escalation in southern Lebanon and the region as a whole,” Aoun told French Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin as he visited Lebanon.
Israel’s military asserted later that it is committed to the agreement, but would continue to “remove threats” from Hezbollah.
The Iran-backed group has condemned the deal, insisting that Israel must withdraw completely from Lebanon before it will end hostilities.

Hollywood blacklisting: Susan Sarandon shares her support for Palestine has cost her film roles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:56:03 UTC
15:56:03 KST

The 79-year-old actress has been vocal with her support for Palestine amid the ongoing conflict in Gaza and shared that her activism carries professional consequences. Her comments follow several artists coming to the defence of actor Mark Ruffalo, who has also been the victim of a "smear campaign".
Susan Sarandon has shared that her support for Palestine has led to her losing film roles and that parts of the film industry continue to shun her over her activism.
The 79-year-old American actress spoke at the Venice Film Festival about how her stance on Israel’s actions in Gaza has affected her work: "In terms of the power structure, I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still.”
The Oscar-winning actress noted that despite losing out on film roles she feels "the narrative has completely changed in terms of the historical relevance of Palestine and the ties of Zionists with America in our politics".
She added: “That has been a major revelation for people, how much money the United States gives to Israel, nobody really understood that.”
Recent opinion polls have shown a distinct softening in US support for Israel since the start of the Gaza war in 2023. According to a July survey from Pew Research Center, US public opinion toward both the Israeli people and the Israeli government has grown increasingly negative and Americans now view the Palestinian people nearly as favourably as they view the Israeli people.
Sarandon was attending a press conference for her upcoming film The Echo Chamber, and thanked director Andrea Pallaoro for not "listening to the warnings" from those opposed to her working in cinema.
The veteran star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Thelma & Louise and Dead Man Walking has been one of Hollywood's most outspoken pro-Palestinian campaigners, alongside others like Joaquin Phoenix, Javier Bardem, and Marc Ruffalo, and was dropped by her talent agency UTA in 2023 after remarks she made while attending pro-Palestinian rallies one month after the Hamas attack on Israel.
Her words anchor themselves in growing fears regarding Hollywood blacklisting,and follow comments made by George Clooney, who came to the defence of Mark Ruffalo following accusations of antisemitism.
Speaking at the Venice Film Festival, where he received the festival’s Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement, Clooney defended Ruffalo’s right to criticise the proposed $111bn Paramount takeover of Warner Bros Discovery.
“I worry when a big company swallows up another company,” Clooney said. “I always worry whenever big companies are consolidating because it means a lot of people are going to lose their jobs.”
He continued: “I support Mark Ruffalo’s ability to speak freely. We’re not going to ban speech. I believe in free speech even when I completely disagree with it. That’s important, right? In fact, it’s part of how a democracy works.”
He added: “There are going to be people tonight in the room that are going to disagree with most everything I say or stand for. Fair enough. That’s how it’s supposed to be. We’re supposed to argue these things out and come to a conclusion based on the information that we take in … I will always support Mark Ruffalo’s ability to speak freely. I like him. He’s a good man.”
Ruffalo had previously expressed concern regarding the proposed studio merger over its potential consequences for Hollywood, while also turning his criticism on the family behind Paramount. David Ellison, the company’s chief executive, is the son of Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison. Ruffalo accused the Ellison family of being complicit the “genocide” of Palestinians, arguing that it was “built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle”.
Ruffalo highlighted Oracle’s ties to the Israeli military, and his comments prompted a backlash from Paramount, which accused him of invoking antisemitic tropes.
Ruffalo rejected the accusation and more than 170 Jewish artists, academics and public figures subsequently signed an open letter defending the actor, warning against attempts to silence criticism of Israel or the proposed merger.
The open letter titled “Enough!”, signed by the likes of Joel Coen, Joaquin Phoenix, Ilana Glazer, Todd Haynes and Hannah Einbinder, read: “We are Jewish artists, writers, creative professionals, faith leaders and thinkers who have, in response to the outrageous smear campaign against our respected colleague Mark Ruffalo, a simple message to share with the world: Enough!”.
“Enough with the false and dangerous weaponization of charges of antisemitism against those who are brave enough to point out the obvious: that the assault on the Palestinian people and the assault on our liberties at home are deeply interconnected, and there is nothing antisemitic about recognizing that fact.”
The letter notes that the proposed merger of Paramount and Warner Brothers Discovery will “destroy thousands upon thousands of livelihoods” and “further consolidate the oligarchic control of our media” as part of a “larger project of tech-driven domination.”
“Larry Ellison and his partners have never been shy about trumpeting - and one they themselves have explicitly linked to their support for the ongoing depredations being visited on the people of Palestine and their silencing of critics of those horrors,” the letter reads.
The letter ends with the signatories stating that they “stand proudly with Mark Ruffalo, and with all decent people who are bravely rising and speaking truth to power.”
Susan Sarandon stars in The Echo Chamber, which is one of 21 films competing for Venice’s Golden Lion award. The prize will be presented on 12 September.

More than 1 million users affected in Mathspace data breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:53:31 UTC
15:53:31 KST

More than a million people, including students, school staff, and parents have been affected by a data breach across Australia and New Zealand.
Learning provider Mathspace says "unauthorised parties had accessed an internal reporting system" and the exposed information included names and email addresses.
What's next?
The compromised reporting system has been taken offline and individuals who are affected are being contacted.
More than a million people, including students, school staff, and parents, have been affected following a data breach at Mathspace, according to the learning provider.
The company said, in a blog post, "unauthorised parties had accessed an internal reporting system used by Mathspace" and the exposed information included names and email addresses.
It said the attackers accessed the system between August 10 and August 27 during a period when a security patch had not been installed.
Mathspace said "attackers exploited a security vulnerability" in its self-hosted installation of software.
"We're truly sorry this happened and are taking steps to prevent similar breaches in the future," the company said.
"Protecting the information entrusted to us by students, families and schools is our responsibility."
Mathspace confirmed a total of 1,079,819 people were affected in Australia and New Zealand.
The hackers exported information that included user IDs, usernames, first names, last names, email addresses, countries, time zones, user types, email-verification status, last-active date, last-login date and date joined.
But the company said not every person had all those fields of data stolen.
Mathspace make clear that no academic records, learning activities, results, assessment records, passwords (hashes), authentication tokens, SSO credentials, or API credentials were exposed.
"The exposed data did not include records linking user accounts to their schools," the blog said.
Mathspace advised people to:
Check unexpected messages independently
Do not disclose passwords or verification codes in response to a message
Use a unique password for each account.
It also urged people to watch for unusual account activity, and if anybody wanted to report suspicious messages or activity they should contact data-breach-response@mathspace.co.
The compromised reporting system has been taken offline.
Mathspace said it had contacted schools, cyber security authorities and education departments and was now contacting affected individuals.
The company said it did not yet know who was responsible for the breach and had found "no evidence so far" that the stolen information had been published, shared or sold.
Steve Hunter, director of engineering, APAC, at cybersecurity and AI company Arctic Wolf, said the Mathspace incident highlighted how difficult it could be for organisations to keep on top of software vulnerabilities.
"Rather than playing 'Whack-a-Mole' every time a new vulnerability appears, organisations need to take a more risk-based approach," he said.
"The priority should be knowing what systems and software you have, understanding where the biggest risks sit, and having a clear process for acting when a critical security warning comes through."

Berlin (dpa) – German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt outlined plans to increase the country’s defences against hybrid Russian attacks following a recent failed drone attack at a major airport in remarks to the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild tabloid.
“Russia’s hybrid attacks involving explosive-laden drones targeting airports, agents operating in our cities, cyberattacks on our networks, and sabotage of our infrastructure are a daily reality,” Dobrindt said.
He predicted that the attacks would increase but said Germany could defend itself.
The newspaper reported on specific plans to improve protection against drones and hacker attacks, citing information from the Interior Ministry.
The airspace over critical transport hubs, airports, railway stations, and Berlin’s government district was reported to be fully protected against drones by means of “new, rapidly deployable units,” it said.
Companies operating critical infrastructure, such as water utilities, electricity providers, and defence contractors, are also to be given legal authority to actively defend themselves against drones.
A national protective shield known as a “Cyberdome” is to be established, comprising a dense network of digital sensors designed to detect and intercept attempted hacker attacks.
A drone laden with explosives was intercepted at Leipzig/Halle Airport near Ukrainian transport aircraft in August.

Unknown Publisher

14:52:07 CST
15:52:07 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's retail sales growth moderated to 1.5 percent year-on-year in July, from 4 percent in June, the Department of Statistics said on Monday.
On a seasonally adjusted month-on-month basis, retail sales increased 0.9 percent in July, it said in a statement.
Total retail sales were estimated at 4.4 billion Singapore dollars (3.47 billion U.S. dollars), with online sales accounting for 15.4 percent, down from 16.4 percent in June.
Recreational goods led growth among retail industries, with sales rising 13.9 percent year-on-year, followed by watches and jewelry at 11.1 percent, mainly on higher sporting goods and jewelry sales.
Sales of computer and telecommunications equipment increased 5.1 percent.
However, food and alcohol sales fell 5.1 percent, while department store sales declined 3.5 percent year-on-year. ■

Israeli strikes on southern Lebanese town kill 11, state news agency says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:51:58 UTC
15:51:58 KST

Israeli strikes on southern Lebanese town kill 12 as fears of escalation mount
BEIRUT, Sept 7 - Israeli strikes on a southern Lebanese town killed at least 12 people including two children early on Monday, Lebanon's health ministry said, in one of the deadliest days of Israeli bombardment in recent weeks.
Fears of a renewed Israeli military campaign are mounting in Lebanon after days of escalating strikes despite a June ceasefire that was meant to halt fighting between the Israeli military and Lebanese armed group Hezbollah.
A woman who said she was related to at least three of the dead said one attack hit a residential building as children were getting ready for school. The Israeli military said it struck people seen transferring weapons in the area of the town, Kfar Rumman.
At the site, Reuters reporters saw children's schoolbooks strewn between chunks of concrete where the building once stood. Rescue workers with heavy machinery had worked throughout the morning to pull bodies out from underneath the rubble.
Eight-year-old Mustafa Farhat lost his grandparents and his mother in the strike, locals said. Rescue workers were still searching for his father's body on Monday morning while the boy lay in the hospital being treated for his wounds, they added.
One of his relatives, Mona Farhat, told Reuters it was their home that was hit in the run-up to school-time.
"What did they target? What is the goal they are targeting? Do they want us to leave our land? They are mistaken," Farhat said at the hospital.
Lebanon's health ministry said 11 people, including two children and four women, were killed in that attack on a residential building on Monday. State media had earlier said the attack happened after midnight.
A separate Israeli drone strike on a civilian vehicle in the town killed one medic, the health ministry said. Two other medics were wounded in the strike, the ministry said.
The strikes on Kfar Rumman came without an online evacuation warning from the Israeli military.
ISRAEL REVIEWING REPORTS OF CIVILIANS HURT
Israel's military said steps had been taken to mitigate harm "to uninvolved individuals, including the use of precise munitions and aerial surveillance." The military said it was reviewing the report that "uninvolved individuals" were harmed as a result of the strikes.
The Israeli military said Hezbollah had launched two explosive drones overnight towards Israeli troops operating near the Ali al-Taher ridge, a strategic cluster of hills in southeastern Lebanon where Hezbollah is thought to have built an underground military complex.
Israel said last week that it had cleared Hezbollah fighters out of the ridge. Hezbollah has not commented and Reuters could not independently confirm the military situation at Ali al-Taher.
In the days since, Israel has ramped up deadly strikes on towns to the ridge's north and west where residents had returned after the June ceasefire, Lebanese security officials told Reuters.
The officials said they were anticipating continued escalations in the south in the coming weeks.
On Sunday, at least 11 people were killed in Israeli strikes on three towns near the ridge, Lebanon's health ministry said in an updated toll.
Two of the dead were women killed in strikes on the town of Arab Salim, where Israel's military had issued an online evacuation warning at 6:04 a.m. local time (0304 GMT).
The health ministry said separate Israeli strikes on Sunday had destroyed the Ghandour hospital in the town of Nabatieh al-Fawqa.
Four other people were killed on Friday, including a woman, it added. Those strikes came without evacuation warnings.
Israeli strikes on Lebanon have killed more than 4,300 people since Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel on March 2 — two days after the start of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran — triggering an Israeli air and ground offensive.
The dead include more than 250 children, nearly 400 women and more than 130 medics, according to Lebanon's health ministry. The ministry does not otherwise distinguish between civilians and militants, and Hezbollah has not issued a toll for its own fighters.
The ceasefire saw violence decrease dramatically, but Israeli troops occupying swathes of southern Lebanon have continued razing villages in the self-declared security zone. Israel's military has continued carrying out strikes both within the zone and to its north, mostly without evacuation warnings. REUTERS

China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:51:50 CST
15:51:50 KST

VIENTIANE, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese medical support team participating in the China-Laos "Peace Train-2026" joint humanitarian medical rescue exercise arrived in the Lao capital Vientiane on Sunday morning.
The team will conduct a 17-day joint exercise and medical service program with the medical support team of the Lao People's Army.
Bouasing Inthavong, deputy director of the General Logistics Department of the Lao People's Army, joined representatives from both sides in attending a warm welcome ceremony.
Song Caiping, captain of the "Peace Train" medical team, said at the ceremony that the Chinese participants had completed 11 rounds of intensive medical skills training before departure and had conducted realistic combat drills en route.
Bouasing expressed gratitude for the assistance China has provided to Laos in the health sector in recent years. He said that, with the continued and in-depth development of the "Peace Train" series of activities, medical support exchanges and cooperation between the two militaries have established a sound mechanism and system, marking a new stage in mutual trust and cooperation in the medical field between the two sides.
According to a member of the Chinese command and coordination group for the joint exercise, this year's exercise is being held against the backdrop of the 65th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Laos, the "China-Laos Friendship Year," and the fifth anniversary of the opening of the China-Laos Railway. It is the sixth time the two militaries have held this series of joint exercises.
The exercise will further enhance the two militaries' capabilities in joint command, joint rescue, and joint prevention and control in medical support, demonstrating their deep military friendship and mutual trust while continuing to build a model for bilateral military cooperation and exchanges.
Following the exercise, the medical team will travel to Vientiane, Savannakhet, Champasak, and Attapeu provinces to provide medical services, including specialized diagnosis and treatment and academic lectures.
These activities are expected to further deepen strategic mutual trust, expand practical cooperation, and promote medical exchanges between the two militaries toward more comprehensive, in-depth, and regularized development. They will also contribute to advancing the building of a China-Laos community with a shared future toward higher standards, higher quality, and higher levels. ■

====================================================================================================

Alternative for Germany's victory, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's nightmare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:50:47 UTC
15:50:47 KST

Good morning, readers. Angela Skujins here holding the pen for this week’s newsletter, where a seismic regional election in Germany’s east has seen the far-right, anti-migration Alternative for Germany (AfD) sweep to power, with the blow ricocheting as far as Berlin.
No alternative: With voters turning out in droves, preliminary end results from Sunday’s Saxony-Anhalt ballot show the AfD securing 43.8% of the vote, representing 39 seats of the 83-member state parliament.
Although this is short of an outright majority, with the official results expected Monday night, it is already being interpreted as a major loss for Merz’ centre-right Christian Democratic Union of Germany (CDU) party. This is a party that has led the region of Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years, but only scraped through 17.2% of the votes.
Nothing short of a disaster: AfD co-chair Alice Weidel told CNN she expects Merz to be out by Christmas. The German chancellor has so far stayed out of the spotlight, but is expected to front-up to his cabinet today in the capital for crisis talks.
CDU member of the German Bundestag Günter Krings just admitted to Europe Today that this was a "devastating result" and "the perception and credibility of our party is a low". Asked about how this impacts the European Union, he said the right would feel "emboldened". "The European Union also should ask, 'What did we contribute to this anger, and what do we have to change?'" Watch.
Interesting to note: European Council President António Costa will be in Berlin on Wednesday and will hold court with Merz. It’s part of Costa’s tour of the capitals — a weeks-long voyage around the member states aiming to collect intel from leaders about their hopes, desires, and gripes with the state of EU affairs. The election results could factor into these talks.
Officially, though, it has to do with the EU’s multi-annual financial framework, aka the long-term budget. As an aside, keep an eye on his Thursday meeting with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, where the Ceuta migration crisis could widen.
Onto Kyiv: The envoys of US President Donald Trump, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, cracked new ground when they visited Ukraine for the first time on Sunday. The aim? Talks with the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. As my colleague Sasha Vakulina writes, there was no ostensible breakthrough, but the visit is a clear sign of renewed diplomatic momentum led by Washington.
EU officials will also be talking — albeit virtually — to politicians in Ukraine today. Jorge Liboreiro writes that Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi will speak with European Commissioner for the Economy Valdis Dombrovskis to discuss the country’s widening budget shortfall.
Money talks: As financial woes for the war-battered country grow, the focus on immobilised Russian state assets held in Europe intensifies. Last year, an ambitious plan to mobilise the funds fell apart because Belgium was concerned about spiralling damages for Euroclear, the depository in central Brussels that holds the bulk of the immobilised assets. But what if the money were moved from Euroclear into an EU-owned custodian?
The idea is gaining traction as a potential solution to break the political deadlock. Jorge envisions what the custodian could look like.
Brussels watches Serbia: The funeral of convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić is expected to take place today in Belgrade without state honours or the presence of government officials, despite a Serbian cabinet minister initially vowing to give the “Butcher of Bosnia” a burial with "all military and state honours".
As Mared Gwyn reports, the the optics around Mladić’s funeral have already sparked outrage in Brussels, with the EU’s Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos on Friday delaying her planned trip to Serbia, an EU candidate country, saying that the “glorification surrounding his (Mladić’s) death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built.”
Mladić died in late August while serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in the Bosnian war. His body was returned to Belgrade last Thursday on a government plane, his body draped in the Serbian flag, in the presence of a cabinet minister.
Kos said that the events surrounding his funeral and commemoration would be an “important test” in terms of Belgrade’s alignment with EU values, a key requisite in its bid to join the bloc. “The values that underpin our common future are not negotiable,” she said on social media.
Straying close to the red line: While no state funeral will be held, Serbia’s Justice Minister and the President of Bosnia’s Serb-majority Republika Srpska joined tributes to Mladić over the weekend at the state-owned Army House in Belgrade, according to local media.
A diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Euronews that any commemoration by Serbian state officials would be completely unacceptable and inevitably weaken the support for the country's EU bid among member states. Brussels had been pushing to open talks on economic growth and competitiveness under Chapter 3 of the accession process.
“Anyone even considering opening Cluster 3 will think twice,” the diplomat told Euronews. “It seems very unlikely that anyone would want to push for that now.”
Hungary, out of the wilderness? The European Parliament is on track to bring Budapest from out of the cold by reversing what is known to be the EU’s “nuclear option”. Article 7 is a legal mechanism that allows the EU to suspend certain rights for a country if deemed necessary. In Hungary’s case, it was triggered in 2018 to assess violations of EU values and alleged democratic backsliding during the government of former prime minister, Viktor Orbán.
With Péter Magyar at the helm, the country is revising several laws from the Orbán era, which is prompting Parliament to reconsider its position. But will this be the good news story Budapest is looking for? Vincenzo Genovese has answers.
Going green: On top of this, we have European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen continuing on her multi-day trip to Greenland. Yours truly wrote an article about how the trip coincides with Brussels reforming its much needed Arctic policy, particularly when it comes to military and economic threats. I have the story below.
EU races to rethink Arctic policy as the global power grab continues
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is completing her two-day whistlestop tour of the Greenlandic capital, Nuuk, on Monday to further European Union-Arctic relations — and gather intelligence as the European Union maps out a new Arctic Policy.
When the policy's first iteration was published in 2021, it made little reference to growing security threats. Instead, the then-EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell emphasised climate change, raw materials and geostrategic influence as central to the document.
But in the years since, the European Commission has admitted the policy needs an urgent revamp to address the changing security and defence environment in the region — a more militarised Russia, for one thing, as well as China's effort to expand its economic footprint as melting ice opens new Arctic Sea routes. The site of the Lin Family Murders:  Gikong Presbyterian Church
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:49:44 UTC
15:49:44 KST

In a quiet backstreet off Section 3 of Xinyi Road in Taipei City sits an unassuming prayer space: Gikong Presbyterian Church. However, in 1980 this tranquil spot was the scene of an event that shocked Taiwanese society: the murders of family members of veteran pro-democracy activist Lin I-hsiung, who then lived at this address.
In the wake of murder
On February 28, 1980, during the military trials of defendants in the case arising from the Kaohsiung Incident—a violent clash between pro-democracy protestors and the Kuomintang government in late 1979—Lin I-hsiung was being tried at the Military Law Division of the Taiwan Garrison Command, and his wife Fang Su-min was attending the trial. That day, around noon, Fang tried to call home several times, but there was no answer, so Lin I-hsiung’s secretary Tien Chiu-chin was asked to go to the family home and check things out.
When Tien arrived, she found the family’s eldest daughter, Lin Huan-chun (today Judy Linton) lying inside the house with multiple stab wounds. Huan-chun was rushed to the hospital and fortunately survived. When police, family, and friends later entered the home’s basement, they found the murdered bodies of Lin’s mother Lin Yu A-mei and his seven-year-old twin daughters Liang-chun and Ting-chun. The case has never been solved.
After the homicides, the Lin home remained under surveillance. As the site of multiple murders, the property could also not readily be rented out or sold. It was only in 1982 that the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan bought the building and converted it into a religious space.
In the course of creating this church, many people came forward to contribute money but were unwilling to leave their names. Some even just threw their contributions into the basement. This reflected the oppressive social atmosphere of the White Terror at the time.
From residence to church
According to Wang Ming-tse, one of the pastors at Gikong Church, the name “Gikong” (Mandarin yiguang), meaning “light of justice” or “light of righteousness,” derives from the Bible, Psalms 89:14–15, and expresses the hope that “the light of God’s justice will shine down on this place.” The desire is to prevent such an atrocity from ever occurring again.
Since its founding, Gikong has continued to stand by the side of victims and their families, and to show concern for the disadvantaged and social issues. In 2014, Lin I-hsiung’s hunger strike to call for a halt to construction of the Fourth Nuclear Power Plant also took place here.
Through successive renovations, Gikong has endeavored to preserve some traces of the old Lin home. A few red bricks left over from conversion of the building have been placed beneath a crucifix, to remind people that this is the former Lin family residence as well as a church. A commemorative piano remains at the entrance to the first floor; according to the church, Lin’s three daughters all used to play it.
As for various rumors, such as one claiming that bloodstains were left on the stairs and were later covered up with carpeting, Pastor Wang says that some of these stories were passed down among early churchgoers by word of mouth and are hard to either verify or disprove. His solution is to tell the different versions of the church’s history when giving tours and allow each visitor to form their own understanding of the truth.
From memory to public space
Memories of the Lin Family Murders are also preserved at the Chilin Memorial House in Yilan County. Lin I-hsiung and Fang Su-min founded the Chilin Education Foundation in 1991 in hopes of using cultural and educational activities to cultivate a better understanding of Taiwanese society and concern for public affairs among citizens.
In 1993, the foundation transformed the home where Lin grew up in Yilan County into the Chilin Memorial House. It commemorates Lin’s mother and his twin daughters, displaying funeral scrolls, elegies, and some personal belongings. In 2001, it was registered by the county as a historic building.
In 2025 Gikong Church was designated by the National Human Rights Museum as a “site of significance for transitional justice.” A plaque was formally unveiled on April 5, 2026, making the church the first site in Taiwan approved by the government under new rules calling for ordinary citizens to initiate applications for this designation.
Gikong Church is the place where the Lin Family Murders occurred, whereas the Chilin Memorial House preserves family memories and historical materials. From two different perspectives, the two institutions keep people aware of the same stretch of history.
Where history happened
Today, the church not only holds services and gatherings, it also offers tours to visiting groups from home and abroad. Pastor Wang, who has served at Gikong for five years, says that through his interactions with victims of political repression and their families, he has gradually come to understand that period of history and also comprehend that “faith and life must be linked together.” He says: “Victims’ families aren’t looking for you to give them a clear-cut answer, but simply need someone who will listen to them.”
In the transformation from the Lin family home to Gikong Church, the light of justice represented by the church’s name has pierced through a historical tragedy and come to shine on the freedom and democracy that Taiwan enjoys today. It also illuminates the hope that people feel for peace and the future.

Easton says China doubtful of US 'Hellscape' concept in Taiwan Strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:49:18 UTC
15:49:18 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Beijing is concerned about the US’ “Hellscape” drone strategy to defend Taiwan in an invasion but is convinced it has not come to fruition yet, Ian Easton, an associate professor at the US Navy’s China Maritime Studies Institute, said in a CMSI report.
The US Pacific Command first used the term Hellscape in August 2023 to describe what a conflict in the Taiwan Strait would look like in the future, Easton said. That same month, the command announced the Replicator Initiative, which seeks to quickly deploy thousands of drones that could make the hellscape strategy a reality.
On June 10, 2024, PACOM Commander Admiral Samuel Paparo described the hellscape strategy as massive swarms of unmanned weapons targeting Chinese forces, per the report. “I want to turn the Taiwan Strait into an unmanned hellscape using a number of classified capabilities so I can make their lives utterly miserable for a month, which buys me the time for the rest of everything,” Paparo said.
Later that month, Chinese defense ministry spokesman, Senior Colonel Wu Qian, said that “some Americans” wanted to use Taiwan to contain China and flood the Taiwan Strait with drone swarms, calling them “extremely psychotic.” Wu claimed America would end up abandoning Taiwan.
In July 2024, Ren Guozheng, an expert on Taiwan affairs at the PLA Academy of Military Science, wrote that the hellscape strategy was part of American cognitive warfare and the US was trying to scare China with its plans and operations, according to Easton.
A Taiwan affairs program in China discussed the hellscape concept and Replicator Initiative during one episode that same month. The host, Li Hong, said the US was militarily inferior and called Paparo’s remarks “full of provocative intent.” She suggested America was in decline and could not keep up with the PLA.
In August 2024, another military affairs program about the Hellscape concept and Replicator Initiative was aired. Commentators said that US unmanned systems could be easily countered with electronic jamming and cyberattacks. They claimed that PLA air defense units could shoot down the drone swarms.
Despite Chinese propaganda dismissing the Hellscape strategy, many Chinese military experts are taking it seriously and respect its basic idea of using large numbers of cheap drones, seeing it as important for future warfare, Easton said.
In August 2025, the PLA Navy’s top magazine, Navy Today, published an article linking Hellscape to several US Navy advances in different types of unmanned surface vessels. “Its current state of equipment development is comprehensive, focused on actual warfighting, and cutting edge,” it said.
In January 2025, Shipborne Weapons, a China State Shipbuilding Corporation military magazine, called the Hellscape plan a “threat” and said shipborne laser weapons could be a potential countermeasure to swarms of unmanned vessels and unmanned aerial vehicles. It argued that missiles like the Hongqi-9 and Hongqi-16 were too expensive. One shot of a solid-state laser weapon would only cost a few thousand RMB.
Additionally, lasers are not limited by ammunition and are faster and more accurate. They can also destroy anti-ship missiles that are impervious to electronic jamming, the magazine said.
In a Modern Weaponry report, authors said the Replicator Initiative was a work in progress and not yet battle-tested. They said it was “basically still conceptually immature.”
The authors said the US would need to transport huge numbers of drones close to Taiwan, which would strain limited long-distance logistics and put ships within range of PLA missiles. “This means the ‘Replicator’ plan’s large numbers of unmanned systems could be destroyed before they can even be deployed,” the report said.
Easton pointed out that while Chinese propagandists are dismissive of America’s Hellscape plan, Chinese military experts take asymmetric warfare seriously and are worried about the increased US military support to Taiwan. He added that the experts view drone swarms as integral to future warfare.

Jamaica to petition King Charles over slavery reparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:49:00 UTC
15:49:00 KST

Jamaica to petition King Charles over slavery reparations
September 7, 2026
The Jamaican government will petition King Charles III on Monday as the country seeks "reparations for the African ancestors who suffered under hundreds of years of enslavement," the Culture Ministry said.
Culture Minister Olivia Grange is leading a delegation which will ask the king, Jamaica's head of state, to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the island's highest court of appeal in London.
The three questions on the legality of the trans-Atlantic slave trade are:
- Whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English law
- Whether it broke international law, and
- Whether Britain now has a legal duty to provide redress
Jamaica says the petition would be the first time a Commonwealth country has used the legal route to pursue reparatory justice.
What did Jamaica say about reparation for slavery?
Grange pointed to Britain's £20 million (€23.28 million) compensation payment to slave owners following the abolition of slavery in 1833.
"Up to 2015, Britain was paying the slave masters, because we were being considered property," Grange said.
"The question really should be: if in modern times we're still paying back the slave masters for the property that was our people, our ancestors, for property that was because of the abolition of slavery, then why shouldn't we be pursuing some remedy at this time?"
Grange said Jamaica wanted the legal questions answered before deciding on its next steps.
The Jamaican delegation will also meet British Museum officials to discuss the return of colonial-era artefacts.
A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said the king has expressed his "commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs."
While Caribbean nations, in recent years have called for an apology and measures including debt relief, the British government has said it will not pay slavery reparations.
Trans-Atlantic slave trade then and now
The trans-Atlantic slave trade between the 15th and 19th centuries involved Europeans (and later Americans) facilitating kidnappings, then transporting and enslaving of millions of Africans to their colonies in the Americas and the Caribbean.
An estimated 12–15 million Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic over four centuries, with about 10.7 million surviving the journey to the Americas. Up to 2 million died during the crossing.
Haiti gained independence from France in 1804 after a successful slave revolt, but France forced the new state in 1825 to pay 150 million gold francs to former slaveholders as compensation for "lost property," threatening war if it refused.
It took Haiti more than a hundred years to settle the debt plunging the Caribbean into a long-term cycle of poverty.
The legacy of slavery remains a contentious issue. Earlier in March, when the United Nations General Assembly voted to recognize the enslavement of Africans during the trans-Atlantic slave trade as "the gravest crime against humanity," the United Kingdom and European Union member states abstained, while the United States, Israel and Argentina voted against the resolution.

According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,332 tanks, 25,284 armored combat vehicles, 145,026 vehicles and fuel tanks, 49,311 artillery systems, 2,103 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,609 air defense systems, 441 aircraft, 355 helicopters, 2,516 unmanned ground systems, 502,717 aerial drones, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.

While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs).

Nepal flood survivor found alive 10 days after presumed death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:40:00 UTC
15:40:00 KST

A 64-year-old woman believed to have died in Nepal's devastating floods was found alive Saturday after spending 10 days trapped inside the remains of her home, surviving in a narrow pocket of air beneath water, mud and debris.
Chandrika Shrestha was rescued from her collapsed four-story house in Betrawati, one of the areas hardest hit by the disaster, after police officers heard a faint voice calling for help.
"The four-storey house was swept away by the floods and was left in the middle of quicksand. While walking around it, we heard a voice, 'Save me,'" police officer Mahendra Darnal said.
Darnal and his team spent about 45 minutes reaching Shrestha, who was trapped in a confined space inside the mud-covered structure. She was taken to an army hospital for treatment.
The rescue came after her family had already begun mourning her death.
"I was in touch with the family and they had started the 11-day mourning period," Darnal said.
Shrestha's survival offered a rare moment of hope as rescuers continued searching for thousands of people missing after a catastrophic wall of water and debris tore through Nepal's mountainous districts on Aug. 26.
The disaster, triggered by a glacial and mountain collapse along the China-Nepal border, destroyed homes, roads, bridges and other infrastructure and buried entire communities under thick layers of mud and debris.
Nepali authorities said Sunday that 1,342 bodies had been recovered in the country, while about 4,996 people remained missing.
The disaster agency's figures, combined with casualties reported in China's Tibet Autonomous Region, put the overall death toll at 1,385, with more than 5,500 people still unaccounted for.
Betrawati has become one of the main centers of the search. Much of its market and residential area has been buried under deposits that have hardened almost like concrete, leaving rescuers to dig through collapsed buildings with shovels and search for pockets where survivors might still be trapped.
Workers wearing hard hats have crawled through gaps in the rubble, periodically blowing whistles in the hope of hearing a response.
Five days before Shrestha's rescue, 24 badly decomposed bodies were recovered from a building in Betrawati's market area that had housed a small shop, Darnal said.
Despite the scale of the destruction, rescuers have continued to find survivors.
Two Nepali hydropower workers were pulled alive from the Trishuli 3A tunnel a day before Shrestha was rescued. A Chinese man was also found alive Saturday inside another hydropower tunnel near the Trishuli River.
Three of the recent survivors were found inside hydropower tunnels, where authorities had initially believed more than 100 workers could still be alive.
"Search and rescue is going on at the tunnels despite geography, adverse weather and lack of connectivity," Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
At least 12 hydropower projects were affected by the disaster, further complicating efforts to reach people believed to be trapped underground.
Authorities estimate that more than 900 people could be trapped in the area around the Trishuli River.
Other extraordinary stories of survival have emerged from the disaster. An 8-year-old boy was rescued and reunited with his mother, while school principal Rajendra Dawadi quickly ordered an evacuation as the floodwaters approached, helping save hundreds of students.
"If the information was wrong, we would lose a day of schooling," Dawadi told AFP. "But if it was true, we were going to lose our lives."
As search operations entered their 12th day Sunday, hopes of finding more survivors were beginning to fade, but rescue teams continued working through mud, collapsed structures and tunnels.
Hundreds of bodies have been swept down rivers and recovered far from the worst-hit Rasuwa district. In Chitwan, hundreds of miles away, authorities have conducted mass burials for unidentified bodies that had become badly decomposed.
Police have taken DNA samples from the bodies before burial in the hope that they can eventually be matched with relatives. Only about 100 bodies have so far been identified and returned to their families.
Nepal is scheduled to observe a national day of mourning Monday, the 13th day after the disaster, in accordance with a traditional Hindu mourning period.
The United Nations has warned that the scale of the destruction has made the delivery of aid extremely difficult and launched a $50 million appeal to assist more than 84,000 people affected by the disaster.
U.N. Resident Coordinator Lila Pieters Yahia described the speed of the catastrophe as devastating.
"You lose your home, you lose your livelihood, you lose your loved one and you lose the breadwinner of your family," she told AFP in Kathmandu on Sunday, describing how people's lives were transformed within "one to two minutes."
Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has called the disaster a "Himalayan tsunami" and warned that rebuilding could cost billions of dollars.
Energy officials are also working to restore electricity to isolated communities, including through solar power in areas that remain inaccessible.
The disaster also caused significant loss of life in China's Tibet Autonomous Region. China's state news agency Xinhua reported Sunday that the death toll there had risen to 43, with another 519 people missing.
Foreign journalists are not permitted to travel freely in Tibet and generally can visit only on tightly controlled trips organized by Chinese authorities. Chinese state media have focused largely on rescue operations and the scale of the disaster.
The exact cause of the glacial collapse remains unclear. Scientists have warned, however, that rising temperatures are accelerating the melting of glaciers worldwide and increasing the risk of floods and other disasters in vulnerable mountain regions.
For rescuers in Nepal, the search continues despite the worsening odds.
In Betrawati, Shrestha's rescue has become a powerful reminder that beneath the hardened mud and shattered buildings, there may still be people waiting to be found.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah said her survival had "given hope to the entire nation."

Nepal holds a day of mourning and rescue efforts continue after flash floods kill 1,300
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:37:45 UTC
15:37:45 KST

Rescue efforts have increasingly focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said.
Nepal held a day of mourning on Monday to remember the victims of the devastating 26 August floods, with government offices lowering flags and family members carrying out mourning rituals.
Monday is the 13th day since the flooding that has killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left some 5,000 missing including foreigners, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.
In Hindu-majority Nepal, mourning periods last 13 days and close family members stay at home and relatives visit to pay respect. On the 13th day, rituals are held to pray for the departed souls.
Several people whose family members are still missing have performed symbolic funerals with mourning rituals. In Hindu tradition, cremation is an important final rite and for some families, performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provides a sense of spiritual release.
In Kathmandu, family members gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the government speed up the search and rescue for the hundreds of people who were working on hydropower plants and were either swept by the rushing Bhotekhoshi river buried by the debris.
Search efforts were continuing for hundreds of people who are still unaccounted for.
Rescuers pulled out a Chinese man from a power plant on Saturday and two Nepalese were rescued from the plant on Friday.
Rescue efforts have increasingly focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said.
Unprecedented challenge
The disaster posed an unprecedented challenge, Australian rescue expert Arnold Dix said on Monday, with multiple search operations underway in hydropower tunnels.
"We are facing something I have never faced before," said Dix, president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, in a post on social media.
"Not one rescue, but multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties, and lives that may still be saved."
Rescue efforts continue "with the same tempo we had on day one," Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told the AFP news agency on Monday.
"Our focus is on search and rescue at three levels - on ground, by air, and in the tunnels. We are making sure that no one is still stranded."
The rescue of three workers from deep inside tunnels at the weekend buoyed hopes of finding other survivors.
Specialised rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects, hoping to find survivors.
"We are measured not only by the lives we save, but by the lives we refuse to abandon," said Dix, a key adviser during the Indian rescue of 41 men trapped for 17 days inside the collapsed Silkyara tunnel in Uttarakhand state in 2023.
"Silkyara taught me never to confuse unlikely with impossible," he said.

Saxony-Anhalt: Germany wakes up to 'unsettling' AfD victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:36:00 UTC
15:36:00 KST

Saxony-Anhalt: Germany wakes up to 'unsettling' AfD victory
Published September 6, 2026last updated September 7, 2026
What you need to know
- Far-right AfD hails 'sensational' results in the Saxony-Anhalt vote
- AfD expected to struggle with coalition building as many parties reject cooperation
- Left-wing populist BSW open to working with AfD on some issues
- Merz's CDU suffers worst Saxony-Anhalt result since German reunification
- Merz says CDU shaken 'to its very foundations' by AfD win
- The European press calling the results an "unsettling new page in German history"
Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state held an election on Sunday, September 6. Follow all the developments on Monday, September 7, here.
CDU's Jürgen Hardt: Result also shows lack of confidence in federal government and Merz
The CDU's Jürgen Hardt, a senior party figure on foreign policy and lawmaker in the Bundestag in Berlin, spoke with DW's Chief Political Editor Michaela Küfner about the implications of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt.
He said the federal government and party leadership should be under no illusions that the result was "not only due to the internal questions of Saxony-Anhalt," but also due to a lack of confidence with the federal government and Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
"To be frank, it should that our concept to minimize the results of the AfD did not work out yet," he said. "We tried to counter AfD support by doing good politics, expecially in the field of migration," Hardt said, pointing to the sharp reduction in asylum applications over the last two years and a gradual return towards economic growth.
"But this is not what voters in Saxony-Anhalt are interested in," he surmised. "They probably want to show 'we are [not] confident in the chancellor and his policy,' and this message needs to be heard by us."
Asked what should be done, Hardt effectively said more of the same — but better and with better communication and salesmanship. He said he hoped the results would not derail or complicate either domestic reforms programs or foreign policy issues like support for Ukraine.
Hardt 'expects' that AfD's Siegmund will lead the state government
Hardt also said, even as the AfD casts doubt on this in the aftermath of the vote, that he believed the party would ultimately lead the state government — with or without a majority, saying he "expected" Ulrich Siegmund to become state premier.
"He has 39 votes, he needs three extra votes and I am sure that from BSW he will get those votes in the end," Hardt said, referring to the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance or BSW.
But even if not, Hardt said that with "a relative majority of 39 seats" Siegmund and the AfD would still have more parliamentary control than the CDU, Social Democrats and Greens combining their 32 seats.
"I'm sure that Siegmund will do that. He's now talking about new elections — something like that — but at the end of the day, he wants to become state premier, he has to deliver, and he cannot hide away," Hardt said.
Even if this came to pass, Hardt said a state government cannot have "much influence" on foreign security issues in German politics, "and therefore I am not in panic" about what it might mean for Germany or its allies.
He did however warn about the AfD's stance on Ukraine and Russia, calling the party a Russian "trojan horse" in German politics that he said advocated policies which would lead to Germany "depending on Russia" and having "to follow the directives of this dictator" Vladimir Putin.
German Chancellor Merz rules out cooperation with AfD but says CDU 'shaken to foundation'
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Monday doubled down on his refusal to work with the far-right populist AfD while at the same time admitting that Sunday's election drubbing had shaken his own conservative CDU "to its very foundations."
AfD has siphoned off CDU voters and pushed Merz's conservatives farther to the right, now it is hoping to win over some of its lawmakers in the state of Saxony-Anhalt in order to form a ruling coalition as it fell just short of winning an outright majority.
Merz said during a press conference on Monday in Berlin after the election: "This shakes our party to its very foundations. We cannot simply carry on as before, nor can I, nor can the federal government."
"We have a strong constitution; we have all the tools to defend the constitution against a right-wing extremist state government," added the deeply unpopular Merz, "but our party system is undergoing a tectonic shift."
Both AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla and top candidate Ulrich Siegmund have called on CDU lawmakers in the state to drop the "deeply undemocratic" firewall and work toward creating a "center-right conservative majority" in Saxony-Anhalt — with Chrupalla saying, "Partisan games really ought to be a thing of the past."
Neighboring France voices concern over rise of the AfD
Speaking with RTL Radio on Monday morning, French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said the far-right AfD's resounding victory in German state elections, "sends a very, very worrying signal."
Lescure called the victory part of a "populist wave" that is "spreading around the world today," saying "we must resist" it.
Lescure's comments echoed those delivered by France's Minister of European Affairs Benjamin Haddad, who called the victory "a very grave moment for Europe."
For years, France has faced the prospect of a far-right government as Marine Le Pen's ultraconservative National Rally (RN) party has come ever closer to gaining power in successive elections, a situation that will repeat itself during federal elections there next year.
It should be noted that RN ended cooperation with the AfD in the European Parliament for its revisionist view of Nazi Germany, it's ties with far-right extremists and allegations that it aided Chinese and Russian agents in Brussels.
AfD leaders say migrants 'have nothing to fear as long as they contribute to making Germany a better place'
Candidate Ulrich Siegmund said he would seek to become the state's premier during a Q&A session after Monday morning's press conference but noted that he would need a stable majority if he was to have a chance to turn the state around.
He also said those with immigration backgrounds need not fear the AfD, claiming that even anti-fascists had been convinced about his earnestness during discussions in which he engaged with protesters outside campaign rallies.
Party co-leader Alice Weidel said the AfD is not anti-immigrant per se and that it welcomes all foreigners willing to "contribute to making Germany a better place" before railing against unqualified immigrants receiving German taxpayer funds as welfare.
Neither Siegmund nor Weidel provided evidence or data to back up their claims.
She also emphasized what she called the fears of women, children and others in the face of "criminal immigrants" and called for far tighter borders, pointing out that Germany's major parties had lost touch with reality in opening them.
This came despite the fact that crime statistics show that immigrants make up only a small minority of criminal suspects, with age and gender being a much more decisive factor.
Moments after saying the party was not against immigrants, Weidel then doubled down on the party's promise to deport as many immigrants as possible as soon as it took power, saying Germany could not afford what she called an "open-border policy."
Germany has increased border controls and security in recent months and net migration and asylum applications have already dropped significantly over the past two years.
AfD calls for political cooperation, ultimately federal leadership at press conference
In their first press conference since yesterday's Saxony-Anhalt state elections, Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, alongside top state candidate Ulrich Siegmund, called the Sunday result "historic" and suggested other parties reconsider the "failed concept" of the so-called "firewall" to honor voters' wishes and help the AfD run the state.
Weidel started off by thanking voters who came out to show support for the party despite "negative press coverage" — the charge of "fake news" and "unfair media coverage" was a through-line for all three party representatives during the press conference.
Weidel praised historically high voter turnout before slamming existing political parties, specifically Chancellor Friedrich Merz, for whom she has a particular animosity, and running through a laundry list of issues that motivated AfD voters — immigration, immigrant crime, high prices, energy policy and de-industrialization being foremost among them.
Weidel then went on to declare that the country's two largest popular parties, the CDU and SPD, would "never win another election" because they had failed to find solutions to those problems.
Co-leader Tino Chrupalla praised candidate Ulrich Siegmund before also slamming Merz — whom he called "arrogant" for dismissing the AfD as a laboratory for political malcontents — while looking forward to coming elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and criticizing German support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.
After claiming the so-called political "firewall" had collapsed, Chrupalla said the AfD is prepared to hold talks with other political parties, including the CDU, which he said would "disappear" if it did not change course.
After thanking AfD leadership, candidate Siegmund joined in slamming the CDU, Chancellor Merz and the media. Siegmund claimed that tens of thousands of supporters had turned out for AfD rallies during the election campaign — though such numbers have been seen as being exaggerated.
Siegmund said Sunday's result had shown that hope had triumphed over "fake news" to deliver a clear mandate for the AfD to form a government.
Further, Siegmund railed against broken political promises — focusing specifically on Merz and the CDU — vowing that he and the AfD would "stay true to our values" and claiming, "people are finally trusting politicians again."
Lastly, Siegmund claimed the vote was, "not only important for the state of Saxony-Anhalt but the entire nation," saying he needed a "Chancellor Alice Weidel" to help him turn the country around, before promising to slash foreign aid to help Germany and its citizens.
"This is not just about Saxony-Anhalt, it's about Germany," he said. "We want our old, safe Germany back again."
What are the coalition possibilites in Saxony-Anhalt?
Holocaust survivor: 'This election result scares me'
Holocaust survivor Eva Umlauf, president of the Berlin-based International Auschwitz Committee, on Monday told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA), "this election result scares me."
Umlauf then asked, "What path is Germany on? The one that it traveled before?"
After saying Holocaust survivors "never thought it possible" that a right-wing extremist party would again be voted into power at the state level — the AfD was also the largest faction voted into Thuringia's state parliament in 2024 — she added that she would continue to fight for democracy and for the memory of those six million Jews killed during the Nazi era.
Umlauf said survivors "owe it to our murdered relatives" to keep their memory alive, calling it "our obligation to young people in Germany."
Far-right AfD on the rise (mostly) for 10 years now
Germany's far-right AfD has seen an almost constant rise in popularity since it was founded as an anti-euro party in April 2013.
After capitalizing on concerns about then-Chancellor Angela Merkel's immigration policies, the party saw a slight drop in popularity in 2019 amid infighting and backlash against right-wing political violence before latching onto its next theme — what it described as "government overreach" during the Coronavirus pandemic.
Preliminary official results confirm AfD short of ruling majority despite landslide victory
The preliminary official results from Sunday's state elections have confirmed the AfD's historic win with tabulations remaining unchanged from a few hours prior.
The far-right party captured 39 seats in all, meaning it eclipsed all other competitors, yet fell just shy of winning an outright ruling majority.
International press calls AfD win a 'clear signal'
Outside Germany, international observers have called Sunday's AfD electoral victory in Saxony-Anhalt a "clear signal" for establishment parties.
New York's Wall Street Journal pointed to liberal immigration policy and weak economic performance as major contributors to the win, writing that conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz had disappointed voters despite exhibiting the right economic and foreign policy reform instincts. The WSJ called the victory a "warning" that voters could ultimately gamble on letting the AfD lead the country alone.
In Italy, La Repubblica described an "unsettling new page in German history," noting that Saxony-Anhalt's voters — who represent only three percent of Germany's overall population — had betrayed the vow "never again" by choosing a rightwing extremist party espousing the "inhumane ideas" of the Nazi era to run their state.
Milan's Corriere della Sera echoed that sentiment, saying that Germany would "never be the same," and emphasizing that the whole of Europe seems as if "hypnotized by the extreme right."
And in Spain, El Pais wrote that the vote would force Europe's democrats to rethink the tired approach of either imitating far-right extremists in hopes of siphoning off voters or attempting to isolate them. The paper pointed to the AfD in Germany but also France's National Rally (RN) as examples of establishment parties failing to hold back extremists despite the clear moral and political imperative of rejecting cooperation with parties that "question the founding principles of post war democracies."
Elon Musk congratulates AfD on election victory in Saxony-Anhalt
Tech entrepreneur and the world's richest man, Elon Musk, who has backed Germany’s far-right AfD, congratulated the party on its Saxony-Anhalt election victory.
"Gut gemacht!" (Well Done!) Musk wrote on his social media platform X in response to a post by AfD co-leader Alice Weidel congratulating the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund on the result in Saxony-Anhalt.
Siegmund promptly replied to Musk, thanking him for his "support."
"If we take responsibility here, I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation. Germany would once again be a place worth investing in," Siegmund wrote.
Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, the AfD has strengthened its ties with Washington, with Alice Weidel calling the US president a role model and AfD representatives attending his inauguration.
Elon Musk, then a close Trump adviser, openly campaigned for the AfD and continues to back far-right political figures.
Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance sees a 'political reset'
Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the populist BSW, called for a "political reset" in Saxony-Anhalt after the party narrowly cleared the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament.
"There are hopefully now majorities in the Magdeburg state parliament for a change in energy policy, an end to the Russia sanctions, better education and a fundamental reform of public broadcasting," Wagenknecht told dpa.
Since its founding in January 2024, Wagenknecht’s BSW has positioned itself as economically left-wing but culturally conservative. She supports higher minimum wages and rent caps but also backs tougher immigration policies.
She has repeatedly blamed the West for Russia’s war in Ukraine and opposed sanctions against Moscow. BSW politicians, like some AfD figures, have also been accused of maintaining ties with supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"The BSW’s comeback has begun," she said, adding "the result would boost her party’s campaign ahead of state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin."
The far-right AfD fell short of an outright majority, leaving the shape of a government in Saxony-Anhalt unclear. Wagenknecht has ruled out a coalition with the AfD but not cooperation, potentially giving her party the balance of power.
"The policy of keeping the AfD out of government has failed. Simply trying to form another coalition to exclude the AfD would be an affront to voters." she said.
AfD faces uncertain coalition options after Saxony-Anhalt win
According to preliminary official results, the AfD emerged as the largest party but fell short of a governing majority in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. The far-right party therefore faces challenges in forming a government.
AfD lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt Ulrich Siegmund said his party’s result represented "a clear mandate to govern."
At the same time, the 35-year-old said he currently saw no potential coalition partners. However, he added that he did not know what might happen in the coming days.
"I don’t know whether there are individual lawmakers who might say: 'That’s it, I’m not playing along with this anymore,'" he said, adding, "A lot can still happen." Following the historic win, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said: "Ulrich Siegmund will definitely run as a candidate for state premier in the state parliament. That much is certain."
If efforts to form a government fail, Siegmund said a new election could also be an option. "In the worst-case scenario, there would simply be new elections, and then we would get 50% or 55%," he said.
Is coalition without AfD possible?
The only coalition that would have a numerical majority without the AfD would be an alliance of all the other parties. However, under a resolution adopted previously, the center-right CDU rules out not only a coalition with the AfD but also with the Left Party. This policy is known as the " political firewall."
That would also be a stumbling block for a CDU-led minority government. In addition, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) could potentialy hold the balance of power with five seats. Its leadership has ruled out supporting CDU.
Following the election, the previously governing coalition of the CDU, SPD and FDP will end. However, state premier Sven Schulze and his Cabinet will remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new state premier is elected.
Is Germany’s "political firewall" against the AfD collapsing?
Germany’s mainstream parties have long maintained a "political firewall" against cooperation with the far-right Alternative for Germany. But that firewall is under growing pressure following the AfD’s historic win in the Saxony-Anhalt state election and prospects in other forthcoming state elections.
The term refers to efforts by established parties to prevent extremist parties from gaining political influence through cooperation or shared votes. The center-right CDU formally rejected cooperation with the AfD in 2018.
But in January 2025, a CDU motion in the Bundestag passed with AfD support, prompting accusations that Chancellor Friedrich Merz had breached the firewall.
The AfD’s growing electoral strength is now raising fresh questions about how long the firewall can hold and what its future means for Germany’s political center.
Read here for more context: What is the 'political firewall' against Germany's far-right AfD?
AfD wins most votes in Saxony-Anhalt, preliminary official results show
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% of the vote in Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state election, according to preliminary official results, making it the largest party, but falling short of a governing majority in the regional parliament.
Six parties will be represented in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt, which has 83 seats:
- Alternative for Germany (AfD) — 43.8%, 39 seats
- Christian Democratic Union (CDU) — 17.2%, 15 seats
- Social Democratic Party (SPD) — 9.3%, 8 seats
- Green Party — 8.9%, 8 seats
- Left Party — 8.6%, 8 seats
- Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) — 5.3%, 5 seats
Meanwhile, the business-focused Free Democrats (FDP) secured only 2.6% of the vote, failing to reach the 5% threshold.
According to the preliminary results, turnout was almost 78%, the highest in Saxony-Anhalt since German reunification in 1990.

“China has made no secret of what it is doing. It is in their five-year plan.
“China doesn’t want to be a raw material supplier, it wants to be a finished product supply. They want to be in key product supply chains because they know that once they control the supply chain, they own the complete value chain.”

JLR job cuts show UK car sector faces 'near-perfect storm'
