Bailey explains that JLR’s latest job cuts are much more than just another round of corporate restructuring:
“Demand is weak and uncertain. Chinese manufacturers are becoming increasingly formidable competitors. Trade tensions and tariffs are reshaping global supply chains. UK industrial electricity prices remain exceptionally high.
Manufacturers face enormous investment requirements to move towards electric vehicles. And the wider global trading environment is becoming more difficult and unpredictable.
“So, it is too easy, and ultimately too superficial, to portray the difficulties facing JLR simply as the consequence of the cyber-attack or poor management decisions.
Bailey adds that governments also make choices, and urged ministers to treat the current situation as a “strategic industrial emergency”.
The UK cannot simultaneously demand rapid electrification, impose increasingly challenging zero-emission vehicle targets, have some of the highest industrial electricity costs among major economies, and also expect manufacturers to continue investing billions of pounds in British factories and supply chains as though these pressures do not matter. Something has to give.
If the UK loses automotive manufacturing expertise, then it could also lose the industrial capacity needed to deliver decarbonisation.
We could reduce emissions from cars made in Britain while importing an increasing proportion of the cars, batteries and technologies from overseas.
“That is not a successful industrial transition; it is deindustrialisation. JLR’s job cuts should therefore be seen as a warning shot. The question is whether Westminster hears it and acts.”

This case was brought by 3,540 claimants, who accused Next of paying its retail sales staff – who are overwhelmingly female – lower hourly wages than its warehouse workers, the majority of which are male.
The appeal judgment endorsed NEXT’s position that it should not have to pay shop assistants and warehouse operatives the same amount of Basic Pay, in circumstances where the market and working conditions are very different.
The importance of this decision is that the Appeal Tribunal has confirmed that it was justifiable for NEXT to rely on market forces to distinguish between different groups of employees, where there was a good rationale to pay one group more than the other.

Ukraine peace talks – full of symbolism, but differences of opinion remain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:32:50 UTC
15:32:50 KST

The peace talks in Kyiv were full of symbolism, as US President Donald Trump’s envoys set foot on Ukrainian soil for the first time since the start of the full-scale invasion, writes the BBC.
The American negotiators had to travel to Kyiv by train to avoid attacks by Russian drones – weapons launched at the behest of Russian dictator Putin, and just hours earlier the US envoys were sitting at his table in Moscow. It was also symbolic that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Kyiv’s Saint Sophia Cathedral, which is not only a monument to Ukrainian history but also lies just a few meters from the headquarters of the state security services, which was attacked by Russian drones on the 4th of September.
The two sides spent several hours in talks, and later the Ukrainians and Americans were joined by security advisers from several European countries, including Britain’s Jonathan Powell. The negotiators then spoke favorably of the important discussions that had taken place and expressed hope that trilateral talks could be resumed, involving both the Americans and the Europeans.
However, fundamental differences of opinion remain. The US envoys had come straight from Moscow, where Putin had told them that Russia was making “tangible progress” on the battlefield. In Ukraine, Americans heard a different story. Ukrainian officials said that more territory had been regained than lost since August, and that the number of casualties on the Russian side had reached 42,000.
Putin told Witkoff and Kushner that the root causes of the conflict must be addressed,
including his demand for territory that belongs to Ukraine, Kyiv’s rejection of the idea of joining NATO, and the significant reduction of the Ukrainian army. Zelensky said after the talks that Ukraine needed firm and clear security guarantees, including a strong army. He also made it clear that he would not give up Ukrainian land in the east of the country to the Russians.
Meanwhile, Witkoff insisted that progress had been made and that everything was in place to reach an agreement. At the same time, he also acknowledged that there are serious disagreements between the parties involved, and a compromise is needed, but it is currently difficult to predict how this might happen.
For now, Kyiv is preparing for the continuation of hostilities, and expects a harsh winter ahead. Some diplomats talk about a window of opportunity next spring, while others are much more pessimistic.
Zelensky thanked the US envoys for their visit, as the brief pause in attacks has given the people of Kyiv a much-needed respite, but few believe it will last.

AfD's historic win splits Europe as populists cheer and Warsaw warns of 'traitors'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:30:21 UTC
15:30:21 KST

Alternative for Germany's landslide victory in Saxony-Anhalt has drawn celebration from Europe's populist right and sharp condemnation from Poland's prime minister.
Alternative for Germany's dominant showing in Sunday's Saxony-Anhalt election has triggered starkly divided reactions across the continent, exposing the widening fault line between Europe's establishment centre and its emboldened populist right.
AfD won 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin.
That was far ahead of Merz’s Christian Democratic Union, which polled 17.2% — losing about half its support — and won 15 seats. The center-left Social Democrats polled 9.3%, the Greens 8.9% and the Left Party 8.6%, winning eight seats apiece.
In Berlin, the result landed as a direct blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who watched the count from CDU headquarters without addressing the public.
General secretary Franziska Hoppermann called it "a very difficult result for us," while state premier Sven Schulze offered only muted congratulations to AfD.
AfD Co-leader Alice Weidel declared "we have received a very clear mandate to govern here."
“We ran on a clear platform of representing the interests of our country, not those of Ukraine or any other country," Weidel told reporters.
"If we receive the mandate to govern at the federal level and assume governmental responsibility, we will cut all unnecessary spending. We will control our borders. We will deport all those required to leave the country and all criminals. We will close the borders.
"I also expect early federal elections, and I expect the current chancellor to be replaced before Christmas."
Lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund also needled Merz, saying "a very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz. Every day this man is in the chancellery is one too many."
Reaction from Warsaw was openly critical. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on X that "only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD," naming members of Konfederacja and PiS among them.
Elsewhere on the continent, Europe's populist right treated the outcome as validation. Italian Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini declared that "another Europe is possible."
Spain's Vox leader Santiago Abascal called the result "a great hope for Germany and for Europe," while Portugal's André Ventura hailed AfD's "historic" victory, linking it to public anger over immigration.
The split reactions underline how a single German regional vote has become a proxy battle for Europe, with mainstream leaders alarmed and nationalist movements energised heading into a string of more German state elections this month.

UN General Assembly Votes to Promote Equal Earth Projection for More Accurate World Maps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

The United Nations General Assembly has voted to promote the use of world map projections that more accurately represent the relative size of continents. The resolution was presented during a session at the UN headquarters in New York on September 4 and received 164 votes in favor, with one country voting against and six abstaining. Sponsored by Togo, the resolution encourages governments, educational institutions, international organizations, and technology companies to use equal-area projections when geographic scale is relevant. The resolution does not formally replace or prohibit the use of the Mercator projection, which has been widely used since the 16th century. Instead, it calls for greater use of projections that preserve the relative area of landmasses and encourages education about the limitations of representing the Earth's curved surface on a two-dimensional map. The 2018 Equal Earth projection is identified as one example of a map that more accurately represents continental scale.
The vote took place during the 80th session of the UN General Assembly, following discussions around the geographic and perceptual effects of commonly used world maps. Togo's Foreign Minister Robert Dussey introduced the resolution, emphasizing the role of cartographic representation in shaping how geographic relationships are understood. The United States was the only country to vote against the resolution, while Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia, and Ukraine abstained.
The Mercator projection was developed by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 as a tool for maritime navigation. Its ability to preserve angles and compass directions made it particularly effective for plotting courses, but this comes at the expense of accurately representing the area of landmasses. As a result, geographic regions appear increasingly enlarged as they move farther from the Equator. The distortion is particularly apparent when comparing Africa and Greenland. On a Mercator map, the two landmasses can appear relatively similar in size, although Africa covers approximately 30.4 million square kilometers, making it about 14 times larger than Greenland. Northern Europe and North America are similarly enlarged in relation to regions closer to the Equator.
Related Article
On Africa Day 2026: Revisiting Architecture’s Role in Identity and Collective Memory
Despite being developed for navigation, the Mercator projection has remained common in educational materials, media, digital mapping, and other forms of geographic representation. Its continued use has prompted debate among cartographers, geographers, and educators about how map projections influence perceptions of geographic scale and the relative position of different regions.
Equal Earth was developed in 2018 by cartographers Bojan Šavrič, Tom Patterson, and Bernhard Jenny as an equal-area world map projection. Unlike Mercator, it preserves the proportional area of landmasses, allowing the relative size of continents and countries to be compared more accurately. However, it introduces other distortions to shape, distance, and direction, making it more suitable for geographic visualization than for navigation.
The resolution has received support from several governments, including France, whose Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot announced shortly before the vote that the country would move away from the Mercator projection in its own cartographic materials. France plans to use the Eckert IV projection, another equal-area system, with different projections selected according to their intended purpose. The discussion also brought questions of territorial representation into the UN debate. Ukraine and the European Union raised concerns about the depiction of disputed territories on some alternative world maps, while emphasizing that the resolution itself has no effect on sovereignty, territorial status, or internationally recognized borders.
The UN vote does not establish a single new global standard for world maps. Instead, it recognizes the limitations of existing projections and encourages the use of different systems according to their intended purpose. As no flat map can simultaneously preserve the Earth's areas, shapes, distances, and directions, the choice of projection remains closely connected to how geographic information is communicated.
Recent developments have drawn attention to architecture, landscape, and spatial practice across Africa. In January 2026, the World Monuments Fund and Knoll named Australia-based practice Architectus as the recipient of the 2026 World Monuments Fund/Knoll Modernism Prize for its conservation of the United Nations' Historic Africa Hall in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. At a larger territorial scale, initiatives such as the Great Green Wall demonstrate how landscape, agriculture, and infrastructure intersect in response to desertification and climate change. Meanwhile, the inaugural Pan-African Biennale (PAB), taking place from September 7 to 11, 2026, in Nairobi, will bring together architects, studios, research collectives, and material practitioners from across the continent.

15:27:00 KST

Inflation in Estonia slowed for third consecutive month in August
The consumer price index (CPI) rose by 1.5 percent on year to August 2026, Statistics Estonia reported.
Goods were 0.9 percent and services 2.4 percent more expensive than in August last year, the agency said.
The CPI rose by 0.4 percent between July and August, which together with the preceding two months' figures makes for the slowest price rises in over five years, Statistics Estonia added.
Commenting on the results, Lauri Veski, the Consumer Price Statistics Service Manager at Statistics Estonia, said that the year‑on‑year increase in prices has been very modest in the last three months – the last time that prices rose so little came in spring 2021.
"Although housing and transport costs have risen on year to August, the CPI was driven down by the decrease in the prices of food and non‑alcoholic beverages," Veski said.
"Food and non‑alcoholic beverages is the commodity group with the biggest weight in the consumer price index. Prices in this group fell by 2.6 percent year on year, which limited the overall price increase. The 4.6 percent decline in clothing and footwear prices also had a considerable impact on the year‑on‑year change," he added.
Housing costs were influenced by the rise in the prices of refuse collection (which went up by 53.6 percent in a year), wood fuel (a 10 percent rise) and electricity (up 3.7 percent) compared with August last year. Fuels were the main contributors to the increase in transport costs, as petrol was 7.9 percent and diesel fuel 27.9 percent costlier than in August 2025.
Year‑on‑year inflation in August was driven by higher costs for fish (which went up by 4.8 percent), fresh fruit‑bearing vegetables (up by 16 percent) and ready‑made food (up by 3.5 percent), while prices fell for fruits and nuts (down by 15.7 percent), dairy products (down by 4.1 percent) and oils and fats (down by 19.2 percent, with butter down by 28 percent). Compared with July, fuel prices rose (petrol up by 2.3 percent, diesel up by 11.2 percent), electricity cost 3.1 percent more and housing rentals increased 2.7 percent, while natural gas prices fell 6.2 percent from July but remained 18.3 percent higher than a year earlier. Among food products, coffee (down by 3.5 percent), citrus fruits (down by 12 percent) and other fresh fruits (down by 9.6 percent) were cheaper than in July, while bread and bakery products (up by 1 percent) and fresh fruit‑bearing vegetables (up by 4 percent) cost more.
Statistics Estonia compiled the above report on behalf of the Ministry of Finance. More detailed information is available from Statistics Estonia here, here and here.

Bangladesh dengue outbreak surges as hospital admissions hit year-high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:24:15 UTC
15:24:15 KST

Bangladesh's dengue outbreak is accelerating, with 42,590 people hospitalised and 117 deaths recorded this year, as a sharp September surge strains hospitals and raises fears the mosquito-borne disease could intensify further in the coming weeks.
At least four dengue patients died and 1,558 others were hospitalised in the past 24 hours, according to health ministry data, marking the highest daily admission tally recorded so far this year.
The disease, which can cause fever, severe headaches and potentially fatal complications, has spread sharply in recent weeks, reviving concerns after Bangladesh's deadliest dengue outbreak in 2023. The outbreak has further strained a healthcare system already grappling with a nationwide measles outbreak that has killed nearly 1,000 children this year.
Health experts warn September could prove even more severe than August, which recorded the highest monthly dengue caseload of the year.
Professor Kabirul Bashar, a medical entomologist at Jahangirnagar University, said his surveillance and forecasting model suggests hospitalisations could exceed 30,000 this month if current trends continue, with weather conditions likely to support transmission into October.
"The peak has not been reached yet," Bashar said. "If the current trajectory continues, September may become the worst month of the year for dengue infections."
Hospital beds in short supply
For Zahid Hasan, 32, the outbreak became a personal ordeal when his four-year-old son developed a high fever and was diagnosed with dengue.
As the child's condition worsened, Hasan took him to three government hospitals but could not find an available bed.
"I was terrified. As a father, it was unbearable to watch my child getting worse without knowing where he could be admitted," Hasan said.
He eventually secured a bed at a private hospital with the help of a relative. His son received seven bags of blood and plasma before being discharged.
"Those days were a nightmare for us. We were constantly afraid something could happen to him," Hasan said. His son remains weak and is recovering slowly.
Dengue patients can deteriorate rapidly after their fever subsides, developing complications such as plasma leakage, low blood pressure, shock and severe bleeding, making close monitoring during the critical post-fever phase essential.
"Patients are flooding hospitals, and warning signs such as abdominal pain, dizziness and unusual lethargy must not be ignored," said Professor Tarek Alam, a physician treating dengue patients in Dhaka.
Bashar said the spread of Aedes mosquitoes beyond Dhaka and other major cities was fuelling infections in districts and rural areas. Dengue cases have now been reported in all 64 districts, although the capital continues to account for the largest share.
The government has intensified prevention efforts as the outbreak worsens. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has ordered nationwide cleanup and awareness campaigns, urging people to remove stagnant water and other mosquito-breeding sites while encouraging greater community participation in mosquito-control measures.
"Fogging alone cannot control dengue if breeding sites remain untouched," Bashar said. "Control efforts must target areas where Aedes mosquitoes are actually breeding. The biggest weakness in dengue control is the lack of evidence-based interventions."

Iran raises price of petrol as US applies economic pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:22:45 UTC
15:22:45 KST

Motorists drive past a large billboard pledging revenge against US President Donald Trump along Jomhouri Street in central Tehran on July 27, 2026. (Photo by AFP)
Iranian authorities have announced they were raising the price of petrol for heavier consumers, as the United States steps up sanctions seeking to isolate the country's economy.
Iran's quota system prices petrol in three tiers: 1,500 tomans per litre for a consumer's first 60 litres in a given month, 3,000 tomans per litre for their next 50, and 5,000 tomans per litre after that. The toman is an informal unit equivalent to 10 Iranian rials.
On Sept. 6, government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani said the price for the third tier would double to 10,000 tomans (about 4.5 US cents).
"The rate will increase to 10,000 toman rials from the morning of Sept. 8," Mohajerani said in remarks carried by state media.
"Different numbers were mentioned in expert meetings, but because the president had promised the people, the rate of 10,000 tomans was set," she added.
She later clarified that the price of the first and second tiers would not be changed.
Iran, a major oil producer with some of the world's cheapest fuel, has for years heavily subsidised petrol, making any changes to pricing politically sensitive.
The development comes as the Iranian currency was trading on the black market on Sept. 6 at more than 2.2 million rials to the U.S. dollar, according to websites that track the rate.
Before the start of the Middle East war on Feb. 28, the rial traded at around 1.7 million to the dollar, and in late April it hit what was then a record low of 1.8 million.

On a Kyiv maternity ward, babies are born during air raids

On a Kyiv maternity ward, babies are born during air raids
KYIV, Sept 7 - The air raid alert in Kyiv was live, warning of approaching Russian jet-propelled drones, but fortunately there were no explosions nearby during the final phase of Alyona Bohatyrenko's labour.
"I gave birth during an air alert!" beamed the 32-year-old, as she lay in her hospital bed cradling her baby daughter minutes after she was born. "None of this is normal, but ... you get used to it somehow."
Doctors at Kyiv City Maternity Hospital No. 2 took a calculated risk by delivering Bohatyrenko's baby on the ward while the skies over the city were under threat.
The same was true for Yuliia Ishchuk, 26, who also gave birth there last Wednesday.
Her husband, 30-year-old serviceman Vitalii Ishchuk, recalled the moment the couple knew the baby was close.
"At three in the morning, the waters broke, but we hadn't packed anything, and nothing was ready," he said. Kyiv was under attack, as it has been almost non-stop since August 27, when Russia significantly escalated its bombing campaign.
"We thought the house was going to be blown to pieces. We called an ambulance; they came, and everything turned out fine."
BIG LIFE CHOICES AHEAD
In an escalating air war between Ukraine and Russia, in which each side is pounding the other's energy and logistical assets to force an advantage, Moscow has fired swarms of high-speed jet drones that are more destructive than older models.
In the last fortnight, air attacks in Kyiv and the surrounding region have been around-the-clock rather than mainly at night, disrupting everyday life for millions of residents.
Officials say conditions are likely to worsen as winter sets in and Russia targets Ukraine's energy system that provides electricity, heating and running water.
Russia says its attacks have a military purpose; Ukraine says they are designed to break civilian morale and persuade the government to give up territory.
For both young families at the hospital, growing threats are forcing them to consider moving into safer accommodation in Kyiv or away from the city altogether.
"We'll have to move somewhere to find better shelter - not a basement in a school or a store - that's no shelter at all," said Vitalii Ishchuk.
Bohatyrenko ruled out moving overseas, but added: "We're thinking about going somewhere this winter after all. We'll have to see how things go, because based on the forecasts, it'll be very difficult to stay in Kyiv this winter with a small child."
'NO ONE WANTS TO GIVE BIRTH'
Beneath the hospital, several pregnant women walked into a shelter with their partners in response to a fresh air raid warning.
Yuliia Kukhar, 29, said that she had only noticed a handful of women with her on the maternity ward.
"No one wants to give birth," she told Reuters.
Ukraine is facing a demographic crisis, with birth rates plunging because of economic factors before the full-scale invasion and, since February 2022, due to partners serving in the military and concerns over the country's security.
Kukhar was expecting her third child. After two daughters, she had thought it would be good to have a boy, but the war, and the risk men faced of being called up to serve, made her think twice.
"We wanted a boy. But there's a war going on, and I don't need a boy. Let's just have girls." REUTERS

Dutch schools must make space for languages spoken at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:21:46 UTC
15:21:46 KST

Dutch schools must make space for languages spoken at home
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch primary schools are now expected to make room for the languages pupils speak at home, like Turkish, Polish and Arabic. New national curriculum standards will encourage teachers to allow students to use their mother tongue to prepare for class or better understand material if it helps them.
The change comes from updated core objectives (kerndoelen) for the Dutch language, which became law in August and set out what children are meant to learn. Current affairs programme Nieuwsuur reported on the new rules on Friday.
About a quarter of people aged 15 and over mainly speak something other than standard Dutch at home – a dialect, a regional language such as Frisian or Limburgish, or another language such as English, Turkish or Polish, according to the national statistics office CBS.
What the schools actually do with the new standards is largely up to them. Attention to multilingualism and pupils’ linguistic identity is obligatory, but the more concrete idea – letting children talk through difficult material in their home language, or prepare for a lesson in it – is advice rather than a strict requirement.
Not everyone agrees
 Language expert Joanneke Prenger, who advises on primary education, said parents should “speak the language you know best” with their children, reversing years of guidance to use Dutch at home. Doing so, she told Nieuwsuur, gives pupils a richer base for learning Dutch and other languages.
Thomas Hendriks, who teaches Dutch in an Amsterdam bridging class for pupils with a language gap, said the steady stream of new advice “comes across as a whim, a trend”, even as more young people leave school unable to read and write properly. In his classroom, he added, letting pupils switch languages also means losing track of what is being said.
The debate comes amid years of concern about basic Dutch skills. The Netherlands was once seen as a strong performer in reading, but scores have fallen sharply, and a national programme worth hundreds of millions of euros has yet to turn things around.
A tougher line elsewhere
 The classroom shift runs alongside a harder line on Dutch in other areas. Ministers want to raise the language level required for naturalisation to B1, and are drawing up stricter rules for welfare claimants who do not speak adequate Dutch.
For international families, the change means a child’s English, Turkish or Polish is now something schools are meant to work with rather than discourage. Regional languages count too – Friesland already requires schools to actively teach Frisian.
Schools have until 2031 to fold all the new objectives into their teaching, and for now decide for themselves how to handle home languages.

5 killed as Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:21:00 UTC
15:21:00 KST

At least five people were killed Sunday when an Amazon Prime Air cargo plane overran a runway while landing at Miami International Airport and struck several vehicles on the ground, local officials said.
Prime Air Flight 7598 overran the airport’s diagonal runway shortly before 2:00 p.m. EDT (6:00 p.m. GMT), crashing into multiple vehicles, officials said at an afternoon news conference.
Five other people were injured, including three who were in critical condition, Miami-Dade Fire Chief Ray Jadallah said.
At least two of the injured were trapped inside vehicles struck by the aircraft, while the pilot and co-pilot were trapped inside the plane following the crash, Jadallah said.
Officials did not immediately identify those who were killed.
More than 60 rescue units and about 200 emergency personnel responded to the crash, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said in a statement.
Emergency crews were still dealing with an active fuel leak from the aircraft late Sunday afternoon, Jadallah said.
Although the airport halted all flights immediately after the crash, two of its four runways had reopened by Sunday evening.
The plane, which departed from San Juan, Puerto Rico, was a 32-year-old Boeing 767-300 freighter that had operated as a passenger jet for various airlines from 1994 to 2015, according to flight-tracking service Flightradar24.
Cargo airline 21 Air operated the plane for Amazon, an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement.
“We are devastated by the accident involving one of our aircraft in Miami today,” 21 Air said on its website. “Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”
Reuters photos taken after the crash showed the jet with its nose on the ground and its tail tilted upward. The right side of the plane had what appeared to be scorch marks.
Flightradar24 said the plane was traveling at 112 knots (129 mph) when it exited the usable runway.
The National Transportation Safety Board, which investigates U.S. civil aviation accidents, said it had sent a team led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate the crash. The agency said it would hold its first media briefing in Miami on Monday.
Amazon was still gathering details about what happened, company spokesperson Kelly Nantel said.
“We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Nantel said in a statement. “Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being and care of everyone involved.”
Boeing and 21 Air said they would support government investigations into the crash.
Sunday’s incident was not the first time an Amazon Prime Air plane has been involved in a fatal crash.
In February 2019, Atlas Air Flight 3591, a Boeing 767-300 freighter operating on behalf of Amazon Prime Air on a flight from Miami to Houston, entered a rapid descent and crashed into Trinity Bay in Texas.
All three people on board were killed.

Finland's former President Tarja Halonen has criticised government cuts to funding for social and healthcare NGOs, saying they could weaken Finland's civil society in a "shattering" way.
She points to the Finnish Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (Kehitysvammaliitto) and the Finnish Centre for Easy Language (Selkokeskus) as examples of organisations whose work could be almost completely halted.
Halonen's criticism is unusual, as former Finnish presidents rarely comment on domestic political issues. She also served as Social Affairs and Health Minister in the 1980s.
A recent survey by SOSTE, which represents 200 social and health NGOs, and Hali, the Finnish Association of Private Care Providers, found that 40 percent of organisations fear the cuts could force them to shut down.
The government's change to the rules governing so-called STEA grants came into force at the end of August. STEA grants for social and healthcare organisations will be cut by around 80 million euros, a reduction of about one-third in next year's state budget.

AI data centers are less thirsty now, tech giants say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:18:38 UTC
15:18:38 KST

Meta's Stanton Springs Data Center is visible Jan. 13, 2026, in Newton County, Georgia, U.S.. (AP Photo)
Data centers are running into a wall of public anger in the United States over their thirst for water and power.
The tech giants spending billions of dollars on them say the water part, at least, is solvable.
Data centers are the warehouses full of computer servers that run the internet and increasingly artificial intelligence.
The computers get hot, and keeping them cool takes water.
American chip giant Nvidia said in a June report that it can eliminate water consumption almost entirely at some facilities when deploying DSX, its newest system for designing and managing AI data centers.
It's a bold claim, and one the industry is under mounting pressure to make good on.
In 2025, data centers consumed 222 billion liters (59 billion gallons) of water worldwide for cooling, according to consultancy Rystad Energy.
Without adaptive measures, the figure could nearly triple to 644 billion liters by 2030, Rystad estimates. Steps to limit the growth could keep it under double.
Nvidia's new method uses a closed-loop cooling system in which liquid flows directly through the servers, as close as possible to the chips, whose temperature can rise above 80 degree Celsius.
The problem is that "there's a pretty direct trade-off between how much water is used and how much energy is used" for temperature control, said Andy Masley, an independent researcher who covers AI and data centers.
Cutting back on water use usually means more power as the liquid in those sealed pipes still has to be cooled down somehow, usually by blowing air over it and that takes electricity.
Nvidia gets around some of this by letting the liquid enter the servers warmer than usual, at 45 degree Celsius.
Most other closed-loop systems ran at about 32 degree Celsius in 2024, according to the Uptime Institute, which certifies data centers.
By starting with warmer water, Nvidia does not need to pump in cooled air year-round.
"Simple fans circulating the air" are often enough, though sometimes a mix of methods is needed, said Josh Parker, Nvidia's head of sustainability.
At sites in extreme climates, or during a heat wave, chill airflow or water evaporation is still necessary.
Microsoft, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Meta told AFP that they also use closed-loop systems, which they said involve no net water loss.
The two cloud computing giants, which have been expanding their already huge data center footprints, used more water overall between 2022 and 2025, but their water use efficiency improved by 25 percent at Microsoft and 37 percent at AWS, according to their most recent sustainability reports.
There is no industry-wide consistency, however, in how companies report data on so-called environmental, social and governance (ESG) efforts.
Elon Musk's SpaceX, now a major player in data centers after it acquired his artificial intelligence company xAI, has never published an ESG report.
In June, ratings agency MSCI gave SpaceX its lowest ESG score.
"Because water is generally much cheaper than electricity," companies have less incentive to cut water use on cost grounds alone, said Shaolei Ren, an engineering professor at the University of California, Riverside.
"There are incentives," Ren said, but they have more to do with public relations amid the growing backlash to data centers across the United States.
Another obstacle is that upgrading an older data center to newer, less thirsty technology is expensive.
That may matter less than it sounds.
Older data centers are smaller and less powerful than the enormous new ones being built now, so they need less cooling in the first place, said Minh K. Le, who leads data center and hydrogen research at Rystad.
And the water a data center uses directly is only part of the story.
Water is used to generate the electricity that powers the data center, and to manufacture its chips and servers.
In the United States, that hidden water use can be twice the amount a data center consumes on its own.

How can the EU help you repair your broken electronics? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:15:02 UTC
15:15:02 KST

Discarding repairable goods generates 35 million tonnes of waste and 261 million tonnes of greenhouse gases annually. Brussels wants to change this by promoting repairs over replacements. But how does it make fixing products easier? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot.
Throwing away your broken washing machine seems easier because it’s quicker and cheaper than fixing it. This is changing as the EU wants you to use your goods for longer.
The EU's Right to Repair Directive encourages consumers to repair broken products rather than replace them by making repairs easier, more accessible, and more appealing. The directive was adopted in June 2024, and member states had until 31 July 2026 to transpose it into national law.
The goal is to keep products for longer, reduce e-waste, promote sustainability, and help consumers save money. The rules cover appliances such as washing machines, vacuum cleaners, mobile phones, and tablets.
Under the directive, manufacturers must repair fixable products, can’t refuse repairs for economic or prior repair reasons, and must offer spare parts at fair prices. Repairs should be free or fairly priced and completed quickly. They must provide spare parts and repair information to independent repairers and clearly display repair service and price information online or in manuals.
The rules also extend the legal warranty by an extra year. If goods are under warranty and consumers opt for repair, they get an additional 12 months of protection.
The European online repair platform helps consumers find local repair shops, refurbished goods sellers, buyers of defective items, and community-led repair initiatives. Customers can also use a European information form to discover and compare repair offers and services.
Do you want to know more about your rights under the Right to Repair Directive? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot!

Zverino – where the Bulgarian spirit lives on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:14:43 UTC
15:14:43 KST

Author
Elena Karkalanova
Monday 7 September 2026 07:35
Monday, 7 September 2026, 07:35
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Nestled among the winding bends of the Iskar Gorge is Zverino, a relatively populous Bulgarian village with an unusually active cultural life. Here, children dance and learn to play musical instruments, while adults preserve traditions and reenact important historical events, making the past a living part of the community today.
“Fakel 1926”, the local community cultural center, which celebrates its centenary this year, is at the heart of this rich cultural life. It is a place where people meet, create and learn, bringing together generations.
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
I have been working at this cultural institution for 10 years. It is the main spiritual and cultural center of the village. There are 1,400 people living here, and we have a school that provides education through 12th grade, as well as a kindergarten. The strong spirit of the people and the close-knit community make our initiatives particularly impactful. This year, we are also celebrating the 100th anniversary of our community cultural center, which has preserved our culture, traditions and way of life over the years”, says Stiliyana Stoyanova, secretary of the local community cultural center.
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
“Fakel 1926” community cultural center is home to a children’s dance ensemble with 60 children divided into three age groups, as well as a music school where young people learn to play various musical instruments. It also has women’s and men’s folklore groups, a handicrafts club, and an arts and creative club featuring 36 local writers, artists and photographers. Their works have already been compiled into five almanacs.
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
“We are proud that very young people take part in our amateur groups. The events we organize have a strong impact and motivate more and more people to get involved. This is also due to the good dialogue and cooperation between the community cultural center, the mayor’s office, the school and the kindergarten, but above all, it stems from the people’s own attitude toward what is Bulgarian and toward traditions – to preserve them and pass them on to future generations”, Stiliyana Stoyanova says, as she shows us the cultural center – its spacious hall, renovated library, and dressing rooms filled with the traditional costumes of the local dance groups.
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
Zverino has a particularly strong connection to Bulgarian history. In 1876, during the struggle for liberation from Ottoman rule, Hristo Botev’s detachment passed through the area. The residents of Zverino welcomed them, fed them and helped them cross the river.
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
This story comes to life every year on June 4, Zverino Day. The local “Botev’s Chetniks” group reenacts the detachment’s descent from the Balkan Mountains. A commemorative plaque dedicated to the event has been placed at the nearby “The Mill” house museum.
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
“The group wears distinctive Chetnik uniforms, and we reenact the descent from the Balkan Mountains with torches. We literally cross the Iskar River, having first prepared and secured the river with rope. This is how we recreate the Chetniks’ crossing of the river”, Stiliyana Stoyanova explains.
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
Zverino’s festive calendar begins on January 6 with Epiphany, one of the major Orthodox Christian holidays. After the festive liturgy at the local church, residents proceed to the Zlatitsa River, where men “rescue” the Epiphany cross and perform a traditional male horo dance in the icy waters. On Bulgaria’s National Day, March 3, Zverino holds a celebration together with the neighboring villages of Oselna and Ignatitsa. Everyone gathers in the village square, and the festivities end with a large Bulgarian horo dance, Stiliyana Stoyanova explains.
One of village’s major events is the National Folklore Festival “Zmey Goryanin”, which brings together more than 500 amateur performers from across Bulgaria including singers, dancers and solo artists. Its name is linked to the local folklore tradition, while its aim is to preserve and promote Bulgarian folk art. The traditions of Christmas caroling and Lazaruvane are still alive, and the community cultural center’s secretary hopes that the old local ritual “Brashlenkyu”, associated with so-called silent water and wishes for a bountiful year, will soon be revived as well.
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
The community cultural center has a specially designated ethnographic corner, where household items used by local residents are displayed, along with authentic traditional costumes from the area, all donated by residents of Zverino.
But what makes people stay in Zverino? The answer is not easy, especially when job opportunities are limited. The village has greenhouse vegetable production, but opportunities for local employment remain scarce. As a result, many residents work in the capital city and travel to Sofia every day, covering just over 100 kilometers in one direction.
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
And yet, some young people choose to stay – the reasons are largely emotional:
''As the saying goes, ‘A stone weighs most in its own place'. It is something that cannot be put into words. The place itself simply has such a powerful energy and beautiful nature”, Stiliyana Stoyanova says.
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
Zverino also has another valuable asset – its natural surroundings. It is part of the Iskar Gorge, a picturesque area in western Bulgaria stretching along the Iskar River, between Sofia and Mezdra. Nearby are the Cherеpish Monastery, the Ritlite rock formation, the Dyado Yotso Monument near Ochindol, and the “Baba Iliitsa” house museum – the birthplace of the heroine from Ivan Vazov’s short story One Bulgarian Woman.
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
In 2025, the local community center and the Vrachanski Balkan Nature Park Directorate launched the project "Eco Destination Iskar Gorge", bringing together the area’s natural and cultural attractions. Two hiking trails have been upgraded. One of the sites attracting tourists is the beautiful Bigora Waterfall, which can be reached via a 7-kilometer hiking trail along the Zlatitsa River.
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
For now, the area is more of a destination for day trips, but the people of Zverino dream of more. They do not simply want to preserve their past; they want to turn the heritage passed down by their ancestors into a reason for young people to see their future here.
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova

Turkey lifts inflation forecast to 28.4% as Middle East conflict pushes outlook higher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:14:25 UTC
15:14:25 KST

Turkey lifts its inflation outlook as the Middle East conflict weighs on the country's economic projections.
Turkey has raised its year-end inflation forecast to 28.4%, Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said on Sunday when he unveiled the country's medium-term economic programme for 2027-2029.
"We expect inflation to start declining again in the fourth quarter of 2026 and to reach 28.4% by the end of the year," Yilmaz said in a televised address.
The new forecast is significantly higher than previous projections.
In last year's medium-term programme covering 2026-2028, the government had forecast year-end inflation at 16%.
Under the new programme, inflation is projected to fall to 21% in 2027, 13.5% in 2028 and 9% in 2029.
Turkey's annual inflation rate eased to 31.51% in August from 31.75% in July, according to official data.
Yilmaz said the war in the Middle East had played a key role in the upward revision of the inflation outlook.
"According to our central bank, the direct and indirect effects of the war on inflation have been estimated at approximately seven percentage points," he said.
Annual inflation, which has remained above 30% since December 2021, peaked at more than 75% in May 2024 before beginning to slow.
Yilmaz said the government had made "significant progress in combating inflation", which remains the top priority of its economic programme.
"Inflation, which had risen to 75.5% in May 2024, has begun to show a clear downward trend as a result of the policies we have implemented," he said.

Türkiye expands Mediterranean marine protection effort
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:10:10 UTC
15:10:10 KST

Türkiye is launching what it describes as the Mediterranean’s largest environmental protection campaign in Fethiye, targeting the removal of millions of cubic meters of accumulated seabed sludge and the protection of the bay’s fragile marine ecosystem.
Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum said the campaign was designed to ensure that the region’s marine environment remains healthy for future generations. “We are launching the Mediterranean’s largest environmental protection campaign so that the blue of our seas reaches future generations,” Kurum said in a social media post outlining the initiative.
The project, implemented by the Turkish Environmental Agency (TÜÇA), will focus on Fethiye Bay, where extensive preparations are underway to remove accumulated seabed sediment. The operation is planned to cover approximately 600 hectares and will target 16,268,925 cubic meters of seabed sludge, which reaches depths of up to 2.7 meters in some areas.
Two dredging vessels operated by TÜÇA are expected to carry out the cleaning operation, which is scheduled to be completed within three years. Following the removal of the sludge, authorities aim to increase the bay’s average depth to about 3.4 meters, improving circulation and supporting the marine ecosystem.
The campaign will also extend beyond dredging. According to Kurum, a mooring system using fixed buoys and mooring lines will be introduced to reduce the need for vessels to drop anchors. The measure is intended to protect seagrass meadows, which provide important habitat for marine life and contribute to the health of coastal ecosystems.
The new system will also seek to prevent uncontrolled boat mooring and bring greater order to maritime traffic in the bay.
The project is due to be officially presented at a launch event on Sept. 8, which will be attended by Kurum and Emine Erdoğan, chair of the UN Environment Programme’s Zero Waste High-Level Advisory Board.
The campaign represents a broad effort to combine seabed restoration, marine habitat protection and more regulated maritime activity in one of Türkiye’s major coastal tourism destinations.
Türkiye’s coastal tourism hub, Antalya, recently launched the “Blue Mediterranean” initiative to preserve and restore local marine ecosystems. Spanning the coastline from the eastern district of Gazipaşa to the western resort town of Kaş, the project aims to eliminate pollution at its source, remove ghost nets from the seabed and deploy artificial reefs to boost biodiversity.

When the Fighting is Over: Will Ukraine War Vets Pose a Threat to European Security?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:09:31 UTC
15:09:31 KST

For Evgeniy Polishchuk, an injury brought an early end to the war in Ukraine. But coming home was only the beginning.
He remembers putting his khaki baseball cap on his wife’s head, a symbol he had finally returned, and holding his family in his arms. But very quickly, he understood that he would have to find his way in the world again – while his friends continued to fight.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I realized that although one chapter had ended for me personally, nothing had actually ended because many people were still defending my country,” he told TVP World.
Eventually, Polishchuk settled into a new rhythm in the southern Polish city of Kraków; just one of many Ukrainian veterans who have moved to the EU after completing their service.
Many more could follow in his footsteps when the war with Russia ends, and this has started to set alarm bells ringing in some European countries.
                                                                                                                                                                         
TVP World has confirmed that the police forces of Poland, Germany and Czechia, the three nations home to the largest Ukrainian populations in the EU, are jointly preparing an analysis of security threats that could emerge in the aftermath of the conflict.
Ukraine Counts on US Passing New Russia Sanctions, Zelensky Says
The possible arrival of battle-hardened Ukrainian veterans, many, perhaps, baring the psychological scars of combat, is considered one such threat.
In April, Czech police chief Martin Vondrášek said that influx of war veterans when the fighting stops poses “the biggest security risk for the Czech Republic that I perceive at this moment”.
But for others, these concerns are overblown and could be exploited by hostile actors eager to fuel fear and resentment against Ukrainians living in the EU.
‘We must be prepared’
The details of the analysis being prepared by Poland, Germany and Czechia remain closely guarded.
The Czech Police confirmed to TVP World the existence of the joint assessment, saying the three countries were “preparing an analysis of security threats that may arise after the end of the war in Ukraine”.
However, they said the document was still being worked on and had not reached its final form.
The Polish Police also confirmed it was working with its Czech and German counterparts, but said it would not comment on the “work and analyses” being carried out as part of the “trilateral cooperation”.
Nevertheless, it pointed to several ways the end of the conflict could create security risks for neighboring nations.
“After the end of the war beyond our eastern border, there is a risk that the demobilization process will contribute to the growth of organized crime, a real and historically proven phenomenon,” the Polish Police told TVP World.
It warned of increased weapons trafficking, drug smuggling, extortion and money laundering, as well as recruitment of veterans by criminal groups.
“War corrupts, and those with combat experience often face enormous difficulties returning to civilian life,” it said. “We must be prepared for various scenarios in the period after the end of the war in Ukraine.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
That preparation extends beyond conventional crime.
Poland, as a “key logistical hub” for aid and support to Ukraine, has become particularly exposed to sabotage, disinformation and cybercrime, the police added.
It argued the answer is to prepare before the threats materialize, for example by creating a new National Police Investigation Bureau to tackle organized crime.
The Polish Police said its approach was based on “hard statistical data, not generalizations or stereotypes”, and pointed to the experience of previous conflicts in the Balkans and Afghanistan.
It added that it would monitor the potential presence of veterans “with full professional attention”, while ensuring that the military community is not stigmatized.
War’s toll
Andriy Kucher, a Ukrainian war veteran, acknowledges that some former combatants will struggle with PTSD, substance abuse or aggression in civilian life. He told TVP World this will be “a huge challenge” for them in the years ahead but believes the problem will not be widespread.
“Mostly it’s normal people who want to have a peaceful life,” he stressed. “They want to go back to their family or have some quiet place to stay alive and just live their lives.”
Kucher had been fighting near Marinka in Ukraine’s Donetsk region when a sniper narrowly missed him and killed his commander. Later that same day a missile struck his position; he was wounded, while his 23-year-old friend died in his arms.
                                                                                                                                                                         
That day, he says, was a turning point – a brutal reminder of how quickly life can change, but also of what he had to be grateful for.
He later set up Strong 300, an organization supporting wounded soldiers and veterans through community, rehabilitation and sport. Rebuilding his own life became inseparable from helping others rebuild theirs.
Yana Chapailo, director of the Ukrainian Defenders Leadership Center, which works with veterans to strengthen their leadership potential, rejects the idea that veterans pose a collective security threat.
“I would not put veterans and criminals in the same sentence,” she told TVP World.
Any crimes they commit should be dealt with by the police on a case-by-case basis, she says. But “you cannot take the behaviour of individual people and apply it to millions of those who are defending their country”.
‘Harmful clichés’ and propaganda
The concern is that fears about Ukrainian veterans could be deliberately amplified by foreign actors to drive a wedge between Ukrainians and their neighbors.
“I think all Europeans need to understand that this is all part of a hybrid war,” Kucher said. “And Russians, unfortunately, are the best at propaganda.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
For Maria Piechowska, an analyst at the Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM), this socio-political lens is the most concerning.
“The police, the Polish state has its tools to fight the security issues,” she told TVP World. “But if we talk about disinformation, if we talk about Russian propaganda, we are not so well prepared.”
She pointed out that Polish-Ukrainian relations have already been vulnerable to political disputes and Russian disinformation, and that just a handful of incidents involving veterans would provide fresh material for turning public opinion against Ukrainians.
Iryna Dobrohorska, an expert from Adam Smith International, a global advisory company, warns that a lack of available data could augment the problem.
Millions of Ukrainian women and children have already moved to Europe, creating a potential pull factor for veterans.
But it is too early to estimate how many would move, Dobrohorska said, because much will depend on how the war ends, as well as factors like employment opportunities abroad and the EU’s temporary protection scheme.
“What I am worried about is the matter of veterans becoming politicized,” Dobrohorska told TVP World. “Without any grounded data, that may become a major risk.”
Piotr Łukasiewicz, Poland’s chargé d’affaires in Ukraine, has previously warned that European governments need to be very careful about how they the approach the issue.
“The worst thing we could do… would be to succumb to harmful clichés,” he said, warning against claims that Ukrainian veterans will “set up mafias” or become a criminal or drug problem after the war.
“We must understand this phenomenon and participate in it, rather than frighten ourselves with it,” he added.
Opportunity, not threat
Asked about the security plans Poland, Germany and Czechia are preparing, the Ukrainian Veterans’ Ministry stressed that those defending the country are among the people most invested in a peaceful and secure future.
                                                                                                                                                                         
“Most veterans came into military service from civilian life – they were entrepreneurs, engineers, doctors, IT specialists and teachers,” the ministry told TVP World. “Many will return to these professions, build businesses and continue contributing to their communities after service.”
For Chapailo, the war-vets wets should be seen as an asset rather than a threat.
“They’ve already established that they have numerous tools and expertise in their hands,” she said. “They are resourceful, they are fast in decision-making, they’ve survived the war.”
She pointed to one former prisoner of war who spent two and a half years in Russian captivity. While imprisoned, he made a mental list of what he wanted to do when he returned. One ambition was to teach.
After coming home, Chapailo helped him become a tutor for other veterans, sharing his expertise in analytics.
“That was his plan when he was sitting in his cell,” Yana told TVP World. “And right now he’s working with these veterans.”
Kucher argues that far from being a threat, Ukrainian veterans could enhance European security, for example by passing on their knowledge of high-tech warfare to the militaries of their adopted homelands.
“The world has changed and each country must rebuild their own security as soon as possible,” he says. “Our unique experience can be useful for you.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry has said previously that veterans are “not a threat, but a security factor for Ukraine, Poland and the whole of Europe.”
“We are convinced that the brave Ukrainian men and women who stood up to defend their country and the world against Russian invaders deserve the highest respect.”
The challenge, then, is not simply how to manage veterans returning to civilian life, but how to make sure their experience is not lost.
“We have to think about a challenge, but not a problem,” Piechowska told TVP World, suggesting that ex-combatants could also be extremely useful in emergency services. “We have to think about opportunity and how we can use their skills.”
So, what next?
None of this means security risks can simply be ignored.
Asked about concerns from Ukrainian veterans and trusts, Poland’s Interior Ministry told TVP World that ensuring public safety and monitoring the consequences of the war are its “absolute priority”.
“We are considering various scenarios, including the risk associated with the illicit trade in weapons and ammunition, and the increased activity of organized crime groups,” the ministry said.
It added that it was continuously sharing information with Ukraine, including cooperation between police and border services.
                                                                                                                                                                         
But experts and veterans argue that preparation should extend well beyond policing.
The challenge of helping ex-combatants return to civilian life will be greatest in Ukraine itself, which is already building a system to support them, covering healthcare, rehabilitation, mental health, housing and much more.
For Kucher, European countries could help expand these efforts rather than waiting until veterans move to the EU.
He argues for dedicated funding programs for veterans, separate to wider humanitarian resources, and had a simple message for governments looking for practical ways to help.
“You need to support veteran NGOs,” he says. “We already work with wounded soldiers. Each week I visit wounded soldiers in hospital, and I understand them and what they need the most.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Piechowska agrees that preparation needs to start early, and that EU states will also need to invest in their own healthcare systems, but she stresses preparation is not only about services. It is also about communication.
She argues that European governments need to think now about how veterans will be discussed in public and how to prevent legitimate concerns becoming a source of social division.
That means developing a “conscious communication policy”, she says, alongside better media and cyber literacy.
Living without fear
After several years away from the frontline, Polishchuk has found a home in Polish society, rebuilding a life close to his family while working, building a business and remaining useful.
In a Kraków restaurant not long ago, he met a young Polish man who was looking for work. There was nothing available, so Polishchuk gave him 100 złoty (€23). The man asked where he was from.
                                                                                                                                                                         
“I told him I’m from Ukraine. And his immediate question was, why aren’t you fighting?”
Polishchuk explained that he was a war veteran who had fought, but was now rebuilding his civilian life in Poland.
The young man was surprised. The veteran had followed him into the street not to ask for help, but to offer it.
“Sometimes society itself, it’s not fully prepared for veterans to return,” Polishchuk told TVP World. “There is an enormous difference between the life experience of someone who has been through a war and someone who has not.”
His principle is straightforward: “A veteran should absolutely be treated as an equal member of society. Not as a victim and not as someone who will come to Europe needing assistance or creating a problem.
“A veteran can be someone who works, builds businesses, participates in society, and helps other people.”

The conservation design for the Rail Baltica overpass span built over Lastādijas Street and Ģenerāļa Radziņa Embankment, together with its support structure in the Daugava River, will require 81,414 euros including value-added tax (VAT), according to an information report submitted by the Ministry of Transport for coordination on the Legal Acts Portal.
Eiropas dzelzceļa līnijas (EDzL) told LETA that the total length of the overpass is 140 metres. The overpass is a significant and technically complex section of the previously planned bridge project. The exposed section of the overpass span above the Daugava now needs to be preserved until construction of the bridge begins.
The next step towards completing the bridge will be the construction of the overpass supports and crossing from Zaķusala, which will be carried out once appropriate financing has been secured and in line with Rail Baltica priorities.
The Ministry of Transport’s information report states that, based on information provided by EDzL, the estimated cost of conservation works for subsection 3A of Riga Central Station, which includes the overpass and support structure, amounts to approximately 551,000 euros excluding VAT under a long-term conservation scenario extending to 2035. This includes both the conservation design and the conservation works themselves.
Meanwhile,
the minimum maintenance work required until conservation begins or construction resumes is estimated at 31,069 euros
excluding VAT. The total identified conservation and maintenance requirements for subsection 3A therefore amount to approximately 582,069 euros excluding VAT.
To ensure that further action complies with regulatory requirements and to prepare the basis for procuring the conservation works, 67,284 euros excluding VAT is required to develop the conservation design for the engineering structure in subsection 3A of Riga Central Station. The indicative amount including VAT is 81,414 euros.
The ministry stresses that financing the development of the conservation design should be regarded as an urgent preparatory measure rather than the allocation of full financing for the conservation works. Developing the conservation design will allow EDzL to specify the scope of work, technical solutions, costs and procurement requirements, as well as enable the subsequent procurement of conservation works in accordance with public procurement legislation.
The development of the conservation design for the engineering structure in subsection 3A of Riga Central Station is only one part of the broader package of measures for conserving Riga Central Station and clearing the construction site. The Cabinet of Ministers will be informed separately about these measures.
The ministry stresses that allocating the funding should be regarded as an urgent preparatory measure
aimed at preventing further deterioration of the structure’s technical condition, ensuring that documentation for the conservation works is prepared and reducing the risk of potentially higher costs to the state budget in the future.
Once the conservation design has been completed, information on the financing required and other circumstances related to carrying out the conservation works will be prepared for consideration by the Cabinet of Ministers.
As previously reported by LETA, the Rail Baltica main line in Latvia is planned to be implemented in its existing scope during the first phase. This includes establishing the Rail Baltica cross-border connection from Lithuania to the Estonian border, as well as completing construction works at Riga Airport and the southern section of Riga Central Station to enable Rail Baltica to connect with the existing railway network.
Therefore, the first phase of the project does not include the so-called “Riga loop”.
It has also been reported that the cost of the first phase of Rail Baltica in the Baltic states could reach 14.3 billion euros, of which 5.5 billion euros would be required in Latvia. However, after indexation, Latvia’s share could rise to six billion euros.
According to the project’s cost-benefit analysis, the total cost of Rail Baltica across the Baltic states could reach 23.8 billion euros. The previous cost-benefit analysis, carried out in 2017, estimated the total cost of the project at 5.8 billion euros.
The Rail Baltica project envisages the construction of a European-standard-gauge railway line from Tallinn to the Lithuanian-Polish border, connecting the Baltic states by rail with other European countries. A new 870-kilometre European-gauge (1,435 mm) railway line is planned across the Baltic states, with trains reaching a maximum speed of 240 kilometres per hour.

Germany seeks to quash 'facilitating genocide' in Gaza case brought by Nicaragua at top UN court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:08:10 UTC
15:08:10 KST

The court could either side with Germany and throw out the case completely or rule against Berlin, meaning the case would then be considered "on the merits" in more detail.
Germany will ask the top United Nations court to toss out a case brought against it by Nicaragua on Monday, which accuses Berlin of "facilitating genocide" with its support of Israel.
Lawyers for Germany will kick off four days of hearings at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the court based in The Hague that rules on disputes between countries.
The case dates back to 2024, following the start of Israel's offensive in Gaza. Nicaragua urged ICJ judges to impose emergency measures to force Berlin to halt all aid to Israel, in particular military equipment.
The court threw out Nicaragua's request in April of that year, saying "the circumstances, as they now present themselves" did not justify emergency orders.
The case is nevertheless ongoing and Germany is now seeking to have it removed, either by persuading judges they do not have the power to rule in the case or that Nicaragua's argument does not stack up.
Berlin has filed so-called "preliminary objections to the jurisdiction of the Court and to the admissibility of certain claims" presented by Nicaragua, according to an ICJ statement.
The detail of Berlin's case has not yet been made public.
Genocide claim
After Germany presents its case on Monday, Nicaragua will respond before both countries get another chance to address the court on Wednesday and Thursday.
It takes on average six months for the court to hand down a ruling in such cases.
The court could either side with Germany and throw out the case completely or rule against Berlin, meaning the case would then be considered "on the merits" in more detail.
During hearings at the court in April 2024, Nicaragua said Germany was "pathetic" to provide aid to Gaza while also simultaneously furnishing Israel with weapons.
Nicaragua's ambassador to the Netherlands, Carlos Jose Arguello Gomez, told the court: "Germany seems not to be able to differentiate between self-defence and genocide."
Germany retorted that Nicaragua's case was "grossly biased," strongly denying the accusations that it was in breach of the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.
Israel launched its offensive in Gaza in response to the deadly 7 October 2023 attacks against it by Hamas-led militants.
Due to its Nazi past, Germany has placed Israel's security "at the core" of its foreign policy, its representative told the court in the 2024 hearings.
Germany said its arms trade with Israel was subject to "detailed scrutiny...that far exceeds the requirements of international law."
This procedure is separate from a high-profile case also before the ICJ, in which South Africa has accused Israel of perpetrating genocide in Gaza, which Israel denies.
The ICJ's rulings are binding but it has no power to enforce them.
For example, it ordered Russia to stop its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a demand that has been ignored by Moscow.

Estonia seeks clearer domestic and psychological violence punishments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:08:00 UTC
15:08:00 KST

Estonia seeks clearer domestic and psychological violence punishments
Estonia is preparing to transpose an EU directive aimed at combating violence against women and domestic violence, with the Ministry of Justice pledging to amend draft legislation to strengthen protections against domestic and psychological violence.
Statistics on violence against women and domestic violence in Estonia are among the worst in Europe. As these problems are widespread across Europe, Brussels has adopted a directive requiring countries to address them.
"The directive was adopted because it was clear that countries were still not doing enough to tackle the problem. Services exist, but there are not enough of them, not enough is being done on prevention and some forms of violence, for example, are still not punishable. The directive must be transposed as it stands and compliance will also be monitored very strictly," said Kristiina Luht, head of victim support policy at the Ministry of Social Affairs.
According to Luht, Estonia has been preparing for this for some time and has already taken many important steps, but some provisions have yet to be incorporated into Estonian law. One example she cited concerns protecting children when people close to them are violent.
"In cases of domestic violence, it must indeed be assumed that minors need protection in all circumstances, even if the attack was not directed at them. This will be written into the Code of Criminal Procedure. Another requirement is that every victim's need for assistance must be assessed, meaning specialists really have to think very carefully about what that particular person needs — what kind of protection and what kind of support," Luht explained.
Another important provision to be written into law concerns cooperation within the support network, meaning close collaboration between victim support services, law enforcement agencies and local authorities. Luht said this has so far been done in high-risk domestic violence cases, but in future it will be required in all cases. A stronger legal basis will also be established for situations where the system has failed a person and the case needs to be analyzed, requiring different authorities to exchange information.
Concern for domestic and psychological violence
Under the directive, countries must draw up national action plans to prevent and combat violence against women and domestic violence. Certain offenses must also be criminalized. Both the Ministry of Social Affairs and civil society organizations are concerned that domestic violence is not criminalized under Estonia's Penal Code. According to Luht, the term "domestic violence" is currently used only in the Victim Support Act.
"There should at least be a specific offense in the Penal Code so that everyone clearly understands what domestic violence is. Psychological violence should also be criminalized — that, too, should be punishable, not just physical violence. We are somewhat concerned that we may be missing an opportunity here. If transposing this directive is such a major process and involves such significant changes, then why not go as far as defining domestic violence very clearly in criminal law as well?" Luht said.
She cited several problematic Supreme Court rulings which, in effect, state that an intimate relationship ends when a couple separates or divorces, even though the reality is different.
"Especially when people have children, they actually remain connected for the rest of their lives and a child can be used to manipulate the other person and harass them endlessly. Unfortunately, that is what they do," Luht said. She stressed that perpetrators of violence are unfortunately very resourceful in such situations, sometimes surprising even those who have spent years helping victims.
Estonia has also seen a case in which a woman was killed the day before she was due to leave her home, illustrating how dangerous leaving an abusive relationship can be.
Draft legislation to be complemented
When ERR approached the Ministry of Justice to ask why these forms of violence were not addressed in the draft legislation, several days passed before the ministry announced that it did, in fact, plan to amend the bill in these respects. Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta also confirmed this in an interview.
"It is certainly not true that the Penal Code does not address domestic violence. On the contrary, we have a problem with the police not initiating proceedings. If violence has occurred, proceedings must be initiated under the Penal Code and the perpetrator can then be removed immediately for up to two months. The bill also broadens the definition of an intimate relationship so that violence between former partners or violence that continues after cohabitation has ended will also be considered intimate partner violence."
According to Pakosta, Section 121 of the Penal Code will be given a new title so that it no longer covers only physical abuse, but any harm to a person's health. The substance of the section will remain broadly unchanged, but it will also become possible to punish psychological violence on the same grounds.
The Penal Code's provisions on threats are also set to be broadened so that a person can face penalties when the victim experiences serious and well-founded fear. Penalties for physical abuse will become more severe. Forms of violence and harassment committed in digital environments will also become punishable, including publishing sexually explicit material depicting a person without their consent, as well as threatening to publish such material.
Officials still engage in victim-blaming
One concern that cannot be addressed through legislation is people's attitudes, Kristiina Luht said. According to Luht, feedback from organizations that assist victims shows that some professionals still hold attitudes suggesting that victims themselves are to blame for their situation.
"I do believe that laws can have an educational effect, but if a professional thinks the victim is to blame, then the law won't help with that. People can be harmed again both by law enforcement and within the social services system. A person is hurt all over again because people don't understand, for example, how difficult it can be for a victim to leave their family or how hard it is to move on with their life after experiencing violence for a long time. These attitudes are actually the hardest thing to change," Luht said, describing accounts she had heard from volunteers.
To some extent, these issues will also be addressed through the European directive, as the law will stipulate that victims must not be revictimized when they enter the system. All professionals, including judges, police officers and victim support workers, must also receive training to understand the nature of domestic violence and the suffering experienced by victims, and to make sound decisions.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Urmet Kook
