EU diplomatic service scraps new high-level defence group amid pressure from member states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:06:36 UTC
15:06:36 KST

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has scrapped a new defence advisory group days after unveiling it, following pushback from member states.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas announced the new group just last week to advise on Europe's defence needs, but the initiative was scrapped following strong opposition from member states.
At an informal meeting of defence ministers in Ireland last week, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas announced a new advisory body bringing together political and military leaders to help design a new approach to European defence.
"The aim is to have some of the brightest minds on security and defence come together and really provide out-of-the-box solutions on how we can be faster in fulfilling these gaps and how we can be more effective," Kallas said during the press conference.
Only days later, the initiative was quietly shelved. Invitees to the launch event, a fireside chat with Kallas, due to take place on Monday in a cosy venue in Brussels, received word of the cancellation on Sunday afternoon.
The abrupt decision came after several member states opposed the move, viewing it as the wrong path to pursue, despite the group having been intended solely as an advisory body rather than one empowered to make decisions on behalf of member states.
"The diagnosis has not changed that Europe needs to deliver faster on defence. Europe still needs to confront the question the group was designed to address, how to strengthen European defence faster," an EU official told Euronews, asking not to be named.
The European External Action Service (EEAS) is already under pressure, as Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has steadily sought more say over the bloc's foreign policy, clashing with Kallas over major issues such as relations with Israel.
The latest Franco-German proposal would place the EEAS under the direct supervision of the President of the European Commission, though it would also give the High Representative a much broader portfolio.
The pressure to scrap the initiative before it was even launched — before the names of its participants had even been announced — is a significant political defeat for Kallas, who had only recently put in place a new EEAS leadership to shore up her position.

Kyiv • UNN
In the Zaporizhzhia sector, soldiers of the 423rd Regiment destroyed a Russian "Osa" surface-to-air missile system worth approximately $10 million. This is already the third such target of the unit.
The pilots of the 423rd Separate Regiment "Scythian Griffins" hunted down another major prize on the Zaporizhzhia front. It was an enemy Osa self-propelled surface-to-air missile system, valued at approximately $10 million, UNN reports.
According to our soldiers, despite the Soviet origin of this weapon, the Russians still use it as a short-range air defense element, and it poses a serious threat to Ukrainian reconnaissance and strike UAVs. The Osa is capable of shooting down aerial targets at an altitude of up to 5 km and operating at a distance of approximately 10 km. Unlike other systems, it is fairly compact and easy to conceal. The destruction of such SAM systems gives our wings access to the enemy's rear logistics.
As noted by the "Scythian Griffins," this is the third Osa they have destroyed over the past year and a half. It will join the collection of special trophies that already includes an "antique" Russian T-54 tank, an intercepted reconnaissance UAV "'ZALA Z-16", a "tank-shed" destroyed together with an infantry unit, a downed Lancet strike UAV, a Strela-10 SAM system, a 2S1 Gvozdika self-propelled howitzer, an Akatsiya self-propelled gun, as well as dozens of Shahed-type strike drones.
As previously reported, at the end of August, soldiers of the 423rd Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment seriously wounded Dmitry Shabaev, commander of the 64th Separate Guards Motor Rifle Brigade of the Ground Forces of the Russian Armed Forces.

Germany’s Merz Under Pressure From Far-Right Election Triumph
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:02:39 UTC
15:02:39 KST

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will huddle Monday with his CDU party to discuss and digest their thumping defeat at the hands of the far-right AfD party in a state election in the ex-communist east.
The anti-immigration Alternative for Germany scored its biggest win yet Sunday with 44 percent of the vote in the Saxony-Anhalt, against about 18 percent for the centre-right CDU, according to broadcasters’ projections.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The visibly dejected CDU state premier Sven Schulze said his campaign was not always helped by national government policies, saying that “we often faced headwinds, and that wasn’t always easy”.
The ballot box triumph put the pro-Trump and Moscow-friendly AfD -- officially listed as “right-wing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency -- within reach of running its first-ever state government.
However, it appeared to have fallen just short of an absolute majority, setting the stage for lengthy haggling before a new government is formed in the state assembly in Magdeburg.
Nonetheless, the result sent shock waves through Germany, which in the post-war era had so far managed to keep extremist parties at bay.
“For the first time since the end of World War II, the AfD -- a party whose state branch is classified as right-wing extremist -- is close to securing an absolute majority,” said Daniel Guenther, the CDU premier of Schleswig-Holstein state. “This is a shocking moment for our country.”
Germany Unveils Anti-Sabotage Plan After Leipzig Airport Attack
- AfD winner mocks Merz -
For Merz -- who watched the results come in from Berlin party headquarters late Sunday, but did not speak in public -- the result is another blow at a time when his approval ratings have dipped sharply.
The AfD’s triumphant lead candidate in the state election, 35-year-old Ulrich Siegmund, took pleasure in mocking 70-year-old Merz, calling him “a very good campaigner” for the AfD.
Siegmund said his party had “made history” and that voters had sent “a signal to Berlin”. Every day with Merz in the chancellery was “one day too many”, he added.
AfD national co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla urged the state branch to seek to take over the government, viewing it as a blueprint for national elections in 2029.
According to projections by German public broadcasters, the AfD fell just three seats short of an absolute majority of 42 seats in the regional parliament.
In the other camp, but also without a clear majority, is a grouping of parties opposed to the AfD -- the CDU, centre-left SPD, Greens and the far-left Die Linke.
One option would be for the tiny BSW -- a leftist party that veers hard-right on immigration -- to act as kingmaker, provided it manages to cross the five-percent hurdle to enter parliament.
The AfD could also try to poach lawmakers from other parties who might want to defect and join its ranks.
Siegmund said his party stood ready to “extend a hand to all forces that want to bring about a fundamental political shift with us”.
- ‘Watershed moment’ -
Rumblings of discontent meanwhile came from within the CDU, which is ruling Germany in coalition with centre-left Social Democrats.
Dennis Radtke, chairman of the CDU’s employee wing, called Sunday’s vote a “watershed moment” and said that “the usual platitudes about a ‘bitter evening’ and the need for analysis won’t cut it”.
Thorsten Frei, leader of the centre-right parliamentary group, called for calm and noted that the chancellor was elected for a four-year term.
He therefore warned against drawing “wrong conclusions” from the result in Saxony-Anhalt.
Political scientist Oliver Lembcke of Ruhr University Bochum agreed however that the election result is “more than a severe electoral defeat for the CDU”.
“We are witnessing a tectonic shift in the party system,” he said.
“A protest and opposition party is transforming -- at least in parts of east Germany -- into a party with a realistic prospect of holding power.”
The AfD, founded in 2013 as a eurosceptic protest party, soon transformed into an Islamophobic and anti-immigration party, railing against the open-door policy of former CDU chancellor Angela Merkel.
Merz has vowed to return the CDU to its conservative roots and launched a crackdown on irregular immigration while trying to reboot a stagnant economy.
Lembcke recalled that last year Merz “took office with the promise of pushing back the AfD -- yet instead, the party has grown even stronger, despite the Union’s shift to a more conservative course.
“This confronts Merz with a question of renewed urgency: what strategy can the CDU use to reverse this trend?”

S. Korea's new jobless claims fall for 2nd month in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:01:59 CST
15:01:59 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's new jobless claims fell for a second straight month due to weaker demand from the construction and manufacturing industries, government data showed Monday.
The number of new applicants for job-seeking benefits retreated 0.3 percent from a year earlier to 81,000 in August, after contracting 2.2 percent in the previous month, according to the Ministry of Employment and Labor.
While sectors such as retail and public administration saw an influx of new claims, a steep drop in claims from the construction and manufacturing industries dragged down the overall figure.
The construction sector recorded the sharpest decline of 22.6 percent in the cited month, while the manufacturing industry posted a double-digit reduction of 11.6 percent.
New claims in the wholesale and retail sector jumped 11.3 percent, and the public administration sector logged the highest growth of 53.5 percent.
The government offers job-seeking benefits to help the unemployed find work, accounting for the majority of unemployment benefits. It is financed by the state employment insurance fund.
The number of benefit recipients totaled 615,000 in August, down 3.6 percent from a year earlier.
It was driven by a substantial contraction of beneficiaries in the construction industry, the number of which tumbled 27.7 percent last month.
The total payout for job-seeking benefits reduced 2.4 percent to 1.01 trillion won (751.3 million U.S. dollars) in the cited month. ■

S. Korea's Q2 industrial loans grow on strong demand from service sector
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
14:01:35 CST
15:01:35 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's industrial loans grew steadily in the second quarter on the back of strong demand from the service sector, central bank data showed Monday.
Debts owed by all industries to the deposit-taking financial institutions totaled 2,065.3 trillion won (1.53 trillion U.S. dollars) at the end of June, up 30.6 trillion won from three months earlier, according to the Bank of Korea.
While the quarterly growth slightly slowed down from an increase of 30.8 trillion won in the January-March quarter, the overall expansion of industrial loans continued to pick up steam.
The trend was largely influenced by banks aggressively expanding corporate lending to align with the government's policy to support productive finance.
Loans to the service industry rose to 1,313.1 trillion won in the second quarter, marking the steepest increase since the fourth quarter of 2022.
It was driven by the real estate sector, the loans to which jumped 6.2 trillion won on the expanded guarantee limits for real estate project financing.
Loans to the finance and insurance sector soared 6.2 trillion won due to the raised margin requirements in the derivatives market.
Loans to manufacturers swelled 8.4 trillion won to 521.5 trillion won in the second quarter, cooling down from the growth of 11.0 trillion won in the first quarter.
The slowdown was attributable to corporate efforts to manage their financial ratios ahead of the half-year closing, alongside early debt repayments by some manufacturers.
Lending to construction companies was almost unchanged in the second quarter compared to the previous quarter.
Industrial lending for operating funds expanded 23.8 trillion won, while lending for facilities' funds increased 6.9 trillion won in the cited quarter. ■

‘We can win here’: Zack Polanski presses the flesh in Holborn and St Pancras
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:00:28 UTC
15:00:28 KST

Zack Polanski has said he will remain as Green party leader even if he loses the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in a high-stakes contest for the left of British politics.
Speaking to the Guardian while door knocking in the north London constituency, Polanski calls the Greens underdogs in the race but says he is confident he could beat Labour, which won the seat with a majority of more than 11,000 at the 2024 general election. The seat has been vacated by Keir Starmer, who announced last Tuesday he was leaving parliament having resigned as prime minister in June.
The Greens are confident about their chances, with party activists having already “knocked on thousands of doors”, according to Polanski, but the race comes as the party has fallen in the polls. There have been murmurs that it might have reached its peak in dying days of Starmer’s premiership, exemplified by the party’s seismic win in the Gorton and Denton byelection in February.
Polanski is not yet formally the Green’s candidate for Holborn and St Pancras but local members are likely to select him. The race will test the electoral heft of his eco-populist party and Andy Burnham’s Labour. The byelection will be Labour’s first electoral challenge since Burnham became prime minister six weeks ago.
Some critics saw Starmer’s decision to announce his intention to leave Westminster on Burnham’s first day in the Commons as prime minister as a way to twist the knife against his successor on his way out of parliament.
Polanski joined volunteers in King’s Cross over the weekend to speak to local voters. It was his fourth visit to the constituency in a week. Should he win, Polanski says he will not move to the area but cycle from his flat in Hackney. “I can cycle to the constituency really quickly. In fact, the length of the constituency is just as fast for me to cycle,” he says. “I’d regularly be here, doing surgeries and representing people.”
Some political commentators have said the seat is a difficult one for the Greens to win and that his run is a high-risk proposition. “I think it’s nonsense,” Polanski says. “I think people are trying to up the stakes because they want some drama.” Nigel Farage ran for election eight times before he won, Polanski says. If he does fall short of winning, he says he definitely stay on as Green leader.
Polanski appeared popular while canvassing. Members of the public stopped him several times between knocking doors to express enthusiastic support for him. At one point, an eager procession of young men who say they have seen Polanski on TikTok gather around him before shaking his hand one by one, making off to the side in an orderly fashion once done. “I feel like the Queen!” the Green leader says.
Starmer won the seat with a 11,572 majority in 2024. The anti-apartheid activist Andrew Feinstein, who is on the left, came second with 7,312 votes and the Greens were third with 4,030. Even if the vote for Feinstein, who will not run this time and has endorsed Polanski, and the Greens was tallied up, the party would be more than 7,500 votes shy of unseating Labour based on the general election figures. Despite this, Polanski still fancies his chances. “We know we can win here,” he says.
It was slow going on the doorstep at first and not many people answered, but things soon picked up. The first woman who answers the door via her buzzer is a big fan. She has arthritis and is unable to come downstairs but she tells Polanski she loves him. “This is a great response. Thank you. I love you too,” he shouts into the buzzer.
Shortly after, Usman Ayyub stops Polanski in the street and shakes his hand. “He is standing on his principles,” says the 27-year-old section manager, who plans to vote for him. He is unimpressed by Labour, who he says has “completely lost the plot”.
“They don’t know what they’re doing,” Ayyub says. “Sometimes they’re falling towards the far right, sometimes they say they’re for the left or the centre. They are not standing for anything.”
After another door knock, a man who claims he worked with Polanski at an adventure summer camp in 2002 stops him. “I saw you on TV and said: ‘That’s Zack!’. Very well done,” he says.
Polanski says he has spoken to Labour voters who are considering a switch to the Greens. “It’s a very easy conversation to have with people. Even if you support Labour or you want to give Andy Burnham a chance, voting Green in this election still makes sense because it’ll make him be a better Labour prime minister,” he says.
“We’ll make sure that we keep pushing him left rather than listening to Nigel Farage. That argument has been resonating with people.”
Pointing at Scala, a famed nightclub in the constituency, Polanski says he worked the door there years ago. He also says his barber is in the constituency. “I come here every week,” he adds.
Some sources in the party have expressed frustration about Polanski’s social media use, with one saying he is “terminally online”. When asked about that, Polanski says: “I think people really appreciate the fact that I’m accessible. With other politicians you get corporate politicians where every single part of their life is micromanaged.
“Every sentence that comes out of their mouth is focus-grouped and I think people absolutely see it as more of a benefit that they know I’m genuine and authentic.”
The issues of housing, the NHS and local crime come up on the doorstep. Burnham has spoken at length about the north-south divide, but Polanski believes there is stark poverty in London and the constituency he is vying for.
“Regional inequality exists so it is important that we talk about supporting all communities,” he says. “It’s also true though that there’s a sense that London is wealthy, but actually somewhere like Holborn and St Pancras has deep poverty and deprivation and often it lives side by side with huge pockets of wealth.”
As the clock passes 11am, Polanski buzzes on a door across from King’s Cross station as people rush pass with suitcases, hoping to catch their trains. Instead of saying “Hi, this is Zack from the Green party” as he normally would, he has begun using his full name, even though it feels “odd”. It appears to work. The man over the buzzer can’t believe it. “Is this Zack Polanski, seriously?” he says.
“Yes, it’s Zack Polanski seriously,” he hears back.

England’s housing courts at breaking point as renters battle no-fault evictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:00:28 UTC
15:00:28 KST

It is a Wednesday afternoon at Stratford housing court, and every seat in the waiting room is full. Over the next few hours, a conveyor belt of tenants and lawyers file into the courtroom to discuss their housing disputes – up to 29 cases are dealt with in a single day.
In one case, a tenant is trying to buy more time after receiving a section 21 no-fault eviction earlier in the year, before they were banned. He has had no luck finding emergency housing with his local council.
His landlord wants him out in the next 14 days, but he says he needs more time. He is off work due to chronic ill health, and has three children aged eight, five and one – the two eldest are due back at school next week. He wants the maximum 42 days, but the judge grants 28, meaning he could be facing homelessness by the end of the month.
In another case, the judge postpones a section 21 eviction order made just before the new Renters’ Rights Act came in, as some of the documentation was proven to be out of date. This gives the tenant more time to find a new home.
While tenants try to delay their evictions, landlords make requests for their cases to be moved to the high court in an attempt to speed things up – the current wait for bailiffs in this part of London is seven months.
Lawyers have said a wave of last-minute no-fault evictions, and a growing number of landlords selling their properties, is pushing more renters into homelessness and driving England’s housing courts to breaking point.
Mustafa Sidki, a litigation partner at south-east law firm Thackray Williams, said: “We saw a huge increase in section 21 evictions just before the act came in. Now we’re getting a lot of instruction from landlords wanting to serve section 8 eviction notices [used when a tenant has breached a tenancy agreement] because they’re selling up as they say it’s no longer financially viable.
“The courts are overloaded – there’s just not enough court time or judicial time to deal with it. And tenants are living in absolute stress because they don’t know how long they’ve got. It used to take two to three months to get a hearing; now it can take up to a year.”
Official data released last week showed a 16% increase in section 21 evictions between April and June this year, compared with the same period in 2025, as landlords rushed to remove tenants.
“In every section 21 notice we served, the tenant didn’t move out, they have refused to vacate and are asking the courts to give them more time to find alternative accommodation,” said Sidki, who represents landlords and tenants.
This issue, along with the rising number of landlords selling their properties, had created a “perfect storm” in the court system, he said.
Savills estimated that 254,000 buy‑to‑let homes were listed for sale in the year to March 2026, a 28% increase on 2024. About 93,000 landlords left the market in 2025, with a further 110,000 forecast to leave during 2026, according to property industry analysts. In London, former rental properties accounted for 30% of all new sales, compared with 13% across the rest of the country.
“There was a lot of talk about no-fault evictions ending, but technically they haven’t – we’re getting a lot of section 8 notices where the tenant isn’t at fault, but the landlord has a right to sell,” Sidki said. “Sometimes these are tenants who have lived in the property for a decade, and they can’t find anywhere else to go.”
Lawyers said the lack of affordable homes for renters to move into meant they were increasingly delaying eviction as long as possible. Many local authorities have also told tenants they must resist eviction in order to access emergency housing support.
Neli Borisova, a senior associate at the law firm JMW, said: “Even where the tenants and landlords want an amicable resolution without having to go to court and all of that stress and expense and time, tenants regularly get advised to basically not leave until they’re evicted by the bailiffs, which puts them in a difficult place.
“I think that is going continue to be quite a frustration on the system.”
Nye Jones from Generation Rent said: “The fact so many landlords uprooted tenants’ lives just because they still could, shows how badly we needed greater protections and the end of section 21.
“Ideally local authorities should be providing more support to people who are on the cusp of homelessness than just ‘stay at home until the bailiffs come’. But it’s a sad fact that they want to avoid putting them in temporary accommodation as long as possible.”

Ministers propose converting female prison estate into cells for men
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:00:27 UTC
15:00:27 KST

Ministers will seriously examine converting parts of the female prison estate into cells that can safely house male prisoners, as the government looks to reduce numbers of women in prison to ease strain on the system.
The prisons minister Catherine McKinnell is to look into the practicalities of converting female spaces to male over the coming months, after warnings from governors and experts that it would pose significant challenges.
Andy Burnham said earlier in the summer that the government was keen to examine freeing more women from prison as a way of building capacity in the system to avoid the early release of more dangerous male prisoners.
But in the details released this week on ways the government planned to free up more space, the emphasis was on deporting foreign offenders and reducing the number of prisoners serving highly controversial imprisonment for public protection sentences, which keep people inside for an indefinite spell.
After a backlash from victims and families, Burnham changed plans for the early release of some prisoners as part of a plan to ease overcrowding. He said he would be preventing the early release of offenders guilty of all forms of manslaughter, as well as rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers.
About 4,500 prisoners are due to be released early in 10 tranches from October under the plans, 1,500 fewer than before Burnham’s interventions. Experts including the former justice secretary David Gauke have warned that the government is taking a big risk running prisons so close to capacity.
But the Guardian understands that officials have told ministers that plans to reduce the number of female prisoners will need much longer-term planning. Andrea Coomber, chief executive of penal reform charity the Howard League, said a genuine reduction in the number of female prisoners would be welcome, but not simply happen to free up space for men.
“[It] does nothing to fix a prison system that is fundamentally too full – it just moves the crisis from one part of the estate to another,” she said. “Without real investment in women’s centres and community alternatives, women risk being sacrificed to the scramble for more beds for men.”
Women currently represent less than 5% of the total prison population in Britain, with 12 dedicated jails. Government sources also said those who would be more likely to be freed would be those on mother and baby units where they cannot be replaced by male prisoners.
The victims minister Alex Davies-Jones said the government still believed that the “vast majority of women who are in prison, many of whom are mothers and have young children, shouldn’t necessarily be there. They are victims in their own right, and they can be appropriately managed in the community through women’s centres.”
But she said that the government could not take a “one-size-fits-all approach” to converting female prisons into male spaces, telling LBC: “There are some women who absolutely should be in prison, and they will remain there.
“But where there is a case to answer that we can re-purpose the female estate, because we know the prison capacity problem is in our male estate, 98% at capacity in the male estate, then we will look to re-purpose to see what we can do to free up capacity and move the estates around.”
Pia Sinha, chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust, said a smaller women’s prison estate could be a positive step if it reduced the number of women jailed and increased the support in communities, who had complex and often unmet needs.
“Any decision about the future of the women’s estate must recognise this reality,” she said. “Rather than viewing a women’s prison as a solution to overcrowding in the men’s estate, the government’s priority should be implementing the Women’s Justice Board’s recommendations and building the community support that can deliver better outcomes for women and safely reduce the number of women in custody in the first place.”

Going for gold: an early autumn road trip across Finland’s sparkling lake district
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:00:27 UTC
15:00:27 KST

I wasn’t sure what to expect from an autumn trip to Finland, my first ever to the country, but spending an afternoon sprawled on a deck chair beneath blazing blue skies certainly wasn’t part of it. After a morning walking beneath the leafy canopy at the Mustila Arboretum – the oldest, most extensive botanical garden in the country – and a lunchtime wine-tasting (more of which later), my friend Sara and I pitched up at the Sahanlahti resort, deep in the Finnish Lakeland, only to find sun-drenched scenery that felt far more Mediterranean than Nordic.
Sahanlahti was the second stop on a mid-September road trip from Helsinki to the shores of Lake Saimaa; a journey in search of ruska, the spectacular autumn colours that blaze for a few short weeks before the long Finnish winter sets in. However, on our opening drive east from the airport to the Radalla resort, set on Lake Urajärvi, most of the thousands of trees we drove past were resolutely green, with just the very tips of the leaves tinged with auburn, like a foliage balayage.
“You’re too early,” the waitress told us, cheerfully, after we had checked in to our chic waterfront cabins, and were tucking into hefty plates of crispy garlic chicken, scattered with freshly picked chanterelles, in Radalla’s quiet dining room. “But you might get some sun tomorrow.” Later, walking back to our cabins through thick drizzle, we agreed she was most probably just being kind.
The Radalla resort is just one of dozens of lakeside hotels scattered across southern Finland – many with self-catering cabins, sauna complexes and gleaming metal steps that lead from wooden piers down into the chilly waters of the lake. The grey drizzle we awoke to made a dip less than appealing, and instead we decided to set off for our next stop, taking in the arboretum en route before finding a place for lunch.
Driving in southern Finland turned out to be quite different from other countries. Most settlements fringe the lakesides, so they tend to be tucked away down side roads leading off from the main highway. Instead, trees – those resolutely green trees – rolled past us for mile after mile, until slowly the fields began to melt into lakes, one after another, the road snaking alongside the blue-grey waters, or stitching together small islets that lay scattered between them.
Googling somewhere for lunch, Sara came across the Ollinmäki winery, an unexpected find in a country that grows absolutely no grapes. Instead, berry wines are hugely popular, and once settled in at our table, we were persuaded to try a flight of six, accompanied by a bowl of hearty elk soup (which tasted considerably better than it looked) and a leaf salad with local cheese. One wine, the white currant and berry Myllärin Matti was particularly delicious, with the tang of a crisp sauvignon – although I wouldn’t want to find out what a Finnish hangover feels like.
From the winery it was an easy drive to Sahanlahti, by which time the weather had cleared and pin-sharp blue skies gleamed above the shores of Lake Saimaa. The main house – painted butterscotch-yellow and dating back to the mid-18th century, when the owners presided over the local sawmill – had a languidly old-fashioned air, but dinner at the Koskivahti restaurant was anything but: rich mushroom soup, slivers of goose confit with lingonberry sauce, wafer-thin beetroot carpaccio with tangy goat’s cheese.
It might have been too early for the leaves to turn, but we had arrived right in the middle of harvest season, when heading out into the fields and islands to pick wild mushrooms and berries (of which there are 35 different varieties) is practically a national sport. We had barely set down our bags at our final stop, Järvisydän resort, before we were whizzing out across Saimaa on a small motor boat, baskets tucked between our feet, to hunt for chanterelles and look for rare ringed seals and ospreys.
The sky was flawlessly blue as we whipped across the water, disembarking first to pick the mushrooms – slashes of bright yellow among the green undergrowth. We were guided in our harvesting by Sebastian, the 12th generation of the Heiskanen family to be running Järvisydän. “Back in 1654,” he told us, “my family were given a portion of land by the Russian tsar, to build a tavern on the route between St Petersburg and Helsinki.” More than 350 years later, the tavern has morphed into a 100-room resort, offering everything from starkly modern glass-walled cabins, high in the forest, to hexagonal log houses with bedrooms set off a central, fire-lit atrium, and camping pods.
It’s an extraordinary place: everything – from the vast reception, dwarfed by a replica Viking longship hull hung above reception, to the restaurants, bar and the Hobbit-like spa – is built entirely from local stone and timber. A visit to the spa seemed the perfect way to warm up after our chilly boat trip, with six different saunas to dip into – although the “sunken log” sauna, where the temperature reached 70C, gave me some sense of how an ice-cream might feel if left out in the sun.
Of the three resorts we visited, Järvisydän was the standout – for its history, for the spectacular scenery of Lake Saimaa that surrounds it, for the delicious mushroom soup and for the long, sunlit walk we took on our final afternoon, through the dense pine forest, where red squirrels skittered around in the branches above. It was a wrench to leave on our last morning, but as we sped back along quiet roads to Helsinki, we agreed Finland had – in spite of our foliage fail – outstripped our expectations. It was more beautiful, more peaceful, more sunkissed than we could ever have imagined.
Ruska (the vibrant colours of autumn foliage) begins in the north of the country in early to mid-September, reaching the Lake Saimaa region in the south by early October.
The trip was provided by Discover the World. A four-night bespoke self-drive trip staying at Radalla, Sahanlahti and Järvisydän resorts starts at £794pp, including B&B and car hire, but not flights.

Pixel 11 review: Google sets the bar for standard flagship phones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:00:26 UTC
15:00:26 KST

Google’s Pixel 11 continues to set the standard for what you should expect from the base model of a flagship phone with class-leading cameras, long software support and almost all the bells and whistles of its most expensive phones.
The regular Pixel 11 costs £879 (€999/$899/A$1,499) making it £80 or equivalent more expensive than last year’s model as the cost of RAMageddon continues to bite. It’s not cheap by any stretch of the imagination, but it comes with 256GB of storage and is £200 less than the Pixel 11 Pro, matching rival Samsung’s Galaxy S26.
At a glance the Pixel 11 looks very similar to the previous two Google phone iterations: glass front and back with flat aluminium sides and large pill-shaped bar at the back, which is much slimmer this time. Stick it in a case and the protruding camera all but disappears.
The 6.3in OLED screen is crisp and super bright with up to a 120Hz refresh rate to keep your scrolling smooth. The in-screen fingerprint scanner is fast and accurate, while the camera-based face recognition works well during the day and is secure enough for use with banking apps, unlike similar systems on most Android rivals.
Specifications
- 
  Screen: 6.3in 120Hz FHD+ OLED (422ppi)
- 
  Processor: Google Tensor G6
- 
  RAM: 12GB
- 
  Storage: 256 or 512GB
- 
  Operating system: Android 17
- 
  Camera: 48MP+ 13MP UW + 10.8MP 5x tele; 10.5MP selfie
- 
  Connectivity: 5G, eSIM, wifi 6E, UWB, NFC, Bluetooth 6 and GNSS
- 
  Water resistance: IP68 (1.5m for 30 minutes)
- 
  Dimensions: 152.8 x 72.0 x 8.6mm
- 
  Weight: 197g
Faster and more efficient Tensor G6 chip
The Pixel has a new generation of Google’s chip, the Tensor G6, which is up to 20% faster in tests. It significantly lags top-end rivals from Qualcomm and Apple, so won’t win any raw performance awards, but feels snappy in daily tasks and can handle mid-level gaming just fine.
The battery life is also improved over previous models, lasting about 54 hours of light use between charges. That includes actively using the screen for more than seven hours for browsing, messaging, apps and photos across a mix of 5G and wifi.
Gaming and more demanding use hits the battery harder, but the Pixel should be able to see out even the heaviest of use days.
Android 17 with more proactive AI
The Pixel 11 runs the latest Android 17 out of the box with operating system and security updates provided until August 2033.
The software is slick, nicely animated and well optimised, with plenty of colourful customisation if you want it. As with previous Pixels, it is a showcase for some of Google’s most advanced AI systems, many of which run on-device, making them fast.
The most interesting of the tools remains Google’s proactive AI systems, which vary a bit depending on where you live. In the UK the expanded Magic Cue from last year pops up in messages and a few other apps with information such as your schedule, flight or order details, and suggestions for good local restaurants from Google maps or photos to share in a chat. In the US, Canada, Australia and a few other regions, the feature is called “Gemini Proactive Assistance” but has similar powers. If you use a supported app, such as Google Messages, the suggestions are low-key great. Unfortunately it doesn’t work in WhatsApp, Signal or other third-party apps I’ve tried, which limits its usefulness.
In the UK and US, Gemini can go further, proactively taking action for you, such as booking a restaurant via OpenTable, which is the type of assistance that has long been promised by various AI agents.
Another useful AI feature is built directly into Google’s keyboard called Rambler, which is voice typing on steroids. You can speak naturally to it and the system will remove your ums and ers and other deviations to produce a succinct, fully formed sentence or paragraph. It makes trying to dictate a rushed messaged while hustling for public transport a lot easier, although it doesn’t show your text until after you hit the stop button, unlike most other dictation tools.
Camera
The Pixel 11 has three cameras on the back and a solid 10.5-megapixel selfie camera in the screen.
The improved main 48MP camera captures excellent photos across a range of lighting conditions, including low light where its larger sensor helps capture more of what’s available. The 13MP ultra-wide camera is one of the best on a phone of this class, helpful for fitting more in the shot or providing a different perspective. But it is the 10.8MP 5x telephoto camera that sets it apart from the competition, capable of meaningfully closing the distance to objects. In bright light it can digitally zoom to 30x magnification with surprisingly good results.
Entirely new for the Pixel camera this year is the “Looks” feature, which allows you to customise how the phone captures and processes your photos for very different styles far beyond simple filters applied after the fact.
There are three versions of the default look available – natural, vanilla and shadows – plus six more-distinctive looks, including “digi” that replicates the look of the old digital cameras that has recently become popular. Each look can be customised in colour, tone, grain and sharpness, so you can get arty or replicate a particular film style.
If you are a Pixel user who has ever thought its photos look a little too cold, dramatic or overly processed, this is for you.
The Pixel shoots great video at up to 4K at 60 frames a second. The new Magic Capture feature is a one-button shooting mode that records video and photos automatically that is best used during events such as birthday parties where you want to be more in the moment but still capture the scene.
Google has also added a “Creator Suite” mode to the video capture, which shoots straight to a folder you can quickly storyboard and trim to create a video. It also has a teleprompter mode for shooting face to camera, a social media grid to get the alignment correct and speech enhancement that cuts out background noise.
All these features are in addition to Google’s popular Auto Best Take, Add Me and Camera Coach from last year, which makes the new Pixel camera one of the most feature rich available.
Sustainability
The battery is rated to last in excess of 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google, third-party shops or self-repair with manuals and parts available.
The Pixel 11 is contains 33% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report and will recycle old devices for free.
Price
The Google Pixel 11 costs from £879 (€999/$899/A$1,499) in a choice of four colours.
For comparison, the Pixel 10a costs £499, the Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079, the Pixel 11 Pro XL costs £1,279, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from £1,799, the Samsung Galaxy S26 costs £879 and the Apple iPhone 17 costs £799.
Verdict
The Pixel 11 isn’t the most advanced Google phone, nor is it the cheapest. But this middle-ground model offers more than enough to beat the competition and question whether you really need to spend more on a Pro phone.
It offers, yet again, a very high-quality experience, great triple camera, long software support and very good battery life. It won’t win any raw performance awards, so those looking for a gaming phone should look elsewhere, but it feels fast and responsive in daily use.
Google’s AI tools are second to none, particularly its Rambler dictation feature in the keyboard and the proactive Gemini features, which offer genuinely useful help even if they are not available in every third-party app.
The new camera looks feature provides more control over photos than ever before on a Pixel, so you can tailor it to your preferences or get creative far beyond simple filters.
It may not have changed all that much from last year’s equally excellent Pixel 10, and it isn’t quite the bargain the Pixel 10a is, but the Pixel 11 is the best phone you can get under £900.
 Pros: seven years of software updates, great camera with 5x telephoto, great screen, impressive local AI features, Qi2.2 wireless charging and magnetic accessory support, long battery life, good size, fast fingerprint and face recognition, 256GB starting storage.
Cons: face unlock option not as secure as Face ID, raw performance short of rivals, no physical SIM card slot in the US, heavier than rivals, not a big upgrade on previous model, no wifi 7.

‘This is what I have to do to survive’: the Sudan refugees forced into sex work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:00:26 UTC
15:00:26 KST

Sudanese women who fled to Egypt to escape the war in their country are facing increasing levels of sexual exploitation, with the Guardian told of single mothers forced to sell their bodies to survive and feed their children.
Many of the women have not previously worked in Sudan, where conservative social norms dictate that men are usually responsible for financial support. Without established trades or professions, and with their husbands and other family members dead or missing, many female refugees are struggling to pay for food, medical care and rent.
The Guardian spoke to 19 aid workers, refugees and medical professionals who say a lack of access to healthcare, education and, at times, food has made the situation for Sudanese women in Egypt increasingly desperate.
Sudan’s civil war triggered the world’s worst displacement crisis, forcing more than 4.5 million people to flee to neighbouring Chad, South Sudan, Libya and Egypt. The situation in Egypt, which took in the largest number of arrivals, with an estimated 1.5 million people crossing the border, has also become significantly worse.
Thousands have found themselves trapped with few resources after a funding shortfall at UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, and the dismantling of USAID eliminated what little support had been available. Unable to work legally, living in poor and often unsafe neighbourhoods, women – who have been among the hardest hit by the war – are acutely vulnerable.
Mariam*, who runs a refugee outreach group in Cairo, says 90% of Sudanese women in her neighbourhood, where rent is cheap, have been subject to sexual exploitation.
“A woman without a husband, who has children, they target her knowing she won’t have enough to feed them,” Mariam says. “She thinks of doing this just once to cover her immediate expenses, but you’re going to be forced to do it every time.”
Even many of those who have spouses are not safe, because their husbands are away from home working long shifts or looking for work in other cities.
Khadiga*, who works in the same refugee outreach group, says: “I know a girl who was taken advantage of and the same man who abused her then began abusing her daughter. Her husband divorced her when he became aware of what had happened.”
Without legal status or proof of their university degrees, even women with professional qualifications, such as teachers and doctors, struggle to find work. Most end up either working informally in factories, where a 10-hour working day nets about 150 Egyptian pounds (EGP; about £2.20), or as domestic workers, where they often go unpaid and sexual assault is commonplace.
Sex work has increasingly become a last resort for women seeking a way out of grinding poverty. “These women have been here since the war started and they are desperate,” says Alaa*, who works for an organisation that helps the women.
Five women described their experiences to the Guardian, speaking on the condition of anonymity.
Before the war, Maha* says she worked as a supervisor at a poultry farm in Sudan, living what she describes as a simple but happy life with her three teenage children, after divorcing their father. She was captured and detained by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who accused her of collaborating with the Sudanese military.
At the time, Maha says, her children had been staying with her former sister-in-law. Unable to find them after she was released and afraid she would be detained again, she fled to Egypt in 2024. She worked informally in a pharmaceutical factory until four months ago, when she lost two fingers in a workplace accident. Struggling to find other work to pay her bills, she started doing sex work. “I do this to cover my rent. If I don’t pay, they will kick me out.”
At night she stands in the street, waiting for passing cars to signal. Payment is about EGP300-600. “I get into cars with strangers. This is what I have to do to survive.”
Maha does not know if her children are still alive in Sudan. “I pray to God to be reunited with my children. But I worry that because I’m doing this, God will never give my children back.”
Sara*, a single mother who fled to Egypt in 2023, says she is “forced to sell herself” to be able to feed her two teenage daughters, but struggles to keep them away from sexual violence. She says her 14-year-old was attacked on the staircase of their apartment building by a Sudanese man, who tore the clothes from her body in an attempted sexual assault, before she was rescued by neighbours.
Workers at refugee organisations also describe how some women are lured into sex work when they first arrive in Egypt, with offers to expedite their residency paperwork. Aisha*, an aid worker, says homeless women are “easy targets” and often engage in sex work for cash or food. “The person who hands her a meal will tell her, ‘I can give you more if you come with me for a few hours’; she will go. Anyone who just arrived from Sudan won’t refuse such an offer,” she says.
Even women who find jobs frequently report being sexually exploited. Zeina*, 21, says her factory boss started visiting her home in the evenings, demanding sex and threatening to withhold her pay and fire her if she did not comply. Desperate to put an end to the abuse, she began shouting at him outside her apartment one night, hoping the neighbours would intervene. Instead, they suggested she was at fault. Feeling trapped, she decided her only option was to return to Sudan.
Zeina’s story highlights a cruel but common dilemma for women being sexually exploited or engaging in sex work. Despite having already survived a gauntlet of bombings, killings, rape and violence at the hands of armed militias to get to Egypt, returning to Sudan often becomes their only escape for many.
Aid workers say exploitation remains under-reported because fear and shame surround the subject of sex outside marriage, even in the context of abuse. Some women fear they could be killed by their own families, but most are wary of becoming outcasts in their community.
Mohamed*, a doctor at a healthcare organisation in Cairo, says he treats at least 10 women every week who report being sexually exploited or engaging in sex work. Many come to him pregnant and seeking abortions. He says the high number of unwanted pregnancies that he and colleagues are witnessing indicates the scale of the problem.
For women, pregnancy presents another impossible situation: in Egypt, children born outside marriage are not legally recognised, while abortion is illegal. Mohamed says those who can find the EGP3,000-4,000 will buy parallel-market tablets of misoprostol – an abortifacient drug that triggers uterine contractions.
But those without money must often resort to dangerous home abortions. Just last month, says Mohamed, two pregnant women who did not have money to buy the pills died after they attempted to insert pieces of wood into themselves, after they had been told it would dilate the cervix and cause a miscarriage.
Mohamed says the lack of legal reproductive healthcare and the high cost of drugs imposes a cruel secondary burden on women who are already traumatised. “It is exploiting the outcome of previous exploitation,” he says.
* Names have been changed to protect their identities

More Chinese pet owners choose TCM for chronic pet illnesses using herbs, bee stings, acupuncture

An increasing number of Chinese pet owners are turning to traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) to address chronic diseases and provide hospice care for their senior pets.
On one social media platform, the hashtag #petTCM has amassed over five million views, reflecting a growing willingness among people to share their experiences with TCM treatments for their pets.
A pet owner from Beijing took his dog, Iron Man, a seven-year-old mix of a border collie and golden retriever suffering from severe gastrointestinal issues, first to a Western veterinary clinic.
The veterinarian there diagnosed Iron Man with inflammatory bowel disease and prescribed medication; however, his condition failed to improve.
Seeking alternatives, the owner decided to explore TCM to “give it one more try.”
The TCM practitioner assessed Iron Man by taking his leg pulse, examining his tongue, eyes, and mental state, and inquiring about his medical history, past treatments, daily diet, and activities. The doctor then prescribed Chinese patent medicine pills and dietary therapy.

Hungarian Media Tycoon’s Firm Formed Dubai Subsidiary While Under Investigation at Home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Reported by
Hungarian media tycoon Gyula Balásy broke down in tears in a May television interview, stating authorities had frozen the accounts of his companies, which had received lucrative public relations contracts under the administration of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.
Following that admission, the National Investigation Bureau of the Emergency Police released a statement about its investigation into “suspicion of fraudulent misrepresentation in connection with overpriced contracts.” The investigation involves the National Tax and Customs Administration, and has been active since at least April in 2024.
Corporate records obtained by OCCRP and Átlátszó reveal that one of the companies that had its accounts frozen created an offshore firm in 2024, as the investigation was ongoing.
In October 2024, the records show, Balásy’s New Land Media formed a subsidiary in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) city of Dubai.
Balásy also owns a luxury apartment in Dubai, according to property records.
He began the process of buying the apartment for approximately 3.2 million UAE dirhams (roughly $870,000) in May 2023, according to leaked property records obtained as part of the Dubai Unlocked project. The land registry shows that the purchase was officially completed in 2025.
Also in 2025, Hungarian corporate records show that New Land Media provided approximately 1.3 billion forints (nearly $4.2 million) in long-term loans to a subsidiary. New Land Media’s records list only two subsidiaries at the time — the Dubai firm and another based in Hungary. The Hungarian subsidiary’s financial statement for 2025 does not record receiving the loans.
In his response to questions from reporters, Balásy did not clarify whether the funds went to the Dubai subsidiary. The Dubai firm is involved in “Education & Training Computer Software,” according to its UAE business license.
While the investigation into Balásy’s companies is more than two years old, authorities did not freeze the accounts until Orbán was ousted in national elections this April, after 16 years in power. Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, has made moves to investigate the misuse of public funds under the previous government.
In a response to questions about the Dubai apartment and the transfer of funds from New Land Media to a subsidiary, Balásy said: “I do not wish to comment on the details of the individual transactions.”
“We are fully cooperating with the competent bodies of the Hungarian state and the investigative authority,” he said. Cooperation has included providing “all requested information and documents.”
“I strongly reject any allegation or suggestion that I have absconded or hidden any assets,” Balásy added.
There is no evidence that the transfer of funds or the purchase of the Dubai apartment were illegal, and the ongoing Hungarian investigation has not resulted in any charges against Balásy.
But Balásy is now facing even more scrutiny. On September 1, Hungarian authorities raided the premises of several of his companies. The action came after Átlátszó revealed that toy vehicles distributed during political campaigns appeared to be overpriced.
Balásy did not respond to a request for comment about the raids.
Controversial Campaigns
In April 2024, Hungary’s chief prosecutor revealed that the National Investigation Bureau of the Emergency Police had launched a probe into alleged “misappropriation of funds and other crimes” by firms that received state communication contracts.
Six months later, in October 2024, the same firms under investigation — owned by Balásy — won another major state communications framework agreement worth up to 75 billion forints ($243 million). Balásy’s companies continued to receive Hungarian state contracts until Orbán lost elections.
During Orbán’s tenure, Balásy’s companies won contracts from the National Communications Office for coordinating advertising campaigns, media buying, event organization and public outreach projects for government institutions.
His network of advertising and event-management companies — collectively known as Lounge Group — designed and distributed the government’s political and ideological campaigns for more than a decade. Some campaigns were criticized for vilifying migrants, Ukraine, the European Union, and LGBTQ+ communities, along with American-Hungarian billionaire George Soros.
New Land Media is the unit of Lounge Group that specializes in media planning and buys advertising space across television, radio, print and outdoor billboards. It decided where and how often government ad campaigns would run. Reporting by Átlátszó and other Hungarian media shows it overwhelmingly spent that public money on pro-Orbán media outlets.
New Land Media has served as a main contractor for government communication and state-backed campaigns overseen by the Cabinet Office, which was headed by Antal Rogán and includes the National Communications Office.
The Hungarian police and the National Tax and Customs Administration both said they could not provide further information about ongoing investigations.
Frozen Funds
Last week, Magyar’s administration initiated the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, which is tasked with investigating the alleged misuse of public funds under Orbán’s government.
Magyar had launched his political career with a 2024 live interview on the YouTube channel Partizán in which he broke with Orbán’s ruling Fidesz party, and lambasted its alleged systemic corruption.
Among his claims in that interview, Magyar said he had quit as CEO of the state-owned student loan center because he refused to continue signing severely overpriced government communication contracts with the Balásy companies.
Balásy has not responded directly to Magyar’s allegations. However, he told OCCRP and Átlátszó: “All transactions between my companies, or between my companies and external parties, have been and are taking place within a strictly controlled, approved legal and financial framework in accordance with the laws in force at all times.”
Setting the scene in 2024 for his future run for prime minister, Magyar vowed to root out what he alleged was cronyism. He also promised to dismantle the state-controlled public media network built by Orbán and his associates, which he called a "propaganda machine.”
Balásy’s companies were central to the Orbán government’s public relations strategy.
In a television interview in May this year, Balásy said Hungarian authorities had frozen bank accounts linked to his companies — including those connected to New Land Media.
A teary-eyed Balásy offered to hand over control of his business empire to the Hungarian state, insisting that he had “nothing to hide” and had done nothing unlawful.
In a Facebook post in response, Magyar appeared to suggest that the action against Balásy's companies was part of a broader effort to dismantle the patronage system built under Orbán. Quoting his 2024 interview, he wrote: "This system could collapse much faster than many people think."
The following day, the National Bureau of Investigation confirmed in a statement that it had frozen company bank accounts as part of an investigation into the alleged misappropriation of public funds and money laundering.
The National Bureau of Investigation said it was also conducting a separate probe based on suspicion of allegedly "overpriced contracts" related to the group of companies.”
It is not known if the Dubai subsidiary, or Balásy’s apartment in the city, are part of the investigation. Balásy declined to clarify whether authorities had questioned him about either.
“I do not wish to comment on the details of my private investments,” Balásy said in his emailed response to questions. “However, I consider it important to state that all my investments — whether in Hungary or abroad — are made in full compliance with the relevant laws and tax regulations.”
The OCCRP Research and Data team contributed research.

Iranians recount horrors of suspected US missile attack on first day of war
Missiles that struck the southern city of Lamerd on February 28 dispersed tungsten fragments, killing at least 21 people
Thirteen-year-old Mohammad Reza Barfar remembers the free kick more clearly than almost anything else on February 28 when the US-led attack on Iran began.
The football-loving schoolboy went to a local field after classes for a match between his village and another team. He scored from a free kick and his brother captured the goal on video.
Hours later, Mohammad Reza was lying wounded amid smoke and debris after a series of explosions struck Lamerd, an industrial city in Iran’s southern Fars Province.
“This was the last time I touched the ball,” Mohammad Reza told Kyodo News, as he showed the video of the goal.
Four pieces of metal struck his body, according to his family and medical treatment records, mangling the sole of his right foot and the heel of his left, and injuring his head and right arm. Damage to a bone in his left leg has left him dependent on a wheelchair.
After the match, Mohammad Reza went to his family’s flower shop and he was resting there when a powerful explosion shook the ground.

Hong Kong’s tourism watchdog has revoked the licences of two travel agencies and a guide after finding they failed to protect members of mainland Chinese tour groups from “coerced shopping”.
The Travel Industry Authority said on Monday that the licences of Go Go Ming Travel Services, Grandee Travel Company and guide Sun Kwun-ying had been revoked with immediate effect.

Taiwan cooling suppliers target thermal resistance with new designs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:56:55 UTC
14:56:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Thermal resistance between AI chips and cooling plates is emerging as a new challenge for the cooling industry, with Taiwanese companies pursuing new designs to improve heat dissipation, CTEE reported Monday.
In conventional AI chip designs, heat generated by a chip passes through thermal interface material (TIM), a metal lid covering the chip package, and another TIM layer before reaching an external cold plate, where coolant carries the heat away. Each additional interface can increase thermal resistance while also creating challenges related to coating thickness and material aging, according to Pocket Securities.
As AI chips consume more power, Auras Technology Co. is seeking to reduce the number of materials and interfaces that heat must pass through before reaching the coolant. The company said microchannel technology will become increasingly important.
Microchannel technology creates tiny channels within the metal lid covering the chip package. Coolant can then flow through the lid itself, bringing it closer to the chip and reducing the distance heat must travel, according to Sinotrade.
Auras said the designs require precise control of coolant flow and hot spots. The shift is also pushing cooling companies further into chip packaging, requiring changes to packaging equipment, manufacturing processes, and yield management.
Jentech Precision Industrial Co. is developing a removable-lid design for Nvidia’s Rubin Ultra platform. The approach allows part of the metal lid covering the chip package to be removed during system assembly, eliminating the second TIM layer and enabling the cold plate to sit closer to the chip.
Jentech also plans to eventually combine vapor chamber and microchannel technologies to bring cooling closer to the chip’s main heat sources.
Asia Vital Components Co. is pursuing cooling systems that cover a larger area and cool both sides of the chip. Some of its newer designs extend cooling from the front of the chip to the back of the motherboard.
Which approach gains wider adoption will ultimately depend on decisions by AI chipmakers and cloud service providers. Industry players expect microchannel technology to enter mass production as early as 2028.

French mechanical elephant parade draws 150,000 in Taipei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:56:32 UTC
14:56:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Taipei Arts Festival’s opening outdoor spectacle, “Three Elephants Pass...,” concluded its second and final procession in Shilin on Sunday (Sept. 6).
Guided by glowing red torches, three massive mechanical elephants paraded alongside mechanical phoenixes and a tin-soldier band through busy streets and night-market arcades.
Accompanied by bagpipes and double-reed instruments, performers representing five continents marched alongside tens of thousands of spectators, turning Shilin into an immersive outdoor theater.
According to the Taipei Performing Arts Center (TPAC), the two-day event drew more than 150,000 visitors, while official livestreams attracted over 220,000 views.
Produced by French street theater company Compagnie Oposito, the performance drew on Taipei’s local history.
The procession’s precise 7:14 p.m. start time honored 1914, the year Taipei’s first zoo was established. For longtime residents, the parade also evoked memories of 1986, when crowds lined the streets to watch animals being relocated from Yuanshan to Muzha.
Taipei Department of Cultural Affairs Commissioner Tsai Shih-ping (蔡詩萍) said the record turnout resulted from long-term cultural cultivation rather than a short-term campaign.
Tsai said the effort began in 2025 after local borough chiefs proposed revitalizing the commercial district. The city subsequently collaborated with TPAC on a multiyear initiative to promote urban regeneration through the performing arts.
Tsai said sales for vendors at Shilin Night Market doubled over the weekend compared with typical days, demonstrating a successful connection between public cultural policy and the local economy.
Founded in 1982, Compagnie Oposito is a pioneer of European street theater.
Co-founder Jean-Raymond Jacob maintains that “the street is both a battlefield and a stage,” emphasizing that the urban environment is a living component of the work rather than merely a backdrop, according to TPAC.
Jacob likened adapting productions to “mixing anise liqueur with water,” noting that while cities, laws, and physical spaces vary, the core structure and rhythm remain intact.
TPAC said Jacob’s choreography relies on geometric concepts such as circles, straight lines, and M-shaped formations. The troupe adapts the performance to each city by recalculating travel times based on distance, road conditions, and slopes.
Technical director Veronique Charbit highlighted the logistical realities of outdoor productions, saying tools suited to indoor stages often fail on uneven street pavement. Charbit works closely with local authorities in each host city to review safety protocols and mitigate risks.
Jacob cited the troupe’s past work “Blue Skins,” which explored the Black experience in France by inviting actors to share their stories and control their choreography, attire, and music rather than reproduce societal stereotypes.
For the Taipei production, the troupe partnered with Taiwanese groups Sun Son Theatre and Hsuan Yu Music, along with dozens of local volunteers, to adapt the performance to its setting.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei District Court issued a wanted notice Monday for legislative aide Chang Chun-chieh (張俊傑) after he allegedly damaged and discarded his electronic monitoring device before disappearing.

Police and the judge later found the damaged device, but Chang could not be located. The court also reported him to prosecutors for allegedly damaging public property.

After the case was transferred to Taipei District Court, a judge granted Chang bail with travel restrictions and electronic monitoring. Chang appeared in court on Sept. 1 and denied fraudulently obtaining legislative assistant subsidies while admitting to offenses including document forgery.
He said he had performed legitimate work as a legislative aide and denied intending to fraudulently obtain the subsidies.

Germany’s anti-Russia stance helped drive AfD election victory – expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:55:13 UTC
14:55:13 KST

Germany’s anti-Russia stance helped drive AfD election victory – expert
The German government’s increasingly hostile stance toward Russia, mounting economic problems, and concerns over migration have helped propel the Alternative for Germany (AfD) to a historic election victory in Saxony-Anhalt, Professor Vladislav Belov, head of the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Center for German Studies, has told RT.
The AfD won 43.8% of the vote, more than doubling its result from the previous state election, according to official preliminary results. It is set to hold 39 of the state parliament’s 97 seats, falling short of the 49 required for an absolute majority.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which has led Saxony-Anhalt’s coalition government since 2021, finished a distant second with 17.2% and 15 seats. Sven Schulze, the party’s lead candidate and outgoing regional head, conceded defeat and congratulated the AfD on its success.
Speaking shortly after polls closed on Sunday, Belov recalled his earlier assessment that the anti-Russian positions adopted by German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt would benefit the AfD among certain groups of voters.
The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), founded in 2024, entered the Saxony-Anhalt parliament for the first time after securing 5.3% of the vote.
“I did not expect the BSW to cross the 5% threshold, so congratulations to Sahra Wagenknecht,” Belov said, describing its performance as another surprise and attributing the result to the party’s “broad peace-oriented position.” “Sahra said that right-wing extremists were those who wanted war and militarization. That also resonated with voters.”
Belov argued that the campaign had been unusually dominated by federal issues, despite voters formally electing a state parliament.
“For the first time, the AfD presented itself not merely as a protest party but as a party with governing competence,” he said, identifying migration, education, and Saxony-Anhalt’s economic and political situation as key campaign issues that other parties had failed to address.
The predominantly rural state is also home to a sizeable chemical industry that has been affected by higher energy costs since Germany abandoned inexpensive Russian pipeline gas. Unemployment stood at 8.1% in July, compared with 6.4% nationwide.
Belov attributed the Greens’ result to tactical mobilization rather than voter support for their policies. He described the ‘Taktisch Wählen’ initiative, which used door-to-door canvassing and an online tool to encourage support for the SPD or Greens in order to block an AfD majority, as “scandalous.”

US, South Korea and Japan begin five-day military exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:53:47 UTC
14:53:47 KST

The US, South Korea and Japan began a five-day joint military exercise on Monday aimed at strengthening their operational and joint response capabilities across multiple domains, local media reported.
The Freedom Edge exercise began in international waters east and south of South Korea’s Jeju Island, Yonhap News Agency reported, citing a statement from the country’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS).
The drill began as scheduled despite US President Donald Trump’s administration shortening last month’s bilateral Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise with South Korea in an effort to encourage North Korea to return to talks.
“The three nations will leverage the drills to enhance operational capabilities and joint response capabilities across multiple domains, including maritime, air and cyber, while maintaining a robust and stable cooperative relationship,” the JCS said.
The exercise will involve major maritime and air assets from the three countries, with a joint exercise control group overseeing operations to ensure their systematic and safe execution.
The South Korean military said the drills were aimed at strengthening deterrence and response capabilities against North Korea’s nuclear and missile threats while safeguarding regional peace and stability.
North Korea has long denounced the allies’ military drills as rehearsals for war.
The three countries will deploy six Aegis-equipped destroyers, along with maritime patrol aircraft, fighter jets and refuelling tanker aircraft, Yonhap reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The South Korean Navy is deploying the 7,600-tonne ROKS Yulgok Yi I and ROKS Seoae Ryu Seong-ryong destroyers, according to the sources.
Japan’s Joint Staff said last month that it would deploy the 7,700-tonne Atago and 5,100-tonne Asahi destroyers, P-1 maritime patrol aircraft, SH-60K helicopters and F-15 fighter jets.
The US Navy announced last week that its 6,900-tonne Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Benfold had arrived at a port in the southern South Korean city of Busan, in a possible indication that it would participate in the trilateral exercise.
No US aircraft carrier is expected to take part in Freedom Edge due to the ongoing US war against Iran, according to sources.
