Bangladesh dengue fever surge strains hospitals as case numbers pass 42,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:29:52 UTC
14:29:52 KST

Bangladesh's dengue outbreak is accelerating, with 42,590 people hospitalized and 117 deaths recorded this year, as a sharp September surge strains hospitals and raises fears the mosquito-borne disease could intensify further in the coming weeks.
At least four dengue patients died, and 1,558 others were hospitalized in the past 24 hours, according to health ministry data, marking the highest daily admission tally recorded so far this year.
The disease, which can cause fever, severe headaches and potentially fatal complications, has spread sharply in recent weeks, reviving concerns after Bangladesh's deadliest dengue outbreak in 2023. The outbreak has further strained a healthcare system already grappling with a nationwide measles outbreak that has killed nearly 1,000 children this year.
Health experts warn September could prove even more severe than August, which recorded the highest monthly dengue caseload of the year.
Professor Kabirul Bashar, a medical entomologist at Jahangirnagar University, said his surveillance and forecasting model suggests hospitalizations could exceed 30,000 this month if current trends continue, with weather conditions likely to support transmission into October.
Hospital beds fall in short supply
"The peak has not been reached yet," Bashar said. "If the current trajectory continues, September may become the worst month of the year for dengue infections."
For Zahid Hasan, 32, the outbreak became a personal ordeal when his four-year-old son developed a high fever and was diagnosed with dengue.
As the child's condition worsened, Hasan took him to three government hospitals but could not find an available bed.
"I was terrified. As a father, it was unbearable to watch my child getting worse without knowing where he could be admitted," Hasan said.
He eventually secured a bed at a private hospital with the help of a relative. His son received seven bags of blood and plasma before being discharged.
"Those days were a nightmare for us. We were constantly afraid something could happen to him," Hasan said. His son remains weak and is recovering slowly.
After fever, some patients deteriorate, develop complications
Dengue patients can deteriorate rapidly after their fever subsides, developing complications such as plasma leakage, low blood pressure, shock, and severe bleeding, making close monitoring during the critical post-fever phase essential.
"Patients are flooding hospitals, and warning signs such as abdominal pain, dizziness and unusual lethargy must not be ignored," said Professor Tarek Alam, a physician treating dengue patients in Dhaka.
Bashar said the spread of Aedes mosquitoes beyond Dhaka and other major cities was fueling infections in districts and rural areas. Dengue cases have now been reported in all 64 districts, although the capital continues to account for the largest share.
The government has intensified prevention efforts as the outbreak worsens. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has ordered nationwide cleanup and awareness campaigns, urging people to remove stagnant water and other mosquito-breeding sites while encouraging greater community participation in mosquito-control measures.
"Fogging alone cannot control dengue if breeding sites remain untouched," Bashar said. "Control efforts must target areas where Aedes mosquitoes are actually breeding. The biggest weakness in dengue control is the lack of evidence-based interventions."

Putin backs proposal to allow volunteers with blindness, deafness, schizophrenia, and other severe medical conditions to serve in regional drone-defense units
Yevgeny Poddubny, a “war correspondent” for Russian state broadcaster VGTRK who heads United Russia’s electoral list, asked Vladimir Putin to allow volunteers with a Category D fitness classification to serve in regional units defending against Ukrainian drone attacks.
During a medical examination, conscripts and volunteers are assigned one of five fitness categories — A, B, V, G, or D — based on their health. Only people in Categories A and B may be called up for regular conscript service or alternative civilian service.
People in Category V are exempt from regular conscript service and assigned to the reserves. Category G grants a temporary deferment of up to one year, followed by another medical examination. Category D exempts people from military service entirely.
Poddubny claimed that wounded soldiers themselves were asking for the change.
“Of course, people in this category have severe medical conditions, but there are cases where […] people are capable of carrying out certain tasks — for example, serving in regional BARS units for air defense and destroying drones. Obviously, not everyone can. But there is a core group of volunteers who have assessed their own abilities and are pleading for an exception that would allow them to serve in regional units that protect facilities from drones. Obviously, this is not about the front line. Their own city, their own village, their own workplace,” Poddubny said.
Putin replied, “Zhenya, I support it.”
Poddubny made the proposal amid rumors that Russia will see another large-scale wave of mobilization this fall. Russian authorities deny having any such plans. Vladimir Putin has called the mobilization rumors “complete nonsense.”
Category D is assigned to people with severe, irreversible medical conditions, including blindness, deafness in both ears, and schizophrenia.

Explainer-Options for UK finance minister Healey to tax wealth in October's budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:22:04 UTC
14:22:04 KST

Explainer-Options for UK finance minister Healey to tax wealth in October's budget
LONDON, Sept 7 - British finance minister John Healey faces pressure to raise billions of pounds in tax at his first budget to offset higher borrowing costs and fund Prime Minister Andy Burnham's plans for expanded social care and more defence spending.
Following are some tax increase options for Healey, who is due to announce his first budget on October 28.
LOTS OF PLEDGES, NOT MUCH LEEWAY
Burnham said last year when he was mayor of Greater Manchester that Britain overtaxed workers and undertaxed wealth. He also pledged to keep Labour's commitment not to raise the rates of income tax, value-added tax, corporation tax or social security contributions.
Britain raised £1.1 trillion ($1.5 trillion) in tax in the 2025/26 financial year.
Budget forecasts in March showed the government had a relatively narrow £24 billion of leeway to meet its target of balancing day-to-day spending and tax revenue by 2029/30. Many economists think that headroom has narrowed sharply since.
CAPITAL GAINS TAX
Capital gains tax raised £24 billion in the 2025/26 tax year. Britain's previous finance minister, Rachel Reeves, increased the rate to 18% for basic-rate taxpayers and 24% for higher-rate taxpayers.
That is lower than income tax rates of 20% and 40% paid by basic and higher-rate tax payers. Earlier this year, Wes Streeting, then a potential challenger to Burnham and now defence minister, suggested CGT rates should match income tax.
The left-leaning Institute for Public Policy Research has made a similar proposal.
In August 2025, the University of Warwick's Centre for the Analysis of Taxation estimated that a comprehensive reform to CGT would raise an extra £11 billion a year.
As well as raising rates to the same level as income tax, this reform ends the exemption on CGT when someone dies but includes a new tax-free allowance to exempt normal investment returns. CGT would also be charged on unrealised gains when someone emigrates from Britain.
However, the sums raised from increasing CGT are disputed. In June 2025, Britain's tax office estimated that raising the higher CGT rate by 10 percentage points would lower revenue by up to £3.6 billion a year due to increased tax avoidance.
PROPERTY TAXES
Council tax, an annual levy paid by property occupiers, raises £54 billion a year while stamp duty on property purchases raises £17 billion.
Council tax is based on the relative values of properties in 1991. Up-to-date valuations would sharply increase payments in London and much of southern England and lower them elsewhere.
Most economists view stamp duty as an inefficient source of revenue as it discourages people from moving house to find work and older households from downsizing.
Last month, in an IPPR paper, University of Oxford Professor Ben Ansell proposed a 0.65% property value tax to replace revenue from council tax and stamp duty.
Before he was prime minister, Burnham was listed as a supporter of a proposal from the Fairer Share campaign group to merge both taxes into a single 0.48% levy on property values.
However, in July Burnham ruled out scrapping stamp duty or council tax at October's budget. He said he wanted to make tax "fairer" and backed plans announced last year which will charge extra council tax from 2028 on homes worth more than £2 million.
WEALTH TAX
Charity Oxfam and campaigners Tax Justice UK have called on Labour to introduce a 2% annual levy on assets over £10 million, which they say could raise £24 billion a year, extrapolating from a University of Warwick estimate.
Asked in a July podcast about the possibility of a "wealth tax ... on the super rich", Burnham said he wanted to take his time before making a decision but would not rule this out.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies said last year that annual wealth taxes were hard to implement, due to the difficulty of accurately valuing assets such as private businesses.
Most developed countries had abandoned wealth taxes due to the administrative burden and political pressure for exemptions which led to relatively little revenue being raised, it said.
Predicting how much a wealth tax would raise in Britain over the long term was hard due to the difficulty of knowing how many people would emigrate in response or find other ways to avoid it, the IFS added. REUTERS

Tech giants know honesty can cost billions. Do we trust them with the truth?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:20:08 UTC
14:20:08 KST

analysis
The Zuckerberg lesson: do we trust AI companies to tell us when things go wrong?
It's not often that we get an actual price tag on the cost of our previous actions, but last month Meta did.
The social media and now AI giant agreed in August to pay up to US$18 billion as it settled litigation by US state-attorneys over claims it knew it was harming young people and didn't do enough about it.
At the centre of Meta's current legal fights over its products' impacts on teen mental health is a single presentation slide that's been more damaging to Meta than anything other than the Cambridge Analytica social media data harvesting scandal.
It's a 2019 internal document saying, "We make body images worse for one in three teen girls." (The company responded to the story by saying its internal data was not accurate.)
The slide, first released in the 2021 Facebook Files, has been a catalyst for criticism that Meta staff knew its products caused harm but did not do enough to address it.
In 2020, the company halted another piece of internal research that has preliminarily shown that surveyed people were told to quit Facebook for a week after early findings included that participants "reported lower feelings of depression, anxiety, loneliness and social comparison." .
The company alleged the research was stopped because it was a flawed methodology.
The alternate explanation posited by lawyers representing schools suing Meta (and other tech companies) was that it was trying to avoid incriminating evidence against itself. A point also made by one Mark Zuckerberg in a 2021 email, released in a lawsuit this year.
"The media is more likely to use any research or recommendations produced to say we're not doing everything we can (implying for craven purposes) rather than that we're taking these issues more seriously than anyone," he said.
Even with legal discovery, we're only getting part of the picture. We can't know exactly what research Meta is doing now. Perhaps it has doubled down on this work to try and make sure its products are safer for everyone. Perhaps.
But what this makes obvious is that there are plenty of incentives for companies to not look too hard at what's going on, lest it become their responsibility to fix any problems that may emerge.
Loading...
As social media finally faces a crackdown, AI arrives
Last weekend was the 20th anniversary of Facebook's Newsfeed, which opened the door for the algorithmic feeds that rule our lives now. We're only really starting to grapple with what this means.
Meanwhile, it hasn't even been four years since the launch of ChatGPT, which set off the generative AI boom that's impacting almost every part of our lives.
It still feels like we're very early in many senses: there's new advances every week, we're only beginning to see how the technology is affecting us and the AI companies remain remarkably unguarded.
Last week, OpenAI released its latest cutting-edge model GPT-6 Astra. In addition to its retro-inspired video, the company released another document at the launch that was much less promotional.
Its "system card", a document almost like a nutritional information or prescription medicine label, identified Astra as its first ever release to reach the "critical" threshold for cybersecurity risks. It said that testing had observed the model carrying out sabotage in tasks, falsifying research data and even launching attacks in a small number of circumstances.
These kinds of detailed evaluations and disclosures are the norm in frontier AI companies. Competitor Anthropic also released a detailed report with the release of Claude Fable 5.1 earlier in the week. They say it's to help people understand the risks posed by the technology.
These risks feel particularly pertinent given revelations only a few weeks ago that OpenAI's models had hacked into the servers of another company, HuggingFace. (The disclosure prompted a number of similar disclosures from other AI companies including Meta.)
Since then, we've learned even more about the incident from OpenAI and a group of independent researchers allowed to review the logs of the company's AI.
What they found was even worse than first shared. They found that hundreds of AI agents had worked together to try to find secret ways to communicate, attempted to cover their tracks by editing records and even convinced each other to sacrifice themselves to achieve their goal of completing a goal.
(Yes, this sounds like a dystopian sci-fi plot. It's also now a real problem we need to deal with.)
Both the system cards and the independent investigation are examples of transparency and openness that, frankly, are surprising to see from a company. OpenAI deserves to be commended for it, as do other AI companies doing similar things.
Loading
The peril of hoping for disclosure
But there was another event that reminded us of the peril of hoping for disclosure.
Over the weekend, Reuters reported that OpenAI's escaped AI models had invaded yet another website, exchanging secret messages and battling a human moderator who was trying to fight the swarm.
And, the researchers who discovered it allege, there's evidence suggesting that OpenAI staff were aware of this further outbreak but had not disclosed it.
OpenAI has since acknowledged this and announced that it will come up with guidelines for how to disclose these kinds of incidents in the future.
But whether they had simply not yet been ready to disclose it, or had other ideas in mind, it reveals just how much of our own potential safety depends on good will.
This kind of incident is something that the federal government is worried about.
Senior Australian government officials pressed Anthropic in a private meeting about how the AI company would disclose critical incidents, according to documents I obtained under Freedom of Information earlier this year.
The government has also commissioned CSIRO research on how to monitor and control a potentially super-intelligent AI.
There are models for forcing disclosure. California, notably the jurisdiction containing Silicon Valley, has passed a state law requiring disclosure of critical incidents and model capabilities. There's no reason why Australia couldn't pass something like that here.
Such a law would also have the benefit of addressing whether these companies are over-egging these incidents by making it a legal matter.
We currently have no laws regulating these cutting edge models, even though we now can see they are able to wreak havoc.
This seems particularly important given that our government's explicit goal is to lure the very major AI companies that are carrying out experimentation with this technology to make Australia their second "node". That would presumably make it even more likely we'll be in the blast radius for the next time an AI breaks out (and there will be a next time).
As part of this, the prime minister outlined his vision to make sure we get a social license for the companies — but so far this has mostly focused on the rules for the physical data centres.
It's hard to think of any event that would jeopardise social license more than finding out an AI company covered up the breakout of a rogue AI.
At least, that's what happened when we found out about Meta's internal research and Cambridge Analytica years after the fact. It's not just what the company knew — both controversies have grown from individual incidents into an enduring stain on Zuckerberg and Meta's trustworthiness on privacy and youth wellbeing — but the fact that it was hidden from us, the public.
Mandating disclosure rather than trusting the AI companies behind the technology could save them from their own worse impulses. And maybe it'll save us, too.

British Finance Minister Healey walks fiscal tightrope before first budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:17:00 UTC
14:17:00 KST

British Finance Minister Healey walks fiscal tightrope before first budget
LONDON – Britain’s new Finance Minister John Healey, a former trade unionist who has backed light-touch rules for banks, must soon decide on the right balance for a budget that could be the defining moment for Andy Burnham’s premiership.
Bond investors want to see how the 66-year-old advances Burnham’s ambitions – from house-building and social care to defence – while keeping fiscal discipline.
Ahead of his debut budget on Oct 28, Healey makes his first major speech on Sept 7 on how to accelerate the world’s fifth-biggest economy, a challenge that has eluded his predecessors for 20 years.
Against the backdrop of rising borrowing costs globally, the budget is also likely to include some tax increases.
People who have worked with Healey, the son of a prison physical education officer, say he is decisive and good at communicating complex issues.
“Events will be raging around him and he’ll keep his cool and his courtesy. He’s got that gift,” said John Monks, a former head of the Trades Union Congress, who hired Healey as his communications officer in the 1990s.
“I wanted someone who could make the economic argument, someone who was capable of not just selling a story but was also able to have discussions with the Bank of England and the Treasury. All those things, he could do,” Monks said.
Healey risked his dream of becoming a Labour lawmaker when he and Monks clashed with party leader Tony Blair and his communications chief Alastair Campbell over union reforms.
“He went toe to toe with Blair and Campbell, as did I, and they didn’t proceed with the proposal,” Monks said.
From the mining belt to the City of London
As a junior finance minister in the 2000s, he showed he was no Labour traditionalist, telling lawmakers of “the importance of a light-touch, principles-based approach” to rules for the City of London.
More recently, as defence minister in Keir Starmer’s government, Healey decommissioned two warships and retired a drone system to spend the money elsewhere.
“There’s no question that he knew what the right things were to do,” Kevin Craven, chief executive of aerospace and defence trade body ADS, said.
But in June, Healey quit as defence minister, dealing a blow to Starmer who resigned as prime minister 11 days later.
Healey told Starmer: “You have been unable and the Treasury has been unwilling to commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats.”
But when the media reported in August that he would not immediately raise defence spending to the levels he previously sought, opposition lawmakers accused Healey of hypocrisy, prompting Burnham to say a timetable would come in 2027.
It remains to be seen how hard Healey will push for the extra money to raise defence spending to 3 per cent of economic output by 2030, a level he said was needed when he resigned.
Former British army chief Richard Dannatt said Healey was unlikely to create his own power base at the Treasury, calling him a “relatively old-fashioned, professional Labour politician who understands the hierarchy”.
While unlikely to be “a revolutioniser” at the Treasury, he would probably be able to overcome internal opposition and find the money he wants for defence, Dannatt said.
The bond market and the budget
Healey’s first test will be to compile a budget that does not upset the bond market – an experience that ended Liz Truss’ short-lived government in 2022 – but offers help to voters with an election less than three years away.
In her first budget two years ago, then Finance Minister Rachel Reeves raised taxes on employers, souring relations with business and leading to a hiring slowdown.
Healey will need to show progress on Burnham’s priorities including giving more powers to local areas while finding money to make up an immediate £5 billion (S$8.6 billion) shortfall in defence spending.
That job is being made harder by Burnham’s commitment to the mechanism for state pension increases and rising welfare spending.
But in contrast to Reeves’ warnings of tough times ahead, Healey has sought to sound upbeat about Britain’s economy.
Burnham’s government rushed out small domestic power bill cuts, a bus fare cap and a tax cut for some hospitality firms when he took office.
The head of a major UK consumer-facing business applauded Healey for saying he was as worried about the cost of doing business as the cost of living.
But two decades on from his last stint at the Treasury, Healey acknowledges how much harder it is now with the debt burden three times bigger, writing on social media that “conditions then were so benign compared with what this country, this government and people and businesses now face”. REUTERS

BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Finance said on Monday that it will soon issue 300 billion yuan (about 44.25 billion U.S. dollars) in special treasury bonds to support eight state-owned financial enterprises directly administered by the central government in replenishing their core Tier 1 capital.
This move is expected to further strengthen these institutions' operational capacity, resilience to risks and ability to serve the real economy, providing stronger support for the country's steady and sound economic growth, according to a circular issued by the ministry.
The eight institutions include two major state-owned commercial banks, namely Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) and Agricultural Bank of China (ABC); two policy financial institutions, the Export-Import Bank of China, and China Export & Credit Insurance Corporation; and four state-owned commercial insurers, which are the People's Insurance Company (Group) of China, China Life Insurance (Group) Company, China Taiping Insurance Group and China Reinsurance (Group) Corporation.
For listed enterprises of them, the capital replenishment is also expected to help create greater value for investors and deliver stable long-term returns, the circular noted.
The eight institutions are currently operating steadily, with stable asset quality and major regulatory indicators remaining within safe and healthy ranges, it said, adding that the capital replenishment endeavor will be carried out prudently in accordance with market-oriented and law-based principles.
Monday's announcement came after the eight firms on Sunday unveiled specific plans to strengthen their core Tier 1 capital, with a combined 360 billion yuan to be raised or received. Of this total, ABC and ICBC plan to raise up to 260 billion yuan through A-share issuances to designated investors.
Core Tier 1 capital is the highest-quality form of capital used to absorb losses and serves as a key buffer against financial risks. For banks, a stronger core Tier 1 capital position generally provides more room to expand lending while maintaining regulatory capital ratios. ■

A eulogy to figs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:10:22 UTC
14:10:22 KST

Figs mean summer — they represent the summer heat, where the sweet scent of fig trees mingles with the chirping of crickets and the singing cicadas. The scent of fig leaves on sleep-inducing lazy afternoons and the indescribable honey-like taste of a fig, chilled in the refrigerator, could be delightful, idle, happy moments of summer. Fig is a fruit steeped in mythological symbolism. In ancient Rome, the phrase “Prima Ficus” was said to signal the end of summer. “Prima Ficus” literally means “First Fig.” It was an expression used to indicate that when the sweetest figs of the season appeared, summer was coming to an end and fall was on its way. Prima Ficus is also the time when one feels the first chill of the autumn months coming. September has already kicked in; fall is near. These days are past the days of first figs; they are fully ripe now, at their peak, so it’s worth celebrating figs before summer waves goodbye.
Fig tree
There’s an expression: “To plant a fig tree in one’s heart of the house.” It’s truly an apt description. A fig tree has the ability to take root anywhere — so much so that it bursts through the ground where it takes root, leaving no solid stone or wall intact with its powerful roots. No matter which ancient archaeological site you visit along the Aegean and Mediterranean coasts, you’ll see a fig tree that has taken root there. Sometimes it takes refuge at the base of garden walls; other times it stands tall and proud, like a solitary monument. Every faith has imbued the fig tree with meaning. In Hinduism, it has become the tree of life, seen as the tree that connects the earth to the heavens. In Jewish and Christian cultures, being under one’s own fig tree has meant feeling safe, being in one’s rightful place, homeland, and on one’s own land. Buddhism has viewed the fig tree as a means of enlightenment. The fig tree certainly has a place in paradise as well. It is recognized as a sacred tree in the Quran. The fig tree has a common symbolism that connects cultures and faiths under one peaceful umbrella.
Fig leaf
There is a great deal of symbolism hidden in a fig leaf. In Western culture, a fig leaf also represents hidden secrets and topics that are kept under cover. It’s no coincidence that Adam and Eve used fig leaves to cover their private parts after being expelled from the Garden of Eden. Fig leaves can grow so large that they can be used to conceal many things. They can also be a good wrapper. In Mediterranean countries, particularly in southern France and Italy, fig leaves are used to wrap cheese. As the leaf dries around the cheese like a paper wrapper, its protective qualities come into play, but most importantly, its wonderfully beautiful scent adds a completely unique aroma to the cheese.
The scent of fig leaf is so distinctive that it instantly transports you to warm summer afternoons in the Aegean and Mediterranean, filled with the sound of singing cicadas. Perhaps that’s why there’s a growing trend in professional kitchens: combining fig leaves with olive oil to create an incredibly aromatic oil. Of course, this oil is so concentrated that it can only be used drop by drop. But even a single drop makes the crickets ring in your ears, while on the palate, a whole tree full of fig leaves bursts forth.
Fig seeds
There is an expression in Turkish that can be translated as: Worrying about things that won’t fit in a fig seed! The English equivalent could be, ‘Making oneself miserable over something that amounts to a hill of beans.’ With so many worries in the world these days, this should be everyone’s life motto. But fig seeds are important, tough being miniscule, their presence is huge. So don’t let fig seeds be missing from your table; the crunch of a fig seed in your mouth is like no other. Fig seeds go perfectly with pastries, cookies, cakes, even savory buns, salads, and yogurt-based appetizers. Sometimes you’ll have very ripe figs going bad — never waste the seeds. Rinse them in a colander to let the sweet pulp drain away, leaving only the seeds. Dry them on parchment paper, or if you prefer, you can dry them in the oven at a low temperature. Keep them on hand — just like poppy seeds, you can sprinkle them wherever you like, and they’ll add a little crunch to your life.
Last of figs
Figs are truly the highlight of summer — the sweetest and most succulent of all fruits. For us, figs equal summer, but above all, they remind us of the Aegean. In the summer, the whole Aegean region smells of fig leaves. The intoxicating perfume of the fig tree lingers in the air, alluring passers-by. Our province of Aydın is undoubtedly the fig capital of the world. Aydın’s dried figs have been shipped to the entire world from the port of İzmir. That is why dried figs have been known as “Smyrna figs,” after İzmir’s ancient name. Aydın’s Sarılop fig is ideal for drying, while İzmir’s Bardacık fig, with its skin almost cracking and bursting open, is the best for eating fresh. Bursa’s black figs, with their purple skin, which can withstand long journeys, even make their way to the British royal palace. Ripe figs taste like nectar from heaven. Now is the best time to enjoy them all — we must savor them before they’re gone.

U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner left Kiev early on Sept. 7 without a breakthrough after talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, although both sides said negotiations on ending the war with Russia would continue.
The meeting on Sept. 6 marked the envoys’ first official visit to Ukraine and followed talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow a day earlier.
A senior Ukrainian presidential official told AFP that the U.S. delegation had brought proposals that were “more effective” than previous plans. No details were released.
Zelensky said the sides agreed to hold a follow-up meeting involving Ukraine, the United States and European partners, with the venue yet to be decided. Senior French, British and German officials joined part of the talks in Kiev.
The discussions covered security guarantees, reconstruction and support for Ukraine through the winter. Zelensky said Kiev was seeking additional air defenses, including Patriot systems, protection for energy infrastructure and substantial supplies of U.S. liquefied natural gas.
“We hope for the support of European partners if the war continues into the winter,” he said.
Witkoff said both Russia and Ukraine would have to compromise, adding that Washington believed it had “the ingredients” to move the process forward. Kushner said the visit had produced possible new ways to advance the talks.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov described the Moscow meeting as “highly useful,” while the White House said the two sides had discussed “substantive plans” that would be announced in the coming weeks. Neither Moscow nor Washington reported a breakthrough.
Fighting continued during the diplomatic effort. Zelensky accused Russia of intensifying attacks ahead of the Sept. 20 State Duma election and said Ukraine was working with 67 domestic companies to develop systems capable of intercepting jet-powered drones.
Ukraine said it struck the Ryazan oil refinery inside Russia on Sept. 6. Moscow, meanwhile, said a Ukrainian drone attack killed a girl and wounded three people in Russian-held Sevastopol. Russia also claimed that it struck a Ukrainian cargo vessel carrying Western military equipment.

Lai pledges more opportunities for Taiwan taxi drivers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:07:45 UTC
14:07:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) attended a Ghost Festival banquet hosted by the Taipei Taxi Drivers' Union on Sunday, pledging better integration for taxis into the country's transportation system to create more opportunities for drivers.
Lai said taxis are an important part of public transportation because not everyone can use the MRT or buses. He said his government is considering a role similar to a “yellow bus" for elderly passengers and more of a supporting role in the Long-Term Care program, per a press release.
He said he has relatives who have worked as taxi drivers. Seeing the drivers at the event made him feel as if he were among his own brothers and sisters. Lai wished taxi drivers safe journeys and successful business, saying he hoped they could leave home happily and return safely every day.
Lai said a stronger economy should naturally generate greater demand for taxi services as people travel more and businesses expand. For example, 360 Taiwanese companies have been encouraged to return to Taiwan and invest as of August, creating additional business opportunities for taxi drivers.
Taiwan's economy is indeed expected to expand sharply this year. The Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics raised its 2026 growth forecast to 11.05% in August, up from its previous forecast of 9.64%.
The government has taken several measures this year to address operating issues facing drivers, such as, in April, a fuel subsidy of NT$6,000 (US$180) per taxi because of higher oil prices. The transport ministry later increased the maximum subsidy to NT$15,000 through the end of 2026, per a transport ministry press release.
The government also tightened regulations governing taxi companies with new rules on Aug. 13 prohibiting taxi companies from improperly charging drivers for affiliation or vehicle-license fees. It also prevented companies from forcing drivers to purchase vehicles, obtain loans, or get insurance from designated providers. Violations result in fines of up to NT$90,000 and, in serious cases, revocation of a taxi company's operating license, per LTN.
The government is also trying to increase the number of taxis equipped to serve passengers with disabilities. Lai also cited the government's long-term care system, saying Taiwan now has more than 15,000 long-term care facilities and more than 100,000 personnel providing services to elderly people and people with disabilities, per the press release.
Lai said the government would continue strengthening support for taxi drivers while seeking to expand their role in Taiwan's transportation network. He concluded by saying that economic growth should be accompanied by stronger social support, particularly for working-class families caring for children, elderly relatives, or people with disabilities.

Russia, North Korea hold completion ceremony of first car bridge between allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:07:38 UTC
14:07:38 KST

Russian and DPRK prime ministers set to join the ceremony remotely, 1.5 years after construction began
		
		
Russia and North Korea opened their first new car bridge to vehicle traffic on Monday, Russian wire services reported, at an official ceremony marking the completion of the crossing across the Tumen River.
Russian state-run TASS News Agency reported on the opening of the new motorway link, with Interfax adding that Russia has also completed the construction of its Khasan border checkpoint.
Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin joined the ceremony remotely along with his counterpart Pak Thae Song to launch the infrastructural project, according to the outlets.
		 
The bridge bears the name of Soviet officer Yakov Novichenko, who saved North Korea’s first leader Kim Il Sung from an assassination attempt in 1946.
The existing Korea-Russia Friendship Bridge, a railway crossing located upstream on the Tumen River, has been the only link connecting the two countries since the late 1950s.
Automobile columns from each side crossed the bridge following Mishustin and Pak’s speeches, with a car that belonged to Novichenko leading the Russian procession, according to TASS.
		 
Russian Minister of Natural Resources Alexander Kozlov, Transport Minister Andrei Nikitin, Minister for the Development of the Russian Far East and Arctic Alexei Chekunkov, Primorsky Krai Gov. Oleg Kozhemyako and DPRK Ambassador to Russia Sin Hong Chol also attended the ceremony.
The roughly kilometer-long bridge will form part of a larger 4.7-km Russian border crossing project linking the Russian and DPRK checkpoint facilities on both sides of the river. 
The bridge features 16 sections between columns, with the seventh and eighth sections built jointly by the two countries. The foundations reach depths of up to 45 meters on the North Korean side and up to 30 meters on the Russian side.
The Russian crossing will have 10 lanes and the capacity to process 300 vehicles and 2,850 people each day, according to Russia’s transport ministry.
Mishustin and Pak kicked off the large-scale construction project remotely at a ceremony in April 2025. The two countries held another ceremony marking the physical connection of the bridge the following year. 
Preparation for the project began months in advance, with early signs reported in Nov. 2024. Russia initially agreed to allocate some $100 million for the project and hired an obscure company named TonnelYuzhStroi as its main contractor.
		 
Construction on the North Korean side was largely finalized in the summer, while Russia is still adding finishing touches to its crossing facility following the installation of the main and auxiliary buildings in recent weeks.
NK News/NK Pro investigations found the project’s cost had at least doubled as of late August, while TonnelYuzhStroi appeared to be a front for a large Chechen construction conglomerate and ultimate beneficiary.
The two countries initially planned to open the crossing on June 19, which marks the second anniversary of the summit between Russian and DPRK leaders Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong Un in Pyongyang, where they agreed to spearhead the construction.
The project faced delays, with a local official later reporting that the two sides aimed to finalize construction in early September. As of late August, Russian authorities reported that the crossing was only 65% complete.
Despite the completion ceremony, it remains unclear whether the bridge will see regular inbound and outbound vehicle traffic between the two countries.

Far-right AfD scores historic win in German state vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:07:13 UTC
14:07:13 KST

People react to exit polls during the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) election party following Saxony-Anhalt state election, in Magdeburg, Germany, Sept. 6 2026. . EPA/FILIP SINGER
Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won the Sept. 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt by a wide margin but fell short of an outright majority, leaving its bid to form its first state government unresolved.
The AfD took 43.8 percent of the vote, more than doubling its share from 2021. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) fell to 17.2 percent from 37.1 percent, according to provisional results.
The AfD won 39 seats in the 83-member state parliament, three short of a majority.
Germany’s mainstream parties have long refused to govern with the AfD, a policy known as the political “firewall.”
An outright majority would have allowed the party to govern alone, but it will now need outside support to take office.
The result adds pressure on Merz, whose party also trails the AfD in national polls.
The far-right party sees Saxony-Anhalt as a step toward victory in the 2029 federal election.
Its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, 35, is a former fragrance salesman who left the CDU and joined the AfD in 2014. He has built a large following on TikTok.
Siegmund campaigned on tougher deportation policies, promising a task force to remove migrants who do not work or integrate.
He also pledged to ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the construction of new wind farms.
His campaign appealed to discontent among eastern Germans who feel they are treated as second-class citizens.
EU affairs analyst Can Baydarol told Milliyet that the AfD’s rise was troubling for Turks in Germany but that he did not expect an immediate change in relations with Türkiye.
He argued that Germany’s concerns about Russia and its interest in closer defense cooperation with Türkiye would continue to shape bilateral ties.
“I do not expect much change in this area,” he said.
Hüsamettin İnaç, a professor at Kütahya Dumlupınar University, told Milliyet that economic insecurity and unresolved migration and integration problems were helping the far right gain support.
He said migrants often became targets when living standards and stability declined, warning that the trend posed particular risks to Germany’s Turkish community.

Pesticides cause 400 million farmer poisoning cases a year, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:04:09 UTC
14:04:09 KST

Nearly half the world's farmers get poisoned with pesticides annually, while global pesticide use continues to rise, a study finds.
Between 402 and 433 million cases of acute pesticide poisoning occur among farmers and farmworkers worldwide every year, according to a new study.
Human poisoning by pesticides has long been seen as a severe public health problem. Despite global efforts to reduce pesticide use, millions of people’s health continues to be impacted, according to a new study published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health.
With a global farming population of approximately 934 million, researchers estimate that around 46% of farmers are affected each year.
They also warn that, despite two decades of international efforts to address the harms of pesticide use, global annual consumption has doubled since 1990, reaching 3.8 million tonnes in 2023.
“We can no longer accept that those who work in the fields and grow our food are exposed to harmful pesticides and become sick,” said Susan Haffmans, from Pesticide Action Network (PAN) Germany, the organisation that commissioned the report.
The hardest-hit countries are in southern Asia, followed by Southeast Asia and East Africa, with Burkina Faso recording the highest national rate at nearly 84% of farmers poisoned every year.
Europe is the only major region to see a decrease in pesticide consumption since 1990, which the authors attribute to strict regulatory efforts.
While these measures have kept the estimated annual fatalities very low —ranging from just 2 deaths in Western Europe to 60 in Eastern Europe— a significant burden of non-fatal poisoning persists among farmers and workers.
Southern Europe is the most affected sub-region with a 32% poisoning rate and over 1.5 million estimated cases each year. In Western and Eastern Europe, rates are much lower at approximately 6%.
However, the researchers note that data for Eastern Europe is particularly thin, as it is currently represented only by Hungary, suggesting that the full extent of the regional burden may still be under-monitored.
Need to address data gaps
The authors call for urgent actions at the international, national, and research level, including better monitoring systems, improved training for professionals working with these substances, and implementing the United Nations target to phase out highly hazardous pesticides by 2035.
They warn, however, that such actions are hindered by a lack of available data, making it difficult to compare estimates across countries and pesticide use patterns.
“Underreporting remains widespread, driven by limited access to healthcare and a lack of clinical training or systems to recognise or record pesticide poisoning,” said Sheila Willis at PAN in the United Kingdom.
She added that, based on the new data, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.

Slow travel in the Spanish Pyrenees: Exploring Taüll, Vall de Boí and Val d’Aran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:40 UTC
14:00:40 KST

From mountain walks and Romanesque churches to glacial lakes and medieval villages, discover a slower side of Spain on a journey through the spectacular Pyrenees.
Here’s a confession – this is actually “take two” of this specific travel tale.
Originally, I had started writing about how a relaxing week-long outdoorsy holiday in Spain had evolved into a mega summer road trip starting in Barcelona, spending a few days in scenic mountain villages and then taking an “eclipsed-sized detour” to San Sebastian. And back again.
Then I realised, just like my itinerary planning and driving skills, that it was all getting a bit too chaotic and veering away from what I really wanted to talk about: and that is the Spanish Pyrenees.
Had I continued venturing towards the road trip storyline, you would have read a lot about spending hours behind the wheel as we criss-crossed our way through Catalonia, Aragon, Navarre, and the Basque Country – where we ended up to watch the eclipse on 12 August. Not a bad tale, but that’s one for another day, maybe.
While Barcelona and San Sebastian are brilliant cities with so much to see and do, it’s only right that the focus here is on slow travel in a lovely part of Spain that I had never been to before.
So, without any more talk of roadworks, dodgy satnavs and drastic searches for petrol stations, here’s how we explored a small section of the Spanish Pyrenees.
A coolcation with great views
Having flown into Barcelona from London, where it was already warm enough, we had feared that a last-minute trip to Spain in mid-August may have been slightly rash considering the rising temperatures across Europe that week.
However, in the Vall de Boí the weather was just perfect. Warm during the day, cool at night, with a few storms thrown in here and there for good measure. It is the mountains after all.
After a 297km, near four-hour drive to the Boí valley from Barcelona (sorry, but it’s worth adding in the journey details for context), we found ourselves in Taüll, a small village located on the edge of the Aigüestortes i Estany de Sant Maurici National Park – the only national park in Catalonia.
Known for its two UNESCO-listed Romanesque churches, Taüll was to be our base for the trip. Sitting at an altitude of around 1,500 metres, it’s an ideal spot for a summer coolcation and you can enjoy scenic walks to nearby villages – up the valley to Pla de l'Ermita or down the hill to Boí. On the walk back down from Pla de l'Ermita you’ll get some great views of Taüll from above.
And if hiking or walking isn’t really your thing, then there’s a few restaurants for relaxed al fresco lunches and dinners. In Taüll, we stayed in a one-bed rental above a selection of eateries – Llesqueria l'Empriu, Tribulosi, and Restaurant El Fai – which all serve local dishes and drinks.
The walking is what we were here for though and the views are what make the journey really worth it.
In Taüll itself, a must-do is the Santeta Viewpoint. You can walk from the Church of St. Climent through the village to the Church of Santa Maria, where a short 15-minute trail starts to the viewpoint. From here you’ll get panoramic views of the valley below and the villages of Boí and Erill la Vall.
There’s plenty more to explore around Taüll, particularly if you want to stay active. The national park has hiking trails past lakes and waterfalls, while the Boí Taüll resort offers adventure activities like e-biking and ziplining during summer and skiing in winter.
Further down the valley, around El Pont de Suert, you can enjoy rafting and kayaking.
From Vall de Boí to Val d’Aran
If you have a car and want to explore the wider area then we’d certainly recommend doing a few day trips to some nearby towns and villages.
Around an hour’s drive from Taüll, Val d’Aran offers mountain scenery, glacial lakes and some of the region’s prettiest villages.
One of its standout walks is the Circ de Colomèrs, a spectacular glacial basin containing almost 50 lakes. The popular seven-lake circuit covers 5.7 kilometres and takes around five hours, with quite a few short climbs included.
Elsewhere, you can explore the town of Arties, known for its Romanesque church, historic houses and lively restaurants, or head higher into the mountains to Bagergue, the highest village in Val d’Aran at 1,419 metres.
Both are among the valley’s most picturesque villages, though we really loved Bagergue. Here you can wander around its cobbled streets and see traditional stone houses. There are some nice restaurants that serve local cuisine and there’s also a cheesemaker and museum to visit, too.
And further afield to Aínsa…
One road trip that we should discuss is the journey from Taüll to Aínsa – which is around 95 kilometres and two hours by car. Although it’s a fair drive, you do get some scenic Pyrenean views and the end destination is just lovely.
On our long list of places to see while in Spain, Aínsa is a medieval town in the Aragonese Pyrenees. It has a beautifully preserved old town and the cobbled Plaza Mayor is lined with restaurants, cafés and small shops.
Another attraction here is Aínsa Castle, which has an elevated walkway along the top of its walls and offers sweeping views of the surrounding mountains.
Slow down and stay a little longer
Barcelona and San Sebastian are undoubtedly two of Spain’s great city break destinations, but this trip proved that there’s plenty worth exploring in between.
In the Pyrenees, slowing down is pretty much the order of the day. Rather than racing between attractions, you can spend your time walking between villages, stopping for lunch on a sunny terrace or heading into the mountains for a trek.
If you have the time to venture away from the cities and explore at a slower pace, this corner of Spain is definitely worth the journey.

Exclusive: MEPs on track to end article 7 'nuclear option' against Hungary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:34 UTC
14:00:34 KST

MEPs are on course to end the long-standing measure, which was introduced over alleged violations of EU values under Viktor Orbán’s government. A mission to Hungary in October would assess the progress of Péter Magyar’s administration, with a final decision expected in early 2027.
The European Parliament is on track to end the long-running Article 7 procedure, the EU’s so-called “nuclear option" against Hungary, which was launched in 2018 over concerns about violations of EU values under then-prime minister Viktor Orbán.
With Péter Magyar now leading the Hungarian government, the country is revising several laws dating back to the Orbán era, prompting the Parliament to reconsider its position, according to several MEPs and officials who spoke to Euronews.
“Hungary has completed many reforms that bring the country into closer alignment with the EU," said a senior MEP from the European People’s Party (EPP), the Parliament’s largest political group. "I see it as reasonable that the procedure ends soon, and I hope it will,” he added.
The EPP is among the political forces prepared to push for the withdrawal of Article 7, in a bid to secure a political victory for Magyar’s Tisza party, which is a member of the party.
The Article 7 procedure is an exceptional measure that can ultimately strip a country of its voting rights if a serious breach of EU values is established. MEPs triggered it against Hungary in 2018, citing concerns over judicial independence, corruption, media freedom and fundamental rights, as well as the rights of minorities and migrants.
A fact-finding mission to Hungary is planned for late October, with meetings scheduled with institutions, stakeholders, authorities and NGOs to gain a comprehensive picture of the rule of law situation in the country.
MEPs taking part in the mission will then draft a report and are expected to recommend withdrawing the procedure if they conclude that EU values are no longer being violated. Some Parliament officials say this could happen as soon as December, while Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, who is leading the file, expects the report to be ready in early 2027.
“There is a whole checklist with criteria which we will assess: one of the elements is the withdrawal of the anti LGBTI+ law,” she told Euronews.
Strik referred to a controversial piece of legislation on minors' protection which restricts children’s access to books, films and other content promoting or depicting a deviation from biological sex, gender transition or homosexuality.
So far, the Hungarian government has not repealed the law, nor has it announced its willingness to do so.
The final decision to withdraw the procedure requires a two-thirds majority, meaning at least 480 of the Parliament’s 719 lawmakers must vote in favour of ending it.
Left-wing groups such as the Greens and The Left could oppose the withdrawal, while conservatives and far-right forces are expected to back it, having consistently viewed Article 7 as an unwarranted intrusion into national politics. The European Conservatives and Reformists, Patriots for Europe and Europe of Sovereign Nations together account for almost 200 MEPs.
With the EPP’s 184 lawmakers likely to back the move, the centrist Socialists and Democrats (S&D) and liberal Renew Europe groups will be crucial to the decision. Both acknowledge Hungary’s progress but stress the need for a thorough assessment that takes into account the full body of legislation.
Renew will discuss the issue at its first meeting of the new parliamentary season in Paris next week, MEP Sandro Gozi told Euronews.
“The end of the procedure should be based on real changes; otherwise we give the impression it is just a political decision,” he said.
The procedure has been triggered only twice in the EU’s history: by the Commission against Poland in 2017 and by the European Parliament against Hungary the following year. In neither case has it reached the sanctions stage, which requires unanimous support from EU member states to suspend a country’s voting rights.
The procedure against Poland was closed in 2024, after a coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk replaced the far-right Law and Justice (PiS) government, bringing the country back in line with the Commission's requests on judicial independence.

As assisted dying bill returns to Commons, families recall loved ones’ battle to ‘go out on own terms’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

The feeling, said Sarah Burns of her sister’s last days, is one of overwhelming guilt.
“You feel really guilty, and helpless,” she says. “Because we knew what she wanted. We really did know. But we couldn’t do anything.”
When time eventually ran out for Elise Burns, a 52-year-old woman who worked in publishing, the circumstances were “absolutely her worst nightmare”. Initially treated for breast cancer and subsequently diagnosed with terminal secondary cancer, which had spread to her liver, lungs and bones, Elise had campaigned passionately for the assisted dying bill, daring the peers who ensured it ran out of time to “look me in the eye”.
As part of the Dignity in Dying campaign, she was one of eight terminally ill people who appealed directly to MPs in powerful videos, filmed by the world renowned British photographer and director Rankin.
She died on 22 July – the second of the eight terminally ill people who featured in the Rankin videos, which were filmed in May, to go. The first, Keith Williams, a 77-year-old former welder who became a social worker, died of lung cancer on 16 June, having also been denied, according to his son, his desperate wish to “go out on my own terms”.
The controversial bill, reintroduced by Lauren Edwards, the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood, returns to the Commons for a second reading on 11 September. Andy Burnham has already said he will not vote to avoid influencing the emotional debate.
Burns will be at the Commons, carrying the baton for her sister, who was from Faversham, and was one of the last people Edwards heard from before reviving Kim Leadbeater’s private member’s bill, bringing it back to parliament after it foundered under the weight of hundreds of amendments by peers in the Lords.
“I would simply like the chance to put a human dying face to what this debate really means for terminally ill people like me,” Elise Burns wrote to Edwards. “For me this is not about politics or ideology, it’s about dignity, compassion and the possibility of having some choice at the end of life.”
After her secondary cancer diagnosis, Elise wanted to “live life to the full” but also started talking seriously about Dignitas, the Swiss assisted dying clinic. “She said all along ‘I do not want a painful death’. And literally every day was painful,” said her sister.
In the end, the speed of events deprived her of that choice. At the beginning of July, just two months after shooting her Rankin video, she developed an infection and was hospitalised. Sixteen days later, she was moved to a hospice, dying two days later.
“The hospice was incredible, trying to make her as comfortable as possible, all the time,” said Burns. “But legally there is only so much they can do. They all knew her wishes.”
The family were left feeling utterly helpless.
More than 100 cross-party peers have written to MPs urging them to send the bill back to the House of Lords so that it can complete its passage through parliament.
The signatories, including the former cabinet secretary Gus O’Donnell, the former Labour leader Neil Kinnock and the former Scottish Tory leader Ruth Davidson, said the upper house’s failure to pass the legislation in the previous session had let terminally ill people and their families down and blocked a measure which had public support.
They accused a minority of peers who had opposed the backbench bill of filibustering after hundreds of amendments tabled by just seven opponents meant it ran out of time.
They wrote: “As even opponents of the principle of assisted dying in the Lords have acknowledged, the elected chamber has every right to ask us to do this. The overwhelming majority of the public – who vote for you but do not vote for us – expect the same.
“And the many terminally ill people and their families who are depending on parliament to pass this long overdue change to the law should not be asked to wait any longer than absolutely necessary for us to come to a decision.”
Marc Williams, Keith Williams’ son, has written directly to Burnham, describing the circumstances surrounding the death of his father, who was a committed campaigner for the bill.
“Dad could have chosen to fly to Switzerland to end his life, but he would have needed to go in November to ensure that he was still fit enough to be able to travel and to endure the loneliest journey imaginable,” Williams, a civil servant, told the prime minister. For the “dignified death” he sought, his father “would have been forced to end his life prematurely”.
Keith Williams, who was a canoeing instructor from Tonyrefail, the Rhondda, was diagnosed in 2023 with prostate cancer and undergoing radiotherapy, which left him with distressing long-term side effects. Last October, he was diagnosed with lung cancer and pulmonary fibrosis. He died on 16 June.
“Dad had some red lines. He wanted to die at home. He was: ‘I want to go out on my own terms. I am desperate to go out on my own terms at home.’”
He shot the Rankin video in early May. Within days he was in hospital struggling to breathe. On returning home, his wife, who suffers from arthritis, was now physically unable to care for him, “much as she wanted to”, said Williams. He was moved to a hospice and died the following week.
“He wasn’t just in pain,” his son said. “He was suffocating to death. The pain, they could give him medication for, but no one could breathe for him.”
Four days from death, a physiotherapist gave him a pint of water and two straws, telling him to exercise his lungs by blowing through the straws, said Marc. “He was four days away from dying! It was ridiculous.”
“He didn’t want any of that. He was ready a long time before that to say goodbye and have his peace.” His children and grandchildren could do nothing but sit and watch him deteriorate because “there is nothing you can do”.
His father was “chuffed to bits” about the bill being back. “Because he wanted it for us,” said Williams. “Obviously it was too late for him, but that’s what he wanted all along, for other people.”

  Additional reporting by Pippa Crerar

Israeli ministers keep telling everyone their brutal plans – so why doesn’t the world take them seriously? | Nesrine Malik
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

The gap between what is being inflicted on Palestinians and the appropriate reaction on the part of the international community has always been vast. But now it yawns so wide that it swallows reality itself. As arms export licences for Israel from states such as Germany surge, talk of harsher measures and sanctions on the part of other European countries remains talk. People continue to be killed in Gaza, Palestinian families remain besieged in the West Bank, and the Israeli political right has been removing all doubt that these violations are intentional, by telling the world of its hopes and plans.
A sample from only the past few days. On Thursday, Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, detailed a scheme for the illegal ethnic cleansing of all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip. He also posted an AI-generated video, now deleted, of Palestinian men entering a conveyor belt into detention, emerging emaciated and tearful. Also a few days ago, the defence minister, Israel Katz, stated that the country was “organised and prepared” to expel Palestinians from Gaza “by every way possible”.
This macabre theatre continues to unfold, its performances less plausible by the day. The Board of Peace promises Gaza will be “redeveloped for the benefit” of its people, while the notion that those same Palestinians in Gaza cannot be allowed to thrive is expressed by Israeli politicians with consistency and a frequency that makes a mockery of the declarations. Last month, the former head of Israel’s national security council, Giora Eiland, pointed out the fact that Israel’s acceptance of Donald Trump’s 15-point plan was a matter of temporary military tactics, rather than long-term peace. “Israel has no interest in Gaza being rebuilt, it’s better for us that it be destroyed for generations to come,” he said.
Moshe Feiglin, previously a “far-right outcast” according to the Times of Israel, is now within reach of a cabinet position as a result of an alliance with the finance minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist party. In a recent interview, Feiglin said that those who didn’t want to leave Gaza should be compelled to by “every way possible. We’ll shut off his water pipes, for example.”
This sort of talk, from within the very ranks of government, is often dismissed as unrepresentative of the Israeli state and, as there are elections ahead, is written off as the lurid but ultimately unserious rhetoric of electioneering. But people such as Ben-Gvir and Katz are not fringe voices, they are ministers with high-impact executive briefs – security and defence – that they have indeed used to push policy that matches their statements.
Ben-Gvir has reopened the underground Rakefet prison, one closed in the 1980s for being inhumane. He has successfully pushed for the death penalty for Palestinians convicted of terror attacks, and celebrated the legislation with a noose-themed cake. Torture and sexual abuse in Israeli prisons are widely documented, the latter earning Israel a spot on the UN’s sexual violence in war zones blacklist. As Ben-Gvir himself is fond of saying, “we promised, we delivered”.
Katz has approved the biggest settlement expansion in the West Bank in decades and justified the move on the grounds that it “prevents the establishment of a Palestinian state that would endanger Israel”; he recently advanced legalisation of outpost settlement farms in the West Bank, and instructed the IDF to hand over law enforcement in the West Bank to the Israeli police, which is a stealth move towards annexation.
As the Knesset member Ahmad Tibi wrote in Haaretz earlier this year, a fiction exists at the heart of Israeli politics, where politicians’ efforts to explain and justify policy to international opinion proceed as though “the racism and extremism now driving government policy exist only on the margins”. When really, it lies at the heart of the state.
And if some of the more extreme statements are just electioneering, what does that say about the parameters of discourse in the country if your campaign is mass ethnic cleansing? What does that say about not only the future of Gaza, but all Palestinians in occupied territories who are labouring under home demolitions, militant settlers and the de facto annexation of the West Bank?
Even if these figures are a minority, both in terms of the seats held in the Knesset and the relative number of people who have voted for them, they still hold the levers of power, there is no substantial domestic mobilisation against them, and the rest of the system is unable or unwilling to stop them. The distinctions around how big their constituency may be or how representative they are of Israelis in general matters not a jot to the fate of Palestinians over whom they have been given executive dominion.
The question now is, why are these people not being taken at their word? Why is there no sense of urgency and outrage. Why are these policies and stated goals from the Israeli state not taken seriously and met with appropriate sanctions, trade and arms embargos, and international censure? There is a wild asymmetry when it comes to the perceived potency of Israeli rhetoric and action. “From the river to sea”, for example, as expressed by Palestinians and their supporters has become stigmatised and its use censured. But the most extreme interpretation of that phrase, that it means only one sovereign people in the mentioned land, is commonplace in Israel.
The founding charter of Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party states that “between the sea and the Jordan there will only be Israeli sovereignty”. Netanyahu himself last week attended a gathering at a religious-Zionist yeshiva, nodding along to a Kahanist song belted out by the attenders. “Remember me, please, give me strength just this time, O God, to take revenge, if only for one of my two eyes, on Palestine,” they sang, adding “May their name be erased!” “There are no more red lines,” was how a Haaretz writer described the scene.
The international community has averted its eyes as red lines are trampled over. This can only be a combination of cowardice and acceptance, barely obscured by feeble statements of condemnation here and there, and grounded in the belief or resignation that Palestinian lives shall be consigned to hell. The facts are clear and plentiful. The Israeli right has a plan and a sense of direction, one that it has nursed for a very long time, and now given nourishment by the 7 October attacks.
Some may not be realisable (ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in Gaza is limited by the fact there are no countries that can or will receive them), but much of it is. The direction of travel is clear and there have been some huge successes so far. There is a line connecting the hundreds of thousands of Palestinians expelled or forced to flee in 1948 and today. The security and carceral state that Palestinians exist in, the destruction of their homes and infrastructure, the settlement and fracturing of their territories, and the extension of Israeli sovereignty over them in ways that dehumanise and oppress, all serve to ensure that a future in which Palestinians are free, let alone thriving in self-governance, never emerges.
- 
  Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

Starwatch: Waning crescent moon gets close to brilliant beacon of Jupiter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

Those already out and about at 5am this week will be rewarded with a beautiful waning crescent moon approaching Jupiter, while Mars watches on from a little further away.
The chart shows the view looking east from London at 5am on Tuesday. The waning moon will be easily visible with about 10% of its visible surface illuminated. The brilliant beacon of Jupiter will be close by. The two are drawing together ahead of a conjunction later that day when the moon will pass less than a degree north of the giant planet. For comparison, the moon appears to be about half a degree wide in the sky.
Unfortunately, the conjunction itself takes place at 7.11pm, after both objects have set from the UK. The following morning offers another opportunity, with the moon now on the other side of Jupiter.
Mars adds to the scene. Look upwards and to the west and the red planet will be identifiable because of its colour. Mars lies in Gemini, while the moon and Jupiter are in neighbouring Cancer.
From the southern hemisphere the pairing is also visible before dawn, with the moon and Jupiter generally appearing higher in the morning sky.

Bereaved parents to give evidence at independent review of Sussex maternity services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:25 UTC
14:00:25 KST

Susan Cacciacarro was almost 37 weeks pregnant with her daughter Chiara when she woke up one morning in 2021, unable to feel her baby kicking.
“My belly just didn’t feel right,” she said. “I didn’t feel any movements.”
Chiara, her first child, had been diagnosed with a hole in her heart during a 20-week scan. Since then, Cacciacarro’s pregnancy had been classed as high risk and the growth of her baby had been regularly monitored in hospital.
But when a 34-week scan revealed Chiara had lost weight over the previous two weeks, maternity staff at Worthing hospital in Sussex did not make a plan to expedite her birth, which was planned to take place at 39 weeks.
On the day Cacciacarro woke up and realised Chiara was not moving, she rushed to the hospital, which is run by University hospitals Sussex NHS foundation trust.
Staff were unable to find the baby’s heartbeat and Chiara was delivered stillborn. “I’ve never felt so devastated and so crushed,” Cacciacarro said. “Your world turns upside down and suddenly it’s black.”
She is among the bereaved parents who will give evidence at a major independent review into maternity and neonatal services in Sussex, led by the senior midwife Donna Ockenden.
The review launched on Saturday with a public meeting in Brighton after months of campaigning by bereaved Sussex families. In February, a joint investigation between the New Statesman and the BBC revealed the deaths of at least 55 babies might have been avoidable if they and their mothers had received better care from University hospitals Sussex.
Ockenden, an expert on maternity safety, led the landmark review into maternity care at Shrewsbury and Telford and another into maternity services at Nottingham University hospitals NHS trust. She is also chairing a review into maternity and neonatal services at two Leeds hospitals.
At the meeting on Saturday, Ockenden discussed the review’s terms of reference with the families who will be most affected by it. “We need to get the finer details right to make sure that no family is left behind,” said Cacciacarro, who is now a mother of two. “I felt robbed when we lost Chiara … I’m hoping this review will provide answers to all harmed and bereaved families.”
As well as accountability and transparency, she said what was most important to the families was that the review brought about an improvement in the safety of maternity care services. “We definitely don’t want other families to go through this.”
When her appointment was announced, Ockenden said it was an honour to be asked to chair the review, which is expected to investigate more than 1,000 maternity and neonatal cases dating back to 2018.
“I am absolutely aware of the responsibility I have to the families and babies across Sussex,” she said. “My priority will be to listen carefully to harmed and bereaved families and to engage comprehensively across communities and with staff ‘on the ground’ here in Sussex.
“We will proactively reach out to ensure that the voices of seldom-heard families are heard through this review. It is vital that the scope of the review now reflects the experiences of families and enables a thorough and meaningful examination of care, so that improvements can be made as the review progresses.”
The bereaved campaigners, who are members of the Truth for Our Babies group (TFOB), are urging other affected families to come forward and participate in the review.
Dr Andy Heeps, the chief executive of University hospitals Sussex, said: “Our thoughts remain first and foremost with the families whose babies have died or who have suffered harm when receiving care in our hospitals.
“We welcome Donna Ockenden’s review and remain committed to fully supporting the process so families can get the answers they need, and we take any possible opportunity to learn and improve. Our overriding priority is always to provide the safest possible care for mothers and babies – that is why our maternity teams have implemented many positive changes in recent years, and why we will work with the review team to find new ways of making our services better, and safer, still.”
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Our thoughts and sympathy are with Susan [Cacciacarro] and all women and families who were failed by maternity services in Sussex.
“Through the national maternity and neonatal taskforce, increased investment in maternity safety, and the wider reforms following the previous Ockenden and Amos reviews, we are working to ensure families receive safer, more compassionate and more consistent care in every part of the NHS.”
