====================================================================================================

Israel loses 1,370 doctors in three years as brain drain intensifies: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:34:59 UTC
11:34:59 KST

Zein Khalil and Tarek Chouiref
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
At least 1,370 doctors left Israel between 2023 and 2025 according to a new study by Tel Aviv University, highlighting a deepening brain drain from the country’s medical sector.
The findings were published Sunday by the Israeli newspaper Haaretz.
The study classifies doctors as having left if they spent more than 270 days abroad during their first year away and did not subsequently remain in Israel for more than three consecutive months.
Prof. Itay Ater, one of the study’s authors, said economists had warned since 2023 of an accelerating departure of skilled professionals amid Israel’s political and security turmoil.
He said concerns first emerged during the government’s judicial overhaul push and intensified after the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and the war that followed.
Researchers focused particularly on doctors over 45, who have typically completed specialist training and play a central role in training younger physicians.
One in five doctors who left Israel during the three-year period was over 45, a trend the study described as worrying.
The losses were particularly pronounced in several specialties.
Some 116 ophthalmologists, dermatologists and ear, nose and throat (ENT) specialists left Israel, equivalent to 6.2% of physicians in those fields, while 188 surgeons – around 6% of the total – also departed.
The Tel Aviv area recorded the highest departure rate, with 5.4% of doctors leaving, according to the study.
The findings follow a report by the Israeli Finance Ministry last week showing that around 24% of specialist doctors in public hospitals are expected to reach retirement age in the coming years.
Another 25% have already passed retirement age but continue working amid shortages in medical staff.
Ater warned that the trajectory, rather than the current situation alone, was the greater concern, saying the trend could worsen after Israel’s general election scheduled for Oct. 27.
The study adds to broader signs of rising emigration from Israel.
Another Tel Aviv University study published in August found that 268,509 Israelis left the country between 2023 and 2025 for at least three months, a figure the Israeli public broadcaster KAN described as a record.
Israeli reports have linked the rise in departures to the war, high living costs and the political crisis surrounding the government’s efforts to weaken judicial powers.
A Kantar poll for KAN in August found that around one in five Israelis had considered emigrating over the previous two years, while 12% said the outcome of the upcoming election could affect their decision to remain in the country.

Taiwan finds new uses for agricultural waste
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:33:04 UTC
11:33:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is turning agricultural waste into new products as part of efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, with the initiative generating NT$150 million (US$4.7 million) in output, according to the Ministry of Agriculture.
The drive toward net-zero agriculture began in 2022, when the ministry unveiled a strategy to cut emissions by 2040. Since then, Agriculture Minister Chen Junne-jih (陳駿季) said the program has helped develop 49 products made from agricultural waste.
A total of 19 companies have joined the initiative, with combined investment reaching NT$320 million as businesses seek ways to put materials that would otherwise be discarded to new uses.
One example is yarn made from discarded oyster shells by a textile company in Tainan. The firm has also combined oyster shell powder with recycled plastic bottles to produce functional fibers, according to CNA.
Agricultural waste can also be reused as an energy source. A dried longan farm in Tainan, for instance, processes pruned branches and other dry wood from its grounds into biomass pellets. The pellets are then burned as fuel to dry longan.
Chen said cutting emissions from agriculture requires more than reducing energy consumption. Changes in farming and livestock practices are also needed, including measures to reduce methane emissions from rice cultivation and livestock manure, as well as nitrous oxide emissions linked to fertilizer use.
Farmers have increased their use of nitrogen fertilizer to boost crop yields. However, excess nitrogen can be released as nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas that traps nearly 300 times more heat than carbon dioxide, according to the Agricultural Technology Research Institute.
Taiwan’s agricultural sector emitted about 6.5 billion kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024, accounting for approximately 2.38% of the country’s total emissions. The figure includes emissions from crop production, livestock, forestry, and fisheries, according to the Climate Change Administration.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:29:33 UTC
11:29:33 KST

An oil depot in the Russian city of Sochi appeared to reignite on Sept. 7, three days after being struck by Ukrainian drones, Russian Telegram media channels reported.
Videos posted by Sochi residents on social media appear to show the oil depot, owned by Russia's state energy company Rosneft, ablaze and billowing smoke. The Russian monitoring Telegram channel ExileNova+ reports that authorities are asking local residents to close their windows due to heavy smoke in the coastal vacation destination.
At the time of publishing the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the reports nor the extent of the damage caused.
It was not immediately clear as to what caused the oil depot to reportedly reignite. Russian Air raid alerts in the region were not activated ahead of the blaze.
The latest fires come days after Ukrainian forces launched several waves of attacks against targets in Sochi on Sept. 3-4, including a naval drone strike on a Russian vessel.
Known as Russia’s "Second Capital," Sochi is home to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s official summer residence. Considered a winter playground for Russia’s elite, the city is located approximately 650 to 700 kilometers (400 to 435 miles) from the Ukraine border.
For months, Ukraine has conducted a sustained campaign of drone and missile strikes against Russian oil infrastructure. Damage to energy facilities has prompted Moscow to impose export restrictions as domestic supplies have tightened and long queues have formed across the country.
Ukraine's General Staff announced on September 4 that two major Russian oil facilities have suspended operations following Ukrainian drone strikes in August. 
Lukoil's NORSI refinery in Kstovo, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, located about 800 kilometers (nearly 500 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was shut down due to damage suffered in a Ukrainian drone attack on Aug. 26. The facility is Russia's fourth-largest oil refinery and second-largest gasoline producer, processing around 15-17 million metric tons of crude oil annually. 
The General Staff also said the Novatek-Ust-Luga complex in Slobidka, Leningrad Oblast, had suspended operations following Ukrainian drone strikes on Sept. 1. Located about 850 kilometers (nearly 530 miles) from the Ukrainian border, the facility is one of Russia's largest ports on the Baltic Sea and home to an oil terminal that serves as a major hub for exporting crude oil and petroleum products.

Homebuyers left in the dark as embattled property developer Bathla confirms major lay-offs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:26:52 UTC
11:26:52 KST

in brief
- More than 210 of Bathla's 350 staff were stood down at a meeting in Sydney on Monday morning.
- Homebuyers who bought off-the-plan have been left in the dark, uncertain when, or if, their properties will be completed.
Property developer Bathla Group has stood down almost two-thirds of its workforce following its entry into voluntary administration earlier this year.
About 213 of Bathla's 350 staff were stood down at a meeting in Sydney on Monday morning, and construction on several projects has halted as the embattled firm clings to life.
Bathla is one of Sydney's largest residential developers, with 45 projects under construction.
Administrators said they had secured short-term funding to keep some of the firm's projects going.
Insolvency adviser Teneo announced it had secured the funding through five lenders linked to the projects, but the amounts and participants were kept confidential.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Administrator Stephen Longley said the funding would enable Bathla Group to maintain limited operations for a further two weeks while longer-term solutions were explored.
"Our immediate priority has been to secure sufficient short-term funding to maintain a minimum viable operating structure," he said.
"The arrangements agreed allow us to provide the central support required for construction to continue on projects associated with the lenders participating in the funding package.
"Significant work remains to secure the funding required to progress and ultimately complete all projects currently under construction. We will continue to work closely with lenders and other key stakeholders to pursue those arrangements."
NSW premier reacts
NSW Premier Chris Minns said the government was talking with administrators, but defended not spending public money bailing out the Sydney-based business.
Minns described Bathla's corporate structure as strange and highly reliant on debt from private lenders.
"I can't just hand money over to an administrator, particularly when the finances of this particular firm are so opaque and difficult to decipher," Minns said.
"There's been a lot of commentary about the way this company ... was managed and run, particularly the enormous amount of debt it ran up.
"This is a very strange corporate structure involving a hell of a lot of debt, largely collected from private credit, not through the banks and traditional finances."
Figures presented to creditors put Bathla's total debt at $3.4 billion, including $3.08 billion to secured lenders, $130 million to unsecured lenders, $145 million to the tax office and $4 million to employees.
The home developer entered voluntary administration in late August after the NSW government declined to bail it out.
'Slow-moving trainwreck'
Former NSW building commissioner David Chandler said issues with Bathla were widely known and called the firm a "slow-moving trainwreck".
"I've had lots of contractors come to me since I retired as commissioner, saying they'd been approached by Bathla to come and actually finish or undertake projects for them," he told ABC TV.
"They said to me there was no way because they were such a difficult group to work with ... it was hard to get paid."
Chandler said those who bought an uncompleted Bathla home off the plan should be able to get their deposit back, because the money was supposed to have been held in trust.
"The people who will be most caught out here will be trade contractors and suppliers who haven't been paid, and some not paid for a very long time," he said.
According to the company's website, the group has 20,000 apartments and 7,000 dwellings in its delivery pipeline, comprising a significant share of the NSW government's target of 75,400 new homes a year for five years until 2029.
Homebuyers who bought off-the-plan have been left in the dark, uncertain when, or if, their properties will be completed, while contractors have been left scrambling to recoup debts.
Founded in NSW in 1997, Bathla is among a long list of Australian home developers that have recently entered voluntary administration or liquidation.

US must drop ‘hegemon’ mindset for Ukraine peace – Jeffrey Sachs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

US must drop ‘hegemon’ mindset for Ukraine peace – Jeffrey Sachs
US backroom diplomacy on Ukraine cannot achieve peace without Washington accepting that it is no longer the world’s sole superpower, economist and public policy scholar Jeffrey Sachs has told RT.
The comments follow separate closed-door talks held by US special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky in Kiev over the weekend. Details of the proposals exchanged during the meetings have not been made public.
“The US still has a grandiose idea that it is the world’s hegemon and the sole superpower, and it is not. Clearly, we are in a multi-polar world,” Sachs told RT in an exclusive interview on Sunday.
Sachs argued that a peace settlement requires taking Russia’s security interests into account and abandoning the expansionist foreign policy the US has pursued for more than 30 years.
“It seems to be psychologically very difficult” for Washington to openly accept that “basic reality,” he argued, saying this is why it resorts to “backroom negotiations” and secrecy that ultimately produce no tangible results.
Sachs also described the situation in Ukraine as an “endgame situation,” arguing that Kiev is in a desperate position militarily, socially, and politically.

Watch: CCTV captures moment Delhi's Satya Niketan building collapse, leaving 6 dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:20:26 UTC
11:20:26 KST

The CCTV footage showed the building suddenly giving way, sending debris crashing onto the road
NEW DELHI: CCTV footage has captured the moment a multi-storey building collapsed in Delhi's Satya Niketan area, killing six people and triggering a major rescue operation.The building, which housed a boys' paying guest accommodation near Delhi University's South Campus, collapsed around 1.30 pm on Sunday while repair and construction work was underway. The death toll rose to six after one more person rescued during the night was declared dead.The CCTV footage showed the building suddenly giving way, sending debris crashing onto the road. Rescue and search operations continued through the night as teams searched the rubble for anyone who may still be trapped.
Multiple agencies, including the Delhi Police, Delhi Fire Service, National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and Delhi Disaster Management Authority, have been involved in the operation."One more person was rescued during the night but was brought dead, taking the toll to six," Deputy Commissioner of Police (Southwest) Amit Goel said, PTI reported.Police have registered a case against the building owner and others, while a magisterial inquiry has also been ordered. Officials are continuing efforts to trace people allegedly connected with the incident.To the residents, the collapse felt like a quake. “We felt the ground shake.
When we ran outside, we saw that a house had completely collapsed,” said Roshan Pal, a student from Lucknow.“When I came out, a cloud of dust was spreading in all directions. That’s when we realised that the building had collapsed. We started removing one part of a wall soon after. Seven students were under it,” said Rahul Gaur, a resident, TOI reported.
10 patients taken to Trauma CentreAccording to AIIMS, the JPN Apex Trauma Centre received 10 patients injured in the building collapse. Of the 10 patients, five were brought dead, while another patient who was in critical condition later succumbed to injuries.Three patients have been admitted and are undergoing treatment. One of them underwent limb surgery, while another patient with minor injuries was discharged after observation.Investigators are examining whether construction work carried out in the basement may have contributed to the collapse.Initial inquiries suggested that the basement was prone to waterlogging, which may have weakened the structure. Investigators are now examining whether construction work aggravated the situation and contributed to the collapse.The MCD is also looking into the matter. Similar concerns over basement work, water accumulation and the structural condition of the building have emerged in the preliminary probe.Police are likely to examine whether permission had been obtained for the work and why construction was being carried out during the monsoon, sources said. "The building owner, contractor and labourers will be interrogated," an investigator said, TOI reported.It was not immediately clear whether the building owner had obtained permission for the construction or whether the work was being carried out illegally, allegedly in connivance with local authorities.
MCD orders demolition of dangerous buildingAccording to the MCD, the premises of Building/House No. 13, Satya Niketan, New Delhi, was found to be in a "ruinous, dangerous condition" and posed a threat to people occupying, visiting or passing by the building as well as those in the neighbourhood.Under Section 348 of the DMC Act, 1957, read with Section 491 of the Act, the MCD has ordered the property to be demolished within three days of receipt of the order.The order said that if the owner fails to comply within the specified period, the MCD will demolish the building and recover the demolition charges as arrears of tax.The collapse has raised fresh questions over the safety of buildings being used as paying guest accommodations and the enforcement of construction and fire safety norms in densely populated areas of Delhi.Congress leader and AICC Uttarakhand in-charge Kumari Selja questioned the BJP government over the safety of students living in such accommodations.“What is the BJP government doing? They have forgotten what happened at the coaching centre. A mafia is operating in Delhi. These children are sent away with so many hopes. They are the only support for their parents. Who is responsible for their safety?” Selja said.
Former Delhi chief secretary Omesh Saigal said the incident should not be viewed in isolation and raised concerns over unauthorised construction in parts of the capital."Look at the kind of buildings constructed in Delhi—I would say that in some areas, one in five buildings is unauthorised; either the blueprints weren't approved, extra floors were added, or the construction is substandard," he said.
Saigal also called for restrictions on new construction in areas that are already overcrowded. "At the very least, we should ban new construction in these areas. We must halt new construction or stop sanctioning building plans, for areas that are already over-congested and over-built. These are the things that need to be addressed," he added.
Kanchan Yadav is a writer at The Times of India, where she covers business, politics, international affairs and social issues. Her reporting also focuses on policy, governance and economic developments, with a close lens on how decisions in corridors of power affect everyday lives and community well-being.

Israel orders demolition of 5 Palestinian homes north of occupied Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:16:55 UTC
11:16:55 KST

Awad Rjoob and Tarek Chouiref
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Israeli authorities have ordered the demolition of five Palestinian homes north of occupied Jerusalem, giving residents as little as 24 hours to evacuate, the Jerusalem Governorate said Sunday.
One of the homes is located near the Jaba military checkpoint, while four others are in the Coptic neighborhood of Al-Ram, according to the governorate.
The owner of the house near the checkpoint was given 24 hours to leave before demolition, while residents of the other four homes were ordered to evacuate within two days.
The governorate said Israeli forces carried out 40 demolition and land-clearing operations targeting Palestinian structures in Jerusalem during August.
In a separate statement Sunday, it said Israeli authorities issued around 15 orders barring Palestinians from Al-Aqsa Mosque during the first six days of September alone.
The new orders brought the total documented since the beginning of 2026 to 800.
That figure is already close to the 23 exclusion orders recorded during July and August combined, including 17 in July and six in August.
By the end of August, the governorate had documented 785 such orders since the start of the year, including 762 during the first half of 2026.
Most targeted Palestinians were barred from Al-Aqsa Mosque particularly in the period leading up to and during Ramadan, the governorate said.
It said the sharp rise in September reflected an intensified use of exclusion orders ahead of the Jewish holiday season, which runs from mid-September into early October.
Around 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in 194 illegal settlements and 400 outposts across the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem. They carry out almost daily attacks aimed at forcibly displacing Palestinians from their land.
Since Israel launched its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip on Oct. 8, 2023, the occupied West Bank has witnessed daily raids by the Israeli army and attacks by Israeli occupiers.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:15:51 UTC
11:15:51 KST

A 23-year-old Israeli was killed in a motorcycle accident in Vietnam on Friday, the ZAKA rescue and recovery organization announced on Sunday.
The victim, David Ben Lulu from Jerusalem, had dual Israeli-French citizenship, and as such the Foreign Ministry had to coordinate between Vietnam and France in order to retrieve his remains for burial in Israel.
"Since we learned of the case, we have been working non-stop with the French, Vietnamese and Israeli authorities," Serge Ben Chaim, commander of ZAKA France, explained. "This morning I personally arrived at the French Foreign Ministry, where the necessary instructions were given to the team in Hanoi, and at the same time we are in direct contact with the French consulate and the family. Following the efforts, the consulate in Hanoi was opened today specifically to promote the processing of documents."
Motorcycle accident victim's remains hundreds of km. from Hanoi
Ben Chaim added that Ben Lulu's remains were hundreds of kilometers away from Hanoi, and that ZAKA was working on a way to arrange his transfer to Israel as soon as possible.
Chaim Weingarten, ZAKA's VP of Operations, described the situation as a "complex case," which required cooperation between several countries' agencies.
"ZAKA's international unit is working together with ZAKA France and the family to overcome the difficulties and expedite the procedures as much as possible," he said. "We hope to quickly complete all the necessary actions and bring the late David for burial in Israel."

Israel weighs destruction phase at Ali Taher Ridge as Hezbollah seeks Iranian response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:10:12 UTC
11:10:12 KST

Lebanese media reported at least 10 people killed overnight in Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon as the IDF weighs how to complete the destruction of remaining Hezbollah infrastructure on the strategic Ali Taher Ridge.
The escalation comes after Hezbollah terrorists launched two explosive drones toward IDF forces controlling the security zone in southern Lebanon. One of the drones was intercepted by Israeli troops, and no Israeli forces were injured.
The IDF described the launches as a blatant violation of the ceasefire agreement and responded with a broad wave of strikes in the Nabatieh area and elsewhere in southern Lebanon, targeting Hezbollah weapons depots and military buildings.
Lebanese reports said one of the targets was a three-story building in the village of Roumine in the Nabatieh area. According to the Hezbollah-affiliated Al Mayadeen network, nine people were killed in the strike, which it described as a “massacre.”
Reports also said a vehicle was struck in Roumine, killing one of its occupants.
According to the IDF, one of the targets was an active Hezbollah command center established inside a building that had previously served as a hospital. The military said terrorists had recently operated from the site to advance attack plans, conduct surveillance and direct artillery fire.
The IDF said precautions were taken before the strikes to reduce harm to civilians, including an urgent evacuation warning issued to residents of the village of Arab Salim, who were instructed to move around 300 meters away from the targeted facility.
The military also issued an Arabic-language evacuation warning to residents of Deir al-Zahrani in the Nabatieh area.
“Following the blatant violation of the ceasefire, after Hezbollah launched a drone toward IDF forces, we are being forced to respond,” the military said. “Civilians in the area must evacuate immediately.”
The latest strikes come as Israel prepares for a decision on the next phase of operations at Ali Taher Ridge.
After IDF commandos and the elite Yahalom combat engineering unit, operating under the 36th Division, completed the clearing of the ridge, the military is now determined to completely eliminate the remaining Hezbollah terrorist infrastructure in the strategic area.
Israel’s security establishment is expected to decide in the coming days how to carry out the destruction phase in the most effective way.
The IDF’s moves to destroy Hezbollah assets on the ridge have deeply concerned the terrorist organization’s leadership, which is trying by every means possible to stop them. Hezbollah is seeking to involve Iran in the confrontation in an attempt to establish a new deterrence equation with Israel that would prevent the destruction of those assets.
At the same time, Israel’s security establishment is closely watching the response from Washington and President Donald Trump, hoping it will not be required to halt the operation.
Once a decision is made to fully complete the operation, the IDF is expected to withdraw to defensive lines farther back. Forces are already preparing for that possibility.
The main objective is to establish a significant, fortified defensive line ahead of the holiday period while continuing to preserve the framework of the agreement with the Lebanese state in the pilot areas. The IDF acknowledges, however, that there has not yet been satisfactory progress on the ground.
The military said its forces would continue operating forcefully on Ali Taher Ridge and across southern Lebanon to remove any threat and would not allow Hezbollah to harm Israeli soldiers or civilians, while remaining committed to the ceasefire agreement.
Tensions surrounding Ali Taher Ridge are expected to continue in the coming days as Israel determines the most effective way to destroy the remaining infrastructure there.
For now, the IDF’s goal is to complete the operation without triggering repercussions that could spill over into other arenas.

Pro-Ukrainian partisans sabotaged communication tower ahead of oil refinery strike, Atesh group claims
A Russian servicemember defected and destroyed a communications tower deep behind Russian lines, allowing Ukrainian forces to strike one of Russia’s largest oil refineries, the Atesh group claimed on Sept. 5. 
The pro-Ukrainian saboteur reportedly contacted the Atesh group, a partisan force operating behind Russian lines, and burned through wiring in a communications tower around the Russian city of Perm, roughly 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukraine, in August.
The Russian servicemember joined the Ukrainian resistance group due to his "disagreement with the country's leadership and the lawlessness he witnessed in the army," the Atesh group claimed on Telegram.
The loss of the tower reportedly disrupted data transmission in the area, leaving security personnel and Russian military units unable to maintain reliable coordination. Ukrainian drones then struck the nearby LUKOIL-Permnefteorgsintez on Aug. 21. Operations at the refinery were temporarily suspended following the strikes. 
The Kyiv Independent cannot verify the claims made by Atesh.
Owned by Lukoil, one of Russia's largest oil producers, the Permnefteorgsintez refinery is among the country's largest. The facility processes more than 13 million metric tons of crude oil annually and produces gasoline, diesel fuel, jet fuel, and lubricating oils.
Ukrainian forces had previously struck the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery on July 29 as part of Ukraine's broader missile and drone campaign against Russian energy and oil infrastructure far from Ukraine. 
The Atesh partisan group regularly sabotages Russian military infrastructure in Ukraine's occupied territories and in Russia.
The group claimed credit for the sabotage of an electric substation powering a military plant in southern Russia on June 20. Members of Atesh allegedly sabotaged an electric locomotive used by the Russian military in Russia's Lipetsk Oblast on May 10.
The group is also active in Russian-occupied Crimea, where it has reported an increase both in people wishing to join and in those willing to pass on important information about Russia's military facilities and weapons.

MOSCOW, September 7. /TASS/. Since the beginning of this year, Ukraine has paid $4.81 billion toward servicing and repaying its national debt, according to TASS calculations.
The largest portion of the funds, $1.587 billion, was paid to the IMF. Ukraine spent $3.224 billion on payments to the World Bank, on foreign-currency government bonds, to the EU, and to other creditors.
Ukraine’s national debt continues to break records. As of the end of August, it stood at approximately $218-219 billion, according to TASS estimates. It is increasing by $4-5 billion per month. According to forecasts by Ukraine’s finance minister, it will reach approximately $240 billion by the end of the year. Consequently, by the end of 2026, each Ukrainian will owe approximately $8,500, and by the end of 2027, about $10,400.

Poland’s anti-Ukrainian turn spills into violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:01:00 UTC
11:01:00 KST

WARSAW — Poland’s nationalist right is turning hostility toward the country’s roughly 1.5 million Ukrainians into a potent political issue, tapping into local resentment over social benefits and wartime history just over a year before a pivotal parliamentary election.
During Poland’s 2025 presidential campaign, politicians began portraying Ukrainians in Poland as freeloaders straining the country’s public finances.
This summer, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, of Poland’s highest honor, the Order of the White Eagle, in reaction to Zelenskyy’s decision to name a military unit after the World War II-era Ukrainian Insurgent Army, or UPA. The group murdered tens of thousands of Poles during an ethnic-cleansing campaign in 1943-1945, although it also fought against the Soviet Union.
Advertisement
Warsaw has been one of Kyiv’s strongest supporters against Russia since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. But the nationalist camp, which Nawrocki seeks to lead, has sought to capitalize on tensions over the Ukrainian presence in Poland and the wartime massacres.
Anti-Ukrainian rhetoric is already intensifying ahead of the fall 2027 parliamentary election, when Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s broadly pro-Ukraine coalition will face the nationalist Law and Justice party and two other far-right parties. Polls show Tusk is far from certain of victory.
The libertarian Confederation party denounced Ukrainians getting social welfare, while Gregorz Braun, the European Parliament member who leads the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown party, said: “The Kyiv regime is neither our ally nor our friend, it is our enemy,” during a summer gathering commemorating the wartime killing of Polish civilians by Ukrainians.
Przemysław Czarnek, the candidate for prime minister from the Law and Justice party, said July: “Military aid to Ukraine must be suspended until that country changes its historical policy.”
Rafał Pankowski, a sociology professor at Warsaw’s Civitas University and co-founder of the Polish anti-racism group Never Again, believes that while the Polish population is broadly supportive of Ukraine, fissures are beginning to show.
“Solidarity with Ukrainians remains strong among many Poles, but populist anti-Ukrainian rhetoric has created fertile ground for attacks, turning a large and visible minority into a target and helping verbal hostility spill into violence. Russian propaganda seized on the opportunity, too,” he said.
Advertisement
Ukrainian Ambassador to Poland Vasyl Bodnar is worried about politicians using Ukraine as a wedge issue.
“Part of Poland’s political class is trying to exploit the Ukrainian issue for political gain. Some focus on developments in Ukraine, others on the behavior of Ukrainians living here. One way or another, Ukraine features in the narrative of every political group — it is simply packaged differently,” he told POLITICO.
In the line of fire
The latest Polish-Ukrainian row might have faded from the headlines, but the fear it helped instill has not.
Vasyl Bodnar is worried about politicians using Ukraine as a wedge issue. | Adem Altan/AFP via Getty Images
“I’ve lived in Poland for about 10 years. I came here to study and stayed,” said Olena, a guide at a Warsaw cultural institution whose name POLITICO changed at her request because she feared for her safety.
“It took me quite a while to integrate, but I have never felt as alienated as I have over the past year. I have become afraid to speak Ukrainian in public, and I have started worrying about my friends and loved ones who live here or come to Poland to visit,” she said.
Opinion polls show a decided shift against Ukrainians.
Advertisement
In an annual survey by the state-run pollster CBOS, sympathy among Poles toward Ukrainians fell from 51 percent in 2023 to 29 percent in January 2026, while antipathy rose from 38 percent to 43 percent over the last year.
Another CBOS poll found that 45.4 percent of those polled attributed the deterioration to disputes over the wartime massacres and historical policy, with social benefits for Ukrainians in second place at 36.4 percent.
Ivan, a Ukrainian national who works at the University of Warsaw and asked to only be identified by his first name, said a neighbor confronted him over Zelenskyy’s decision to name a military unit after the UPA.
“We were in the elevator. My neighbor started yelling at me, telling me to go back to Ukraine and explain to Zelenskyy that he shouldn’t have done that. It was absurd,” Ivan said.
Olena recalled a Polish woman following the group she was guiding and complaining that hearing her speak Polish was “an embarrassment” to her as a Pole.
“I said loudly that Polish was not my native language, that I came from Ukraine,” Olena said.
Advertisement
For Ivan and Olena, the hostility remained verbal. For other Ukrainians, it has turned violent.
In July, two men were arrested after two Ukrainians, Anastazja, 20, and her 21-year-old partner Maksym, were beaten outside a Wrocław grocery store. The attack was denounced by Poland’s Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha thanked the police for the arrests.
Earlier that month, an off-duty employee of Bielsko-Biała’s municipal bus company hurled nationality-based abuse at three Ukrainians, including two 11-year-old schoolgirls, on a bus.
Donald Tusk attends a ceremony in London on May 27, 2026. | Pool photo by Jack Taylor via WPA/Getty Images
In August, a Ukrainian man was attacked on a tram in Poznań.
The Polish police recorded 180 reports of ethnically motivated crimes against Ukrainians in the first half of this year, a 30 percent increase over the same period last year, reported the Rzeczpospolita newspaper.
The Polish government — which has tightened Ukrainians’ access to welfare, even though their collective contribution to Poland’s economy far exceeds public spending on them — set up 50 specialist prosecution teams in early 2026 to investigate hate crimes.
Advertisement
Between February and June, Polish prosecutors sent 283 cases to court. Ukrainians were the victims in more than 80 percent of such cases, up from 4 percent in 2014 and 74 percent in 2023.
Tusk said in July that attackers had become bolder because they believed they enjoyed political protection and called on Nawrocki to speak out on the matter.
“I am appealing directly to the president to stop remaining silent on this matter,” Tusk said. “We must wage a decisive fight against this violence, because the bandits, the hooligans, this violent pathology has gained courage and audacity because it has also received political patronage.”
The Roman Catholic Church has also weighed in, issuing an appeal “not to fuel nationalistic sentiments.”
Ambassador Bodnar hopes politicians will stop inflaming relations between the two countries.
“The best response will be effective communication — from politicians, the media, and, of course, government officials — who would communicate in a positive manner and resolve those issues that are painful or important to both sides,” Bodnar said.
Advertisement
For Ivan, the change in tone is making him more wary of drawing attention to himself in Poland.
“I still speak Ukrainian, and I wear a pin with the Polish and Ukrainian flags. What has changed is the way I feel about potential conflicts. I used to not be afraid to speak up and stand up for myself if someone attacked me because I’m Ukrainian,” he said. “Now I’m afraid no one would help me and that I would be accused of violating some law and simply deported, even though I’ve already built my life in Poland.”
The government’s policy is to deport Ukrainians even for minor offenses — one Ukrainian 18-year-old was kicked out of Poland for jumping a barrier at a concert.

Russia has entered Sweden’s election campaign, center-left front-runner warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

STOCKHOLM — Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson must urgently take action to address claims that his potential far-right coalition partner may have been infiltrated by Russia ahead of this month’s general election, the front-runner in the race told POLITICO.
The call by Magdalena Andersson, leader of the center-left Social Democratic Party, which polls have on course to win the Sept. 13 election, comes after the campaign was rocked by claims that an official inside the far-right Sweden Democrats party had longstanding ties to Russia.
If Andersson wins, she’ll join embattled Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez as one of the few center-left politicians around the European leaders’ table. However, the gap between her coalition and a right-wing faction led by Kristersson has been narrowing as the election draws near. If Kristersson wins, the Sweden Democrats stand to enter government for the first time after the prime minister said he would govern with the far-right party.
Advertisement
“Ulf Kristersson must come clean about the security crisis,” Andersson told POLITICO in an interview. “These are extremely serious allegations … Russia is the greatest threat to Sweden.”
The claims, laid out in a Sept. 3 article by non-governmental group Expo, allege that a female Sweden Democrats official promoted pro-Kremlin narratives for a decade, cultivated ties with a Russian state-backed group in Sweden, and brought Russian family members onto the grounds of the Swedish parliament. The official, Polina Malaberg, who remains employed by the Sweden Democrats, previously held roles linked to parliamentary committees focusing on EU affairs.
Malaberg’s partner, Gustav Gellerbrant, is a senior civil servant and Sweden Democrats member who heads the party’s Coordination Office inside the government, acting as a liaison between the party and Kristersson’s current governing coalition. While Gellerbrant himself is not accused of Russia ties, his relationship with Malaberg raises questions about his security clearance, Andersson argues.
“Is there information relating to national security that may have been exposed?” Andersson asked. “What measures has the prime minister taken and what measures does he intend to take?”
Both Kristersson and Jimmie Åkesson, leader of the Sweden Democrats, have publicly addressed Expo’s claims. Kristersson said Malaberg should be fired if the allegations turn out to be true. “We are in a European war … You can’t have people who sit around promoting pro-Russian narratives and work in the Swedish parliament,” he told newspaper Aftonbladet.
Advertisement
Åkesson said his party had been unaware of the pro-Kremlin posts by Malaberg but conceded “we have to look at this and sort this out,” adding that the party was investigating the claims and that Malaberg could not continue to work for them if she maintained her pro-Russian views.
But these answers aren’t enough, said Andersson, a former finance minister and prime minister of Sweden. “When did the prime minister’s office become aware of this, and what information has been given to the prime minister?” she asked, adding: “This is about Sweden and the security of the Swedish people.”
Speaking to POLITICO from her parliamentary office in Stockholm, Andersson argued that the risks of having the Sweden Democrats in government go beyond security. “We’ve seen journalists threatened” since Kristersson started ruling with backing from the Sweden Democrats, she said. “NGOs are threatened if they criticize what the government is doing. They’ve been threatened to have their state support withdrawn.”
Ulf Kristersson has been in power since 2022. | Pool photo by Jaimi Joy via EFA/EPA
“There could be a Swedish government where half of the ministers, including the foreign minister and the EU minister, come from a party that thinks we should have an inquiry on exit” from the European Union, she added.
The question is whether Swedish voters will agree with Andersson that it’s time for a change (Kristersson has been in power since 2022).
Security and migration remain top campaign issues. Kristersson’s camp vows to crack down harder on gang violence while ramping up deportations, including plans to deport some migrants who have been schooled in Sweden when they turn 18.
Advertisement
Quizzed about her migration stance, Andersson said Sweden’s previously open border policy was “unsustainable.” The country now requires a “very strict” migration policy, she said, adding that her party is open to supporting third-country “return hubs” — external deportation centers for migrants whose asylum applications have failed — if she wins.
But she said a Sweden Democrats proposal to strip permanent residency from some migrants crosses a line. “Once you have permanent residency, it’s permanent, right? You can’t say yes and then ‘no, we changed our minds’… That’s not how Sweden works. Many of these people work. They are bus drivers. They are entrepreneurs creating work… It’s insane.”
Asked whether she was closer to Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen or Spain’s Sánchez on migration, Andersson sidestepped, citing both as close contacts in Europe’s center-left camp.
Andersson touted strong support for Ukraine, a continued “frugal” stance on EU budget negotiations, and tough-on-crime policies as areas where she would maintain continuity with Kristersson’s government. She also favored using Russia’s frozen assets to help fund Ukraine and opposed “decoupling” with the United States.
“Many people say it’s enough now” with Sweden’s current government, Andersson concluded. “We’re the Social Democratic Party. Jobs and household economy, together with welfare, schools, hospitals and elderly care. These are the main issues.”

Author's YA book partly inspired by experience as sex educator in schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:55:22 UTC
10:55:22 KST

Bad Queer by Gayathiri Kamalakanthan and Chi Nwosu tells affirming coming-of-age story
Surya feels like a bad queer. When an ice cream man misgenders them, they stay silent.
"I pray for a sharper tongue," they think when a classmate harasses them for not looking like either a boy or a girl.
Surya is the protagonist of Bad Queer, a young adult novel-in-verse written by London-based Gayathiri Kamalakanthan and illustrated by Chicago artist Chi Nwosu.
Coming into their final year at school, Surya has come out to their parents, who are queer and non-binary, and their close friend Maha, but not to everyone.
They're also yet to have their first romantic relationship.
"I would really like to like someone.
But I know I can't force it," they reflect.
'Poetry and illustration are a beautiful match'
Throughout Bad Queer, Nwosu's line drawings help develop Surya's journey of self-acceptance.
Sometimes the illustrations capture a detail from the text, like Surya's hands writing in their journal or the tiles in a family game of Scrabble.
Elsewhere, they take us into Surya's internal emotions, like a flurry of stars and swirls that surround the text as Surya practices deep breathing in a bathroom stall.
"I think poetry and illustration are a beautiful match because they're both asking the reader to interpret and really be part of co-creating the story," Kamalakanthan says of the book's unusual format.
Nwosu, a Black, non-binary, queer Nigerian American artist and designer, relates to how Surya feels connected to their ancestors and how they're searching for representation of their queer and non-binary self in Tamil culture.
"I find myself looking towards Igbo history in a similar way," Nwosu says.
"I want to know where are the others? Where are the outliers? How did folks treat people who were different or had a different orientation towards the world?
"[Surya's story] reflected my own experience as someone who didn't fit neatly into a binary."
One aspect of the project Nwosu particularly enjoyed was learning about Tamil symbolism and incorporating it respectfully into their work.
"A lot of my own art incorporates cultural and spiritual symbols as a way to learn, remember and honour my Igbo culture and the histories of global solidarity and queer solidarity," they say.
Finding themselves on stage
Surya's life changes when, on a whim, they audition for their school's youth theatre.
"It's as if this one audition is a mini protest
against all the times I've said nothing" they think.
The group, led by the enthusiastic Mr Ali, proves a safe space for Surya to explore and embrace their identity.
In this new environment, Surya soon befriends Akhil, who proudly wears a "GAY AF" badge and Sade, who gives Surya a worry stone to soothe their pre-audition anxiety.
Then there's Blessing, a newcomer with a "perfectly crooked" smile. Surya is soon smitten.
Kamalakanthan says their own experiences working in the theatre, including writing a play, Period Parrrty, were "foundational" for them.
"I gained confidence to really step into the intersection of my Tamilness and genderqueerness," they say.
"There's something about theatre being a communal act. You're not just writing in a room by yourself. You're in rehearsal rooms, trading mood boards, figuring out a shared vision with a director and cast, and that collective imagining really opened up my confidence."
'I wanted him to get things wrong and keep trying'
As Surya's relationship with Blessing develops, they gain the confidence to live as their true self.
While Blessing is kind and empathetic, it's also a journey for him to embrace being in a queer relationship.
"Because of the binary world we live in, [Blessing] has a difficult time understanding Surya's transness," Kamalakanthan says.
"I wanted him to get things wrong and keep trying and not shy away from doing his own thinking and research about what he doesn't understand yet."
Kamalakanthan says the arc of the relationship was inspired by their previous work as a sex and relationships educator.
"I noticed students were often more fluent in naming sexual harm than articulating consent and the type of touch they might be comfortable with," they say.
"I wanted characters in Bad Queer to model those exact conversations: fumbling, hesitant and laughing nervously through the words … and importantly working out their boundaries before any touch happens.
"There's so much in books and TV about sexual violence, which is of course an important topic to understand.
"But I also wanted to write consensual, caring relationships. We need templates for those conversations too."
'Stories that I really longed for as a young person'
Kamalakanthan and Nwosu hope Bad Queer strikes a chord with young people coming to terms with their gender identity and sexual orientation.
"As a young person, I felt like I didn't quite have the words to describe the feeling of queerness that I had inside," Nwosu says.
"To understand what it means to find dignity for yourself as a queer and genderqueer person and to learn to accept the parts of yourself that maybe make other people uncomfortable was one of the profound takeaways from the book for me.
"It was incredible to work on a book intended for young people and to know they will have these stories that I really longed for as a young person."
Kamalakanthan says they want to present a different kind of narrative around queer and trans youth, who often don't get support or understanding from their parents.
"I wanted to write a family where being trans is incidental alongside the usual messiness and tenderness of any family," they say,.
"Surya's parents won't always have all the answers, but they're people who Surya knows are safe enough to express worries and anxieties to, including if anything unsafe or harmful is going on.
"For a lot of queer people I know, our teenage years were spent hiding, feeling unsafe and managing how we were perceived, rather than discovering the fullness of who we could be.
"I want the characters in my stories to have the teenage adolescence a lot of us didn't get to have, that I hope young people get to have now."
Bad Queer is published by Allen & Unwin.

AfD wins Saxony-Anhalt election with 43.8% of vote — election commission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:47:01 UTC
10:47:01 KST

BERLIN, September 7. /TASS/. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party secured a decisive victory in the the Saxony-Anhalt election, receiving 43.8% of the vote, the regional election commission said in releasing preliminary official results.
This is the best result the AfD has ever achieved in a German state election, doubling its share of the vote compared to five years ago. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) came in second, losing about half of its votes compared to 2021. The party received only 17.2% of the vote, marking the CDU’s worst performance in Saxony-Anhalt to date. Conservative candidates failed to win a single constituency seat.
The Social Democratic Party of Germany received 9.3% of the vote, Alliance 90/The Greens 8.9%, and the Left Party 8.6%. The BSW (formerly the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance - Reason and Justice party) also entered the state parliament with 5.3% of the vote.
Approximately 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in Saxony-Anhalt. Voter turnout was the highest in the region since German reunification, with about 77.8% of eligible voters casting ballots.
Following the election, the formation of a state government became extremely complex, as all parties except the BSW refuse to cooperate with the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. Moreover, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party rules out cooperation with the Left Party as well. Meanwhile, the Alternative for Germany party narrowly missed securing an absolute majority. However, it could form a regional cabinet for the first time if it receives support from the BSW.
Experts view the CDU’s defeat as a personal defeat for Chancellor Friedrich Merz and as evidence of the public's rejection of his government's policies, including those regarding Russia.

Said Amori and Tarek Chouiref
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Israel is preparing to destroy two underground routes in southern Lebanon and intends to prevent displaced residents from returning to areas its forces may leave, the Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported Sunday.
The routes, located beneath the Ali al-Taher Heights, are expected to be blown up in the coming days, KAN said, citing unnamed military officials who claimed that no “living armed operatives” remained at the site.
The army is then expected to begin a phased withdrawal from what Israel calls its “security belt” in southern Lebanon.
The plan is due to be presented this week to the head of the Israeli army’s Northern Command before being sent to the political leadership for approval.
Under the proposal, Israeli troops would pull back from the so-called “yellow line” to a “gray line” roughly 2 to 4 kilometers (1.2 to 2.5 miles) from the Israeli border, where the army plans to establish around 20 permanent military positions.
On Thursday, the Israeli army claimed it had established “operational control” above and below ground in the Ali al-Taher Heights area. The Hezbollah group did not comment on the claim.
KAN also said Israel had relayed a message to the Lebanese government through the US that displaced residents would not, for now, be allowed to return to areas vacated by Israeli forces.
The issue is expected to be raised in direct Israeli-Lebanese talks due to resume this month in Rome.
The report comes amid heightened tensions in southern Lebanon where Israeli attacks have intensified in recent days after the Israeli army claimed it intercepted a drone that was allegedly launched by Hezbollah toward its forces operating in what Tel Aviv calls a “security zone” in southern Lebanon.
The strikes come despite a US-sponsored framework agreement signed between Israel and Lebanon on June 26 which provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army.
Israel has carried out attacks on Lebanon since March 2, killing 4,362 people and injuring 12,378 others while displacing more than 1 million people, according to Lebanese authorities.
Israel continues to occupy areas of southern Lebanon, including territory it has held for decades and other areas occupied during the 2023-2024 conflict, while its forces have advanced more than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) into Lebanese territory during the current conflict.

Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing Concludes State Visit to Vietnam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:36:00 UTC
10:36:00 KST

Myanmar’s military-appointed President Min Aung Hlaing yesterday wound up a three-day visit to Vietnam, during which he and Hanoi’s top leaders agreed to expand cooperation across a broad front.
The former general arrived in Vietnam on Friday, part of a diplomatic campaign aimed at consolidating ties with regional governments and normalizing relations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
In addition to meeting top leaders including President To Lam and Prime Minister Le Minh Hung, Min Aung Hlaing also held meetings with top Vietnamese firms such as VinFast, a local EV manufacturer, and the military-run telecoms group Viettel, which operates Mytel, one of Myanmar’s major telecom operators.
According to a Vietnamese government statement quoted by Reuters, a key focus of the talks between Lam and Min Aung Hlaing was defense and security cooperation, which the two leaders elevated to a key pillar of bilateral ties.
In particular, the two leaders “agreed to expand cooperation in military training, exchanges between young officers, search-and-rescue operations and disaster response, while stepping up information sharing and coordination against crimes,” the statement said.
“Vietnam stands ready to share its experience in national development, ensuring economic security and fostering sustainable growth,” the statement quoted Lam as saying during the talks.
Economics and trade were also high on the agenda. Trade between the two nations has fallen in recent years, as Myanmar has become engulfed in civil conflict. According to statistics cited by the Associated Press, two-way trade totaled $853 million in 2020 but then fell to $590 million in 2025.
Speaking at the Myanmar-Viet Nam Business Forum in Hanoi yesterday, Min Aung Hlaing called “for greater bilateral economic cooperation and increased Vietnamese investment in Myanmar,” the Global New Light of Myanmar reported. In particular, he said that Myanmar was “seeking to expand cooperation with Vietnam in telecommunications, technology, manufacturing, agriculture, energy, tourism and human resources development,” in the newspaper’s paraphrase.
Both sides also reaffirmed a commitment not to allow any individual or organization to use one country’s territory for activities against the other – a similar arrangement to the one that Lam made during his visit to Thailand in May.
During his meeting with Min Aung Hlaing on Saturday, Le Minh Hung “congratulated Myanmar on achieving significant results in national governance under the leadership of President Min Aung Hlaing,” Vietnamese state media reported. He also “affirmed Vietnam’s support for the Myanmar government in continuing to implement measures to promote stability, reconciliation, dialogue, economic development, and improve people’s lives.”
Vietnam was the eighth country that Min Aung Hlaing has visited since taking office in April, and the third member state from ASEAN, with a fourth – Cambodia – to follow later this week. He has also paid visits to India, China, Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan. In all of these places, he has sought to consolidate diplomatic relationships and to drum up foreign investment, as evidenced by the large business and political delegations that have accompanied him on each trip.
A top priority, which Min Aung Hlaing flagged in his inauguration speech in April, is to normalize relations with ASEAN, which since late 2021 has excluded the country from its summits over its failure to implement the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan. This plan calls for a cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and inclusive dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
Myanmar’s government has rejected the Consensus, in both word and deed, while cultivating relations with those ASEAN member states most sympathetic to its reintegration into the 11-nation bloc.

Saxony-Anhalt: Preliminary official results show AfD tops vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:35:00 UTC
10:35:00 KST

Saxony-Anhalt: Germany wakes up to 'unsettling' AfD victory
Published September 6, 2026last updated September 7, 2026
What you need to know
- Far-right AfD hails 'sensational' results in the Saxony-Anhalt vote
- AfD expected to struggle with coalition building as many parties reject cooperation
- Left-wing populist BSW open to working with AfD on some issues
- Merz's CDU suffers worst Saxony-Anhalt result since German reunification
- Merz says CDU shaken 'to its very foundations' by AfD win
- The European press calling the results an "unsettling new page in German history"
Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state held an election on Sunday, September 6. Follow all the developments on Monday, September 7, here.
CDU's Jürgen Hardt: Result also shows lack of confidence in federal government and Merz
The CDU's Jürgen Hardt, a senior party figure on foreign policy and lawmaker in the Bundestag in Berlin, spoke with DW's Chief Political Editor Michaela Küfner about the implications of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt.
He said the federal government and party leadership should be under no illusions that the result was "not only due to the internal questions of Saxony-Anhalt," but also due to a lack of confidence with the federal government and Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
"To be frank, it should that our concept to minimize the results of the AfD did not work out yet," he said. "We tried to counter AfD support by doing good politics, expecially in the field of migration," Hardt said, pointing to the sharp reduction in asylum applications over the last two years and a gradual return towards economic growth.
"But this is not what voters in Saxony-Anhalt are interested in," he surmised. "They probably want to show 'we are [not] confident in the chancellor and his policy,' and this message needs to be heard by us."
Asked what should be done, Hardt effectively said more of the same — but better and with better communication and salesmanship. He said he hoped the results would not derail or complicate either domestic reforms programs or foreign policy issues like support for Ukraine.
Hardt 'expects' that AfD's Siegmund will lead the state government
Hardt also said, even as the AfD casts doubt on this in the aftermath of the vote, that he believed the party would ultimately lead the state government — with or without a majority, saying he "expected" Ulrich Siegmund to become state premier.
"He has 39 votes, he needs three extra votes and I am sure that from BSW he will get those votes in the end," Hardt said, referring to the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance or BSW.
But even if not, Hardt said that with "a relative majority of 39 seats" Siegmund and the AfD would still have more parliamentary control than the CDU, Social Democrats and Greens combining their 32 seats.
"I'm sure that Siegmund will do that. He's now talking about new elections — something like that — but at the end of the day, he wants to become state premier, he has to deliver, and he cannot hide away," Hardt said.
Even if this came to pass, Hardt said a state government cannot have "much influence" on foreign security issues in German politics, "and therefore I am not in panic" about what it might mean for Germany or its allies.
He did however warn about the AfD's stance on Ukraine and Russia, calling the party a Russian "trojan horse" in German politics that he said advocated policies which would lead to Germany "depending on Russia" and having "to follow the directives of this dictator" Vladimir Putin.
German Chancellor Merz rules out cooperation with AfD but says CDU 'shaken to foundation'
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Monday doubled down on his refusal to work with the far-right populist AfD while at the same time admitting that Sunday's election drubbing had shaken his own conservative CDU "to its very foundations."
AfD has siphoned off CDU voters and pushed Merz's conservatives farther to the right, now it is hoping to win over some of its lawmakers in the state of Saxony-Anhalt in order to form a ruling coalition as it fell just short of winning an outright majority.
Merz said during a press conference on Monday in Berlin after the election: "This shakes our party to its very foundations. We cannot simply carry on as before, nor can I, nor can the federal government."
"We have a strong constitution; we have all the tools to defend the constitution against a right-wing extremist state government," added the deeply unpopular Merz, "but our party system is undergoing a tectonic shift."
Both AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla and top candidate Ulrich Siegmund have called on CDU lawmakers in the state to drop the "deeply undemocratic" firewall and work toward creating a "center-right conservative majority" in Saxony-Anhalt — with Chrupalla saying, "Partisan games really ought to be a thing of the past."
Neighboring France voices concern over rise of the AfD
Speaking with RTL Radio on Monday morning, French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said the far-right AfD's resounding victory in German state elections, "sends a very, very worrying signal."
Lescure called the victory part of a "populist wave" that is "spreading around the world today," saying "we must resist" it.
Lescure's comments echoed those delivered by France's Minister of European Affairs Benjamin Haddad, who called the victory "a very grave moment for Europe."
For years, France has faced the prospect of a far-right government as Marine Le Pen's ultraconservative National Rally (RN) party has come ever closer to gaining power in successive elections, a situation that will repeat itself during federal elections there next year.
It should be noted that RN ended cooperation with the AfD in the European Parliament for its revisionist view of Nazi Germany, it's ties with far-right extremists and allegations that it aided Chinese and Russian agents in Brussels.
AfD leaders say migrants 'have nothing to fear as long as they contribute to making Germany a better place'
Candidate Ulrich Siegmund said he would seek to become the state's premier during a Q&A session after Monday morning's press conference but noted that he would need a stable majority if he was to have a chance to turn the state around.
He also said those with immigration backgrounds need not fear the AfD, claiming that even anti-fascists had been convinced about his earnestness during discussions in which he engaged with protesters outside campaign rallies.
Party co-leader Alice Weidel said the AfD is not anti-immigrant per se and that it welcomes all foreigners willing to "contribute to making Germany a better place" before railing against unqualified immigrants receiving German taxpayer funds as welfare.
Neither Siegmund nor Weidel provided evidence or data to back up their claims.
She also emphasized what she called the fears of women, children and others in the face of "criminal immigrants" and called for far tighter borders, pointing out that Germany's major parties had lost touch with reality in opening them.
This came despite the fact that crime statistics show that immigrants make up only a small minority of criminal suspects, with age and gender being a much more decisive factor.
Moments after saying the party was not against immigrants, Weidel then doubled down on the party's promise to deport as many immigrants as possible as soon as it took power, saying Germany could not afford what she called an "open-border policy."
Germany has increased border controls and security in recent months and net migration and asylum applications have already dropped significantly over the past two years.
AfD calls for political cooperation, ultimately federal leadership at press conference
In their first press conference since yesterday's Saxony-Anhalt state elections, Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, alongside top state candidate Ulrich Siegmund, called the Sunday result "historic" and suggested other parties reconsider the "failed concept" of the so-called "firewall" to honor voters' wishes and help the AfD run the state.
Weidel started off by thanking voters who came out to show support for the party despite "negative press coverage" — the charge of "fake news" and "unfair media coverage" was a through-line for all three party representatives during the press conference.
Weidel praised historically high voter turnout before slamming existing political parties, specifically Chancellor Friedrich Merz, for whom she has a particular animosity, and running through a laundry list of issues that motivated AfD voters — immigration, immigrant crime, high prices, energy policy and de-industrialization being foremost among them.
Weidel then went on to declare that the country's two largest popular parties, the CDU and SPD, would "never win another election" because they had failed to find solutions to those problems.
Co-leader Tino Chrupalla praised candidate Ulrich Siegmund before also slamming Merz — whom he called "arrogant" for dismissing the AfD as a laboratory for political malcontents — while looking forward to coming elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and criticizing German support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.
After claiming the so-called political "firewall" had collapsed, Chrupalla said the AfD is prepared to hold talks with other political parties, including the CDU, which he said would "disappear" if it did not change course.
After thanking AfD leadership, candidate Siegmund joined in slamming the CDU, Chancellor Merz and the media. Siegmund claimed that tens of thousands of supporters had turned out for AfD rallies during the election campaign — though such numbers have been seen as being exaggerated.
Siegmund said Sunday's result had shown that hope had triumphed over "fake news" to deliver a clear mandate for the AfD to form a government.
Further, Siegmund railed against broken political promises — focusing specifically on Merz and the CDU — vowing that he and the AfD would "stay true to our values" and claiming, "people are finally trusting politicians again."
Lastly, Siegmund claimed the vote was, "not only important for the state of Saxony-Anhalt but the entire nation," saying he needed a "Chancellor Alice Weidel" to help him turn the country around, before promising to slash foreign aid to help Germany and its citizens.
"This is not just about Saxony-Anhalt, it's about Germany," he said. "We want our old, safe Germany back again."
What are the coalition possibilites in Saxony-Anhalt?
Holocaust survivor: 'This election result scares me'
Holocaust survivor Eva Umlauf, president of the Berlin-based International Auschwitz Committee, on Monday told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA), "this election result scares me."
Umlauf then asked, "What path is Germany on? The one that it traveled before?"
After saying Holocaust survivors "never thought it possible" that a right-wing extremist party would again be voted into power at the state level — the AfD was also the largest faction voted into Thuringia's state parliament in 2024 — she added that she would continue to fight for democracy and for the memory of those six million Jews killed during the Nazi era.
Umlauf said survivors "owe it to our murdered relatives" to keep their memory alive, calling it "our obligation to young people in Germany."
Far-right AfD on the rise (mostly) for 10 years now
Germany's far-right AfD has seen an almost constant rise in popularity since it was founded as an anti-euro party in April 2013.
After capitalizing on concerns about then-Chancellor Angela Merkel's immigration policies, the party saw a slight drop in popularity in 2019 amid infighting and backlash against right-wing political violence before latching onto its next theme — what it described as "government overreach" during the Coronavirus pandemic.
Preliminary official results confirm AfD short of ruling majority despite landslide victory
The preliminary official results from Sunday's state elections have confirmed the AfD's historic win with tabulations remaining unchanged from a few hours prior.
The far-right party captured 39 seats in all, meaning it eclipsed all other competitors, yet fell just shy of winning an outright ruling majority.
International press calls AfD win a 'clear signal'
Outside Germany, international observers have called Sunday's AfD electoral victory in Saxony-Anhalt a "clear signal" for establishment parties.
New York's Wall Street Journal pointed to liberal immigration policy and weak economic performance as major contributors to the win, writing that conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz had disappointed voters despite exhibiting the right economic and foreign policy reform instincts. The WSJ called the victory a "warning" that voters could ultimately gamble on letting the AfD lead the country alone.
In Italy, La Repubblica described an "unsettling new page in German history," noting that Saxony-Anhalt's voters — who represent only three percent of Germany's overall population — had betrayed the vow "never again" by choosing a rightwing extremist party espousing the "inhumane ideas" of the Nazi era to run their state.
Milan's Corriere della Sera echoed that sentiment, saying that Germany would "never be the same," and emphasizing that the whole of Europe seems as if "hypnotized by the extreme right."
And in Spain, El Pais wrote that the vote would force Europe's democrats to rethink the tired approach of either imitating far-right extremists in hopes of siphoning off voters or attempting to isolate them. The paper pointed to the AfD in Germany but also France's National Rally (RN) as examples of establishment parties failing to hold back extremists despite the clear moral and political imperative of rejecting cooperation with parties that "question the founding principles of post war democracies."
Elon Musk congratulates AfD on election victory in Saxony-Anhalt
Tech entrepreneur and the world's richest man, Elon Musk, who has backed Germany’s far-right AfD, congratulated the party on its Saxony-Anhalt election victory.
"Gut gemacht!" (Well Done!) Musk wrote on his social media platform X in response to a post by AfD co-leader Alice Weidel congratulating the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund on the result in Saxony-Anhalt.
Siegmund promptly replied to Musk, thanking him for his "support."
"If we take responsibility here, I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation. Germany would once again be a place worth investing in," Siegmund wrote.
Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, the AfD has strengthened its ties with Washington, with Alice Weidel calling the US president a role model and AfD representatives attending his inauguration.
Elon Musk, then a close Trump adviser, openly campaigned for the AfD and continues to back far-right political figures.
Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance sees a 'political reset'
Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the populist BSW, called for a "political reset" in Saxony-Anhalt after the party narrowly cleared the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament.
"There are hopefully now majorities in the Magdeburg state parliament for a change in energy policy, an end to the Russia sanctions, better education and a fundamental reform of public broadcasting," Wagenknecht told dpa.
Since its founding in January 2024, Wagenknecht’s BSW has positioned itself as economically left-wing but culturally conservative. She supports higher minimum wages and rent caps but also backs tougher immigration policies.
She has repeatedly blamed the West for Russia’s war in Ukraine and opposed sanctions against Moscow. BSW politicians, like some AfD figures, have also been accused of maintaining ties with supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"The BSW’s comeback has begun," she said, adding "the result would boost her party’s campaign ahead of state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin."
The far-right AfD fell short of an outright majority, leaving the shape of a government in Saxony-Anhalt unclear. Wagenknecht has ruled out a coalition with the AfD but not cooperation, potentially giving her party the balance of power.
"The policy of keeping the AfD out of government has failed. Simply trying to form another coalition to exclude the AfD would be an affront to voters." she said.
AfD faces uncertain coalition options after Saxony-Anhalt win
According to preliminary official results, the AfD emerged as the largest party but fell short of a governing majority in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. The far-right party therefore faces challenges in forming a government.
AfD lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt Ulrich Siegmund said his party’s result represented "a clear mandate to govern."
At the same time, the 35-year-old said he currently saw no potential coalition partners. However, he added that he did not know what might happen in the coming days.
"I don’t know whether there are individual lawmakers who might say: 'That’s it, I’m not playing along with this anymore,'" he said, adding, "A lot can still happen." Following the historic win, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said: "Ulrich Siegmund will definitely run as a candidate for state premier in the state parliament. That much is certain."
If efforts to form a government fail, Siegmund said a new election could also be an option. "In the worst-case scenario, there would simply be new elections, and then we would get 50% or 55%," he said.
Is coalition without AfD possible?
The only coalition that would have a numerical majority without the AfD would be an alliance of all the other parties. However, under a resolution adopted previously, the center-right CDU rules out not only a coalition with the AfD but also with the Left Party. This policy is known as the " political firewall."
That would also be a stumbling block for a CDU-led minority government. In addition, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) could potentialy hold the balance of power with five seats. Its leadership has ruled out supporting CDU.
Following the election, the previously governing coalition of the CDU, SPD and FDP will end. However, state premier Sven Schulze and his Cabinet will remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new state premier is elected.
Is Germany’s "political firewall" against the AfD collapsing?
Germany’s mainstream parties have long maintained a "political firewall" against cooperation with the far-right Alternative for Germany. But that firewall is under growing pressure following the AfD’s historic win in the Saxony-Anhalt state election and prospects in other forthcoming state elections.
The term refers to efforts by established parties to prevent extremist parties from gaining political influence through cooperation or shared votes. The center-right CDU formally rejected cooperation with the AfD in 2018.
But in January 2025, a CDU motion in the Bundestag passed with AfD support, prompting accusations that Chancellor Friedrich Merz had breached the firewall.
The AfD’s growing electoral strength is now raising fresh questions about how long the firewall can hold and what its future means for Germany’s political center.
Read here for more context: What is the 'political firewall' against Germany's far-right AfD?
AfD wins most votes in Saxony-Anhalt, preliminary official results show
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% of the vote in Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state election, according to preliminary official results, making it the largest party, but falling short of a governing majority in the regional parliament.
Six parties will be represented in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt, which has 83 seats:
- Alternative for Germany (AfD) — 43.8%, 39 seats
- Christian Democratic Union (CDU) — 17.2%, 15 seats
- Social Democratic Party (SPD) — 9.3%, 8 seats
- Green Party — 8.9%, 8 seats
- Left Party — 8.6%, 8 seats
- Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) — 5.3%, 5 seats
Meanwhile, the business-focused Free Democrats (FDP) secured only 2.6% of the vote, failing to reach the 5% threshold.
According to the preliminary results, turnout was almost 78%, the highest in Saxony-Anhalt since German reunification in 1990.
