Jamaica to file slavery reparations petition during UK visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:34:57 UTC
10:34:57 KST

Jamaica to file slavery reparations petition during UK visit
Petition to King Charles questions the legality of slavery under English law and UK’s responsibility for reparations.
A Jamaican delegation to the United Kingdom has said it will file a petition addressed to King Charles III to seek legal guidance on the question of slavery reparations.
This is the first time a British Commonwealth state will use this legal route “for the cause of reparatory justice”, the Jamaican delegation said, as the visit to London kicks off Monday.
Jamaica’s Ministry of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport said its minister, Olivia Grange, will lead the delegation “to advance Jamaica’s push for reparations for the African ancestors who suffered under hundreds of years of enslavement”.
The ministry added that it will meet with the British Museum to discuss “the repatriation of cultural artefacts taken from Jamaica”.
The petition will ask the king, Jamaica’s head of state, to answer three questions on the transatlantic slave trade to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the Caribbean island’s highest court of appeal based in London.
Under the Judicial Committee Act of 1833, the UK monarch has the authority to refer legal matters to the court for an advisory opinion.
The questions include: whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English common law, whether it violated international law, and whether the UK has a legal obligation to provide a remedy for the harm caused by slavery.
Grange said she would not speculate on whether Jamaica was asking the UK to pay reparations for the slave trade.
“We want the answers. Once we get the answers, or once we get a response to those questions, then the next steps will be determined,” she said.
“We understand the Jamaican government is seeking a petition to be heard before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council,” a Buckingham Palace spokesperson said in response to Jamaica’s inquiry.
The palace acknowledged the king’s constitutional role in the petition as Jamaica’s head of state but said he had no role in deciding the substance of the claim.
British merchants enslaved and forcibly transported 600,000 to 1 million Africans to Jamaica between the 17th century and the early 19th century.
Shortly after abolishing slavery in 1833, the UK paid slave owners $27m in compensation, amounting to 40 percent of the Treasury’s annual income. To raise the cash, the government took out considerable loans, finally paying off its debts in 2015.
The Jamaican government estimates that the country is owed about $10bn, but the UK has repeatedly refused to pay for historical slavery.

Robert Pattinson Is Disturbing and Alluring in Primetime, a Sordid Movie About a Sordid TV Show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:17:33 UTC
10:17:33 KST

In the early 2000s, if your idea of a cheap thrill was to see presumed sicko pedophiles caught on camera as they advance upon their ostensibly underage prey, NBC’s To Catch a Predator was your show. The host, Chris Hansen, had once been considered a serious journalist, spearheading investigative reports on events like the Columbine shootings and the World Trade Center attacks. But on the sleazy, sensationalistic To Catch a Predator, he was more of a vigilante showman. The show worked like this: A crusading organization called Perverted Justice would initiate conversations in online chatrooms designed to attract potential sex offenders. Then they’d be lured to sting houses outfitted with hidden cameras, where Hansen and his crew would await their arrival, ready to enact a pruriently dramatic Gotcha! moment, generally followed by an arrest. Nobody likes a pedophile, and without leaving the Barcalounger, viewers could revel in the self-congratulatory certainty that they too were helping to keep the world safe for the kiddos.
Documentary filmmaker Lance Oppenheim’s first fiction feature Primetime—premiering here at the Venice Film Festival—fills in some background pixels on the show’s rise and fall, focusing particularly on an ambitious, egotistical, and at least somewhat delusional Hansen, played by Robert Pattinson. It’s 2006, and Hansen and his beleaguered producer Andie (Merritt Wever, bringing an edgy nervousness to the role of a woman struggling to stay afloat in the ruthless world of TV news) get a chance to move their show into a primetime slot. The stakes are high, but the potential rewards are great. Hansen’s hubris balloons, and he infects others with his own inflated sense of the public service he claims to be providing. To complete its mission of reeling in the bad guys, the show employs youthful-looking decoys posing as underage kids. One of these is an elflike performer named Del (singer-songwriter Phoebe Bridgers) who can impersonate either a boy or a girl; she passes some tips along to a nervous newcomer who will come to be known as Decoy Dan (Skyler Gisondo, in a performance laced with touching eagerness). Though he hopes to become a real actor and thinks this is his way in, he wants to quit when he sees how demeaning the gig actually is. But Hansen, with his crocodile smile and purring, almost sultry intonation, persuades him to stick with it, assuring him that he’ll be helping to cleanse the world of evil.
Hansen has gotten high on what he perceives as his own power, and his ambitions grow even greater as he and his team try to draw in a “whale,” ideally a major government figure, rather than the pathetically sad—though still dangerous and repellent—lowlifes who tend to creep into their trap. These thankless roles are heroically played by an assortment of actors including Tony Revolori; despite his character’s unsavory and illegal intentions, his tremulous shock at being caught underscores the show’s legally questionable entrapment methods.
Hansen’s unfolding mania is one of the chief features of Primetime, and Pattinson’s performance is one of the only reasons to see it. As he practices dialogue that he’ll use in the show, drawn from the chatroom fodder that has lured the show’s marks into its trap, he relishes the prurient material a little too much: “I will undress you, you will undress me.” His theatrically precise diction is both disturbing and weirdly alluring.
Still, it’s not exactly clear what Primetime is aiming for: it seems to be making the point that while sexual predators are unequivocally bad, the people who make trash TV—particularly a sordid show that’s masquerading as a means of protecting kids and meting out justice—are also immoral, scheming, and just all-around unpleasant. That’s a shaky equivalence. Oppenheim, director of docs like Spermworld and Some Kind of Heaven, structures the film as if he were shaping a mosaic from disorienting shards; sometimes the scenes feel jaggedly disconnected. He and cinematographer David Bolen have given the picture a grubby, grainy look, including sections that mimic early-2000s-style video recording. If you feel dirty watching it, that’s by design—and if you enjoy feeling dirty, that’s your choice.

Trump supports renaming New Mexico to New America

WASHINGTON, September 7. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump expressed support for a proposal to rename New Mexico "New America" on his Truth Social page.
"Many people suggested changing the name of New Mexico, one of the great vote cheating states of all time, to New America. So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible state. Wow, I love it!" the US leader wrote. An AI-generated video accompanying the post shows the president changing the state’s name on a roadside sign in New Mexico while dancing to the Village People’s hit "YMCA."
According to the US Constitution, the federal government cannot change state names; this is the prerogative of state authorities and residents. After the new name is approved by the state legislature and then by the population in a referendum, the relevant amendments must be made to state law. If the proposal is approved, state authorities will inform Congress and the US government of the changes. New Mexico media outlets have reported that residents do not support renaming the state.
Previously, the president signed executive orders renaming the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario the Gulf of America and Lake America, respectively. These orders change how the federal government and federal maps refer to these places. However, future presidents could sign executive orders reversing these changes.

Ancient roots: China pioneering sex therapist warns of rise of ‘relationship blind’ phenomenon
Tong recalls a client whose single father advised her to ‘wear more clothes’ after she faced school sexual harassment
Behind many sexual difficulties lie questions that extend far beyond the confines of the bedroom. After years of assisting clients in navigating issues of intimacy and relationships, one of China’s pioneering sex therapists has observed how gaps in education and communication shape individuals’ most private struggles.
Originally from Taiwan, Tong Songzhen began her career as a nurse before attaining a doctorate in sexology from Shu-Te University. Since 2016, she has established sex therapy practices in Beijing, Shanghai, and Shenzhen.
Tong shared with the SCMP that most of her clients are between the ages of 30 and 50, with men comprising about 80 per cent of her clientele. While male clients often seek help for sexual dysfunction, women typically experience greater insecurity in intimate relationships.
Her clientele has included two PhD holders who lacked fundamental sexual knowledge and mistakenly believed that pregnancy could result merely from sharing a bed. She also worked with an 80-year-old man who, after enduring the effects of a stroke for two decades, sought to rekindle physical intimacy with his partner.
“Sex is never solely about sexual organs. It encompasses an entire system that involves the body, psychology, and social relationships,” she emphasised.

Ukraine lost $1.2 bn to defense fraud and waste in one year – NYT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:12:05 UTC
10:12:05 KST

Ukraine lost $1.2 bn to defense fraud and waste in one year – NYT
Ukraine lost around $1.2 billion to fraud, waste and mismanagement in military procurement in 2024 alone, the New York Times has reported, citing confidential government audits and court records.
Seven of the country’s ten largest military contractors continued to receive new orders despite fraud investigations, previous failures to deliver, or the arrest of executives on corruption charges, the paper wrote on Sunday, describing the pattern as a “persistent phenomenon.”
Auditors also identified 18 companies awarded contracts despite earlier defaults, six of which had failed to fulfill a single deal.
Defense industry fraud is “a longstanding tradition” in Ukraine, American anti-corruption expert James Wasserstrom has told the NYT. “Anything that isn’t nailed down in Ukraine will be stolen,” he said.
Among the cases highlighted by the Times was the state-owned Pavlohrad Chemical Plant, which supplied the military with 233,000 unusable mortar rounds. Nevertheless, the company later received more business, including a contract to supply nearly all of Ukraine’s 122mm artillery rounds in 2025.
The audits also found that cheaper offers were sometimes bypassed. In one tender, Kiev reportedly bought Turkish-made munitions for multiple-launch rocket systems through a Czech intermediary for around $5,100 each despite the manufacturer offering them directly for roughly $4,200.
The losses accumulated as Vladimir Zelensky repeatedly appealed to Western governments for more weapons, warning of critical shortages on the battlefield. In April 2024, he said Kiev was in “dire need” of increased support and pressed its backers to deliver promised arms and ammunition.
The report comes amid a series of high-profile graft investigations involving top Ukrainian officials and figures close to Zelensky. In August, the Ukrainian leader sacked the deputy head of his office, Irina Mudraya, while other recent corruption probes have implicated former ministers, diplomats and senior officials.
Former Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov, meanwhile, accused the government of “systemic corruption” following his dismissal in July. Fedorov, who had sought to overhaul military procurement, has claimed that entrenched defense-industry interests resisted his reforms and has since called for wartime elections.
Zelensky’s five-year presidential term expired in May 2024, but he has refused to hold a new election, citing martial law imposed after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022.
Moscow has long argued that the scandals are evidence of systemic corruption in Ukraine. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said earlier this year that corruption “permeates the entire Ukrainian power structure, including Zelensky’s inner circle and Zelensky himself.”

Volcano eruption in Indonesia leaves 170,000 travellers stranded as seven airports remain closed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:11:34 UTC
10:11:34 KST

Seven Indonesian airports – including two serving Jakarta – remained closed on Monday morning because of volcanic ash from eruptions at Mount Anak Krakatau, the transport minister said.
Ash from Anak Krakatau, which sits halfway between Java and Sumatra islands, has blanketed Jakarta and several surrounding areas since it erupted late on Friday, leading to the closure of the airports for safety reasons.
The transport ministry said 170,000 people have been affected by flight cancellations.
The suspension at Jakarta’s main airport was extended until 6pm Monday local time, along with six other airports, the airport authority said. The airports include ones serving Jakarta’s nearby provinces of Lampung and West Java.
“We cannot ascertain when this will end due to the dynamic weather,” the transport minister, Dudy Purwagandhi, said.
“To date, 1,558 flights have been delayed at the eight affected airports, with 170,000 passengers stranded,” the ministry said in a statement on Sunday. More than 900 affected flights were to and from the Soekarno-Hatta, it added.
Schools across Jakarta were also affected with classes moving online on Monday, the city said in a statement, without specifying how long the measure would be in place.
Some shipping has also been disrupted.
Eruptions of Anak Krakatau on Saturday produced a fountain of lava and booming sounds that could be heard up to a few hundred kilometres away, the geology agency said.
There were more eruptions on Sunday, with the volcano monitoring agency’s website showing the most recent occurring on Sunday at 8.23pm.
The agency warned on Monday that “the probability of further eruptions in the coming periods remains high”.
Ash from the volcano was detected in the airspace surrounding Soekarno-Hatta international airport, prompting authorities to suspend operations, the ministry said.
The disruption left some passengers scrambling to find alternative flights.
Henny Yensan, 44, who had hoped to go back to her home town with her mother, said “everybody was disappointed”.
“No one flew into a rage because, after all, this is due to natural disaster,” the businesswoman who had to reschedule her flight to Tuesday told AFP.
Volcanic ash also reached the city of Bandar Lampung in the southern tip of Sumatra, blanketing parked cars and roadsides.
Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatau, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra.
Ships passing through the strait were asked to increase vigilance for possible disruption to navigation safety due to volcanic activities.
Vessels are prohibited from approaching an exclusion zone of a 3km radius from the volcano, local port authorities said in a statement.
The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera that formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatau.
That disaster was one of the deadliest and most destructive in history with an estimated 35,000 people killed.
Geology agency head Lana Saria warned against approaching Anak Krakatau, saying materials ejected from the volcano could endanger those within the exclusion zone.
She said the most recent series of eruptions do not have the potential to trigger a tsunami.
A 2018 tsunami triggered by a collapse of parts of Anak Krakatau killed 429 people and left thousands displaced.
Indonesia, a South-east Asian archipelago nation, sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the meeting of continental plates causes high volcanic and seismic activity.

Why is Kenya cracking down on foreign traders and small retailers?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:08:55 UTC
10:08:55 KST

Why is Kenya cracking down on foreign traders and small retailers?
President Ruto says small businesses should be reserved for Kenyans as his government moves against foreign traders.
Kenya is beginning a crackdown on foreign nationals operating small retail shops and engaging in hawking, after President William Ruto directed authorities to shut down such businesses from September 7.
Ruto made the announcement on September 2 while addressing micro, small and medium-sized enterprise (MSME) traders at State House in Nairobi.
He said foreigners should not compete with Kenyans in businesses such as hawking and small retail, while foreign investment was welcome in activities requiring greater capital and investment.
What is Kenya doing?
Ruto directed authorities to begin shutting down small businesses operated by foreign nationals from September 7, saying hawking and small-scale retail should be reserved for Kenyans.
He said the government would take administrative action while the Parliament of Kenya considers the proposed Local Content Bill, 2025.
He also directed National Assembly Majority Leader Kimani Ichung’wah and Trade Cabinet Secretary Lee Kinyanjui to accelerate the bill’s passage through Parliament.
Why is Kenya moving against foreign traders and small retailers?
Hesbon Hansen Owilla, a professor at Aga Khan University in Nairobi, said the policy would help protect Kenyan traders.
“Yes, this is the best way to protect Kenyan small businesses and traders,” he told Al Jazeera. “Kenya is trying to bring in only investors who are bringing capital that can spur economic development by creating jobs rather than allow small-time foreign traders who only stifle Kenyan small traders while enjoying the robust infrastructure that Kenya has built and social securities.”
“It’s like expatriates. A country cannot allow expatriates in for jobs locals have expertise in,” he said.
The proposed Local Content Bill, 2025, would require foreign companies to increase local sourcing and employment, among other measures.
The bill is still being considered by Parliament and has not yet been enacted into law.
What businesses and traders are affected?
The directive is aimed at foreign nationals operating small retail shops and engaging in hawking. Ruto specifically referred to hawking and small shops when announcing the crackdown.
Kenya’s broader micro, small and medium-sized enterprise (MSME) sector covers a wider range of businesses. The government has not publicly provided a comprehensive list of all businesses covered by the September 7 directive or an estimate of how many foreign nationals will be affected.
Ruto also directed Ichung’wah to engage the State Department for Immigration’s principal secretary and establish the requirements governing permits issued to foreign investors and traders. It is therefore not yet clear how the directive will apply to foreign nationals who already hold permits to conduct business in Kenya.
Foreign Affairs Principal Secretary Korir Sing’Oei said on September 6 that foreign nationals who meet Kenya’s legal requirements, including holding the necessary work permits and licences, remain legally protected to operate businesses in the country. He said Ruto’s remarks had been taken out of context and were made in the context of the Local Content Bill, 2025.
How significant is foreign investment in Kenya?
Kenya’s 2024 Foreign Investment Survey, the latest such survey published by the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS), put the country’s stock of foreign direct investment at 1.458 trillion Kenyan shillings ($11.27bn) at the end of 2023, up 8.5 percent from 1.343 trillion Kenyan shillings ($10.4bn) at the end of 2022.
These figures cover foreign investment across the Kenyan economy and are not limited to the small-scale trading activities targeted by Ruto’s directive.
Surveyed foreign-invested enterprises employed 224,769 people in June 2024, including 221,267 Kenyan employees. Foreign employees accounted for 1.6 percent of the workforce in those enterprises.
What is the Tata Chemicals case?
The Tata Chemicals dispute is separate from the small-business crackdown.
Tata Chemicals Magadi operates a soda ash business at Lake Magadi in Kajiado County. On July 28, the Kenyan government suspended the company’s mining operations, citing alleged compliance issues under the country’s mining laws. The suspension also affected its soda ash exports.
On September 3, Ruto said he had ordered Tata Chemicals to leave Kenya, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local community in Kajiado County. He said the government would bring in two new companies to establish glass and chemical manufacturing facilities in the area.
Tata Chemicals said it had submitted the information requested by Kenyan authorities and was awaiting further communication. The company has said it complied with regulatory requirements and remained committed to resolving the matter through legal and regulatory channels.
The Tata dispute concerns the company’s soda ash operations at Lake Magadi. This is separate from the directive targeting foreign nationals operating small retail businesses and hawking.
What does this mean for foreign investment?
International business consultant and Sols Inclinations Ltd Managing Director Solomon Kinyanjui said the distinction was not between welcoming foreign investment and rejecting it, but between foreign capital that complements Kenyan enterprise and activity that displaces it.
“The issue is not whether foreign capital is welcome, but what role it should play in Kenya’s economy,” he told Al Jazeera. “Foreign investment should complement Kenyan enterprise, not substitute for economic activities Kenyans can competitively undertake themselves.”
He said the stronger case for foreign investment was where it brought capital, technology, skills, industrial capacity and access to export markets, but warned that the government needed to draw the boundary clearly and apply its rules predictably.
Hafsa Abdiwahab Sheikh, a journalist, said the policy could have both benefits and costs depending on how it is implemented.
“The policy could create more jobs for Kenyans and encourage skills transfer, while helping protect local employment,” she told Al Jazeera.
“However, if implemented unpredictably, it may discourage foreign investment and increase business costs, leading to higher prices. It could also affect relations with foreign communities if foreigners are blamed for unemployment.”

Hong Kong’s top financial regulators have urged local banks to make greater use of the city’s growing pool of offshore yuan liquidity, while also flagging the need to prepare for a coming wave of autonomous AI systems used in the financial sector.

Kyiv introduces tiered air threat alert system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
00:36:00 UTC
09:36:00 KST

Kyiv introduces tiered air threat alert system
According to Ukrinform, the Kyiv City State Administration announced this on Telegram.
From now on, city residents may receive the following alerts:
Yellow level: “Drone danger”;
Red level: “Massive drone threat”; “Missile threat”; “Missile and drone threat.”
Green: “All clear” – no threats or dangers.
Each new alert indicates the current type and level of threat.
If the type of threat changes, a new alert automatically replaces the previous one.
A separate “All Clear” is not issued between different types of threats.
For example, if a “Missile Threat” alert follows a “Drone Danger” alert, this means that a missile threat is now active.
An “All Clear” alert means that none of the listed air threats have been detected in the city at this time.
The Kyiv City State Administration noted that the differentiated alert system is currently in place in all districts of Kyiv except Pecherskyi.
In the Holosiivskyi and Sviatoshynskyi districts, it is partially operational. This is because, in certain areas, differentiating between types of threats is not yet technically feasible.
Therefore, the procedure for audible alerts remains unchanged there: in the event of any air danger or threat, a standard siren signal is sounded without separate differentiation by threat type and without an “All Clear” signal.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Ukraine will update its air threat warning system, specifically introducing a “yellow” threat level for drone attacks and a “red” level for missiles. There are also plans to differentiate the audio signals and the geographic scope of the alerts.

While both he and the US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had given upbeat assessments of the talks, neither announced any breakthroughs on ending the conflict.
But the senior Ukrainian official told AFP: "It's not the same as it was before. This one now is more effective. They're still talking. This is actually the most important part."
Witkoff, who is President Donald Trump's business ally, and Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, travelled to Kyiv a day after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow -- the latest of several visits to the city.
Ukraine's rail operator announced their departure from Kyiv in a post on Telegram early Monday, accompanied by a photo of the two envoys' standing under a station sign announcing the "Peace Express".
Sunday's visit to Kyiv was their first to the Ukrainian capital, which has been enduring deadly Russian strikes for more than four years.
Zelensky said: "We very much hope that we will be able to reach agreements with our American partners, and we are counting on the support of our European partners if the war continues in winter -- and this is how it appears at the moment."
Zelensky also said Ukraine would hold talks with the US, France and Germany, but did not elaborate. And he repeated his call that only a meeting between the two leaders could solve territorial issues.
Thanking the US envoys for their visit, Zelensky said on X: "The main thing is to achieve peace for Ukraine -- a dignified, reliable, and lasting peace. We are directing all our efforts toward this."
Read moreUkraine-Russia talks: What are the US objectives?
'On same side'
Moscow occupies large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine and the Kremlin told the Americans on Saturday it was feeling "confident" it would advance more.
Moscow has said it wants not just the territories it occupies but the land it claims as Russian to be recognised as its own -- terms unacceptable to Kyiv.
Witkoff said both sides would need to compromise, adding: "We think we have the ingredients to get to that place.
"We've had a very meaningful discussion, substantive, important, and we are very encouraged and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes."
Kushner added: "Hopefully this trip has come out with some new ways to advance forward. I think we've learned a lot from the trip."
Witkoff and Kushner travelled to the region hoping to revive the Trump administration's push for peace in Europe's worst conflict since World War II, after a summer of escalation.
British, French and German representatives attended a separate round of the talks.
Zelensky said he was grateful the Europeans were there, adding: "Here we are all on the same side."
Like all visiting officials, the US delegation had arrived by train, with "Peace Express" written on the platform at Kyiv Central Station.
Ukrainian airspace has been closed since Russia launched its invasion in 2022.
Russia and Ukraine vowed not to strike each other's capitals during the US envoys' trip.
Read more'A bad sign': US envoys head to Kyiv after three-hour talks with Putin
'Substantive plans'
Moscow's invasion has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
A White House official said in a statement to AFP that in Moscow the envoys had "discussed substantive plans which will be announced in the coming weeks".
Without elaborating, the Kremlin said the Americans had "put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement".
Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine, and Russia increased deadly strikes this summer.
Since Putin launched the invasion in February 2022, the war has dragged on with no end in sight.
In Kyiv, few people appeared to believe in a breakthrough.
Nataliia Lipekh, 67, said it was "absolutely necessary (for them) to be here" and to see that "our land is already soaked with this blood and that we need some help".
"At the moment, I have no grounds for hope," said 29-year-old Yaroslav, saying he had seen "far too many of these negotiation processes".

EU to boost Greenland investment amid Trump annexation claims

Her two-day visit signals support for Greenland and Denmark amid US President Donald Trump’s push for American control of the Arctic territory.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is expected to unveil on Monday a boost in EU investments in Greenland and closer political ties with the Danish Arctic territory, which Donald Trump has insisted should belong to the United States.
Von der Leyen arrived in Greenland on Sunday for a two-day visit serving as a show of support for the governments of Greenland and Denmark, which have strongly rebuffed Trump’s campaign to annex the world’s largest island.
The head of the 27-nation European Union's executive body, von der Leyen is expected to unveil plans to invest in sectors including critical minerals, satellite communications and renewable energy in Greenland, a semi-autonomous part of the Danish realm.
Read moreNATO's Arctic activity poses 'direct threat' to Russia, Lavrov warns
On Sunday in Nuuk, the capital, von der Leyen said the package would be "substantial" but gave no details. Greenland Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen said his country wanted to build on its "close friendship and good partnership" with the EU.
Von der Leyen's visit reflects the increasing geopolitical importance of the Arctic to major powers, such as the United States, Russia, China and Europe, as melting ice opens new shipping routes to make the region’s mineral wealth more accessible.
"Greenland's stunning landscapes and natural beauty will stay with me for a long time. But so will the visible scars of climate change on the ice sheet," von der Leyen posted on X after a boat trip under clear blue skies in a fjord scattered with chunks of ice.
"As the ice melts, a new reality is taking shape."
Trump, the US president, sparked a crisis in US-European ties and turmoil within the transatlantic NATO military alliance this year when he stepped up his demands for the US to control Greenland, arguing that fellow NATO member Denmark could not defend it.
Read moreTensions in the Arctic: Greenland issues sharp rebuke to Trump-linked oil company
European officials stressed Greenland is part of NATO territory, meaning it is covered by the alliance’s mutual defence pact, and that the US already has the right to increase its military presence there under a longstanding treaty.
Tensions lowered after Trump and NATO boss Mark Rutte agreed in Davos in January that the United States, Denmark and Greenland would begin talks to resolve their differences and NATO would step up its role in Arctic security.
However, the trilateral talks have yet to yield an agreement and, at a NATO summit in Turkey in July, Trump restated his insistence that the US should control Greenland.
While Denmark is a member of the EU, Greenland left the bloc in 1985. But its people, as Danish citizens, are also citizens of the EU.
The EU has long provided funding to Greenland, mainly to pay for fishing rights and support its education system. The package to be announced by von der Leyen will represent not only a big increase in funding but a broadening of the sectors that will receive EU cash, according to EU officials.

Marnus Labuschagne will travel to South Africa for next month's Test tour of South Africa after being named in a 16-man squad.
There have been calls for the number three to be dropped after more than three years without a Test century, but the 32-year-old has kept his spot for the tour despite being left out of the side for six ODIs leading up to the Test series.
Australia's men's team will play three ODIs against Zimbabwe in Harare followed by three more 50-over games against South Africa in Durban, Johannesburg and Potchefstroom before the Tests in Durban (October 9-13), Gqeberha (October 18-22) and Cape Town (October 27-31).
Chairman of selectors George Bailey said a pure focus on red-ball cricket "may be a benefit" for Labuschagne.
"Not shying away from the fact we'd like some more runs from Marn, that's clear," he said.
"But we're also confident he can still make a positive contribution to that squad."
Labuschagne has never played a Test in South Africa, where he was born and spent the first 10 years of his life.
Big-hitting Cooper Connolly, spinner Matthew Kuhnemann and seamer Michael Neser, another South Africa-born Australian, have been added to the group that contested the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay last month.
Bailey said Connolly, who bowls part-time spin, had been selected primarily for his batting, with Josh Inglis the only other batter in the squad outside the XI from the Bangladesh series.
Both players have traditionally batted in the middle order in first-class cricket.
It leaves the team without a huge number of options for change if the batting line-up continues to struggle.
"Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn't been functioning as successfully as we would like," he admitted.
"But we've continued to win a lot of Test matches over that period and that ultimately is the key, scoring more runs than the opposition."
Connolly, 23, is one of three players in the squad under 30, along with 29-year-old Kuhnemann and 27-year-old all-rounder Cameron Green, with the latter the only incumbent in the team.
It raises concerns about an impending transition as the majority of the team ages out with little Test experience in younger players behind them.
"Age is a big focus for some, performance I think is important," Bailey said.
"We're confident around where that group's at and also over the ensuing months years as the transitions occur, be that through performance or players dropping out of formats, there'll be good people that are well placed to come in and perform in whichever team that is."

North Korea deploys warship ‘capable of annihilating retaliatory strikes’
Leader Kim Jong Un says vessel will form part of Pyongyang’s nuclear response system, strengthen naval forces.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attended the commissioning of a warship he said could deliver “annihilating retaliatory strikes on an enemy”, citing “constant threats”, according to the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
The Kang Kon, named after the North Korean military leader who was killed in action during the Korean War, was formally deployed at a ceremony at the eastern Wonsan Port in Kangwon Province on Sunday.
Recommended Stories

- list 3 of 3North Korea fires ballistic missiles as US-South Korea drills near end
In his address, Kim said the warship “represents the self-respect and will” of North Korea to defend its rights and interests, KCNA reported.
“The time has come for us to exercise our sovereignty at sea and under water,” Kim said, according to KCNA.
He said that “dangerous shadows must be erased” and that North Korea was under constant threat in the “sea east of the Korean Peninsula and nearby waters”, KCNA reported.
KCNA did not specify what weapons systems might be deployed on the Kang Kon, but said it has the same weapons systems as the 5,000-tonne warship Choe Hyon launched in June.
A previous KCNA report said Choe Hyon-class destroyers can carry a range of weapons, including missiles that analysts say are capable of carrying a nuclear payload.
The ship was commissioned a day before the US, South Korea and Japan were set to begin a five-day military exercise in waters east and south of South Korea’s Jeju Island.
South Korea’s military said in a statement that the Freedom Edge exercise is defensive in nature and meant to respond to North Korean nuclear and missile threats as well as promote regional peace and stability.
North Korea has previously slammed the trilateral drill as a “reckless show of strength”.
Sunday marks the third launch of the Kang Kon; the destroyer partially capsized during the first commissioning in May 2025 before it was repaired and relaunched the following month. It underwent further repairs and sea trials before completing weapons testing in July this year.
Kim said he would demonstrate another stage of North Korea’s naval buildup in eight months, KCNA said, without giving details.
North Korea has accelerated efforts to modernise its navy as Kim pursues a broader expansion of the country’s nuclear-capable forces.
He also said the construction of naval bases on North Korea’s east coast was under way and that the country would create new naval units and build different classes of warships.
Pyongyang, which calls itself an “irreversible” nuclear state, frames the build-up as deterrence against Washington and Seoul. The Korean Peninsula remains technically at war, and Kim has accused the allies of driving the region “to the brink of a nuclear war”.

Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:01:32 BST
09:01:32 KST

Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school
- Published
As the new school year begins in Austria, a law banning headscarves in schools for girls under 14 has gone into force.
The law forbids "traditional Muslim" head coverings, such as hijabs or burkas, in public and private schools across the country.
Integration Minister Claudia Bauer, from the conservative People's Party (ÖVP), says the headscarf is "a sign of oppression and a means of controlling girls from the earliest childhood".
But critics say the new law is fuelling anti-Muslim feeling in the country and could be unconstitutional.
The law was brought in by the conservative-led coalition of three centrist parties, the ÖVP, the Social Democrats (SPÖ) and the liberal Neos. They say the law is a "clear commitment to gender equality" and is intended to protect the rights of young girls.
Carla Amina Baghajati, from the official Islamic Community in Austria (IGGÖ), told the BBC that the organisation "firmly opposes the ban".
"We believe it unjustifiably restricts the fundamental right to freedom of religion and disproportionately affects Muslim girls," she said.
"Rather than protecting children, it singles out a specific religious practice and risks excluding the very children it claims to support."
The IGGÖ said it would support legal challenges by girls and their families "who believe that their fundamental rights are being infringed" and who wished to bring their cases before the Constitutional Court.
The court struck down a previous ban on headscarves in primary schools in 2020 on the basis that it contravened the principle of Austria's religious neutrality.
Teachers are expected to enforce the new ban if they see a child wearing a headscarf by holding a series of talks with the student and their legal guardians.
If there are repeated violations, child services must be notified and as a last resort, guardians could face fines of up to €800 (£685).
Some teachers have expressed concerns about having to enforce the ban.
The Green Party's Sigi Maurer accused Education Minister Christoph Wiederkehr, from the liberal NEOS, of "creating new conflicts and offloading them onto the teachers".
She said teachers were "already under enormous strain" and that Wiederkehr wanted to "foist the role of police officers onto them" on top of their other duties.
The opposition far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) says the current ban doesn't go far enough. It is calling for a general prohibition on headscarves and face coverings in schools for students and teachers alike.
The FPÖ's Ricarda Berger said there was "no place for political Islam in Austria, and certainly not in our schools".
Austria's Chancellor Christian Stocker, leader of the ÖVP, recently called for a constitutional ban on political Islam, telling Austrian public broadcaster ORF he did not "want to live in an Islamic state".
In France there has been a ban on wearing any conspicuous religious symbols, including headscarves, turbans and kippas, in schools for more than 20 years.
The Austrian law differs from French legislation in that it specifically targets head coverings worn by Muslim women.
Austria, like several other European countries including France, Belgium and Denmark, bans the full face veil (niqabs or burkas) in public.
Baghajati said the IGGÖ was concerned about "a troubling trend" across Europe "in which complex social challenges are reduced to symbolic measures aimed at minority groups."
"Such approaches may generate political attention, but they rarely solve the underlying problems," she said.

China marks major tunnel milestone for Central Asia railway bypassing Russia
Conceived in 1997, the 500km China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway will offer the shortest land route from China to the Middle East and Europe
This marks the first milestone for the flagship project under Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative, offering China a critical trade corridor bypassing Russia.
The 210-metre (690-foot) tunnel was the first drilled through in the Kyrgyz section since full-scale work began in June 2025, China’s state broadcaster CCTV reported on Saturday. Overall progress on the section had reached 17 per cent, it said.
The CKU Railway spans over 500km (310 miles), including about 305km in Kyrgyzstan alone. It runs from Kashgar in China’s western Xinjiang region through the mountains of Kyrgyzstan before terminating in Andijan, Uzbekistan.
It will also provide a vital trade gateway for southern Xinjiang, according to CCTV.

Nuclear waste plan for Japanese resort town sparks backlash: ‘not our problem’

The rural Japanese town of Hitachiomiya sprawls down the Naka River valley in northwest Ibaraki prefecture, surrounded by lush forests and overlooked by the picturesque Yamizo mountains. Just 140km (87 miles) from Tokyo, its golf courses attract weekend players, while onsen hot spring resorts in the surrounding hills keep local business steady year-round.
The local tourism association’s website highlights traditional festivals, campsites, hiking and cycling routes, alongside unique sights – including a complex of cave tombs on Mount Raijin, an ancient cedar grove and centuries-old temples and shrines.
Today, however, tourism representatives and municipal officials are more tight-lipped about the area’s attractions.
This week, Hitachiomiya Mayor Sadayuki Suzuki accepted a request from the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry for his community to undergo a preliminary survey to determine whether the town’s geology is suitable for a repository to store Japan’s large – and growing – stockpile of highly radioactive nuclear waste.
In a statement issued on Monday, Suzuki said the area showed a “relatively high probability of exhibiting favourable characteristics according to the scientific characteristics map”, adding that land was available “to install above-ground facilities for final disposal”.

How cognitive shortcuts fuel American political divisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
00:00:07 UTC
09:00:07 KST

When politically engaged individuals clash over public policy, their mutual dislike is often driven by how recognizable and organized their beliefs are. People who consistently hold strong liberal or conservative views express much more animosity toward opposing thinkers than those with moderate or mixed political opinions do. These findings, published in Political Behavior, suggest that the structure of a person’s worldview plays a central role in driving modern political divisions.
Political scientists often trace interpersonal hostility back to disagreements over specific public policies. In recent years, researchers have identified a divide in American politics based on political engagement. This divide separates individuals deeply involved in political conflict from bystanders who lack strong attachments to political parties. Not everyone approaches politics with the same level of intensity or organization.
Some voters possess highly structured belief systems. For these individuals, a stance on one issue reliably predicts their stance on another. Other citizens hold a mix of liberal and conservative views, or they remain ambivalent on major national issues. Tadeas Cely, a political science researcher at Masaryk University and Dartmouth College, wanted to find out how these different belief structures influence political hostility.
Past research often combined all policy disagreements into a single category. Cely sought to test whether clashing with a staunch ideologue generates different emotional reactions than clashing with a moderate. The research focused on two main traits: opinionatedness and belief alignment. Opinionatedness describes the tendency to hold strong views rather than neutral ones.
Belief alignment refers to how consistently a person’s views match a single political ideology, such as modern liberalism or conservatism. Together, these traits define what political scientists consider an ideologue. Cely hypothesized that disagreements among ideologues result in higher expected disagreement and greater mutual animosity.
When confronted with broad policy agendas, individuals often rely on cognitive shortcuts to inform their political decisions. In the context of public policy, belief patterns that follow recognizable structures provide mental cues for emotional reactions. Foundational literature on this topic describes a specific type of political thinker who knows which political ideas typically group together. For these individuals, a single political stance serves as a reliable indicator of a much larger worldview.
These politically sophisticated individuals can infer an entire belief system from a few distinct opinions. When ideologues encounter someone who expresses unambiguous, organized views, they instantly recognize the structural pattern. If the pattern aligns with their own, it signals a likable, belief-congruent peer. If the pattern opposes their own, it triggers an immediate emotional response of dislike, long before every individual policy is debated.
To investigate these dynamics, Cely conducted a large survey experiment involving 2,000 adults in the United States in early 2024. Participants reviewed hypothetical profiles of fellow citizens, each displaying stances on eight different public policies. The hypothetical citizens represented varying degrees of opinionatedness and ideological consistency. Participants then rated their feelings toward each profile on a standard thermometer scale measuring interpersonal warmth, ranging from completely cold to completely warm.
The results revealed that the nature of the opposing belief system heavily influences interpersonal affection. Disagreeing with an opinionated counterpart resulted in a substantial drop in positive feelings. For every single issue where opinions strongly clashed, warmth ratings plummeted. When participants disagreed with a centrist profile, meaning someone holding neutral positions on the issues, the resulting animosity was nearly four times lower.
The specific topic also mattered. Disagreements on highly debated issues like abortion, firearms regulation, and immigration produced the largest drops in warmth. The organization of a participant’s own beliefs also altered their emotional response. Participants with aligned beliefs, meaning they were consistently liberal or conservative, reported steep declines in affection when faced with an opposing profile.
Among these ideologically aligned individuals, the warmth gap between a similar-minded profile and a different-minded profile was massive. At the exact same level of policy disagreement, these structured ideologues experienced a much colder emotional reaction than non-ideologues. Participants with mixed or unstructured beliefs showed much less hostility toward profiles they disagreed with. They did not feel particularly warm toward similar-minded counterparts, but they also did not react with extreme animosity toward differing views.
A second large experiment, also involving 2,000 United States adults, explored why these structured belief systems produce such strong reactions. This survey tested whether ideologues expect to disagree more than others, even when the observed level of disagreement is identical. Participants read text-based descriptions of hypothetical citizens featuring four specific political opinions. These profiles represented either consistently liberal, consistently conservative, centrist, or mixed viewpoints.
Participants were then told the hypothetical citizen held opinions on two additional, unrevealed issues. These hidden issues were student debt relief and a ceasefire in Gaza. The participants had to predict the citizen’s stance on these hidden issues and estimate how often they would disagree with the person overall.
Cely found that ideologues use recognizable belief patterns as a mental shortcut. When a consistent liberal or conservative recognized an opposing ideological pattern in a profile, they anticipated high levels of disagreement on the unrevealed issues. Participants without a structured ideology did not make these same sweeping assumptions. This lack of assumptions among non-ideologues led to lower expectations of future conflict.
The anticipation of conflict was most pronounced among politically sophisticated participants. These individuals successfully recognized which political views typically group together. Because they could easily fill in the blanks of an opposing worldview, these politically savvy individuals expected the highest levels of overall disagreement. This assumed friction appears to fuel greater animosity before a specific policy is even discussed.
The research relies on a simplified measure of moderate beliefs. The survey design does not distinguish between participants who hold genuine, centrist policy preferences and those who are simply ambivalent. Separating these two groups could provide a more precise understanding of how moderation affects interpersonal hostility. Additionally, the study design measures the outcomes of differing belief systems but does not isolate the exact psychological mechanisms at play.
The heightened animosity among ideologues might stem from a general tendency toward closed-mindedness or intolerance of differing worldviews. Future research could involve directly manipulating the presentation of belief structures to isolate these cognitive processes. Expanding this framework to democracies outside the United States, where two to five distinct belief systems often coexist, would help determine how broadly these patterns apply.
The study, “Hatred Takes An Ideologue: Recognizable Belief Patterns Lead to More Animosity and Disagreement,” was authored by Tadeas Cely.

6 killed in Satya Niketan building collapse; FIR against owner
NEW DELHI: The death toll in the Satya Niketan building collapse in Delhi rose to six as search and rescue operations continued at the site, with teams clearing heavy debris and looking for any remaining trapped persons. Hours after the building collapse in a student-dominated area near Delhi University’s South Campus, the MCD has ordered action against illegal buildings with four or more storeys.One more body was recovered during late-night operations, taking the total number of fatalities to six.
Teams from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), Delhi Fire Service, Delhi Police and other agencies continued rescue operations at the site as they worked to remove the debris.The collapse that took place on Sunday afternoon, has raised fresh questions over the safety of buildings being used as paying guest (PG) accommodations and the enforcement of construction and fire safety norms in densely populated parts of the national capital.The Rekha Gupta-led Delhi government has ordered a magisterial inquiry into the incident and directed that an FIR be registered against the building owner, the chief minister’s office (CMO) said.
The decision was taken following an on-site review and a preliminary assessment of the incident, the CMO said.“Following an on-site review and based on the preliminary assessment, the chief minister has ordered a Magisterial Inquiry of the incident and an FIR against the building owner,” the CMO said.It added that those found responsible for the incident would be held fully accountable and face the strictest provisions of the law.Meanwhile, Congress leader and AICC Uttarakhand in-charge Kumari Selja questioned the BJP government over the safety of students living in such accommodations. She said students are sent to Delhi with hopes of building their future and questioned who would be held responsible for their safety.“What is the BJP government doing? They have forgotten what happened at the coaching centre. A mafia is operating in Delhi. These children are sent away with so many hopes. They are the only support for their parents. Who is responsible for their safety?” Selja said.Former Delhi chief secretary Omesh Saigal said the incident should not be viewed as an isolated case, claiming that similar incidents occur every few months. He also raised concerns over unauthorised construction in parts of Delhi.Saigal alleged that some buildings either have unapproved blueprints, additional floors added later or substandard construction, and questioned whether authorities responsible for approving building plans had adequately checked their safety."Look at the kind of buildings constructed in Delhi - I would say that in some areas, one in five buildings is unauthorised; either the blueprints weren't approved, extra floors were added, or the construction is substandard," he said.He also called for restrictions on new construction in areas that are already overcrowded and over-built, saying authorities should consider stopping the sanctioning of new building plans in such areas and examine the safety of existing structures."At the very least, we should ban new construction in these areas. We must halt new construction—or stop sanctioning building plans—for areas that are already over-congested and over-built. These are the things that need to be addressed," he added.NSUI President Vinod Jakhar described the situation as extremely grave and said rescue operations were continuing under difficult conditions."Rescue operations are ongoing, and conditions are dire. Almost all the students being pulled out are dead. We tried our best to get those students out; we actually succeeded in rescuing about three of them. Had the medical facilities, medical teams, police, and fire brigade arrived on time—had all necessary resources and responsible officials been present promptly—perhaps more students could have been saved. But the BJP has no disaster management plan. Just look at how the country's Home Minister inaugurates a grand BJP office in Goa today, while here, a building collapses. BJP offices never collapse because they are built using money extorted from PG and coaching centre operators. Our only demand is justice for the students. Several of our colleagues have also sustained serious injuries. There is absolutely no accountability," Jakhar told news agency ANI.Meanwhile, Delhi Bharatiya Janata Yuva Morcha president Rajat Choudhary said the situation remained serious and appealed for speedy rescue efforts. He said ambulances and doctors were present in large numbers and urged both the Delhi and Central governments to ensure that those trapped were rescued quickly.Choudhary also appealed to political parties to avoid politicising the tragedy and instead extend support to the affected families and those involved in the rescue operation.
"This is not the time for politics; those affected were someone's children. Instead of playing politics, one should offer support. The opposition should not do this; they should stand in solidarity," he said.In a separate response, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) ordered the immediate sealing of all illegal constructions with more than four floors and warned of strict action against officials found responsible.
“All illegal constructions with more than four floors will be immediately sealed, and strict action will be taken against the guilty officials, leading to their immediate dismissal. These orders will be implemented with immediate effect,” the MCD said.

Hormuz traffic dips to lowest since May after US, Iranian strikes on ships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06

Hormuz traffic dips to lowest since May after US, Iranian strikes on ships
- Ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dropped to an average of 10 per day, the lowest since May, following strikes by US and Iranian forces on oil tankers.
- US attacked three Iranian oil tankers on Sept 5, and Iran's IRGC retaliated by targeting three tankers using unauthorised routes and US vessels.
- The conflict has escalated maritime risks, with 27 projectile strike incidents since July, greatly raising danger for commercial shipping in the region.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – An average of 10 commodity ships transited the Strait of Hormuz per day over the past 10 days, the lowest since May, according to shipping data on Sept 7, after US and Iranian strikes on tankers.
The 10-day moving average was 10 on Sept 6, down from more than 15 on Sept 4 and nearly 13 on Sept 5, data from analytics firm Kpler found.
Only two vessels passed through the strait on Sept 5 while six went through on Sept 6, mostly using the Iranian route.
US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers on Sept 5, US Central Command said, including one off Kharg Island, Iran’s key oil export hub, following attacks by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on US warships in the region.
In retaliation, the IRGC navy said on Sept 5 that it targeted three oil tankers travelling unauthorised routes in the strait as well as three additional US vessels in other areas.
The three Iranian tankers were Downy, Stark I and Kylo, also known as Noxen, maritime intelligence firm Marisks said in a note.
The Sept 5 attacks represented a “major escalation in the maritime conflict”, Marisks said.
“Commercial tankers are now being deliberately used as instruments of reciprocal economic pressure, substantially weakening the previous distinction between military confrontation and commercial shipping,” it added.
“Risk is therefore assessed as extreme for Iranian/Iran-linked tonnage and materially elevated for US-linked or US-escorted shipping throughout the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman.”
There have been 27 projectile strike incidents since July 6, resulting in damage to vessels operating in and around the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said in its weekly report.
On Sept 6, one very large crude carrier (VLCC) and three bulk carriers laden with metals, grains or oilseeds entered the strait, Kpler data showed.
A tanker carrying refined products loaded from a Saudi port attempted to exit but was turned back, data from LSEG showed.
No VLCC has exited the strait since Sept 2, according to Kpler data. REUTERS

‘Mayday’ film review: Kenneth Branagh plays ‘a good Russian’ for a change as a former KGB officer who loves Top Gun and fights like Liam Neeson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
23:46:01 UTC
08:46:01 KST

‘Mayday’ film review: Kenneth Branagh plays ‘a good Russian’ for a change as a former KGB officer who loves Top Gun and fights like Liam Neeson
A film about a downed U.S. Navy pilot and a former KGB officer who become friends while trying to escape the Soviet Union in 1987 is now streaming on Apple TV. Shakespearean actor Kenneth Branagh once again plays a Soviet citizen — hardly new territory in his career — while Ryan Reynolds sticks to his familiar persona. The film was commissioned by Skydance Media, a studio that reportedly has close ties to the Trump administration. Critic Eduard Zhuravlev examines what a campy, cliché-ridden Hollywood portrayal of the Soviet Union can look like in 2026.
It’s 1987. Dashing U.S. Navy pilot Troy Kelly (Canadian actor Ryan Reynolds) accepts a secret CIA mission: fly a reconnaissance plane into the Arkhangelsk region to find out whether the Soviet leadership is building missile silos there. The mission goes wrong. Kelly’s plane is hit, and he is forced to eject over the snow-covered taiga. In the forest, the wounded American is rescued by bearded carpenter Nikolai Ustinov (Irish actor Kenneth Branagh), a former KGB officer who is anti-Soviet and a huge fan of the action movie Top Gun. Ustinov agrees to help Kelly escape; a ruthless “Red Army” led by “head of internal security” Alexander Volkov (Polish actor Marcin Dorocinski) is already hunting him.
Mayday may seem like just another streaming action movie destined to fade from memory before the credits finish rolling. These movies usually star some Chris — Evans (The Gray Man, Ghosted), Pratt (Mercy, The Tomorrow War), or Hemsworth (Extraction, Extraction 2). This time, though, viewers got lucky — and not because the lead happens to be a Ryan. Reynolds has plenty of streaming junk on his own résumé.
Mayday is a funny, propulsive buddy road comedy that holds its own even against 1980s genre classics. It also reimagines the caricatured Soviet clichés Hollywood produced in abundance during the Reagan era, from Red Dawn and Rocky IV to Red Heat and Rambo III. That makes it a politically charged film.
John Francis Daley and Jonathan Goldstein wrote and directed the film. Their credits include the reboot of the 1980s comedy series Vacation, the hilarious and hard-edged comedy Game Night, the brisk fantasy Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves, and the screenplays for Horrible Bosses and Spider-Man: Homecoming. The pair could easily rank among Hollywood’s most skilled comedy filmmakers working today.
Skydance Media is another important “author” here — the same studio that merged with Paramount, plans to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, and reportedly has close ties to the Trump administration. Its résumé includes not only the Terminator and Mission: Impossible sequels and a good half of the mass-market schlock starring the Chrises mentioned above, but also films about the complicated relationship between East and West, including The Gorge and Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit.
Branagh, incidentally, directed Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit and played its main villain, Russian oligarch Viktor Cherevin, who plots a terrorist attack on Wall Street. Branagh, an award-winning filmmaker known for adaptations of Shakespeare and Agatha Christie — plus one Marvel outing — has played a Russian character roughly once every six years. After Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit came Tenet, in which the Irish actor played another Russian oligarch, Andrei Sator. International relations are almost beside the point for Sator: dying and bent on revenge, he is prepared to destroy the world. Now Branagh has unexpectedly played “a good Russian.” True, Ustinov is a former KGB officer who tortured people on the job, but the filmmakers show little interest in that detail.
This is one of the first roles in Branagh’s career that has asked him to throw punches. The 65-year-old Irishman does a remarkably convincing Liam Neeson impression in action scenes, at times staged with the choreographic swagger of Atomic Blonde and the John Wick films. In one scene, filmed almost entirely without cuts, the unflappable comrade takes out a group of volunteer patrolmen with a pool rack to the tune of Belaya cheremukha; in another, he dispatches an entire train car full of Red Army soldiers — literally.
Branagh’s unexpected performance — his character recalls Robin Williams’s Soviet saxophonist in Moscow on the Hudson — easily overshadows Reynolds’s efforts. Troy Kelly is yet another exhausting, chatty wisecracker in Reynolds’s career; the actor has not dropped the persona even off camera in roughly 15 years. Still, the two actors have chemistry to rival Deadpool and Wolverine.
The filmmakers bring plenty of wit of their own. For starters, Mayday is both the international distress signal Kelly transmits and simply “a day in May” — the final showdown unfolds on Red Square in the middle of the Victory Day parade.
Moscow was filmed in Budapest, as usual, but with respect and humor. Ustinov drinks moonshine and eats bear meat, but the clichés are played for laughs rather than treated seriously. The actors playing Russian characters either speak Russian without a foreign accent or clearly make an effort. A Party apparatchik keeps The Atheist’s Dictionary and The Luzhin Defense at his dacha; a village grandmother keeps a jar of chicory on a shelf. There is even a Wes Anderson-style montage of a ride in a Zhiguli past Stalinist skyscrapers, Khrushchev-era apartment blocks, and a combined heat and power plant — all set to Bruce Springsteen.
Volkov, a revanchist played with impish gusto by Polish actor Marcin Dorocinski — who also played chess player Vasily Borgov in The Queen’s Gambit and the unnamed captain of the sunken submarine Sevastopol in the latest Mission: Impossible films — keeps a portrait of Chernenko in his office. Before you have time to think the filmmakers are off by two years, Chernenko is replaced by Gorbachev. “I didn’t want to hang a portrait of the man who’s destroying my country,” Volkov says. He dreams of restoring the empire and putting an end to glasnost.
At the same time, the filmmakers urge people to get along, discard propaganda slogans, and stop equating “Party policy” with individual citizens. At first, Kelly says, “Silence is complicity,” and calls everyone living in the Soviet Union part of the problem. He gradually changes his mind both about supposedly faceless Soviet people and about American democracy, after learning that his father developed cancer from asbestos exposure. Ustinov also revises his view of America, which had been shaped by the militaristic propaganda in Top Gun.
The filmmakers’ love for the biggest hit of 1986 is, of course, another meta-joke. It is hard to imagine a KGB officer born in the 1920s — even a former one — watching a bootleg VHS tape of an action movie about young, muscular pilots facing unidentified MiGs 100 times a year. The joke seems intended to remind us that ideological manifestos can be found in pop culture, not just in scientific communism classes.
Skydance Media also made Top Gun: Maverick, the sequel released 36 years after the original — and the highest-grossing film of Tom Cruise’s career. In 1986, Ustinov had to watch the movie on a bootleg VHS tape (“You could go to prison for that!”); by 2022, Maverick was playing in theaters near Arkhangelsk through gray-market distribution. The franchise makes a fitting symbol: a book about the brief period without a Cold War could well be titled “From Top Gun to Top Gun.”

What is celebrated on September 7 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:42:10 EEST
08:42:10 KST

What is celebrated on September 7 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On September 7, Ukraine observes Military Intelligence Day, while under the auspices of the UN, it is Clean Air Day. Brazil celebrates Independence Day.
On September 7, Ukraine celebrates Military Intelligence Day, the International Day of Clean Air for blue skies is held under the auspices of the UN, and Brazil celebrates Independence Day. According to the church calendar, under the new style it is the Forefeast of the Nativity of the Theotokos and the day commemorating the Martyr Sozon, while under the old style it is the Translation of the Relics of the Apostle Bartholomew and the day of the Apostle Titus, UNN reports.
Military Intelligence Day of Ukraine
An official holiday established by a Decree of the President of Ukraine in 2022 to honor the special importance of military intelligence in protecting the national interests, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of the state. The date commemorates the issuance, on September 7, 1992, of the decree establishing the Directorate of Military Strategic Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
Unique special operations, the acquisition of critically important strategic information, and the analytical work of intelligence officers play a decisive role in countering military aggression and planning the defensive actions of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
International Day of Clean Air for blue skies
An official environmental observance under the auspices of the UN, established in 2019 to draw attention to the problem of air pollution, which is considered one of the greatest environmental risks to human health.
The observance calls on governments, businesses, and society to strengthen international cooperation, reduce harmful emissions, introduce renewable energy, and ensure every person's right to a clean environment.
World Duchenne Awareness Day
A global medical and social initiative aimed at spreading information about a rare genetic disease that leads to progressive muscle wasting in children.
The event encourages the mobilization of resources for research in gene therapy, expanded access to early diagnosis, and support for patients and their families around the world.
Independence Day of Brazil
The country's main national holiday commemorating the proclamation of independence from Portugal on September 7, 1822, by Regent Prince Pedro, known as the "Cry of Ipiranga."
The day is marked by large-scale military parades in the capital, Brasília, mass cultural festivals, and ceremonial events throughout the country.
Victory Day in Mozambique
A public holiday commemorating the signing of the Lusaka Accord in 1974 between the Mozambican liberation movement FRELIMO and the government of Portugal, which ended the colonial war and paved the way for the proclamation of a sovereign state.
Forefeast of the Nativity of the Theotokos
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers observe the Forefeast of the Nativity of the Theotokos—a day of prayerful preparation for one of the twelve greatest Christian feasts.
The day also commemorates Saint Sozon the Martyr, who suffered for the Christian faith at the beginning of the fourth century in Cilicia, and Saint John, Archbishop of Novgorod.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate the Translation of the Relics of the Holy Apostle Bartholomew and also remember the Holy Apostle Titus of the Seventy, a disciple of the Apostle Paul and the first bishop of Crete.
In the folk calendar, this day was called "Titus the Leaf-Faller" or "Titus the Mushroom Gatherer," as the date was considered the deadline for the mass gathering of wild mushrooms and marked the beginning of the active autumn leaf fall.

Bus plummets from cliff in Cabo Verde killing at least 25, mostly children
At least 25 people, mostly schoolchildren and teenagers, have died after a bus fell into a ravine on Cabo Verde’s island of Fogo. The deadly crash prompted the authorities of the archipelago nation to declare a two-day mourning period.
The accident occurred on Saturday, when the bus, carrying children on a field trip, plumetted off a cliff while en route to the village of Cha das Caldeiras. The village, known for its unique wines, is located within the large crater of the active Pico do Fogo volcano.
The annual trip was set up by a private individual. The organizer, who is believed to have been behind the wheel, was killed in the crash. Most of the 32 people aboard the bus were killed in the accident, while others received injuries of varying severity.
“I am heartbroken. This is an irreparable loss, a part of the future that is being said goodbye to: the overwhelming majority of the victims are young people and teenagers,” The country’s president, Jose Maria Pereira Neves, said in a Facebook post.
The president, alongside other top officials, attended the funeral of some 18 victims of the crash on Sunday, while other deceased were buried in a separate ceremony earlier in the day. The country’s authorities are investigating the accident.

Yemeni Coast Guard intercepts oil tanker after ‘unauthorized’ delivery to Houthi-held port
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
23:32:38 UTC
08:32:38 KST

Aziz Ahmadi and Rania Abushamala
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Yemeni Coast Guard forces intercepted an oil tanker Sunday after it unloaded an “unauthorized” cargo at the Houthi-held Ras Isa port in Al-Hudaydah governorate, government media reported.
The Comoros-flagged tanker Nerida unloaded the cargo without prior approval from the Yemeni government or undergoing established procedures through the UN Verification and Inspection Mechanism for Yemen (UNVIM), Yemen’s state-run television channel quoted an unnamed Coast Guard Authority source as saying.
Based in Djibouti, UNVIM inspects goods and cargo bound for Houthi-controlled ports to ensure compliance with an international arms embargo.
The source said the tanker disabled its Automatic Identification System (AIS) during parts of its voyage before its signal briefly reappeared south of Al-Hudaydah after it departed Ras Isa port and headed toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
“After the vessel left areas under the militia’s control, a government Coast Guard patrol intercepted it in the Gulf of Aden,” the channel reported.
“The vessel initially failed to comply with orders to stop, and armed men aboard opened fire on the patrol boat before it later responded to the call and was escorted to the port of Aden,” it added.
No casualties were reported, and there was no immediate comment from the Houthi group.
UNVIM was established in December 2015 at the Yemeni government’s request to ensure that vessels sailing to ports outside its control comply with UN Security Council Resolution 2216.
It is managed by the UN Office for Project Services.
The incident comes amid escalating clashes between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis in recent weeks.
Government forces said Saturday that they had made battlefield advances on fronts in Taiz and Al-Hudaydah governorates while the army captured dozens of Houthi fighters.
