====================================================================================================

China Focus: China's top grain-producing province turns paddies into tourist destinations
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:26:45 CST
06:26:45 KST

This photo taken on July 29, 2026 shows a panoramic view of rice paddy art pieces at a rice park in Fujin City, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province. (Xinhua)
HARBIN, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Surrounded by four rice paddy art pieces stretching across the vast fields in northeast China, a giant piece in the form of a QR code catches many people's attention. It can be scanned to access an online store for agricultural products.
These art pieces, spanning 120,000 square meters, are located in a rice park in the city of Fujin, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province. Heilongjiang, China's top grain-producing province, has transformed vast paddies into thriving tourism destinations, boosting local incomes.
Turning a design into a giant field canvas requires multiple steps, including design, positioning, layout marking and transplanting. Rice varieties are selected to match the palette: black rice for black and brown sections, edible rice for green, and ornamental rice for yellow and white.
However, this form of art was far less precise in its early days.
"When we first tried in 2017, field positioning relied entirely on manual labor. Workers even had to stand high with megaphones to direct the placement," said Wang Chao, head of the office at the Fujin Tourism Development Service Center.
"The designs were mostly flat. Now, GPS positioning and 3D composition techniques have made the lines and layers much sharper," Wang noted.
This rice landscape is drawing growing numbers of visitors.
Zhao Zihan, a tourist from the neighboring city of Shuangyashan, visited the spot in Fujin with her family on a Saturday. "I've passed by several times but never had the chance to stop. This time I came specifically to see it," she said. "The vast rice paddy art lifts my spirit and fills me with hope for the future."
Beyond admiring the scene, visitors can now engage in increasingly diverse and immersive experiences, from transplanting rice and milling grain to exploring rice growth and camping beside the paddies.
Many of the park's service staff come from surrounding villages, and the visitor flow has spurred the growth of nearby farmstay restaurants. Wang said related services earn participating villagers across 10 villages an extra 4,000 yuan (about 590 U.S. dollars) per person each year.
The story of agritourism is unfolding across Heilongjiang's vast landscape.
In Xinghuo Village, a Korean ethnic village in Huachuan County, the transformation is vivid.
Home to 407 households and over 7,400 mu (around 493 hectares) of farmland, the village sits beside a highway amid scenic surroundings, yet was once just an ordinary village focused on rice cultivation.
"Back then, the roads were mostly dirt paths. There was no work for me in the village, so I had to go out and make my way," said Han Liuhua, 45, who left for cities like Shanghai and Qingdao, both in east China, at age 18.
In 2018, she gave up her urban career and returned to the village, becoming the first migrant worker to come back in over 20 years.
"When I first opened the restaurant in 2022, the villagers weren't very optimistic about me. Visitor numbers were low back then," Han said, noting that the scenic area has since brought a surge in foot traffic, and the restaurant's daily sales can now reach more than 16,000 yuan.
"The distance from my office to my restaurant is less than 50 meters. But when tourists are at their peak, it takes me five minutes just to squeeze through," Han said. "I'm one of the biggest beneficiaries of the village's transformation."
In 2025, the village's scenic area opened, welcoming 1.33 million visitors, generating 300 million yuan in revenue across the full industrial chain, and creating jobs for over 800 people.
The scenic area has renovated farmhouse exteriors in the traditional Korean style, built ecological picking gardens, and created an 8,000-square-meter giant rice paddy art piece to develop diversified, immersive and year-round products.
Inside the park, visitors can immerse themselves in Korean ethnic culture and agricultural experiences, from making kimchi and brewing rice wine to transplanting and harvesting rice.
The same trend is unfolding elsewhere in the province. In the city of Wuchang, a renowned rice-growing area, local enterprises are also actively developing agritourism products.
"I often come here after work. Rice has always been close to my heart, and seeing the vast paddies is far more relaxing than visiting a regular park," said a local resident surnamed Hu, who was picnicking at Qiaofu Dayuan Agricultural Co., Ltd.
The company hosts a variety of rice culture events each year, including rice-planting festivals and harvest ceremonies, while also serving as an experimental education base for primary school students, welcoming tens of thousands of visitors from across the country annually.
"Premium rice isn't just about taste. It is about the experience," said Qiao Wenzhi, head of the company, adding that by combining product customization with experiential value, the premium for their rice has risen by up to 40 percent.
Heilongjiang's broader push for agritourism also comes as China moves to diversify its tourism offerings and cultivate new growth drivers for the industry.
"Developing the multiple functions of agriculture" has been incorporated as a measure in the outline of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), referring to efforts to ensure food security and supply while integrating agriculture with culture and tourism.
The latest five-year tourism development plan, approved by the State Council and released in July 2026, calls for nurturing new drivers of tourism growth and enriching the supply of high-quality tourism experiences. ■

This photo taken on Sept. 5, 2026 shows a rice paddy art piece at a rice park in Fujin City, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province. (Xinhua/Ji Hang)

TEHRAN, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei has said that his country would announce a restricted zone outside the Strait of Hormuz in the coming days and place any ship attempting to transit the area on Tehran's sanctions list.
In an interview with state-run IRIB TV, which was broadcast Sunday night, Rezaei said that the zone would extend from "the line where the U.S. naval blockade begins to the Strait of Hormuz region and inside the Persian Gulf on the other side (of the strait)."
Ships that enter the zone without coordination with Iran, he added, would face sanctions affecting their insurance coverage and future passage through the waterway.
Rezaei framed the move as part of a broader strategic shift in Iran's approach to war and diplomacy, aiming at increasing pressure on Washington.
The security official stressed that the Strait of Hormuz is completely closed, dismissing the U.S. claim that ships and oil tankers are crossing the waterway as a "lie."
While acknowledging that some vessels attempt to cross the strait via a route near Oman, often switching off their navigation systems to evade detection, Rezaei said most of those ships "receive blows."
Yet he added that Iran does not intend to sink them for now due to environmental concerns.
Rezaei further revealed that Iran had test-fired for the first time a domestically developed anti-destroyer missile above a U.S. aircraft carrier 48 hours ago, describing it as a warning that the U.S. naval blockade is vulnerable.
"The special missile created a hell for the Americans, and they fled," he said.
Rezaei said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed unless the United States takes practical steps to fulfill its obligations under a peace memorandum of understanding signed between Tehran and Washington in June.
In the coming days, he added, a new international corridor designated by Iran and Oman for passage through the strait would be announced, emphasizing that the corridor would be under Iran's management.
Following U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, Tehran restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz, while U.S. forces imposed a naval blockade targeting vessels traveling to or from Iranian ports and coastal areas. ■

China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

Valentin Debise of EASTROC ZXMOTO Evan Bros Factory competes during the race 2 of WorldSSP at the FIM Supersport World Championship French Round in Magny-Cours, France, Sept. 6, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Huiwo)
MAGNY-COURS, France, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Chinese motorcycle brands are gaining visibility both on the racetrack and among French enthusiasts, as strong results in international competition coincide with growing consumer interest in one of Europe's major motorcycle markets.
At the FIM Supersport World Championship's French Round, which concluded Sunday at the Nevers Magny-Cours Circuit, riders Valentin Debise and Federico Caricasulo delivered a strong weekend for Chinese manufacturer ZXMOTO and the Evan Bros Racing team.
The pair secured a historic one-two in Friday's Superpole, with home rider Debise taking his first career WorldSSP pole ahead of Caricasulo. They finished third and fifth respectively in Race 1, while Debise claimed another third-place finish and Caricasulo finished eighth in Sunday's Race 2.
Speaking to Xinhua ahead of the race, Debise said ZXMOTO's approach to motorcycle development was one of the reasons he decided to join the fledgling racing project.
"At the beginning, that's what convinced me to join ZXMOTO, because that's what they told me: 'We want to make the best motorcycle. That's what matters,'" Debise said.
The French rider, who made his first trip to China during the recent summer break, said the drive for constant improvement he observed there had strengthened his confidence in the potential of China's motorcycle industry in France and across Europe.
For ZXMOTO, its debut WorldSSP campaign is also part of a broader push into Europe. Huang Qin, head of the company's foreign trade department, said the largely European championship provides a platform to raise its profile in a key overseas market.
In France, ZXMOTO is working with motorcycle importer and distributor DIP. Anthony Barneaud, who oversees the brand at the company, said it had already received "a significant number of pre-orders" ahead of the first deliveries to French dealers.
Valentin Debise of EASTROC ZXMOTO Evan Bros Factory reacts after the race 2 of WorldSSP at the FIM Supersport World Championship French Round in Magny-Cours, France, Sept. 6, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Huiwo)
Barneaud said ZXMOTO's WorldSSP performances had created a "real surprise effect," generating greater interest from riders and dealers. More broadly, he said Chinese brands were gradually changing perceptions by showing French motorcyclists they could offer reliable, well-equipped motorcycles at competitive prices.
Away from the track, Chinese manufacturers were also drawing attention from spectators browsing motorcycle displays around the circuit.
"Chinese motorcycles offer very good value for money," said Ludovic, a French motorcycle enthusiast. A long-time fan of Italian brands, he said Chinese manufacturers had increasingly caught his attention.
Interest is also visible online. The 2026 ZXMOTO 820RR attracted more than 10,000 unique visitors to its model page over the latest quarter on French motorcycle website Motoplanete, making it the site's most-viewed motorcycle model page during the period. The CFMOTO 1000 MT-X 2026, from another Chinese brand, ranked second.
Other Chinese manufacturers were also visible at Magny-Cours. A QJMotor display drew a steady stream of spectators during the weekend.
A staff member from SIMA, QJMotor's importer in France, told Xinhua that Chinese manufacturers' progress in international racing had helped increase their visibility among French riders. "It's important for us," he said.
Valentin Debise (front) of EASTROC ZXMOTO Evan Bros Factory competes during the race 2 of WorldSSP at the FIM Supersport World Championship French Round in Magny-Cours, France, Sept. 6, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Huiwo)
The interest comes as Chinese motorcycle brands continue to expand their presence in France. In May, they accounted for 15.7 percent of new motorcycle registrations, according to French publication L'Automobile Magazine. Registrations rose 58 percent year-on-year that month, meaning roughly one in six newly registered motorcycles was from a Chinese brand.
Huang said attracting attention through racing and new products was only a first step. Building lasting consumer trust in mature overseas markets would also require competitive products, sustained participation in top-level racing, a strong dealer network and reliable after-sales service.
"Only then can we achieve sales in mature markets and build a strong reputation for the brand," Huang said. ■

Far-right AfD scores record win in German state election
China
Unknown Publisher

05:26:17 CST
06:26:17 KST

A voter arrives at a polling station in Magdeburg, Germany, Sept. 6, 2026. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has won Sunday's state election in Saxony-Anhalt with a record 44.5 percent of the vote, according to an exit poll released by public broadcaster ARD. (Xinhua/Zhang Haofu)
MAGDEBURG, Germany, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has won Sunday's state election in Saxony-Anhalt with a record 44.4 percent of the vote, according to an exit poll released by public broadcaster ARD.
The Christian Democratic Union (CDU), led by incumbent state leader Sven Schulze, suffered a heavy blow, plunging to 18.4 percent, down from 37.1 percent in 2021, the poll showed.
The Left party came in third with 9.3 percent, followed by the Greens with 8.7 percent and the Social Democratic Party (SPD) with 8.4 percent.
The newly formed Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) hovered right on the 5-percent threshold to enter the state parliament, while the business-friendly Free Democratic Party (FDP) crashed out with just 2.2 percent.
Conceding defeat, Schulze acknowledged the AfD's clear victory, while urging political leaders across Germany to heed the message sent by voters.
In Berlin, head of the Chancellery Nina Warken called the election outcome a "watershed moment" for the CDU, describing it on broadcaster ZDF as a "very, very difficult result." Warken also insisted that the federal government would resolutely press ahead with its planned reform agenda.
In the 83-seat state parliament, the AfD is projected to secure 39 seats, three seats shy of an absolute majority needed to govern alone.
The AfD's 35-year-old state lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund hailed the result, declaring that "the people have sent a clear signal."
Speaking to ARD, Siegmund also signaled a shift from his pre-election stance of only seeking office through an absolute majority, noting that his party is now open to a coalition.
However, all other mainstream parties have repeatedly ruled out entering a coalition with the AfD. It remains unclear how a viable state government will be formed. ■

RAMALLAH, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- The new school year started Sunday across the West Bank, with Palestinian schools trying to keep classes going despite ongoing challenges.

Amjad Barham, the Palestinian education minister, said during a ceremony marking the start of the school year at Beit Fajjar Girls' Secondary School, near Bethlehem in the southern West Bank, that more than 15 new schools had opened this year.
He said the ministry had developed plans to ensure the continuation of education despite the existence of barriers, checkpoints, closures and the demolition of schools in villages and towns affected by settlement activities.
But behind efforts to keep schools operating, Palestinian education officials say a deepening financial crisis is placing additional pressure on the education system.
"The new academic year began amid field and financial challenges that have affected various aspects of the educational process," said Sadiq al-Khadour, spokesperson for the Ministry of Education.
Al-Khadour said that the financial crisis had affected the renewal of school furniture, completion of administrative buildings and equipping of some schools.
He attributed the difficulties affecting teachers and students to the financial crisis facing Palestinian Authority institutions and widespread job losses among Palestinians since the outbreak of the latest round of Palestinian-Israeli conflict in October 2023.
For 10-year-old Suleiman Khaled, the economic hardship was reflected in a simple part of the new school year: his school bag.
"I wished I could have a new bag, but my father has been unemployed for almost two years," Khaled said.
The financial burden is also being felt by teachers, who are struggling to meet the educational needs of their own families while continuing to work amid rising living costs.
Palestinian teacher Hussam Aghbaria, 45, from Hebron in the southern West Bank, said the financial difficulties facing teachers had directly affected their daily lives.
Aghbaria, a father of four, including two elementary school students, said rising prices of stationery and school supplies had added pressure on families already facing difficult economic conditions.
"Teachers find themselves in a difficult situation. On the one hand, they have to fulfill their role in teaching students at school, while on the other hand, they have to provide educational supplies for their own children at home amid deteriorating economic conditions," Aghbaria said.
Alongside financial difficulties, students and teachers face daily obstacles in reaching schools, including checkpoints, road closures, military gates and raids.
Al-Khadour said these circumstances were affecting the regularity of education, adding that the ministry had developed alternative plans to help students and teachers reach schools under difficult conditions.
According to a report issued by the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs in April, as of December 2025, the number of movement restrictions imposed on Palestinians in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, reached 925. The figure is 43 percent higher than the annual average of 647 movement obstacles in the preceding 20 years.
Such restrictions have also raised concerns over the ability of students and teachers to reach schools regularly.
Ramallah-based educational expert Youssef Abu Ras said the readiness of schools for the new academic year should not be measured solely by whether they open their doors.
"It should also be measured by the availability and stability of educational conditions and the ability of students and teachers to reach schools and continue their studies regularly," Abu Ras said, adding that the field and financial crises could become permanent rather than exceptional circumstances.
He warned that reduced school hours or disruptions to the academic schedule could negatively affect the future of coming generations. ■

Antonelli storms from 19th to win F1 Italian GP
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:26:09 CST
06:26:09 KST

By F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
BEIJING, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Kimi Antonelli produced a remarkable comeback from 19th on the grid to win his home Italian Grand Prix on Sunday, passing Mercedes teammate George Russell late in a dramatic race at Monza.
Antonelli took the lead for good from Russell at the Ascari chicane on lap 50 after the two Mercedes drivers had traded places repeatedly earlier in the race.
Max Verstappen finished third for Red Bull, ahead of McLaren's Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris, while Lewis Hamilton took sixth for Ferrari.
Antonelli became the first Italian to win his home Grand Prix since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966. No Formula One driver had won from as far back as 19th on the grid since John Watson triumphed from 22nd at Long Beach in 1983.
The victory was Antonelli's seventh of the season and extended his championship lead over Russell to 66 points, with Hamilton a further 10 points behind in third.
Mercedes also strengthened its grip on the constructors' championship and now has 468 points, 122 ahead of Ferrari, with McLaren third on 287.
Alpine's Pierre Gasly had claimed a surprise first pole position and initially held off Russell, but the Mercedes driver swept into the lead at the start of lap two.
Moments later, Ferrari's Charles Leclerc crashed heavily at the Parabolica after running wide and losing the rear of his car, causing the race to be halted while barriers were repaired.
Antonelli had already climbed seven places to 12th by the stoppage, which allowed him to discard the hard tires he had started on.
Russell led Gasly and Verstappen at the restart, but Antonelli continued his rapid progress, passing Norris and then Gasly before moving ahead of Hamilton and Piastri to reach third by lap 13.
He caught the leaders soon afterward, beginning a frenetic battle with Russell in which the Mercedes pair repeatedly exchanged first place while Verstappen remained close behind.
Antonelli first took the lead on lap 18 before Russell responded, with the pair trading places several more times as Mercedes attempted to manage their battle.
A virtual safety car following Lance Stroll's retirement on lap 28 changed the complexion of the race. Antonelli and Verstappen pitted while Russell stayed out, leaving Antonelli to fight his way back through traffic.
The Italian quickly dispatched Gasly, Norris, Hamilton and Piastri to return to second and began closing a gap of more than 13 seconds to Russell.
With Russell struggling with tire graining, Antonelli was within striking distance by lap 47. An initial attempt at Turn 1 two laps later sent him briefly through the gravel as Russell defended stoutly, but the Italian recovered before making his decisive move at Ascari on lap 50.
Russell held on for second, with Verstappen third after a race-long battle with Piastri. Norris finished fifth, ahead of Hamilton, Gasly, Arvid Lindblad, Franco Colapinto and Yuki Tsunoda.
The next round of the 2026 season is next weekend's Spanish Grand Prix, which will be held for the first time at the new Madring circuit in Madrid. ■

Once disgraced, twice-resigned, ex-PM Keir Starmer is now ex-MP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
21:22:03 UTC
06:22:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Once disgraced, twice-resigned, ex-PM Keir Starmer is now ex-MP
Even in resignation, Keir Starmer is a liability for the Labour Party. One of the most unpopular Prime Ministers in British history, the former Labour leader had transformed an admittedly shallow Parliamentary majority into a succession of by-election defeats, shrinking municipal power, and a perpetual spate of Reform UK polling leads.
Just as Andy Burnham has inaugurated a new period of Labour resurgence by distinguishing himself from his predecessor, operating as a far savvier politician, prioritising Mamdani-style affect and vibes, and even, in a limited way, introducing some cost-of-living reforms, Starmer has caused the new PM a headache by resigning. He will no longer serve as the Parliamentary representative for Holborn and St. Pancras, a seat he has held for eleven years.
Starmer, the man who backed Israel’s genocide of the Palestinians to the hilt and sought to strip the disabled of benefits and pensioners of winter fuel payments, ended his Parliamentary career after six weeks on a summer wage. Putting a damper on Burnham’s hard launch, he also opened himself up to a career that does not involve him declaring his earnings. Starmer’s resignation is a final parting shot to his successor.
This by-election is the first substantive test of the new PM’s wager to rebuild an electoral coalition which binds together significant parts of the Northern electorate with Labour’s disloyal, leftwards-moving voter base in the larger, metropolitan cities.
Starmer’s resignation, as venal and self-obsessed as his time in office, might symbolise a potential challenge to this ambition. Formally, it shouldn’t. The Burnham poll bounce hasn’t been enormous, but it has been significant. He has dragged Labour back to the top from oblivion.
With the opposition in disarray, as Farage faces a litany of financial scandals and Zack Polanski’s Greens struggle to find their feet against a more nimble Labour leader, there is an argument to say that Burnham’s Labour should be commanding far larger polling leads.
There should not be any comfort walking into this by-election, however. The Holborn and St. Pancras constituency, like many London areas, is an almost Dickensian tale of two cities. Sandwiched between London Euston and King's Cross station is the historic working-class Somers Town neighbourhood, just as behind the leafy Victorian and Georgian terraces of Kentish Town and Camden lies a legion of working-class estates.
This seat, in many ways that have been actively papered over in the national political conversation over the past decade, is a classic Labour constituency. It brings together a multiracial working class with a professional middle class that has grown in size both as a component of the area and of Labour’s electoral base.
The Labour Party will hope that the Burnham charm offensive is enough to win the seat, supplementing its superior ground game. Of the Labour candidates on offer, there is a real estate developer, the former leader of Haringey council, and a spate of other councillors in the race. The favourite is likely Sagal Abdi-Wali, the current Camden council leader, former Constituency Labour Party chair, and a Somali refugee.
The New Statesmen’s Ben Walker in a Britain Predicts poll has Labour with a thin 5% lead over the Greens in Starmer’s former constituency. Whilst this is certainly the poll with the most generous tilt towards the eco-populists, the prize for the Greens is clear.
Zack Polanski, who has confidently declared that he will run for the seat so long as he wins the support of the local party, has an opportunity to send a shockwave through London Labour and build upon the Greens’ growing clout across the capital, having won control of five London councils in the recent local elections.
Without the jeopardy of worrying about the seat falling to either the Conservatives or Reform UK, Polanski can confidently claim, as Russell Warfield has argued on PoliticsJOE, that if you want to make good on Andy Burnham’s promise to end neoliberalism, getting another Green into Parliament will be a far better means for making good on that than simply getting another Labour MP elected.
To achieve this, the Greens would need to capitalise on their growing inroads in wards across the constituency whilst also finding firmer footing as they try to pivot against a more capable, Janus-faced Labour leader.
Keir Starmer’s last act as a politician could also be his final gift to the Green Party, handing them an opportunity to regain their momentum and position themselves as the effective opposition to Andy Burnham’s muddied attempt to revive Labour’s fortunes.
Jonas Marvin is the author of forthcoming The Breaking of the English Working Class, due out for Verso Books in August 2026. He also cohosts Life of the Party podcast and blogs at Marx’s Dream Journal.

Popular brain supplement linked to shorter lifespan in men
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
21:21:25 UTC
06:21:25 KST

Popular brain supplement linked to shorter lifespan in men
A common amino acid found in protein-rich foods and supplements may be linked to a shorter lifespan in men.
- Date:
- September 6, 2026
- Source:
- Impact Journals LLC
- Summary:
- A large study involving more than 270,000 people has linked higher blood levels of the amino acid tyrosine to a shorter lifespan in men. Using both observational data and genetic analysis, researchers found that elevated tyrosine could potentially reduce male life expectancy by nearly a year, while no significant effect appeared in women. Tyrosine is found naturally in protein-rich foods and is also sold as a supplement for boosting focus and mental performance, making the finding especially intriguing.
- Share:
A large study involving more than 270,000 people suggests that one common amino acid may be tied to how long men live.
Researchers led by Jie V. Zhao, Yitang Sun, Junmeng Zhang, and Kaixiong Ye from the University of Hong Kong and the University of Georgia examined whether phenylalanine and tyrosine, two amino acids involved in metabolism and brain function, are connected to lifespan (lifespan). Their results point to a notable difference between men and women. Higher tyrosine levels were associated with shorter life expectancy in men, while no significant effect was detected in women.
The findings could eventually help scientists better understand why aging and longevity differ between the sexes, although much more research is needed before the results can be translated into health recommendations.
The research was published in Aging-US titled "The role of phenylalanine and tyrosine in longevity: a cohort and Mendelian randomization study."
Why Tyrosine Matters
Amino acids are the molecular building blocks that the body uses to make proteins. Phenylalanine and tyrosine are both found in foods that contain protein, and they are also available in dietary supplements.
Beyond their role in protein production, these amino acids participate in important biological processes. Tyrosine is especially interesting because the body uses it to produce neurotransmitters such as dopamine. Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers that allow nerve cells to communicate, and dopamine helps regulate functions that include mood, motivation, and thinking.
Despite these important roles, scientists still do not fully understand how long-term differences in phenylalanine and tyrosine levels might influence aging.
More Than 270,000 People Studied
To investigate, the researchers analyzed information from more than 270,000 participants in the UK Biobank, a large research database containing health and genetic data from people in the United Kingdom.
The team used two complementary approaches. First, they looked for associations between blood concentrations of phenylalanine and tyrosine and outcomes related to death and predicted lifespan. They also used genetic methods to investigate whether the relationships might go beyond a simple association.
One of those approaches was Mendelian randomization. This method uses naturally occurring genetic differences among people as a way to test whether a particular biological factor may contribute to an outcome. Because genes are assigned before many lifestyle choices and diseases develop, the technique can sometimes provide stronger clues about cause and effect than an observational study alone.
At first, higher levels of both amino acids appeared to be associated with an increased risk of death. But when the researchers examined the relationships more closely, tyrosine was the one that consistently stood out.
Tyrosine Linked to a Shorter Lifespan in Men
The genetic analyses suggested that elevated tyrosine levels may have a potentially causal relationship with reduced life expectancy in men. According to the researchers' estimates, higher tyrosine could shorten male lifespan by nearly one year.
The same pattern was not seen in women. Researchers found no significant effect of tyrosine on female lifespan.
The relationship also remained after the researchers accounted for phenylalanine and other related factors, strengthening the possibility that tyrosine itself may have an independent connection to aging.
The team also found that men generally have higher levels of tyrosine than women. That difference could potentially contribute to the well-documented gap in average lifespan between the sexes, although the findings do not establish that tyrosine is responsible for that gap.
"Phenylalanine showed no association with lifespan in either men or women after controlling for tyrosine."
Why Might Tyrosine Affect Longevity?
Scientists do not yet know exactly why higher tyrosine levels might be associated with shorter lives in men.
One possible explanation involves insulin resistance. This occurs when cells become less responsive to insulin, the hormone that helps control blood sugar. Insulin resistance is associated with several diseases that become more common with age and could therefore provide one possible link between tyrosine and longevity.
Tyrosine is also used by the body to make neurotransmitters involved in the stress response. Hormones and related signaling pathways can function differently in men and women, which could help explain why the apparent lifespan effect emerged only in men.
These mechanisms remain hypotheses, however, and will require further investigation.
What the Findings Mean for Tyrosine Supplements
Tyrosine is widely sold as a dietary supplement and is often promoted for improving focus, alertness, and mental performance. The new findings therefore raise questions about whether chronically high tyrosine levels could have unintended long-term consequences.
Importantly, the researchers did not directly test tyrosine supplements. The results therefore do not show that taking a tyrosine supplement shortens lifespan.
Instead, the study examined tyrosine levels in the body and their relationship with longevity. The researchers suggest that people with unusually high tyrosine concentrations could potentially benefit from dietary changes designed to lower those levels.
One possible strategy is restricting protein intake, which could reduce tyrosine exposure. However, it remains unclear whether deliberately lowering tyrosine through diet would actually extend lifespan or improve health.
More research will be needed to confirm the results, uncover the biological mechanisms involved, and determine whether diet or lifestyle changes can safely alter tyrosine levels in ways that promote healthier aging.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Impact Journals LLC. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Jie V. Zhao, Yitang Sun, Junmeng Zhang, Kaixiong Ye. The role of phenylalanine and tyrosine in longevity: a cohort and Mendelian randomization study. Aging, 2025; 17 (10): 2500 DOI: 10.18632/aging.206326

NEW DELHI: Uttarakhand waqf board's plan to introduce a revised marriage contract, or nikahnama, within a month "to align it with the Uniform Civil Code" has not gone down well with All India Muslim Personal Law Board (AIMPLB), which has challenged UCC in the high court.AIMPLB spokesperson SQR Ilyas said that the board opposes any such move by state waqf board and state govt and wants to reiterate that the nikahnama should not be revised till Uttarakhand HC gives its judgement. "Our view is clear that Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act exists and is a valid Indian law. Conversion solely for marriage will no longer be permitted, requiring individuals wishing to convert to follow procedures outlined under Special Marriage Act of 1954. The mandatory waiting period known as 'iddat' will no longer be enforced, giving women the autonomy to determine the duration themselves.

Stray US glide bomb likely hit wedding in Iran – WaPo
A US munition likely landed a direct hit on a wedding in Iran last week after it veered off its designated target, the Washington Post reported on Sunday, citing a person familiar with the operation.
The incident occurred in Kuhestak, Hormozgan Province, amid a new wave of airstrikes unleashed by the US on Iran on Tuesday. One of the munitions hit a residential home with a wedding party underway, killing at least five and wounding nearly 70. The Iranian authorities said the victims were three women and two children aged four and 16.
The explosion at the party was highly likely a result of a direct hit by a US munition, according to the WaPo. The US Navy dropped six glide bombs at a communications tower in the town, with all but one striking the designated target. The stray munition missed the tower, reportedly hitting the house located around 135 meters (440 feet) away. The comms tower was the only designated target within the town during the Tuesday strikes, the source told the WaPo, ruling out any prospects the home was attacked intentionally or mixed with some other target.
The reporting is consistent with earlier pieces run by AP, the New York Times, Reuters, and other outlets, which indicated that the wedding party was hit by a US-guided weapon, most likely a JSOW glide bomb, rather than debris or a faulty anti-aircraft missile fired by Iran.
US Vice President J.D. Vance said on Thursday that Washington is looking into the incident. “We’re investigating it because obviously we care. We want to know,” he told reporters. The US military has insisted it does not target civilians and has not taken responsibility for the strike.
The attack on the wedding party has become the latest in the string of civilian mass-casualty incidents that occurred amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
On the opening day of the US-Israeli war on Iran, US forces hit an elementary school in Minab, killing 175 people, predominantly young girls. At least 21 civilians, roughly a third of whom were children, were killed in Lamerd that day. Tehran has repeatedly accused the US of committing war crimes throughout the conflict, reporting some 3,000 civilian casualties since it began late in February.

Govt in a tangle over Supreme Court ruling on 'creamy layer'

NEW DELHI: The Centre is in a tangle over Supreme Court's landmark judgement on "creamy layer" that paved the way for induction in the elite civil services of OBC candidates who had cleared the examinations over past ten years but were denied appointments.On Aug 25, govt approached the apex court seeking clarification on the Rohit Nathan judgement that laid down that "salary" could not be added to the "income" to determine if a candidate from a PSU background falls in the "creamy layer" - like it is done for OBCs from non-PSU families. Govt, while seeking that it be allowed to go ahead with allocation of service for Civil Services-2025 without implementing the Nathan judgement, also raised questions about the SC's definition of "creamy layer".But barely a week ago, Centre told Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) that it intended to execute the SC order of March 11. "A decision has been made to implement the decision in terms of the judgement rendered by SC in Union of India vs Rohit Nathan," the ASG told the principal bench of CAT.On Aug 19, CAT was hearing a contempt petition against Centre as an OBC candidate, Basant Singh, had sought that the bench enforce its earlier order for his induction in civil services.
His case was similar to those of candidates in whose favour SC delivered the Nathan judgement."It is further submitted by the learned ASG that 56 similarly placed candidates are also being considered along with the applicant," CAT quoted the ASG as submitting. CAT put off the case based on Centre's undertaking that necessary steps were being taken to implement the Nathan judgement.The apparently contradictory stands taken by govt within a week's interval have disappointed OBC candidates who felt the SC judgement in March had ended their wait for induction in civil services.The case pertains to department of personnel and training (DoPT)'s differential implementation of the "creamy layer" criterion for OBCs from a PSU background and others. While, as per 1993 office memorandum, "salary" and "agricultural income" are not included in computing the "income" of a family, DoPT has been taking "salary" into consideration for candidates with parents in PSUs. Govt has cited the absence of "equivalence of posts" - categorising posts in PSUs, banks, universities, etc.
But, according to guidelines, while Group A and Group B are ineligible for quotas, others are eligible if their "annual income" does not exceed Rs 8 lakh.After a long wait, following orders by three high courts in support of the candidates, SC ruled in March that "salary" cannot be the criterion for determination of "creamy layer" for any category as per the 1993 judgement and that candidates who have suffered should be inducted in civil services.

At least five killed after Amazon cargo plane crash in Miami airport
The cause of the crash is being investigated.
At least five people have died after an Amazon cargo plane crashed in the United States, overrunning its runway while landing at Miami International Airport and disrupting one of the country’s busiest airports.
The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said in a social media post that a Boeing 767-300 overran the runway at 2pm ET (18:00 GMT) upon arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket explodes on launchpad in Florida
- list 2 of 3Amazon’s Zoox secures US federal approval for steering-wheel-free robotaxis
- list 3 of 3Jeff Bezos consortium nears deal to buy stake in Liverpool FC: Reports
Five people were also injured in the crash, three of whom are in critical condition, and two others were hospitalised with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials said in a news conference.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said that “multiple vehicles” were struck by the plane, which caught on fire after it crashed. The department said more than 60 fire rescue units were working to extinguish the blaze and assess the status of people affected.
The fire rescue chief, Ray Jadallah, said some people were trapped inside motorised vehicles following the crash. The pilot and copilot were also trapped in the plane. It is not clear how many crew members or passengers were on board.
Fire crews were dealing with a fuel leak on the plane several hours after the incident, Jadallah said.
An Amazon spokesperson said the plane was operated by 21 Air and experienced “an incident” while attempting to land.
“We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said. “Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, wellbeing, and care of everyone involved. We’re doing everything we can to support those affected.”
Videos circulating online show black smoke billowing from the scene near the runway. The aircraft appeared to be largely intact despite the fire.
The 32-year-old plane had been a passenger aircraft for more than two decades before being repurposed as a cargo carrier in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.
Early reports indicated that the aircraft veered off the runway and crossed a road near the airport.
The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), which investigates major transportation-related accidents, confirmed that it was aware of the crash and would provide additional updates as more information became available.
US Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said his agency had issued a full ground stop in Miami after the incident, urging travellers to anticipate “significant delays”.
The cause of the incident is unknown. The FAA said it is investigating.

China’s secret lifeline to Russia’s killer drone producer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
21:10:37 UTC
06:10:37 KST

A Chinese state-owned firm has supplied Russia with the materials required to build hundreds of kamikaze drones, according to internal Russian company shipping documents obtained by POLITICO.
The records, which have been reviewed by Western governments, provide the clearest evidence yet of a Chinese-state corporation continuing to aid a sanctioned company in the Kremlin’s military industrial complex.
The shipping and customs documents reveal the Chinese firm disguised the shipment of 46 tons of carbon-fiber chemicals to a subsidiary of Russia’s Rosatom earlier this year. The corporation develops the key components of the kamikaze drones Moscow used to attack a shopping mall in central Ukraine in August, killing at least 16 people.
Advertisement
Chinese components have long been retrieved from Russian drones following strikes on Ukraine. Yet the documents gathered from Russian sources by the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre — a Kyiv-based think tank close to the Ukrainian government — detail for the first time how a Chinese state firm exported crucial drone-making components directly to Russia.
The USCC has shared the documents with the U.K. and U.S. governments.
These revelations “would allow the [U.S.] State Department to sanction” the Chinese supplier, because they “establish” shipments to Rosatom’s subsidiary after it was sanctioned by much of the West, said David Albright, founder and president of the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security think tank. The shipment, he points out, is disguised with a customs code for exports like nylon and polyester.
“Rosatom and its enterprises operate in full compliance with applicable laws and regulatory requirements,” said a spokesperson for the Russian state firm. “Any claim to the contrary is false and demonstrates a lack of understanding of how Russia’s customs authorities operate.”
Chinese state firm Jilin Chemical Fiber Group did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Both the State Department and the U.S. Treasury Department can impose sanctions “to disrupt the networks and channels through which Russia procures technology and equipment from abroad to support its war effort,” the State Department said in a statement last year.
Advertisement
“This evidence provides irrefutable proof that Chinese state-owned companies are involved in the supply chains of raw materials to Russia,” said Serhii Kuzan, head of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre. International sanctions on Russia mean that “China has become arguably the main, and in fact the only, source of supply for the materials needed to manufacture the composites used in Russian weaponry,” Kuzan said.
The U.S. House Select Committee on China has reviewed the documents and determined they are “legitimate,” according to a U.S. government official familiar with their contents. The Ukrainian government has also reviewed the documents and confirmed their authenticity, a Ukrainian official said. Both officials were granted anonymity as they were not authorized to speak on the record.
The Treasury Department declined to comment on the specific allegations of Chinese shipments of materials essential to Russia’s weaponized drone program, but said in a statement it takes “allegations of sanctionable conduct extremely seriously.”
The State Department didn’t respond to a request for comment. Britain’s Foreign Office has reviewed the documents and did not push back on the revelations. The U.S. Central Intelligence Agency declined to comment.
Chinese President Xi Jinping told Russia’s Vladimir Putin in a meeting in late August that ties between the two nations are set to strengthen.
Advertisement
From the outset of its war on Ukraine, Moscow has signaled Beijing’s support is essential to its ability to resist foreign pressure to end the conflict.
“In essence, we have built a stable system of mutual trade that is protected from external influence,” Putin said in May. Beijing’s cooperation with Moscow has blunted the impact of foreign sanctions aimed at starving Russia’s military industries of key components.
Xi-Trump summit
The revelations come as U.S. President Donald Trump prepares to meet Xi in Washington later this month.
New evidence of China’s support for Russia’s war on Ukraine may intensify pressure on Trump from pro-Ukraine lawmakers to push Xi to stop such shipments in a meeting that both leaders would likely prefer to devote to extending the fragile truce in the U.S.-China trade war.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
In August, Putin appointed a general to head up drone warfare in a newly established branch of Russia’s military to strike deep inside Ukraine. Ukraine is meanwhile intensifying attacks on Russian oil refineries, threatening the foundation of the country’s economy.
During a trip to Moscow last month, CIA Director John Ratcliffe warned Russian officials not to escalate the conflict in Ukraine with America’s NATO allies amid suspected Russian-linked sabotage and drone incursions across Europe. Moscow has made a series of recent threats against countries that support Kyiv.
The Chinese government has consistently denied providing weapons to support Russia’s war on Ukraine. “We would not add fuel to the fire, and above all we would not profiteer” from the conflict, Chinese leader Xi said in 2023. Washington has repeatedly accused Beijing of providing dual-use items — materials usable in both civilian and defense manufacturing — that go directly to the Russian military.
Advertisement
The scale of the shipments and the military importance of the Russian company receiving them, however, suggest Chinese officials are either turning a blind eye to that assistance or are actively facilitating it, said multiple U.S. weapons experts, former intelligence officials and diplomats.
Evidence of Chinese support for Russia’s weaponized drone program “smear and scapegoat China,” Beijing’s embassy in Washington said in a statement. “We have never provided lethal weapons to any party to the conflict, and strictly control dual-use items,” the embassy said.
The Russian embassy in Washington didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Former U.S. officials familiar with Chinese government oversight of state-owned companies dismiss those claims.
“They are doing it knowing that the Chinese government will not bust them for it,” said Dennis Wilder, former CIA deputy assistant director for East Asia and the Pacific. “The idea that Chinese state-owned enterprises can hide things from the Chinese government just doesn’t wash.”
The shipment “could not have escaped Chinese government attention,” said Washington-based weapons expert Albright. He and his organization, the Institute for Science and International Security, have conducted years of in-depth research on Russia’s drone production.
What the docs show
The Russian-language documents establish the shipment of the carbon-fiber chemical between the warehouse addresses of Chinese state-owned Jilin Chemical Fiber Group and Alabuga-Volokno — a subsidiary of Russian state firm Rosatom’s advanced materials and composites division UMATEX.
The firm is based in a factory complex in Russia’s Tatarstan region. There, in the Alabuga Special Economic Zone, Alabuga-Volokno supplies high-spec carbon-fiber to Moscow’s mass production of the long-range kamikaze drones, built on the design of Iran’s Shahed, USCC and Albright’s research shows.
Alabuga-Volokno and UMATEX have faced a variety of Western sanctions since 2023, including sanctions imposed by the U.K. and under a White House executive order.
Advertisement
Its operations are also sanctioned by Ukraine, the EU, New Zealand and Switzerland. The U.S. government prohibits exports that can be used by the Russian military.
Jilin, a large Chinese state-owned enterprise specializing in the production and sale of synthetic chemical fibers, doesn’t currently face Western sanctions.
Disguised with a customs code for civilian synthetic fiber exports, the shipping documents dated 2026 and marked with the Rosatom Alabuga-Volokno logo, set out “a full range of freight forwarding services, including cargo transportation, customs clearance, and cargo insurance” between the companies for two 40-foot shipping containers filled with a maximum total of 46 tons “of polyacrylonitrile tow (PAN-precursor) for manufacturing purposes,” according to a translation.
So called PAN-precursor fibers are the key chemical component to make military-grade, light weight carbon fiber. The correct customs code would have identified the shipment as a dual-use item that has both military and civilian applications, said Albright.
The mislabeling of customs codes “points to a company hiding a more sensitive order,” said Kerri Bitsoff, a former Treasury official who designed and enforced sanctions against Russian weapons procurement networks.
“The company takes a controlled item, finds a plausible cover code, and ships it under that category,” she said. “The same cover will often be used across different companies for similar items.”
Advertisement
None of the sanctioned Alabuga SEZ companies imported goods using the customs code normally used for PAN-fiber, according to a review of 2022-2025 trade data from Sayari, a risk and data intelligence company.
Metadata scraped from the shipping document shows the document was created by a Russian state official serving the Tatarstan region.
Alabuga-Volokno’s key role is providing Russian strategic industries with high-spec structural carbon fiber, with 89 percent of the company’s production expected to go to defense industry enterprises by 2030, according to the USCC’s calculations. Internal company product lists shared by the USCC think tank with POLITICO show Alabuga-Volokno makes 39 items containing carbon fiber with various types of polymer binders for aviation, rocket engineering, drones, shipbuilding and armor.
The Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre says it has tracked at least eight tenders to contract shipments of PAN precursors in containers to Alabuga-Volokno from Jilin Chemical Fiber Group since 2022 up to this year.
Sanctions violations
The Ukrainian government believes the shipping documents show potential sanctions evasion, the Ukrainian official said. A British government official said “it would not be appropriate to speculate about any potential future sanctions designations as to do so could reduce their impact.”
Jilin is providing “a critical part of making the carbon fiber necessary” to make weaponized drones, Albright said. “Without it, you can’t build the airframe,” he explained, noting it’s used to strengthen the wing and internal structures, including the fuel tank and engine. The amount of PAN shipped from Jilin would be enough to produce carbon-fiber for as many as 1,300 kamikaze drones, he estimated.
Advertisement
Albright, who has long studied kamikaze drone-making in the Alabuga SEZ factory complex, says Russia has been “totally dependent on China” to supply the specialized PAN acrylic fiber that is the primary ingredient used to manufacture high-performance carbon fiber.
“Dual-use goods from China and Hong Kong keep Russia’s weapons programs running despite Western export controls,” the U.S. House Select Committee on China said in an August report. Beijing provides more than 60 percent of components necessary to keep Russia’s military functioning, per data published in June by the Kiel Institute, a German nonprofit economic analysis foundation.
“The number of companies in China that have provided dual-use capabilities to Russia’s military industrial complex is in the dozens now, and those connections are deep,” said Kurt Campbell, former deputy secretary of state in the Biden administration. In exchange, he added, Moscow provides Beijing technology transfers to upgrade “some military capabilities that they have sought.”
With China’s support, the Russian defense industry “is able to continue to grow its manufacturing base for a wide range of drones, components for missiles, and other types of weaponry, which are then used in its attacks on Ukraine,” said USCC’s Kuzan, noting that ongoing shipments only deepen the industrial sector integration two of the West’s strategic rivals.
“Combating these channels through secondary sanctions, export controls, and enforcement of sanctions restrictions, financial pressure on intermediaries, and coordination with Asian partners,” he said, “must be a priority for the defense and economic policies of the U.S., the EU and their allies.”
John Sakellariadis contributed to this report.

Iran says it will declare ‘prohibited zone’ near Hormuz Strait in coming days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Iran says it will declare ‘prohibited zone’ near Hormuz Strait in coming days
TEHRAN - Iran’s top security chief Mohsen Rezaei on Sept 6 said his country would establish a “prohibited zone” near the strategic Strait of Hormuz, state media reported.
“In the coming days, a prohibited zone will be announced outside the Strait of Hormuz. This zone will start from the US Navy’s blockade line and include areas of the Persian Gulf. Any ship entering this new zone will be placed on the sanctions list” of Iran, Rezaei told the state TV.
Iran’s top negotiator on Sept 6 threatened a more forceful response to any further US attacks after Tehran targeted American warships in their latest round of clashes.
The exchanges of fire, which began with US raids last week, come amid a deadlock in the six-month war between the two foes.
Iran has maintained its stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz while Washington continues a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Washington is also seeking to choke Iran’s economy, rolling out sanctions on entities with financial links to the Islamic republic in a bid to force it into submission.
Iranian Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has acted as chief negotiator in talks to end the war, said on Sept 6 that “the era of proportionate responses has come to an end”.
“Any aggression against Iran’s interests and security will receive a faster, more intense and more painful response,” he added, in a speech carried by state media.
Vessels targeted
On Sept 5, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees American military operations in the region, said Iran had unsuccessfully fired at two American warships – an aircraft carrier and a destroyer.
In response, the US struck three oil tankers it said were linked to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards (IRGC).
Video posted by the military showed large fireballs and billowing flames after projectiles slammed into the ships.
The three vessels were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies”, CENTCOM said.
Iran quickly retaliated, with the Guards saying their naval forces “targeted three oil tankers on the unauthorised route of the Strait of Hormuz and three vessels affiliated with the child-killing America in other areas”.
It warned ships not to attempt to transit the key trade waterway via routes not approved by Tehran.
Early on Sept 6, Iran’s Guards also said they attacked a US naval drone trying to enter the strait, according to a statement carried by state television.
CENTCOM spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins, however, called the claim “a complete lie”.
‘Clinging on to power’
CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper had said after the exchange of strikes: “If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost – taking out three of yours.”
The Iranian foreign ministry condemned the attacks on its oil tankers as “illegal and aggressive actions”.
The administration of US President Donald Trump has tried to downplay the significance of the six-month conflict, which has proven increasingly unpopular at home as midterm elections near.
US Vice-President J.D. Vance has gone so far as to say that he “wouldn’t call it a war”.
Trump reiterated that view on Sept 4, calling the war “small potatoes” for Washington.
Iranian officials have maintained their defiant tone, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told ABC’s This Week programme on Sept 6 that Iran was “doing everything they can to cling on to something”.
“They know their nuclear programme’s coming to an end. Their navy has come to an end. Their air force has come to an end. They’re clinging on to power,” he said.
A fragile ceasefire between the two sides collapsed in July after attacks on commercial ships in the Hormuz strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.
Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly threatened to claim sovereignty over the strait, even posting a map showing it as “new US territory”.
Vance has insisted the US will not reopen talks with Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping in the strait. AFP

ABC Business Daily: Are we headed for 'Bondmageddon'?
Probably not a question you thought you'd ever ask, but our intrepid business unit podcasters not only ask it but answer it for the same price!

Domestic energy market not hit by surging global LNG prices: CBA
While motorists know all too well how the US-Iran war has hurt them at the pump, it's perhaps a surprise that a doubling in LNG spot prices hasn't impacted the cost of energy generation across the Australian winter.
Indeed, baseload power futures in a key segment of the east coast electricity market are now tracking back towards pre-war levels.
Back in 2022, a spike in global LNG prices that followed the Russian invasion of Ukraine contributed to much higher electricity prices across the Australian grid over winter, thanks to its dependence on gas in the generation mix.
CBA's commodities analyst Vivek Dhar says worries that east coast Australia would suffer through a winter as it did in 2022, where domestic gas prices linked up with international gas prices, which, in turn, contributed to surging electricity prices, have thankfully not come to pass.
With around a fifth of global LNG production offline in, stuck in Qatar and Europe boosting gas storage levels ahead of its winter, Mr Dhar says Australia's east coast energy market has exceeded expectations in weathering the increase in international gas prices this year.
"To be clear, the 2022 winter experience for Australia's electricity market was largely due to a perfect storm of events — unplanned dispatchable power outages, electricity and gas demand being stronger due to a colder than usual winter and renewable generation underperforming expectations," Mr Dhar wrote in a research note.
"Batteries, both utility scale and behind the meter, have proven the decisive difference.
"East coast spot gas prices have traded at a significant discount to international gas prices as the influx of batteries has reduced gas demand from gas power generation (GPG)."
Mr Dhar said the proposed Domestic Gas Reservation Scheme due to kick in next year has also provided a disincentive for gas producers to link domestic and international gas prices.
"On the electricity side, batteries have meant more electrons are competing in the morning and evening price peaks, reducing the role of GPG but also, more importantly, reducing the influence of GPG on electricity prices.
"Given GPG typically influences the price of the marginal electron in the morning and evening peaks, batteries have effectively lowered electricity prices.
"And to put this price reduction in perspective, NSW baseload power futures are now tracking below pre-war levels over the next 30 months."
Key Event
Clearance rates hold up, volumes fall as spring auction season opens
The spring home auction season opened with mixed results.
While the national clearance rate remained unchanged for the fourth consecutive week at just under 53%, the number of properties put under the hammer was noticeably lower, down 31% from the opening day a year ago.
However, property market researcher Cotality said auction activity is anticipated to lift over the coming weeks, rising to about 1,640 this week and 1,900 next week.
Melbourne held the most auctions, with 662 homes on the block, up 2.8% on the previous week, though 28% lower than the same week a year earlier.
The preliminary clearance rate rose to 58.2%, up from 54.9% the previous week and a four-week high.
In Sydney, the preliminary clearance rate rose 1.4 percentage points to 57.7%, an 18-week high, with 523 homes auctioned.
Key Event
Iron ore hits more than a 1-month high on elevated freight rates, restocking hopes
Iron ore prices have risen for a third straight session to hit a more than one-month high, supported by elevated freight rates and expectations of restocking by steelmakers ahead of the National Day holiday in China, the world's biggest buyer of the commodity.
The most-traded iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange climbed 1.5% to $US108.33/tonne this morning.
The benchmark October iron ore contract on the Singapore Exchange rose 1.3% to $US100.90/tonne, the highest since July 15 and trading above the key level of $100 for a second straight session.
Lending support to the key steelmaking ingredient was a rally in freight rates fuelled by strong energy prices amid renewed tensions between the United States and Iran, analysts said.
Moreover, anticipation of growing appetite for steelmaking ingredients as steel demand seasonally picks up this month also boosted market sentiment.
Ore consumption has shown signs of recovery, with average daily hot metal output, a gauge of iron ore demand, ticking up 0.1% from the week before to 2.37 million tons after two weeks of falls, data from consultancy Mysteel showed.
However, thin steel margins curbed gains in ore prices, according to Guiqiu Zhuo, an analyst at broker Jinrui Futures.
"There is a seesaw effect between iron ore and coal, with the former strengthening while the latter weakening, but steel margins remained squeezed," Zhuo said.
Other steelmaking ingredients tumbled, with coking coal and coke down 3.4% and 3.0%, respectively.
Steel benchmarks on the Shanghai Futures Exchange were mixed.

Corporate Travel Management (CTM) class action inches closer
We (rightly) talk about KPMG Australia a lot as its failings continue to be examined by a parliamentary committee, the Department of Finance and creditors.
But the other firms aren't having a great time, either.
Class action law firm Phi Finney McDonald has said that it is "well advanced in its investigation" into a class action against Corporate Travel Management (CTM) Limited and its former auditor PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) Australia concerning financial misreporting over several years.
If you don't recall the disaster, there's a great read at the bottom of this post. I mean, seriously, this is just the first two paragraphs.
An Australian travel giant embroiled in a $100 million overcharging scandal for refugee accommodation was invoicing a government for more rooms than a hotel actually had, the ABC can reveal.
Brisbane-based Corporate Travel Management, a former share market darling valued at $2 billion, was also double-billing the UK government during the refugee program or charging for exclusive use of hotels when no exclusivity existed.
When the overcharging scandal exploded, raising questions about the rigour of the PwC audit, the company halted trading in its shares.
When trading resumed, just last week, the value of the company slumped 86% in one day.
The law firm says the potential class action would allege "CTM misled investors in its annual financial reports over a multi-year period up to 2024, in contravention of its obligations under the Corporations Act".
"PwC Australia is alleged to have engaged in misleading or deceptive conduct and making false statements about auditing CTM's financial reports in accordance with the applicable standards.
"A class action would allege that this conduct resulted in a loss to investors who bought shares during the claim period."
Here's Roop Sandhu, principal lawyer at Phi Finney McDonald:
"Investors have a right to expect that financial statements from their listed investments are a true and fair reflection of the company's performance.
"They are rightfully concerned about what has happened to their investments in Corporate Travel, after a long-term suspension and subsequent shattering of the share price.
"Likewise, investors have a right to assume that an auditor's standards meet the relevant legislation and regulatory requirements."

ASX earnings upgrade 'a flash in the pan': J.P. Morgan
With the dust settling on the ASX's August reporting season, J.P. Morgan's equity team has taken a deep dive into the results and has come away disappointed.
The investment bank's Australian equities chief strategist, Jason Steed, said the high hopes earlier in the year had turned out to be merely "a flash in the pan".
"Post February's results season, we declared a thaw in Australia's long, dark earnings winter. August has put paid to that thesis, with the earnings outlook souring and most sectors going into reverse," Mr Steed wrote in a research note to clients.
"Through the course of the season, only Healthcare generated upgrades, albeit from a depressed base."
Mr Steed said Australia stands alone across developed markets in recording negative revisions over the past month; all headline indices are in the red — ASX 200 (-1.4%), ASX 50 (-1.3%) and Industrials (-0.7%).
"Looking forward, earnings growth remains buttressed by the mid-caps, where we estimate the 3-year CAGR (compound annual growth rate) will come in at 11.1%. Our largest companies (ASX 20), however, are set to generate a pedestrian 4.9% over the next three years," he said.
Here's the J.P. Morgan scorecard:
- The upgrade/downgrade ratio deteriorated through the season. The proportion of companies generating upgrades, at 22%, slid below the long-run average, while earnings downgrades climbed to 43%.
- Notable earnings upgrades: Ramsay Healthcare +6%, Super Retail Group +7%, Virgin Australia +12%, Mineral Resources 14%.
- Notable earnings downgrades: JB Hi Fi -5%, Endeavour Group -10%, Seek -11%, Life360 -14%.
One area where upgrades abounded was in showering investors with dividends.
"The income-centric nature of the Australian market, thanks in part to franking, means that boards are very reluctant to cut dividends even in a softening earnings environment," Mr Steed said.
"This mindset was on show through the course of the season, with DPS (dividend per share) upgrades above the historical average and downgrades well below."
Super heavyweight bout: Labor vs One Nation
Labor and One Nation are back in the ring this morning, boxing on about One Nation's policy to divert a portion of super back into pay packets.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has accused One Nation of wanting to "end superannuation as we know it" by allowing renters or mortgage holders to access some of their super early.
"It's now beyond doubt that any Coalition government with One Nation in it will cut your super. This means less money and less economic security for millions of Australian workers," he says.
"Every time One Nation is asked to support the financial interests of Australian workers, they oppose the financial interests of Australian workers. By ending super as we know it, by making Australian workers poorer as a consequence … this is exactly why One Nation poses an unacceptable and dangerous risk to Australian workers."
One Nation Treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce says he can't see why the government would have an issue with One Nation's proposed superannuation plan.
"This is not a seismic shift in administration. It's a change in attitude; that if you're doing it tough, you get some of your own money back," he argued at a press conference in Sydney this morning.
"What we are doing here is giving people back some of their own money from the future, not taking it out of their current balance, but [out of] some of their own money in the future. And what we have to realise [is] that superannuation is not a national asset. It's individuals' asset," he says.

Saxony-Anhalt: Digesting the AfD's landmark election win
September 6, 2026
After an unusually quiet evening at the press center for the Saxony-Anhalt state election, journalists, camera crews and technicians were suddenly running around, jostling and shouting. Ulrich Siegmund, the leading candidate of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), went running off with his bodyguards, looking for the best place to stand so that he would be clearly visible on camera when the election projections started appearing on the screens.
And then, a few minutes later, the commotion started up again, as AfD party leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla arrived, beaming just as broadly as Siegmund. Another scramble ensued, and the bodyguards shouted: "Stay back!"
At 6 pm, when the preliminary results finally came in, the AfD was well above 40%. For the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which governs the region between the Elbe and the Harz Mountains, it is a nightmare — there's no other way to put it. Weidel subsequently declares the result a clear mandate for her party to form a government. It's hard to disagree with her on that. She tells reporters that even before Christmas rolls around, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) will be replaced following this election result.
Weidel: 'This is a mandate for us to form a government!'
After all, Merz, whose popularity has hit record lows across the country, was rarely seen during this election campaign. And his party here in Saxony-Anhalt was glad about that.
AfD co-chair Tino Chrupalla also spoke of a blow to the chancellor, who he said only makes grandiose announcements. He also accused the chancellor of "unnecessarily escalating" tensions with Russia recently. Once the cameras were off, Chrupalla admitted that even he hadn't expected such a clear victory.
The AfD, which the domestic intelligence agency classifies as "confirmed far-right extremist," held its election party at the Altes Theater, just a stone's throw from the press center. Before entering the building, journalists and visitors were searched by police dogs, and bags were checked twice.
"This feels less like a state election and more like a G7 summit," said DW correspondent Matthew Moore, after finally getting into the Altes Theater. To maintain order over the weekend, 1,800 additional police officers were dispatched to Saxony-Anhalt from other federal states.
'Like a trip to the dentist': The CDU at the Maritim Hotel
And what about the CDU, which has governed Saxony-Anhalt for the last 24 years? The voters' rejection of the party could hardly be more decisive. That Sven Schulze, the incumbent premier, did not resign immediately could even be seen as an act of bravery. With a stony expression, he told his supporters: "This is democracy!"
At the beginning of the year, Schulze succeeded Reiner Haseloff as head of government in Saxony-Anhalt. Seventy-two-year-old Haseloff was highly respected in the state and yet did not wish to run for another term. But when he stepped down, it was too late for Schulze to counter the force of support for the AfD.
The CDU election party — which turned out to be not much of a party at all — was held at the four-star Maritim Hotel. In the hotel ballroom, only die-hard CDU supporters remained to witness the debacle. This year's results were half of what they were in the previous state election. It was a difficult defeat for the party that remained the strongest political force in Saxony-Anhalt for the last twenty years. "It's a bit like being in the dentist's waiting room," a CDU supporter told DW reporter Bernd Riegert with a bitter smile. "You know it's going to hurt, but you can't run away."
Uncertainty regarding the BSW
No matter how big the right-wing populists' election victory may be, the AfD has little chance of governing with an absolute majority. And so far, all other parties have ruled out entering into a coalition with it.
It will likely come down to the economically left-wing and politically conservative Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which could narrowly make it into the state parliament.
Meanwhile, Eva von Angern, the leading candidate for the socialist Left Party in Saxony-Anhalt, spoke of a "dark day" for the state, because of "the consequences this result could have for Saxony-Anhalt and the people of Saxony-Anhalt." And by that, she was also referring to the AfD's hardline policy toward refugees. During the campaign, the AfD made it clear time and again that asylum seekers whose applications were rejected would be deported on a large scale "from day one."
Hope within the SPD for a majority without the AfD
As for the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the junior partner in Chancellor Merz's federal government struck a surprisingly optimistic tone. Despite predictions that they would fare much worse, the Social Democrats are now assured of representation in the state parliament. In distant Berlin, SPD Secretary-General Tim Klüssendorf was not yet ready to give up hope that a coalition of all mainstream parties might be able to bypass the AfD and form a coalition: "If such a majority exists, then it should be formed with the participation of all the parties represented in this state parliament," he said.
Greens between euphoria and shock
The environmentalist Greens spent election night somewhere between euphoria and shock. Actually, the party should be delighted with such an unexpected result. Predictions had long suggested they might fail to clear the five-percent threshold, but now they're safely in. DW reporter Giula Saudelli said that some staff members at the Green Party's election party had tears in their eyes when the projections appeared on the screens: tears of relief for their own party and tears of shock at the AfD's gains.
"There's no reason to jump for joy when it's still unclear whether far-right extremists will be able to govern this state," party co-leader Felix Banaszak told DW. He had spent a lot of time campaigning in Saxony-Anhalt. Videos on social media showed him being openly attacked and verbally abused. But he continued nonetheless. People close to him say that this may have contributed to the Greens' election success — a success that doesn't quite feel like one.
… and in Berlin, the chancellor remains silent
But this much is clear: it was an historic evening in Saxony-Anhalt: a defining moment. Much remains unclear, such as who will eventually govern the state and what consequences this will have for Chancellor Friedrich Merz. A press conference has been scheduled with him for midday on Monday.
This article has been translated from German.
