Health Minister Mark Butler has stepped up to answer and has accused the Coalition of overseeing an increase in the tobacco excise when it was in government.
Butler says enforcement is the best way to go about reducing the illicit tobacco industry, and has commended the SA and Queensland government's efforts to bring it under control.
The health minister has pointed to Canada's experience in cutting the tobacco excise, saying it could lead to an increase in smoking rates.
"We're open to sensible ideas. We're not going to do a discount war with organised crime, and we won't be led by the One Nation like you are," Butler says.
Coalition leaving health policy to organised crime: Burke
We're now on the topic of illicit tobacco as Angus Taylor asks why the government won't just adopt the opposition's plan to slash the tobacco excise.
The Coalition is arguing that by cutting the tobacco excise to 80 per cent it would reduce the number of Australians buying tobacco on the illicit market.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke gets pretty fired up in response.
"The last thing this parliament should ever do is outsource its health policy to organised crime," he says.
Burke says the raw cost of an illicit pack of cigarettes is one sixth of the cost of legal cigarettes before you get to the excise.
"So even if you do reduce the excise in the way the opposition are saying, you still have a massive price differential," he says.
Jim Chalmers hoses down suggestion to introduce income splitting
Kennedy MP Bob Katter has the first question from the crossbench and has suggested to the treasurer he introduce income splitting and a birthing payment.
The idea was suggested by former Queensland senator Gerard Rennick in early 2025.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says income splitting will cost the federal budget "substantially" about $70 billion over the medium term.
Chalmers says income splitting would primarily benefit higher wealth and income couples.
He says income splitting would encourage economic dependence and reduce incentives for women's workforce participation.
"I hear the proposal at the core of his question, the government has decided to go down a different path when it comes to providing that cost-of-living relief that families need and deserve," Chalmers says.
Minister stands by house price modelling
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson is up next.
He references a recent downturn in house prices in Sydney and asks if the government still stands by its modelling.
Housing Minister Clare O'Neil takes this one.
She starts by saying the government "could not have been more clear" about the impact changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount were estimated to have on prices. 
The budget wound back the capital gains tax discount for investors in established housing and limited negative gearing to existing investments and new builds.
O'Neil says the budget papers outlined Treasury's modelling. It estimated the changes would add about 75,000 additional owner occupiers and prices would grow by 2 per cent less over a couple of years.
"We've been transparent in the budget," she said, questioning why the Coalition hasn't used opportunities to ask Treasury themselves about the modelling.
Manager of Opposition Business Dan Tehan did his best to say she wasn't being relevant to the question, but Speaker Milton Dick lets this one pass.
We move on.
Albanese refuses to say whether Labor will release house price modelling
The first question of the day goes to Opposition Leader Angus Taylor who has asked about Labor's budget tax changes.
"Will the prime minister release Labor's secret housing modelling so Australians can know how much further prices are going to crash?" Taylor asks.
The prime minister has refused to say whether he would release the government's internal modelling.
But Anthony Albanese has been quick to spruik reporting saying there were a record number of loans for the construction of new dwellings in June.
"When people choose to invest in housing, they're not investing in their future wealth and assets, they're investing in the future wealth and assets of the nation," Albanese says.

Iran says it will declare 'prohibited zone' near Strait of Hormuz in coming days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
21:00:29 UTC
06:00:29 KST

Iran's top security chief has said that Iran would establish a "prohibited zone" near the Strait of Hormuz in the coming days.
"This zone will start from the US Navy's blockade line and include areas of the Persian Gulf,” Mohsen Rezaei told Iranian state TV on Sunday.
“Any ship entering this new zone will be placed on the sanctions list of Iran,” he added.
Rezaei also said Iran and Oman would sign an agreement in the coming days on the new corridor through Hormuz, with its entry and exit points under Iranian control.
He said the Strait of Hormuz was “completely closed and under the control of the armed forces,” dismissing US President Donald Trump’s claim that the strategic waterway remained open as a “big lie.”
Before Iran closed the strait, more than 100 ships carrying over 100 million tons of cargo passed through it daily, Rezaei said. He added that only seven or eight ships carrying essential goods for Iran were now transiting the waterway.
The latest development comes as Tehran’s chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned of a more forceful response to any further US attacks after Tehran targeted American warships in their latest round of clashes.
The exchanges of fire, which began with US raids last week, come amid a deadlock in the six-month war between the two foes.
Iran has maintained its stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz while Washington continues a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Washington is rolling out sanctions on entities with financial links to the Islamic Republic.
Ghalibaf, who has acted as chief negotiator in talks to end the war, said on Sunday that "the era of proportionate responses has come to an end".
"Any aggression against Iran's interests and security will receive a faster, more intense and more painful response," he added, in a speech carried by state media.
Vessels targeted
On Saturday, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees American military operations in the region, said Iran had fired at two American warships, an aircraft carrier and a destroyer.
In response, the US struck three oil tankers it said were linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC).
Video posted by the military showed large fireballs and billowing flames after projectiles slammed into the ships.
The three vessels were "part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies", CENTCOM said.
Iran quickly retaliated, with the Guards saying their naval forces "targeted three oil tankers on the unauthorised route of the Strait of Hormuz and three vessels affiliated with the child-killing America in other areas".
It warned ships not to attempt to transit the key trade waterway via routes not approved by Tehran.
Early on Sunday, Iran's Guards also said they attacked a US naval drone trying to enter the strait, according to a statement carried by state television.
CENTCOM spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins, however, called the claim "a complete lie".
'Clinging on to power'
CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper had said after the exchange of strikes: "If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost - taking out three of yours."
The Iranian foreign ministry condemned the attacks on its oil tankers as "illegal and aggressive actions".
A fragile ceasefire between the two sides collapsed in July after attacks on commercial ships in the Hormuz Strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.
Trump has repeatedly warned in recent weeks and claimed sovereignty over the strait.
Vance has insisted the US will not reopen talks with Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping in the strait.

War update: 206 clashes on front line, fiercest fighting in Pokrovsk sector

“A total of 206 combat engagements have taken place since the beginning of the day. The enemy carried out 59 airstrikes, dropped 208 guided aerial bombs, and used 5,308 kamikaze drones to strike targets. It also carried out 1,957 shelling attacks on populated areas and positions of our troops,” the statement said.

LONDON, September 6. /TASS/. The armed conflict between the United States and Iran may continue for six months more, former Pentagon chief (2011-2013) and former CIA director (2009-2011) Leon Panetta said.
"I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved," he said in an interview with The Guardian.
"It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end," he said, adding that the Trump administration is risking to be dragged into a protracted war in the Middle East.
According to Panetta, the conflict seems to be on course to become "another failed war" in the Middle East "like Iraq and Afghanistan." The United States’ adversaries "see weakness in terms of our ability to be able to really implement our military capability of defending our country," he noted.
US President Donald Trump, in his words has "boxed himself in" and now has three options: to "admit that it’s a failed war" and walk away, which he thinks to be highly improbable; to continue exchanging strikes, with both sides attempting to "avoid the startup of a more dangerous war" but refusing to negotiate or surrender, which he believes will lead to a protracted war; and to finally take control of the Strait of Hormuz and this way strip Iran of its "most dangerous leverage point" over the US.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding envisaging an immediate ceasefire on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, the United States resumed large-scale attacks on Iran overnight to July 8, having accused it of breaching the existing agreements in what concerned the Strait of Hormuz, a global chokepoint for approximately 25% of oil and some 20% of LNG supplies.
The Trump administration recently signaled an end to any large-scale use of force against Iran and a transition to putting economic pressure on the Islamic Republic through sanctions instead.

Isro dismisses privatisation speculation, says role will only strengthen
NEW DELHI/BENGALURU: Allaying the fears of some of its staff that the organisation will be privatised and its role reduced to an R&D lab, Isro Sunday dismissed “speculation” about any diminution of its role as “misinformation”.“These assertions are completely baseless and incorrect. We wish to categorically state that Isro will neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished,” it said.Isro further said it would continue to remain “India’s principal institution for advanced space research and technology development, national and strategic missions, space science and exploration, and critical and frontier space capabilities”.Space promoter and regulator Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (INSPACe) chairperson Pawan Goenka also said Sunday that Isro would “remain the bedrock of the Indian space sector” and at the core of India’s space programme leading frontier research and the next generation of national missions like the space station and Gaganyaan.The agency said, “Participation of private sector in space is not about reducing its role.
It is about enabling Isro to focus even more strongly on the next generation of India’s space programme, while industry scales mature technologies and capabilities. What is changing is not the importance of Isro, but the scale and structure of India’s space ecosystem. The transition is therefore towards an Isro-led national space ecosystem.”The agency also said its role would progressively strengthen in areas where “its scientific expertise matters most: frontier R&D, advanced technologies, human spaceflight, next-generation launch systems, deep-space and planetary missions and strategic national capabilities. It will continue developing cutting-edge technologies, including advanced payloads for communication, navigation and Earth observation, sensors, propulsion systems and other critical technologies”.After nine Isro staff associations representing thousands sought clarification from the agency chairperson on the private sector shift, Goenka said on X, “Let me say it unequivocally: Isro’s role is by no means diminishing.”On scaling up the production of rockets and satellites in India, the INSPACe director declared that the country had set an “ambitious target” of 50 launches a year by 2030. “A goal of this scale cannot be achieved by one organisation alone. Govt and private industry have to build this future together,” he said.The INSPACe chairperson said, “The reforms since 2020 are about expanding India’s overall space ecosystem. IN-SPACe will facilitate and authorise greater non-govt participation, while NSIL will help commercialise mature capabilities.”Goenka said the idea of space reforms is to “let industry increasingly manufacture and scale mature launch vehicles, satellites and other systems, while Isro focuses on what it is uniquely placed to do: advanced R&D, scientific missions, strategic missions, new technologies, and infrastructure that is too complex for the private sector to develop on its own”.
Assuring staff that they were going to handle big projects, he said, “Isro will remain at the core of India’s space programme, leading frontier research and the next generation of national missions, including Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035, an Indian crewed mission to the Moon by 2040, next-generation launch systems, and sustained lunar and planetary exploration.”“The direction is not a smaller Isro. It is a larger Indian space ecosystem, with Isro pushing the technological frontier,” he added.

Ukraine cannot be settled like a business deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:11:19 UTC
05:11:19 KST

Fyodor Lukyanov: Here’s why it’s hard for Witkoff and Kushner to close the Russia-Ukraine deal
Diplomatic efforts to end an acute and bloody armed conflict should always be welcomed and the persistence of Donald Trump’s administration, which has pursued this goal for more than a year and a half, also deserves recognition, even if the results so far can hardly be called outstanding.
At the very least, the White House remains the only actor in the West both attempting to change the situation and possessing significant leverage over it. Trump and his closest associates probably do genuinely want the war to end as its continuation distracts Washington from foreign policy priorities they regard as more important. But why, then, does Trump’s diplomatic initiative keep going round in circles, with each new attempt ending in another disappointment?
Trump and his principal envoys tend to approach the conflict as an extraordinarily difficult but essentially technical problem, as a puzzle to be solved in isolation from the wider international system. This reflects the worldview of the current White House, where international affairs are a collection of practical problems to be resolved in ways that strengthen America’s position, preferably with some commercial benefit attached. Given the professional backgrounds of the president and his two principal intermediaries, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, this is hardly surprising.
Such an approach can be useful as an instrument, but it becomes less useful when it substitutes for an understanding of the processes that produced the conflict in the first place and, to use the Russian formulation, its root causes. Any durable settlement requires some understanding of what must change in relations between the major powers if similar confrontations are to be avoided.
Trump repeatedly insists that the war would never have begun had he been president in 2022 with the implication that Joe Biden and the Democrats were simply too incompetent to prevent it. Trump has occasionally acknowledged that NATO’s long expansion eastward contributed to the crisis, but he generally shows little interest in the broader military and political processes behind it.
Yet American and NATO policy towards Ukraine wasn’t created by one administration or a handful of officials in Washington and Brussels, rather it developed over decades from a particular conception of Western strategic interests. The crisis that entered its most acute phase in 2022 was, from Moscow’s perspective, the culmination of processes underway since the end of the Cold War.
This helps explain why Washington continues to underestimate how much the outcome matters to the principal participants. For both Russia and Ukraine, too much is at stake for the conflict to be settled through the kind of transaction Trump instinctively favors, given their interests are obviously opposed, but both regard the outcome as fateful. Western Europe, having invested heavily in Ukraine’s cause, also has a direct political stake in the result, so every new attempt by Washington’s two brokers therefore encounters the same obstacle in that none of the parties sees this as simply another deal.
There’s another contradiction in the American position because Washington wishes to become the principal mediator in a conflict whose continuation it has materially supported.The US position has certainly changed under Trump as Washington’s previous fixation on Ukraine has diminished considerably. Trump would prefer America to step back while retaining decisive influence over what happens next, but that is precisely where the difficulty begins.
Transferring the financial burden, political responsibility and risks to the Western Europeans while continuing to dictate the terms requires a degree of obedience from junior partners that Washington can no longer guarantee. EU governments and Kiev have also learnt how to deal with this unconventional president and when they can’t persuade him, they have become increasingly adept at circumventing his pressure.
The one American instrument against which there would be little defence is a complete cessation of military support, but Trump is unlikely to take that step, even if he were personally inclined to do so because facilitating an outright Russian victory isn’t his objective. He may care less than his predecessor about the precise shape of the eventual settlement, but a complete Ukrainian defeat would be another matter. Nor would abandoning Ukraine enjoy much support across the American political establishment, where there is virtually no constituency for a fundamental rapprochement with Russia.
The White House therefore doesn’t envisage the radical change in American policy that would be necessary to transform the conflict, but without one, events tend to return to their previous course as a prolonged and extremely fierce confrontation whose duration nobody can confidently predict.
In such a confrontation, those fighting the war and bearing its risks ultimately matter more than mediators or outside sponsors. None of this means Witkoff and Kushner’s shuttle diplomacy is pointless, given communication between adversaries is indispensable, and the present infrastructure for official dialogue remains inadequate. Also, informal channels can help restore understanding where formal diplomacy has broken down, but informal diplomacy has limits.
Friends and business associates may establish contacts and discover areas in which compromise is conceivable, but they don’t themselves make peace. The shuttle diplomacy of a presidential son-in-law and a trusted business partner may eventually serve as a catalyst for serious negotiations, however, if that moment comes, the settlement will have to be negotiated by officials and institutions possessing state legitimacy and the power to implement what they sign. Personal connections can open the door, but they can’t, by themselves, end a war.
This article was first published by Russia in Global Affairs, translated and edited by RT.

Far-right AfD wins key state vote in eastern Germany
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
23:09:23 EEST
05:09:23 KST

Germany’s Alternative for Germany has won the state election in Saxony-Anhalt with about 44% of the vote, putting the party in first place by a wide margin and raising the prospect of a far-right state government for the first time in postwar Germany. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU finished second on about 18%.
Exit polls and early projections showed the AfD more than doubling its 23.7% share from the 2021 election.
The result gave the party its strongest state-level performance since its founding in 2013. Whether it will govern remains unclear because the final distribution of seats depends on the performance of smaller parties.
AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund told supporters in Magdeburg that the party had “made history in this state”.
“We have achieved exactly what we wanted to achieve,” he said after the polls closed.
The AfD said the result gave it a mandate to govern. Party co-leader Alice Weidel described the result as historic and said the party would speak with other political groups about the formation of a government.
Germany’s main parties continue to reject governing with the AfD under the political “firewall” intended to keep the party out of coalition governments.
The CDU suffered a major defeat after governing Saxony-Anhalt since 2002. Its state leader, Sven Schulze, conceded that the election had been difficult and said the party would have to respond to the result.
CDU general secretary Franziska Hoppermann called the outcome a defeat for the party but rejected suggestions that Merz’s position should be reconsidered.
The result places further pressure on Friedrich Merz, whose federal coalition with the Social Democrats has struggled with weak economic growth and falling public support.
Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, who also leads the SPD, said voters had sent a “signal to Berlin”.
Turnout was high. The Guardian reported participation at 76.5%, while other projections placed it closer to 78%. Reuters cited broadcaster ZDF as estimating turnout above 80% during counting.
Saxony-Anhalt has about 2.1 million residents and formed part of communist East Germany before reunification.
The AfD has built much of its strongest support in eastern Germany. The party also recorded gains in western states earlier this year and now leads some national opinion polls ahead of the next federal election, due in 2029.
A recent INSA poll placed the AfD on 28% nationally and the conservatives on 20%.
The AfD campaigned on tighter immigration controls, changes to education and cultural policy, opposition to new wind farms and closer relations with Russia.
Siegmund has also promoted a “remigration” policy. The party says the term refers to deporting people who are in Germany illegally or have committed crimes. Critics argue the policy risks extending beyond those groups.
The AfD branch in Saxony-Anhalt has been classified as right-wing extremist by the state domestic intelligence service. The party rejects that designation.
A possible route to power will depend on the final seat count and whether smaller parties enter parliament.
The left-wing BSW crossed the 5% threshold in some early projections. The party has ruled out a formal coalition with the AfD but has worked with it on selected policy questions.
If the AfD fails to secure an absolute majority and no party agrees to govern with it, the CDU and other parties would need to negotiate a multi-party coalition to keep the AfD out of the state government.

What the Pentagon’s Sweeping Polygraph Hunt Has Revealed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:08:02 UTC
05:08:02 KST

Pentagon investigators administered polygraph tests to dozens of military officers and civilian employees in August as part of an investigation into disclosures about the nation’s dwindling weapons stockpiles.
The polygraph tests, first reported by The New York Times last week, followed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement in July that the Pentagon was forming a joint task force with the Department of Justice to identify and prosecute what he called the “unauthorized disclosure of sensitive” information to the press.
Spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement to TIME that the Pentagon does not comment on investigative matters but “takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly.”
“Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world,” the statement said.
The August interrogations included some 50 members of the Joint Staff, according to the Times. CBS News also reported that several dozen officials were tested earlier this summer, including those from the U.S. Central Command.
Why did the Pentagon polygraph dozens of officials?
Sources familiar with the matter told multiple outlets this summer that U.S. supplies of certain critical munitions—including long-range precision-guided missiles and air-defense interceptors—had fallen dangerously low. They suggested that its inventory would likely dwindle further amid the ongoing war with Iran.
Sources told The Washington Post that Trump clashed with Hegseth over the matter during a visit to Camp David on July 31, claiming that he had been “misled on extreme munitions shortages that now threaten to limit military options with Iran.”
Trump refuted the idea that there were any shortages in a Truth Social post on Aug. 6.
“The U.S. has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types,” Trump wrote in his post. “Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed.”
The President called for lengthy imprisonment for those caught leaking information to the press.
“The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down,” he added. “Long term jail sentences will be sought!”
In a separate post that same day, he denied that he’d fought with Hegseth, calling the reports “completely unfounded rumors.”
“I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing,” he said.
Trump intensified his attacks on the coverage on Sept. 3, calling media outlets who reported on the shortages “treasonous scum” who refuse to “accurately report” on the conflict with Iran.
Despite Trump’s repeated denials of a broad munitions shortage, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated in late July that missile interceptor inventories have dropped—with Patriot inventories now under 1,000 and THAAD inventories at about 250.
Exact figures about the U.S. weapons cache are classified—and that’s for a good reason, according to Harrison Mann, a former defense intelligence official and a senior fellow with the advocacy group Win Without War.
“That is valuable information to any U.S. adversary,” he tells TIME. “Obviously, if they know that we're out of ammo in some significant way, it changes deterrence calculations for U.S. adversaries.”
At the same time, however, he argues that any shortage would likely be clear to the public and to Iran.
“Smart people can put together pretty accurate estimates of what the U.S. has used up between looking at what's been produced, which isn't necessarily a closely guarded secret, and looking at what has been expended on the battlefield,” he says. “Maybe not with the same amount of fidelity [as Pentagon officials], but the Iranians can tell when they're not getting hit by as many standoff munitions, and certainly everyone can tell when U.S. and partners have run out of interceptors.”
Mark Cancian, a senior adviser with the CSIS Defense and Security Department, says he and his colleague created CSIS’s July report on dwindling munitions using only “unclassified” sources.
“If two people at a think tank can do this analysis with entirely unclassified sources, then the Chinese, with tens of thousands of intelligence operatives, and way better sources of information can get much better numbers,” Cancian says.
What Pentagon polygraph rules require—and what the tests found
The Pentagon adheres to specific guidelines and restrictions when administering polygraph tests. They are most commonly used in pre-employment and vetting for intelligence agencies like the National Security Agency and the Defense Intelligence Agency. They are also administered when personnel are seeking or maintaining access to top-secret, special-access, or other sensitive information—as well as in the event of unauthorized disclosures of classified information. 
Pentagon rules require an examinee’s written consent and allow the person to end the examination at any time. For an issue-specific counterintelligence examination, investigators must have interviewed the person, reasonably believe that the person knew about or was involved in the matter, pursue other investigative avenues as thoroughly as circumstances permit, and determine that the polygraph is essential to the investigation.
The Defense Secretary is also required to establish a process for monitoring the “responsible and effective” use of polygraphs and to make information about their use available to congressional defense committees.
The Pentagon has not released enough information to determine whether investigators followed all those requirements. It also has not disclosed the investigation’s findings. CBS News, however, reported that no one had failed the questions meant to determine whether any officials had leaked information to the media.
It also said that the polygraph tests included a wide range of questions pertaining to national security. Specifically, The New York Times reported that officials were asked if they had disclosed classified information to members of the press, according to information provided by its sources close to the investigation, and if they had provided information about diminished munitions stocks.
People familiar with the effort told the Times that the tests appeared intended not only to identify a leaker but also to deter officials who might leak classified information to the media in the future.
How unusual are polygraphs in Pentagon leak investigations?
While the use of polygraphs is not unheard of, the sheer number of people targeted during this investigation is uncommon, officials told CBS News.
David Pozen, a law professor at Columbia University, pointed TIME toward his article for the Harvard Law Review that assesses information leaks within the federal government.
“Periodically, task forces have recommended that the White House take concerted steps to facilitate leak investigations, such as regularizing the use of polygraphs and requiring government employees who speak with the press to provide advance notice, followed by summaries of what was discussed,” he wrote.
This was notably implemented during Ronald Reagan’s presidency in 1983. Reagan authorized polygraph testing in investigations of unauthorized classified disclosures, although he barred agencies from using the results alone to discipline employees.
Polygraphs have been considered or used in leak investigations under more recent administrations, as well. During the George W. Bush administration, the FBI interviewed nearly 100 members and staff of congressional intelligence committees while investigating leaked intelligence connected to the Sept. 11 attacks. Agents commonly asked whether they would take polygraphs, but most declined.
In subsequent years, publicly documented operations involving dozens of senior military officials appear exceedingly rare. But the Trump Administration has used polygraphs in previous leak investigations.
In early 2025, the Department of Homeland Security administered lie detector tests to identify people suspected of disclosing plans for immigration raids. That year, members of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s office were reportedly polygraphed in response to a leak investigation. At the direction of Director Kash Patel, the FBI also began using polygraphs in leak investigations in 2025. In a separate episode this year, more than two dozen current and former members of Patel’s security detail—in addition to some information-technology employees—were reportedly tested in an effort to identify sources of leaks about his leadership.
Still, Cancian says that polygraph use is more common at intelligence agencies than among senior military staff. He characterizes a polygraph hunt of this scale as incredibly unusual.
How the Pentagon’s polygraph hunt could affect future disclosures
While no leakers have been identified to the public, and it remains unknown whether the efforts uncovered any, the tests may serve a secondary purpose—which is to dissuade officials from sharing information in the future.
Cancian says the investigation stems from an “understandable” desire for senior Pentagon officials to have candid conversations with their employees without worrying about leaks to the press.
“Every administration is concerned about that. I think this one is particularly concerned about that,” Cancian says. Otherwise, officers may hesitate to put concerns in writing, circulate formal objections, or talk openly within authorized channels. The Joint Staff is tasked with giving civilian leaders candid assessments of readiness, risk, and operational sustainability, while coordinating with combatant commands around the world.
“Meetings get smaller and smaller, fewer and fewer people can attend because of concerns that larger groups, you know, might leak,” he says.
Mann adds that a polygraph test is known as an “inconclusive” tool.
“You can game them. You can get false positives,” he says. “So, you certainly won't necessarily get to the bottom of whatever you're searching for by running a lot of polygraphs, but it is quite effective as an intimidation tool and as a deterrent against leaks.”
He says that many officials are “still nervous” about doing routine polygraph tests, even if they have “nothing to hide.”
“They know it's something that you can fail and that can then disrupt your career or suspend your clearance if you can't pass it, even if it's just because you were nervous that day,” Mann continues.
He says that this polygraph hunt is a way for Hegseth to test the loyalty of his employees amid pressure over the continuation of efforts in Iran. Just this week, Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina urged Trump to replace Hegseth as Defense Secretary.
“Independent of the Iran war, [Hegseth] has been trying quite hard, in my view, to streamline that bureaucracy to more personal loyalty—often at the expense of readiness or combat effectiveness,” Mann says. “This is one of the products of somebody who is trying to have a very, very tight grip on the bureaucracy he leads.”

Swans show what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like in Brisbane boilover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:07:07 UTC
05:07:07 KST

Fri, 28 Aug, 7:40 pm, Final score, Bulldogs 96, Magpies 93
analysis
Swans show exactly what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like in Brisbane boilover
When Sydney chairman Andrew Pridham declared his side's premiership hopes "torpedoed" after suspending five players, he was right.
Preparing for a finals campaign is a delicate exercise. A little shift here or there can have major impacts. The less things change, the better.
At least, that is what conventional wisdom says.
Last year, Adelaide's excellent home-and-away season was detonated by Izak Rankine's suspension for a homophobic slur on the eve of the finals.
Rankine's actions drew a dark cloud over the entire football club, and without him on the field in the finals, the Crows unsurprisingly limped out in straight sets.
Winning a final with five of your first-choice players sidelined? That seemed like mission impossible for the Swans.
A lot has been made of Sydney's famed "Bloods" culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. What is it? What is it supposed to look like? Is it real or just a PR myth?
While the club rightly admitted the culture was not what it once was off the field, on the field there appears to be little sign of slippage.
With Sydney decimated by the suspensions, the Swans appeared to be their rivals' easy ticket to a deep September run, the helpless carcass hungry animals in an African savanna would feast upon.
Brisbane, by virtue of a slight percentage edge over Hawthorn, had the apparent gift of facing the Swans in one qualifying final while the Hawks looked doomed as they headed to Perth to take on Fremantle in the other. How quickly things can change over one weekend.
Sydney has been one of the AFL's model clubs over the past two decades as a picture of professionalism from the top down, and performances like the one against Brisbane remind you exactly why the Swans have been revered for so long.
Turn on a Swans game, and you know what you're getting. Regardless of who is in the line-up or who is in the coaches' box, Sydney shows up with a baseline of effort and intensity, backed by a relentless never-say-die attitude.
All of these traits make up Sydney's true "Bloods" culture on the field.
If you wanted an example of what it looks like, the culture was on full display as Sydney eviscerated the two-time reigning premiers in front of an SCG crowd that was as raucous as it has ever been.
The louder the crowd got, the better the Swans played. The better the Swans played, the louder they got. The crowd and the players worked hand in hand like a beautiful symphony, and the tidal wave they created swallowed Brisbane up entirely.
It is hard to imagine an 18-5 team flying under the radar, but that is exactly what Sydney has done so far this season, right up until the Pullman Hotel scandal.
While the AFL world was consumed by Fremantle's leap from a cute team to a bona fide premiership threat and Brisbane's bid to threepeat, Sydney quietly ticked along in the background to the best home-and-away season in its history.
What Sydney couldn't recoup in terms of talent in the absence of Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — arguably three of its top six players by any metric — it made up for with sheer, unadulterated hard work against Brisbane.
That is not to say the Swans are a team bereft of star power in the absence of the suspended five.
In Charlie Curnow, Sydney still has the AFL's most terrifying key forward, in the metronomic Brodie Grundy, it still has arguably the best big man on his day in the non-Max Gawn division, in Errol Gulden, it has a Rolls-Royce of a midfielder capable of being the lead actor in any team's engine room, and in the incandescent Tom Papley, it has a small forward that can bend the energy of a match like no other.
It is no surprise that all of these guys, as well as many others, were excellent in the win over Brisbane.
"The two weeks of training up to that point, we trained the house down," Papley told Nine's Sunday Footy Show about the lead-up to the Lions game.
"That's the best we've trained all season. The drills we did were all about pressure, closing space, chasing, tackling, and surging the ball forward, and we trained so well and came together on game day.
"I'm so proud of the boys. It was amazing.
"There were board members in the rooms after the game saying it was the best win in the club's history apart from the premierships.
"The job's not done yet, but the desire and passion we played with … inside the four walls we believed and that's what we kept doing."
Sydney has played in, and won, bigger games in its history. It will continue to do so going forward as well.
But with the context of everything that has happened in the lead-up to this one, and then the Callum Mills injury sprinkled over the top as an additional bit of nightmare fuel, Sydney will have to go a long way to find a performance it is prouder of.
The Swans still face an uphill task to win this year's flag, even with a home preliminary final to come in a fortnight.
As the Swans have experienced in their past four Grand Final appearances since their last premiership in 2012, even the best-laid plans with a perfect lead-up can go up in smoke on the final day of the season.
But for one day at least, the Swans showed everyone just exactly what "Bloods" culture is supposed to look like.

Amazon cargo plane overshoots runway at Miami airport, striking vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:06:43 UTC
05:06:43 KST

Amazon cargo plane overshoots runway at Miami airport, killing five
MIAMI – An Amazon cargo plane overran a runway at Miami International Airport and burst into flames on Sept 6, killing at least five people and shutting down the airport’s runways.
The Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air as Prime Air Flight 7598, overshot the runway at around 2pm after arriving from Luis Munoz Marin International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
The plane slammed into multiple vehicles near the airport, trapping some people inside, according to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, which reported heavy flames and smoke when it responded to the incident.
Along with the five people who were killed, another five were injured, three of whom were in critical condition, Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said at a news conference.
“We’ll continue to update you as soon as information is confirmed, and tonight our entire community is joined in prayer and grieving for those who are affected,” she said.
“Prime Air Flight 7598 overran Miami International Airport’s diagonal runway and is disabled at the north-west end of the airport,” Indira Almeida-Pardillo, a spokeswoman for Miami International Airport, said in a statement.
She said all runways and taxiways were closed as at 3pm local time (3am on Sept 7, Singapore time) and a ground stop was in effect.
Several hours later, at least two of the runways had opened, said Greg Chin, another airport spokesperson.
There was “a very complex fire”, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue chief Ray Jadallah said at a news conference, and the engine compartments were on fire during the “search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot who were trapped in this aircraft”.
A total of 60 fire units responded to the scene.
“They arrived within 30 seconds after getting a call,” he said.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned of significant delays and possible cancellations in a post on social media platform X.
21 Air, a Miami-based cargo airline, began operating Boeing 767-300 freighters on behalf of Amazon in 2024.
In a statement on its website, 21 Air said it was cooperating with the FAA, the US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and local authorities.
“Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives,” the company said.
Amazon confirmed that one of its planes, operated by 21 Air, experienced an incident while attempting to land in Miami.
“We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokeswoman, said in a post on X.
“Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being and care of everyone involved,” she added.
The FAA said it would investigate the incident, and the NTSB said it was also starting a probe and would hold a media briefing on Sept 7.
Amazon’s in-house cargo airline has tilted its focus to larger aircraft that can handle longer distances and bulk shipping, with the 767 model that crashed in Miami now accounting for the largest portion of its fleet.
Amazon Prime also has 10 Airbus A330-300 freighters, as well as smaller narrow-body 737s for regional routes.
21 Air, which also provides dedicated transport for DHL Express, is owned by Jim Crane, the chairman of the Houston Astros baseball team, according to a 2021 letter to the Department of Transportation.
While the circumstances of the accident remain unknown, the crash stands to be the worst cargo-related incident since UPS Airlines Flight 2976 was destroyed on Nov 4, 2025, when it impacted the ground shortly after take-off at Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport in Kentucky, killing the three crew members on board and 11 people on the ground.
Freight planes make up only a small part of commercial air traffic, but cargo operations have been prone to proportionally more crashes over the years, partly because flights can be longer and planes are often older.
The most common accidents in the industry in 2025 were tail strikes, landing-gear malfunctions, runway excursions and ground damage, according to the International Air Transport Association’s 2025 Annual Safety Report.
The aircraft involved in the Miami crash was more than 32 years old, having first flown in June 1994.
Over the decades, it changed hands, including operations for Air Europa, Kenya Airways and Atlas Air, a cargo specialist, after being converted into a cargo aircraft in 2016, according to data compiled by the Planespotters website.
The Boeing 767 is no longer in production as a commercial aircraft but still widely flown.
The manufacturer still makes the plane in low numbers as military refuelling planes. BLOOMBERG

At least five killed in New Delhi building collapse

Kushner refrains from saying is US will toughen pressure on Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:03:28 UTC
05:03:28 KST

WASHINGTON, September 6. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner has refrained from saying whether the United States is going to increase pressure on Russia if no visible progress is made toward settling the Ukrainian conflict in the foreseeable future.
"There's no such thing, you know, in the world as forever enemies or forever allies," he told a news conference after talks with Vladimir Zelensky in Kiev, answering a relevant question.
According to Kushner, Trump is looking at the Ukrainian conflict through the prism of the "idea of what the best outcome could be and what benefits all people." "You know, President Trump comes from the business world. In the business world you think about things in the context of win-win," he said. "War is negative sum, you know. Everyone loses from war, whereas you know business and peace is positive sum, and hopefully you can find big benefits from that in a big way."
"Our role is to try to be the ones who are pursuing the peace," he stressed, adding that attempts to settle the conflict in Ukraine are "a very important and noble pursuit."
"And we're going to keep doing it with everything we have," Kushner noted. "And President Trump obviously has a lot of different ways to play it, but he's always focused on what are the best interests of America and the United States.".

In France, the far-right leader wants Ukraine to pay for Europe's aid - Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
Jordan Bardella, leader of the "National Rally," is demanding guarantees of repayment for aid to Ukraine. He proposes spending funds only on European weapons.
The president of France’s far-right party "National Rally," Jordan Bardella, called for replacing unconditional support for Ukraine with relations under which France would receive something in return. If his political force comes to power, financial and military aid to Kyiv could be provided under new conditions. Bloomberg reports this, writes UNN.
Details
According to him, the difficult state of French public finances requires Paris to receive some return for military aid to Kyiv. The 30-year-old politician is considered one of the most likely candidates for the post of prime minister of France if Marine Le Pen wins next year’s presidential election. At the Ambrosetti Forum in Cernobbio, Italy, Bardella said that France has serious problems with public debt and the budget deficit.
We are drowning in debt. We are drowning in deficits. And it is irresponsible to take on spending commitments and promises of financial support for a country without any guarantees
Bardella stressed that the current approach needs to be completely reconsidered. He spoke positively about the policy of the United States, which demands certain commitments from Ukraine in exchange for support. As an example, the politician mentioned agreements granting the United States access to Ukrainian natural resources, including rare-earth materials, as part of guarantees related to loans and other aid.
At the same time, Bardella assured that France would not abandon Ukraine if Marine Le Pen wins; she is the "National Rally" candidate for president after Emmanuel Macron. However, he proposed changing the mechanism for providing support. In particular, Ukraine could guarantee that financial aid received from European states would be used to purchase military equipment exclusively from defense-industry companies in those countries.
As the publication notes, French President Emmanuel Macron has sought to coordinate Europe’s response to Russia’s war against Ukraine and strengthen France’s position as one of Kyiv’s main allies and a leader of the Western bloc. Bardella’s position differs substantially. His views on international politics and the economy are much closer to Trump’s approach.
Bardella also criticized the European Union’s regulatory policy. He took a position close to that of the American president and major U.S. technology corporations, whose influence the EU has sought to limit with new rules in recent years. In the politician’s view, France could use its significant nuclear-power capacity to attract data centers needed for the development of artificial intelligence.
We remind you
National Rally Vice President Louis Aliot promised to halt aid to Kyiv if Le Pen wins the election. The leader of the National Rally’s parliamentary group has already announced her participation in the presidential race.

The psychological effects of padel and pickleball, according to science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:00:38 UTC
05:00:38 KST

Pickleball participation was associated with greater happiness, life satisfaction, social integration and lower depression, while padel was more closely studied in relation to confidence, anxiety and mental fatigue, according to a systematic review published in Frontiers in Psychology.
Physical activity is widely linked to better mental health, yet many people do not meet recommended activity levels. Padel and pickleball have attracted attention because they are social, relatively accessible and can be played across a range of ages and skill levels. Padel is played on an enclosed court where the ball can rebound from the walls, while pickleball uses a smaller court, a perforated plastic ball and slower-paced play that emphasizes strategy and interaction.
The researchers conducted the review because most previous studies had concentrated on physical fitness, injuries and sporting performance. Less was known about whether these sports were related to mental health and wellbeing. The review ultimately revealed a stark divide in the existing literature: padel has mostly been studied in competitive settings, while pickleball research has frequently focused on recreational play among older adults.
Led by Lena Lauxtermann at the University of Vienna, the researchers searched for studies published through October 8, 2024. Of 71 records screened, 14 studies were included, representing 1,403 participants. Eight padel studies included 538 people and six pickleball studies included 865. Women represented 42% of the overall sample, or approximately 589 participants.
The pickleball findings were mainly linked to wellbeing. Participation was associated with greater happiness, stronger social connections and higher life satisfaction. One study found that happiness was positively related to participation, while another linked more serious involvement in pickleball with lower depression. Social integration appeared particularly important for female players. During the COVID-19 pandemic, reduced opportunities to play were associated with increased loneliness and poorer mental health, suggesting that the social contact provided by the sport may be part of its benefit.
The padel studies focused more on athletes’ performance-related emotions. Higher-level players generally reported greater self-confidence and lower physical symptoms of anxiety. Anxiety also changed according to ranking, gender, match stage and whether players won or lost. Mental fatigue increased across consecutive matches and was linked to slower reactions and poorer accuracy. Motivation sometimes rose during mentally demanding matches, which may help explain why players continued performing despite feeling mentally tired.
The findings suggest the two rapidly growing racket sports may offer different mental-health benefits, but stronger research is needed to determine whether playing them directly causes improvements.
The authors summarized: “Padel studies primarily target performance aspects like self-confidence, anxiety, and mental fatigue, while pickleball research highlights wellbeing gains in life satisfaction, happiness, and social integration.”
Some limitations are to be noted. The results should not be interpreted as proof that either sport prevents depression or anxiety. For example, many studies relied on self-reported experiences, and all of the included studies were observational rather than randomized controlled trials. Padel research also overrepresented elite and competitive players, while pickleball research focused mainly on older adults. Additionally, the available research was geographically narrow, with all included studies originating from just three countries: the United States, Spain and Finland.
The study, “Padel, pickleball and wellbeing: a systematic review,” was authored by Lena Lauxtermann and Brendon Stubbs.

The US now has access to more than half Australia’s military bases – could it drag the country unwillingly into war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
20:00:14 UTC
05:00:14 KST

US military interests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil, in what some analysts describe as a “saturation” – even a “colonisation” – of the Australian continent.
New data compiled by the Nautilus Institute and published by Guardian Australia maps the extent of US militarisation. The US military controls 17 facilities on mainland Australia and has access to 75 more Australian-run military installations. US defence corporations have access to an additional 18.
In total, the US military and US defence corporations have control of or access to 110 facilities on Australian territory, well over half of all the military installations in Australia.
“We have been thinking about American influence on Australian defence policy as a matter of penetration,” the database’s author, Prof Richard Tanter, tells the Guardian, “and we’re aware of the closeness of the alliance, the integration of the armed forces …
“But what this database shows is it’s not a matter of penetration, it’s a matter of saturation. Over half of the defence facilities that we have looked at have some level of American access: that means American personnel, it means American corporations, some of the biggest armaments companies in the world.”
‘Aligning ourselves completely’
The US military controls or has access to 92 defence facilities on Australian soil for:
- 
  Gathering intelligence, accessing satellite data for targeting information and communications intercepts.
- 
  Training, including for 2,500 marines on dry-season rotation in the Northern Territory.
- 
  Pre-positioning warfighting assets such as Osprey aircraft.
- 
  Logistics hubs holding weapons, munitions and fuel, stored in case of a war in the Pacific.
Some bases, including Pine Gap, play critical roles in identifying targets for US strikes overseas and are well known by Australians, even if their operations are highly classified.
Others are massive – the Bradshaw field training area in the Northern Territory is the size of Cyprus – but barely known.
Announced in June, Bandiana base in Wodonga will be the site of tens of millions of dollars worth of pre-positioned US weapons, munitions, fuel and vehicles, stationed for rapid deployment in the event of conflict in the Pacific.
Beyond the military’s presence, at least 42 Australian military facilities are accessed by US defence contractors – some of the biggest weapons manufacturers in the world – which use Australian sites for manufacturing, testing and training of weapons systems deployed by militaries across the globe.
Lockheed Martin assembles guided missiles in Port Wakefield, South Australia. Northrop Grumman signed a multimillion-dollar contract this year to build rocket motors for guided weapons at Mulwala in New South Wales. Collaboration with US manufacturers will “promote allied interoperability and provide a second source of supply for critical munitions”, the Australian defence force says.
Of the military bases that operate under US control, with Australian access, Pine Gap is the best known. But its precise role in US warfighting is hidden from public view.
Like several large military bases across Australia, Pine Gap hosts multiple defence facilities, each with distinct functions: a ground-control station for signals intelligence satellites; a relay ground station for early-warning missile launch systems; and a site for intercepting foreign satellite communications.
The Nautilus Institute database counts defence facilities, rather than bases, so Pine Gap consists of three distinct, co-located facilities.
Critical to US operations around the world, including conflicts in the Middle East, it is formally a “joint defence facility” but it is always commanded by an American.
The Force Posture agreement – “with full respect for Australian sovereignty” – gives US forces and contractors “unimpeded access to and use of” agreed Australian facilities, including for deploying forces and materiel, bunkering vessels and refuelling aircraft.
The US military presence will continue to expand. From next year up to 1,200 uniformed military personnel will operate from the HMAS Stirling submarine base just off Fremantle. The government insists that technically this will not be a US base – rather a “rotation” – but there is little contestation of its actual implication.
Arguing in favour of the Aukus nuclear submarine agreement, the former defence minister Christopher Pyne told a public inquiry the multibillion-dollar deal was “a lot more than the submarine procurement”.
“From a strategic point of view, it’s not something that’s ever really discussed in the public, but it’s one of the most important aspects of it: Aukus is also a new United States submarine base in the Indian Ocean.
“For the Americans, being able to have a submarine base in the Indian Ocean is a massive strategic advantage.”
Tanter, a senior research associate at the independent public policy thinktank the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability and an honorary professorial fellow at the University of Melbourne, says the US military’s expanding presence is not in service of its junior alliance partner but rather US interests alone.
“Over more than a decade, the United States has been preparing the capacity for high-tempo warfighting operations with China, springboarding from Australia,” he says. “And that means we are aligning ourselves completely with American strategic planning.
“From a Chinese perspective, Australia is not so much hosting US bases on its territory, it’s a US base in its own right … Australia is a serious piece of real estate in the US warfighting machine.”
There exists no comprehensive public record of foreign military access to bases on Australian territory. This database has been compiled from open-source information, responses provided to parliament, and government and commercial reporting.
Tanter argues that the acceptance of the US military presence has become so ingrained within the government and defence that unwinding Australia’s enmeshment within the world’s most powerful military is increasingly difficult.
“This is a massive institutional failure in Australia, a kind of learned incapacity at a political, parliamentary and bureaucratic level,” he says. “We’ve learned how not to ask those questions.”
‘Waltzing its way into a war’
At a press conference in June, the defence minister, Richard Marles, demonstrated the breadth of the US military presence in Australia.
Speaking in Rockingham, Western Australia – across a narrow bay from HMAS Stirling – Marles was announcing the establishment of a $30m US logistics base in Wodonga, Victoria.
“We are seeing a growing US footprint in Australia that is important in terms of building our own military capability but also it’s very important for Australia’s national security,” Marles said.
Marles said the “hugely significant American presence” in the region was a balance to China’s “very significant military buildup”.
Earlier, the minister told the Defending Australia Summit that US military presence in Australia was indispensable to deter conflict in the region.
“We will see an increasing American military footprint on our continent over the course of the next few years.”
Just last week Marles met the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where both leaders “agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”.
The Guardian put a series of questions to Marles’s office about the implications of an “increasing American military footprint” across Australia. A spokesperson for the defence department said Australia held a fundamental principle of “having no foreign bases on Australian sovereign territory”, and that the Australian government retains sole control over deployment of the ADF and over the use of Australian territory.
But, the spokesperson said, Australia’s 2026 national defence strategy reiterated “Australia’s alliance with the United States remains fundamental to our national security and the Australian Defence Force’s (ADF) capacity to generate, sustain and project credible military capability”.
The alliance with the US allowed Australia to “pursue our national security interests far beyond what we could achieve alone”, they said.
Australians’ fragile faith
Government ministers are fond of the reassuring line that the Australia-US relationship is broader, deeper and more enduring than the tenures of prime ministers and presidents.
But Australians’ faith in the US is fragile and fracturing.
A Lowy Institute poll showed Australians’ “trust in the United States to act responsibly in the world” has fallen to 31%, the lowest level in its polling history.
Just 21% of Australians have confidence in “Donald Trump to do the right thing in world affairs”, the lowest level of confidence in a US president yet.
Just more than half of Australians (55%) said they were either “strongly” or “somewhat” in favour of allowing the US to base military forces in Australia, down eight points from 2022 (63%).
Australians feel the alliance with the US remains important: 73% rate it as either “very important” or “fairly important” to the nation’s security.
Other findings are more damning: a poll for the Australia Institute found more than half (52%) of Australian voters believed Trump was a greater threat to global security than Vladimir Putin (17%) or Xi Jinping (16%).
More than twice as many Australians (59%) now believe Australia’s interests are best served by a more independent foreign policy rather than a closer alliance with the US (23%). Just 13% of Australians believe the US is a “very reliable” security ally.
This represents, Dr Emma Shortis says, a “seismic shift” in Australia’s perception of its once-great and powerful friend.
“After following the US into nearly every war since World War II, Australians have had enough. They see tangible risks in being so close to President Trump’s bleak and violent version of America.”
Shortis, the director of international and security affairs at the Australia Institute, argues that the Trump administration has repeatedly demonstrated that the US is willing to jettison security commitments made to allies. US bases across the Middle East have been repeatedly attacked by Iran.
“Trump has demonstrated that it’s all contingent, it’s all insecure,” she says. “And what he has also highlighted – particularly with his illegal war in Iran – is the way those US bases themselves become targets.
“It doesn’t matter what you do, it doesn’t matter how much you give him, you can literally give him a plane, and it’s not enough, he will not defend those bases.”
Shortis says Australia’s increasing integration with the US military has resulted in “an accelerating erosion of Australia’s independent, sovereign, decision-making power”.
“Instead of having the option of saying ‘no’ to involvement in United States wars, involvement becomes the default position.”
She cites the March attack by a US nuclear-powered submarine on an Iranian frigate, sinking it and killing more than 100 people. Three Australian naval personnel were onboard, part of the submarine’s crew: the US did not forewarn Australia of the attack.
“Australia might maintain the pretence of sovereign decision-making power, but that’s not the reality.”
Dr Albert Palazzo, an adjunct professor at the University of New South Wales Canberra and formerly the director of war studies for the Australian army, tells the Guardian the US military’s accelerating buildup carries danger for Australian security.
“The Australian government seems to be waltzing its way into a war between the United States and China, by allowing this country to become an outpost or bastion of the US military, and as a platform from which they will launch military force against China,” he says.
Dr Vince Scappatura, the author of The US Lobby and Australian Defence Policy, described US base access across Australia as a kind of “second wave of colonisation”.
“Today we are shaping up to be the ‘tip of the spear’ for US power projection into the region – that’s what the sprawling US base access represents,” he says.
“Each one of those dots on the map represents a point of leverage Washington has over Canberra when it comes to matters of defence and foreign policy. Not that they really need to use it.”
Scappatura says the phrase “empire by invitation” was originally coined to describe US hegemony over western Europe “but it is applicable equally here. I sometimes describe it as ‘voluntary subordination’.”
- 
  The Australian bases & US involvement database is coordinated by Prof Richard Tanter at the Nautilus Institute

Fact check: Election fraud claims spread in Saxony-Anhalt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:59:00 UTC
04:59:00 KST

Fact check: Election fraud claims spread in Saxony-Anhalt
September 6, 2026
On Sunday, Saxony-Anhalt held one of Germany's most consequential elections in years. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a decisive lead, putting the party in a position to potentially form the first far-right state government in Germany since World War II.
In the days before the vote, false and misleading claims seized on the election's importance, with social media users alleging fraud, vote-rigging and irregularities in the handling and counting of ballots.
DW Fact Check previously documented some of these tactics as part of Matryoshka, also known as Operation Overload, a Russian-linked influence operation targeting German elections.
Below, we take a closer look at some more recent claims.
Fake video shows election workers destroying AfD ballots
Claim: "German election workers recorded themselves outright destroying ballots that were cast for the populist party 'Alternative For Germany' (AfD), during Germany's recent elections," reads a post viewed 10,000 times on X, posted by a QAnon-associated account, a far-right American political conspiracy theory and political movement.
A one-minute video shows a white-gloved man unpacking ballots from red envelopes, laying them on a table, and drawing a black X through ones that select the AfD. A ballot marked for the CDU is set aside, as a voice says in German, "these are OK."
The same video was shared by numerous other accounts, in German and English across social media platforms X and YouTube.
Verdict: False
There are several telltale signs that this video is staged. Most obviously, all three crossed-out ballots contain the same name.
They're also missing a hole punch in the top right corner, a regulation that ensures ballots can be used with a template for blind or visually impaired voters. The envelopes are also already unsealed.
The Gnida Project, a Russian disinformation watchdog group, said the video was part of the Storm-1516 campaign.
Storm-1516, a unit controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, was also active ahead of Germany's 2025 federal election.
Read more on disinformation around Germany's postal voting system
Russian disinfo campaign alleges CDU fraud
Claim: The CDU is engaging in fraud in the Saxony-Anhalt election. "The social media pages of deceased residents of Saxony-Anhalt have become a platform for the #CDU's election campaign," reads one post on X, sharing a spoofed DW video.
"According to T-Online, non-existent citizens are set to vote by post for the #CDU in the Saxony-Anhalt election," reads another.
Verdict: False
DW Fact check reviewed five videos following a near-identical template: each was about a minute long and was posted by an account with zero followers and nearly no other posts. The videos feature a reputable news outlet's logo in the corner — including DW, ARD, WIRED, and BBC — and make claims about the CDU committing election fraud.
The claims range from the CDU using a database of Nazi soldier names to register fake ballots, to residents receiving campaign messages from deceased relatives.
Each video ends with a message urging viewers to "share this video with your family and friends in any way you see fit".
One of the videos claims T-Online disinformation reporter Lars Wienand had "obtained evidence that the CDU will attempt to rig the election." Wienand confirmed he had reported no such thing, writing to DW that "it's not the first time that suspected Russian disinformation had misused my name and image."
Julia Smirnova, disinformation expert and senior researcher at the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy, told DW the posts were part of the Matryoshka Russian disinformation campaign, also known as Operation Overload.
"As with other Matryoshka videos, the reach is mostly inauthentic," she wrote in an email to DW.
DW Fact Check has previously documented the same operation targeting candidates in Germany's state elections. We identified more than 180 fake posts on X, Bluesky and TikTok, many of them using the logos and formats of established media outlets to spread fabricated allegations about politicians.
Read more on Russian disinformation targeting German elections
Did Halle start counting ballots too early?
Claim: "Unbelievable scandal! In Halle, absentee voting ballots are already being counted before 6 p.m. That's blatantly illegal!" reads a post on X with over 160,000 views, posted by a right-wing journalist.
Below is a screenshot of German newspaper ZEIT's online news blog, with an entry, originally written in German, titled: "Counting of absentee ballots from 60 polling districts begins in Halle-Neustadt".
Verdict: Misleading
The screenshot accurately shows a screengrabbed ZEIT liveblog entry, published at 3:15 pm.
Only ZEIT made an error, with the reporter clarifying to DW over email that their reporting was just describing "preparatory tasks" and not the actual counting of ballots.
The ZEIT blog entry has since been corrected with a "transparency note" that reads, "An earlier version of this blog post stated that the count had already begun. In fact, preparations were only underway. We have corrected the error."
The Saxony-Anhalt's state election regulations specify that ballots are not supposed to be officially counted until the voting period ends at 6 p.m. They can, however, be opened in advance to facilitate later ballot-counting.
Edited by: Sarah Steffen

Iran plans new ‘exclusion zone’ outside Strait of Hormuz after ship attacks
Iranian security chief threatens sanctions on transit ships as US blockade and tanker strikes escalate tensions
The new head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council on Sunday said Tehran plans to announce an “exclusion zone” outside the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels it believes are attempting to transit the waterway.
Mohsen Rezaei’s comments to Iran’s state broadcaster came with few details, a day after the US struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran launching ballistic missiles at US warships. Experts called the launches a dangerous escalation after Iran’s previous attacks at sea targeted commercial shipping.
The new zone should be announced in the coming days and weeks and “will begin from the line of the US naval blockade, extend toward the Strait of Hormuz, and from this side continue into the Persian Gulf,” Rezaei said. “Any ship that enters this area with the intention of passing through the Strait of Hormuz and is identified will be placed on our sanctions list.”
It is not clear where Iran defines the location of the weekslong US blockade, which is aimed at Iranian ports and keeping Tehran from shipping out its oil. The US military has said over 20 warships are supporting the blockade, which as of Sunday had redirected 92 commercial ships and disabled three.
The US has been introducing new measures to increase the economic pain on Iran after negotiations collapsed and no end to the intermittent fighting appears in sight. Meanwhile, Iran continues to attack some ships trying to transit the strait, which has become an important source of leverage for Tehran in the war that began February 28 with US and Israeli strikes.
Iran earlier Sunday said it struck an unmanned US vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, a claim that the US military dismissed as a “total lie”.

Iran raises price of petrol as US applies economic pressure
TEHRAN – The Iranian authorities on Sept 6 announced they were raising the price of petrol for heavier consumers, as the United States steps up sanctions seeking to isolate the country’s economy.
Iran’s quota system prices petrol in three tiers – 1,500 tomans per litre for a consumer’s first 60 litres in a given month, 3,000 tomans per litre for their next 50, and 5,000 tomans per litre after that. The toman is an informal unit equivalent to 10 Iranian rials.
On Sept 6, government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani said the price for the third tier would double to 10,000 tomans (about 5.7 Singapore cents).
“The rate will increase to 10,000 toman rials from the morning of Sept 8,” Mohajerani said in remarks carried by state media.
“Different numbers were mentioned in expert meetings, but because the President had promised the people, the rate of 10,000 tomans was set,” she added.
She later clarified that the price of the first and second tiers would not be changed.
Iran, a major oil producer with some of the world’s cheapest fuel, has for years heavily subsidised petrol, making any changes to pricing politically sensitive.
The development comes as the Iranian currency was trading on the black market on Sept 6 at more than 2.2 million rials to the US dollar, according to websites that track the rate.
Before the start of the Middle East war on Feb 28, the rial traded at around 1.7 million to the dollar, and in late April it hit what was then a record low of 1.8 million.
Late in August, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent laid out plans for the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran, hoping to use financial pressure to hasten the end of the war.
The new measures build on a sanctions regime by the US and allies that has been in place since 2018, when President Donald Trump withdrew from an international deal struck with Tehran on its nuclear programme.
The US has also put Iran’s ports under a naval blockade, attempting to reduce its oil exports to zero. AFP

'Now measured in the millions': The common process being used to scam Australians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:35:54 UTC
04:35:54 KST

in brief
- Scammers are exploiting the growing use of CAPTCHAs to trick people into running malicious code outside their browser.
- An expert has practical tips on how to minimise your risk.
CAPTCHAs are meant to protect our online infrastructure from bots. Scammers, however, are turning them against us.
Cybersecurity experts have seen a rise in fake CAPTCHA scams, with the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) releasing a warning this week about the ruse.
The fake CAPTCHAs direct internet users to input code outside of their browser, which grants hackers access to the device and, in some cases, browser session information.
The scams often ask them to paste a script into a computer's terminal, allowing the attacks to bypass anti-malware security systems.
Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at UNSW School of Computer Science and managing director of the Digital Lies & Cyber Literacy Foundation, said the ability to bypass anti-malware protections made fake CAPTCHA scams particularly dangerous.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"You haven't got very many of the protections of the operating system working for you," he told SBS News.
Previously, CAPTCHAs were commonly required for creating online account. However, they're now common when making the first connection with a website, greatly increasing the number that internet users are asked to complete.
Pearce attributes this to "the explosion of AI agents online" as websites attempt to prevent artificial intelligence from going through them.
The increased prevalence of CAPTCHAs means it's easier for dodgy ones to slip through.
Pearce said he'd "expect it more on slightly dodgier websites" but hackers "can try and hijack your connection so that you get that when you're trying to get to a normal website".
Pearce also said the number of fake CAPTCHA attacks "are now measured in the millions".
How to avoid fake CAPTCHAs
According to Pearce, it's now much harder than it used to be for criminals to leverage a person's internet connection against them.
Major browsers such as Chrome, Firefox and Edge have used significant resources to make themselves "about the safest piece of technology there is on your computer", Pearce said.
He said users should be suspicious if a CAPTCHA asks them to type something or leave the window.
"If it's actually asking you to type some random thing on your keyboard, you should immediately start getting suspicious," Pearce said.
"Be very wary of anything that might take you out of the safety of the web browser."
He says that, if something feels off, internet users should ask themselves: "Why? Why do I need to do this?"
