IDF expected to make historic change for more inclusive combat soldier profile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
18:23:47 UTC
03:23:47 KST

The IDF is expected to make a historic change to its system for profiling candidates for potential combat roles, lowering the minimum “score” required to be eligible for such a role to provide more soldiers for combat in an era when the military faces a massive shortage.
While there have been numerous reports over several months suggesting that such a change might be approved, KAN News reported first on Sunday that the decision has finally gone through.
Prior to the decision, the lowest profile a soldier could have and still serve in any combat role would have been 72 out of 100.
Soldiers who received a 64 profile because of some kind of minor, though not insignificant, medical condition were automatically disqualified from consideration.
IDF introduces new profile score of 70 instead of 64
Under the new system, many soldiers who might once have been dropped from a 72 profile to a 64 profile will instead be dropped only to a new profile score of 70.
This 70 profile score will still allow them to serve in particular combat roles, such as artillery, air defense, certain other air force functions, and additional roles, though they would still not serve in infantry units like the Golani or Givati brigades.
Since Hamas’s October 7, 2023 invasion, the IDF has talked about a shortage of 7,000 combat fighters and of 10,000-12,000 soldiers in general, due to the large number of soldiers killed and wounded in recent years, as well as the increased standing army requirements to ensure that future such invasions are not possible.
With no major increase in haredi (ultra-Orthodox) enlistment from the current government, the drop in profile standards, while controversial, has been viewed as one way to handle the issue in the near and medium term.
The IDF had not responded by press time despite repeated requests, prompting speculation that some controversy might still be blocking or delaying the move.

France Plans to Receive 47 Rafale F5 Fighters by 2035
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
18:21:16 UTC
03:21:16 KST

The French Air and Space Force plans to receive 47 Rafale fighter jets in the latest F5 configuration by 2035.
This is set out in the updated French Military Programming Law (LPM) for 2024-2030.
The aircraft are primarily intended for France’s Strategic Air Forces (FAS), which carry out nuclear deterrence missions.
The Rafale F5 will be a significantly more comprehensive upgrade of the fighter than previous standards. The aircraft will receive new weapons control systems, an improved radar, electronic warfare systems, a new onboard defensive suite, new weapons, including MICA NG missiles, and improved data-link capabilities.
The Rafale F5 is also expected to be capable of carrying the future ASN4G hypersonic nuclear missile.
In addition to the aircraft itself, France is developing a combat drone designed to operate alongside the Rafale F5. The first development contracts have already been signed with Dassault Aviation, Thales and Safran.
The drone is intended to operate in complex environments, including suppressing enemy air defenses, and is to be used alongside Rafale F5 fighters.
However, despite France’s plans, the program to develop the new version of the aircraft is facing financial difficulties.
In April, it was reported that France would fully finance the development of the Rafale F5 after negotiations with the United Arab Emirates on joint financing of the program ended without an agreement.
The negotiations ended in December 2025. Paris proposed that Abu Dhabi join the program in exchange for investment, but without the participation of local companies in the development or the possibility of obtaining technology.
The UAE was expected to contribute up to €3.5 billion to the program, whose total cost is estimated at approximately €5 billion.
Following the UAE’s refusal, all financial commitments related to the program will be borne by the French Ministry of Defense, which could potentially affect the pace of its implementation.

Common artificial sweetener aspartame makes brain cells more vulnerable to stroke damage, mouse study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
18:00:36 UTC
03:00:36 KST

Recent research in mice provides evidence that consuming the common artificial sweetener aspartame may worsen the brain damage caused by a stroke. The findings indicate that the sweetener disrupts cellular energy centers and blocks protective signaling pathways during periods of oxygen deprivation, making brain cells more vulnerable to injury. The study was published in Ecotoxicology and Environmental Safety.
Aspartame is a non-nutritive sweetener widely used in zero-calorie beverages and processed foods. While regulatory agencies generally consider it safe for human consumption within established daily limits, ongoing scientific debates have raised questions about its potential effects on the nervous system. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that mothers of boys with autism had more than tripled odds of daily exposure to diet soda or aspartame during pregnancy.
Additionally, a 2023 study indicated that treating human brain cells with aspartame led to oxidative stress and damage to mitochondria, the energy-producing structures inside cells. The new research, led by Yan Bai and Ji Feng at Fudan University, aimed to test whether aspartame consumption might make the brain more susceptible to injury during the intense stress of a stroke.
When an ischemic stroke occurs, a blockage prevents blood and oxygen from reaching parts of the brain. When blood flow is finally restored, the sudden rush of oxygen and nutrients can paradoxically trigger a cascade of inflammation and oxidative stress, causing additional tissue damage. This secondary wave of damage is known as cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury.
The scientists conducted their research using both living mice and lab-grown mouse brain cells. For the animal model, they divided 50 male mice into groups. The experimental groups were given drinking water containing either 0.1% or 0.2% aspartame for seven days. These concentrations were specifically chosen to approximate the upper limits of an acceptable daily intake for humans.
After the week of aspartame consumption, the researchers temporarily blocked the mice’s carotid arteries for two hours to simulate an ischemic stroke. They then removed the blockage to allow 12 hours of reperfusion.
The findings indicated that mice pretreated with aspartame suffered worse brain damage than those that drank regular water. In mice exposed to a simulated stroke without aspartame, the area of dead brain tissue was about 24.3%. In mice given the 0.2% aspartame water, the dead tissue area expanded to 58.6%.
Microscopic examination of the brain tissue showed that aspartame worsened the physical breakdown of neurons in the cortex and hippocampus, two brain regions involved in memory and thinking. The aspartame-treated mice had fewer surviving neurons and showed more severe signs of cellular degeneration.
To understand exactly how aspartame caused this added damage, the researchers isolated neural stem cells from the brains of newborn mice. They grew these cells in a laboratory dish and pretreated them with aspartame for 48 hours. They then subjected the cells to oxygen and glucose deprivation to replicate the harsh conditions of a stroke.
Similar to the animal experiment, aspartame increased cell death in the dish. Cells treated with the sweetener experienced an approximate 25% larger reduction in viability compared to cells that underwent oxygen and glucose deprivation alone. Interestingly, other common artificial sweeteners tested in the study, such as sucralose and acesulfame potassium, did not produce this added toxic effect.
The researchers observed that aspartame caused a massive buildup of reactive oxygen species within the mitochondria of the cells. Reactive oxygen species are unstable molecules that can cause severe structural damage when they accumulate beyond normal levels. This buildup was accompanied by a loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, a sign that the cells’ energy centers were failing.
The sweetener also suppressed the ERK/CREB1 pathway, a sequence of chemical signals that normally helps cells survive stress and promotes neuronal resilience. When the researchers added specific chemical compounds to activate this protective pathway and neutralize the reactive oxygen species in the mitochondria, they were able to partially reverse the cell death and inflammation caused by the aspartame.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding these results. The study exposed the mice to aspartame for only seven days, which does not reflect the long-term, daily consumption habits of many people who drink artificially sweetened beverages. It remains unknown how chronic, low-dose exposure might alter the brain’s resilience to injury over a lifetime.
The animal experiments also relied exclusively on male mice, meaning it is uncertain if females would show the same neurological vulnerabilities. The researchers did not test the mice for behavioral or cognitive changes, so it is not entirely established how this cellular damage might translate to physical or mental impairments after a stroke.
Future research will need to explore how artificial sweeteners alter metabolic pathways over longer periods and whether these mechanisms hold true in human clinical scenarios.
The study, “Aspartame exacerbates cerebral ischemia–reperfusion injury via mitochondrial dysfunction and ERK/CREB1 pathway suppression,” was authored by Yan Bai, Ji Feng, Xiao-Yu Wu, Zhi-Sheng Yao, Yue-Tong Liu, Yu-Hong Li, Guo-Dong Lu, and Kun Xue.

SEC sues ISS as Trump administration ramps up scrutiny of proxy advisers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:53:53 UTC
02:53:53 KST

The Securities and Exchange Commission sued Institutional Shareholder Services, seeking to force the influential proxy adviser to turn over information as the Trump administration steps up scrutiny of firms that help investors decide how to vote their shares.
The SEC filed the subpoena-enforcement action Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, saying ISS had refused to fully comply with an administrative subpoena seeking information about its proxy recommendations and voting activity.
The agency's Division of Examinations began reviewing ISS in March and requested data related to the firm's recommendations and votes, the SEC said. After ISS did not produce all of the requested information, the enforcement division opened an inquiry and issued a subpoena on July 21.
The SEC said ISS has continued to withhold some records despite extended deadlines and repeated efforts to resolve the dispute. The regulator said its investigation remains in the fact-finding stage and that it has not concluded ISS violated federal securities laws.
ISS argued in correspondence with the SEC that the subpoena raised First Amendment concerns and could expose ISS and its clients to retaliation over their voting activity.
ISS did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
The lawsuit comes amid a broader Trump administration push to tighten oversight of proxy advisers, which provide institutional investors with research and recommendations on shareholder votes covering issues including board elections, executive compensation and shareholder proposals.
President Donald Trump signed an executive order in December directing the SEC to review its rules and guidance on proxy advisers, enforce securities-law antifraud provisions and consider additional disclosure and regulatory requirements.
The order specifically named ISS and rival Glass Lewis, which the White House said together control more than 90% of the proxy-advisory market.
ISS is registered with the SEC as an investment adviser. The SEC is asking the court to order the firm to comply with the outstanding subpoena.

Sting Interceptor Drones Integrated With MAGURA MV11 Naval Drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:52:34 UTC
02:52:34 KST

Sting interceptor drones developed by Ukrainian company Wild Hornets have been integrated with the MAGURA MV11 naval drone. The interceptors and communications systems were upgraded specifically for operation in the maritime environment.
Wild Hornets told Militarnyi about the integration.
According to the company, the work had been underway for quite some time but was not widely disclosed at the military’s request. In particular, the first targets were intercepted by Sting interceptor drones launched from unmanned surface vessels (USVs) back in the spring.
Throughout this period, alongside their combat use, the company continued working to improve the platform, interceptors and communications systems, as operations in the maritime environment have their own specific requirements.
The company separately highlighted the Hornet Vision digital communications system as an important component of integrating the interceptors for operation from maritime unmanned vehicles. The system uses an omnidirectional antenna with 360-degree coverage.
“In other words, it can simply be installed on the carrier platform to provide a stable connection without the need to develop an additional rotating mechanism, as is the case with directional antennas. It has been upgraded to operate in particularly harsh conditions,” Wild Hornets said.
In addition, the Hornet Vision Ctrl remote-control system, which provides low signal latency, became an essential part of effective operation with high-speed interceptor drones launched from platforms.
The MAGURA MV11 was designed by the UFORCE design and R&D bureau in Portugal with international investment and a focus on carrying out missions for Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
The MV11 is the largest drone in its class. Unlike earlier models in the family, it is a transport platform capable of carrying other unmanned systems and equipment for carrying out missions.
With its larger dimensions, payload capacity of up to 2,200 kilograms and endurance of up to seven days, the MV11 can operate as a carrier platform, delivering, launching and supporting other drones far from shore.
The model is designed for reconnaissance, surveillance, support of amphibious operations, as well as delivering fuel and equipment for other unmanned surface vessels.
A key feature of the drone is its ability to launch a larger number of unmanned systems directly from its deck. The platform thus becomes a mobile maritime base for other unmanned systems.

Beyza Binnur Donmez
06 September 2026•Update: 06 September 2026
Belgium's asylum and migration minister said Sunday she opposes allowing 13 Palestinian students from Gaza to enter Belgium despite having scholarships and visas to study in the country.
Anneleen Van Bossuyt told Belgian public broadcaster VRT that authorities should consider the potential consequences of allowing the students to enter, warning of a “domino effect.”
“It is presented as if it concerns only 13 people, but we must not forget the domino effect,” she said, noting that they could later seek family reunification or apply for asylum.
Van Bossuyt questioned why similar arrangements would not then apply to people from other conflict-affected countries, including Yemen, Sudan and Afghanistan.
“Why would that not apply to people from Yemen or Sudan? Or why not Afghan girls who want to study here?” she said.

Herwig Leirs, rector of the University of Antwerp, said allowing them to come was a matter of political will.
Flor Didden of the Belgian development organization 11.11.11 criticized the minister's position, stressing that the students had been invited by a Belgian university and awarded scholarships.
“It concerns 13 students who have been invited by a Belgian university and for whom there is a scholarship. In some cases, your services issued a visa. They have the right to come to Belgium,” he said.

The United Nations’ top official in Nepal has issued an emotional appeal for international aid, warning that survivors of the catastrophic Himalayan flooding last month saw their lives transformed “in one to two minutes”.
The UN Resident Coordinator, Lila Pieters Yahia, said communities along the China-Nepal border were struggling to comprehend the scale of devastation after torrential floods on August 26 tore through mountain districts, destroying roads, bridges and hydropower dams.
“You lose your home, you lose your livelihood, you lose your loved one and you lose the breadwinner of your family,” she told the AFP news agency in Kathmandu. “And you know, this happened in one to two minutes.”
At least 1,384 people were killed and more than 5,500 others remain missing in Nepal and the Tibet region of China. Among the missing are more than 800 foreigners from at least 34 countries, including tourists and pilgrims.
Many communities near the epicentre remain cut off, with roads washed away and journeys that once took hours now stretching into days. The UN, working with Nepal’s government, has launched a $50m appeal to support more than 84,000 people affected.
The UN’s Pieters Yahia warned of the risk of cholera and other communicable diseases, citing the deaths of 5,000 cattle and urging urgent investment in sanitation, hygiene and protection for vulnerable women and girls.
“My plea to the international community is: this is the time to help Nepal,” she said. “We can’t leave them alone.”

Court orders return for Jalud Palestinian families home after extremist settlers drove them out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:49:56 UTC
02:49:56 KST

The High Court of Justice ordered Israeli authorities on Sunday to arrange within 14 days for three Palestinian petitioners and their families to return to their homes in the West Bank village of Jalud, after months of nationalist violence by Israeli extremists drove residents out and left the houses open to repeated takeover.
The order requires the IDF and police to protect the families as they return and allow them to bring in supplies needed to repair the homes and restore water and electricity. Updates to the court are due by September 22.
The justices also issued a conditional order requiring the state to explain why it has not restored the residents to their homes and removed barriers from the access roads. A sworn response is due by October 8.
The decision moves the case beyond the state’s general promise to coordinate the families’ return and requires concrete action and detailed answers about investigations that have produced few visible results so far.
The court said the state largely did not dispute the central sequence of events.
How an unauthorized outpost led to a de facto siege on Palestinian families
The case concerns an unauthorized outpost known as Givat Hatzmabarim (short in Hebrew for tzamig bo’er, which translates to “burning tire”), established on April 19 inside Area B near Jalud, south of Nablus. Area B is under Palestinian civilian administration, while Israel retains overall security responsibility.
According to the petition, the outpost’s establishment was followed by more than four months of incursions, threats, stone-throwing, roadblocks and damage to the residents’ property and infrastructure. The petitioners said attackers cut their water line, uprooted trees, grazed livestock on their land, set fire to a family vehicle, and blocked the road to their homes with large rocks.
On July 22, the first two petitioners and their families left their homes after what the court described as a prolonged de facto siege. Intruders then broke through a wall of one house and smashed its doors and windows. The third petitioner’s house was also used as a place for members of the group to stay.
The three Palestinian petitioners and their families have not returned.
More than two weeks later, the military issued a seizure order and removed the intruders from the first house. They moved to the second house, and when soldiers removed them from there, they moved to the third, according to the decision.
The petitioners submitted video showing soldiers and the intruders playing soccer together in the courtyard of one of the houses. An IDF officer told the court that the soldiers were reinforcements who had not been properly briefed on the relevant orders and had since been removed from combat duties.
When the military left the first two houses on or around August 24, the intruders returned that same day and unloaded equipment and supplies near an army vehicle, according to video described in the ruling. The parties disagree over whether they resumed living inside the homes.
The state told the court that it had conducted eight enforcement operations against the outpost, declared the area a closed military zone, reinforced the troops stationed there and initiated patrols. It also pointed to new procedures, dedicated Border Police forces, administrative exclusion orders and a task force established to address nationalist crime.
Authorities said enforcement is repeatedly frustrated because suspects scatter before forces arrive, mobilize large groups to obstruct operations and submit false reports intended to divert the troops.
Authorities detain four Israelis carrying clubs, knives, pepper spray
The state also cited two specific incidents. On May 5, security forces stopped a vehicle carrying four identified Israelis, construction materials, two clubs, two knives, and two containers of pepper spray. Authorities took one person to the Ariel police station. On August 23, forces arrested another Israeli near the outpost and transferred him to police.
The state asked the court to dismiss the petition, arguing that the military commander was acting within the resources available and that no permanent force could be stationed at the homes.
The justices were not persuaded that the measures described had produced effective enforcement.
Israeli authorities had the names and identification numbers of people found at the outpost, as well as vehicle registration details and extensive photographic evidence, the court said. The state nevertheless gave no answer when asked what enforcement action had been taken against those identified or why vehicles used in the activity had not been seized.
“The picture that emerges is very grim,” the court said, adding that there were many questions but few satisfactory answers.
The judges said the military’s measures largely consisted of revised procedures, troop adjustments and limited improvements in enforcing administrative orders. What remained missing was criminal enforcement - the “finishing leg,” as a brigade operations officer described it during the hearing.
While police are responsible for criminal investigations, the court stressed that overall responsibility rests with the military commander, who is required to protect all residents living under Israeli military control.
The case reaches the court amid a broader increase in nationalist violence against Palestinians and a persistently low rate of prosecution.
Police figures obtained by the Movement for Freedom of Information recorded 779 complaints in 2025 in a category covering nationalist offenses against Palestinians and offenses attributed to Jewish extremists. The published figures said 307 investigation files were opened and 52 indictments were filed that year, although the indictments were not necessarily connected to complaints submitted during the same period.
Yesh Din, which tracks a separate group of complaints involving ideologically motivated offenses against Palestinians, reported that 93.6% of the investigations it monitored between 2005 and 2025 ended without an indictment. Only three percent resulted in a full or partial conviction.
The High Court referred to several other recent petitions involving Palestinians driven from their homes and warned against treating the violence as unavoidable. It said the phenomenon had grown over years, diverted troops and resources from other security missions and damaged Israel’s international standing.
More fundamentally, the court said, nationalist violence against Palestinians is entirely unacceptable and contradicts the basic moral principles of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state.

====================================================================================================

Gafni’s ouster marks a changing era for Israel’s haredi parties - and for Netanyahu - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:49:52 UTC
02:49:52 KST

You think Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been in power for a long time? Consider Degel Hatorah’s Moshe Gafni.
Gafni, the Knesset’s longest-serving MK, was unceremoniously dropped from the party’s Knesset slate on Saturday night, along with Uri Maklev, on the instructions of Degel Hatorah’s spiritual leader, Rabbi Dov Lando.
When Gafni first entered the Knesset in 1988, Israel had only one national television channel; Rabbi Elazar Menachem Shach led the Lithuanian haredi (ultra-Orthodox) world with which Gafni is associated; Yitzhak Shamir was prime minister; Ronald Reagan occupied the White House; and Mikhail Gorbachev led the still-intact Soviet Union.
Netanyahu and Gafni were first elected together in 1988. Netanyahu left the Knesset in 1999 and returned in 2003. Gafni, apart from a two-year absence from 1992 to 1994 and a brief break in 1998-99, has served almost continuously for close to 38 years.
And while he obviously never wielded anything approaching Netanyahu’s power, Gafni became one of the country’s ultimate power brokers and kingmakers, a symbol of the disproportionate influence that haredi parties have often exercised over Israel’s political system.
The era of haredi influence over Israeli politics may be coming to an end
As October’s election approaches, that era may be coming to an end. Several opposition parties have made military or national service for all a central condition for joining the next government. And now the man who, perhaps more than anyone else, came to represent the old system is also on his way out.
Degel Hatorah’s rabbinic leadership thanked Gafni and Maklev for their years of loyal service but said they would not be included on the party’s next Knesset list, citing the need to “refresh” its parliamentary representation.
Gafni will also be replaced as Degel Hatorah chairman by Yakov Asher, slated to head both Degel Hatorah and United Torah Judaism (UTJ), the party it forms with the hassidic Agudat Yisrael. This is therefore not merely the departure of a veteran MK; it is a changing of the guard.
The reference to “refreshing” the list is a courteous formulation. The obvious inference is that Gafni and Maklev are being held responsible for the failure of the haredi parties to secure the comprehensive legislation their rabbinic leadership demanded to protect the status of yeshiva students from conscription – even in a Knesset in which the haredi parties repeatedly held the balance of power.
There is a considerable irony here. As a longtime MK and seemingly permanent chairman of the powerful Knesset Finance Committee, Gafni was perhaps the most accomplished parliamentary tactician in haredi politics. He mastered the political system, knew how to work its levers, and succeeded in channeling tremendous budgets to his constituents.
Yet all that parliamentary mastery could not deliver the one result his community – or at least its most respected rabbis – considered essential. And that raises a broader question: Has the traditional haredi method of working within the parliamentary system to protect and preserve the yeshiva world run its course?
For decades, the model worked.
The haredi parties generally avoided taking strong positions on diplomacy and security, were willing to align themselves with whichever major party could best meet their communal needs, and they used their pivotal position to secure budgets and preserve military exemptions.
But the war, the IDF’s manpower shortage, repeated court rulings, and mounting public anger over the unequal sharing of the security burden have made that model increasingly difficult to sustain.
What was once viewed by much of the public as an irritating but tolerable political arrangement is now seen by many as immoral, fundamentally unjust, and a long-term threat to a country that is badly in need of more soldiers amid a prolonged, multi-front war.
Is Degel HaTorah breaking away from Netanyahu?
The removal of Gafni and Maklev may also be intended as a message to Netanyahu that the alliance between Likud, the haredim, and the religious Right can no longer be taken for granted.
Lando said as much earlier this year, during the failed effort to secure the draft-exemption legislation, declaring that Degel Hatorah no longer trusted Netanyahu and that, as far as the party was concerned, the old right-wing bloc no longer existed.
Netanyahu and Gafni entered the Knesset together, and their relationship came to symbolize the Likud-haredi alliance. The arguments could be fierce, but both men knew that, at the end of the day, they needed one another and would find a way to get back to business.
Taking Gafni off the list deprives Netanyahu of a key ally in the haredi world and of his most dependable political channel to the Lithuanian haredi leadership. It also leaves him dealing with new political leaders who may feel less bound by decades of shared history and personal commitments.
That should not necessarily be interpreted as Degel Hatorah abandoning the prime minister. Ideologically, culturally, and politically, the party remains far more comfortable with Likud and the religious Right than with most of the parties in the anti-Netanyahu camp.
It does suggest, however, that Netanyahu can no longer assume that history and personal relationships will automatically restore the alliance to what it once was.
Does this mean that Degel Hatorah is winking at Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett?
Possibly. The leadership change may be a signal that the party is open to working with the “change bloc” – or at least wants Netanyahu to believe that it is. By portraying itself as potentially available to either side, Degel Hatorah could try to regain the kingmaker status the haredi parties once enjoyed.
If, as recent polls indicate, the anti-Netanyahu bloc finishes a few seats short of the magic 61 needed to form a government, UTJ – with the seven it has been receiving consistently in the polls – could theoretically push it over the finish line.
But “theoretically” is the operative word.
Such a move would depend not only on what Degel Hatorah and its new political leadership want but also on whether Bennett, Eisenkot, and Avigdor Liberman – who have all made haredi conscription central to their campaigns, though with somewhat different nuances – would agree to in order to bring UTJ into a coalition without a fundamental change in its position.
A change in Degel Hatorah’s position on this matter is very unlikely. Gafni’s departure does not mean Degel Hatorah is softening its opposition to the conscription of haredim. Nor does Asher’s elevation – even though he served for several months in the IDF’s abbreviated Shlav Bet framework – signal a more accommodating position on the draft.
The change is therefore less about ideology than political positioning. Degel Hatorah is trying to move from being perceived as a captive part of the Netanyahu camp to being seen once again as a potential swing vote between the blocs.
The party has not crossed the political aisle. But by pushing Gafni out of the next Knesset, its rabbinic leadership has served notice that Netanyahu will have to win the haredim back rather than simply count them in.

Netanyahu trial resumes as defense phase moves beyond prime minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:49:37 UTC
02:49:37 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s criminal trial resumed at the Jerusalem District Court on Sunday after the summer recess, beginning a new stretch of the defense case in which the remaining witnesses for Netanyahu and his three co-defendants will take the stand.
Netanyahu completed his own testimony in June after 98 hearing days spanning a year and a half. Sunday’s hearing focused primarily on organizing the witness schedule and determining which defense witnesses will be called, rather than hearing new evidence.
Four hearing days are planned this week. According to a notice submitted by Netanyahu’s defense, MK Ze’ev Elkin’s cross-examination is scheduled to continue on Monday.
Ronit Mandelbaum is expected to testify later that day if necessary, while Police Chief Superintendent Shmuel Sharvit is scheduled to take the stand on Tuesday and Wednesday. The defense asked the court to issue summonses for Mandelbaum and Sharvit.
Their testimony will form part of the defense effort to challenge the prosecution’s account of how the investigations in the case were conducted, and whether evidence was lawfully and properly obtained.
The trial is also returning to its original venue in Jerusalem. Netanyahu’s testimony was heard at the Tel Aviv District Court building under special security arrangements.
The most consequential unresolved question as proceedings resume is the bribery charge in Case 4000, the Bezeq-Walla affair.
Judges continued to see evidentiary difficulties in proving bribery
After Netanyahu completed his testimony, the judges told the parties that their assessment from June 2023 had not changed: They continued to see evidentiary difficulties in proving bribery and believed the prosecution should consider withdrawing that charge.
This was not an instruction, nor was it very detailed. The prosecution has not withdrawn the charge, and the indictment remains unchanged.
Case 4000 alleges that Netanyahu, while serving as prime minister and communications minister, advanced regulatory decisions benefiting Bezeq and its then-controlling shareholder, Shaul Elovitch. In exchange, prosecutors allege, Netanyahu and his family received unusually favorable and responsive treatment from the Walla news site, which Elovitch also controlled.
Netanyahu and the Elovitches deny that there was any such exchange. Netanyahu has argued that Walla remained hostile to him and that the regulatory decisions were professionally justified.
Even if prosecutors withdraw the bribery charge, Case 4000 would not disappear. Netanyahu would continue to face allegations of fraud and breach of trust over the same affair, alongside fraud and breach of trust charges in Cases 1000 and 2000.
Case 1000 concerns gifts, including cigars and champagne, that Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, allegedly received from wealthy businessmen, principally Arnon Milchan. Prosecutors allege that Netanyahu provided official assistance in matters affecting Milchan while receiving those gifts. Netanyahu says they were presents exchanged within a genuine friendship.
Case 2000 concerns recorded conversations between Netanyahu and Yediot Aharonot publisher Arnon “Noni” Mozes. Prosecutors allege that the two discussed improving Netanyahu’s coverage in exchange for steps that could have weakened the newspaper’s principal competitor, Israel Hayom. Both men deny wrongdoing.
Mozes and Shaul and Iris Elovitch are standing trial alongside Netanyahu and will also be able to call witnesses in their defense.
The dispute over the Case 4000 bribery charge is closely connected to the battle over how quickly the trial should now proceed. Netanyahu’s attorney, Amit Hadad, has said that if the charge remains, the defense may seek to call hundreds of witnesses to challenge the prosecution’s account.
The judges have instead been pressing the parties to narrow the witness lists and accelerate a trial that began in May 2020. Beginning October 4, hearings are scheduled to take place five days a week, from Sunday through Thursday.
Both the defense and prosecution opposed the five-day schedule when it was discussed in June. Hadad argued that it would leave Netanyahu’s lawyers without sufficient time to prepare witnesses and warned that members of the defense team could withdraw if they could not provide adequate representation.
Court instructed the defense teams to prepare witnesses and alternatives
The court has nevertheless instructed the defense teams to prepare witnesses and alternatives for each hearing day to avoid further cancellations.
The timetable is particularly pressing because the head of the three-judge panel, Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman, is expected to retire in March 2028. The panel also includes Judges Moshe Bar-Am and Oded Shaham.
For now, the trial remains in the evidence stage. Once Netanyahu and the other defendants finish presenting their witnesses, the prosecution and defense will submit their final arguments. Only then will the judges deliver a verdict on the charges that remain.

On Saturday, Huckabee said it was in Israel's own interest to take action against settlers carrying out what he described as "criminal behavior and terrorism."

Greece wants deeper ties with both Israel and Arab countries

Breadcrumb
Greece wants deeper ties with both Israel and Arab countries
Greece will press ahead with its strategic defence cooperation with Israel but also wants to deepen relations with other states in the Middle East, Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said Sunday.
Greece-Israeli ties and defence, security and energy cooperation have grown closer over the past decade, and Mitsotakis enjoys a friendly rapport with his counterpart, Benjamin Netanyahu.
Shared concerns about Turkey have helped boost ties. The two countries signed a 3-billion-euro ($3.5 billion) deal on 31 August for Israel to build an air defence shield in Greece.
Mitsotakis told reporters in Thessaloniki that Greece is one of only five NATO countries spending at least 3.5 percent of its GDP on core defence.
Greece’s traditionally high spending has been fueled by almost constant tensions with Turkey, and its questioning of Greek sovereignty over parts of the Aegean Sea and the Eastern Mediterranean.
Greece recognises only the demarcation of the two countries’ respective maritime zones as an issue to be negotiated or sent to international arbitration.
Asked about US President Donald Trump’s expressed desire to sell the advanced F-35 multirole combat aircraft to Turkey, Mitsotakis replied that he will not tell the US what to do, but noted that legal obstacles remain as Turkey was sanctioned for buying the S-400 air defence system from Russia.
Greece will take delivery of its first 20 F-35s in late 2028, with an option to buy 20 more.
Mitsotakis also said he planned to visit Saudi Arabia soon, and that the recently concluded Mecca Joint Defence Agreement among Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey changes nothing in Greece’s relations with Riyadh.
Greece has maintained an air defence battery in Saudi Arabia since 2021, and has used its Patriot missiles four times since July to down drones and ballistic missiles, allegedly from Yemen, aimed at the kingdom’s oil refineries.

US energy secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday morning that the US may not be able to reach a nuclear agreement with Iran that would prevent the country from having nuclear weapons.
Asked on ABC on Sunday morning about any sign of such a deal, as negotiations appear stalled and the US-Israel war on Iran continues, Wright said: “There may not be a nuclear agreement.”
He talked about options for ending the “existential threat” of a nuclear armed Iran coming about by further US military action to knock out the country’s capacity to manufacture and deploy such missiles, saying: “It may be simply [a case of] destroying their capabilities to do it” or else “an agreement may await the next administration in Iran”.
He later said on CBS that the US was not shutting down diplomatic outreach and was “always open for a deal”. Wright told that network’s Face the Nation show that the “biggest role” of the US military in the Gulf region currently was to stop Iranian energy exports.
“We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said.
In an earlier interview with CNN on Sunday, Wright declined to declare the strait of Hormuz safe for oil tankers – unless they are being escorted by the US navy – and stopped short of saying whether the navy would need to remain in the Gulf region “indefinitely” in order to keep the vital energy passageway operating, as the conflict drags on.
This came despite Donald Trump’s repeated claims that ships can safely navigate the narrow marine waterway, and the US president’s insistence last week that the US controls the strait, while floating the idea that it be named after him – statements that were followed by further strikes from both sides in the area.
Wright, appearing for an interview on CNN’s State of the Union show on Sunday as well as ABC and CBS, was asked whether he could “unequivocally” assure safety to merchant ships transiting the strait. The question came after a New York Times report found that August was the deadliest month for merchant vessels in the area since March.
“We’re working cooperatively with fleets that do want to transit. Some ships aren’t transiting, and, of course, that’s their choice. But the United States is working with teams from all the nations in the Gulf to get transits and to continue to ramp them up,” Wright said.
“But you’re not saying that it’s currently safe?” host CNN Dana Bash asked, to which Wright replied: “We’re getting a lot of ships through, but, of course, it requires the US military to do that. We are not [at] pre-conflict levels, if that’s what you’re asking.”
Bash then asked: “If a country or a company wants to send its tanker through the strait of Hormuz, can they do so safely?”
“Well, if they want to work with the United States navy, I think they can,” Wright said.
Bash then asked whether the US navy would remain in the region “indefinitely” and whether its presence in the strait was becoming “the new normal”.
Wright responded: “Well, it is today, but I think, as you look forward, other nations will come and work with us in this endeavor. Certainly, trade for the world is important. It shouldn’t be just the United States’s responsibility.”
“But until Iran changes their position or changes their government, we’ll have to deal with them. But, slowly, their capabilities are being degraded and ours are being enhanced,” he added.
Nuclear and diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran appear to have stalled after a June interim agreement to end military operations collapsed without producing a lasting settlement on peace or the future of what remains of Iran’s nuclear program after US strikes last summer caused huge damage.
Wright was also asked by CNN if he would say the US is still at war. “We’re still in a conflict, for sure,” he said. On Thursday, the US vice-president JD Vance said at a White House press briefing: “I wouldn’t call it a war,” instead referring to a military conflict. Trump then defended Vance, saying: “A lot of people do not call it a war, I would call it a military conflict, because it’s small potatoes for us … it’s not a big thing.”
The Republican US senator John Kennedy of Louisiana was asked on Sunday by NBC if the war would be over by November.
“Probably not,” he said.
The conflict passed the six-month mark in late August. The former defense secretary Leon Panetta warned in an interview with the Guardian this weekend that it could last a lot longer.

06 September 2026•Update: 06 September 2026
Kimi Antonelli produced a remarkable comeback to win the Italian Grand Prix on Sunday, charging from 19th on the grid to victory at his home race and becoming the first Italian driver to triumph at Monza since 1966.
The 20-year-old Mercedes driver passed teammate George Russell on Lap 50, with three laps remaining, and held on to secure a memorable victory.
Russell finished second to complete a Mercedes one-two, while Red Bull’s Max Verstappen took third.
McLaren’s Lando Norris was fourth ahead of teammate Oscar Piastri, with Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton finishing sixth.
The race was interrupted on Lap 2 after Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc crashed heavily at the Parabolica, prompting a red flag. Leclerc walked away from the accident and was cleared following medical checks.
Antonelli, who had qualified seventh, started from 19th after receiving a grid penalty for exceeding his permitted allocation of power-unit components.
His victory equaled the second-furthest-back starting position from which a Formula 1 World Championship race has been won, behind John Watson’s victory from 22nd in 1983.
The Italian quickly made his way through the field following the restart and took the lead from Russell at the beginning of Lap 18.
Antonelli and Verstappen later pitted for fresh tires during a virtual safety-car period, while Russell remained on track and attempted to preserve his hard tires.
Antonelli returned to second place by Lap 38 and gradually reduced the gap to his teammate as Russell struggled with tire wear.
The Italian briefly ran through the gravel while battling Russell on Lap 49 but recovered and completed the decisive pass one lap later.
Russell tried to respond over the closing laps but could not regain the lead, allowing Antonelli to cross the finish line to a huge reception from the home crowd.
The victory strengthened Antonelli’s position at the top of the drivers’ standings.
He arrived at Monza leading Russell by 59 points and increased his advantage to 66, moving to 267 points.
Russell’s second-place finish lifted him to 201 points, while Hamilton dropped to third with 191 after collecting eight points for sixth place.
Mercedes’ one-two contrasted sharply with Ferrari’s fortunes at its home race. Hamilton could manage only sixth, while Leclerc’s early retirement left the Italian team without a podium.
Antonelli became the first Italian driver to win the Italian Grand Prix at Monza since Ludovico Scarfiotti triumphed at the circuit in 1966.
Pole-sitter Pierre Gasly was unable to maintain his qualifying advantage and finished seventh for Alpine.
Racing Bulls rookie Arvid Lindblad took eighth, ahead of Alpine’s Franco Colapinto and Racing Bulls driver Yuki Tsunoda.
Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto finished 11th, followed by teammate Nico Hulkenberg, Williams’ Carlos Sainz, Red Bull’s Liam Lawson, Haas pair Oliver Bearman and Esteban Ocon, Williams’ Alex Albon and Cadillac’s Sergio Perez.
Valtteri Bottas, Lance Stroll, Fernando Alonso and Leclerc failed to finish.

AfD claims landslide victory in German regional election
The opposition right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has won Sunday’s regional election in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt with 43.8% of the vote, the local election commission has said. The AfD is set to claim 39 out of 97 seats in the local legislature, falling short of a governing majority.
The vote was marked by a record turnout of 78%, the highest since the reunification of Germany in 1990.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party finished in a poor second, securing just over 17.2% of the vote and 15 seats, according to official preliminary results.
AfD lead candidate in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, said the party has “written history” and that the outcome of the vote would “shake all of Germany.”
“We are going to get our country back, and we are starting with Saxony-Anhalt,” he said.
The Germans have given the AfD their trust and it “will not disappoint them. We will not become like these other parties,” Siegmund added.
AfD co-chair Alice Weidel earlier did not rule out forming a coalition government in the region, including with Merz’s Christian Democrats, should the right-wing party fail to secure an absolute majority.
After the exit polls gave victory to the AfD, Sven Schulze, the CDU lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt and the outgoing regional head, conceded defeat, congratulating the opponents on their electoral success.
“That’s democracy,” Schulze said, adding that voters have sent a clear message which must be heeded, both at the regional and federal levels, as quoted by German media.
Schulze attributed his party’s poor showing to the unpopular policies pursued by the federal coalition government, which is comprised of the CDU and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).
SPD co-leader and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil similarly spoke of a “signal to Berlin,” insisting, however, on the continuation of the so-called ‘firewall’ policy, under which all major parties refuse to cooperate with the AfD.
AfD co-chair Tino Chrupalla said that the outcome of the Saxony-Anhalt regional elections have demonstrated that voters reject the controversial ‘firewall’ policy by ‘voting out’ the mainstream parties.
According to preliminary results, the SPD has finished third with 9.3% of the vote, followed by the Greens and the Left Party with 8.9% and 8.6%, respectively. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) has also narrowly secured the spot in the legislature with 5.3%.
Over the past several months, opinion polls have consistently shown that the AfD is the most popular party nationwide, enjoying the support of 28% of respondents.
Having the largest opposition faction in the Bundestag, the party campaigns on an anti-immigration platform and is also highly critical of the German government’s support for Ukraine, as well as sanctions against Russia.
An INSA poll published by Bild in late August indicated that support for Germany’s governing Christian Democratic CDU/CSU bloc had fallen to 20%, with some 78% of respondents dissatisfied with Merz’s coalition government.

Dennis Ross: Iran’s resilience during US war continues to ‘surprise’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Dennis Ross: Iran’s resilience during US war continues to ‘surprise’
TEHRAN — The clearest path to a deal to end the US war on Iran may lie in the dispute over shipping fees through the Strait of Hormuz, according to former US negotiator Dennis Ross, as Washington confronts the reality that months of military and economic pressure have failed to force Tehran into submission.
The United States and Israel launched their war against Iran on February 28, apparently expecting that sustained military pressure would weaken the Islamic Republic and compel its leadership to make far-reaching concessions. Instead, Iran has maintained its political and military footing while continuing to challenge US pressure, particularly around the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has repeatedly demonstrated that it can absorb severe pressure while retaining significant leverage over the course of the confrontation. Despite the heavy economic costs imposed by US sanctions and the naval blockade, Tehran has rejected demands that it sees as compromising its sovereignty and has continued to insist that any settlement must address the consequences of Washington’s military campaign.
Ross said Iran could abandon any demand for a formal toll on shipping while retaining the right to charge for legitimate navigational, security or environmental services. Such an arrangement, he argued, could give both sides a way to claim a political victory, allowing Tehran to step back from its demand without appearing to capitulate.
“The Iranians have consistently surprised us in terms of their resilience,” Ross said, adding that he doubted economic and military pressure alone would force an Iranian retreat.
The Strait of Hormuz has become the central pressure point in the confrontation. Washington has sought to use its naval power and economic blockade to restrict Iran’s oil exports, while Tehran has maintained that the strait cannot simply be treated as an instrument of US power. Recent military exchanges around the waterway have further demonstrated the risks of trying to resolve the dispute through force.
“If you could announce that the strait were reopened, I think Trump would do a deal,” Ross told The Associated Press.
For Washington, such a deal could provide a face-saving way to end a costly confrontation. For Tehran, reopening the waterway while preserving its sovereign rights and securing an end to the pressure campaign could equally be presented as a victory.
After months of war, the emerging lesson is that Iran’s resilience has become one of the central factors pushing the US to search for an exit from the conflict.

Iranian writer, poet and artist Javad Mojabi passes away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Iranian writer, poet and artist Javad Mojabi passes away
TEHRAN- Javad Mojabi, the prominent Iranian writer, poet, satirist, painter and literary and art critic, passed away on Saturday following a period of illness. he was 87.
Mojabi was one of the prominent figures of contemporary Iranian literature and art, whose career spanned more than six decades and encompassed literature, visual arts, journalism and art criticism.
Born in 1939, in Qazvin, Mojabi began his literary and artistic activities in the 1960s. He produced more than 50 works in various forms, including poetry, short stories, novels, satire, plays, screenplays and research.
His first book, the poetry collection “A Season for You,” was published in 1965 when he was 25. Mojabi later recalled that the publication of the book served as his formal entry into the literary world of his generation.
Alongside literature, painting remained an important part of his artistic life. He began painting as a child with his brother, Hossein, and later became recognized as one of the pioneering figures in the field of painting criticism and research on visual arts in Iran.
Mojabi pursued his professional career in journalism as well, while continuing to write extensively on literature and contemporary art. His critical and research works on painting and Iranian artists appeared in various publications and books, further establishing his position as a figure active across several branches of the country’s cultural life.
He was also widely known for his contribution to contemporary Iranian satire, which he explored through different literary and artistic forms. His fiction output included works such as “The Lost Garden,” “Naked Narrative,” “In This Weather” and “Speaking While Saying Nothing.”
Mojabi remained artistically active during the final years of his life. In 2026, while he was hospitalized at Iranmehr Hospital, a collection of his paintings titled “White Nights of the Hospital and Me” was put on display, reflecting his continued engagement with painting despite his illness.
Through a career extending over more than six decades, Mojabi became part of a generation of Iranian intellectuals and artists who moved between literature, visual arts, journalism and cultural criticism. His multifaceted body of work left a lasting presence in Iran’s contemporary cultural landscape.

The fire erupted aboard the vessel on September 5, with Russian emergency services deploying 52 firefighters and 10 pieces of equipment to the shipyard. The blaze covered an area of roughly 80 square meters before being brought under control, according to Russian Telegram channel 112.
Firefighters extinguished within approximately two hours. No casualties were reported. The cause of the fire and the extent of damage to the icebreaker have not been disclosed.
Admiral Makarov is a Project R-1039 diesel-electric icebreaker built by Wärtsilä in Helsinki, Finland, in 1975 as part of the Yermak class constructed for the Soviet Union.
The vessel has a displacement of approximately 20,247 tonnes and is nearly 135 meters long. Its propulsion system produces about 30.5 megawatts of power, allowing the icebreaker to navigate through continuous ice up to 1.5 meters thick at around two knots.
Admiral Makarov previously operated in Russia’s Far East and Arctic regions before being transferred to Rosmorport’s Northwestern Basin Branch in late 2025. After completing repairs, the vessel was expected to escort ships to Russian ports in the eastern Gulf of Finland during winter navigation.
The icebreaker has been undergoing repairs since spring 2025, including work on its hull, propellers, three propeller shafts, and main engines. Repairs to the engines were scheduled to continue through the end of 2026.
Kronstadt, located on Kotlin Island in the Gulf of Finland, is also home to a major Russian naval base. In June 2026, Ukrainian drones struck the Russian Project 20380 missile corvette Boykiy at the Kronstadt naval base, causing a fire aboard the vessel.
In October 2025, another major accident hit a Russian shipyard when the unfinished PK-700 heavy floating crane capsized at the Sevastopol Marine Plant in temporarily occupied Crimea, killing two people and injuring at least 20 others.

Iran attends 39th Moscow International Book Fair
TEHRAN – The Iranian Book and Literature House attended the 39th Moscow International Book Fair, held from September 2 to September 6, with a collection of 500 book titles, a series of illustrations, and various cultural programs.
The pavilion of Iran presented a diverse collection of works from Iranian publishers and executed various programs to introduce the country’s cultural capacities, promote the Islamic Republic of Iran’s “Grant” program, and follow up on contracts previously established with Russian publishers during the Tehran Publishing Fellowship, Mehr reported.
The titles displayed at the Iran pavilion covered topics such as literature, culture and art, children and young adults, and themes related to religion, faith, and Iranian national and cultural identity.
In this event, a collection of works by Iranian illustrators was also put on display for the audience. This section was designed with the goal of introducing Iran’s artistic and creative capacities, particularly in the field of children’s and young adult literature.
In the design and visual space of the pavilion, an effort was made to bring together elements of the country’s culture, history, and identity. On one side of the pavilion, an illustration of Ferdowsi and his enduring poems, alongside images inspired by the art of Persian painting and miniatures, showcased the grandeur of Iran’s literary and artistic heritage. On the other side, a composition featuring Iran, the Persian Gulf, and the Strait of Hormuz could be seen.
This year, a special section of the pavilion was dedicated to images of the martyred leader of the Islamic Revolution and a memorial for the child martyrs of Minab, emphasizing concepts such as national identity, territorial integrity, Iranian culture, and honoring the memory of the martyrs and the culture of resistance.
Alongside the exhibition of books and artworks, various attractive programs were arranged at the Iran pavilion. These included cultural and literary meetings and events, programs related to illustration and art, as well as participation in the fair’s collective activities. Meetings with publishers, booksellers, and officials from the host country’s publishing industry were also among the programs planned during the fair.
The focus of the Iran pavilion was to introduce the capabilities and products of the country’s publishing industry, clarify national and cultural identity, represent Iranian literary and artistic luminaries and works, address religious and faith-based themes, and provide narratives related to the history and civilization of Iran. Furthermore, topics such as war and its impact on children and families were addressed in some of the works and programs presented.
The presence of the Iranian Book and Literature House at the Moscow International Book Fair was an opportunity to introduce the country’s publishing and cultural capacities, familiarize Russian audiences with Iranian works, and develop connections between the publishers, authors, illustrators, and publishing industry activists of the two countries—a connection that can pave the way for greater cooperation in the fields of translation, rights exchange, joint production, and cultural interaction between Iran and Russia.
Over the course of five days, 300 publishers from Moscow and various Russian regions, along with foreign participants from Iran, India, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and China, presented hundreds of thousands of titles at the 39th Moscow International Book Fair.

Settler violence has risen sharply in the West Bank in recent years. Palestinians and human rights groups have repeatedly accused Israeli authorities of failing to adequately investigate or prosecute attacks.
The United Nations and most countries consider all Israeli settlements in the West Bank illegal under international law and regard the territory as occupied. Israel disputes that characterization, saying the territory is disputed rather than occupied.

Sydney art exhibition highlights Minab tragedy, voices of war, resilience

Sydney art exhibition highlights Minab tragedy, voices of war, resilience
TEHRAN – The “When the Earth Embraces the Sky” art exhibition, featuring works addressing war, loss, displacement and resilience, has opened in Sydney, Australia, with the Iranian section focusing on the Minab school tragedy and commemorating the children who lost their lives in the attack.
The exhibition opened on Sunday at the Frank Oliveri Community Centre in Heckenberg, New South Wales, and will remain open to the public through September 13. The event brings together more than 50 artworks from artists and community members from diverse backgrounds, including Iranian, Afghan, Iraqi, Lebanese and Palestinian communities.
Organized by the Conference of Birds – Shia Hub for Art & Culture, the exhibition explores the human consequences of war and displacement while emphasizing memory, resistance, resilience, connection and hope for renewal.
The event brings together representatives and artists from communities whose countries have experienced war and military conflict in recent decades. Through painting, drawing, photography, mixed media, sculpture, calligraphy and other forms of visual art, the exhibition seeks to transform experiences of loss and destruction into a broader reflection on human dignity and resilience.
The Iranian section has been dedicated to the tragedy at Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Hormozgan province, and serves as a memorial to the children killed in the attack.
The Minab tragedy occurred on February 28, when the school was struck during the opening phase of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Iranian authorities reported that 168 people were killed and at least 95 others wounded in the attack, which struck the school while children and teachers were attending classes.
As part of the program, the documentary “Minab,” directed by Iranian filmmaker Maryam Yousefi-Sadr, was screened on Sunday following the opening ceremony. The screening was proposed by the Benevolent Iranian Women Association, which is also participating in the exhibition’s Iranian section.
The exhibition’s broader theme draws on the enduring concepts of memory, loss and rebuilding, while seeking to present the experiences of communities affected by conflict beyond images of destruction alone. According to the organizers, the event aims to highlight the capacity of individuals and communities to remain rooted, rebuild and envision a more hopeful future.
Inspired in part by the spirit of Karbala and Imam Hussein (AS), the exhibition also seeks to create a space for dialogue among Sydney’s multicultural communities and demonstrate the ability of art to bring together people with different cultural backgrounds around shared experiences of grief, displacement and hope.
The exhibition is free to the public and continues at the Frank Oliveri Community Centre in Heckenberg until September 13.

Iran’s retaliatory fire sends US warships fleeing, exposes American vulnerability

The released imagery debunked Washington’s claims of effectively escorting and supporting trespassing vessels through the maritime choke-point.
“The United States is the greatest threat to the security of regional countries and maritime trade; US support and escort operations are nothing but a big lie!” the IRGC cautioned. Since February 28, Washington has repeatedly violated international law, targeting sovereign territory, critical national infrastructure, and civilian neighborhoods. However, Tehran's defense strategy has transformed the confrontation into an operational strain on the US military.

Interceptor exhaustion: US stocks of key interceptors, including Patriot PAC-3 and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missile systems, have been depleted by well over half.
Strategic vulnerability: Defense intelligence estimates indicate that the rapid consumption of these high-cost interceptor inventories has pushed American air defenses in multiple theaters to critical levels, creating global operational gaps that will take defense manufacturers years to rebuild.
While Washington faces a rapidly shrinking stockpile of high-grade munitions and logistical strain, Iran’s defense doctrine—built upon domestic production, underground missile facilities, and vast stockpiles of asymmetric assets—has demonstrated enduring strength.
Despite sustained military pressure and illegal blockades from Washington, the national resilience of the Islamic Republic remains unbroken. The defensive actions executed by the IRGC have consolidated popular support across Iran, proving that threats and military coercion cannot alter Tehran's posture.

Thales to Localize Production of 70 mm Rockets in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:13:37 UTC
02:13:37 KST

India will establish assembly and partial local production of guided and unguided 70 mm rockets.
Thales announced this in a press release.
Thales and Kalyani Strategic Systems Limited (KSSL) have signed a strategic alliance agreement under India’s Make in India program to establish advanced manufacturing capabilities for 70 mm rocket systems in the country.
Thales’ 70 mm rockets are already used by Indian HAL Rudra and HAL Prachand attack helicopters equipped with compatible launchers from the FZ family. In addition to engaging ground targets, the guided version of Thales’ 70 mm rockets can be used to engage drones.
As part of the cooperation, Thales will provide technological expertise in 70 mm rockets and launchers developed in Belgium.
KSSL, for its part, will use local manufacturing and testing facilities to produce and integrate components from Thales’ certified supply chain. The first fully assembled rocket made in India is planned for early 2027.
“Thales has partnered with India for decades and this collaboration with KSSL is a testament to our deep and long-standing engagement with the local defence ecosystem. By combining our combat-proven 70 mm rocket expertise from Belgium with KSSL’s engineering and manufacturing strengths, we are co-creating capabilities that will enhance India’s operational readiness and advance its vision of self-reliance in critical defence technologies,” said Ankur Kanaglekar, Thales’ vice president in India.
Kalyani Strategic Systems Limited (KSSL) is a wholly owned subsidiary of Bharat Forge Limited and is responsible for the defense business of Kalyani Group, one of India’s leading engineering and technology industrial groups.
The company’s portfolio includes artillery systems, armored and protected vehicles, small arms, ammunition, naval systems and unmanned platforms.
This is not Thales’ first attempt to localize 70 mm rocket production in India.
In 2023, the company signed an agreement with state-owned Bharat Dynamics Limited to establish manufacturing capabilities for the FZ275 rocket and integrate Indian components into Thales’ global supply chain.
In 2024, Thales signed another memorandum, this time with Adani Defence & Aerospace. The agreement covered the localization of production of both the guided FZ275 LGR and unguided FZ90 FFAR.

"We held three rounds of talks today. All of them were very substantive," he said.
According to him, the talks focused heavily on the challenges of the winter period and possible support for Ukraine.
"We devoted considerable attention today to the winter period and all the challenges that may arise. We very much hope that we will be able to reach agreements with our American partners, and we are counting on the support of our European partners," Zelensky said.
He noted that despite the possibility that the war could continue through the winter, the teams are positively assessing further opportunities.
"If the war continues through the winter, we are counting very much on the 'winter package,' which I discussed in great detail today with Steve, Jared and our European partners. We are counting on support for air defense and energy, and we are also counting on significant volumes and the ability to use American LNG," Zelensky said.
According to Zelensky, the partners support these proposals.
He thanked the U.S. for resuming the negotiation process after a pause.
"I want to emphasize the role of Steve and Jared in restoring the negotiation process today. They were in Russia. I think it would be right for Jared and Steve to talk about Russia. [...] What is important is that the American team met with the Russian president and also with me today. And we discussed all the possibilities, including the possibility of resuming the talks," Zelensky said.
According to him, a trilateral meeting of national security advisors was also held.
"We had a trilateral meeting of national security advisors. I think all sides will do everything possible to resume these talks," Zelensky said.
Zelensky said the territorial issue remains on the agenda and stressed the need to resolve such complex matters at the leaders' level.
He also stressed that the talks provided an opportunity to discuss security guarantees and Ukraine's future. According to him, these include not only security guarantees but also economic guarantees to help Ukraine recover and rebuild.
"We are talking about a prosperity plan. We are talking not only about security guarantees, but also about economic guarantees for Ukraine to recover and rebuild," he said.
Zelensky stressed that Ukraine will face a number of challenges after the war ends, including the need to maintain a strong army.
"We all understand what challenges will exist after the war ends, and we are discussing them among ourselves. We understand that our army must be strong, and this is the main security guarantee for us. And all of this requires resources... The guarantees must be strong and clear for Ukraine... We must not be afraid of any future challenges," he said.

Palestinian farmers battle settler sabotage to save Hebron crops, livestock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:03:20 UTC
02:03:20 KST

Palestinian farmers battle settler sabotage to save Hebron crops, livestock
West Bank farmers defy daily settler attacks, sheep theft, and military restrictions to protect their land from agricultural sabotage.
Amid the grapevines that once provided a steady income for her family, 56-year-old Palestinian farmer Theeba al-Sabaa spends much of her day guarding her home and farmland in the occupied West Bank from settlers.
From dusk till dawn, she works on her land in the town of Beit Ummar, north of Hebron, known by locals as “Jabal Sabaa”.
Theeba is engaged in a daily battle against the encroaching settler outposts that have emerged among the rolling hills that surround her, and which block access to sections of her land.
“By God, the land has taught me patience, and to cling to my right, for as long as I have a right, I must take it and never let it go,” she told Al Jazeera.
“I will never leave it because I worked hard on it, I toil and sweat on it, so I will not leave my toil and sweat, or the toil of my children and my husband, to go to someone else.”
Weaponising livestock
Since mid-2024, when settlers established new outposts on the nearby hills, every one of Theeba’s moves has been monitored.
Settlers frequently approach the perimeter of her home and deliberately release livestock into the cultivated fields.
“They enter with their sheep into our land after we plow and fix it, grazing in it, trampling the crops, and stomping on them with their sheep, leaving nothing,” Theeba said.
“As soon as they feel any movement or anyone entering the land, you find them attacking us immediately.”
This intimidation extends to the adjacent fields, where 59-year-old Anwar Sabarneh lives with his extended family of seven brothers.
Due to the repeated settler violations, two of his brothers have been forced to abandon their land.
Sabarneh, who supports a family of 14, owns several dunams of vineyards located just 300 metres (980 feet) from his home. With aggressive settlers around, reaching them has become a dangerous ordeal.
Military complicity
Sabarneh said that the Israeli army even demands permits from Palestinians to work on their own land.
“The army came with the settlers to ask me for a permit so I can work in my home, in front of my house’s door, and on my land where I am the rightful owner,” Sabarneh said.
Farmers are also barred from building anything on their land. Sabarneh’s sheep have also been locked in a barn for over eight months due to the dangers posed by settlers.
“If they see me taking the sheep out, the settlers chase me, kidnap them, and steal them,” he said.
When Sabarneh’s children have tried to retrieve their stolen sheep, Israeli soldiers have arrested and beaten them.
A forced exodus
Repeated pogroms by settlers against Palestinian farmers reflect a broader strategy targeting agriculture across the southern West Bank.
Settlers and the Israeli troops carried out 11,074 attacks in the West Bank during the first half of 2026, according to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission. This includes 3,488 carried out by settlers.
Hasan Breijieh, a settlement affairs expert and director at the commission, told Al Jazeera that continuous settlement expansionism, alongside restrictions on Palestinian movement, are the primary reasons that so many Palestinians have been forced to flee their farms.
“Military gates erected at the entrances of Palestinian communities have tightened control over… access to their orchards and vineyards,” he said.
Bypass roads, built by Israel, have also hindered “connectivity between Palestinian communities”, Breijieh said.
Under such restrictions, Palestinian farmers have faced a fourth consecutive season without being able to harvest olives, grapes, or guava. Their lands have been “neither plowed nor pruned”, and have been forcibly abandoned.
In the face of such oppression, Palestinian women like Theeba al-Sabaa have continued to play a pivotal role in protecting their land, particularly when men have been killed or detained by Israeli forces.
“They continue to maintain their leadership role in preserving the family’s agricultural legacy today,” Breijieh said. “This land was historically the primary source of livelihood for families, and a Palestinian cannot leave it voluntarily, no matter the sacrifices.”
He recalled his own grandfather, who went to his fields to bid farewell before dying. “Goodbye, vineyard,” he said to his land.

EU faces 300,000 factory job cuts as China ‘colonises’ supply chains, industry warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:00:10 UTC
02:00:10 KST

Job losses in EU manufacturing will rapidly increase unless Brussels stops the “colonisation” of industry by Chinese component manufacturers, a leading industry trade body has warned.
Eurometal predicts 300,000 job losses in manufacturing in the rest of 2026 because of expanding competition from China, which is now enjoying a record €1bn-a-day trade surplus with the bloc.
On Monday, Eurometal will bring its concerns to decision-makers in Brussels, staging a protest using 10 symbolic coffins in a procession around the European Commission headquarters.
The coffins will be marked with phrases such as “EU competitiveness”, “industrial jobs” and “European factories”.
European manufacturers fear that the commission is not fully alive to the cannibalisation of their industries as China becomes embedded in supply chains through the sale of components.
Alexander Julius, the president of Eurometal, told the Guardian: “China has made no secret of what it is doing. It is in their five-year plan.
“China doesn’t want to be a raw material supplier, it wants to be a finished product supply. They want to be in key product supply chains because they know that once they control the supply chain, they own the complete value chain.” He wants the commission to understand fully the impact of Chinese exports at component level, including metals and chemicals used in 90% of manufacturing.
The EU has already taken action on electric vehicles by imposing tariffs on Chinese imports in 2024, and in June introduced higher tariffs on imports of foreign steel. The bloc’s trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, has also said the EU’s €360bn (£310bn) annual import/export imbalance with China is “not sustainable”, with both sides agreeing to hold three months of talks, ending in October, to try to avert a trade war.
“You look at the job losses stacking up in industries in places like Germany. The media, the politicians can see the consequences, but they don’t go after the virus that is causing it,” Julius said. “They don’t see why it is happening or ask why companies are either relocating to China or India or going bust.”
Among the conditions allowing the “virus” to spread is the increasing costs borne by European metal manufacturers with tariffs on steel imports and carbon emissions taxes for those high-energy sectors.
Components manufactured in China face none of those levies, said Julius, and that, combined with the undervaluation of the Chinese currency, the yuan, makes it challenging to compete with Chinese rivals, he added.
Companies have to satisfy shareholders and will continue to buy from China, whatever the political rhetoric coming out of Brussels, he said.
“When manufacturing leaves Europe, Europe not only loses production but investment, knowhow and long-term economic resilience,” Eurometal said ahead of the protest.
Analysis by the European Commission in June projected potential job losses of more than 1m on the back of high energy costs and global competition, which will include the 100,000 job cuts at Volkswagen confirmed by the German carmaker last week.
China has repeatedly accused Europe of protectionism. It threatened “resolute countermeasures should the EU further target Chinese companies or products”, according to the state-owned Xinhua agency earlier this year. Since then, the EU and China have agreed a three-month truce.
